I have dozens of games in my steam library, and this is one of a handful that I felt compelled to finish. If you've ever wondered what it feels like to try to survive in a war-zone, this game is about as close as you will get, while being both challenging and fun.
Warning - There may be some small spoilers in the pro/cons below
Pros:
- Great Balancing: The game is pretty difficult/hardcore. However it does not force you to grind endlessly or add completely illogical elements for the sake of making you suffer. It is difficult because each choice you make has a dramatic impact. For example, take scavenging. Due to the way the scavenging mechanic works, you can only bring back a certain amount of loot each day. You can't clear out an entire house in one night, which is very realistic if you think about it. Furthermore, some locations/ways of acquiring loot are more dangerous than others. Murdering innocent people and taking theirs stuff will have negative consequences, just as it would in real life. Since you have a limited amount of supplies to work with, there is complex strategy as to how to use these supplies to survive, and discovering a good strategy is a ton of fun.
- Good Needs System: Each survivor has needs that need to be fulfilled. They must be fed, they must be kept healthy, and they must be kept sane. I won't go to far into detail because finding out how the game works is part of the fun, but keeping your survivors alive is very manageable if you take care of important things like security and careful rationing of food. However, if you waste your food or medicine, or put your survivors in dangerous situations, they will quickly get injured/sick or begin to starve.
- Decent Crafting System: What I like about this game is that each building upgrade has its own unique benefit and its own niche in the game-play. There are no superfluous elements added just for the sake of variety. You aren't going to be able to craft 10 different types of food. However, everything that you do craft is very important in its own way, and spending your precious resources on the work-station at the wrong time in the game will give you a hard time.
- Decent Combat/Stealth: Some people may complain that the combat system is too unpredictable. To them I would say that in a real life war zone, a civilian wouldn't Rambo his/her way through a group of armed thugs every night and expect to survive for long.The game encourages you not to kill or steal by making these activities dangerous. Sometimes they may be necessary, but you shouldn't seek out combat for no good reason. In fact, it may be helpful to avoid it completely.
- Excellent Atmosphere/Background: I really enjoyed the atmosphere of the game. The visuals and background music set a mood of desperation that I haven't seen in any other game.
- NPCs/PCs: The characters in this game truly seem alive. The graphics/animations fulfill cater to this purpose pretty well. When your survivors are injured they limp. When they are sick they cough, when they are cold they shiver. In other words, they react to their surroundings pretty well. Also, they each have their own stories that they reveal gradually over the course of weeks. The NPCs in the different locations also have their own worries, whether it be a son trying to protect his parents from robbers (You), or a bandit trying to find ammunition for his gun. There are many stories out there, and trying to discover them all is a lot of fun.
-This is going on for longer than I intended, so I am going to stop with the Pro's here...
Cons:
- Ocasional Bugs: As of 11/16/2014, I have encountered two bugs over 20 hours of in-game time. One of them was a CTD when returning to my safehouse, but it was pretty minor and I was able to continue my game from the previous day. The other was a workbench bug after about 12 days (about 2-4 IRL hours), which was more annoying since it forced me to restart from day 1. The game just got released, so I assume these bugs will be patched soon. Overall, I really enjoyed the game, so having to restart on one of my playthings wasn't too annoying and it seems to be a very rare bug.
-Time Scale: It would be nice to be able to speed up time during the day. There is an option to end the day early, but you risk having a trader show up at your door or a random event taking place, and not being there for it. This is a minor complaint though, since usually there is plenty of stuff to do during the day (building, cooking, etc.) and no reason to skip to night.
Overall: I would strongly recommend this game to any mature gamers out there. It has a depth that most AAA games lack, and is far better than any other indie survival game I have played (some examples being Don't Starve or Zafehouse Diaries )

Not to say it's a bad game or beyond salvaging in any way. Coming from former Blizzard North developers, guys behind Diablo 1 and 2, and carrying over its visual identity from FATE it's definitely easy on the eyes and manages to have a lighthearted, vibrant atmosphere despite its world ending state of things. Along with some welcome features like sending your pet to sell your loot, Torchlight is definitely worth checking out all things considered. Shame about the lack of multiplayer, though.

This game may be easily seen as a Minecraft style shooter that tries to get popular from this tactic, and as such it could make you think it has nothing to offer. This can obviously stimulate people to ignore it or read reviews skeptically. If you are reading this, you either probably want to get this game or think you may want to. I am going to tell you what this game really is and why you may want to spend your time in Blockstorm.
Blockstorm is obviously indeed a Minecraft with guns scenario, though the features this game brings are much more than you would expect. You can find most of these nowhere else. Here are my pros. This game has a very in depth editor for every single visual element in the game. Whatever you see here you can make look different and as such personalize it for yourself or others depending on what you want your role to be in this community. These visual elements include weaponry, edited based on class, (such as making an assault rifle or knife skin), maps, characters, and even NPCs. Each of these are produced in an also voxel based editor with small blocks used to make them. Next, all of the maps in the game are fully destructible minus forcefield blocks. This and the weapon editor makes everything in the game extremely dynamic, to a level of Battlefield if not more. For example, say you are on an oil rig. You walk up a building to shoot two people on a bridge battling. You pull out your nyan cat rocket launcher and begin aiming at your prey. You easily realize Big Smoke and that Spetznaz guy aren't going to enjoy this. The rocket is fired, blowing the entire bridge up and making it fall into the water to be gone the entirety of the match.
Now for the much smaller list of my cons. Blockstorm is faced with the extremely unfortunate lack of funding. The creators are led by IndieGala, who no longer pay GhostShark for this game's development. This means since the game wasn't popular to begin with, it certainly began to lose the little steam it had to begin with. Fortunately though, there are still 156 and counting dedicated players in this community, and they are here to stay. This means that the community is more connected, which may not be seen as a con to some people. Also, as you can't sprint, grenades can be op in this game. This is an issue that can be avoided, though not easily sometimes. It seems to appear in this game that it has a lower ping refresh rate, so people won't get hit sometimes in higher ping servers.
Overall, this game has immesurable dynamisism, and a dedicated community for all the fps needs you should have, regardless of its numbers and other minor development bugs. Thank you for reading this, I hope it helped you decide.

If you ever wondered why all your friends always loved the Diablo franchise while you absolutely hated it, you probably missed the mysterious initiation those complacent souls went through by the time those games were still fresh. Well, it's your chance again. Torchlight is your way inside the secrets of the hack-n-slash RPG's, and it surely can make you a lover of the genre, no matter how contrary to that you might think you are. It is a gem, no doubt, although it has some flaws too, but in the end, rest assured that the pros easily overcome the multiple cons. Let us talk a little about the cons. The story is not memorable, nor the characters, but we are all used to that already nowadays. Also, the game looks cartoon-ish. Even if that actually doesn’t bother as much as one could think, it’s still an issue. There are only three classes, and the characters are not customizable – except for their names and pets – but that’s not so big of a deal too. To be honest, the only real problem with the game is it being too easy overall. If you have half a brain functioning, you shouldn’t play it on any difficulty other than very hard. On normal difficulty, once past half of the game and with the latest skills at hand, one can pretty much one-click anything to death that is not a boss or a mini-boss – literally. Probably only on very hard some old good player’s awareness skills might be better than just spamming the RMB, the default character skills button – probably. We hope this game can be anything of a challenge somehow. On top of all that, the game also starts to get a little repetitive on later levels… Well, from what has been said, one can understand there are some issues, but despite all of that, the game is still so much fun it would be a shame to let it be overlooked, and nothing of that mentioned above should prevent it from being highly recommended for any kind of player. Torchlight is simple, colorful and fun. The entire monster killing and the beautiful visual effects keeps the player interested in the action. The weapons are interesting, so are the drops: one doesn’t have to go anywhere outside the run at hand for help with his survivability. Indeed, because of things like this, the simplicity of the game could arguably be a plus in its favor, instead of a detriment. If one doesn’t want to sacrifice all his spare time grinding, farming, and even buying from other players (sometimes even with real cash) only to be able to survive at later levels, like, for example, one is supposed to do in Diablo III, Torchlight offers a fantastic alternative. It is made for casual players, and anyone could play it on the hardest difficulties without having to resort to anything other than what he finds and does at that particular level with that particular character. Add to all of that the super low price and it becomes an absolute must buy, at least if you’re not a fool. Are you a fool?

Battlerite attempts to bring in the free to play MOBA audience by offering a much more fast-paced experience with constant combat, eliminating the wait times of "laning" phases from other games, but does it succeed in replacing the rest of the gameplay from those titles?
Battlerite is an isometric, champion-based arena combat game. It uses a small team structure and a much more fast paced combat system to make the fighting more exciting and force most game-deciding actions in each match to be split second decisions. It also uses elements from free to play games like purchasable crates for cosmetics and a quest system that offers chests as rewards.
First things first, Battlerite is in early access, and in this case, it’s a game that’s planning on going free to play once it fully releases. This is something to keep in mind throughout the whole review, as of writing the game costs $20 to purchase, while players who decide to jump in later will be getting an improved experience and saving money. That said, if the game sounds interesting, some may want to jump in right now, and for them, that’s entirely possible and gives users a chance to give feedback on balance and bugs prior to release.
The game is a multiplayer-only title that focuses on having intense and fast-paced 2v2 and 3v3 engagements with very little interference. It borrows mechanics from other champion-based games like roots to hold enemies in place and charging ultimates by dealing damage to enemies or finding pickups placed around the map. Unlike its contemporaries, however, the focus on being fast-paced is enforced by the mechanics in an appropriately harsh manner. Matchmade games are decided by a best of three rounds series of fights with a two-minute timer on them. When the timer hits zero, a circle will appear on the outer edge of the arena and start closing in towards the center of the arena, and anyone caught outside the circle takes damage every second.
Battlerite can be found on Steam for $19.99.
Being a multiplayer-only title that focuses on champion-based combat, this game lives and dies based on a couple different factors. The community has to be large enough that matchmaking times don’t take far too long, the champions have to be interesting and/or fun to play, the cast has to be reasonably diverse so the gameplay doesn’t get too samey, and lastly the game must be properly balanced to keep the sense of intense arena combat and skill that keeps the whole package exciting. Battlerite does a decent job of keeping their cast of characters interesting and mostly balanced. The champions are split into ranged and melee attackers and a set of support characters built around buffs, debuffs and healing in various ways with damage dealing as a secondary objective.
Something worth mentioning here with the game is the appearance of the community, while Steamcharts reports seven thousand to four thousand players a day depending on the time, it’s not uncommon to run into an issue where the matchmaking will take several minutes to put players together. This is odd considering the game consists solely of 2v2, 3v3, training and A.I. modes to play in, so the player base isn’t being diluted by playlists for DLC in any significant way. Unfortunately it gives the appearance that the community is smaller than it really is, hopefully, this is something to be fixed sooner rather than later. It’s also weird to see a bug like this in a game that’s been so far relatively bug-free as far as we could tell. The worst experience so far being the game soft-locking after a multiplayer match which required closing the game entirely to fix, ouch.
We’ve covered the small bugs and what the game needs to do to be successful but not the actual gameplay. To put it in a sentence, it’s perfectly serviceable. It doesn’t introduce any crazy new ideas to champion-based games or does anything especially unique with being an arena combat game outside of forcing a faster pace with the round timer. The champions are generally enjoyable with no real slumps or standouts in the cast and there is a bit of choice both in how your team composition is made when playing with friends as well as how the champion is built. After every round regardless of win or loss, each player can choose one of three preset “Rites” that alter the character’s abilities. Some of them are focused on rewarding more skilled play like reducing the cooldown of an ability depending on how many targets are hit by it, while others serve to improve abilities or create advantages, like improving the healing done to allies and damage done to enemies when using a teleport ability that phases through targets.
This is the strongest aspect of the game, by offering each player their own set of choices, each match can play out differently in a way that legitimately impacts the overall game, as the split second decisions have much more impact in a game that lasts a maximum of ten minutes as opposed to something like League of Legends where decisions can be corrected or accounted for over the course of over forty minutes to an hour. Each character build can excel in a specific circumstance and bring a level of synergy to the team that wouldn’t exist with the base characters, like having a character root the enemy in place to setup for a penetrating shot that punches through all of the rooted targets from a Jade in stealth. It’s the best selling point for the title, and potentially the only one, as the game doesn’t really have much to offer outside of the fast-paced arena experience with variance offered through champions and different builds using the Rite system.
Graphically, the game is nothing special. The art style very closely matches that of other MOBAs like the previously mentioned League of Legends and DoTA 2 and following in their style all three games run very well. Maxing the game out and getting a consistently high framerate is by no means a difficult feat so the play experience will be very similar in terms of visuals, and the low system requirements won’t restrict many people from playing the game. In addition, the sounds and music are also effectively a non-element, the music isn’t anything noteworthy and just serves to a small backdrop while the meat of the game takes place, while the sound effects are all par for the course. In regards to the graphics and sound, “Battlerite” doesn’t do anything special, and while it isn’t a good or a bad thing in itself, it does hurt the game given that it has so little to sell itself on.
Overall, while Battlerite isn’t particularly groundbreaking in any way, it doesn’t need to be. It has an art style that conveys what it needs to with filler music playing in the background and builds itself on making the combat fun and diverse as opposed to making the rest of the experience particularly enthralling. It doesn’t focus on crafting a story through lore in the characters and arenas like some other recent champion-focused games have, but instead, it goes all in on the idea of crafting a fast-paced arena experience. It’s laudable that the focus is so tight on what the developers are trying to accomplish, but as a game in itself, it’s not hard to see players being left wanting with the current cast of characters and maps, as well as with a price tag that will later be dropped. It’s fun and enjoyable, but that fun comes at a cost right now, so it’s hard to recommend at the moment for anyone who’s got other games in their backlog to hit or other multiplayer-centric titles to play.

It's said that the greatest despair that a parent can face in life is the loss of a child.
Shelter is a small story that you play which mimics parental love and the sorrow of loss by making you take care of five young badgers (You're the mommy badger) who need to be fed and protected as you go across the dangerous wilderness through day or night.
I've noticed you should always try to keep them more or less fed at the same level or else the one that's least fed doesn't grow as much and becomes slower, therefore your possibility of loss of that young one is higher.
I've loved playing this little story/simulation for it actually makes you want to protect the little ones as if it is your responsability - and when you lose one, it actually hurts.
It also has a very distinct and great look to the game, with various textures to give that abstract depth of the wild life, the soundtrack choices are great for each moment...
All I can say is that I loved it. Now it's time for you to find out if you're able to feel the pain of a mother.

“Water, water, everywhere,
And all the boards did shrink;
Water, water, everywhere,
Nor any drop to drink.”
Thankfully water is not something your character requires in the slow-paced adventure lovers dream that is Salt.  I purchased this game on a whim one day, and I can say that it did not disappoint.  Salt is not a game for Action lovers.  It's not even a game for adventure buffs looking for an engaging story, but Salt provides a beautiful open-world sandbox adventure game with just enough mythology and folklore to keep you sailing on.  Travelling can be dull at times, especially when you sail for long periods of time without even seeing another island to explore, but these moments are not overly common.  There are a plethora of items to find, gather, craft, etc. though the crafting and inventory menus are still a little rough around the edges for me. (I should note here that I have not played the game since the latest update and the developers say they have addressed some of the issues with the inventory/equipped items etc.)  The beautiful scenery is the real star of Salt.  The sunrise and sunset will never disappoint you, and the islands, though all fairly similar in appearance other than elevation, look nice enough.  Grass blows in the wind, fires crackle in the distance at night, and combing through a dense island at night with nothing but a dim torch to light your way can be truly haunting.  After playing the game for some time I really only have two outstanding issues I would like to bring up.  One, the enemies of Salt are the biggest nemesis of the game itself.  The graphics just seem sort of lazy and the AI is almost nonexistent.  I'm not a stickler on graphics and I love playing older games, but with the polished look that the rest of the game has you will find yourself wondering why the developers fell flat in this regard.  The other issue I want to address is the absence of other ships in the game.  While sailing you will literally never encounter anyone.  I don't mean to imply that the game should be known for ocean battles, but it would be nice to include something like a trade ship that sells supplies and upgrades for your ships, or even just friendly passersby who could give you missions and what not.
My overall rating for Salt would be 7/10
If you like adventure games where you have a minor story overview but also largely craft your own story i think you will enjoy this game.  Gathering supplies and crafting never seemed repetitive as long as I had something to gather for.  Eventually you will most likely run out of missions, but I can honestly say even though I have largely completed what the game initially had to offer I feel It was an absolute deal for the price.

The gameplay itself is absolutely outstanding, the game world is gorgeous and the music is fantastic.

Good: Excellent visuals, fun combat, great story(-telling), good character backstories.
Bad: One-dimensional characters, mostly linear gameplay
The paradigm system is a great new feature for party configuration in battle. Party paradigms dictate what roles each party memer plays, as well as giving bonus buffs to the whole party depending on the configuration. This can be likened to how in football, where you have your standard offensive and defensive lines, and also special teams, except expect to be making frequent paradigm shifts in battle as the situations change.
I never experienced the stereotypical JRPG grind in this game. The paradigm system and the Active Time Battle system keep the combat refreshing. Most battles can be tackled with proper selection of paradigms. In fact, I never upgraded any weapons, didn't complete many sidequests at all, and yet the ending was still comfortable and appropriately challenging. The pacing is definitely on point.
One of the major drawbacks is that the game is mostly very linear. However, this is only until about Chapter 11, which is the point where you're thrown into an absolutely massive map to explore, with lots of things to kill and numerous sidequests.
The story was enjoyable, and it was deep and complex. However, character development for the most part missed its mark. With a few exceptions, many characters seemed very one-dimensional in their mentality throughout the game. However, the storytelling partially makes up for this. The intricately connected character backgrounds are gradually revealed through the game, and the connections are revealed in an interesting way.
Final Fantasy XIII also features one of my all-time favorite characters: Sazh. He is the most well-developed character in the entire game. The black dude with a chocobo in his 'fro might raise eyebrows, but he is the most relatable character, and acts as the sole voice of sanity while everybody else around himseems to try to pound into your brain their "I'm a hero" spiel (looking at you, Snow).

Overall, Beyond Earth is disappointing.  There are glimpses of interesting evolutions of the mechanics introduced in Civ V, but they really are few, and this game feels more like an extensive mod of Civ V, rather than an expansion or evolution.
Some plusses of the experience include an affinity system, which changes the way your military units, as well as aspects of your society grow as you spec into one of three directions.  Additionally, the alien faction in the game is much more omnipresent than the barbarian camps you see in vanilla Civilization.
On the negative side, you still have the lackluster diplomacy and interactions with the other factions in the game, and the City States that were present (and largely unnecessary, in my opinon) in Civ V make their return in the form of Outposts.
I think ultimately your enjoyment of Beyond Earth is largely dependent on how much you enjoyed Civilization V.  If you're like me, and weren't a big fan of Civ V, then Beyond Earth doesn't really warrant your attention.  If you loved Civ V and want to play a sci-fi twist on familiar systems and gameplay, then Beyond Earth is perhaps worth your time.

For me, I've gone through two playthroughs of this game. Honestly after that, I can't really find a good reason to go through and do it again. The game is okay, but compared to what was available with the first iteration of Civ 5 (which changed almost everything) This game, despite not being a DLC (which would have made more sense to me, this is just what happens after a space victory.) Doesn't feel like it was meant to be a standalone game. All the units, despite their distinct looks, are very obvious reskins of eachother, and really the differences are negligible. Affinities serve no real purpose in-game other than cosmetic appearance, and a few unique units only available to certain affinity levels. The tech web, while it is different, doesn't really add much to the game--and it's not very well explained as to what your goal is supposed to be with it. The game feels too well balanced. There's no definite reason why you should go with a certain affinity over another depending on your playstyle. As a person who's accustomed to seeing similar skins in RTS games like Wargame and Command & Conquer, there are definite advantages to playing for a particular side/team depending on your playing style. Affinities, are a half-baked attempt to do so. They don't actually add any elements to cater to a particular playing style, and given the lack of unit variety ultimately don't add definitive advantages to  choosing a particular affinity over another--they're ultimately cosmetic.
Conclusion:
All in all, I did sort of enjoy my two playthroughs of the game. I didn't feel quite like I do when I play Civ 5, and have to cater my strategy to each person. The graphics arent better, nor are they different enough to actually consider it a separate game from Civ 5,  it would have made more sense as just another DLC. There are some improvements to the game over Civ 5, but not enough to justify the high price it's been given.

To start off, I have been playing the Civilization series since Civ 4. I really enjoyed this one! It basically took the core gameplay mechanics of Civ 5, and changed over to a Sci Fi setting. It is a still a relatively different game from Civ 5, and I think that does need to be stated. The buildings are different, the units are different, the culture trees are different, and the tech is different. It still has that Civilization gameplay, with a lot of core mechanics still in place though. I enjoy how it took a bit of the clutter from Civ 5 and touched it up to where it feels much more natural (such as the trade routes, and the culture trees). The aliens are interesting, and I'm hoping they add more since there does only seem to be a handful of different critters you run into throughout the galexy, and all of them can be found on every planet which kind of takes away some of the excitement of starting a new game (just like how every planet has miasma, and endless chasm canyons). There are three different affinities which really define how you build your Civilizations; those being: Purity, Harmony, and Supremacy. All three are fairly different, and have very interesting and unique units and styles. It makes it very interesting since you can definitely see the difference in the technology you decide to go with every playthrough. With that being said I thought it was interesting that your sponser doesn't effect the appearance of cities and buildings in anyway like it did in Civ 5, but I can't really say I would have expected everything to add diversity to every playthrough. Overall I was happy with this game and would definitely recommend it for anyone out there who's looking for a good turn based strategy game and is sick of a historical setting.
Beyond Earth: I'm writing this part now since Beyond Earth came out and I have had a chance to play that expansion. So for Beyond Earth it basically makes the water tiles just as useful as land tiles on top of adding four new factions, the ability to cross/class affinities, a couple new biomes, and finally a few more alien monsters. The water tiles thing is a neat concept, and it illiminated the desperate need for a good start (every game of Beyond Earth I played I landed on the coast, and the AI, up to Vostok difficulty, rarely expanded in water tiles, no matter how resource filled they were). The new factions were definitely needed to bring a unique feel to every game since now you can no longer get every faction into one game; the new factions are Space Korea, Space Vikings, Space Germany, and Space Middle East, and both the Space Vikings and Space Korea can start with their capitols in water tiles. The cross/classing affinites was cool at first, but became annoying when I would accidentally get the wrong upgrades to my units when I research into upgrading roads into railways so it altered my gameplay a bit and it became a little clumsy when I wanted to get specific with my builds. The two new biomes were pretty, but frigid world already had a planet type that catered to those who wanted to play on ice worlds which leaves the primordial worlds as the only really new unique biome. Lastly there is the new aliens which I definitely liked, and I liked how the aliens now change their colors in different biomes, but it would still be cool to see some biome specific species.

Get your guns and assassin equipment ready, because Mr. 47 is in another adventure. After the long wait after Blood Money we got Absolution which shows pretty much a complete overhaul compared to the its predecessors.
Starting with the stunning graphics (yes, I said stunning graphics will leave you really amazed about the level of detail the developers put into it), but the beautiful display, colors, detail and everything comes with a cost to PC specially, because the game seems not to be fully optimized (and by optimized, it means you could have the latest GPU and drivers and even with those the game will have its FPS drops).
Lots and lots of improvements were made to the game, like the controls were simplified and are more easy to get use to; the stealth part of the game is all about the perfect timing some times and with practice gets easier to figure out patterns guards or events happen.
A great addition to it are the challenges per mission which if you do them all, you can discover even more ways to finish your targets. Every mission has now a score system which is calculated in how you approached your targets or how you handled the situation, of course getting the perfect score is pretty much getting the Silent Assassin rating like the previous games in the series, which most of the times mean "kill only your target and get out without being seen".
Now, the disguise system is little different from Blood Money; in Blood Money, when you weared a disguise guards or any other NPC will have like a suspicion level and anyone was able to spot you if you were not careful enough; in Absolution all of this changed to if you grabbed a disguise only NPCs with almost the same clothes will see through it, i.e.: if you get a garner outfit all of the garners in the mission will know you are not a garner, and they will be able to spot you. Of course some of the disguises dont work in certain areas, but there are some missions where you can have a VIP disguise and do almost whatever you want without anyone really knowing you are Mr. 47. After a while you get use to or if you are completing the challenges, you will find how difficult the game can be by not using a disguise in certain areas.
The way to handle guns is much easier and smooth; a great addition is the "Point Shooting" feature which is similar to the "mark and execute" system from Splinter Cell Conviction; which some time will be really handy when you are in a difficult situation.
Absolution will give you a more linear story and unlike the previous games where almost every mission was like a sandbox where you could wonder for hours discovering new ways to get your target; Absolution broke most of the missions in parts, some where you have to go from A to B without being detect and some where you have to eliminate a target so in the end you get your score based in how you handled the mission through the set of parts of the mission.
The story is really interesting and can say the developers did a great job doing almost if not every single cut scene in the game, because you will be able to see how detail the character models are and how they are voice perfectly. Music as the other Hitman games goes really good and gets you into the game.
and finally, another addition to this game is the Contracts mode where you can go through any of the missions of the game and complete it in whatever way you want, like eliminate the target you want with certain weapon, while wearing some disguise, etc. After you complete all of this you will successfully create a Contract which you can send to a friend to see if they are able to complete it or even get a better score you did.
So after all of this, if you are wondering if the game is good, well it is. Took me almost 80 hours to complete it at 100% (completing all the challenges, missions, etc) and let me tell you I had a blast while going through it, so grab that silver baller, sneak on those targets and eliminate them!

I'm a space enthusiast.  I work in the aerospace industry.  I love space-themed games and I love the civilization franchise.  All the planets were aligned for me to really enjoy this game.  And I do enjoy it, as demonstrated by the amount that I've played it.  However, I don't feel like I should recommend it.
I must say, the in-game music is great.  However, many of the other aspects of the game that could really capture the wonder and awe of exploring another planet are lacking.  The technologies are kind of bland, unlike Alpha Centauri's techs which almost seemed like legitimate branches of physics.  The wonders in the game mostly provide meager bonuses that don't make them all that exciting, and gone are the days of elaborate, thought-provoking cut scenes for wonders.  To top it all off, winning the game is the most anti-climactic experience you'll ever encounter.  You get a small pop-up window with a pat on the back and then are dumped to the main menu.
However, all the aforementioned disappoitments are not the real reason why I don't recommend the game. Here's the real reason:
It's abundantly clear that the developers intentionally released a partial game at full price with the intention of bilking us later with expansions and DLC.  For a game that was pretty much built off of its predecessor, why else would many of the features from the predecessor not be in this game?  Answer: because they want to sell those features to you later.
This trend of games only being complete after you've effectively paid double the initial price via DLCs will only get worse until the gaming community decides to no longer support that business model.

As for replay value, I don't see myself going back through any of the missions the way I did in the first two hitman games.

Quite honestly a powerful experience and a great game.
A rogeulike that's half base-building survival, clearing out a shelter in a time of war, carefully managing what few resources you have and the skills of your survivors to best suit the needs of everyone. The other half is a tense stealth experience where you are a civilian, not a soldier. You won't be sneaking around like Sam Fisher wiping out whole buildings of enemies. You'll be scared, alone, and the moment you see a man with a gun you pray and pray that he's not out for blood that night. And you run. And you hope that you make it back to the exit in one piece.
Good amount of replay, and it brings attention to the other side of the Hoo-ah go soldier military shooter; the plight of the average men and women caught between two sides, neither one good or evil. No morality system. No good and evil. Just you, trying to survive, and determining if your convictions are worth perhaps dying for, or how far your morals will bend in the name of survival.

I have dozens of games in my steam library, and this is one of a handful that I felt compelled to finish. If you've ever wondered what it feels like to try to survive in a war-zone, this game is about as close as you will get, while being both challenging and fun.
Warning - There may be some small spoilers in the pro/cons below
Pros:
- Great Balancing: The game is pretty difficult/hardcore. However it does not force you to grind endlessly or add completely illogical elements for the sake of making you suffer. It is difficult because each choice you make has a dramatic impact. For example, take scavenging. Due to the way the scavenging mechanic works, you can only bring back a certain amount of loot each day. You can't clear out an entire house in one night, which is very realistic if you think about it. Furthermore, some locations/ways of acquiring loot are more dangerous than others. Murdering innocent people and taking theirs stuff will have negative consequences, just as it would in real life. Since you have a limited amount of supplies to work with, there is complex strategy as to how to use these supplies to survive, and discovering a good strategy is a ton of fun.
- Good Needs System: Each survivor has needs that need to be fulfilled. They must be fed, they must be kept healthy, and they must be kept sane. I won't go to far into detail because finding out how the game works is part of the fun, but keeping your survivors alive is very manageable if you take care of important things like security and careful rationing of food. However, if you waste your food or medicine, or put your survivors in dangerous situations, they will quickly get injured/sick or begin to starve.
- Decent Crafting System: What I like about this game is that each building upgrade has its own unique benefit and its own niche in the game-play. There are no superfluous elements added just for the sake of variety. You aren't going to be able to craft 10 different types of food. However, everything that you do craft is very important in its own way, and spending your precious resources on the work-station at the wrong time in the game will give you a hard time.
- Decent Combat/Stealth: Some people may complain that the combat system is too unpredictable. To them I would say that in a real life war zone, a civilian wouldn't Rambo his/her way through a group of armed thugs every night and expect to survive for long.The game encourages you not to kill or steal by making these activities dangerous. Sometimes they may be necessary, but you shouldn't seek out combat for no good reason. In fact, it may be helpful to avoid it completely.
- Excellent Atmosphere/Background: I really enjoyed the atmosphere of the game. The visuals and background music set a mood of desperation that I haven't seen in any other game.
- NPCs/PCs: The characters in this game truly seem alive. The graphics/animations fulfill cater to this purpose pretty well. When your survivors are injured they limp. When they are sick they cough, when they are cold they shiver. In other words, they react to their surroundings pretty well. Also, they each have their own stories that they reveal gradually over the course of weeks. The NPCs in the different locations also have their own worries, whether it be a son trying to protect his parents from robbers (You), or a bandit trying to find ammunition for his gun. There are many stories out there, and trying to discover them all is a lot of fun.
-This is going on for longer than I intended, so I am going to stop with the Pro's here...
Cons:
- Ocasional Bugs: As of 11/16/2014, I have encountered two bugs over 20 hours of in-game time. One of them was a CTD when returning to my safehouse, but it was pretty minor and I was able to continue my game from the previous day. The other was a workbench bug after about 12 days (about 2-4 IRL hours), which was more annoying since it forced me to restart from day 1. The game just got released, so I assume these bugs will be patched soon. Overall, I really enjoyed the game, so having to restart on one of my playthings wasn't too annoying and it seems to be a very rare bug.
-Time Scale: It would be nice to be able to speed up time during the day. There is an option to end the day early, but you risk having a trader show up at your door or a random event taking place, and not being there for it. This is a minor complaint though, since usually there is plenty of stuff to do during the day (building, cooking, etc.) and no reason to skip to night.
Overall: I would strongly recommend this game to any mature gamers out there. It has a depth that most AAA games lack, and is far better than any other indie survival game I have played (some examples being Don't Starve or Zafehouse Diaries )

This game is Awesome.
I bought this game when it was only $0.89 on steam, but for $2.99 its worth every penny.
The game runs very well even on toasters, although, in high populated servers you can generally expect a lower frame rate, though its manageable enough.
Secondly, this game gives you complete control over each of your weapons and character models, so if you want to customize it to fit whatever design you have, you can do that. If you have the time, and patience you can a really awesome skin, or really awesome weapon. I've got nearly 20 different skins for my weapons, and more when I feel like it. For what it's worth, its probably one of the best purchases I've made.
My main gripes with the game are the melee hit boxes, as I frequently miss people I should have hit, and hit people who I should have missed, although the hitbox is based off the default knife skin, and not so much as whatever skin you have on your weapon. Additionally the damage in the game is very inconsistant, the rifle normally kills people in 1-3 shots(if you hit the head, 3 anywhere but the head, and 2 if the first shot is a body shot and second a head) although there are times when it takes a whole magazine to kill them, and all I get are hit markers. The sniper is also a big concern with the game, as there seems to be a bit of a delay from when you flick your scope onto an enemy and aim to compensate. there will be times when I scope in, over or undershoot my aim, and when I go to move the scope there's about a half to one second delay before you reaim in otherwords, unless you aim right where there at and scope in perfectly, sniping is very hard.
Additionally, when you want to make a new weapon from scratch, you can't break it all the way down, you can only break it down to essentially it's skeleton.(the exeption being the knife that you can make it into whatever you want.) this gets infuriating if you have a very clever design but you are limited to game's coding of the skeleton, which is understandable, but this in turn makes you get even more creative about your problem.
Overall though, I would still say that this game is worth its price, as you can create just about anything in the game, the only limits are what your own imagination can come up with.

Magic Duels Origins is the response we all awaited for Hearthstone and all the other f2p CCGs out there. Sadly it doesn't live up to the expectations many of us had.
The game starts slow, forces you to play a very very slow tutorial, the campaign is bland and uninteresting, The decks you start with are so vanilla, the music is hideous, the sound design is terrible (as expected of a MTG game).
But beneath all this mess, there's MTG! I'm one hour in and I got a headache at how slow paced the forced tutorial/campaigns are. It's nowhere near as fun as previous Duels of the planeswalkers. I'm certain once I get past all the boring missions and unlock a couple booster packs I may be able to get some fun out of it.
The microtransactions are cheaper than real boosters, but still expensive as booster packs are only 6 cards rather than 15 (Last I played MTG booster packs contained 15 cards).
The UI is well polished, but the game pace just feels slow and clunky.
What bothers me is something I read, where they mentioned they may sell DLC later on, now I'm unsure if this future DLC will unlock sets that can be acquired with IGC or will be buy only.
There's also the fact that there are no starter freebies to get you hooked with the game.
It has a lot of potential, but it's just not good at it's current state.
If you're a hardcore MTG fan or used to play, give it a shot, it may be fun with friends. But as it is, it stands as a slow, boring and frustrating experience.
Edit: There are daily quests, you just have to get past an hour of boring tutorial-campaign. I'm a fair person and I'll edit my review as the game improves, as I'm sure it could.

The grandmother didn't understand why Jimmy didn't like his gift.
She knew he enjoyed Bioshock, so why would he not appreciate an improved version?
Jimmy explained: "We are consumers! We have to stand up for our rights and make sure companies know we want a good product! If we shut up about these things, they'll just get away with it!"
But lovely, old granny didn't understand a word of what he said.
"But Jimmy", she said. "I bought you this because I wanted to make you happy. You shouldn't concern yourself with these things. What counts is that I love you."
Jimmy, however, would not budge.
He knew he was in the right. He knew his cause was just.
"I think I'll get an early night. I am very exhausted", said his grandmother, shortly before she left the room.
With nobody do complain to, Jimmy booted up the game and started playing.
It wasn't nearly as bad as he thought it would be.
In fact, he actually came to understand why he had loved the game so much 9 years ago.
It was still a fun experience. Slightly flawed, but still fun.
He didn't even realize how long he had been playing, when he finally went to bed at 4am in the morning.
After a good night's rest, Jimmy got up and wandered into the kitchen to fetch some cereals.
He was wondering why his grandmother wasn't having her usual tea.
"Grandma!", Jimmy shouted. "You're not having any tea today?!"
Worried about his grandmother, Jimmy went to her room and knocked on the door, but there was no reply.
Nervously, Jimmy opened the door to find his grandmother still in bed.
Jimmy's grandmother had died that night.

As someone who is a semi competitive Melee and PM player, this game really clicks with me. If you play Melee and PM at a high level, you can probably pick up a character in an hour or two. If you're a competitive Melee or PM player, you can probably pick up a character in an hour or two.
This game is ACCESSIBLE
The gameplay is fast and smooth, and incredibly user friendly. The learning curve is lessened from Smash due to the lack L-Cancelling, replacing it with low landing lag, making combos smooth and easier to perform. There aren't edges to the stages, making edge-guarding less read based, but, the wall jumping and air dodging lets you mix up your recoveries just enough to keep opponents guessing, but not to the point where you could do 3-4 different things recovering. Also, you can attack and move out of an air-dodge, which makes a missed wavedash off the stage less punishing. There aren't any shields in Rivals. Instead, you have parrying, which keeps defensive play to a minimum.
I haven't even talked about the characters yet.
Wow.
Every character is completely unique, with really well executed ideas. Zetterburn can set opponents on fire, and if he connects a strong attack (the non copywritten name for smash attacks) while the opponent is still on fire, the attack does quite a good deal more knockback and damage (Try aerial side-b into F-smash ;) ). Wrastor is the godlike combination of Falco, Marth, and Jigglypuff. He utilizes a wind current that, if he is inside it, raises his speed and his already insane aerial speed. He also has 4 jumps, so, uh.
BACK AIR BACK AIR BACK AIR.
Anyways, Forsburn can create a clone of himself (ICs anyone?) and can create smoke, store it, and use it to create an explosion around him. He can also Ken combo. Orcane uses a puddle that he creates somewhere on the map. He can teleport to it, make it evaporate into bubble has a trap, and enhance some moves of his. Maypul is an extremely small and fast character that can mark opponents with certain special moves. If she uses a strong attack while the person is marked, they are stunned for a small amount of time, which is a really simple kill setup. If the opponent is marked and she up-Bs, she will pull herself toward the opponent, and control her direction, which is great for mixups. Kragg hits quite hard, but is a good deal slower that the rest of the cast. He can create a big stone that he can throw in a myriad of directions. If he isn't holding it, he can break with an attack, which sends a bunch of rocks in the direction he attacked. Depending on what attack you use and what direction you hit it at. His up-B is really bizarre, he summons a pillar of stone wherever he is. It's really useful for comboing, by getting an opponent between Kragg and the pillar opens tons of combo opportunities.
So, is this game worth buying? Yes, absolutely, One of the greatest games in early access right now.

Good: Excellent visuals, fun combat, great story(-telling), good character backstories.
Bad: One-dimensional characters, mostly linear gameplay
The paradigm system is a great new feature for party configuration in battle. Party paradigms dictate what roles each party memer plays, as well as giving bonus buffs to the whole party depending on the configuration. This can be likened to how in football, where you have your standard offensive and defensive lines, and also special teams, except expect to be making frequent paradigm shifts in battle as the situations change.
I never experienced the stereotypical JRPG grind in this game. The paradigm system and the Active Time Battle system keep the combat refreshing. Most battles can be tackled with proper selection of paradigms. In fact, I never upgraded any weapons, didn't complete many sidequests at all, and yet the ending was still comfortable and appropriately challenging. The pacing is definitely on point.
One of the major drawbacks is that the game is mostly very linear. However, this is only until about Chapter 11, which is the point where you're thrown into an absolutely massive map to explore, with lots of things to kill and numerous sidequests.
The story was enjoyable, and it was deep and complex. However, character development for the most part missed its mark. With a few exceptions, many characters seemed very one-dimensional in their mentality throughout the game. However, the storytelling partially makes up for this. The intricately connected character backgrounds are gradually revealed through the game, and the connections are revealed in an interesting way.
Final Fantasy XIII also features one of my all-time favorite characters: Sazh. He is the most well-developed character in the entire game. The black dude with a chocobo in his 'fro might raise eyebrows, but he is the most relatable character, and acts as the sole voice of sanity while everybody else around himseems to try to pound into your brain their "I'm a hero" spiel (looking at you, Snow).

Not boring, not tedious, not a remake of CIV V by any means. I like it, yet I am a bit irritated at some of the missing features such as strategic mode not being an available mode, and the focusing of a certain income was weird to figure out-I actually found out how to do so on accident. Lag happens regardless of how hot or cold the computer is running. Waiting for more than 10 seconds for a unit you clicked on to catch up with your click is kind of annoying, especially when trying to go to war.
I also experienced a trade route choosing to go a longer way than was necessary-two cities were literally four tiles away from each other, unobstructed by anything. The terrain between them was flat and clear. The trade route, every time, decided the best way to get there was to go five tiles down, two tiles over, and then some odd number of tiles back up to get to the city. At first I thought "maybe I need a road", but even after building one, it still wanted to go the long way-which btw, was riddled with alien siege worms and drones and what not because there was a nest down there. Ended up never even using a trade route for that city to the other one the whole entire game.
Also, wtf. No "Just...one...more...turn" feature? I lost (without knowing how as I was fairly sure I was winning) and there is a button there to continue playing afterwards, but it's blacked out! I don't get it.
Multiplayer online via internet (so you're playing with people you don't know) is terribly put together, in the sense that I did not know there was DLC offered if you pre-ordered. I saw that AFTER the game had dropped and could no longer get that option. So since I don't have the DLC, I can't play online with those who DO. Even in CIV V you could still play with those who had the DLC.
It should have been offered to everyone, not just those who pre-ordered. Like I said, I never even knew there was a way to pre-order or what the rewards were for someone who had.
All in all, I would recommend playing this game, but thinking back to how much the game was hyped...I don't think it's worth 50.00 for a game that isn't even finished, especially since we can't get the DLC that others have. Not fair, and not good business sense, imo.
Would recommend playing, but not buying.

Day 10: My group was hungry.  We were out of food and desperate.  We put our hopes in that there would be food in the apartment complex that was basically blown in half during the shelling.  One half was empty but we knew the other half had a group in it.  We often heard gunfire coming from the building meaning they might be hostile.  It was risky but we were desperate.
It was simple.  We would take from the empty half of the building and let the other half keep their stuff.  Marko went that night.  The only way he could approach was from the inhabited side.  I climbed the ruble to the second story and used a crowbar to break in.  I then headed to the next door inside and peaked through.  There were two women on the other side.  One told of a scavenger on the other half searching for items.  The other responded by saying that, "John" would kill them.  Kill them.  But it's just a scavenger.  He wasn't a bandit breaking into this side.
One of the women went upstairs and the other started walking towards my door.  I quickly got up and hid in the closet.  The women entered the room and checked her items, then left from the same door she came in.  I could hear her go upstairs.  Now was my chance.  I left the closet and opened the door.  Only stairs upwards and another door.  I went through the next door.  I opened it to see a man with a sniper rifle aimed at the next building.  This was John.  standing at the end of the building.  He screamed for the other scavenger to show themselves.  I considered going around but John would see me crossing to the other side.  And he would most likely kill me.  Was this what the gunshots were?  Not self defense but killing scavengers on the other half?
I pulled out the crowbar.  If I don't get these supplies, we'll die.  If I cross to get them, John will kill me.  And he is already threatening to kill another.  This is justified right? I slowly approached him from behind, and swung.  I wounded him but didn't kill him.  He then yelled at me saying, "it would be the last thing I ever did" and brought his powerful rifle around to aim at me.  No.  I can't get shot.  We don't have any food let alone medical supplies.  With new found fear I swung again.  And again.  I saw that one last hit could do it.  And begun to swing.  He then yelled, "please don't kill me!" and began to let go of the rifle.  But it was too late.  I was already swinging at his head.  I hit him and he fell off the second story of the building and down to the ground. Dead.
He was giving up.  I could have taken the weapon and let him live.  If only I hadn't attacked to kill.  I might not have swung so eagerly.  But I was scared.  It was his fault.  He was going to shoot me.
I then heard the women coming from downstairs.  I got ready for another fight.  But they ran right by me.  One got on her knees at the edge of the building and began crying.  The other stood between us.  Fear in her eyes with no weapon.  I paniced.  I did this.  He's dead because of me.  I ran.  Without any of the stuff I needed.  I headed back.  Marko entered the safehouse and the following message appeared.
The night was calm.

If you have played Civ 5, you have played Beyond Earth more or less. There are a few game tweaks here and there but you could just be playing a Civ 5 mod. Not that that is a bad thing though. The landscape and unit skins do make it feel a bit visually different to other Civ games but you do know without a doubt you are playing a Civ game (but instead of barbarians, you are fighting aliens).
Some of the interactions with the AI players seem a tad pointless and, although there are mixed reviews about the Affinity system, I really enjoy the game. To me it feels like Command & Conquer 3 mashed with Civ 5. Apart from the addition of the Affinity system (which is good but needs a bit of tweaking perhaps), this does feel slightly stripped down. As opposed to the plethoras of units from previous Civs that required different tactics to use well, there are around nine units which are upgraded through the affinity system. World events are back as well but overhauled as Quests that appear much more frequently and with more obvious rewards, which is a very nice touch.
The tech tree has had a refreshing overhaul so you can see whaere everything leads easily now, however some quests ask for certain structures/units to be built without any indication of where they are in the tech tree. This caught me out a few times and i had to resort to Googling where some of them sat in the tech tree. Some sort of quest indicator on these would be really helpful.
As some of the other reviews have said, there is a bit of a beta feel to it at time of writing. The tutorial's seem to pop up reletnlessly even once you have gone through them earlier in the same game. For some inexplicable reason the game spends a good three minutes or so at the start screen. I have no idea why; there is no loading indicator and pressing buttons doesn't help. This is a real pain as it happens EVERY time I open the game.
Overall, yes, I would recommend this as I really like the Civ franchise. If you are looking for a finely tuned, highly polished pinnacle of the Civ series, hold on to your money for now. This is a great basis for them to build on but there is a lot of work to be done before it could properly be considered a top-notch game.

While the system tech tree, the alien species and the visuals style is distinctive, these aspects are ultimately not enough to make Civ:BE feel like a fresh entry in the series. Some new features, such as the orbital layer, feel unrealised.
To add further insult to injury, asides from a truly awe-inspiring introductory cinematic, there is far less of an interesting story, and even less of faction personality. Factions lack the broad historical legacy of previous Civilization games, and there are no faction specific units. Everything turns on your affinity, and whilst this is a fair decision, it feels like a missed opportunity. Stations (or City States) are also underwhelming in their gameplay significance. They lack quests, growth or any of the features City States had in Civ:V - they are now trade routes only.
And finally, the same connection issues for multiplayer lobbies in Civ:V remain. On numerous occassions I've had to spend 1.5h just to host a Civ:BE game with 6-8 players, and an equally long time to resume the game another night, if on the rare occassion it allows us to play without continuously disconnecting someone when another connects.
As a full priced release, Civilization: Beyond Earth is not worth the cost. You'll be better served trying the Alpha Centauri mod on the Civ:V Steam Workshop. If you are planning to buy Civilization: Beyond Earth, wait until Firaxis Games have released a roadmap on what they will add to the game - but that will likely come in the form of paid DLC, that doesn't drastically change the formula.

This game is Awesome.
I bought this game when it was only $0.89 on steam, but for $2.99 its worth every penny.
The game runs very well even on toasters, although, in high populated servers you can generally expect a lower frame rate, though its manageable enough.
Secondly, this game gives you complete control over each of your weapons and character models, so if you want to customize it to fit whatever design you have, you can do that. If you have the time, and patience you can a really awesome skin, or really awesome weapon. I've got nearly 20 different skins for my weapons, and more when I feel like it. For what it's worth, its probably one of the best purchases I've made.
My main gripes with the game are the melee hit boxes, as I frequently miss people I should have hit, and hit people who I should have missed, although the hitbox is based off the default knife skin, and not so much as whatever skin you have on your weapon. Additionally the damage in the game is very inconsistant, the rifle normally kills people in 1-3 shots(if you hit the head, 3 anywhere but the head, and 2 if the first shot is a body shot and second a head) although there are times when it takes a whole magazine to kill them, and all I get are hit markers. The sniper is also a big concern with the game, as there seems to be a bit of a delay from when you flick your scope onto an enemy and aim to compensate. there will be times when I scope in, over or undershoot my aim, and when I go to move the scope there's about a half to one second delay before you reaim in otherwords, unless you aim right where there at and scope in perfectly, sniping is very hard.
Additionally, when you want to make a new weapon from scratch, you can't break it all the way down, you can only break it down to essentially it's skeleton.(the exeption being the knife that you can make it into whatever you want.) this gets infuriating if you have a very clever design but you are limited to game's coding of the skeleton, which is understandable, but this in turn makes you get even more creative about your problem.
Overall though, I would still say that this game is worth its price, as you can create just about anything in the game, the only limits are what your own imagination can come up with.

It's Magic. It's free. If that's all that matters to you, play it.
Whether this game is worth your time depends on what you expect from it. For someone who's new to MTG, this is a great way to see whether the game is for you without investing $. For someone who doesn't religiously follow MTG's sets/plot, this is an OK way to keep up to date on (some of) the newer stuff. For someone who wants to play against random strangers for internet bragging points, this is fine too.
Other digital versions of MTG outshine this game in replicating MTG's individual aspects. This game is a serviceable middle ground, leaning frequently towards "ease of use" rather than "replicating the experience". Overall, I'd give it a "meh" if I could. My initial review of this game was negative, but it's grown on me since release, which is why I'm going with thumbs up.
For those of you coming into this with no knowledge of Magic: the Gathering, MTG is a "trading card game", the first physical version of which was released in 1993. The game has seen many digital adaptations over the years, each of which fell somewhat short of replicating the physical experience that made MTG so successful. This game takes the F2P approach - allow users to earn content by investing time, while giving them the option to purchase "shortcuts" and/or cosmetic items.
Let's dig right into the differences. While this game's expansion release dates (now) match paper MTG's ones, not every physical card makes it into the game. The card pool is further reduced by rarity: instead of the usual "4 of a kind" limit per deck, uncommons are capped at 3, rares at 2, and mythic rares at 1 per deck. This developer choice lowers the power disparity between players somewhat, given how often physical MTG's winning decks are packed full of the rarest/most powerful cards (and how in an F2P game time/$ eventually unlock all of them).
The above applies not just to cards per deck but to cards owned - once you get a mythic rare, you won't see it again in booster packs (which, unlike in the physical version, contain only 6 cards each). Deckbuilding isn't hobbled by this, because the cards you unlock are available for any deck you create, regardless of how many decks you've put them into. Trading, however, is non-existant, which means card access is extremely streamlined: earn in-game currency (gold), buy booster packs, get cards. (There is no "draft" or "sealed deck" mode at the moment, so there is no alternate use for boosters.)
Deckbuilding in the Stainless Games MTG adaptations has been steadily improving with each iteration, but there are still hiccups. Unless you are a new player, don't follow the game's "deck archetypes" - the system will often suggest sub-optimal card choices to you. Fortunately, the game no longer requests you win games with archetype-built decks in order to earn gold, so experienced players can safely ignore this feature.
Speaking of new players, one of the good things this game does is how it introduces game mechanics. "Skill quests" are essentially small game setups that require players to properly take advantage of a given card mechanic to succeed. Skill quests are less useful to experienced players, but completing them gives gold, so they're worth running through once.
Same can be said of the story. This game includes a short overview of each expansion's plot. Love it or hate it, getting through the plot rewards gold, and you never have to return after slogging through the plot once.
So let's say you've covered all the above and actually want to PLAY. Your choices for earning gold (to unlock more cards and make better decks and win more often) are playing against the AI, PVP, and various daily/weekly quests. AI is predictably dim, and will only occasionally win games against experienced players even on the hardest setting. PVP matchmaking is...lacking. Each "season" (expansion) tracks your net "wins-losses" score, and randomly matches you against players in the same bracket. This makes no provisions for card unlocks or skill level. Given that you earn no gold for losing, you actually want to stay away from PVP until you have a solid enough deck, which means AI grinding or quests.
There are several good things about daily quests. First, you can "bank" up to three of them, which means you don't have to play this game every day. Second, once a day you can "refresh" a quest, and hope for a better randomly-generated task. This is nice because some of the quest requirements are much harder to achieve, such as requiring PVP. Incidentally, the game promotes daily log-ins by giving extra gold for each first daily PVP win, but prohibits griding by imposing a daily gold cap.
But what about playing against friends? Well, you can do that, but you won't earn gold. Worse, there is no voice or text chat in the game. Still worse, there are no servers, which is why all PVP is random. What this means for friendly games is that you have to hop out into Steam's overlay to invite someone to PVP, and then keep overlay or your choice of voice chat active to actually communicate. It's easy to see why developers decided to exclude chat options (to avoid text/vocal griefing/abuse), but this choice makes the game less appealing to the average user.
To sum things up, this is a serviceable MTG adaptation, but the game carries with it a multitude of annoyances. Whether the game is worth putting up with them is really up to you.

-The swordplay does feel good. You can dismember enemies. Not just with a sword but you can dismember them with projectile weapons too.
-I found the enemies to be dull for the most part. And they can get annoying when a bunch of them gets spawned over and over.
-Too many things explode in this game.
Even bicycles explode. How does a bicycle explode from a sword?
There are bunch of exploding barrels. Gas tanks. Cars explode. Arcade machines explode. Explosions explode. There are exploding enemies…
-Some areas feel very linear while some are non-linear.
There are secrets to find. Including hidden areas that are pixely just like the original game. Glad they included these easter eggs.
There are a lot of references to the original. Including some one-liners
-Unlike SW 1997 where enemies were spread out across the level, with SW 2013 you are locked in an area and must kill hordes or enemies and then the exit will glow yellow (this is where you’ll notice some comparisons with Serious Sam and DukeForever).
-There are alot of ways to regain health: health kits, souls of dead demons, using the healing power, fortune cookies, etc
I would have preferred to be able to carry health packs.
-You can unlock powers, skills, and attachments for weapons.
In conclusion, I prefer Shadow Warrior Classic Redux, however SW 2013 is still a good game. But its too tedious at times.

I personally find it hard, to get a game, perhaps an exploration, that I thoroughly enjoy. Games such as Dear Esther. Shelter has a special glow to it that makes the game extraordinary. Then again, the game is awful. Now don’t get me wrong. I admire the game, and for the small price it is very much worth it. But… the games flaws are big, yet unfixable. The games flaws almost have nothing to do with the game, its the person. But, before I get to the things wrong with it, why don’t I state whats good about it. For one, its a badger simulator, now who wouldn’t want to play that? The game has beautiful graphics and the art style is different and is amazing. The lighting however should be changeable. The entire game is done with a pastel, almost opaque color. It is almost uncomfortable to look at and can get very annoying at times. Especially during the night. When almost everything is a grayish blue, its hard to find food, keep track of the 5 badgers (I had only one at the time) and see where you are going. Besides the colorm I found its hard to keep the badgers with you. Crouching, or pressing control will bring the badgers to you but only as you hold the key. If the young cubs spot food, they will automatically remove themselves from their mother and hop around it. This can get very annoying. Also, if something frightens the badgers they will run to safety. This happened to me, and my 1 badger and soon I was down to 0 badgers. I looked everywhere, but it was at night and the badger was gone. One issue I have is how quickly the badgers will begin to starve. I lost 3 of my badgers to starvation during the bird of prey section in the beginning of the game. There is no food along the path and I got lost with the several safety patches. I mean really, it is so hard to keep the badgers with and keep them alive. Im amazed how long I was able to keep them with me. I have been a bit too negative though. I don’t want it to sound like a bad game because, it is not at all a bad game. Not even close. The gameplay is smooth and the controls are simple and easily mastered. With only 6 keys and the mouse there are no confusing shortcuts and pointless keys to worry about. The sound effects in this game help far more than you’d think, along with shadows. Hearing the call and seeing the shadow of the large bird of prey will ensure that you get to safety soon and give you fair warnings as to when you may be about to be attacked. At night, many sounds may scare your cubs, or you, but the small call you do will help handfuls to find missing cubs. I like the boundaries by the water to ensure that no baby badgers are sent down to their doom. This game is absolutely extraordinary and is sure to have you playing hours straight.

Blockstorm isn't a bad game. It's just poorly executed, and has very little depth. Being an obvious Minecraft clone, it also mixes in mechanics from games like Counter Strike, and the end result is actually fun to play for a dozen hours or so due to the unique abilities to burrow through walls or build your own. That'd be fine and dandy, but the developers decided to add cheap "do this 10,000 times" server-side "achievements," that offer no challenge and force players to grind on even after the game has lost its appeal. Being an indie game, there are at most two dozen people online at any given time, and the only reason anyone still plays at all is because IndieGala regularly gives away thousands of copies for free. Most of the more interesting game modes are always empty because only a single map was included for each, leaving the rest to be filled out by the community, so what's left are staple modes like capture the flag and team deathmatch that have been done better before. Even basic things like being able to remap weapon keys are inexplicably missing! These problems may seem minor, but that's exactly why they should not be there in the first place, and what could be a fun and unique game ends up being a lazy Minecraft cash-in, with few players, and more frustration than anything else.
I love the artwork in this game, It doesn't take to long to beat though. Overall, I would wait for it to go on sale.

The Good: Amazing technical feat, nano suit is awesome, on-the-fly weapon customization is very useful, huge open world, changes pace throughout the game, lots of weapons
The Bad: Very difficult, a bit on the short side, feels like it's missing something
The biggest hype behind Crysis was it's looks. Very few people have the hardware to run the game like it should be: All settings to very high and using DirectX 10, and I am one of the lucky few to have the hardware setup to do so. While most people can run this on ultra settings you won't find too many who can run it above 30 FPS. My setup was able to handle most of the game at above 20 FPS but did dip into the single digits every once in awhile. With that aside Crysis is just stunning even three years later. Every texture is high res and even when looking at something u close you can see all the detail in that texture and not just a blurry or pixelated mess. All the lighting is gorgeous and the physics seem almost real thank to the super advanced Crytek engine and DirectX 10. Everything in the game just look amazing: Every blade of grass sways, trees crumble under fire, leaves on palm trees shear off when fired at. Throughout the whole game you will never get sick of looking at this tropical technical feat.
Now a game can look as good as it wants, but it's no use if the game doesn't play well, and have a good story?. You play as a Special Forces agent called Nomad, and are sent in with a team to investigate an island that the Koreans have occupied. It gets interesting right from the beginning, and stays interesting throughout.
Thankfully Crysis is a solid shooter with some elements that other FPS games have never used before and the biggest thing is the Nano Suit. This thing lets you choose between four different modes to help you out on the battlefield. Stealth turns you invisible for an amount of time. The faster you move the more energy it depletes. Armor...well is pretty self explanitory, and speed gives you a super boost that lets you dash dozens of yards in a matter of seconds, for a few seconds. Lastly strength lets you throw enemies, and melee them to make them fly as well as extra height when jumping. All these are crucial to surviving in this hard and wide open game.
Yeah that's right it's not linear. Surprised? Well with so many linear FPS games out there *cough Halo cough* it's a nice change. The island is huge and wide open and you can take different approaches to each situation. Most of the time you have to infiltrate Korean KPA camps and using stealth along with silenced weapons is a good start. Or you can go in guns blazing. If you prefer the back door approach maybe you can get there by truck or swim across the lake and take them all by surprise. The multi-approach system is useful, but stealth may not always be the best choice, and some times you don't get one.
That brings me to the next element of customizing your weapons on the fly. Have a sub-machine gun and can get an accurate shot? Attach a silencer, and a sniper scope, and set it to single shot and pop off some guys before charging in. Once inside attach a red dot sight, and add an ACOG scope to the top and even a grenade launcher. Being able to change one weapon to another on the fly is just awesome and really does help in every situation. This breaks the monotony of trying to find a gun for specific situations.
The game's pacing takes a turn half way through the game when you start fighting aliens. Of course this makes the game more interesting and is almost like two games in one, and takes a more linear turn. Instead of infiltrating KPA camps your fighting alongside squad mates against aliens. This is fun and I wish shooters would do stuff like this more often. It breaks up the monotony of the open jungle and kicks things up a notch.
Every element in the game works, but of course everything could be better, and that's why Crysis 2 is coming out. My biggest gripe with the game is the difficulty. Even on easy the game is brutal and seems unfair at times such as vehicles blowing up really fast, and having 30+ guys come after you, and not being able to use stealth to get into a camp. This can drive you nuts, but the story is good enough for you to keep coming back for more. If you have the PC power Crysis is a must have.
~Score: 9/10
