I bought two copies of this game. One for me, and one for a friend.
I have told that friend to wait a couple of months, because everything past turn 100 or so is broken and/or badly balanced or simply not finished.
Diplomacy is a joke. The AI makes offers it does does not agree to. I have even been offered *Nothing* for *Nothing* by an AI opponent.
In earlier CIV games you got a sense of when an opponent was close to a tech/culture win and could act accordingly. Here you only get the information "75%" if you know where to look, and then suddenly BAM! YOU LOSE!
I really like the Affinity system, but early victory requires going 90-100% after just one of the three. And don't get me started on units... Their strength is 100% tied into the affinity system. Units upgrade EXPONATIALLY with affinity with huge leaps in strenght. A linear or logistic curve would be much better IMHO. Getting a high enough affinity to enable an "affinity win" should not automatically give you invincible units - going after those wins should be a sacrifice; not an obvious path.
Let's hope DLC's fix this mess. Cheers! :D

I should be a prime fan of this game - I love Civ, I love the sci-fi colony setting...
But CivBE falls short of the series' greatness. There is some minor gameplay variation from Civ V, but not improvement. For example, the new starting options and events/quests are interesting at first but not fleshed out enough. And the lacklustre goes much further...
Opportunities were missed here. Instead of thinking, "Players can scan the world from space, so how can we modify the game to take account of a detailed world map being available from the beginning?", we instead get the same mostly dark world to start with. Instead of thinking, "No need to reinvent e.g. boats and tanks, so what new strategic units can we develop?", we instead just get units in a highly analogous progression to the historical Civ series.
The ending had no build-up and was followed by zero post-game analysis: gone are the histograms etc. The ending was just a single splash screen, positive or negative, not even telling me which victory my opponoent had won. Frankly the game feels unfinished.

-Shadow Warrior 2013 is a combination of Shadow Warrior 1997, Serious Sam and Duke Nukem Forever.
-The story and characters are good. The jokes are good most of the time.
-Gameplay is good for the most part.
Except for when you have to use a power which requires you to double tab a direction key and hold an attack button.
It becomes a problem in the heat of battle when you are trying to dodge enemies and projectiles. And many times its unresponsive.
-Weapons feel underwhelming. There isn’t much kick to them.
I feel like the weapons were downgraded in order to focus more on the sword. You’ll likely use the sword more than all the other weapons combined.
-The swordplay does feel good. You can dismember enemies. Not just with a sword but you can dismember them with projectile weapons too.
-I found the enemies to be dull for the most part. And they can get annoying when a bunch of them gets spawned over and over.
-Too many things explode in this game.
Even bicycles explode. How does a bicycle explode from a sword?
There are bunch of exploding barrels. Gas tanks. Cars explode. Arcade machines explode. Explosions explode. There are exploding enemies…
-Some areas feel very linear while some are non-linear.
There are secrets to find. Including hidden areas that are pixely just like the original game. Glad they included these easter eggs.
There are a lot of references to the original. Including some one-liners
-Unlike SW 1997 where enemies were spread out across the level, with SW 2013 you are locked in an area and must kill hordes or enemies and then the exit will glow yellow (this is where you’ll notice some comparisons with Serious Sam and DukeForever).
-There are alot of ways to regain health: health kits, souls of dead demons, using the healing power, fortune cookies, etc
I would have preferred to be able to carry health packs.
-You can unlock powers, skills, and attachments for weapons.
In conclusion, I prefer Shadow Warrior Classic Redux, however SW 2013 is still a good game. But its too tedious at times.

Torchlight was developed by some of the guys who worked on Diablo 1 & 2. It's essentially very similar gameplay, the most noticeable difference being how bright and colorful the game looks in comparison to Diablo. This may be a turn-off to some, and very welcome to others who are tired to the standard dark and brown color schemes in games these day.
If you're unfamiliar with Diablo, Torchlight is still a very accessible game. ARPGs are quite easy to get the hang of, as far as controls go (clickclickclickclick Q 124356 etc.) It's rather slow-paced, which might bug some people as it starts to feel boring after a few hours in a play session. Having a pet companion helps make the single player descent less lonely/ Pets will fight by your side, and also sell any excess items you give it in town for you. Dungeons are somewhat randomly generated. Loot drops also varies.
The game is quite easy on Normal difficulty due to the abundance of potion drops, and the ability to just spam the potion button when you are in trouble. You shouldn't expect to die very often at all. Although this might give the game a bit of a casual feel, it is still an enjoyable single player game that isn't overly lengthy. You can get a good 25 hours in. Don't expect much on the story front; it's rather bland and not very memorable. Besides, the core of the game is centered on loot.
While this game is worth the price, you may want to shell out an extra $5 for the sequel, which, in addition to fixing how rigged potions worked, the slow pace, adds much more to the game with regards to loot, classes, monsters, skills, and importantly, multiplayer.

This game is special as it hits you right from the very beginning as being something very different from other games. It's simply unique in its simplicity and brings out the beauty of what we seem to have mostly forgotten while living in cities and leading a modern life, ignorant of the continuous struggle to survive in the wild. The simple act of feeding to living another day - it's something that most of us take for granted, but finding food in the wild is an adventure of its own for these wild creatures.
There are no achievements to unlock in this game. There is no button-mashing involved. No alien robots to vanquish. No zombies to kill. It's simply down to the very basics of nature and how we instinctively react to protect our own. The story is touching and the more you play, the more you get involved into the lives of the mother badger and her cubs. This game exhibits a universal appeal, irrespective of the kind of games you usually love to play. There is adventure in protecting yourself and your family. But at all times, you need to make sure that your cubs are fed regularly. This is as real as it gets, with some elements of surprise intertwined into the story to keep the experience fresh and exciting. The graphics might seem somehow washed out or really bright, but the game really distinguishes itself from all the other games out there by drawing your focus and care to the gameplay itself, although the graphics look really good, once you understand the concept and setting and then you can truly appreciate the majestic beauty in doing the simplest things to stay alive and survive.
Forget everything as you dive into this game. There is no 1st place here or any trophy to win. Enjoy nature and living as you would have, all from the perspective of a small creature out on its own to protect its family in the wild. It's magical and well worth the time to experience a great adventure!

I personally adore this game, it's a shame that I can't play it more. If you are looking for cutting edge graphics, linear storylines, well developed NPCs, or  an incredible combat system this may not be the best game for you, but what it lacks in pure aesthetic areas it more than makes up for with game style, originality, and pure joy of exploration. I found myself completely immersed in Salt to a point where I was legitimately freaked out by some of the games content, inquisitive about other things and quite pleased with how serene the randomly generated worlds are. The early access game does leave some things to be desired; multiplayer, smoother graphics, etc. but the content, as lava boots implements it, feels very well placed, there are very few loose ends that are common with many early access games.
I do have a few things that I would love to see in future updates; better sailing mechanics (let's face it, square sails are historically accurate, but are not the most efficient or visually appealing, Assassin's Creed Blackflag found a great balance in the sailing department) The weather cycles and new night sky are in the works, I am very excited about those, they will really help with an already immersive game. The story line could use a little work in order to ease the player into it sooner, but the journey of exploration is indeed a good one. The pirate captain bosses could be a little less random, I had trouble hunting down the last one.
Overall a stellar game, It runs (fairly) smoothly on most machines, the new menu system is great, and I am looking forward to using my controller with the new patch. If you don't feel like buying it now please keep an eye on it, Salt is riding the waves to something great.

Salt - A great time passing casual game, albeit lacking in a lot of areas (EA Review though)
This IS IN EARLY ACCESS, I KNOW. It's not done. Whatever. I recommend this game IF you are wanting to pass some time, maybe wait for Steam to download something else and not suck up bandwidth playing a game.
Tl;dR It's a great time waster if you're into exploration and open worlds and ships and stuff. Plus you can act like a pirate. Arr.
PROS:
- Relaxing! It's a really low stress game. My heart rate climbed above 30bpm only when there were pirates rushing at me with axes. I almost had a heart attack.
- Fun! It's actually pretty fun if you're into exploring and open worlds. The map (I believe) is endless, with random generated islands always coming up on the horizon at some point. You actually do get a small sense of discovery and it's just as intense as Capt. Picard discovering a new planet, or a cheap street walker discovering a new wart in her nether regions.
- Deep(ish/er than I thought it would be)  crafting system. If you don't look up recipes on a guide, it can be mildly entertaining to experiment on things! Also, it's a good way to pass time when sailing between islands, sail time can be long.
- Interesting loot. I actually found myself scouring islands mainly for better weapons and armor, and was surprised at the level of bonuses and whatnot that the devs have put in the game. I wasn't expecting passive skills on different stuff, and armor sets, it was unexpected and interesting trying to find all the pieces of a specific set. It's basically Skyrim on steroids but when i say that I mean after it grows lady lumps and stops and becomes a scrawny chicken man again. So no, it's not Skyrim but it's better than I thought.
- Interesting islands. Scouring for resources on islands and searching for pirate bases and especially traders and treasure hunter islands was a great time waster while I waited for Elder Scrolls Online to take 20 ♥♥♥♥ING HOURS TO DOWNLOAD.
CONS:
- Early access! It's buggy sometimes. It'll still have a ways to go. But it's entirely playable in it's current state so you can't knock it TOO much here. Unlike DayZ which is STILL BUGGY as HELL.
- Graphics. They aren't for everyone. Myself personally it doesn't bug me that they're pretty dated graphics, but to some people they'll be turned off.
- Repetition. Repetition. The game is basically the same thing over and over. Basically it's the same gameplay repeated. It's pretty much the same objectives repeatedly. You'll find yourself doing the same thing over and over. There isn't much variety in the gameplay, it kind of repeats itself a lot. HOWEVER. You WILL have a purpose generally, especially if you're trying to follow the questline, or collect supplies for certain in-game items that are pretty impressive that require mass amounts of supplies to inherit...almost kind of a spoiler what you can find, so i won't ruin it. It was cool discovering one for the first time.
- Pirate AI - Garbage. Might change with early access, but the AI is heinously bad.
Overall, Salt basically boils down to one word. Mild. The game is mildly entertaining, mildly exciting, and mildly deeper than i thought it would be. It's great for playing to pass time while waiting for another longer download if you don't wanna use bandwidth and for just passing the time exploring.

Story:
In Sachen Story kann Crysis 1 nicht beindrucken, relativ schwache Entwicklung der Charaktere und stellenweise noch relativ klischee lastige Erzählweise, leider ist dies nichts neues mehr in der FPS Branche und ich vermisse gute Story-Driven spiele wie Bioshock Infinite. In Sachen Story kann dieses Spiel leider nur mit Charakterbindung punkten diese fallen einem schon relativ ans Herz und man vermisst jeden gestorbenen Kameraden.
Grafik:
Grafiktechnisch kann dieses Spiel selbst nach knapp 8 Jahren noch punkten. Die Grafik ist immer noch anschaulich und setzte seiner Zeit neue Maßstäbe in Sachen Detailreichtum und Grafikanforderungen für Spiele. Deshalb gebe ich hier auch volle Punktzahl. Bei meinen Reviews ist nämlich folgendes zu beachten: Ich achte auf Grafik für die damalige Zeit nicht für die jetzige! Ich hoffe ihr habt Verständnis dafür.
Gameplay:
In Sachen Gameplay muss ich ehrlich sagen ist Crysis 1 vor allem in den höheren Schwierigkeiten echt anspruchsvoll und man kann sogar echte Taktiken verwenden, da die KI relativ realistisch auf diverse Aktionen reagiert, mehr dazu im KI teil. An sich ist das Gameplay realtiv gut, jedoch hätte stealth noch besser umgesetzt werden können und ich vermisse Verbesserungen im Nano-Suit. An sich sticht es trotzdem aus anderen Branchen Konkurrenten heraus.
KI:
Die KI ist eine der besten die ich bis heute in einem Spiel gesehen habe. Auf diverse aktionen wie plötzliches Auftauchen reagieren die Gegner meist relativ realistisch mit Erschrecken oder Starrstehen. Sie wundern sich zudem oft über die stellenweise „übernatürlichen“ Kräfte die man hat und versuchen nicht blind auf einen zuzustürmen und versuchen in  Deckung zu gehen. Zudem zielen diese gut und treffen gut.
UI:
Das UI ist schlicht gehalten und hat ein immersives feeling, da komplett Voice-Acted. Mit neuen VR Headsets kann man sich dann vielleicht wirklich wie im Nanosuit fühlen.

First off: For those of you who are going to say "quit whining you baby! It was a free upgrade! Be grateful!" Don't. That is ,frankly, a flimsy argument. I shouldn't be grateful for a shoddy port. I've paid good money for the original game. Millions have. That should be enough for them to put their all into this remaster. They're also selling this port on the store as we speak alongside the original game for the uninitiated. Anytime you sell a game for money, it should be of the highest quality. This is not going into the artistic and historical significance of this game. How they owe it to game history to properly restore and preserve this work of art. It has been said. Let me begin.
Remaster Impressions:
The game has been decently overhauled. It's not overall dramatic but for the most part does look better. Although, jaringly, some areas of the game actually look flatter than the original. The blood, gun models, and portions of the environment lack that artistic and visual flare that was present in the original. They may be a higher resolution but the originals tend to look nicer because of they way they were rendered. (I also miss the low framerate physics. I always found interesting and just added to the atmosphere by how unsettling it was.) In conclusion, everything is higher quality and is a servicable remaster. However, something is off about it. It lacks a sort of spark or artistic flare that was present in the original game.
PC Port Impressions:
Pretty awful. Literally NO graphical options. NO gameplay customization options. It ran well on my system but I have a decent PC. I feel this remaster will exclude many because of the lack of preformance options. The ones with lesser PC's will not be able to customize this game to meet their specs. This game basically lacks everything that makes PC gaming unique from consoles. Which is strange given the fact the orginal versions all have pretty good ports. Overall, its a pretty disappointing rerelease of a series that deserves so much better.
Closing:
I shouldn't expect more from the pathetic game industry but I can't help but do. These games are landmarks and are a critical part of game history. If they wont do it than we at least owe it to these games to push back and not swallow whats thrown at us. I want remasters of games such as these to be treated with more respect. This should be about preserving the history of the medium, not a rushed cash-in on an opportunity to sell the same game again. This remaster is much better than others but better doesn't mean ideal. The trend has already started but it's up to us to push back against something when it feels inadequate.

I LOVED Assassin's Creed 4, it is absolutely one of my favorite gaming experiences of all time.
I hadn't played an Assassin's Creed game since the original one came out on consoles back in 2007. That was a fun game at the time. It had surprised me because the gameplay was easily accessible and it had a unique concept and setting. I never got back into the series after that since for one, I didn't think the Renaissance setting would be as interesting, but after the success of Assassin's Creed 2 they beat it to death. Also, the original Assassin's Creed was cool in that it gave you a lot to do outside of the main story, but had no tangible rewards for any of it, making the side activities pointless.
So picking up Assassin's Creed 4 was the first time I had bought an Assassin's Creed game since the original. The thing that tipped me over the edge? Pirates.
I love Pirates. See my review of Sid Meier's Pirates for more proof of that.
I think that high seas piracy is a perfect setting for video games in general, but for whatever reason, very few games have tried this setting, and only a couple games have managed to do it well. Assassin's Creed IV is one of those games. It's like the pirate game I've always wanted but never knew it.
So overall, the gist is that you start off as a crewmember on a pirate ship. After being wrecked in a storm, you end up stranded on a Caribbean island, then murdering and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tting your way onto a merchant ship bound for Havana. In Havana, you learn some of the basic controls of the game and get an introduction to the main story before the Big Bad throws you in jail. You break out of jail and steal your own ship with your own pirate crew, and then BAM! you're a real Caribbean pirate and the game opens up, with an open world to explore, items to collect, missions to complete, etc.
You notice how I haven't mentioned anything about Assassins yet?
That's the thing about this game, although the plot and gameplay on land is still reminiscent of the Assassin's Creed series, where the game really shines is where it focuses on the piratical aspects of the experience. Not that I disliked the Assassin stuff. I really did feel powerful and stealthy when utilizing the skills the game gave me to perform assassinations. But they pale in comparison to the feeling you get when you're exploring the seas as a pirate.
I tend to do shorter, to the point reviews so I feel like if I keep going about this it's going to run really long, but there's a lot of stuff this game does right that I want to touch on.
One thing, is that the soundtrack is amazing. The ambient music that plays on land and at sea tends to fit the tone just perfectly. Also, while you're at sea on your ship, your crew will regularly engage in sea shanties. That is traditional working songs sung by sailors while on ship. It's a small but wonderfully atmospheric touch to the game, adding a level of immersion that I wasn't expecting to the experience.
The graphics are utterly beautiful as well, although I wonder how much of that is due to the setting. The game is lucky enough to benefit from the lush tropical islands populating the colonial Caribbean sea as it's backdrop. But in addition to that, this game has some of the best looking water and water physics I've ever seen in a game. In fact, I often wondered how it was possible for the game to accomodate all the intricacies of the ocean physics, as well as my crew and enemy ships in the middle of a battle. I'm impressed just from a technical standpoint. But amazingly it does work, and it works almost perfectly.
Also, you know how I mentioned that one of the problems I had with the original Assassin's Creed game was that it gave you a bunch of things to collect and explore, but nothing really came out of that collection and exploration? AC4 is slightly guilty of that (Animus Fragments) but for the most part the game is very good about there being a reason and a reward for collecting everything that you do and exploring as much of the game as possible.
I love games that encourage exploration, and Assassin's Creed 4 is definitely one of those.
Now that i've gushed a lot, I guess I'll talk about some of the faults.
First of all, like I've sort of already said, this is a great game, and one of the best pirate games ever, but it may not live up to what some people want out of an Assassin's Creed game. It just doesn't feel like an Assassin's Creed game most of the time. In fact, the final mission in particular, felt completely out of place from the rest of the game, as it focused on completely different skills and actions than everything else you'd been doing in the game.
The game also could benefit from cutting out the non-Animus parts entirely (if you've played an Assassin's Creed game you know what I'm talking about) they feel completely pointless and tacked on.
Also, although I enjoyed some of them, the underwater sections of the game were mostly frustrating and not fun.
As I mentioned before, although the game does a good job of actually having a reason for you to do the collecting and exploration, there were a few things that didn't go anywhere, the Animus Fragments being the biggest example, but also, I sorta expected there to be bigger rewards for collecting a large percentage of the collectibles, or for getting the entirety of a certain type of collectible. Also, I don't care about concept art, or multiplayer rewards, I want rewards that translate to things that I can actually use or interact with in the single-player game itself.
Also, the hideout at Inagua was a good idea, but is poorly executed. After you receive the hideout, and purchase the first 3 or 4 upgrades, there's really no reason to return there, or to continue upgrading it all. I was hoping there would be more customization and use to it, but there really wasn't. Also, you can collect several items and artifacts that are stored there, but that's really all that happens with them. You collect them, and then they just sit there in your hideout. It's disappointing.
Overall, this is one of my favorite experiences with a video game, ever, and in appreciation of it, I'm planning on giving more of the Assassin's Creed series a try. Despite the flaws, I think this would be a great game for everyone.
One final note though, the DLC is not worth it. Do not buy.

Alright, while looking through the reviews, I've come to the conclusion that people were expecting the game to be too similar to Alpha Centauri, and are comparing this game to that one.  Let it be known that if you are a true Civ fan that has been playing Civ V for months, and was really looking forward to this one, then you will enjoy this game.  If you are somone who had put maybe 50 or so hours into the previous Civ's, and were wanting to buy this game just to say you did, then you will be disappointed.
PROS
TechWeb- the techweb is something new to Civ titles. In the previous Civ games, the tech tree went left to right, with all the players picking up about the same techs, at about the same time, depending on your science output per turn.  This resulting in EVERYONE getting the same units, wonders, and buildings.  In Civilization Beyond Earth, the technology is all new.  We don't know where the future will take us in terms of tech, where as in previous Civs, we were just repeating history.  With the new techweb, every game, each sponsor (what "civilizations" are called in Civ: BE) could possibly all have different techs. This becomes even more so when many of their techs are chosen because of their affinity - also new to the game. I will go into affinity in more detail, but basically it is your ideaology, and by picking one of them and pursuing it through tech, you will unlock special bonuses, buildings, and units that other ideaologies wouldn't allow you to get. This is very interesting, because many of the technologies that boost your affinity, also unlock wonders.  This makes getting wonders, even on higher difficulties, way easier. You have to choose your techs wisely however, because you will NOT get every tech by the time the game ends, it's just impossible. You'll be lucky to get 3/4's of the entire techweb unlocked. With this new techweb, every single game you play, you will have different techs. I have completed 2 games and still have not been able to fully explore the tech tree.
Affinity- Like I said, your affinity is your ideology - it's what your people belive in for this new world you now live on.  There are some similarities between each - all 3 have a specific vitory you can accomplish, each have a different end game ultra unit, and each use a specific resource to build their specific untis and buildings. There are three affinities in total, each with entirely different looks on the world, bonuses, and units that come with it...
HARMONY- these people believe that this new planet is a beutiful place, and they dont want to repeat the mistakes they made on Earth here. They want to live with the aliens and wildlife, which is represented through their abilities and units.  With a high enough level of affinity, you can heal in miasma - an otherwise poisonous gas. You can attract seige worms to enemy cities through the enhanced spying system. Many of their units encorporate alien life, an example being the xeno swams, which are a combo of human military and many alien melee units. These are only a few of the many bonuses that can be unlocked. This affinity uses Xenomass to build their specific units and buildings.
PURITY- these people think that humanity is perfect where it is, and they dont really care if a few aliens have to die to keep it that way. These civs want the human race to be the dominating race of the planet. They can deploy a dirty bomb in an enemy city, also through the spying system. They can build massive and deadly tanks to fight their foes, and they also really like the color red, which, I guess the the color for the dominating or suppresive factions of most games. Oh, and this affinity can deploy orbital units for a longer time if you have a high enough level, along with other things. This affinity uses Floatstone as its resource to build specific untis and buildings.
SUPREMACY- these people also dont really care about the aliens. But instead of wanting to keep the human race the same, they want to advance it through technology. Many of the supremecy techs are related to robotics or biotic enchancements. Many of their units are high tech and very deadly. This affinity uses Fireaxite as its resource to build specific units and buildings.
All affinities change the look of your characters, cities, and units as the game progresses and your affinity levels. Its really interesting to see how the differnet looks of the Ais changes based on their affinity type.
Virtues- they are essentially your social policies from Civ V. There are 4 virtue types - Might, Prosperity, Knowlede, and Industry. Might mainly improves your army, Prosperity mainly improves your growth, Knowledge mainly improves your science, and Industry mainly improves your production. Unlike Civ V, it does not take culture to unlock the virtue like it did the social policy, and there are 15 choices under each virtue, making 60 virtues in all.  By the end of the game, if your really cranking out culture, you should be able to unlock about 20 or so, give or take a few. The virtues are separated into 3 tiers going verically, Every 5 vitues unlocked in a single one of the categories gives you a bonus related to the category. For example the first five unlocked in knowledge gives you a bonus of 10% culture in each city. Along with the vertical bonuses, you also can unlock horizontal bonuses, from unlocking certain amounts of virtues in total.  For example, I think after you unlock 6 tier one virtues of any category, you recive a bonus of one free virtue, and so on.  The bonuses get relativlely better as you advance into the tier 2 and 3 virtues, although some are deffinatly better then others.
Espionage- Espionage has been greatly improved from Civ V. There are many different things you can do with your spys including stealing energy/science, staging a coup, and bribing units into your empire.  There is also a special action your spy can do for each affinity. The more spy operations done in a city increase its intrigue. The max intrigue is 5, and the better more intersting options take more intrigue to do.
Trading- Just like Civ V, trading is important. Whether it be internal trade routes, that improve food and production, or external trade that improves science and energy, they're all important. Instead of having a civiliaztion wide limit on the number of trade routes, like in Civ V, you now get a base of 2 trade routes per city you own. This number can be improved through many building upgrades. One thing I wish they had done was change the font to a more bright color for "Previous Route" because it blends in extremely well with the rest of the text, and Ive found myself taking sometimes a few minutes to figure out where I last sent a convoy or trade ship.
Quests- This game offers quests throughout the game, that act as a tutorial for new players, and help you prgress to a victory. Some of the quests are triggered from things that you do, and others are random.  Some quests may ask to kill some aliens, take out a nest, contruct a building, or destroy a station (basically a citystate) for either a reward of some sort or to progress your affinity.
Stating Sponors/Options- Although alot of people are giving the game slack for thinking that there are only 8 Sponors in the game, there are way more. Your starter Sponsor is selected based on the sponor you choose(8), the colonists you bring(5), the cargo you bring(5), and the spaceship you use(5). Because of this, technically there are 1000 different settings you may have for your nation.
OTHER PROS
-Workshop Support
-Music
-Graphics
-Orbital Units
CONS
User Interface- This is funky, especially for new players. Techweb can get confusing, and the affinity/virtue aspect can catch newcomers off-gaurd. There needs to be a popup that tells you what you have just finished producing in a city. Also, an end game stats menu would be helpful.
Wonders- pretty boring and non-interesting.

Civilization: Beyond Earth is not a brand new entry in the franchise. It is a rehash of Civilization V's core mechanics with a space-themed reskin and a few tweaks to existing systems. This is a disappointment since previous installments always were significant departures from the previous iteration; by comparison, Beyond Earth feels more like an expansion pack. An expensive one, too, at $50.
Nevertheless, some of the tweaks are interesting. The tech web, and the associated affinity system, give you an amazing degree of freedom in tailoring your colony to your needs and resources. Similarly, there are several different paths you can take with virtues (i.e. policies), such as a broad approach that yields generic bonuses or a specialized one that focuses your colony's efforts towards a particular goal.
However, many other changes are for the worse. Several ways of interacting with your rivals that were present in Civilization V have been removed: no more World Congress, no more Tourism, no more religion, no more vying for city-states' favor... This wouldn't be a big deal if the AI was intelligent and if diplomacy built meaningful relationships: but the AI still spams cities and will never, ever give you a deal that is fair, more often than not contacting you to see if it can get some free energy or science from you with vague promises to repay you later. Trading actual resources for the new "favors", which sounds nice in theory, is just another step to obscure the fact that the AI is trying to shaft you.
The victory conditions have been dumbed down as well due to the removal of the above-mentioned interactions. Aside from Domination, the four other types of victories are all variations of "research tech X, build wonder Y, wait a few turns". Does the AI react to you nearing a victory though? Absolutely not.
And then there are the long-standing problems with the Civ V engine that are still present -- such as the weak diplomacy described above. End of turn unit animation bug? Still in. Random sounds looping or playing over each other? Yup.
All in all, an experiment that can be most flatteringly described as "somewhat interesting". But if you've played your fill of Civilization V already, Beyond Earth is superfluous. I can only recommend it to people who've never played Civilization V and for whom the sci-fi setting sounds particularly attractive.

If you are a fan of strategy games, pick it up, it's fun to play and they did a good job of capturing the sci-fi feel of Alpha Centuari mixed with the better parts of Civ 5. If you are looking at this game as the latest in the franchise, beware.
Sadly the game is a poor entry into the franchise as it stands. The visuals are there, though the maps are often cluttered and too often "alien terrain" is a synonym for "eye-bleeding purple" or "deep-depression brown". The units are few, very few, and often go from woefully underpowered to laughingly overpowered with a single tech.
What makes the game truly underwhelming is the polish. Wonders have no description, nothing in the tech tree marking them as special, and have all the "wonder" of an overdue library book. Buildings are strangely named and poorly described, with each having a "quest" upon completion, a forced RPG like contrivance.
In the polish catergory comes the worst embarrasment: the writing. The quotations are bad. Most of them make little sense and bear no relevance to the tech or building to which they're attached. The voice actor they hired for the English version is equally bad, reading the quotations with a mix of childish pronunciation and undeserved vigour. To fall from the great heights of Civ 5's grand narrator to this street-corner huckster is one of Beyond Earth's worst offences.
In summary, this is a decent game. For $50, you could do an awful lot worse. Had it been released as simply "Beyond Earth" it would recieve my ringing endorsement. As a "Sid Meier's Civilization" game however, it has much to improve upon, and much to apologize for.

After 25 hours playing Beyond Earth, I have to cautiously say that if you haven't purchased Beyond Earth yet, wait. Wait for a sale, wait for possible DLC or expansions.
There's simply not enough content, not enough diversity, to keep me engaged. Without a wider variety of content, most games feel the same, and aside from the early turns, each progresses in the same way. The sponsors (civilizations) differ from one another in only the most minimal way, and other pre-game choices are just as drab. Some of the hype surrounding Beyond Earth touted the number of different ways you could set up your nation before the start of the match, but in practice these choices only have a minimal effect, and one that fades into near-meaninglessness.
This trend, of blandness and shallow choices, permeates the entire game. The list of veterancy promotions for units has been gutted to two: an instant heal and a minor power increase, which is a very boring let down. Wonders offer resource bonuses much like regular buildings, lacking the character and unique abilities seen in the Civilization games, and without the beautiful art and fanfare we used to get. Speaking of fanfare, the victory and defeat screens are also minimalist, and don't offer you any post-game information or statistics. Instead, you are offered the choice of quitting to the main menu or (if victorious) continueing to play. That's extremely anti-climatic. Even Alpha Centauri, if memory serves, offered a turn-by turn territory map so you could watch how the various civilizations grew and shrank.
The tech tree's organization, an interesting departure from tradition, suffers because the icons displayed lack adequate differentiation in shape or colour. Not only does this make the tech screen somewhat ugly, it also leads to needless tech-by-tech searching to find out which technology unlocks the specific unit, building, wonder, or ability you are looking for. That's information you should be able to find at a glance.
Map presets and custom options are both sparse, and even with the preorder DLC they pale in comparison to previous games. You are unlikely to be presented with any novel maps, which is a shame, especially with the new map features (canyons, miasma) that could be used to really spice things up.
The list of available units is slim. Yes, you are presented with options to customize them based on your chosen psuedo-ideology,  but far too many of these choices are dry percentage increases, and they don't alleviate the damning lack of variety. You get one air unit, two navel units, and a scant handful of melee and ranged land units.
Quests are a neat new addition, but again the interesting aspects are mired down by the majority of "quests" prompting you to choose between one of two options.
The trade system, while manditory, is boring and cannot be automated, meaning that by late-game, you're reassigning one or more trade units to its route almost every turn. By late game, on a larger map, you're spending too much time micro-managing trade routes, the interface for which has NO meaningful filtration options, nor does it adequately highlight the route the unit was previously assigned to.
And there is one things that really really gets me, despite being a seemingly trivial issue: there is either a hidden "Time" victory condition or a bug with disabling the Max Turns option, meaning that games end for me after a set number of turns, with victory going to the player currently leading. That's the absolute least satisfying way to win a match, and an extremely frustrating sucker-punch of a loss. The first time it happenedto me, I was dumbstruck. I didn't know it would occur, and it made me feel like the hours I had sunk into that game were meaningless, wasted. And that was a match I "won."
In the end, what is new in Beyond Earth fails to make up for in what has been removed, in either depth or width, and it is disconcerting that the game fails to match the content of Alpha Centauri. There is simply too much missing (great people, the religion system, veterency upgrades, wonders/civilizations/units/maps that look, feel, and play uniquely, and satisfying victories). Consider this along side the overall lack of character (bland... everything) and annoying interface (tech tree, trade routes--Both of which are addressed in various mods, which tells you something), and the game just feels rushed.
I hope we see some heavy content additions, which I believe can salvage the game and give us a reason to come back to it. Until then, wait for a significant price-drop.

It's really hard to talk about this game. I've finally beaten Final Fantasy XIII and the first thing that comes to mind is, it really is a unique experience. So, is it good? Well, I can't say I liked it, but I can see why others would enjoy it or even love it. That's why you'll find so many different opinions about this game. I'm not recommending it because buying it is a risky move anyway. But let me tell you, if you think you're going to like it, you probably will, so go ahead and buy it if that's the case.
I can't say anything that hasn't already been said. The game is extremely linear. No excuses. The problem isn't that you go from point A to point B and you can't do side quests or something else, that's something to be expected in some RPGs to be honest. But here, it's not just side quests that you can't do. You can't do anything. 90% of the game is a hallway. You can't find hidden stuff. You can't pick a different path to get to point B. You can't even *talk* to NPCs (well, you can, but you just have to stand in front of them and that's it). The interaction with the environment does not exist. I honestly can't feel attached to a world that seems to be static and unalterable. But of course, maybe you don't mind playing a game like this.
Once you get to Gran Pulse you are allowed to do a bunch of sidequests, mount chocobos and find treasures, yes, but that doesn't change the fact that the worlds feels... dead. You can't do much, you still can't explore and meet people, explore towns, or at least know a bit more about the main characters. It doesn't feel like an open world game just because you're free to move around.
The story is rather confusing, but that doesn't mean it's bad (especially if that's the kind of stuff you like). And I hope you like it because it's the most important thing that this game has to offer, and if you don't, you're screwed. Same with the main characters, they play a big role in the game, and they're not your typical heroes. Instead, they seem to be taken straight from a shonen anime, with extremely pronounced personalities. That's been done before (remember Palom and Porom? Locke? Zidane?) so keep that in mind.
I think this Final Fantasy has a way better battle system than the previous ones, and most people seem to agree. It's dynamic and relatively fast-paced, and probably my favorite aspect of this game. But since you don't have much to do in the game, you're going to see it a lot.
In short, you have to like the story, the style, and maybe the battle system. That's pretty much what Final Fantasy XIII is. An on-rails RPG with no interactivity, with a long story and lots of battles.

In Sachen Story kann Crysis 1 nicht beindrucken, relativ schwache Entwicklung der Charaktere und stellenweise noch relativ klischee lastige Erzählweise, leider ist dies nichts neues mehr in der FPS Branche und ich vermisse gute Story-Driven spiele wie Bioshock Infinite. Zudem zielen diese gut und treffen gut.
UI:

As another reviewer said, welcome to BADGER SIMULATOR 2013!
I recommend ignoring the hype and deciding what you are looking for in a game before trying.
Your enjoyment of Shelter will be largely influenced by what you look for in a game. If you go into Shelter looking for a fin traditional game then you may be disappointed. What Shelter offers in this department is non-traditional graphics, invisible walls, long corridors with little explorations, lite-survival and caretaking elements, some somewhat neat stealth take downs, and annoying birds of death. Oh, and bugs that will cause your badger children to die.
However, if you are looking for a game that also offeres a unique and harrowing experience that puts you in the shoes of motherhood in the animal wilds, trying to do whatever it takes as an omnivore in the middle of the food chain.
The graphics remind me of picture books from childhood, recalling tales and fables about animals and their children in their world, full of morals and whatnot. This may be bunk to others, but as an artist it drew me into the world and realitic//naturalistc grapics would have had a lesser effect on me.
The soundtrack itself is wonderful, blending into the game perfectly. I cannot say much about it specificly other than it filled the world just right, layering and never pulling me away.
The sound effects are good as they should be, the badgers yip and yap in communication, the predatory birds caws are terrifying when first heard, and other animals sounds serve as environmental clues. This is all as it should be.
So the real meat of this gaming experience comes to down to the scripted experiences you progress through. Your badger children age and grow as you take them through several environments, each containing various hazards such as darkness, fire, and flooding. You must constantly provide them food of either the vegetable of flesh variety.
If you are not the type of person looking to be placed in the role of protector, mother, leader, provider; if you don't find yourself becoming emotionally attached as you play games, then you may want to give Shelter a pass.
I am a white male gamer, age 32 and fall somewhere in the middle of attachment/unattachment. When my first two badger died to something in the darkness I was sad, but I expected it sooner or later. They were weak and scared. When my next child died in a flood it was upsetting but I still had two strong children to look out for. When one of them was taken by a large raptor because I took a wrong turn in some underground tunnels and came out the dangerous end, I was screaming at the top of my lungs at the computer screen.
This game go to me.

This game is awesome. It's very addictive and made me think i'm cryptofarmer or something. Game has interesting economy model which is its main force. Crop's prices changes dependent on amounts of wheat you sell to the market. It forces player to sow different types of crops. There are also timed special demands wchich allows you to sell your crops at double price. You shouldn't have to much equipment at the begining because the maintenance of machines, building, ground, living stock cost you specific amount of money everyday. Hiring workers (bots) to do the most boring job is great solution and prolongs the time of having fun but their work costs money (which is good). Manipluating the flow of time is very usefull tool, especially when you have nothing to do but to wait for crops to grow.
But it has also some negatives. The most annoying of all is the traffic AI (or no AI). They travel at 30 kph no matter what they do which forces you to overtake them constantly. They stop centimeters from the obstacle which often blocked my workers when they were trying to make turn at the end of the field. It's good idea to block the road with some old trailers or something. They enforce turn priority just like as i wasn't there which causes frequent accidents.  They are concrete, solid objects and hitting them is harder than hitting a bunker wall. I can hit them by truck with 60 tons of cargo at 90 kph which causes my truck to do bizzare things and doesn't affect them any way. When they hit me at crossroad once (i had the priority as the car was turning left and i was going straight), my truck flew dozen meters aside and the car which hit me was like: "nah, i don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;. Is there any possibility to turn off the traffic?
When my workers works in the field at night i barely can see them as when they use lights they doesn't illuminate anything, the same goes with the traffic, it's quite easy to hit other cars at night, especially when using outside camera.
Edited: I forgot to mention that breeding of cows, chickens and sheeps is very complex and i was impressed how many aspects of that were put into game.

This one is one of my 3 fav series in franchise with Assassin's Creed II and Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood
Pros:
-fighting system (started from AC3)
-no more complicated crafting windows
-Grand Theft Boat (except you only stay on your own ship)
-charismatic main hero
-Kenway's fleet (you send your fleet on missions and they bring you stuff)
-interesting main story, sequences quite differ from each other by mood, locations and by things you do, unlike in AC1/AC3 (where you basically hunt each templar per sequence)
-THANK GOD no more "wanted" system (on lands), that means no more killing witnesses, bribing heralds and removing poster every 3 minutes
-awesome "wanted" system on the sea: kill boats -> kill bigger boats (bigger rewards) -> kill even bigger boats (even bigger rewards), and when you've had enough, turn off pirate hunters by bribing dudes on the lands
-a lot of upgrades for Edward and Jackdaw, but sometimes they require you to find special recipes
-soundtracks (personally I love all assassin's creed games soundtracks)
Cons for all AC game:
-overstretched gameplay by missions where:
-you have to quietely follow dudes
-you have to take a f***ing walk with NPCs
-viewpoints (srsly I hate them, I usually try to visit ALL viewpoints in the beginning of the game)
Cons specifically for ACBF:
-bad optimisation (srsly, system req says: Nvidia GeForce GTX 470, mine's is a twice of efficient and still 40 fps in big places (cities, jungles etc)), but even worse has AC: Unity
-no more Desmond's Adventures :/, starting from Black Flag the present day scenes go worse and worse :(
Multiplayer (I really suck at it, so I don't want to judge it):
-that's a VERY different expirience: no more waiting around, you mostly have like 1 minute to live
-custom game modes, where you can fully customize session rules, and by fully I mean really fully (e.g make a game where only rifles are allowed)
I suggest you buy console version, or this one if you have latest gen graphic card for 60+ fps performance

Apart from some obvious flaws, this is a nice addition to the Hitman franchise.
I'm just going to say right off the bat that this is a pretty fun Hitman game. As a franchise it should have died with the very first Hitman game. While the original game had fans, I have to say it is one of the worst games I have played. The premise is not particularly interesting. Subsequent Hitman games have improved a great deal on the original but have always had shortcomings, for example, the second Hitman game had some really bad AI bugs which meant that you could quetly walk behind someone who is asking for for ID and politely strangle them. Some of the levels were tedious or pointless etc. So when considering this Hitman game, it is no different.
There are some really interesting ideas in this game that could have been so great but were poorly implemented. For example, hand to hand combat is basically the same 2 animations repeated over and over. this is especially odd considering the H2H was put on display in one particular level that has you in a bar room brawl. It is obvious that 47 is proficient in Karate but the moves on display quickly become a bore. It is also difficult to randomly engage an enemy in H2H. I don't expect it to be on par with Batman: AC but a little effort in this area could have gone a long way.
The other interesting but badly implemented idea is the focus skill. It is basically a rip off from Max Payne with a slight difference, the game almost pauses and you can pick your targets, ready for execution, then push a button and 47 will quickly dispatch a large number of foes. This skill is also put on show in another level that has you doing target practice. However this skill lacks the flare and showmanship of Max Payne, making this "skill" feel more like a cheat. It takes the enjoyment out of dispatching enemies, especially on the PC where aiming is done with precision on the mouse.
Aside from these issues I found the game enjoyable. The story was a little strange though. 47 seems conflicted about being a hitman, but his pysche doesn't lend itself to those feelings. He isn't haunted by the people he has killed, he also has no moral qualms about killing a friend, because those are his orders after all. Aside from this though, the story is logical, believeable and simple. 47's journey to the end of the game is also highly varied. *spoiler* I absolutely loved the corn field level.
Depending on how you play the game, 47's brutality is on show, a ruthless and lethal killer who is pretty much untouchable.
Graphics: Superb use of the Unreal engine with some nice tweaks like tessalation which brings a new level of realness to 47's dome.
Sound: Atmospheric and functional.
Overall I would say it is worth the asking price, but as with all Hitman games, expect flaws.

Day 32. It's been about a week since the cold started and it's snowing every day. My people started fighting during guard shifts during the night and it has started taking its toll on both their mental and physical well-being. And the cold doesn't help. People are wounded and sick and I'm badly in need of meds.
Of the few locations around my safehouse that aren't blocked because of the weather, an old school that was shelled. Rumors say they have a lot of meds, but that it may be dangerous. I decide to send my best scavenger out armed only with a crowbar.
Arriving at the location, it's heavily guarded by militia. One guy approaches me and wants to trade, he has some meds, but I have little and left it all at the house anyway. He tells me we can't trade, but that I can't enter...
The hell I can't! My people need those meds!
While he's waiting for me to change my mind at the door, I sneak past him and his friends through an unguarded floor above. As I silently go deeper inside the school, I finally find some medication and some bandages. Minutes later, after a few close calls short of being discovered, I see a locked cabinet down the hall. Using the only item I brought with me, my trusty crowbar, I break it open. What do I find? About a ton of tobacco and some ammo!
I sneak my way out the way I came, and back at the entrance, that guy is still asking me if I want to trade. The meds I found aren't going to cut it, so I offer him the ammo and the tobacco I stole from him earlier against some more meds and some sugar. He accepts, not knowing I'm actually selling him his own stuff, what a fool!
I run back home, patch everyone up, and we all have a good laugh about the incident around a few glasses of moonshine we made from the sugar we just made ours.

The game is unfinished and lower quality than im used to from firaxis. It has lots of balance issues, its not the 'new' Alpha Centauri that a lot of people were waiting for and the overall production quality is lower than other Firaxis games.
If the high traderoute yields are intentional, you would think that they had the whole game balanced around it. But if you build all traderoutes quickly, you will run into the same problem over and over again: nothing to build, no way to fail.
this makes it pretty clear that the game wasnt even balanced around this high yield, but rather it wasnt balanced at all. The high yields from traderoutes trivialize everything, from city placement to wonders to buildings. On top of that they are a chore to manage, they already were in Civ5, and now they gave you 10x more of 'em.
Take the wonders: Some are ok, but half of them are worse than NORMAL BUIDINGS (for their cost). It looks more like they are placeholders and werent even looked at before the game went live. Same with buildings, the scaling for bigger cities is completely off because they dont offer force multipliers like in Civ5. they didnt add a new take on the Civ formula, they just shuffeled everything around at random, and it doesnt work.
They basically need to massively overhaul everything from the ground up if they rework traderoutes..are they even intending to invest this much ressources into the game at this point? Because they certainly didnt invest enough pre-release.
I am pretty positive that noone of the BNW team worked on this, at least non of the game designers. And dont forget that the writing, voice acting, leaders etc. are all a huge step down from civ5 or even SMAC as well, if you watch AngryJoes Review of the game you can clearly see how bad the production value is compared to Civ5 when he shows the comparison to Civ5 Leaders.
All in all, this looks like a cashgrab from Firaxis to me, its not on par with what i am used to from them in any way shape or form, the production value is very low compared to their other games, certainly not a fullprice title but rather a mod.

This game is actually kinda neat for a blocky shooter. I've played Ace of Spades, which at times may have had some issues, dependant on the kinds of players you played with (Which now is utterly broken with the DLC classes.)
But this is Blockstorm, not Ace of Spades. It's very similar in the general idea, but it's still its own game. Blockstorm is your typical CoDdy-style Insta-ADS shooter, yes. Though one thing I love about it the most is the fact you can create your own models through little voxel cubes. It's chunky looking, but it's just small enough to make enough as a simple design and slap it on the workshop, or keep to yourself. This doesn't just stick to playermodels either, you can make two NPCs, vehicles, weaponry, and whole maps. If you don't feel like making it yourself, you can just go onto the workshop and see if you find something you like.
The only complaint I have is the movement speed. With alot of CoDdy insta-ADS FPS games, you're gonna run at the pace of a snail. What's worse is this game throws in a "Weight system" based on your loadout. Heavier weapons means slower movement. So, I was pretty easy to kill when I started playing my first round. I've been too used to Quake and Doom to get used to slow speeds. But when you get used to it, it's manageable in the least.
Overall, I'd recommend this game.
Just beware, you may come across salty players that will claim hacks or insult you. But y'know, what game doesn't have that these days?

Technical issues on release aside, I'll try to assess the game ignoring those for now:
Seems like they decided to go with a new ftp model and plan to release new cards in the future as DLCs for this game. No more annual stuff like 2013-2015. This game goes for the Hearthstone ftp model. It uses gold as currency to buy booster packs. You get gold by playing the game and doing quests. You can buy gold by spending cash. Simple enough.
PROS
- This one has free deck building! No more preset decks like in 2013/2014. There's a deck wizard to help new players build decks too, so they don't get overwhelmed (I recommend eventually going away from it though, as sometimes it recommends really bad cards for your deck). Ofc the card selection is limited to Origins set (around 250 cards?) for now.
- They put 2 headed giant mode back in the game
- Daily quests for bonus gold (20-60g range)
- Pretty neat tutorial and campaign with stories. Completing them gives you a decent amount of gold to start off.
CONS
- Normal battles and 2HG are currrently the only modes in the game
- The UI is a bit buggy, sometimes makes you select wrong targets by overlapping cards, etc
- The game requires constant Internet connection to save your progress and earn gold. This means that if the servers are down, there's no point playing, pretty much. This is because of the new ftp model.
- For some reason they removed any kind of chat option from the game. in 1v1 it doesn't matter too much since it's like Hearthstone. In 2HG it's a bit awkward since it's 2v2 co-op. If you don't play with friends and talk on skype or some other chat you can't really plan much...
- Playing 2HG doesn't give gold. You can't do quests and achievements in this mode either.
NEUTRAL
- There is a gold cap you can earn every day. Currently 400g (1 booster pack costs 150). For me as a casual player it doesn't matter too much since I can't grind 24/7. For ppl with more free time it might be restricting.
- The whole Origins set revolves around Planeswalker cards. These cards are quite gamechanging. My worry is that it would limit the variety of deck building, since most effective way is having the ones built around planeswalkers. Top "meta" will be set and the game's gonna get dull. This could be fixed by having an option to ban the planeswalker cards in your matches or future DLC cards sets.
If you liked the previous MtG games this one's pretty much your top choice, esp if you like free deck building. And since they don't plan to release more games and build on this one instead... Might aswell stick to it. Hopefully they will fix the bugs and consider adding more modes and options later on. It feels a bit barebones for now.

For those that want to know what I think about this game in one sentence before I get into detail, let me help you with this next one. Riders of Icarus-a beautifully crafted MMO world paired with fantastic gameplay and one ruined by the worst optimization I have ever seen in a game powered by the Cryengine.
Now for more detail. I have never seen a world in an MMO look so lifelike and attractive and lively than this one, and that is due to the game using the Cryengine. The colors are rich, the animations tastefully artistic. The gameplay is simple and to the point, and the art style feels like playing a movie. The characters are very beautifully done, and the animations are spot on right down to character physics without being over sexualized. The mount system is spectacular, allowing you to tame wildlife that makes sense to be able to be tamed with ease, being very intuitive to do so without making it too easy and still with the chance to fail, while allowing you the ability to attempt taming that possible mount all over again should you fail without any need to wait. I have not seen the common pay-to-win aspects most are saying that are in the game here that Nexon is well known for. The community seems to be very pleasant and helpful. I even got a solid mount for free from Alienware Arena with a Steam Key that the devs put out through them. As a big MMO gamer, this seems like everything you'd want in a game if you've got the hardware to support it.
However, it is far from that. This game is quite literally the best example of the worst optimization for a game using Crytek's Cryengine, and is a contender for the worst optimized game I have played PERIOD. With my Dell gaming laptop, on the highest graphical settings, I am running at 60+ FPS. In certain areas where the MAIN QUESTLINE TAKES YOU, I could be running at my normal framerate one second and suddenly dropping off to the low twenties in another, then going up to  my norm again, only to tank again a few minutes later, and this rinses and repeats until I exit the game regardless if I lower graphics settings. I thought it was due to the fact that it was a croweded area, having a lot of plants and enemy NPCs in the area and that I left Google Chrome open with a number of tabs in the background, so I went and closed Chrome. Once I went back to the game, the drops in FPS WORSENED to the teens. This is NOT what I want to have in any MMO, and I'll even list my specs here. This laptop right now has a 1TB hard drive that is a hybrid having 8GB NAND cache memory in it. It's got 8GB DDR4 RAM. I have an NVIDIA GeForce 1050 in this thing with 4GB dedicated VRAM, and my CPU is a quad-core Intel Core i5-7300HQ clocking at 2.5GHz and I am running Windows 10. This laptop is well within the recommended specs, so it's not a lack of having the needed hardware, so what's up Nexon? (EDIT: I forgot to mention the storyline. By choice. It lacks consistency, and where I am in the game, never actually explains what happened to lead to the game or what anything in it actually means. It's like they cobbled together this great idea, forgot a story, so pulled together random ideas, glued them together, and called it good a few days before the publishing deadline. While it works with the concept behind the game, it doesn't explain the taming aspect of the game, barely explains the combat mechanics and the flying mount mechanics, explains a way to get on a mount that doesn't even work in the actual game [it assumes the mount is already present, which it never is as you have to physically call it], and leaves you confused as to why the princess you're trying to save even was captured and what kingdom you are a soldier for and where the hell the Dragon Guard is from, as they're not even affiliated to you in any way, yet are. There's no consistency, and feels like it's just cobbled together at the last minute and barely had enough time to put sosme graphical sequences to it or decided to use some scrapped CGI for them and animate the mouths and record a quick-but-brief voiceover for the characters to make it feel like time was put into it.)
Overall, the game is a beautifully well crafted game with a masterpiece for the world in which it's set. But unless you enjoy losing almost 50 FPS every few minutes once you enter a forest inhabited by killer plants and fairies, steer clear of this one for now.
EDIT: As people obviously do not know how to read or use Google, I'll edit this to clarify here. The rate of power that my CPU might be working at might be lower then the specs state, but it's also a Kaby Lake processor, meaning that they're designed to operate as efficiently as the previous gneration while requiring less power with the new architecture on which they're built in order to lower the temperature of the CPU under heavy workload. As a result that shouldn't have the affect I'm having in this game on framerate alone. I'm not saying that's not playing ANY reason into this, what I'm saying is that it's not the ONLY reason it's happening and you and I both know better, assuming you even know how the Kaby Lakes are designed like myself. I'm not saying that my processor's the best in the world; but considering it's in an $800 budget gaming laptop from Dell, it's a solid one and rates right up with the other quad-cores that ARE at the proper power outputs.
What's happening here, and this is confirmed with the thread I added on the game's Steam page from other players (no dev response yet though) is that the game is just horribly optimized, NOT an issue with my CPU, which DOES overclock to about 3.1GHz when needed.

Magic: The Gathering of Mistakes
A brief first impression: disappointing. For all the wrong reasons.
The Steam release for this game seems to have gone backwards from the iOS version. The tutorials/ skill quests are bugged, sometimes simply not giving the player the required cards to make any progress. Other times the tutorial is completable, but uninformative because the cards that are the focus of the lesson simply aren't on the board (this happened in the trample/ group blocking skill quest, where my opponent literally had no creatures).
These issues wouldn't be such a big deal if acess to the game proper didn't depend on going trough these missions. Most of them you can skip, but it feels like a bit of a waste to, considering that the quests reward you with coins for completing them. The initial 4 tutorials, however, you cannot skip and, if one of them is bugged, you need to quit out and start from the beginning again - and hope that all 4 go ahead smoothly. I had to restart 4 times in order to get through. Just awful.
The game also freezes pretty regularly, mostly after clicking "Okay" or "Don't Show Again" on the hints. Disabling hints reduces the frequency of the crashes, but it doesn't do away with them entirely. Sometimes they just happen for no apparent reason (such as after assigning combat damage, passing the turn, or selecting a card from your library). In a few games, the timer also got stuck on my opponent's main phase, so I had no choice but to quit. It wasn't an outright crash, but it was virtually the same thing.
Finally, server issues can cause your progress to not be saved, preventing you from making any progress in the game's story mode (or, presumably, any other mode). A disconnection here and there I can live with, but when you finally complete a fairly tedious story mission that has frozen on you twice, only to find that, at the end of it, your victory isn't even recorded by the game, and you have to do it yet again, it's incredibly frustrating.
I waited patiently for this game, and didn't even really have such high hopes for it. I played a friend's iOS version and found it satisfactory, so I assumed that an additional month of tuning would polish it up nicely for PC, and do away with some of the (minor) bugs I noticed on the iPad version. Sadly, this hasn't happened, and even my measured expectations have been disappointed. The bugs are far more abundant here, and the crashed are much more frequent. I also never lost connection with the server while playing on the iPad, so there's that too.
At its core, it seems like it could be a decent Magic game, and I can only imagine that it will grow better and better as new cards are released, and user feedback is incorporated (please, Wizards!). But, as it stands, the game is extremely disappointing. As the introductory levels are, presumably, supposed to entice new players, and excite newcomers and veterans alike, I find it pretty concerning that these elements feel so unpolished. The campaign is stale and repetitive. It freezes too frequently, and sometimes fails to save your progress. The awkward angled table view is still there, which is a bit of a pet peeve, but I know I'm not alone. Your first couple of boosters should be easy to get a hold of - boosters are what the game is ostensibly all about: deck customisation, and playing your own way. Instead, you have to slog through a buggy, uninteresting and, most importantly, unfun Story mode in order to get them. It feels like Wizards really dropped the ball on this one, but just decided to roll with it anyway.
tl;dr: If the game wasn't bugged out at every turn, it might be fun. I'd only recommend this one for diehard MtG fans, and even they might not have the stomach for it.

One of the best metroidvanias I've ever played. Unique artstyle, interesting world, great music and fun gameplay (the bosses especially are really well done). The game is massive, much larger than these types of games typically are.
The freedom to choose your path is something that sets it apart from most other games in the genre. In most metroidvanias you unlock a new item or ability and then use that to access the "next" area. In Hollow Knight you can explore the areas much more freely in the order you want. There's an area later in the game that you can access from 3 completely different paths through the use of different abilities.
Finishing the game doesn't even require entering all the areas or collecting all the abilities. All this freedom makes the game great for speedrunning. I'm usually not a fan of doing speedrun achievements in these games, but in Hollow Knight it was really enjoyable since the open-ended nature allows for many different strategies and routes to take. The speedrun was a lot more about planning and thinking than perfect execution.

Cryogenics is the deep freezing sleep technology from the video games DOOM 3 and Fallout 4 and the Alien movies with Sigorney Weaver.  You know the one. Cons:
- Most side events/missions happen off screen and have little impact
- Little to no character interaction, mostly inner-monologues unless theyre depressed
- Characters have little to no personality, only background is flavour text
- Combat cover mechanics are awful
- No manual or explanation of certain game mechanics (heating, addictions etc.)
Possible con

- Some minor bugs, safehouse doors will sometimes be unopenable, fires not raising temperature, teleporting through floors etc
I quite enjoyed the game and definitely got my moneys worth out of it but the lack of character personality really let the overall experience down. I'd recommend playing it all the same, though maybe wait till its on sale if youre not convinced.

I snuck into a house with only my knife.  I heard voices talking but didn't see what they said.  I went through a room on the bottom floor, but there was a hole in the roof, and someone with a gun spotted me through the hole.
"I'll kill you!"  The person went back and came down a ladder looking for me.  I hid myself in the shadows and waited.  They walked by my position, and I lept upon them without even thinking.  Not a chance they saw me coming...My character threw them onto the floor and stabbed them over and over until the person was dead.
More people heard the violence and came down the same ladder.  I couldn't hide again; it was them or me. I charged at the one that came down first, but she just pushed me away and ran past me.  She ran to the person I'd just killed.
"Boenza...No!  Boenza, I don't believe this...."  The female character keeps crying and saying the name Boenza.  She doesn't even acknowledge me.  I loot Boenza's body right in front of her; she doesn't try to stop me.
Another character, a male I believe, came into the room.  He was holding a rifle and could have dropped me right then.  He just looked at me and started shouting.
"Leave! Get out of here!"  I thought he would shoot me.  God knows I deserved it.
Sickened, I turned around and just walked out with the woman audibly crying over Boenza's body.  The man just watched me leave with nothing besides Boenza's gun.
Was Boenza their child?  Why had she yelled that she would kill me?  I guess she was trying to protect her parents; trying to be the hero we see in war far too often.  I didn't want to die, so I killed her with a knife, in what was probably her own home.  I tried to kill her mom, but she was tougher than me and just brushed me aside because trying to care for her daughter was more important.  I looted that girl's body in front of her mother because I needed the gun.
Then there's her father...He saw his wife crying over their dead daughter's body, and past them he saw me with my knife which would have still had blood on it.  He could have killed me with his rifle.  Most of you would have because this is a game, right?  He just shouted for me to leave over and over again.
They were better people than me, including Boenza; I wish Boenza had won our fight.

Having played a solid 40+ hours of this, I feel I can give a fairly straightforward review.
First of all, if you are a fan of Sid Meier's games, especially in the last several years, then you will likely find enjoyment with this. It feels like 75% Civ 5 and 25% Alpha Centauri. I played very little AC in the past, and don't remember a whole lot, but the spirit of that game is noticable in Beyond Earth.
Those familiar with Civ 5 will have no trouble getting started in BE, requiring low in-game-advisory assistance. At first the game feels somewhat like an expansion to Civ 5, but you slowly realize that it separates itself fairly quickly with the tech-web and some of the missions/quests.
It's a lot of fun for a Civ-junkie like myself, but I still question the $50 price tag. There doesn't seem to be much change in the Civ 5 game mechanics to warrant a $60, but also feels much more than a $30 expansion. It also feels incomplete. Not like there are bugs of any kind, most of the errors in the game are the same that exist in Civ 5 and they are pet-peeves that could be worked on to improve stream-lining the gameplay more than "bugs". I just feel that the game was designed with limited flair and depth to make way for future DLC. Looking at how expansions were handled in Civ 5, I can see all sorts of additions to BE such as playing non-humans or a reworking of some units and the tech-web itself.
One thing I have considered from trying to get a broader view of the variety of quests/missions that are unique to this game is the potential for a much deeper story, something that strays from the usual Sid Meier's style, a bit more reminiscent of Warcraft 3 in how that game introduced characters central to a campaign. Your units in BE improve as your affinity levels rise, giving you some customization and beefing up their strength significantly. This makes you slightly more attached to units than previous Civ titles. While this is turn-based and Warcraft was real-time, it would still be neat to see a sort of campaign mode added to set this title apart from others, since it already seems like a hybrid.
Sid Meier's fan rating, despite it seeming prepped to cash in on future DLC: 8/10
Overall rating for casual fans of turn-based 4X styled games: 7/10

In the past, I played Civ 2 (Test of Time) & Civilization 3 Complete. I enjoyed both of those and was realling looking forward to Civilization: Beyond Earth as I was sort of hoping for a more modern version of the Civ 2 (Test of Time) Sci-Fi scenario.
I didn't play Civ 4 or 5 so, fortunately, my view of the game is that of just the game, not how close it is or is not to Civ 5.
I'm definitely enjoying it and recommend it to those who enjoy TBSs and sci-fi games.
Things I like:
1. The quantity of alien "barbarians" - the ammount of aliens on the map can make things very interesting and foce you to stay out of certain areas early on. I enjoy the way the affect the game.
2. The unit evolution system - Its nice that units upgrade automatically now and have several different ways they can look
3. The tech web. While it can be daunting its honestly not that hard to figure out. Play a few times and figure out what you want to do and go that route in the tech web. Want to win fast? Just hyper specialize in your tech training instead of spreading out.
4. Quest. I think the quests are a big help towards at least a minimal degree of immursion. They do get predictable after several play throughs though but overal I like them and the different ways they can affect the game.
5. Virtues, affinities, and quest benefits. I enjoy the many ways you can improve your game through micro benefits gained from various avenues. It feels like I can play the game several times and have very different experiences should I choose so.
Things I think need improvement:
1. The alien AI. They tend to fluctuate heavily from super passive (most frequent) to being completely aggressive (not common) I'd like to see more fluidity in their reactions to how you treat them.
2. Endings. I enjoy the concepts behind the endings but I think there needs to be more "to do" about them. In today's gaming environment I was honestly hoping to see a short cinimatic when I won. As it stands, winning the game seems... sort of anti-climatic
Again, I am enjoying the game and recommend it to other TBS and sci-fi fans.
