Games can be many things, they could provide an escape from the world, interactive environment to challenge one's abilities, learning, discovery and exploration and much more.
From the first look, Final Fantasy XIII is an epic adventure in mindblowingly beautiful world. Enchanting music and wonderful story. Perhaps, it starts a bit slow, reading details of mythos from a log could be a let down. Perhaps, gameplay stresses story over exploration or heavy action. Still, it feels like a grand adventure all the time. Technically, it has gorgeous environments, enchanting music and solid cast of characters. All that with enormous level of attention to the details. Which could be seen and heard everywhere, from the way crystals are glowing to subtle nuances in soundtrack.
But it seems, that this game has an additional unique quality well worthy of praise. In short, it could play a role of therapist or even a friend in a turbulent time of change. It could provide a much needed time off, relief and help to sort things out. Why? It centered around a group of young but dedicated people who are acting against all odds - politics, social values, all authority. It shows corrupting quality of authority and the way it affects society and creates pressure, thus providing a healthy perspective on society. At the same time, it shows a natural value of such human qualities as kindness and compassion. And their independence of any authority, thus helping to clarify confusion for many people (young?) who think themselves to be inadequate outsiders in adequate society. Carefully showing that the society is in a constant flux of chaos anyway. And that any change starts from inside, thus first affecting people who are around. In this way, it shows universality of such qualities as compassion and friendship (even for bad guys, few games/movies do that).
It also touches on a subject that nobody is perfect, but it is never a problem if you don't give up on yourself; it is more like a wrong view to think there is a 'perfect someone'.
In general, the game brings up so many topics (such as conditioning, conformity, authority, society, corruption, friendship, weaknesses) that it can be somewhat considered encyclopedia of modern psyche (albeit very light). Therefore, it can provide a kindly guidance for a confused soul. All that with aesthetics, style and without pressure. One cannot help but wonder, whether such a game is a gift in times of change which could provide so much needed relief from the world and, perhaps, even guidance. While helping to clarify many issues and raise better questions. At the same time, showing that there is always a way and time to cool down.
Is it a grand adventure? For sure. Is it mindblowingly beautiful? My goodness, yes! But what's more, it can play a role of a guide when there is none around. And that is an exceptionally rare trait among... well, anything.

So far, I cannot reccomend this game. This will be my first review as i like to try and be understanding and give games time to mature. This series has had 5 years and every single release is buggy and has issues with saves, card bugs, etc.
So far, the servers in this version are up and down due to a bug allowing people to 'buy' tons of gold on the shop without actually being charged.
Myself and a handful of others i've been chatting with have lost the 3 initial free boosters you receive after completing the tutorial. We opened them and added the cards to the collection, but the cards disspeared after the next login. The game's store links as of this review have been removed, although if you have a link you are able to get to the store page still.
Lots of users are experiencing crashes, and i can confirm at least a few cards within one hour of playing that don't even trigger their abilities correctly.
The gold and campaign progress appear to be stored on stainless' servers, which is why you can't access either of them while not connected to the service. The card unlocks are unknown, but could be tied to a local save which would expllain losing the initial booster contents (though the 3 unopened packs should have been given back..). I know decks at least are stored locally, as i got the dreaded "Choose your save file" from steam cloud once reconnected (note that i didn't know i was disconnected beforehand). I chose local and it still had my deck, but it kept asking me every time i logged back in so eventually i chose the cloud save. This stopped the prompting but i lost the deck.
Combine these frustrations that happen every single duels release with the fact that stainless or wizards don't talk to the community at all until it's too late, and i can't reccomend this game at this time. I skipped the last years version because of issues like this, and swore i'd never buy another one. I decided to try this due to it being free and thinking ok, maybe they're going to take a note from Blizzard and make a solid experience.
As far as features go, the hold priority option is missing, which is sad as it was in the original Duels of the planeswalkers. There aren't proper beginning or end steps, but's the usual for this series. There's NO chat, so you can't even text communicate with your opponent or partners. No voice chat either.
I'll gladly update the review when all this crap is fixed, but until then either stay away or take my advice and don't spend any real money on it, you never know if your cards will stick around at this point.

I'm playing FFXIII for a second time now.  Granted, I'm a Final Fantasy fan (my first being FF7, although I've gone back and played the previous games)...  The main character Lightning reminds me A LOT of a female version of Cloud (FF7), Snow cracks me up with his cheesy Hero lines, and Vanille, I can't help but notice her gasps and comments seem a little weirdly suggestive sometimes.  What I'm trying to say is there is a nice diversity among the characters and you're bound to become attached to at least one of them.
Usually when I'm playing games I quickly tire of some of the repetative music, namely the battle music.  I have to say, FFXIII's soundtrack as a whole is AMAZING.  I even listen to it when I'm not playing the game, as well as got non-gamers liking it too.
The battle system and character growth was a bit interesting.  You have control over your lead party member and if they die, regardless if there are other surviving team members, you lose.  Although, playing the game on normal as opposed to easy, you can still retry at the point just previous of the battle you died in without any penalty whatsoever.  I don't believe this takes away from the challenge of the game, rather I do appreciate saving my sanity of going through blah blah since my last save point just to readjust a battle stratedgy.
You set up a battle stratedgy sorta, kinda, like FF12 in your menu - these are called Paradigrams - before your start running around battling.  For example, while you're leader is attacking, healing, defending, the rest can be attacking or healing or casting magic, etc. according to what Paradigrams you set beforehand that you can change infinitely during the duration of battle. The Paradigram is basically a combination of how many people in your party (max 3) and what skills are available (max 6) (e.g. Ravenger, Medic, Commando). "Staggering" your enemies is important, especially in boss fights.
As you progress through the game, different skills open up to your characters, seems like a different take from FF10's sphere grid.  Except if you decide to use your CP (growth points/experience points essentially) on lets say "Ravenger" (magic skills) it's linear from that point.  Like you can't pick which Ravenger skills you want, you just start from like Ravenger lvl 1 and go up crystal by crystal (Strength +3, Magic +2, Learn Fira, etc).
There's not a lot of exploring I feel in FFXIII until you get to Gran Pulse, which isn't much later in the game, and it's bascially just a very very VAST plain and your sidequest there is to fulfill previous L'cie's goals which involve defeating some monster- there is a lot to defeat though and some extremely challenging.  However even though the beginning of the game is very linear the environments are amazing - it's a very visually appealing game.
But to get down to it, you're doing a lot of fighting and listening/watching the story.  I would say it's a relatively smooth and enjoyable game to complete.
I'd rate this game an 8/10.

Rivals of Aether is a great 2D spiritual succesor to the Smash Bros. series from Nintendo. I love the unique characters with both original moves and moves inspired by characters from the Smash series. The mechanics and rules in the game differ than that of Smash as well, and to that I say "well done!" If it were just a blatant knock off of Smash, it would not feel as original and innovative as it does.
With all that said, I'd like to share some my personal knitpicks about the game.
For starters, the character Kragg feels a bit too overpowered. His movesets are easily abused by campers and veterans, making him extremely difficult to fight against. He also has a good bit of speed behind him for a heavy-hitter. Now I may just be a John or a Scrub for these complaints, but I may also not be the only one that feels this way about him. I just can't help but find myself hating going against this character, especially when they are spamming the rock throw and rock scatter attack. It feels nearly impossible to get around it.
Second, online play can have some SEVERE lag issues. Sometimes it can run fine depending on the connection, but often times, there is a HUGE delay in the controller input when playing online, which can make it extremely difficult to play. I understand if someone I'm playing with has bad wifi, but their has got to be a way to patch this.
Lastly, I think the overall controls are a bit too stiff. It may just be me, but I find myself parrying A LOT when I am simply trying to dodge roll instead. Sometimes my inputs don't match what I am trying to do either.
Now I know this game is in Early Access and it is FAR from done, but I figured I would just give my two cents about my thoughts on the game so far. All in all, for it being in such an early stage of development, it is pretty damn solid! I tip my hat off (if I had one) to Dan Fornace and his team on this game. It's fun, it's innovative, and I absolutely cannot wait to see where this game goes when it recieves it's full release in the next few months! Good luck to you all, and I hope my inputs on this game help you out in anyway.

A wonderful little indie game that takes simple platforming mechanics and makes it very creative.
You play as a space astronaut that has the ability to...well...defy gravity. You have your typical jump mechanics, and even the double jump ability.
What makes this game really fun is your weapon.
You have the ability to either create two types of vortex: a blue or orange vortex. The blue vortex will suck you and other applied objects into/around the hole, while the orange vortex repels anything  that comes near it. In a sense, the game's kind of like Portal.
And other than you having the ability to shield yourself from these vortexes time to time, that's all you really need to know, and traverse across the stage and through a door onward to the next stage.
The game can escalate pretty quick as each level you pass, but when you land on a certain platform, the game checkpoints you on that section, allowing you to continue from where you left off before you self-destructed. This makes the game's awaringly increased difficulty much more tolerable, and you're not left raging into your favorite pillow pet.
With the simple mechanics and the wonderful soundtrack that I'm quite hooked into, and its very low price of a $3 retail, I'd say this game is a must buy. And if you happen to find this game on sale, then even better. (I got this game for literally $0.29, and easily made up for it through steam cards. So its as if I got to play this neat indie for free.)

Hollow Knight is a beautifully drawn game. The characters really come to life with their hand drawn animations. The environments are engaging as you explore a lost and crumbling civilization.
The story takes a lot of digging and researching in order to identify everything that happened to the world prior to your arrival. A lot of the lore is hidden in character interactions, item interactions, and journal entries.
This game requires carefully planned movements and precise attacks. You will not be very successful with a “hack and slash” style of gameplay. Additionally, you will (more than likely) die a lot during your first playthrough, but you do get that sense of accomplishment from finally defeating that enemy that you’ve been struggling with.
The biggest downside (in my opinion) would be the large distances between the save points (benches). This could require a lot of traveling to get back to where you died.
One improvement could possibly be a sort of indication of how much you’ve damaged any particular enemy. Be it a life bar or changing the character model to show the amount of damage that you inflicted. This would give you a representation of how close you’ve come to beating that particular enemy prior to dying or to prevent unneeded weapon swings/jumps.
All in all, I cannot recommend this game enough. This game has me coming back for more and has me constantly looking up additional theories on “What happened to this world”.

TL;DR – As an early access game this has a lot going for it already. It needs to work on balancing resource development and technology progression, but the management systems at the core of the game are excellent and the devs are present in the steam/PA forums so the Q&A available makes getting a grasp on the mechanics more than doable.
This game takes the concepts behind the Anno series and games like Banished and then dives into the mechanics of colonist, resource and technology management and lets you micromanage the heck out of them. Progression is slow and every advance you make, be it adding a food item to the menu or unlocking a new tier of technology, must be meticulously calculated. That’s why I love it.
To give you an idea of resource management, one of the more simple things in the game are plastics: you will need 3 different types (alpha, beta, gamma) throughout the game and a plastic manufacturing chain will be the second or third thing every colony establishes. You need to:
If you don’t have a blueprint or one is not on the market and you don’t have a blueprint left to unlock, then you have a whole separate production chain to work on for researching them. This process isn’t nearly as tedious as it may sound at first and the experience makes getting a production chain up and running that much more rewarding. The game is full of logistical challenges, and as you progress, the systems can become more complicated and rely more on other systems, which speaks to the game balance.
The balance of resources produced to resources used is already great. The balance of technologies researched to technology cost needs some improvement. It can be difficult to expand at all once the technologies to unlock power upgrades (vital for expansion) start requiring core techs/documents, because these take considerable resources to develop, not to mention a lot of time. While completely possible, this does cause long spans in the game where it seems like you’re doing nothing but waiting.
As for foods, ship add-ons, automation stations and power modules, the game offers a myriad of evermore-complex upgrades that make noticeable improvements to every corner of your colony.
Where the game needs the most improvement right now (patch 2.96.2) is in the imparting of information. The game either needs at least a half dozen more tutorials, or a pure sandbox mode. This would go a long way towards teaching non-economic-worldbuilder-veterans how to get a good start, since the slightest mistake early in game could devastate your colony and make you just start over.
At the moment it’s also absolutely necessary to claim some bonus packages at the new colony screen, because without some free blueprints and power modules, you’re asking for a dead colony. It would be nice if there were either more tier-1 blueprints available on the market, or security boxes were easier to get in a level 1 colony.
The game also doesn’t have any resource graphs that I could find, so it’s difficult to track a decline in food or fertilizer or water over time. For that, you have to keep an eye on the numbers of resources in your inventory and try to remember values so you notice if you’re running out of something. Graphs would be a great addition.
There is also nowhere to see a summary of what level colonists you have and the available housing space for that tier. I currently have to manually add up the number of junior, senior and master colonists I have and then visually check to make sure I have enough residences to house them. A summary screen for this info would be a great addition.
It would also be nice if there were some more glitter; 1x1 and 1x2 parks, industrial gadgets, commercial outlets, something to fill in the extra space left over once you’ve completely filled a platform.
Overall I’m happy I bought it and 100 hours in I’m going to be playing it more, even though it’s not finished and things like drones and energy combos haven’t been implemented – I’m excited for when they are.

STATE OF ANARCHY ON PC
I think we all had “those kids” in our classes at school that liked to doodle crude, violent images all over their papers during class. Thanks to developer Andrew Jr. and State of Anarchy, we now know what happens when they graduate. Playing something like a simplified take on the original Grand Theft Auto, this hand-drawn crime spree is basically the natural evolution of those same murderous stick figures, brought to life with minimal effort and maximum mayhem.
State of Anarchy doesn’t waste much time with the likes of story, throwing players straightaway into a violent world where everyone’s out to kill. The gameplay is rudimentary, yet relatively effective for what it sets out to do. Players will guide their bullet-spraying protagonist across the ballpoint-pen landscapes, racking up the body count on their way to complete each stage by taking out the heavy-gunning boss waiting inside a fortified position within a bank.
State of Anarchy Bank
It’s tough for me to really judge State of Anarchy because, while it seems pretty crude and simplistic, it embraces this existence well. There’s no pretense of being anything more than a violent top-down killing spree, and the visual style goes well with the vocal sound effects that accompany it. This isn’t a game that’s trying to be anything more than it is, nor one that feels like it needs to. It is, simply put, a no-frills action title that sees no need to dress itself up in anything fancier.
Despite how well it pulls off the simple approach, State of Anarchy isn’t without some flaws. While your character can level up and obtain new weapons, there’s a strange linear take on the whole thing. Players have no option to use the weapons previously obtained, with each new one replacing the last. New guns are unlocked by defeating each ‘boss’, a repeated identical fight taking place in the center of a very large and densely-populated bank. This repetition begins to grow stale pretty early on, but there’s nothing demanding that players tackle each new stage in any particular timeframe.
In addition to unlocking new weapons, clearing each stage in State of Anarchy also allows players to spend any talent points they’ve earned by leveling up since the last one. Players can spend each point on increased health, running speed, fire rate, or health regeneration. For me, the obvious choice was to go hard on regeneration, but with lengthy healing time hard to find among the swarms of increasingly-powerful enemies, others may find that this is not the best path.

IF YOU USE THIS REVIEW - READ THE ENTIRE THING. IF YOU DO NOT, YOU WILL BE MISLED. I've been a Hitman fan for a loooong time. I can still remeber playing Hitman: Codename 47 on my ancient CRT. But something about this makes it fun, such as figuring out a clever way to assassinate your target (assassination objectives are very rare, but always fun). I'm not sure. When I first played this game, I played it on the easiest difficulty level available.  I beat it, I enjoyed it, it didn't cause me much trouble.
But then I tried to play through it a second time on "Normal" difficulty, and based upon my experiences there I simply cannot recommend this game.  Hitman: Absolution is billed as a stealth-based game where you "hide in plain sight" using disguises, cover, and a blending-in technique referred to as "instinct."  On Easy difficulty, I found myself able to get through relatively nicely because of being able to mash the "Instinct" key... and ONLY because of that.  The disguise system is horrible: I have never seen such an unrealistic disguise system on any video game in my entire life.  The way the disguise system works is that any NPC wearing a similar disguise becomes suspicious if you get too close.  The problem is, though, that the definition of "too close" varies from a few feet to a few hundred yards away.  There are some levels I have played where my disguise was instantly blown, most notably the prison section in the "Skurky's Law" level.  No disguise I have used has been effective there.
Granted, the prison level in Skurky's Law takes place in a small town in South Dakota, but the same principle holds true in the main city in which the game takes place: Chicago, Illinois.  When you have an abandoned library with poor lighting and about fifty police officers searching for a bald guy wearing a suit, then donning a police uniform with a hat should make it easier to get by without being noticed.  But this simply does not work without mashing the Instinct key or diving behind cover.
The disguise system wouldn't be so terrible if the much-vaunted Instinct system were more usable in difficulties higher than "Easy."  In several levels on Normal Difficulty, I start out with absolutely no Instinct whatsoever, and because I'm on Normal, the Instinct doesn't regenerate, and for some reason the things that should increase your instinct tend to be in places where you have to pass by multiple enemies and you have to hope that they didn't actually spot you.  I can understand the concept behind Instinct not regenerating, as it adds to the challenge, but that said the devs could have at least given the player a full instinct meter at the beginning of every level, or even only half.  It's far better than going into a level with none at all and no chance of blending in without it.
Then there is the checkpoint system, which is decent I suppose, but with the major problem being that if you have to leave the game for any reason and then restart later, your progress in the level may be saved but the enemies you have dealt with have not been saved.  So if you had a clear area behind you before going to a checkpoint and leaving the game, upon returning to the game later you have a whole bunch of enemies that have apparently risen from the dead while you were off the game.
Of course, there have been trainers made for this game, that allowed paying customers to make the system more realistic, but alas, IO Interactive apparently doesn't like it when players actually enjoy playing their games, so a recent patch has rendered such trainers useless.  I've heard of trainers that are more compatible with the present version, but unlike the earlier trainers, these require money... and why should I pay a third party even more money after I've already bought the game from the publisher so that I can actually play the game in a way that is satisfying to me, the customer?
The extraordinary frustration I have experienced with Hitman: Absolution is quite common, so much so that I have to wonder if IO Interactive didn't make this game more to anger its customers than to give people an enjoyable, quality stealth assassin game.  There are so many things wrong with the game that the gaming community sought to fix... and the devs deemed the fixes to be "cheating."  I can understand that on the multiplayer version, but not on the single-player campaign.
So all in all, I simply cannot recommend this game.  The frustrations I have endured due to the faulty disguise system, the poor implementation of the Instinct system, and the game's inability to remember all of your progress even through a simple level in this highly linear story-driven game, have made any positives irrelevant.  If the only way I can "hide in plain sight" as the game supposedly allows me to do is to play it on the easiest difficulty level available, then this game simply does not and cannot deliver on such a promise.

To all the haters out there I am glad I didn’t listen and purchased the game anyway.   Let’s start with this, it’s not CIV 5, so stop your complaining!  I have played through and won twice on this game and I am hooked!  There are so many negative reviews, I actually can’t believe I purchased the game at full price.  I am so glad I did because the game has the deep strategy I was looking for.  This game has the deep strategy and content I love about the Civilization series without being a clone of the game set in space.

The Civilization series is a masterpiece of gaming content.  The original game came out in 1991, there is no question it has to be the most enduring PC based game in history.  I have played this game for that long and each version has just gotten better.  Each version has also been different.  Civ B.E. is no different. I truly enjoy the three tracks you can go by as far as alien culture. The Tech Web is much more engaging than the linear tech tree.  The modes of winning have been very fun to explore.
There are three tracks by which you choose your dominant culture for the game.  Each one is a combination of a religious devotion, a cultural belief and provides technology boosts.  Track one is harmony with the alien planet, track two is a balance of the two and track three is pure earth culture all the way. They become religious in the sense that like Civ 5 you anger, annoy and upset your fellow colonists to the point where it could lead to war. This serves the purpose of a political devotion as well.  The nice thing is it is not mutually exclusive you can mix and match as you go so there is a balance there as well.  The technology boosts equate into ways to help with the all aspects of the game.  This makes for a unique sci fi strategy game that I have not seen before.  You get to decide how “Alien” your culture becomes.
The Tech Web is similar to other sci fi strategy games I have played, in that you have a core of technology you start with then branch off in a direction.  What makes this even better is that each sub technology does not have to be researched in a linear way.  This makes it possible for you to jump around and move in a direction when needed based on what your colonies goals or needs.  To the credit of BE it allows you to address specific colony issues.   There may be a building that brings easy health and you have a health problem.  There may be a military improvement or other reason to keep building on a specific technology track.  This is so much better than the tech tree.  You have to pick a track culture, economy or military to get to a goal and even through it has branches it is still pretty linear in nature. After two complete play trough’s each game played differently which I truly enjoyed.
The modes of winning are very different which also makes it fun.  You are not devoted to one over another and do not need to commit as early as you do in Civ 5.  In my second play though I could have easily gone with conquest but I chose Transcendence.  Each victory style has a different end point which also makes winning as satisfying as Civ 5.  I have completed two victory tracks and look forward to completing more.

If you’re a Civilization series fan you will find the game similar as well as very different.  If you have played this series for years as I have, the deeper cultural and artistic touches where not there in the original 1991 game.  No doubt this has made the original game a legend.  Civ B.E. is worth playing now and it will only get better in the future.

Day15. Palve and 2 others are very hungry with 2 portions of meat left. Palve went to "Sniper junction" in search of food. No luck.
Sniper got his leg on the way back.
Day16. Palve, Tired, starving, wounded, bleeding with no bandage to patch up. The other 2 could barely hold on too. "Just one more time tonight" Palve thought, "I'm sure hospital will share something with us".
Palve ate one of the last two portions of meals and lied down on a bed. He is still very hungry, but he will live.
1pm, someone knocked on their door. "Trader!" The chef thought, rushing to the door in hopes of bartering some food and bandages. as the cook opened the door..
"Please help our mum!". What he see is not a trader, it was children. Two of them. "Our mother is sick! She needs medicine or else she won't make it!". Stunned, the cook glanced towards the safehouse. The kids are waiting for a reply, pleading with their eyes. After a few seconds of silence the words came out, "Sorry.". The chef closes the door, trying not to look the kids' face as he turns away, dragging his worn out body back onto the bed. Sitting on a chair with a book, school teacher glared at the chef filled with rage and sadness, but she adverted her teary eyes after.
They have no medicine.
Night time. Palve nagivated through the city with darkness as his cover, bringing some stuffs with him in hopes of trading. As he slowly approached the hospital an armed man looked at him. He says nothing and let him pass. Palve headed straight towards who looked like a nurse. The nurse quickly grabbed him, putting him down on a bench and dressing his gunshot wound. He thanked the nurse and moved in further. Along the way was littered with debris and some places looked like something useful might be there. Palve thought about looking around but his thought immediately vanished as he notices the people around him, shaken, tired, on edge. The last straw could be anything.
Doctor found, Palve exchanged a few words, he managed to strike a deal getting him enough food to last one more day. With his mood lifted and wound patched up, he return through the darkness with more energy than ever.
Day 17, Palve arrived with a handful of goodies. He went straight to the kitchen to store the food as he calls out the other two. As he opens the door he saw both the chef and school teacher.
Chef in a pool of blood, And on the chair was the teacher, with a knife sticking out of her chest. Chef was still breathing, faintly. "i...p.." chef drew his last breath.
Day20, With a bloodied shovel Palve leans to the wall next to the fridge. No more food, no more enemies, no more reasons. Just bodies and blood. "Serves you right." Palve mutters as he tosses his last cigar butt on a nearby figure. A body filled with cuts, bruises and gushing blood. "No more." Palve thought, he closes his eyes letting everything go.
Footsteps, someone is closing in. Palve lazily lifted his eyelids. The sun is high and the rays hits Palve right in the face. Dazed, A figure came onto his sight slowly shadowing over the light. A girl... with a gun.
Palve chuckled, closing his eyes as he takes a deep breath. He can hear footsteps closing in, but he no longer...
"Hey.", The voice was firm, but not threatening. A little curious that he has not been shot yet, Palve looks at the girl.
Her lips starts moving again.
"Do you..."

Final Fantasy XIII is the first part of the Final Fantasy XIII trilogy. The story starts with Lightning (the main protagonist of FFXIII) battle the PSICOM soldiers during the turmoil caused by an event called "The Purge". And as the story progresses, other characters appear to fight off the PSICOM soldiers. Don't worry, I won't spoil you any of the plot.
Expect a bit of confusion since the game starts throwing events at you immeadiately. But as you progress through the story, you'll begin to understand bit by bit why they are fighting for such a cause. Each character or should I say a member of your party has their own reason for fighting off their current foes.
Just like any Final Fantasy game, FFXIII has its own battle system but you only control one character of your party. The game distinguishes the members of your party into roles and the only one you take control of is the Leader. The FFXIII focuses more on formation and the debut of the Paradigm Shift. The Paradigm Shift is a unique battle feature of FFXIII where your party sets up formations applicable to your current situation. As the leader, you have the command to change paradigms suited to the situation or your style of battle. Unlike other Final Fantasy games that involve many characters, FFXIII mostly restricts you to the characters available during the plot or scenario. Since the game is very linear, your party maybe split into multiple teams either alone, by pair or by trio depending on how the plot goes.
The level up system is also linear since the game somehow adapted Final Fantasy X's crystal level up system. The main difference is that in FFXIII, each character has their own roles and each role has its own crystal level up system. So if Lightning has 4 different roles, then you have 4 level up systems for Lightning.
Again, the game very much linear. Digging very deep into the storyline. The game still features an open world but you'll have to grind down up to Chapter 11 to play it. By the way, the game has 12 chapters all in all.
Some Updates of Game:
+ O and X buttons are now well distanguished when using the Asian or Western controls.
+ The "ESC" button issue has now been resolved.
+ The game graphics can now be adjusted to suit your PCs.
My own rating:
Graphics: 10/10
Music: 10/10
Gameplay: 7/10
Story: 9/10
Overall: 9/10
I recommend this game to big fans of Final Fantasy games. If you love dwelling deeper into the storyline and want to experience the new innovation of the Final Fantasy Series, then this is the game for you. If you prefer the traditional way then, this game will surely disappoint you since it IS very linear and very much attached to the storyline. And don't worry about the game's price because this game is very much worth every penny with the game spanning to more than 100 hours of gameplay and the tough boss battles that can span for more than an hour.
If you loved this game, then continue on with the 2nd part of the trilogy, Final Fantasy XIII-2.

This game has my vote for Indie game of the year. The choices you make need to be thought out as some actions have either positive or negitive effects on your suriviors. You start with 2 ~ 4 random people in a shelled out home in the middle of what seems to be a civil war. The games art design is fitting to set the emotion & the somber music helps with this a lot. The game cycles between day ~ night. Day you fix your home ~ build items ~ get rest for the night. Night hits and the fun begins. Pick one of the 3 members to go looting, one to stand guard at home and best to have the 3rd rest for day time activities. You pick where you want to head off too, sometimes you don't see anyone and looting goes smooth, but what fun is that. Some of the survivors you come across are harmless and are just out looking for surplies like you, others maybe living where you go and you need to decided to loot them or leave and of course there is the chance they are bandits. We all know they just want to sell you the best long distance plan. There is plenty of random events and every time you start over your 3 survivors could all be different, the weather might of changed and I can promise you while the locations on the map might be the same going there will not be. Giving this game plenty of re-play ability.
Average game time is between 30 -50 days, thats right a survival game where there is a goal! Finally you have an objective, outlast the war & win, Don't be fooled this is not an easy game and has the ability to make you care about your survivors wanting to see them live to the end & sometimes having to choose who eats and who don't.

Once again, I'm having a hard time deciding whether to thumbs up or down.
Compared to Civ V
Pros:
- It's balanced now, more or less, no more OP cultures like France or Korea.
- Multiplayer stability has been greatly improved, no more disconnecting players every other turn.
- Waiting time between turns has been significantly decreased. Especially on huge maps, you don't get to walk the dog between turns anymore.
- Science fiction theme, nuff said.
- New technology structure allows for far more variety in gameplay, and you can actually decide in which way you want your people to develop.
- Interface is more user friendly, at first I was like 'meh', but after getting used to it, I have to admit that it's really better that way.
Cons:
- It's balanced now. Which makes the different sponsors kinda generic. Part of the fun has always been to play and deal with each culture's weaknesses and advantages.
- No recognizable leaders, units, wonders etc... Civ V lived a lot on those, like meeting your childhood hero Dshenghis Khan, or lead German tanks into battle, or the thrill you got when you built that one world wonder you've always wanted to visit.
So, is this a good game? Definetly yes, but, if you want to play it for the mechanics, strategies and tactics, stick with (or get) Civ V, it's way cheaper, and you don't really miss out that much.

Excellent stealth game. This was my first "Hitman" experience. For the most part, I didn't need to know any backstory, though there were some loopy out-of-place elements like gun-toting latex wearing nuns and a.... a bioengineered mexican wrestler in an otherwise gritty crime story set in a real-looking world.
While the game is linear, the levels themselves have an open-floor format. You can explore an environment entirely to figure out the best way to assassinate your target. About the levels, there are the obligatory strip club and police precinct levels, but the game really soars with some creative environments like a roof-top marijuana commune, chinatown during New Year, and a cheesy roadside motel with accompanying mini-golf. I've never seen crowds done better in a game. In a typical open-world city game, pedestrians are usually sparse, and basically exist as background. But in Hitman, the crowds are thick, you have to wade through them, the streets feel much more alive than similar games like GTA or L.A. Noire.
The game play is solid as well. There are many ways to kill a target. There is a point system, though I would suggest ignoring it for the most part as you'd have to play every level as a silent killer to maximize your points, and to do so would mean missing out on many of the creative kill methods. Try sneaking through one level, then shoot your way through the next, then use environmental kills for another level. You can always replay a level to beat challenges, so vary it up.
One small caveat. I wouldn't call the game full-tilt mysogynist, but your first assignment is to kill an unnarmed naked woman in a shower. The characters in this world- both men and women- are ugly and ruthless, but with the exception of a 50 year old nun, all the women seem to have fallen out of a BDSM mag. And maybe, just once, in some crime game, I'd like to see the obligatory strip club level be a male strip club. Or at least something less betty booped, like a truck stop strip club at noon on a Tuesday where the girls are over 40 and the alcoholic bouncer still hasn't cleaned up the puked mcrib on the floor of the VIP closet.

Final Fantasy XIII, what is left to say about this game that hasn't been said already? Plenty, actually. This game is by no means a flawless game, it is not the best game in the franchise, it represents change and risk; something we gamers fear even when we demand it. Final Fantasy always changes, if they game a good game or a bad game you can be damned sure they're not going to make it twice, the beautiful thing about Final Fantasy is that if you don't like this year's version you can always look forward to the next one which you can be sure will be 100% different in mechanics, story and writing.
GAMEPLAY
The game starts off like an empty bag waiting to be filled, or maybe a tree waiting for the rain. They give you almost nothing. But slowly after the first major plot point in the game they feed you the combat system piece by piece, a strange mixture of the classic ATB, Final Fantasy X's spheregrid leveling and finally a touch of Final Fantasy XII's Gambit system. In Final Fantasy XIII you control only one character but you can change the AI behavior of your allies making them tank, heal or set you up for devistating staggers and chains. The combat has you thinking ahead on the fastest way to defeat your enemies and which paradigms you should switch to inorder to accomplish these means. Having your allies set up staggers and then watching your team tear enemies apart with bonus damage and chain attacks is incredibly fun and rewarding. The better you do in each battle the more Crystal Points you are given, which means you can level up your characters faster and further. Don't be contempt on letting the Auto-Battle AI do everything for you, Final Fantasy XIII's combat is deep but only if you let it.
STORY
By far my favorite story in any Final Fantasy game, but each to their own.
CHARACTERS
Thanks to the incredible voice acting and incredible animations the characters come to life like no other Final Fantasy before. The characters themselves are very human, very flawed and all have their own personal agenda and concerns with what's happening to them. Don't be fooled into thinking Lighting is the main character of the story, each character gets almost equal development and you'll play as every one of them at some point or another.
Oh, and Hope stops being a whiny little ♥♥♥♥♥ after a certain point. You'll probably hate him the most, so I'll just leave that word of 'hope' for anyone wanting to punch him in the face for crying over his mother so much.
EXECUTION
While I might personally love the game, I have to admit that there are things it does wrong. Plenty. The worst offender is the execution of the core ideas. The problem with Final Fantasy is they hand you the game but don't hand you any meaningful gameplay until chapter three. You have to sit though two hours of the game for it to finally begin and get good and that is a serious problem. While it might take longer for older Final Fantasy titles to click with you at the very least they don't limit you to a linear hallway and a single attack for the first two hours of the experience. This makes the game hard to get into and leave the player little reason to come back. If you're like me you probably play the game an hour at a time. Anyone who spends two days playing this on and off is probably going to get more invested in their other games over Final Fantasy XIII and by the time they finally muster into Chapter Three they'll probably forget all the momentum of the story or forget how good it feels to finally be able to do something with the combat system.

I have over 1,500 hours in Civilization 5, a game they invested a lot of development time over several revisions. The game design for Beyond Earth is a great idea and has potential for a start. It was very obvious they used the Civilization 5 base engine to develop the game rapidly. Beyond Earth on the other hand was simply released without thoroughly being tested.
Because of their reputation as a company, they also increased the price tag "Beyond Belief" considering the overall product. I would have just waited a year if I had known of its current state and my trust in the corporation just dropped. The business goal of money, money, and more money with rushed development just doesn’t work in the gaming industry without taking a hit.
I extended game play by building up to understand the tech tree and learn the strategy. I tried a standard sized default map and set it up to only be won by domination. I could not complete this game I set up because of a tech tree game defect, but here is what I did see before I gave up.
1. When you conquer all cities of a player, they are still in the game! They show on the score board (mini option window), they have roaming units, they interact with your leader and are still able denounce you, and they can conduct spy missions (I caught one)!
2. Key resources for the 3 possible paths is not balanced if you choose to focus on only one. I was only able to build at most 3 Supremacy titan units with little remaining resources for much else (some buildings require them). I eventually equaled in Harmony and  I was able to build about 10 titan harmony units with plenty of resources left over. There is an obvious advantage for Harmony.
3. <CRITICAL> The tech tree cannot be fully researched. I was only able to continue my game until I had to pick the last research item and the game locked on its selection screen. I was unable to tab out or focus on a Task Manager screen to kill the game. It kept throwing me back to Beyond Earth. Definitely not ready there.
4. The tech tree is not a good game design because it’s not large enough with the idea that a player should focus on one of 3 main paths. This should have been thought out more and presentation was difficult to see in a quick overview. The zoom in and out feature should just be removed if it cant be done correctly. This should have been wiped and redone in presentation.
5. You can only reach a max of 18 in one of the paths, but there is no reason not to be able to go higher. I was even able to select a greyed out option to increase beyond 18 (took the point away and gave me nothing). There should be no reason to stop it in presentation even if it doesn’t affect game play. I felt cheated out of a point even if it had no value.
6. The initial options to set up a game with bonuses advantages is a great idea over the set advantages in Civilization 5, but it fails to present the initial racial titles even though it is obvious during the game the origins exist when speaking different languages that follow a Civilization 5 format. A simple presentation flaw that doesn’t match achievements either.
7. The AI should be guided by victory conditions, but it became obvious that with only domination allowed, none of the computer teams were trying to achieve it. It felt like this basic direction for AI was completely ignored instead of being the main direction for goals of winning. Where is the challenge?
This is what I saw over the 31 hours I played. Some of these will eventually be fixed, but the game just is not ready for release, so if you are considering buying it, wait.  I am sure there are many other defects, but the game should not lock your computer through poor game design. Join the side that demands better quality from their products.
For game concept I would give this 4 out of 5 stars, it could be so much more than it is and has great potential.

I haven't played the PS3/X360 version when it came out so long ago so when it released on PC (and went on sale for $6) I had to give it a shot.
Warning, FFXIII does have a bad reputation for being linear (it really is except for pretty much one chapter, 11 if you want to know...), but I really did enjoy the story and the battle system. The game takes a while to reach its stride, the true battle system isn't unlocked until Chapter 3, and up until that point, battles are pointless and albeit a bit tedious. And like classic JRPGs, you're in for a lot of cutscenes.
If you're not a fan of JRPGs or if this is going to be your first, I honestly wouldn't recommend this game to start unless you're a stickler for storylines and character development (I know I am so perhaps I'm a bit biased here). For most of the game, it's a lot of running towards the goal mark while making slight detours for treasure orbs. That said, I am a fan of the Final Fantasy series and I truly enjoyed this game.
Is it the best Final Fantasy? No. Would I recommend this game to everyone? Also no.
I think this game is sadly made for a few choice groups of people. Maybe not even the Final Fantasy fans over the ages. I've played my share of FF games and came into this one with an open mind, and I adored the story (it does get a bit confusing in the beginning with flashbacks throughout to fill in the gaps, later it will make sense) and the gameplay. The leveling system reminded me sort of the leveling system in FFX albeit unique for each role and character instead of one giant thing.
If you're familar with JRPGs and you don't mind a linear world, definitely give this game a shot. If not, you might want to try other FF games first.

Rivals of Aether is a fantastic game that balances the best elements of similar games like Super Smash Bros.
Pros:
-It retains some of the technical skill involved in Melee and Project M (i.e. wave-dashing) but does not overwhelm you with constant skills like L-Cancelling or SHFFLing. I have personally found L-Cancelling to be a hassle, so I was happy to find that there is very little (maybe even zero) landing lag in Rivals of Aether.
- The basic attacks are all there, but a lot of characters have much more interesting mechanics (i.e. Wrastor's aerials freezes him in the air.) Combo-ing with these attacks feels awesome due to the small amount of hitlag on each attack.
-There are no more grabs or ledge grabbing which some people find questionable. However, the lack of grabs adds to much more fluid gameplay relying on attacks to start combos rather than grabs. Also, ledge grabbing has been pratically replaced with wall jumping, which is much different to say the least.
-In my opinion, the characters in this game are much more unique than the characters featured in Super Smash Bros. Each character in this game has a unique gimick besides just attacks, specials, and aerials. I hope that future characters will flow as well as the current ones.
-Rivals of Aether is a game that endorses competetive play and is built for it. This game will feel like a Smash Bros. game made for competetive play. If you like Smash Bros. You will like this game.
-Has support for Xbox 360 controllers and keyboard. You can also use a Gamecube controller if you follow these instructions:
-The music is very good, and I personally love the art style. However, due to the lack of stages the music can become   repetetive.
-Comes with a cool training mode that allows you to experiment and play with bots in any way you want.
Cons:
-Many of the fights experienced online will be choppy and filled with button lag. From my experience, most games I've played have been realtively low on the lag scale. Whenever I play with friends there is no noticeable input lag or choppiness in the gameplay.
-The game is in early access, so you don't really know whether this game will really become something with your money. I say this from personal experience with many early-access games that I have purchased, which I'm aware is my own mistake.
-I don't necessarily know if this is a con, but to all the Melee fans out there: Rivals of Aether is not Melee 2.0.

Conclusion:
I definitely missed lots of pros and cons, but overall, I believe Rivals of Aether is very entertaining and worth the price tag due to the replayability of the game. As stated previously: If you like Super Smash Bros. in any way, shape, or form, you will like this game.

This is not a review of the "Bioshock" part.
This is a review of the "Remastered" part.
The "Remastering" isn't even that. It's just new textures and uncapped physics which are admittedly beautiful, but this is supposed to be a game and not a tech demonstration. The same old problems and bugs are back, interestingly enough accompanied by entirely new ones. The mouse is a clusterfig, the interface is horrendous, controls are poorly made for PC, and there are practically no graphics or FOV options. The simple act of saving still grabs you by your wasteband, yanks you towards a loading screen, then kicks your butt right back into gameplay.
"Why complain?" I hear you say. "You got it for free, didn't you?" Yes I did. but other people won't, and they will expect a legitimate attempt at revamping a treasured classic. This is aimed at them: Skip the money grab, get the original version. It's fun, it's charming, and there aren't any lofty expectations.

Most of the other mechanics are not really Souls-like or, like the combat, may have some ties to the Souls formula but they aren't bound in a way that would deserve a "Souls clone" description. In the end, it's an atmospheric 2D exploration, combat and story-driven game that deserves a look if you've ever enjoyed a Souls game or a metroidvania game. But not because it fits a mold nearly so much as because it's a great new synthesis and it executes well on all of them. It's my game of the year for 2017.

Somehow a game which has an achievement for finishing in under 4 minutes 22 seconds made hours fly by. Hours of gameplay and emotional trauma. This game has a superb sense of humour, deftly pulling the amusing and entertaining out of what at its core is just a simple walking simulator with narration. The game goes further though, prompting questions about the nature of video games and other elements of philosophy and life. Too long a review would spoil it (further!), so you should play!
The free demo is a great introduction, although it's definitely not a demo in the traditional sense.

!!TLDR at the bottom of this review!
Project AURA is a very good concept, but unfortunately it's still only a concept. Very specific roadmap but extremely slow development progress. Looking at their old roadmap, this game was to be released earlier this year. It is still early access.
Now I don't have a problem with delays if it's to ensure good gameplay (Software tester myself), but after taking a 6 month break and starting it up again, only to see... Nothing. Absolutely nothing new or any gamebreaking changes.
All they managed to do these past months is to make lots of text horribly hard to read, they introduces a very nice saggy lag (still playing on the same computer as before and no lag earlier), and changes to the "vital reserve" that still looks just like it did before.
However! I still haven't given up hope on this game. They have made a great time killer so far, and it just needs that final touch. So I'm hoping they can stick to the roadmap now.
But to summarize:
Pros:
- Very interesting concept
- Potentially promising future
- Great game for those that love micro management (Not for lazy persons that want everything served on a platter)
- Cozy atmosphere
- Detailed
Cons:
- Very steep learning curve (Don't get this if you think games like sim city is too hard.)
- Not intuative at all. Be prepared for a UI that hates you and never cooporates)
- Lag. Ran perfectly fine before, suddenly it's slow and saggy.
- Lack of logic. E.G. Your "ships" (flying heli-ships) will fly around the world, but can only find seaweed, metals, plastics and old "Vestige" like paintings? And why can we build super advanced flying machines  that does not require fuel, but not a simple boat for fishing?
- Advancement progress is messed up. You build a seaweed farm and an advanced recycling centre during the first 5 minutes, but you need a huuuuge load of research, time, colonists and multiple "farms" before you can bake a loaf of bread?? Baking is currently end game stuff and for a colony that have flying ships with endless fuel reserves... well... lack of logic.
- Power management... h dear... Once again, flying machines with infinite fuel, but maintaining power levels is a B***H.
- Morale system... I'm just gonna go ahead and say that it is completely worthless, and someone thought about it waay too much. And replacing the living quarters to satisfy everyone... oh dear God... just a whole new level of irritating.
So this game has flaws. Lots of them. But I will still recommend this game to people that love micro management. And with that I mean ONLY people that love micro management. Because this game is ALL about micro management. I see a lot of "It's too hard!" in the discussions, and yeah... thats the damn point. Maintaining a post apocalyptic colony would probably be a frikkin hard thing to do...
But I will stick to hope and will absolutely play this alot more when, and IF they manage to add that final touch.
TLDR; If you skipped to this part, this is NOT a game for you. Simple as that. It's hard, takes time to learn, and involved a dung heap of micro management. Get over it and go play The Sims or something.

Don't really know what to put here, so I'll put a recipe for peanut butter cup minicakes.
INGREDIENTS:
1/4 cup REESE'S Creamy Peanut Butter
2 tablespoons shortening
1/2 cup packed light brown sugar
1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract
1 egg
3/4 cup all purpose flour
1-1/4 teaspoons baking powder
1/8 teaspoon salt
2/3 cup milk
1-1/3 cups (8-oz. pkg.) REESE'S Peanut Butter Cups Minis , divided
(hdr) (hdr) PEANUT BUTTER CREME FROSTING (recipe follows)
DIRECTIONS
1
Heat oven to 350°F. Line small muffin cups (1-3/4 inches in diameter) with paper bake cups.
2
Beat peanut butter, shortening, brown sugar and vanilla in medium bowl on medium speed of electric mixer until creamy. Add egg; beat well. Stir together flour, baking powder and salt; add alternately with milk to peanut butter mixture, beating until well blended. Fill muffin cups 3/4 full with batter; lightly press one mini peanut butter cup into center of each batter-filled muffin cup, leaving chocolate partially uncovered by batter.
3
Bake 12 to 14 minutes or until top springs back when center is lightly touched. Cool in pan on wire rack about 10 minutes. Remove from pan to wire rack; cool completely. Frost with PEANUT BUTTER CREME FROSTING. Garnish each frosted minicake with mini peanut butter cup or mini peanut butter cup half. About 3 dozen minicakes.
PEANUT BUTTER CREME FROSTING
1 can (12 oz.) ready-to-spread fluffy white frosting
1/2 cup REESE'S Creamy Peanut Butter
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
Beat frosting, peanut butter and vanilla in medium bowl until well blended and fluffy. About 2 cups frosting.

Let me start off explaining the recommendation. Yes I recommend it, if you love civ and want a slightly different civ game.
However, if you're expecting innovation / a totally refreshing experience... Wait for the expansions, there might be something in there.
The good:
A new unit system, that makes combat a lot more diverse than earlier civ games. The addition of a lot of hovering units makes sea-battles a lot more tactical and stops the "I have more boats, I win" boring checkerboard fights from before.
The affinity system really allows you to diversify yourself from the other civilizations, and adds a contention point similar to religion in civ5.
The aliens are a lot more diverse than barbarians, and make early expansion a bit more difficult (allthough they dont seem to engage outposts, which is a shame)
Health is a great new modifier, allthough its effects should be more drastic.
The bad:
It feels the same as civ 5. The alien planet doesnt really feel alien. A more hostile environment or maybe some more terrain modifiers would be welcome.
The tech web, allthough a good idea, and a welcome change, is kind of pointless. You'll never just follow one tree, when the inner parts of the web start costing 1 turn per technology.
The lack of personality makes the civs feel a bit boring. Perhaps a religion expansion would help.
Conclusion:
Civ:BE is a good game, it doesn't have the launch problems civ5 had.
It's a lot of fun to play. However it feels like they took civ5, redesigned the units and removed some expansions.
Your best bet is to wait for the expansions, however if you want to play it now, it's still a good game on its own merits, and you can expect a stable game at launch.

Firstly, I do not recommend this game until a large amount of issues get cleared up, yet, like Civ5, has plenty of potential ahead.
I would advise for Civ5 fans like myself to hold off another few weeks or perhaps months for a rather large variety of fixes to be brought in.
Perhaps It's best to note some of the obvious faults and cons of the game to give you a more indepth idea of what you could be dealing with:
- Bad wonders; pretty pathetic bonuses after putting in the effort of researching the required tech and a simply bad visual introduction to the wonder once completed.
- Ranged units; melee strengths greatly reduced, averaging around 1:3 ratio to its ranged strength, however, this has obviously been introduced to some substantial increases to ranged units capabilities, but without a melee supporting unit, don't bother taking them outside the city tiles.
-AI / computer players; Don't bother playing any games under Very hard difficulty if you're looking for any kind of challenge. They avoid affinity levels like the plague and bounce around with 1st level units as long as they can. Oh, and they no longer trade resources, just 'favours', which of course can be saved up and used later to sway their minds, but playing beyond 200 turns with a pocket full of favours doesn't get you very far.
- Stations (city states); Low hp, low defence, don't have a ranged attack, don't absorb land, rather poor late game benefits (even at tier 3), they dont call for help, computer players will demand you stop attacking them even when you're the one trading and protecting them!
- Health; The old Civ5 happiness system has been replaced by a health system, which is entirely dependant on buildings which take some time to research and build and rarely benefit you beyond +3 increase. A few late game tile improvements grant you health also, but at rather steep costs. So don't expect to expand your empire beyond 3-4 cities without falling well below the health line.
- Beginning bonuses; plenty of reasonable choice, however scanning for alien nests only works on turn 1, +1 population for capital city is rather poor even on a marathon length game, CIV bonuses are rather poor compared to Civ5 Civ's, but obviously we will need to wait a few months for another 5-10 Civs to be introduced.
- Easy tech; Adopting the Scavenging virtue with the first level purity affinity grants your scouts immunity to alien attacks and are free to roam the world destroying every alien nest in site for a sweet tech bonus, the aliens assult any other unit near nests and rarely end their turn on top of the nest making for easy explorer pickings. This method has bumped myself beyond the AI every game.
There are plenty more issues to touch up on but you start to see a trend affecting almost every element of the game. But I feel that some pros should be listed as well, this is Civ after all!
- Aliens; love them, so much more annoying and stronger than barbarians, with mid-end game units like the siege worm and KRAKEN floating around the world. Making explorers and ships likely to die within a few turns after automation as they blindly stumble into the claws of the local fauna.
- Outposts; Great adaptation to city development, stops those pesky neighbours from landing a city 4 tiles from your capital. easily destroyed, no ranged attack, slow border expansion, great all around.
- Unit evolution; as you gain affinity levels, your units gain strength and unique bonuses! and not to mention a new skin. Instant upgrades for all units is rather unbalanced but this makes for a much more diverse game and interesting wars.
- Tech web; With the choice of rushing to end-game tech or slowly developing every capability, taking away the linear approach has been a fantastic improvement. Of course, being futuristic makes it rather confusing at first, I highly recommend a few minutes reading over potential improvements before selecting what to research next.
- Quests; Needs some work, however its great to have some goals pushing your game play, kill the giant worm! or even free the slaves from far base one! It would be nice to see some foriegn country specific quests encouraging a more violent game.
Well there you have some basics of the game to ponder over, I've met plenty more issues and oddities that need to be worked over in the next few weeks but this game does have great potential just as Civ5 had when it was first released.
I can see that the game has been rushed for release before it's time, but with the next 2 or 3 major updates, this will be worth buying for all the strategy and Civ fans out there.

Many of the reviews seem to be that "the port is good" but lets not ignore this game being one of the most boring games ever invented. If you are used to bioware/american style RPGs, you will be baffled by the utter lack of decision making while playing. If you are used to even quasi-linear J-RPGs like Bandai's Tales of series or previous Final Fantasy - still don't worry about thinking. The game is literally ONE long hallway for a majority of it. I heard there is a more "open" area FAR FAR later in the game but be ready to run straight on one-way paths, fighting pre-ordered creatures and choosing to goto dead ends for some minor treasure. The story has very little explanations or backstory - without reading datalogs don't ever even try to explain or understand any of the terms or geography within the world. With no overworld, there is no "feel" of any connection between any location - just long hallways with different music and backgrounds. One of the game's developers defended the incredibly linear, boring exploration as it allows the player to just "focus on the story". I'm sorry but does he think gamers are so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ they can't acknowledge a story while playing a game?
Positives-
+Graphics are great, obviously.
+Music is quite good
+Xbox 360 controller works great.
+Graphic options are really great.
+Combat is a mixed bag but really pretty simplified-the game chooses your best options by default and really you only need to change paradigms(strategies) to heal or buff/debuff from time to time.
Negatives-
- Feels like a job to play. I cannot stress enough - you are running straight only; I'm not even joking. Mario Brothers 3 had more to explore than this game.
- Only 5 main characters, they're all pretty boring and range from annoying to emo.
- No towns or even pseudo-illusion that you are in a "living, breathing world". It is a huge step back before even Final Fantasy 1. There is no NPCs to give you dialogue or context or illusion that something exists besides monsters just wondering back and forth in groups waiting to be killed.

First off, I have to say the game has a remarkable atmosphere. It's dark, gritty, and it isn't afraid to show what a civilian's perspective of the brutality is like. You make hard choices that affect your groups' mentality and attitudes. You can scar NPC's in the world emotionally by killing their family member or spouse. Basically, each choice you make in this game has huge consequences.
Secondly, the crafting and scavenging of this game, while well done, is quite tedious at first, but then I understood WHY it is tedious. It reflects the scarcity of ingredients and items in a war-torn, blockaded city. I almost felt hopeless at some points in the game with food running scare many times, fuel depleting rapidly without upgrades and bandits trying to attack my home just so they can get the neccesary ingredients to survive too.
Third and finally, the characters themselves of the game, while not too deep, are remarkably likeable even though they don't really speak other than just text boxes. They interact with each other, they offer things to each other such as comfort and support and items. They feel like living people in a very realistic world. At some points, I was almost crying because of my character being broken from killing too many innocent people. He felt hopeless and I did too. I questioned my logic of "It's the best for us" or "It was neccesary" when I gunned down someone or stole from someone.
tl;dr
The game is an emotional rollercoaster with unique storytelling, atmosphere and gameplay mechanics. One of the very best games I have played in... ever!

Stumbled upon this on a Friday evening and spent the entire weekend in a total binge. Just couldn ´t stop playing...
Before i bought it i watched a few minutes on a "let´s play" on youtube by which the game was presented as a "survival game without zombies". Laughed about this comment as it really says alot about the current gaming industry. There is tons and tons and tons of "procedurally generated open world sandbox zombie holocaust survival games " blah, blah, blah. The industry seems to be all out of ideas. This War of Mine is different. Mainly, the setting of the game is more plaussible than other survival games. It emulates events that actually happens when civilians suffers from war. In game where you kill heaps of zombies with a shovel, you as a player really don´t feel affected by it: It´s a faceless monster going after your brains, it´s not a person or even an animal. But when you play a regular person that kills an old man in sheer desperation for food, now that´s something that really gets to you. It´s this that makes This War of Mine great. You are constantly faced with really though ethical decisions. You only have food for two and there is four of you. Who should eat? The hungry, sick old man or the starving young woman? Should we give medicne to that sick old man and hopefully save his life or should we save it to possibly barter for food for everyone?  Where should we go to find supplies? Should we send someone to the hotel eventhough we know it´s very dangerous? Or should we go to a safer location but possibly end up with nothing and starve? How far are we prepared to go for food? Would we steal from the helpless? Would we murder for it? And the desperation rises...
Overall i think this is a great game. Restarted it a few times and it´s always slightly different. Only few cons i can think of is that eventhough it´s slightly different every restart, the replay value isn´t so high that you feel that you would have as fun with it as the first time you finished it. Yet there´s always some "what if´s" left when you finish the game. The character biographies isn´t all that developed and sometimes you lose track of their personal stories. Their stories are mainly about things from the past and doesn´t relate so much to their current situation. If the relations between the characters where more developed, with dialoges and events based on their internal relations, this game would be something you would play over and over and over... This plus some minor tweaks and it would be a total 10 out of 10.
And if they launched a sequel i would be all over it!

Battlerite attempts to bring in the free to play MOBA audience by offering a much more fast-paced experience with constant combat, eliminating the wait times of "laning" phases from other games, but does it succeed in replacing the rest of the gameplay from those titles?
Battlerite is an isometric, champion-based arena combat game. It uses a small team structure and a much more fast paced combat system to make the fighting more exciting and force most game-deciding actions in each match to be split second decisions. It also uses elements from free to play games like purchasable crates for cosmetics and a quest system that offers chests as rewards.
First things first, Battlerite is in early access, and in this case, it’s a game that’s planning on going free to play once it fully releases. This is something to keep in mind throughout the whole review, as of writing the game costs $20 to purchase, while players who decide to jump in later will be getting an improved experience and saving money. That said, if the game sounds interesting, some may want to jump in right now, and for them, that’s entirely possible and gives users a chance to give feedback on balance and bugs prior to release.
The game is a multiplayer-only title that focuses on having intense and fast-paced 2v2 and 3v3 engagements with very little interference. It borrows mechanics from other champion-based games like roots to hold enemies in place and charging ultimates by dealing damage to enemies or finding pickups placed around the map. Unlike its contemporaries, however, the focus on being fast-paced is enforced by the mechanics in an appropriately harsh manner. Matchmade games are decided by a best of three rounds series of fights with a two-minute timer on them. When the timer hits zero, a circle will appear on the outer edge of the arena and start closing in towards the center of the arena, and anyone caught outside the circle takes damage every second.
Battlerite can be found on Steam for $19.99.
Being a multiplayer-only title that focuses on champion-based combat, this game lives and dies based on a couple different factors. The community has to be large enough that matchmaking times don’t take far too long, the champions have to be interesting and/or fun to play, the cast has to be reasonably diverse so the gameplay doesn’t get too samey, and lastly the game must be properly balanced to keep the sense of intense arena combat and skill that keeps the whole package exciting. Battlerite does a decent job of keeping their cast of characters interesting and mostly balanced. The champions are split into ranged and melee attackers and a set of support characters built around buffs, debuffs and healing in various ways with damage dealing as a secondary objective.
Something worth mentioning here with the game is the appearance of the community, while Steamcharts reports seven thousand to four thousand players a day depending on the time, it’s not uncommon to run into an issue where the matchmaking will take several minutes to put players together. This is odd considering the game consists solely of 2v2, 3v3, training and A.I. modes to play in, so the player base isn’t being diluted by playlists for DLC in any significant way. Unfortunately it gives the appearance that the community is smaller than it really is, hopefully, this is something to be fixed sooner rather than later. It’s also weird to see a bug like this in a game that’s been so far relatively bug-free as far as we could tell. The worst experience so far being the game soft-locking after a multiplayer match which required closing the game entirely to fix, ouch.
We’ve covered the small bugs and what the game needs to do to be successful but not the actual gameplay. To put it in a sentence, it’s perfectly serviceable. It doesn’t introduce any crazy new ideas to champion-based games or does anything especially unique with being an arena combat game outside of forcing a faster pace with the round timer. The champions are generally enjoyable with no real slumps or standouts in the cast and there is a bit of choice both in how your team composition is made when playing with friends as well as how the champion is built. After every round regardless of win or loss, each player can choose one of three preset “Rites” that alter the character’s abilities. Some of them are focused on rewarding more skilled play like reducing the cooldown of an ability depending on how many targets are hit by it, while others serve to improve abilities or create advantages, like improving the healing done to allies and damage done to enemies when using a teleport ability that phases through targets.
This is the strongest aspect of the game, by offering each player their own set of choices, each match can play out differently in a way that legitimately impacts the overall game, as the split second decisions have much more impact in a game that lasts a maximum of ten minutes as opposed to something like League of Legends where decisions can be corrected or accounted for over the course of over forty minutes to an hour. Each character build can excel in a specific circumstance and bring a level of synergy to the team that wouldn’t exist with the base characters, like having a character root the enemy in place to setup for a penetrating shot that punches through all of the rooted targets from a Jade in stealth. It’s the best selling point for the title, and potentially the only one, as the game doesn’t really have much to offer outside of the fast-paced arena experience with variance offered through champions and different builds using the Rite system.
Graphically, the game is nothing special. The art style very closely matches that of other MOBAs like the previously mentioned League of Legends and DoTA 2 and following in their style all three games run very well. Maxing the game out and getting a consistently high framerate is by no means a difficult feat so the play experience will be very similar in terms of visuals, and the low system requirements won’t restrict many people from playing the game. In addition, the sounds and music are also effectively a non-element, the music isn’t anything noteworthy and just serves to a small backdrop while the meat of the game takes place, while the sound effects are all par for the course. In regards to the graphics and sound, “Battlerite” doesn’t do anything special, and while it isn’t a good or a bad thing in itself, it does hurt the game given that it has so little to sell itself on.
Overall, while Battlerite isn’t particularly groundbreaking in any way, it doesn’t need to be. It has an art style that conveys what it needs to with filler music playing in the background and builds itself on making the combat fun and diverse as opposed to making the rest of the experience particularly enthralling. It doesn’t focus on crafting a story through lore in the characters and arenas like some other recent champion-focused games have, but instead, it goes all in on the idea of crafting a fast-paced arena experience. It’s laudable that the focus is so tight on what the developers are trying to accomplish, but as a game in itself, it’s not hard to see players being left wanting with the current cast of characters and maps, as well as with a price tag that will later be dropped. It’s fun and enjoyable, but that fun comes at a cost right now, so it’s hard to recommend at the moment for anyone who’s got other games in their backlog to hit or other multiplayer-centric titles to play.

Retro Family have once again composed a beautiful soundtrack to an original and graphically innovative setting in a world of nature where shelter is your only hope and survival your only goal.
