DISCLAIMER: This review is for the Early Access verion of RoA. Things are going to improve and be changed in the future.
As an avid Smash fan, I was extrememly excited for RoA. I even signed up for the beta and played the alpha builds a long time ago. To my unpleasant surprise, not much has changed.
Most of the game feels 'tacky' and rather lazy. The amount of options doesn't come close to matching up with flash projects such as Super Smash Flash or the like. The game has a very limited set of defensive options that don't allow for any creative leeway. That said, there's new mechanics, and they are interesting. Instead of implumenting a defensive shield-based system, Dan opted for a parry system. That's fine, new things ina 'Smash' scenario sound awesome.
The biggest problem is that the game has is it's way to defensive. The way the parrys work currently creates a heavy 'run in, do a combo string, then run the hell away' gameplan. Rinse and repeat.
After my time with the game it seems that the neutral is less about creativity and interesting approaches/follow ups and more about who messes up first and get's punished first. The footsies in the game are rediculious, and I'm sad the game is primarily that. I would have moved to have a better balance between character's defensive and offensive options.
As for reccomending this game, it's iffy. If you like Smash Bros. and have played it for years, I don't reccommend this. The design philosophy will feel foreign to you. For other crowds that want to get into fighting games, this might be a nice stepping stone to start with.

My brother in arms, klaeldemon, recently presented me with a surprise gift of one of the most engrossing strategy games I've ever played. Though I had not played any of the previous incarnations of Sins, Rebellion a natural fit, and offered an amazing degree of depth and PC user-friendly options and extras, including the unparalleled boon of being able to save multi-player games for later continuance. Though there is no story-driven campaign to speak of, skirmish play is great fun and moreso, co-op comp stomp with friends. With support for up to ten players in a game and map sizes varying from a single star system to a vast galactic expanse, a single match can offer many vigorous hours of gameplay. Each of the playable factions has a staggering array of mighty warships and combat abilities, but military conquest is but one path to victory. You can dominate through technological or economic superiority, or even seek the diplomatic path and achieve victory without firing a shot.
Once you get the game running at a steady framerate it is actually pretty great.

Silky: Complexity, depth, longevity of games, replayability.
Rough: Learning curve, documentation.
..oo00oo..
This is a good game IF you're the right kind of audience. That's probably not the most of endearing statements to make but there's a reason for it.
The learning curve, given it's development state and expected evolving documentation, is steep. It took several starts to actually work out what I had to do and I'll be honest, several times I nearly wtfragequit and many times I was heard muttering "ffs" when the game just did not comply or didn't make sense - and I'm the gentle type. It was downright frustrating - having said that, most of the issues seemed to stem (in hindsight) from lack of good documentation for something that is not simple to play.
By perservering (and you should), every new start revealed a little more and what keeps you playing is the complexity - no, it's not overwhelming but it's not a casual game either. This is an intriguing title - parroting much of the sim/build/upgrade genre - but there are some clever tech/progress gates that appear a bit blunt (almost traumatic) until you identify the "right" way to do it - well at least until you're ready to *really* upgrade with extra rings to increase the size of your colony.
(I sincerely hope that's not too cryptic but it's the closest I could get to the inherent beauty of this title - it just sucks you into "just one more build/fix/adjustment" well past midnight).
It will take you hours to identify those nuances embedded that make your colony shine and respond the way you hope and I found the LESS I tried to force the pace (a legacy of devs developing for the time-poor and casual audience these days) the better the game became.
I mentioned the type of audience you need to be here. Let me just say you need to be borderline anal-retentive, analytical, patient, forgiving and self-deprecating (it's probably not the games fault, it's YOU) and it's really helpful if you like the type of game that encapsulates intriguing gameplay, complete with probable lore to explain your situation.
As an EA title at time of writing, the active and listening devs are working on the documentation - among the frequent updates and bug report responses they address almost immediately. There are no faults in this department.
For the price - an easy buy. The test to whether you will like it or not is by considering whether what I wrote made sense to you. If it did, buy it.
If it didn't..... :)

Key to Beyond Earth is to judge it on its own. It is hard, especially with the legacy of Civilization and Alpha Centauri - most games would have a hard time to live up to those giants. Beyond Earth is more than just a Civ V space repaint. It takes many elements from Civ V and refines them, and sadly also loses them. Overall it is a fun game, that excels at some parts such as the new science tree, affinities and unit upgrades, and falters with its clunky UI and lack of Civ personalities.
The Pros:
Firaxis did a fantastic job creating a believable sci-fi alien world. The units and buildings are very detailed. One of the best features are the affinities. You can choose three paths how to react to your alien world. Live in harmony with it, become cyborg, or go with purity. Each path gives you certain advtantages, such as getting huge alien military units. The science tree is more like a web. Its not linear like the Civ V science tree, so you can kind of jump back and forth how you please. Unit upgrades have also been improved from Civ V. They include not just stat upgrades, but visual ones. If you go with the Supremacy Affinity your soldiers will turn into cyborgs. The soundtrack is beautiful, and fits the sci-fi theme nicely.
The Cons:
While Beyond Earth gets many things right, it sadly commits a few blunders. Firstly, the 8 civs have little to no personality, despite changing their look based on their affinity. Playing against Napoleon or Gandhi was much more entertaining and interesting, than the oddly bureaucratic looking civ leaders in Beyond Earth. What makes matters worse, the other civs aren't as important as they were in Civ V, as diplomacy has been trimmed down a lot, and the civs aren't as aggressive. In fact I would go so far and claim diplomacy can be completely ignored. The other problem are the meaningless world wonders. Instead of  a beautiful painting and a historical quote we get a picture of a blue print. Not just that, most world wonders lack statistical oomph, and are glorified city buildings. The UI could also use some streamlining, as it is extremely clunky. Lastly the game suffers of some balance issues. Right now trade routes are insanely powerful, and overall difficulty is just too easy.
The Verdict:
Civ Beyond Earth on its own is a good game. The problem is that many people compare it to Alpha Centauri, or Civ V fully patched with two expansions. While 50 dollars is a bit steep, I think it has enough beef to be its own game. With some balancing and patching this game will be a successful game, if people are willing/able to look past the giants of Civ V and Alpha Centauri, and judge it by its own merits.

Bioshock is still a great game almost a decade later, despite some pacing and difficulty spike issues in the last quarter or so. It plays totally fine with a keyboard & mouse and ran smooth throughout my playtime. I'm not sure how much better this  looks than the original 2007 release as I haven't played that version in a long time, but while it's visiuals do show some age, the game does look good and still retains the strong art direction and atmopshere it always had.
In my experience with the remaster, I encountered a handful of audio bugs where dialouge would skip and stutter, which I don't recall happening in the original whatsoever, but each instance would correct itself after a few seconds. I also had the game crash twice, one of which resulted in an hour of lost progress I was forced to replay.
My biggest issue with Bioshock Remastered is that some aspects of it are not optimzied as well as they should be. The game does not auto-detect your montior's resolution, defaulting instead to the highest possible setting it offers regardless of your setup, which for me resulted in all the icons and windows open on my desktop to be wildly shifted around so I was forced to repostion them every time I quit the game. And both times the game crashed, all my chosen graphical settings were reset, causing the problem to worsen. In 2016, and with a game that's almost a decade old, the remaster simply shouldn't have these problems.
I'm giving this game a recommendation because it's Bioshock and overall the game ran and worked fine for me. But the issues stated above were annoyances that should have been ironed out before release. This is a game you should play, but depending on how you feel about the above issues I stated, you may want to wait for a patch first.

DISCLAIMER: This review is for the Early Access verion of RoA. Things are going to improve and be changed in the future.
As an avid Smash fan, I was extrememly excited for RoA. I even signed up for the beta and played the alpha builds a long time ago. To my unpleasant surprise, not much has changed.
Most of the game feels 'tacky' and rather lazy. The amount of options doesn't come close to matching up with flash projects such as Super Smash Flash or the like. The game has a very limited set of defensive options that don't allow for any creative leeway. That said, there's new mechanics, and they are interesting. Instead of implumenting a defensive shield-based system, Dan opted for a parry system. That's fine, new things ina 'Smash' scenario sound awesome.
The biggest problem is that the game has is it's way to defensive. The way the parrys work currently creates a heavy 'run in, do a combo string, then run the hell away' gameplan. Rinse and repeat.
After my time with the game it seems that the neutral is less about creativity and interesting approaches/follow ups and more about who messes up first and get's punished first. The footsies in the game are rediculious, and I'm sad the game is primarily that. I would have moved to have a better balance between character's defensive and offensive options.
As for reccomending this game, it's iffy. If you like Smash Bros. and have played it for years, I don't reccommend this. The design philosophy will feel foreign to you. For other crowds that want to get into fighting games, this might be a nice stepping stone to start with.

Final Fantasy 13 is a mixed bag.
Pros: The game and the animations are very beautiful and has a fantastic soundtrack
Cons: Phew, where to start?
Characters: none of the characters are likable. Yes, Light and Snow may be quite decent towards the end of the game, but overall I never felt like I WANTED to see what was happening to them, I felt like pressing the 'skip' button more than I would have liked to.
Progression: Compared to previous games, the progression was different, but felt like a chore. It was a mix between "how far does this chapter get me on the board" versus "what do I really need" versus "grinding your a**" off. I think that is where I would have preferred more of a challenge than mindless grinding. Don't get me wrong, I have played all FF games up until 13, so I know about grinding, but never has it felt this slow!
Levels: while beautiful, it is essentially a "walk along a corridor to the next cutscene". Many paths I walked on ranged from "amazing vistas" to "dull caves with one or two large textures changed between them". Compared to previous games in the series it wasn't helped at all by the higher resolution of art assets.
Video sequences / cutscenes: The video sequences in many cases were stunning and of his production value, but the cutscenes ranged from "passable" to "filler" in an attempt to either pace the game (didn't need to do that, it was already a chore) or add some backstory to the characters or exposing plot twists you could see a mile away.
Overall, the game feels dull, slow, a grind. If you are a hardcore FF fan and you want to finish all games of the series then I wish you good luck and patience. If you are in for a challenge, then many other games will enable you to just do that. The setting is nice, the music fantastic, but everything else feels lacklustre, slow paced, a grind, a waste of your time and a grind without ever feeling your choices (other than your progression to add more HP or strength) matter, all put to life with a broring script, way too few "wow" moments and a cast of unlikable characters who moan and whine more than wanting to actually do something.
Most memorable moment: When the characters themselves said "it must be the end soon, surely, this is taking far too long". Exactly my thoughts!
Based on all that, I cannot recommend this game. It took me just over 13h to finish it, I did not complete all side missions.

This game is a great Smash Bros-lite for PC, probably the best attempt at translating the mechanics of smash to another game that I have seen. If you enjoy Smash, you will likely enjoy the basic gameplay of this game. At the time of this review, there are 6 characters, 5 stages, and only 2 modes (2-4 player versus and 1v1 online). While this isn't a huge amount of content, what is there is really good, and there seem to be 2 more characters and I believe 3 more stages planned based on the greyed out options in the menus. There seems to also be two more modes planned, including a story mode. Based on this, I can safely say more content is coming, and the content promised is likely to be delivered as it isn't all that much more than what is already available,
As far as comparing the game to Smash, I would say that for a $15 title it compares well. While it has no where near the amount of characters as Smash, falling short of even the original N64 Smash Bros, the characters available are all quite unique and varied. Most of them have moves and abilities unlike anything I've seen in Smash, and this helps differentiate the game from its source of inspiration. Some particularly original abilities include the Earth Beetle's up special, which pulls a giant pillar of stone from the ground right under the character's feet. So cool! Another example is that the Bird character can shoot a whirlwind that leaves a trail of wind behind, making his movement speed faster inside the trail. The attention to detail is really impressive here, as each character's abilities fit perfectly with their look and the way they handle. The bird is lightweight and has wings, and thus focuses on aerial moves and speed, whereas the beetle is larger and slower, focusing on slower, heavier attacks and keeping his feet firmly planted on the ground. The other 4 characters have their own quirks and specialties, but I won't spoil them for you here. While Rivals doesn't offer the breadth of content of a Smash game, it maintains a similar level of quality with the content it does provide. As someone who sees the Smash titles as some of the most polished games ever made, this is a big compliment.
The graphics  are a simple, 2D, pixelated style often seen in indie games. While this is not out of the ordinary, the art direction and design of each character and stage conveys a unique sense of identity and place. This is the perfect example of a game that uses the pixelated 2D style that is so common and elevates it, making it something original and aesthetically pleasing. I like the choice of anthropomorphic animals, as it ties in well with the four elements theme the game has.
Overall, this is a great game, and one of the best early access titles I've ever played. While I usually avoid early access titles, as they can feel half-baked and unfinished, this game is an exception to that rule. The base mechanics and gameplay are all here, and the additional content to come will simply add to an already great experience. If you want to wait until all of the content is out, feel free, but if you buy now you are still getting a great experience, and will have reason to revisit the game later once further content is released. The game is already in a polished, playable, and (most importantly) fun state, and I whole-heartedly recommend a purchase, especially if you can hook up 4 controllers and gather some friends around your TV or monitor.

The strong points of the game come in the form of great research trees, wonderful diplomacy aspects and an interesting pirate mechanic. There are 3 seperate research paths for each race, with some unique upgrades to each race. Diplomacy has to researched in the respected research path, with the ability to offer pacts and agreements to other players. The pirate system in the game works by having a neutral race (which can be toggled on and off) attack the player with the highest bounty on their head, this often leads to bounty war in order to get the pirates attention off you and onto the enemy.
One of the downsides to the game is that each game takes an eon to complete. We can be talking hours to finish a medium to large game.
Overall I would highly recommend this game to anyone who is interested in Sci-Fi RTS games.

I'm recommending this game because they fixed the grass.
They fixed the grass.
The first time I played this game, grass was so hideously drawn that it was actually a distraction. It was that two-dimenional stuff that rotates with you so that you're always facing it, like in a bad hologram. I looked on the game's blog, and there were a number of complaints about visuals, to which the dev team basically said, "Minecraft proves people don't care about graphics."
But people kept complaining. And I stopped playing the game because I couldn't stop staring at how ugly the grass was.
And they fixed it. The devs defended a position, and when people continued to argue for why it was wrong, they relented, and they responded to what the players value.
It's also a really cool experience with a lot of room for adventure and discovery. But it could have been that, undone by dev tone-deafness. But they fixed the grass.
Next on the list: There is absolutely no excuse in this day and age to have a limited number of save slots in the game.

I recently purchased the game and have played it for a little while (as you can undoubtedly tell), and I thought I would add my perspective.
I really enjoy city builders, and was hoping I would get that when I bought it; what I received wasn't quite what I expected, but in a good way! While it is listed as a city builder, it would be more accurate to call it a base builder (anyone familiar with Stronghold will feel at home with this one).
Please bear in mind that I don't really care for the hard levels which have natural disasters, enemies, &c, preferring instead to have a leisurely and peaceful game; therefore, your experience may vary. Yes, I realise that may make me a wimp, but some of us don't enjoy getting our bases wiped out because we're terrible tacticians. :P
The positive stuff:
1. Very Good: In my opinion, there are two mechanics within Project AURA which are absolutely fantastic; one of them is the item system. Each building has a blueprint that allows you to choose any additional "modules" (for lack of a better term) to add to the main structure, and you can also adjust where everything sits in the blueprint (a very nice feature as well, given the space constraints at the beginning). Once you have everything set up, you click on a button with the Market symbol on it and, once you confirm the purchase, all of the needed materials are bought at once. No more jumping back and forth and writing down/memorising what you need to get and in what amount; that button purchases all of the materials at once (which is extremely helpful for me because the going back and forth s*** makes me want to stab myself in the eye to experience something less agonising).
2. Very Good: The second fantastic mechanic is the ability to find out what anything requires in terms of the "recipe" in order to make it (a la Minecraft, Subnautica, etc). F2 opens up a window that enables you to determine what you need to build something. You click and hold the object, move it over to the window and put it in the appropriate slot, and there you go.
3. Good: No micromanaging!
4. Good: I have a decent graphics card (GeForce GTX 960) and experienced absolutely no lag/stuttering. I have the graphics on High and it works just fine for me.
5. Good: I went to the company's forum page and it would appear they are pretty good at responding to people who post messages, which is a positive sign.
6. Trivial: The different occupations are indicated by different helmets. I must admit that is a new mechanic for me and I don't bother remembering which one goes to what profession, but it's actually pretty cool all the same.
The negative stuff:
1. Bad (conditional): The only real issue I have is the disjointedness in some aspects of the game. While there is nothing game-breaking or requiring anger management courses, some of the item/building/material descriptions can be confusing and/or lack information. By way of example, one of the power creating buildings tells you it increases power intake, but there is no indication in the power screen that it is doing so. I eventually figured out that it delivers a single packet of energy at the beginning of the day. Certain items have requirements that aren't immediately apparent, which has led to some frustration. However, these are easy things to forgive because they are still working on it (and, as mentioned before, the developers seem to be taking an active interest in hearing what players have to say on these issues, so these issues should be eliminated/corrected in a future patch).
2. Trivial: The somewhat primitive camera. You can move in the usual manner with the WASD keys, and zoom in with the wheel, but that's about it. This is not a camera function I am accustomed to, so it took some getting familiar with it.
3. Trivial: You'll be waiting a lot at the beginning while your ships gather items.
All in all, this is your standard base builder like many others of its type, but the very useful mechanics regarding items and the ability to know what you need to build something modestly places it ahead. While it does have some issues, they are expected and/or trivial, making them reasonably negligible.
Regardless, I continue to play it and look forward to seeing what the developers do with this game in the future.

As much as I love Civilization V, I simply cannot recommend this game to fans of the series.
The core gameplay elements are okay, but at the moment, it just feels like there is a lack of content considering the price tag.
You get a total of about 8 different units to choose from throughout the course of the game, regardless of the affinity you choose, which is incredibly disappointing, the AI is practically useless (I was only attacked once throughout two seperate games), The different civilizations feel lackluster in terms of their traits, and their leaders, wonders don't feel special at all, or give you a sense of accomplishment for building them, and to top it all off, there are tons of bugs in the game currently.
The quest system and different types of victories are very interesting, and I enjoy being able to shape my own type of civilization based on my own choices throughout the game, but I wish that some of the decisions were more impactful, and didn't rely basically upon which type of resources you start the game with.
Aliens are in my opinion, an improvement upon the barbarians from Civ V, due to theoir increased difficulty and levels of aggression, leading them to be something to plan for in all stages of the game. The only thing that is annoying about the aliens are the seige worms, which until you are much later in the game, are essentially impossible to kill, which can be a huge problem for a developing Civ.
In a nutshell, If you were expecting better gameplay, I would just stick to the game's predecessor, Civ V, and experiment with modding, or just enjoy a more fleshed out game experience. At this game's current stage, the game itself is just boring, unbalanced, and not very fun in general. It has a few things going for it, but until some developmental changes are made to this game, I cannot recommend a purchase, as much as it pains me to say it.

Years ago I said I'd never play Final Fantasy XIII. Just never cared for the direction the franchise was going. I had played the first Final Fantasy on the NES when it first game out. Final Fantasy II (IV) and III (VI) on the SNES. Was never a big fan of series from there on, although I do like VII (I just don't agree it's the masterpiece Milliennials think it is.). That being said, I saw SquareEnix has this on sale on their website for $6.50, but I still wasn't interested... Then I saw it contained the Japanese audio. SHUT UP AND TAKE MY MONEY! Only a little over 2 hours in, and I can see why people complained about the first few hours calling it a "tutorial." But hey, at $6.50, and Japanese audio, I'm already satisfied! Or... not.
The game is as (or more) linear than Super Mario Bros (NES) in that you follow a directed path with no exploration WHAT SO EVER AT ALL (BORING!). Run down this magically created pathway, kill enemies, proceed to next area, jump up some debris, jump down the debris, battle, enter next pathway. I'm falling asleep walking in a straight line.
Battles attempt to be something special, and the first 20 or 30 battles were ok... But then it's just boring as ****. There is no strategy to it, NONE. None of the thinking or tactics of older Final Fantasy games. Nope, just let AUTO BATTLE do what it has to do, switch up the paradigm IF/WHEN needed. Lack of control over the other characters makes this a completely dull experience.
And then there's the story. The game doesn't even try to explain what fal'Cie, l'Cie, Pulse, Cocoon, Eden, or any frakin' thing is. They just throw it at you like you should already know. Seriously, it's worse than the writing for season 8 of Doctor Who. Somebody should have been fired from SE for this abomination.
I can see why SquareEnix has to re release Final Fantasy IV and VII constantly... They're great games, THIS and most recent Square games are NOT.

"A very suprising game. Definitely a good purchase, spent quite a few hours in the game and had fun playing against AI. Can't wait to get better at this game and play some online some time."
This was my original review when I only had clocked a few hours of game time. After having played more games I would definitely recommend this game to this anyone who is fan of the RTS or 4X genre. The strong points of the game come in the form of great research trees, wonderful diplomacy aspects and an interesting pirate mechanic. There are 3 seperate research paths for each race, with some unique upgrades to each race. Diplomacy has to researched in the respected research path, with the ability to offer pacts and agreements to other players. The pirate system in the game works by having a neutral race (which can be toggled on and off) attack the player with the highest bounty on their head, this often leads to bounty war in order to get the pirates attention off you and onto the enemy.
One of the downsides to the game is that each game takes an eon to complete. We can be talking hours to finish a medium to large game.
Overall I would highly recommend this game to anyone who is interested in Sci-Fi RTS games.

I was wary of the port quality, so I waited until the graphics settings update to buy the game. So far, I've been pretty satisfied. If you haven't played FF13 yet, this is the version to get if you think your computer can handle it. The game looks great, and while the framerate seems locked around 30 most of the time, and ocassionally dips to 20 (and less occasionally gets up to 60), it's very playable. Load times are pretty snappy and faster than I remember them being on the Xbox, despite my HDD being pretty slow (7200rpm). No room on my SSD for this 50GB game.
What's interesting is that after playing with shadow resolution and AA settings, the framerates aren't really affected that much for me. Whether I'm at the lowest shadow and AA settings (512x512 and x2) or the highest settings (8192x8192 and x16), FPS tends to be at 30 more often than not. The only difference is that at lower settings, I'll occassionally see framerates jump to 60 for brief periods, and the dips to ~20FPS are rarer (but still occur). At max settings, 30 is as high as I get, and dips to the 20s are slightly more frequent (and I can hear my fans working a bit harder).
So it's playable, pretty, but not perfect. Definitely room for improvement regarding performance. You probably won't get solid 60FPS by playing with the settings using the default config options, unfortunately. I'm willing to look past the dips and accept 30 FPS because this is a pretty slow paced game and not a twitch shooter - they're annoying, but not terrible or gamebreaking. If you're on the fence about picking this up because of the port quality, I'd say go for it.
Misc info:
1920x1080 resolution, fullscreen (not windowed)
Using an Xbox 360 controller (controls are fine - maybe the camera angling is a bit wonky at times)
i5-3570k @ 3.4GHz
Radeon HD7950, not overclocked
Other stuff I forgot about
The description text for enemies isn't displaying at 1080p, so that's pretty lame.
There is an option to choose English or Japanese voices when you launch the game.
There is an option in-game to specify whether messages about user input should display with keyboard prompts or controller prompts. By default it was set to "keyboard", so I changed it.
I didn't try to play with keyboard settings, but for the controller there was just an image displaying which button did what (i.e. no re-mapping).
Early in the game there is some female-on-male violence that may trigger sensitive MRA types. The scenes would have been loudly protested if the genders were reversed, I imagine.

- PC Port Review by
Final Fantasy XIII was originally a console exclusive title like most of the titles in the FF series, however 13 and some other Final Fantasy games have been recently ported to PC along with some other old-school JRGPs like Valkyria Chronicles.
Unfortunately the quality of port is much below expectation, even though it has been patched several times it still has some serious flaws. Performance is terrible even on most powerful PCs although this game is several years old. The engine also stutters every few seconds if you don't plug-in a controller or use a virtual (fake) one. Also the game provides very little graphic customization options.
Being a very bad port is the only downside of this game. Final Fantasy XIII is one of the best JRPG titles ever released and has won several awards. If you manage to get over the troubled shell, you will find a beautiful gem inside.
Gameplay structure is a bit different than most RPG & JRPG titles available on the market. Most of your playtime will be spent battling various monsters and enemies through game's innovative battle system called ATB (Active Time Battle). ATB is closer to Turn-Based gameplay of traditional JRPG games rather than Real-Time. Your party consists of two or three characters, of which only the leader can be controlled. The rest of your party is controlled by AI which does a pretty good job.
The progression speed of the game is very slow which can frustrate impatient and casual players. Game takes a very long time to unlocks all of its gameplay features. It's basically like a very long tutorial that makes up for almost half of your playtime before showing you the true game. Final Fantasy 13 is mostly linear with paths filled with enemies and a cut-scene at the end.
Overall, gameplay is very addictive and rewarding. It's a difficult game to fully accomplish and some of the optional bosses and enemies need a lot of grinding to defeat.
Story is where Final Fantasy titles shine, Final Fantasy 13 is no exception. It has a very expansive lore and a really intriguing story. Although it may be a little hard to grasp for newcomers, it's what you would remember for a long time once you understand its true nature. Characters are presented in a very good way and as they develop, story becomes more and more interesting.
Final Fantasy 13 is like a living, breathing world that you can live in.
The original game is a relatively old title so we can't except cutting-edge technology and mind-blowing visuals. However, the art design of the game is simply fantastic. As with most Japanese titles, a lot of work has been put into art design. Every single monster you encounter looks alive, every single character you see look real. The world is very beautiful.
Unfortunately, the technical aspect of the game and its weak engine can't really catch up with today's standards but the art design can easily make up for it.
Again, another area in which Final Fantasy titles have always been great is music. Soundtrack is amazing and you feel like you want to listen to it over and over again. Sound Effects are great too and Voice Acting is professional. Both Japanese and English voice actors should be proud of their work.
Final Fantasy 13 is one of the best JRPG games that I've ever played, however the PC port feels very rushed and is done terribly. It still doesn't make the game itself a bad title, but the PC release is really a weak port. I'd recommend getting it on the console if you haven't played it already (and own a console, of course) but if you don't have a console, well PC seems to be your only choice.

Quick list of pros/cons so far (will update as I play more)...
Pro:
+Cool setting
+Production chains seem cool and rewarding once completed though I've seen people complain they're too long.
+I have my first like 7 step production chain running and it makes me happy.
+Colonists can be personalized though you barely see them...
+I actually like the node system - just gotta remember to start production as buildings won't autostart. Perhaps a Preference in options to enable this by default would be good?
+YOU CAN HARVEST POOP!
+So many nodes.
Con:
-Click and drag is very laggy and unresponsive for me. Could just be my PC but the game runs fine.
-Could just be my novice status so far but the Power Grid is annoying and convoluted. I figured it out but I'm still low on power. Starting "Packs" could royally slow your expansion down if you choose the not so ideal ones.
-Info on Research seems quite scant. Wasn't in the tutorials. I think I've figured it out though. You won't be able to trade with all faction on the market without Diplomacy research - wherever that is. Again, starting affinity could slow your expansion down too.
Neutral:
~I'd like to be able to zoom in more.
~Tutorials are good overall but I think could have used some more details (there is in-game text help)
~When splitting stacks, it should just appear in your inventory instead of having to drag the stack back to the inventory from the little window. Should also be able to type in a number in this window.
~Multiple windows open at a time can get annoying. Escape key will close them quickly enough and saves this from being a con.
~Previous untested patches caused people to get locked out of supply chains. Was patched. Hopefully won't happen again.
So, will update as I play more. I'd recommend in its current state despite only 2.7 hours of playtime :)

I have played through several times now. I've got mixed feelings.
Nice is automatic upgrades of units rather than having to spend money to upgrade them(which meant I often had very antique units in my Civ games guarding cities). Nice is the sci-fi elements (no more General Ghandi to worry about). Nice are some of the units, although it takes too long in game to get really sci-fi'ish units unless you're playing harmony. Mostly, tanks, troops, jets.
Overall, I found the game a bit tedious. Too many turns seem to go by with nothing really happening. This is a risk with turn based 4x games, but so far this seems particularly grindy.
Aliens are underdone, more an annoyance and easily eliminated as a factor early in the game. They get to be mobile scenery very quickly once you get purity level 1 and the fence with only the Manticores being a bother. Explorers quickly come to ignore aliens and this lets you move and build your colonies in alien infested areas as you can stack the two. They aren't even "real" aliens, they are more like alien wildlife. The Siege Worms are currently the most underwhelming part. Something is bugged with the bugs' aggressiveness. That said, given the number that seem able to spawn early in the game when there's still a lot of fog of war, under aggressive is probably better than overaggresive
Not stacking units seemed ok given ranged units are more common. But, every map I've place has LOTS of blocking terrain (mountains and canyons). Late game, canyons become less an issue as floaters and large walkers become available.  However, before they are available, choke points become more of a factor. There is no mountain crossing unit I've found yet and aircraft seem to frequently have too little range to reach enemy cities. There is a teleporter sattellite but that leads to the next problem:
Orbital units can be expected to not last 1 turn once your cold wars go hot. they will IMMEDIATELY be shot down by the enemy. I have yet to see an option that allows them to survive the first anti-orbital strike. Orbital lasers, teleporters, etc, are best put out of range of cities, which is a strategy and sometimes gets you around the terrain problems. However, orbital units cannot overlap coverage, making it difficult to place more than one at a time. They also have limited duration before they deorbit, making maintenance of your orbital network a manual process. It makes a new feature an also-ran. You have to use them, but the best orbitals are solar collectors(virtually mandatory to keep your energy levels high in the mid game and even into the late game) and  miasma removers(early on before workers get the option or you get far enough on the harmony track to ignore it).  The "offensive" orbitals end up being either defensive or single use bombs. That would be ok, but you can't even build an orbital in a city if you have one "on the launch pad". Also, there seems to be no list I can find that lists WHERE unlaunched orbitals are waiting, which can be annoying if you don't write it down or forget.
The "you win" or "you lose" screens are just horrible. A bit of text and a back ground image. It doesn't even scroll and I have yet to find a game summary screen of any sort. Just "you win".  The "contact" victory text and "you lose" in particular are horrid.  I lost one game simply because I forgot to pay attention to the AI's progress on victory, but the text telling me I lost told me nothing, so I don't even know what conditions it won on or which AI player won.
Ultimately, this is a spiritual successor to Alpha Centari, but there are a lot of issues that bog it down. I'm giving it a "not recommended" because there's no "mixed feelings" selection. While I'm not the kind that demands every game have a huge story, the lack of  background info and meaningful end game text is very disappointing.
Wonderful loot and potentialy never ending, though it starts to get a little grueling towrds the end of the story.

Black Flag was the first game I ever "reviewed" on my Steam account and as such, I didn't give it any real justice.
Black Flag is herald as one, if not the best of the series and for good reason. It brings us an interesting protagonist with solid, naval gameplay. It has its drawbacks sure but it ultimately turns into a wonderful experience all around.
I'm not usually keen on playing "Yet Another White Male" but Edward's depth really sold me on him. He has a perfectly understandable outlook of "I want walls that hold back the wind and cold, I want food that doesn't taste like dust". This is not an exact quote as I'm reinstalling after probably a year since I've played it last, but that is effectively his motive; To not be poor. This leads him to the pirate life (Or "Privateers" as he tries to convince his girlfriend that going away for a year is what's best for them) and further leads into his snarky devil-may-care attitude. He gets plenty of dialog that shows the full gamut of personality that involves greed, fear, worry, confusion, and bravery. This is how you write a character, people.
The game does not waste time getting Edward in his own ship with mechanics you might recall were tapped into in AC3 but never utilized and was mostly stuck in an optional gimmick. It returns here in full blast with solid broadside mechanics that eventually turn into a melee as you render enemy ships inert. You follow through on a couple of objectives and call it a victory. It's one of my favorite aspects of the game and even includes a sort of ship-based stealth mission or two as you try to navigate your ship through swamps, avoid massive Man O War's, and risk exploring contested waters.
If there's a drawback, it's that the game focuses so much on the naval combat (Which, again, is wonderful) that the on-foot missions suffer greatly. Most of them involve following a mark around and staying within an audio bubble to hear them properly. They are frequently irritating and not as interesting as the more straightforward assassinations that the series is known for.
For those who felt the 'modern day' segments were a blight, they thankfully take more of a backseat here. You step into the role of a voiceless employee that navigate the headquarters on your off-time and suss out the secrets of the company. Ultimately you are whomever you wish to be and exploring is largely optional as most of the time you can just 'log back in' and go straight back into the game proper.
Regardless of one's opinion on Ubisoft and recent business practices; I highly recommend you get this game. Even if you're not a fan of the franchise, Black Flag stands on its own two feet and you won't need to know a lot of lore to be invested in Edward's personal journey. Please get this game.

Verdict: 9/10 (in isolation). However if you already own Civ5, dont bother buying this game. And if you dont own Civ5, I would recommend buying Civ5 instead(with all the expansions), you will get a better and more engaging/polished experience.
Civ5 was one of the best games of all times. Beyond Earth however is dissapointing. Its basically a different skin on top of Civ5, with a few add-ons like quests/mini-missions which IMO they dont really add much value, and I think they will quickly become annoying once you have played through a few games.
The biggest dissappointment compared to Civ5 is however is that there have been NO improvement of the enemy AI whatsoever. And the agression level of your opponents is also basically non-existant. I won the very first game I played basically with no opposition at all. And like Civ5, the only way to crank up the difficulty level is by giving the computer fake advantages. This means on higher difficulty levels the computer dont actually plays smarter, its simply giving various boosts, which means its not really competing with you on a fair level. Its like playing chess with a computer, but instead of the computer getting smarter on higher difficulty level, they give the computer an extra Queen or something. This is why I basically stopped enjoying Civ5/BE, the base AI game is too weak, unless you give the computer unfair advantages.
So I hope for their next Civ game the developers invest more money on improving the AI and making the game more challenging. They have a very sound platform for making an awesome game, they just need to find a way to make the opposition smarter WITHOUT cheating. by giving the computer extra units/build speed. And the computer opponents need to be more aggressive.

A polished sequel to Bloodline Champions with an attentive dev team and a lovingly crafted cast, there are is not currently a better isometric arena brawler on the market.  Using an exact copy of Overwatch's progression system, matches in this game are on an even playing field and character customization is already relatively rich even in early access.  The structure of each round is a fast paced hero deathmatch, focusing on casting powerful skill-shot abilities while simultaneously reacting to and countering enemy ability usage.  Intelligently spending your EX energy (think fighting games) on powerful enhanced abilities or your ultimate ability in each round allows you to employ a wide variety of potential strategies over the course of a match.  Between each round in a match you customize your character with the titular battlerites (passive abilities that modify your active abilities) so that you may better counter your opponent's' character choices, play styles, and their battlerite selections.  If you enjoy fast-paced tactical games that reward reading your opponents and obliterating them with carefully aimed spells then this game is for you.

A short yet beautiful adventure where your maternal/paternal instincts take over.
It's a charming and short game about motherhood and trying to protect your young in a cold world.
The game clocks in a little over an hour yet it doesn't overstay its welcome with its simplistic mechanics of feeding your young, trying to keep them together and keeping them from being devoured. The game is pretty simple but keeping your young alive is surprisingly difficult and over the course of your hour you'll find plenty of twists and turns and new mechanics to keep things free.
You'll mostly be wandering around, trying to feed your children by either knocking down apples or even hunting small animals. There will even be times where you are met with more children than food and you have to choose who to feed (hungry children will fade and grow weaker and slower making them easy prey). Avoiding eagles, creatures of the night, trying to keep them calm when they run away scared and keeping them alive during natural disasters makes you grow attached to them.
My only criticism is that for a game so short there are loading screens (which are quick) but load into very different areas of the forest. Such a short game would have been much better at providing a more seamless transition between the "areas" of the forest.
All in all it's a great game.

How to fix the stutter/lags:
It has nothing to do with your PC or Intel/AMD - Final Fantasy 13 will search a GamePad or Controller. You have now 2 options.
1. Plug-IN a controller (PS3/PS4 GamePad)
2. or Install a Virtual GamePad Device ( you dont need a Gamepad for this - you can still play the game with Keyboard and Mouse)
Its a device driver that bridges the gap between any device that is not a joystick and an application that requires a joystick. (its a "Ghost-GamePad" - something like that).
Download vJoy and install - here is the Link:
This should fix the Problem.

Deutsch/German:
Problemlösung - ruckeln/lags:
Das Ruckeln hat nichts mit dem PC oder Intel/AMD zu tun - Final Fantasy 13 sucht ständig nach einem Gamepad/Controller. Dies verursacht die kleinen Lags. Es gibt nun 2 Möglichkeiten:
1. Spiel mit einem PS3/PS4 Controller
2. oder installiere ein virtuelles GamePad (du brauchst dafür kein richtiges GamePad/Controller - du kannst das Spiel weiterhin mit Tastatur und Maus spielen)
Es ist ein Geräte Treiber der dem System ein GamePad "emuliert" und somit das Problem zwischen Tastatur/Maus und Controller-Suche verhindert.
Man könnte es so erklären: Man gaukelt dem System vor das man ein Controller benutzt; aber dennoch mit Tastatur & Maus spielt.
Das sollte das Problem Beheben.
Best wishes - Flora

Overall, if you're going to play a colony sim, try something else

Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth is no Alpha Centauri reboot or remake. It doesn't even try that hard to hide the fact it's using Civilization V: Brave New World as a baseline - but Brave New World is a damn good baseline. Couple the solid gameplay of Brave New World with new elements such as a non-linear tech tree, greater civ customisation options and an epic sci-fi soundtrack by Geoff Knorr, and you've got a game that's sure to keep you entertained for several hours if not hundreds. Sure the game is still a bit buggy and unpolished at the moment but Firaxis are already aware of some of these issues and once they're done, this will be a solid entry to the Civilization series and highly recommended for those who enjoy hard science fiction or even sci-fi books on planetary ecology, like Frank Herbert's Dune. Just as it was with Alpha Centauri.

Hollow Knight. . . where to begin? Overall is is a fairly difficult platformer with many bosses and enemies. There also NPCs that one may become friends with. There never really seems to be a object without reason here. Everything has a purpose.I will go over many pro and con that may may question whether you should buy.
PROS:
-Its a platformer but is also a difficult game. It balances combat and platforming.
-The art. Its a hand drawn art style that brings evevy detail out.
-The enemies: They all have a unique attributes, an enemy could be there just to block a path or to kill you. . .
-The mechanics: You can nevery realy become OP you are almost always just right. You gain more and more skills throughtout the game. Most of these are platforming based but can help in a pinch. There are also many hidden mechanics of sorts that are extremely help full, such as the Spike Bounce. There are also charms to accmodate your play style. Charms provide boost and abilities to you character The Knight.
-Quest: Beside the main game many characters have quests. For example there is a qeust that give you a hp item.
-Collectables: There are many items that acount for completion percent and that jsut help. For example you need 4 Mask Shard to get more HP.
-Level design: Many level have a large explorable area that can hold many secrets. Some you cant get to until you have obtained a special ability. This game rewards exploration. There may or may not be hidden walls you ahve to hit. wink wink
-Difficulty. This game can be as easy, or as hard as you make it. You can make you charater take more damage for example. But most of the difficult thats already there is not unfair. Alot of difficulties can come from quests, trying to 100% etc.
CONS
-There can be sometimes where you may grind for a good amount, it isnt bad but can sometime be annoying. For example there is a lantern for 1800 Geo (your currency). You need it for an entire area of the game. This area is not optional either. 1800 is a good amount so you may grind an area a few time to afford it.
-Hidden items: This is more of a pro (for me at least) because it promotes eploration. But if you are casually running through and not hitt every goddamn wall, you will miss alot of items, some more important that others. No key item though I believe, taht would just be dumb.
-Hidden Tech: Again more por that con for me. but I put this under cons because its cons for others. There are certain item that you can't get without knowing if an ability can do this. It promotes ecpermenting but again no one wants to try every combination of abilitys to reach a charm.
Final Verdict:
There aren't many Cons as I really like the game. (biased much lol) But I can't see some pros being cons and some cons being pros for other people. Like I dont like grinding, its repetitive and annoying. But the game does feel very polished and well thoughtout. Team Cherry did an amazing job. This game is $15 and even down to $10 during sales. This game could have easily been like $40 and I would buy it. You easily get 100 hours out of this game especially if you truly enjoy it. Would reccomend, this post is kida biased but it is an opinion. There are also 2 more DLCs knwon to come out so this game will be even better soon!

So yeah. I've defended this game against naysayers for a while now but I think it's about time I ate my own words somewhat.
While BE is undoubtedly still a decent game, playing it for the past 10 or so hours has made it abundantly clear why there should have been an open beta. And I'm not referring to complaints about how this doesn't live up to the legacy of SMAC or how it's too similar to Civ 5. I wish those were the only issues. Suffice it to say there are a lot of missteps that really shouldn't have made it past the testing stage. The game is missing a lot of key UI features and shortcuts that were already present in Civ 5 and you'd think would have transitioned quite easily into this title.
For instance, why are we never told when something is built? Unless it's a wonder, the city just prompts you to select something new without ever telling you what was just completed. And while I'm glad to see more trade routes, why do I need to refresh all of them over and over without any option to just leave them to continue trading until canceled? I realize that wasn't an option in Civ 5, but with all the routes we have to micromanage now, it really ought to be.
Meanwhile, things I'd like to have dragged out - such as victory completions - are even more lackluster than in Civ 5. It's just a water color painting and an option to either play a few more turns or leave to the main menu. That's it. Where are the endgame screens with the graphs and maps and a rating of my performance or anything else that would offer the player some semblance of closure and completion? Totally absent. On the other hand, if I lose, why am I never even told what victory condition was used to win the game? I can't even check in the quest log because there's no option to "Keep Playing" if I lose.
There's no way to track the victory progress of rival factions beyond vague quarterly updates, so I'm forced to limit the game to the only victory conditions I can keep tabs on, namely Timed and Domination. There's also no diplomatic view to see which factions are at war with each other, the aliens can more or less be avoided until you're powerful enough to completely crush them, after which they become completely irrelevant, and the quests will occasionally have bizarrely impossible tasks such as constructing a petrochemical plant near a city that doesn't have a petroleum resource.
These are all things that really should've been implemented or ironed out before even setting a release date.
I enjoy the sci-fi aesthetic, I like the darker, almost twilight atmosphere and planetscape, the quests give me things to do instead of just pressing END TURN ad nauseum, espionage is much more rewarding, and the Affinity system offers a sense of direction and purpose that I always felt was lacking in previous Civ games that weren't SMAC. The units are fewer but more versatile, the sense of adventure and discovery more palpable than in Civ 5 and assuming multiplayer works the way it should, I see it being a lot more enjoyable than Civ 5.
That said, it feels like I'm playing an incomplete game. Quotes and voice acting are rather forgettable, attack animations seem to have been an afterthought, with impact explosions not even implemented for most units, Prosperity absolutely trumps all other Virtue trees, orbital layer isn't nearly as useful as the devs made it out to be, and immersion in terms of the overall narrative just isn't there. I mean come on, at least let me check to see how my own faction leader's appearance changes with my Affinity progress. Give me some monuments. Show my workers changing along with my affinity, even if it's just aesthetically. Give me a Planetary Council to exert diplomatic pressure on my rivals. Something. ANYTHING.
Really hoping to see a lot of patching and hotfixes in the coming months.

This is a unique game. It has a lot going for it, but bare in mind that this is not a game for everybody. What you get here is a vary deep production-chain and population manager. It has long production chains like in the Settler series. For instance just to produce the most basic food product- the seaweed portion you need a ship to bring in the raw sea weed. The♥♥♥♥♥♥needs a hangar, and a pilot. The hangar needs a director and a technican to maintain it. Then the seaweed needs to be processed. First you need to fatten the seaweed- for that you need a bioreactor plus a farmer of two. Once the seaweed is fattened you need to dry it, that needs another facility and a operator or two. And then you get the most basic food type. Don't get me even started on bread. And the game is a grind. And that can be disheartening at times. You need to invest a lot time into the game to get anything done. And there is a lot of micromanaging. This game is a micromanagers wet dream. You control everything, every individuals workplace, job, diet. The game is also very atmospheric- if you are into chillout music Stellardrone plays in the soundtrack. I'm having a lot of fun here. It is a breathe of fresh air after simple economic games like Anno. So if you are into micromanagment, complex production chains and you are not pulled off by grinding- thant this is a game for you. If you are looking for a quick, easy game- maybe not so much. There is still much that needs to be implemented to the game for it to truly shine- like disasters or research. But it is already playable and enjoyable and you can see where it is going. I think it is worth supporting in early access.

A polished sequel to Bloodline Champions with an attentive dev team and a lovingly crafted cast, there are is not currently a better isometric arena brawler on the market.  Using an exact copy of Overwatch's progression system, matches in this game are on an even playing field and character customization is already relatively rich even in early access.  The structure of each round is a fast paced hero deathmatch, focusing on casting powerful skill-shot abilities while simultaneously reacting to and countering enemy ability usage.  Intelligently spending your EX energy (think fighting games) on powerful enhanced abilities or your ultimate ability in each round allows you to employ a wide variety of potential strategies over the course of a match.  Between each round in a match you customize your character with the titular battlerites (passive abilities that modify your active abilities) so that you may better counter your opponent's' character choices, play styles, and their battlerite selections.  If you enjoy fast-paced tactical games that reward reading your opponents and obliterating them with carefully aimed spells then this game is for you.

At its core Magic the Gathering is a social game. A game to enjoy with your friends (or frenemies) laughing, talking smack, and dropping game winning bombs. Salt is an early access game that involves you (the character) searching for items and ultimately traveling island to island.
Of the negative reviews on here, I find that most either a). are disappointed at the "early access development" at this stage of the game and/or   b). dislike that this game hands you nothing.  (You are going to have to do some trial and error when crafting things.)
The game itself is great because the point is to find and acquire items so as to defeat pirates and captains; and ultimately, deal with ancient ruins and such that come later in the game.  It's paced a little slower than some may like, but that's the point.
I enjoy the game because it's laid back and I can unwind.  There aren't harsh time tables for which tasks must be completed.
---
I think that Salt has a long life ahead of it with potential to keep evolving as its player base grows.  The maps are vast and there is almost always something to find on an island (whether it be a look out point, items, loot, food; etc.).
The world is beautiful and it is updated by the developers.
On the developers:  I have to give them kudos.  They listen to the community and get to work fixing any and all bugs they find quickly.  The Steam community is just as friendly and helps each other out as necessary.
Yes, the game has its hitches and it's not 100% crystal clear, shiny, and finished - but it is stunning and fun to play.

Well, I have been playing this gem of a game since Early Access, and the game has showed no signs of slowing down. Online can be fun, but don't expect to have a good time if you get paired with a laggy opponent. The story mode is short and fun, but I honestly felt like it was poorly written, with no reason why you were fighting everyone (with the exception of the last character you face in each character's story). After you complete story mode, you unlock Abyss mode, which is essentially Warioware meets Smash bros., with some of the tasks including Multi-man modes, Break the Targets, a "Metal" enemy, so on and so forth. Overall, Rivals of Aether is a great game, and it is absolutely worth every penny spent and second played. Just a warning: if you want to be good, you need to get a controller, keyboard controls do not work with platform-style fighters. Steam controller works great.

The Pirates are challenging, at some point I wandered onto more than a few islands where I had no hope of making it out alive because I had the worst gear, yet still hadn't found the materials to make anything better.
Salt definitly needs improvement in some aspects, but I cannot wait for what else they have in mind to add. I think what I would want added to the game most of all is some sort of rough sea areas where the waves are higher and more chaotic, and toss your boat around.

Despite its stray from the original formula, this game stays true to the principle foundation of what a Hitman game is.  Its added linearity may turn off some players but it helps add to the feeling of being an methodical, engineered killer.  Through every mission there are multiple ways to take down enemies, and a variety of tools to complete objectives.  Believe it or not, the game doesn't improve on the mechanics of Blood Money, but rather Hitman 2.  In Silent Assassin, having a disguise didn't mean you were hidden, enemies who were too suspicious would actually tail you.  Absolution builds on this by allowing you to hide in plain sight with instinct, and also adds a bullet time feature similar to Red Dead Redemption, which only adds to the feeling of bad-assery that this series has been known for.
At its current price tag of $25, this game is more than worth it, for old and new fans alike.

I'd call it a roguelike survival simulator, set in war times. This time, however, you do not play the role of soldiers or any other type of warriors taking part in the conflict, but you're controlling an often overlooked part of military conflict - the day to day life of civilians.
The game will give you a random selection from the survivor menu, some random starting items and some random scavenging locations and off you go. During the day, you manage your shelter (base-building), respond to random encounters when people visit your shelter and monitor the condition of your survivors. During the night, you go out to scavenge for supplies. You will have to scrounge the available locations for items necessary for your groups survival.
My second playthrough got me Zlata, a “consoler” that keeps the morale of the team up, Pavle the runner (again) and 2 old people (Anton, Cveta) with no skills whatsoever. It was an uphill battle, since the food&meds consumption was higher from the very beginning. Pavle or Zlata would go out scavenging, Anton and Cveta stayed and guarded the shelter.
Hunger started creeping in. Anton got wounded in the defence of our shelter. Zlata got sick. I sent Pavle to scavenge, but many locations were closed due to fighting and snow. I was only left with 1 choice – I went to a warehouse guarded by local thugs and I took what I needed by force. The team was not too happy about that, but hey, we got rid of some thugs, that’s O.K, right? Unforunately, after a while there were no more thugs left, and Pavle started stealing from other survivors. He ended up killing some other civilians in self-defence, when he was caught rummaging through other people’s stuff. That brought the morale of the group to an all-time low. But at least we have food and meds.
It’s day 40 and the radio tells me that peacekeepers are supposed to move in within the next two weeks. They better move in fast, there’s no one to steal from anymore.

First play through below (skip to the bottom for the critic of the game).
Promising start to my life in a war torn town. Food, shelter, beds and warmth. What more could you ask for?
Scavenged around buildings, only took what we need. Life was good considering.
We helped our neighbours out and in return they helped us.
Then we were raided during the night, in which the two girls of the group were gravely injured. They lay in bed while the other two survivors picked up the slack, hoping to run into bandages to cure their fatal cuts. After two nights of no luck, sent one of the injured to a near by hospital - they bandaged her up and so she decided to help in return. She searched the rubbled for potential lost medical supplies and she found some!
She went to hand it in to the doctor who has helped her so many times... and then she started getting called a ***** by the guard. The guard proceeded to blast her head off with a shotgun.
Down to three, drastic measures might have to be taken. A survivor travelled to the nearby church in lue of some aid only to find the priest shot down by a bandit. Rightly so, the survivor murdered said bandit with a shovel and aquired a gun. Searched the area for bandages, none to be found! He tip toed through the dark to a neighbouring building, only to be spotted by a bandit and chased. As the bandit closed in he shot the bandit twice in the chest... and paused, thinking that was all the death that would come of that night. He slowly crawled away beaten from this ordeal and promptly recieved a shot in the back by another bandit.
Back at base, the female survivor is in and out of conciousness. Her companion, the chef, having to feed her and keep the place warm. After realising the other scavenger has not come back, he goes to seek revenge - taking down the last of the bandits and aquiring some more guns. No bandages to be seen to save his last friend.
So the next night he goes to a hotel, praying the tradesmen have stashed medical supplies somewhere near. In his depressed state he slaugthers them all in a gruesome battle of guns, barely making it out alive himself. Yet - no bandages to be found.
He travels home to find his friend has died of her wounds... Proceeds to drink some moonshine at 8am in the morning when there is a knock at the door. Two girls asking for medical supplies. The chef slams the door in their face and promptly heads downstairs to find some rope.
Game over.
Critic of the game follows:
Great game and I feel I have barely scratched the surface at 7 hours. You seem to gain a huge sense of attachment to your crew. Lot's of sneaking about to get your needed supplies and building your shelter. However, there is a small amount of storyline to it - however I have never survived long enough to find it :P If you have the cash, and liked the trailer, get the game. You won't regret it!
Post 24 hours of play: After playing this game for such a long time there is no way I would change my recommendation. I managed to complete all the achievements (for those achievement nutters out there, this game is easily completable) and found most of the different variations to buildings. Sadly I have uninstalled the game - for now - because I cannot handle anymore depression from it. Hope you guys have as much fun in this game as I do!
Although the game is challenging, once you understand how the AI works you can easily take any level down in one or two attempts. However, there is always the risk that you end up loosing one of your crew - go in prepared.
I strongly recommend this game if you like farming, good graphics and fun in general. There is alot and by that I mean ALOT of mods you can add to the game, and ofcourse there is dlc's too :P :D

Ah, how to say the right words about this game.
I've been playing for over a year now, every few months I try it out again. And every time I remember why I love it and spend the next 10+ hours playing it nonstop. This game is the pinnacle of resource management games, and will be even better when all features are implemented. But even if development stops tomorrow it'd still be a game well worth the (scrolls down) $16.99. I thought I remembered paying $20 for it, and it was worth every penny. I highly recommend this game to anybody who enjoys balancing inputs and outputs of materials, building ratios, population management, and any other types of administrative gameplay. I loved Sim City (originals, not the crappy 2013 one), I love Cities Skylines, I love Factorio, and if you like those games too then you will enjoy this one.
Development is continuing, and the dev(s?) is always very quick to respond to suggestions/requests on the forums, which makes me more willing to contribute.
Given that it's early access, unimplemented mecanics don't really count as cons.
The only real con is that there is an unusually high barrier to entry. It probably took me a good two hours to figure out all of the mechanics and UI tricks to get to the point where I didn't want to do something and have no idea how to do it. But the depth of the game is comparable to the amount of time it takes to learn. Nobody sits down and understands how to play Europa Universalis IV or Crusader Kings II in the first two hours. This game is to city management as those games are to 4X Strategy.  In other words, the best and most in-depth.
That being said, pretty much all of the keyboard shortcus that you would want are there. It's even pretty easy to figure things out once you realize that you can probably do what you want if you hold shift or ctrl while pressing the button.
Lastly, one thing I love about this game (but could see being off-putting for other city builder liking types) would be that there is very little layout management. Oh, there's a lot of nit picking you can do with exactly how to shape the buildings in the plot size, but mostly the game comes down to the fact that you don't spend a lot of time designing your colony. Rather, you spend your time running it. If you love building roads then this game isn't for you. If building roads and finding the most efficient layout is a sometimes fun but mostly tedious process (as it is for me) then this is the game for you.
All in all, I highly recommend it. Buy it. I hope this game gets big, because it deserves it.

Battlerite is often described as a MOBA without the creeps/jungle/towers/items, and that's relatively accurate. But I think the better description would be a top-down version of World of Warcraft arena. It certainly reminds me more of the latter than the former, mostly because of the pacing (Battlerite matches aren't quite as quick as the typical MOBA teamfight), but also because each character has more abilities than your typical MOBA character.
This game is all about positioning, teamwork, skillshot aim, and timing. It's extremely satisfying, and there's a ton of opportunity to outplay your opponents. When it's working right, there's almost zero danger of the typical MOBA ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t occurring. What I'm referring to are things like being perma-CC'd, or taken from 100%-0% health inside of a single stun, or having battles that go on forever because the healers are just able to keep everyone topped off. The game's systems work in such a way as to discourage or outright prevent all of that, and that's really refreshing.
Definitely worth the purchase if you're sick of any of the stuff I just described, or you're bored of WoW arenas.

Making a game complicated does not mean you made it challenging, once past the learning curve this game offers very little substance. This is a building game that offers one linear path in order to accomplish anything. There is no variation and you can customize very little, other than how things look a little bit. This is a developer in my opinion who needs to spend a little bit of time playing Banished to get an idea of how to make a game feel like you are making choices for your city building survival. The illusion that you are in control of anything is based on when you choose to implement your citizens but it ends there. This game has a long way to go in order to be a great simulation game in my view and based on how it is made, I am not sure we will see the changes necessary to make it such.

As a big fan of the Civilization serie and SMAC, I had great expectations for this game, but it ends up as a big disapointment. It feels like civ5 was before the extensions, but even worse. The main problem with the game is that everything is dull. The faction leaders have no character, the aliens are nothing special and there is nothing exciting about the technologies. The wonders are for the most part stupid +x buildings and it seems pointless to pursue them, which is the complete opposite of what's happening in civ5 for instance.
Another issue is that everything in the game is linked to science and so it feels like there is only one way to play. You get to the victory conditions by pursuing an affinity, you get a better military by pursuing an affinity, etc... so it's not like you are really making a choice at all. The different affinities all play the same way.
Also the game does not seem like it has been play tested. Someone was bound to realize that reassiging the trade units all the time was really boring, right?
There are some nice ideas with quests, but they are also a bit broken. The generic "choose between two bonuses" should probably not have been quests either, it's just a choice. Some quests are impossible to achieve, for instance it asks you to build a certain building in a city which does not have the required resource.
Diplomacy is also dull. Everyone is asking you for resources in exchange for favors (and at the start of the game, I wonder why they want the resources to begin with, it's not like they can do anything with it), and afterwards they don't want to give you anything meaningful in exchange of these favors.
In the end, I wonder how you can have as models civ5 and smac and end up with this game. It's like the design has been made quickly in one day. I had high expectations following the recent releases from Firaxis but this is a big letdown.

I've been playing Project Aura for about a year or so now, and this game is a unique game. The goal of Project Aura is to create a self-sustaining city for survivors of a global climate change disaster. Unlike other city-building games, PA emphasizes the administrative side of running a city - foodstocks, medicines, production of fabrication materials to construct buildings, technology to support said buildings, and the logistical planning for put a functional colony together.
As far as city-builders are concerned, PA is a unique experience. The administrative aspect of running a self-sustaining city requires much planning, critical awareness of systems and supplies, and expanding when the need or ability arises to combat various challenges facing the colony. In my opinion, PA provides a futuristic image of the post-human era, with the last vestiges of humanity attempting to survive on a now-hostile planet.
I would whole-heartedly endorse Project Aura, as it provides hours of entertainment and challenge. The developers have worked hard at creating a cohesive, complex, and creative world respelndant with motifs of crisis, resilience, and survival. If you want something different from shooters, rogue-like clones, flights sims, or an RPG, check out Project Aura. There's a great community of people playing this game, so you'll join a corps of colonial directors determined to save humanity!

With every new Civ release, the strategy element seems to become more well balanced. The restrictions in movement and unit stacking due to the hex system in Civ 5 were part of this progress towards a game that is less sprawling and with a less predictable outcome beyond a certain stage. Although the interface in Beyond Earth lacks finesse, it is functional and unobtrusive. There seem to be more city building options than in other Civ games and the quest system breaks the staleness in strategy that sometimes used to develop in previous Civ Games. The potential to simply insert quests seems like a great way to manipulate the game's dynamics. Let us not forget that this is the base game, and there may be DLC to add layers of sophistication at a later stage. I think the developers could have put more effort into the interface and given the game more atmosphere through the use of cutscenes and so on, but I love it anyway.

--- Review of the game after the Dec. 11 patch ---
Good on Square Enix for coming back and patching in resolution options and graphics settings, essentially fixing most of the technical problems I had with this game on release. Call me fickle, but fixing that alone has greatly increased this game's value for me - especially (pardon any potential snarkiness) as it makes it seem SE actually care about what they release on Steam.
FFXIII, whilst it definitely has some issues - the story seems really overly complex for what it is and the game doesn't open up the full extent of its battle system until way later on (a problem I found was fixed in FFXIII-2, also available on Steam), I couldn't help but find myself enjoying it.
I found that if you experiment with it fully, employing the use of Saboteurs and Synergists alongside Commandos, Medics and Ravagers, the Paradigm system is great fun to use, particularly later on when the battle system finally does fully open up.
The game definitely has some great visual design in both the characters and the world as well in my opinion, with the trip through Nautilus being a highlight for me, showcasing what might be best described as a "Final Fantasy Disneyland".
Though the grindy combat system will understandably turn some people off the game, in my opinion those who can make it through that will find a huge JRPG adventure with a cast of either honestly or ironically enjoyable characters that whilst being incredibly long, never truly gets boring.
