Unlike other games of this genre, Salt is focused on exploration rather than survival, and it's great. You'll sail across a huge ever-expanding procedurally generated world looking for loot, hunting, fishing, fighting pirates, discovering ruins, customizing your ship and crafting new gear to help you on your journey.
Every Salt game starts the same: you wake up on an island with no enemies, a journal, a basic crafting guide, all items you need to build your first boat, weapon and pickaxe. What's next? Engage the high seas and discover!
As other players have said, this game is very relaxing and feel almost therapeutic. Kudos to the sound designer; all ambience sounds are top notch and very immersive. There's music too, but it only plays at the right times, like when you're on deep sea with angry waves, discovering something completely new, etc.
While the graphics are cartoonish, the lighting is very realistic. The sunset in this game is one of the most beautiful I've ever seen on a videogame. It's so beautiful that you'll want to stop everything you're doing just to admire the view. Another element that means a lot in your experience is the waves. They feel like real waves, reacting to the wind with unpredictable patterns. You really feel you're sailing into the unknown as you see your last visited island disappearing and with nothing in front of you. You can craft a sextant or look for a compass to help you find your localization.
The downside of this game is that you can't explore underwater, there's only one biome and there's no weather changes. The good thing is that new biomes and dynamic weather are already planned and are coming soon. To know more about what's planned and the stage of development you can read the devs development blog
. Every friday they post something new. Worth the read even if you don't own the game.
If you don't know if you might like Salt, download the demo. There's little limitation on the demo (you can't go very far, can't use world seeds and can't play on hardcore mode), so you can almost feel like you're having the full experience. If you enjoyed what you played, buy and support the devs. When you launch the game you'll notice that you can continue your adventure from where you left on the demo. How awesome is that?
All in all, I recommend Salt for everyone looking for a relaxing experience. You can play without worrying of dying (you respawn every death) or you can play in hardcore mode with permadeath to see how far you can go. Don't be turned off by the cartoonish graphics. There's an incredible game here. Try the demo and see for yourself.

I can sum it up fairly easily: If you're a Hitman fan and looking for another taste of the series, there's absolutely no reason why you need to play this. It may be a good game for the right audience (lovers of Kayne and Lynch might get a kick out of it) but make no mistake, this isn't a Hitman game. What mechanics have been taken from previous instalments have been put through the grinder a fair bit, and what we're left with is another shooter with stealth mechanics that feel like they were added as an afterthought. Gone are the days where you get to choose how to approach a situation and now you get to grumble frustratedly as you trial-and-error your way towards the particular set of very specific actions that will get you through an area alive.
Stealth is just one of those genres, that if the mechanics aren't implimented smoothly, the whole thing falls apart. And this is one of those games.
But like I said, if you're NOT into stealth games, and you like shooters with some pretence of deeper mechanics, you may find this a good ride.

A few moments later, a man came up behind me with a shotgun and yelled "Die, B*tch!" I qiuckly charged at him and stabbed him with my knife before he could fire, killing him with 3 thrusts of the blade. I assumed that the building was taken by bandits, due to this attack. I ran out of the building, passing the body of my attacker, along with 2 women grieving over it. There have been a slurry of survival games, and most of them are (frankly) crap. Too easy, too predictable, too linear, too beta, there's a thousand things that can be wrong with a survival game. This game avoids those problems, as well as could be expected.
Resources aren't completely scarce, but they're used in large quantities, and even with ~20 of an item, you won't get a lot of use out of it. This feels just right, since I never felt comfortable with my situation, but I was also constantly crafting, building, and shifting priorities. Maybe i was flush for wood/materials, but I was out of food. Once I was good on food, I needed more materials to make water filters, or something like that. It felt difficult to survive, and that's what I want from a survival game.
Alongside food and rest, there's a "emotion" value for each character, too. They become sad when they see atrocities, and will progress into depression and eventually become "broken" and uncontrollable if you don't give them books, music, or other nice things to relieve the stress. I appreciated that in games like Don't Starve, and I appreciate it here, too.
The scripted encounters with NPCs are well done, with decent dialogue and enough ambiguity to keep you guessing what their real intentions were. The only problem with scripting these is that it's too easy to "game" it after seeing the encounter. Your second, third, and subsequent playthroughs will feel less "survival", and more "metagame." Other games (like FTL) solve this problem by randomizing outcomes, or adding other factors into the outcome of a dialogue choice, rather than just your choice (maybe your inventory, character being used to speak to the NPC, or location change the relative outcome of the encounter). But TWOM glues itself to rails. That's forgivable.
But let me level with you, the combat sucks. Unlike the rest of the game, there's no "soft introduction" to combat. And that can be fine, if combat made any sense. You have to deliberately switch to "combat mode", which entirely changes the environment actions you can use. Except that none of those actions are explained to you, and you have to spend a couple minutes examining icons and trying them out, hoping that you don't wind up making noise as you do.
You can never sneak up on enemies, their ESP goes off when you get closer than ~5ft to them - even if they're sleeping. And when you do, in fact, fight them, there's no feedback about how you're supposed to fight them. My first battle was a fistfight with someone whose house I'd broken into - but after madly clicking on the guy, the only thing i'd accomplished was my character sprinting in a circle around him. I tried to flee, but then my character inexplicably decided he couldn't go through the enemy, and wound up being lethally beaten. The next few combat scenarios ended up like this too, with the controls getting in the way, and lack of feedback failing to inform me *what* i was supposed to do. At one point i managed to knife a gunman to death, steal his pistol, and fire it at his compatriot. I was pretty sure that bullets, when they hit someone, were are pretty lethal thing. Unfortunately, they did less damage than punching him, and with one shotgun blast he killed my character.
This really wouldn't be so bad - every game has a learning curve. But when your character is dead forever, your other characters are stricken by grief (sometimes to the point of being suicidal or uncontrollable), and you need to *start a new game* to get back on track, that's a bad deal. It feels distinctly unfair to have the drop on an enemy, execute a well-planned ambush with the right weapon, at the right time, from the right angle, with no possibility of failure - and the game arbitrarily decides that it'll never work. Not just that it *randomly* won't work, but that your ambush *couldn't* work; it'll never work no matter how many times you try. And because you tried that entirely reasonable ambush, you now need to restart the whole game just to get back to where you were. That's frustrating.
Overall, play it. You'll like it. But just be aware that it has some player feedback and logic issues.

This game is basically an improved version of Bloodline Champions.
If you never played that game, it was an action skill-based 3rd person arena 2v2/3v3 deathmatch, where you had to kill your opponents and work in a team in a small arena setting using the abilities of your hero.
Battlerite has exactly the same identical concept and mechanics. All currently available heroes are even very very very similar to the ones in BLC. In this game however, the gameplay is way more fluid, there is less staggering and it overall presents a more fast paced combat than BLC.
In this game, like in BLC, all skills (7 + 2 variations) of your champions are skillshots and require aim to land. There is no random effects, there is no crit chanche, there is no luck. Everything is written in the tooltip of the ability, and works the same way every time. This means that you will get more proficient with your hero the more you play and learn it. Abilities are quite varied between each champion and in general feels really balanced, at least at my skill level (Gold IV). There is no item to buy and there is no gold, all champions start from scratch at the beginning of every match. Battlerites, which are little variations around the champion skills, add even more strategy options, by making you choose between 3 different effects at the beginning of every round. Possible effects include increasing a skill damage, reducing its cooldown, or granting a little defensive bonus on use, for example.
One of the biggest issues with BLC was the economy system. It was a free to play game where you had a free rotation of champions + the ability to buy other champions using game credits or money. This however did not work that well, since you were really limited in which hero you could play in a given match. It required grinding to unlock your favorite champion, and artificially capped your ability to play in a team. Battlerite went instead with the pay upfront route: by buying the game, which is a currently a bit expensive (20€), you unlock all current (14) and future heroes from the beginning. This model in my opinion works better for this kind of game (while I find the BLC model to work better in games like League of Legends).
The game can look frantic and chaotic on first sight, with projectiles flying all over the map. By removing every random factor from the equation however, the game quickly becomes readable and understable. Having said that, a more exhaustive tutorial could have helped a bit, perhaps by briefly introducing every champion in the game, which is paramount to be succesfull at any level in this game.
For now (and the game is still in early access) there are ~15 champions, divided into 3 main categories: Melee (tanks), Ranged (DPS), and Support (Healers). All champions available are quite different from one another, while covering the same archetypes. I don't find any unplayable or overpowered champion, in the current state of the game. I wish there were more champions available tho, because you see a lot of the same characters right now, and it is currently hurting the replayability of the game.
Overall I'm having a great time with this game, and I can safely recommend it to others. I hope it will have a great future, with a bigger player base (that it deserves) and with some more characters available. For now it is a bit expensive for the amount of content available, but it will get better if SLS can keep up introducing fun, fresh and balanced character to the roster.

I found a house with 2 old people.
A husband and his wife.
The wife was sickly and could barely run
The husband asked that I leave. I didn't
He asked that I please leave his wife alone.
They were defenseless
I walked around and poked into their inventory
I couldn't take anything because it would mean I'd be stealing
The husband yelled: "Hey! Stop what you're doing!", "Bandits! Help!", "Oh God please stop!"
I was confused. I had done nothing wrong. I looked, but did not touch.
So I ran out.
I came back the next day with medicine to see if I could trade or perhaps give the medicine to help his sick wife.
No options came up. So I left.
I came back the next day and still nothing.
I thought to myself "Maybe if I sneak around I can get away with stealing their things"
I was caught. They yelled in fear and ran around the house to keep away from me.
I attacked them
They begged for mercy and begged me to stop.
I killed her husband with a shovel.
The sickly wife was in the fetal position on the third floor.
I took everything. And left the wife to fend for herself.
I came back to my shelter.
And stared at my computer screen
I went to my bathroom and looked into the mirror asking myself "Did I really do that?" "Was it needed?"
I tried to tell myself that what I did was for the greater good of my shelter and the people living in it
But I attacked a defenseless old couple, took their things, killed the husband who was trying to protect his sick wife, and left the wife to fend for herself.
Oh God. Please save this lost lamb.

It's another supply chain management game. It does a couple things really well (and a couple of things not-so-well), but ultimately doesn't really have any charm. There's no real objective other than "survive", but surviving never really feels like a struggle until you hit about 50 colonists and morale becomes a gigantic issue out of nowhere (colonists either die to poor health from not enough food/water or if you fix that problem they become rebels from poor morale due to not enough tier 2 food stuffs). The gap in difficulty between tier 1 food and tier 2 food is astoundingly high and feels like one of the biggest flaws in the design of the game's supply chain. It's way too hard to recover seeds, plant and grow said seeds, ensure you have new seeds left over from the previous crop, etc. It requires a fair amount of micromanagement, and inevitably everything goes horribly wrong while you're paying attention to one aspect of the game and another goes kerblewy. You could play the game on pause, but that would only be more tedious than the game already tends to be.
Ultimately, I couldn't shake the feeling that I was on a never-ending quest to get to the next tier of item, which would require progressively more micromanagement to sustain. The game desperately needs some macromanagement capabilities. But even if that got fixed, I don't know that I'd enjoy it, because the game never really gives you a reason to care if your colonists live or die.

As usual, Tom Chick of Quarter To Three puts it perfectly and much more eloquently than I ever could:
I'm a huge fan of the series, there is no other franchise I've spent so much time on as Civilization. So after a dumbed-down, disappointing Civilization V I had high hopes for this installement. Unfortunately it completely failed to deliver. The AI is about as smart as a loaf of bread. The much touted tech web is just a more confusing version of the tech tree. Technologies feel random and arbitrary. The entire setting is very hard to get into. While ordinary Civilization allows you to develop a good intuition about the relative strength of various units (e.g. musketeer vs longbowman) in Beyond Earth you have no idea (quick, is a CNDR or an Apostle the stronger unit?). This is made worse by the fact that you can't even hover over enemy units to find out how strong they are or the fact that there are only a handful of unit categories and units within a category look nearly identical. It is very hard to get the information you need in this game. Want to quickly see who's at war with whom? No luck. Want to see how you are faring in comparison to other civilizations? Except for a rough victory progress and points comparison you cannot see technologies, production, energy output and other vital statistics like this.
The game forces you to make decisions all the time. Not in the good kind of interesting and relevant decisions, but random "quest" decisions that pop up dialogs and force you to make a mostly meaningless A/B choice while ironically blurring out the very information you'd need to make an informed decision.
Diplomacy is even more useless than usual. Except for declaring war you cannot really do anything meaningful. While resource and technology trading used to be an important part of the game it is unnecessary here. You can trade for "favours" with the AI, but they seem to have no discernable value whatsoever.
The game is dumbed down to the point where I could automate everything, including end-of-turn, and watch the game auto win itself. On one of the difficulty settings where the AI gets a bonus too!
Wonders have been castrated to the extend that a first time Civilization player I introduced to the game didn't even realize he built one until I told him. Compare that to the race up to be the first to finish a wonder in older Civilizations. You'd get a rewarding mini video, a building on the map and a significant bonus. Here it's just one more random thing you click on.
On a technical side the game doesn't work in fullscreen mode for some high resolution, high refresh rate settings. And, even more annoyingly, AI turns take inexcusibly long. I don't know if anyone has the patience to finish a huge map - I certainly don't.
Summary: A string of repetitive, boring decisions with no real pay-off to show for it. Civilization IV Beyond the Sword remains the pinnacle of the series. I recommend sticking with that instead.

As a great fan of Civilization V, I have been looking forward to Beyond Earth all year. My expectations were pretty high, and I expected at least all the things that were good in Civ 5 to appear in Beyond Earth, but that hope was idle.
The problems with this game are numerous, and I doubt I will address all of them here. However, before we get to the bad, let's start with the good.
- There are no major bugs that I have seen, except for some odd behaviour when loading the game sometimes.
- The engine runs very smooth.
- Some bold choices have been made, including a tech web and specializing your civilization through an affinity. There are a number of "quests" but for reasons I will go over later, they are extremely shallow.
- Civilizations are bland and boring, and there is almost nothing to set them apart.
- You can choose a few starting parameters for your civilization, but there are clearly "better" options here to the point where taking anything else nerfs you even before you begin.
- Wonders are in the game but are weak, boring and sometimes outright silly.
- Except for Domination, all victory conditions are pretty much the same: build a building, wait around 30 turns, and win. They are completely non-interactive.
- Diplomacy is a complete mess and just doesn't work. It was already bad in Civ 5 but it's worse here. Luckily, because there is no interaction needed for winning, it can be completely ignored.
- Tactical battles are poor. In Civ 5, the 1 unit per tile was good but sometimes a pain. It could be alleviated by choosing certain promotions or getting later game units. In Beyond Earth, the terrain is much worse with lots of mountains, miasma and other impassible terrain. This makes combat horrendous.
- Promotions: these are just utterly boring. You can choose to get either a 50 point heal, or 10% combat strength when your unit levels up.
- Unit upgrades: You get these by increasing your affinity level. You do that by quests or teching. The problem here is that with some luck, you can get affinity pretty fast, in which case your units completely dominate the opponent very quickly.  If not, then you are forced to research in a certain way, meaning that the tech web might as well be lineair. Even if you manage to upgrade your units, they stay bland and boring throughout the game until the very end, when they change from boring to utterly broken.
- Quests: Most quests consist of: build two of this building to choose an extra effect for it. Those effects cannot be seen anywhere, so you can only know what you need to build by committing all of that information to memory after numerous playthroughs. The stat bonuses do not necessarily make sense.
- The removal of city states, great people and luxuries: These three things added a lot of depth to strategical choices in Civ 5. They are completely removed in Beyond Earth and not replaced by anything.
- Happiness: This has been replaced by health, which is an almost irrelevant mechanic. Which is good because staying healthy is reliant only on social policies and buildings, forcing you once again to give up the non-lineairity of the tech web.
- Visually this game is not pleasing at all. Not only does everything look the same, but that same is depressing, unclear and intentionally blurred near the edges of your screen. There is no option to turn that off yet, but they will fix that they said. That doesn't change that everything looks dead, the color scheme is: brown, purple, dark green. It gives me a headache.
- The "story" that develops ends in oblivion after a few quests. No explanations are given anywhere and the end texts (there are no end animations or anything) just say something vague that means nothing at all, under the guise of "we leave it to your imagination".
- Enormous overhead in micromanaging workers and trade routes. This takes up more effort than actually building your empire.
- Orbital units, the new "thing" in Beyond Earth are not very satisfying. They once again add some passive benefits, and some can be used offensively, but it's a mechanic that doesn't add much to the game.
Unfortunately, I cannot recommend this game to anyone. If you don't already own Civilization V, then it's a much better choice than this. If you do own Civ V, then play that instead unless you are completely bored with it (although this won't alleviate your boredom for long). If you are a big fan of Sci Fi, then please just wait until this is on sale and has gotten an expansion.

I'm playing on easy so I can get through the story line and start on XIII-2, so every battle is fun and slightly challenging, but not frustrating or needing super studying and planning and perfecting your loadout. (This is a review of the version: 1.3.1.0 of Salt. By the time you read this, the game might drastically have changed.)
Salt is an open-world exploration game featuring boats, pirates, spiders, islands, and lots of water.
You start off on an island without anything but a book, and you're tasked with creating a boat, or rather, a sailing raft. "How do I create a raft?" Press "u" to open then tutorial book. It'll tell you that you need to find logs and cloths. "Well, how do I find logs and cloths?", you explore the island. Logs are scattered everywhere, and cloth is made out of plant fibers, which is also scattered everywhere.
Once you've made you raft, you're free to explore the ever-expanding, randomly generated world of Salt. On your journey you will discover a lot of different things, and you might have to consult the wiki at times. The wiki is however, not your only way of finding recipes. The are books scattered around the world which contain several recipes, telling you how to craft different weapons, boats, and even potions, among many other things.
As I said earlier, the game contains pirates, spiders and boats. This really adds to the element of the game. It might make you rethink how you approach a pirate camp, or how you  might go hunting for loot, and deer in the night. During the night, it's pitch black. It's hard to see anything, really. You can craft a torch, though, to make it easier to see what's infront of you. However, before you do that, I recommend making a weapon.
Back to the pirates though. Unfortunatly, there are no pirates on the sea yet. You can find abandoned pirate boats, but without pirates in them. You can however, find a variety of pirate establishments on land. They all contain different tiers of pirates, each of them harder than the other. You might not want to fight the highest tier pirates at once in the game, so I suggest you make a sextant and write down the coordinates of that island for later (Recipe can be found on the wiki, or in a book).
Salt is one of those games that lets you explore it's gigantic world without limits. It lets you upgrade your method of transportation to make it faster, and it makes you rethink how you might approach a horde of bandits. I am very eager to see how this game will develop in the future, and I have high hopes for it. This is a game that I would recommend for anyone.

When I first heard of this game, I thought it'd be in line with pretty much all the other "survival" games out there: hunt food, avoid stuff you can't kill, and above all, STAY ALIVE. But boy was I ever wrong... I've never, never ONCE, been one to scorn people (read: game developers) for taking a different approach than the "standard average", but I think it's time to break that streak now. This game had an interesting concept, but it completely failed to deliver on pretty much every single point possible (and some I didn't even think it WAS possible to fail at, too!)
First, we've got the issue of the controls. They're simple enough, sure... but you don't really have any actual CONTROL over things. Least of all your rather rëtarded little cubs. They run around rampantly, stealing food from their starving siblings, and of course, at the worst of times, they follow their dear mother, i.e. the player. For me, this ended with two being killed by predators, and a third to die by starvation (though not in that order exactly).
Then, we've got the rather extreme issue of orientation. There's absolutely no way to know where you're supposed to go, what you're supposed to do, or hell, even what you're NOT supposed to do. There's nothing worth mentioning in terms of a tutorial, so once you've started playing, you're pretty much left completely clueless as to what to do and when, in order to keep your mentally underdeveloped offspring alive.
Next up, we've got the horrifying graphics. I appreciate funky visuals, don't get me wrong, as I focking LOVED Child of Eden for it's colourful style, and I'm a HUGE fan of the pleasantly vibrant style that Bastion has. Aquaria made me have an eyegasm from its gorgeous graphics. But Shelter? It failed to deliver even a nudge, when I expected a whammy. The colours were so horribly watered out and pale that it was a tremendously underwhelming experience, seeing the game itself, and the brightness was so horrifyingly high that even if I'd completely RUIN my monitor's settings just for this game's sake, it STILL wouldn't be worth it.
Following up the last one, we've got that "emotionally instigating sound" the developers are boasting so proudly of. Maybe I've been spoiled with such intense soundtracks as the original Lord of the Rings trilogy's OST, or hell, even the TRON: Legacy music, both of which were awe-inspiring to say the least, but Shelter's sound and music just felt jagged, stale and unstimulating.
And last but not least, an issue among games I've been able to cope with since the dawn of my gaming life at the tender age of three... LENGTH. I found Beyond Good & Evil to be pleasantly bite-sized, and basically every CoD-game ever made to be decently lengthy, considering how they've essentially been 99% MP-oriented since installment #4, but Shelter was so infuriatingly short that I didn't feel satisfied at all. Granted, I didn't pay even half the game's, ahem... "actual value" (*mock-cough* BÜLLSHÏT!) since I bought it during the 2013 christmas sale, but even for the low price of 2,24€ it felt lacking and mind-numbingly short. Honestly, I was mad at whatever shïtheads that anally excreted Blue Shift for making such a horrifyingly short game, but you know what? Whoever you guys are, I forgive you. At least you TRIED. At least you provided MORE than a single hour's worth of "gameplay". Maybe not by much... but at least you TRIED. Shelter, however, is originally priced at a whopping 14€ for barely more than an hour's worth of gaming, which is even MORE than what you'll give for games such as Shadow Complex, Castle Crashers or hell, even Magicka, all of which provide (by comparison) infinite amounts of replayability and content.
All in all, Shelter was without a doubt the biggest gaming blunder of not just 2013, but probably the whole decade. I've seen some bad games out there, like Big Rigs or Nation Red, but most of the games that are bad are that way 'cause of bugs, glitches, imbalanced gameplay, but with Shelter, the fault isn't with the game itself. It's that the developers (a pox on you all) didn't even TRY to deliver anything more than an interactive motion picture at such a ridiculously overdone price that it makes the BluRay copies of Ghibli-flicks seem "fair".
I give this game the lowest rating I've ever given any game ever, and hopefully, it'll remain the ONLY game I'll ever review that I'll give this low of a score to as well... 0.0/10

This game is basically an improved version of Bloodline Champions.
If you never played that game, it was an action skill-based 3rd person arena 2v2/3v3 deathmatch, where you had to kill your opponents and work in a team in a small arena setting using the abilities of your hero.
Battlerite has exactly the same identical concept and mechanics. All currently available heroes are even very very very similar to the ones in BLC. In this game however, the gameplay is way more fluid, there is less staggering and it overall presents a more fast paced combat than BLC.
In this game, like in BLC, all skills (7 + 2 variations) of your champions are skillshots and require aim to land. There is no random effects, there is no crit chanche, there is no luck. Everything is written in the tooltip of the ability, and works the same way every time. This means that you will get more proficient with your hero the more you play and learn it. Abilities are quite varied between each champion and in general feels really balanced, at least at my skill level (Gold IV). There is no item to buy and there is no gold, all champions start from scratch at the beginning of every match. Battlerites, which are little variations around the champion skills, add even more strategy options, by making you choose between 3 different effects at the beginning of every round. Possible effects include increasing a skill damage, reducing its cooldown, or granting a little defensive bonus on use, for example.
One of the biggest issues with BLC was the economy system. It was a free to play game where you had a free rotation of champions + the ability to buy other champions using game credits or money. This however did not work that well, since you were really limited in which hero you could play in a given match. It required grinding to unlock your favorite champion, and artificially capped your ability to play in a team. Battlerite went instead with the pay upfront route: by buying the game, which is a currently a bit expensive (20€), you unlock all current (14) and future heroes from the beginning. This model in my opinion works better for this kind of game (while I find the BLC model to work better in games like League of Legends).
The game can look frantic and chaotic on first sight, with projectiles flying all over the map. By removing every random factor from the equation however, the game quickly becomes readable and understable. Having said that, a more exhaustive tutorial could have helped a bit, perhaps by briefly introducing every champion in the game, which is paramount to be succesfull at any level in this game.
For now (and the game is still in early access) there are ~15 champions, divided into 3 main categories: Melee (tanks), Ranged (DPS), and Support (Healers). All champions available are quite different from one another, while covering the same archetypes. I don't find any unplayable or overpowered champion, in the current state of the game. I wish there were more champions available tho, because you see a lot of the same characters right now, and it is currently hurting the replayability of the game.
Overall I'm having a great time with this game, and I can safely recommend it to others. I hope it will have a great future, with a bigger player base (that it deserves) and with some more characters available. For now it is a bit expensive for the amount of content available, but it will get better if SLS can keep up introducing fun, fresh and balanced character to the roster.

Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag continues the overarching Assassins vs Templars story by placing you in the early 1700s in the Age of Pirates, taking the role of Edward Kenway, a fortune-seeking pirate.
Story-wise, this is the first game without Desmond Miles, where you play as a non-speaking Abstergo Entertainment employee, exploring memories to create a new feature video game. Like other AC games, these modern-day segments don't really accomplish much, as Edward's story is much more interesting, dealing with the consequences of his lust for riches.
Visually, this game is very impressive. Character design is great, locations are styled well, and no visual bugs were noticed. Smooth performace all around.
Gameplay is the greatest strength in this game, letting the player basically do whatever he/she wants to do. Find treasure? Pull out those maps and get hunting. Explore the Carribbean? Planty of explorable and unique locations. Blow up everything in sight? Blast away with a fully upgradeable ship. The gameplay mechanics are slightly improved from AC III, including better sailing, free-aim, and combat.
The only real negative here is the overall story. You spend an extended amount of time not playing as an Assassin, which is strange given the title, Assassin's Creed, but does well in exploring the ideology of both the Assassins and the Templars from a third-person perspective.

You don't control every move for each member in your group, you assign them class roles and let them do thier thing. Usually it's helpful, sometimes they do things that make no sense in the moment, like casting a lightning protection spell on each member becuase the single creature you are fighting uses lighthing, even though just adding water to everyones attack would take it out within half a minute. I'm playing on easy so I can get through the story line and start on XIII-2, so every battle is fun and slightly challenging, but not frustrating or needing super studying and planning and perfecting your loadout. I prefer it that way. The last detail I made sure of was to use Japanese voices with subtitles. Just like in my anime, I find the Japanese voice actors to be leagues ahead of the English speaking talent. I wholeheartedly recommend this game to any RPG enthusiast, especially anyone that loves Final Fantasy and Square Enix.

This review is updated to take the recently added graphic options into account.
I'll start with the port before moving to my opinion about the game itself (which I for some idiotic reason 100% completed).
Graphic options:
The recent patch added graphic options to the game, which include
-Custom resolutions (up to 1080p (+?))
-MSAA Anti-aliasing (up to x16)
-Shadow resolutions (up to 8192 x 8192)
-(and full-screen/windowed mode)
So yeah, it's better than nothing, but it's not exactly amazing. Options are also changed in the launcher, which means that you can't change them in the game. The game runs at 60fps.
(It might be that the resolution goes higher than 1080p and it just doesn't show them to me because I have a 1080p monitor. Let me know if this is the case.)
Performance is poor, as a result of very poor PC optimization. Some people have reported that they are running this with smooth 60fps, but other people have reported huge performance issues even with high-end machines. I myself am getting around 30fps. What seems to be causing this is the UI, which is in some way bugged, and disabling the UI via a thirdy party program actually gives me a huge performance increase. However, you obviously can't play the game without the UI. This is something that Square should really look in to and fix it. FFXIII is not an action game so I found that bareable, but your opinion (and performance) may vary. I'd never play an action focused game at 30fps.
There is still no audio options, which is a problem for some people. There's also both Japanese and English audio, although this heavily increases the file size.
The game is roughly 50gb, so that might a problem for you if you have a small hard-drive or a slow internet connection.
Keyboard and mouse controls are functionable, although I found playing with a controller much more pleasant.
Keyboard and mouse controls are mostly rebindable. Mostly. You can't rebind movement controls from WASD (or whatever AZERTY uses) and selection keys, which are left and right mouse buttons. I really don't see this as a problem because, honestly, would you actually ever rebind those? Rest of the keys are fully rebindable.
So yeah, the port is still very barebones, but if you can deal with that, I think that the game is worth playing.
Final Fantasy XIII is a very story focused game, so if this is not what you are looking for, I wouldn't recommend the game for you. First eleven chapters of the game are very linear, but this allowed them to focus on the story telling in a way that would not have been possible on a more open game, although at times even I found this linearity fairly dull. I actually quite enjoyed the story of the game.
I have one problem with the characters though. In my opinion, Final Fantasy XIII has five well written characters, and then there is Lightning. I just found her incredibly boring character, and aside from one scene in around chapter 4 or something with Hope, she received practically zero character development. This would not be a huge problem if she wouldn't happen to also be the main character of the game. On the other hand, I found all the other characters very well written.
Combat system of the game is fairly unique, and while it starts out as very repetitive, I did find it quite interesting after a while. Although I must recommend that do not use "Auto-Battle" button. Just don't, that makes the combat very dull and isn't always the most optional option anyway. I have some minor problems with it though, biggest one being that you can't change your party leader/controlled character during the combat. I heart that this is changed in FFXIII-2, so I'm quite looking forward to that.
Soundtrack of the game was in my opinion also very good, although thanks to the sound balance (which you can not change due to lack of audio options), it's not quite as loud as I would have liked.
As I said, the game is very linear, but honestly, the side quests that the game introduces in chapter 11 are very dull. I got obsessed with it and got all the achivements, but I really do not recommend that. It is very grindy and takes countless of hours and hours, and hours of time. There is a reason why only 0,64% have the Treasure Hunter achievement. Just, don't do it. Play through the story and do those few side quests (Cie'th Stone missions) that you do during it, and leave it at that.
In the end, I enjoyed FFXIII, despite its faults. Thanks to the linearity, I found some of the chapters fairly boring and doing all the side quests definitely wasn't enjoyable, but the story, combat, and the characters (aside from Lighting) were quite good. I do recommend the game, at least to fans of JRPGs.

/****** UPDATE **********/
Well, 18 months later, I have given Salt another run. A lot has improved -- graphics, combat, and quests come to mind, and the devs are on the brink of releasing multiplayer! But let's see how Salt fares with the specific items for which I docked it 18 months ago:
1. Environments: still lacking. While the game includes a greater variety of tropical and jungle islands, they do not differ very much, and there is still an overall lack of interesting places to explore on the islands themselves.
2. Activities: this has had a big overhaul. There are many quests, a litany of new pirate types and bosses, and ship customization! I still would like to see activities like cave and dungeon crawling, however.
3. Loot: Thumbs up! There far more quest-specific items, items from combat, and items to craft now.
4. NPCs/Creatures: there are more NPCs now, such as merchants and innkeepers, but the game is still heavily lacking in native biology beyond deer and spiders. They did add sea turtles, and I've seen screenshots of sharks (though never encountered them).
5. Sailing has improved twofold. Fishing is still fun, but I love the ability to deeply customize your cruising ship, to manually map out the world (harkening back to windwaker), and to use cartographic tools like the sextant and the compass.
6. Music... better! But still a quiet game. I respect the developers' design decision to make it this way, but I cannot lie that I have a better experience while listening to tracks from Windwaker.
Conclusion: for the price, I do think Salt is now worth a buy, particularly with multiplayer so close. The game is a relaxing nautical adventure across a massive world, and I find myself returning to it again and again in the face of the usual chaotics that occupy the top sellers list on steam. But my recommendation comes with a heavy warning...
Development on Salt is SLOW. At the pace of development, it may be years yet until all of the promised content is delivered. The game now provides 10-15 hours of fun, and up to several dozen more depending on your tolerance for repetition. If you want more than that, Salt is no more than an investment.
For me, it has been a sound investment, if only one that is taking its time to pan out.
/***************************/
This is early access, and while the game is quite stable and beautiful to me, it's also fairly empty. Islands contain mostly the same biome: a standard tropical environment with trees and bushes. Sometimes you'll find deer and rare resources. If you're lucky, you'll find some pirates on an island and some treasure chests. There is an early selection of loot to obtain. Other than that, after 4-6 hours you will have seen most of what there is to see.
Nonetheless I love the premise and potential to this game. A massive, island-scattered world to calmly explore, with manual ship control and plenty of ships to build. The  Windwaker-styled art and seafaring give this game real character. It's all immensely exciting and I do think the developers will succeed. In many ways they already have, as I personally have had a swell time.
But before I can recommend it to the general gaming audience, it needs more of the following:
- Environments. Snowcapped islands, deserts, volcanic peaks and flow, cities, etc. Exploration demands variety here.
- Activities to do on the islands. Let's see some dungeons and homes to explore, castles on cliffs, etc. Quests that aren't fetch quests.
- Loot: more weapons and armor and categories.
- More NPC's and creatures than just pirates and spiders and deer. I'd love to see the developers tap into various mythology for creatures to inhabit the islands and the sea, for example. Imagine leviathans occasionally slithering out of the deep sea and peaceful whales surfacing for air.
- Speaking of the sea: there should be more to do while sailing. Whether that means interacting with creatures, dropping anchors, searching for treasure on the sea floor, anything to reduce the monotony would help. The fishing is good, but could be expanded.
- Music. The main-menu music is a beautiful, Elder-Scrolls-like tune. But music rarely plays in the game itself, and it needs to start a little more often.
The good news is the developer is targeting many of these features and the game is still early in development. I have high hopes for this title, and once I feel it has solved some of these issues, I will update this review accordingly.
(but if you're like me, a gamer who loves nautical and exploration games who can overlook some of the emptiness, then by all means jump right in!)

First off, this is meant to be an honest and unbiased review, so I'll be going through the good in the game as well as the bad, without ranting off too much. I'll be assuming you know the general theme it contains.
The time I spent playing Salt was incredibly relaxing. Like others have stated before, it's almost therapeutic. I believe this is what the game focuses on, instead of your typical Minecraft rip-off. Speaking of which, it's not a Minecraft rip-off. It's an exploration game of its own and definitely has a lot of potential to become an awesome and original game.
If you're looking for a fast paced action game, Salt isn't the game for you. Salt is the game where you'll find yourself idling more often than doing things of major importance, but in my opinion that's what makes it so lovely.
-Relaxing
-Original Gameplay
-Open World
-Good Lighting
-Unique Water Dynamics
-Very 420 Friendly
-Arrow Physics
-Plenty Of Things To Do
-Bug-free (I haven't encountered anything)
-Dev's Seem Active
-Growing Mod Community
-Strictly First Person
-No In-Game Mapping System
-Save files are not local (If you mess up, your items used while fighting will still be gone if you die)
-Delayed Response Time (barely noticeable)
-Pirates Are Landlubbers (they don't leave land)
-Unoriginal Textures & Goofy Models
-Animations need lots of work
-No Guidance (You're often left wondering "What will I do next?" and not in a good way)
-Unbalanced Difficulty (No Actual Combat Scaling)
-Mediocre Combat System
All in all, I downloaded the Demo and shortly after I made a purchase of the game. Is it worth the $15? That's debatable. The Demo contains a lot of what the full game has to offer and will show you all you need to know about how it plays. The game currently offers about 6-24 hours of gameplay before you get less inclined to play it.
Salt is a great game for relaxing after a hard day, and it's the only game I find myself able to play in those moods where nothing seems to be entertaining. It's very smooth and runs great even on my crappy laptop. There's occasional moments where I can see the game could make basic improvements but from what I've seen the developers are working on fixing all of the issues and take their gamers seriously on suggestions. If they keep up the work then Salt will become an endlessly entertaining and unique game.

The characters are all very human, and react realistically to what you do.
Despite being depressing, it's extremely addictive. I spent four hours in the game and the time just flew by. Replayability isn't an issue either, there are several different characters that you might get when you start a new game and loot is kind of random. The buildings are more or less the same each run, but the day that they are available changes, so you'll find yourself entering buildings in different orders and discovering different things.
Easy to pick up and fun to play.

After being a fan favorite, from my early childhood, this game has truly tested time.
With amazing sounds, graphics, and combat, it felt too real for 2010. From the aminious forests and valleys in the northern sectors, to the barren fields where you expect an entire army to start firing at you, this game immerses and involves you.
As well, as being home to coop domination, team deathmatch, and more, Arma 2/Arma 2 OA brought and sustained one of its best, FREE, modded expansions
Drumroll please.........
DAYZ!
Featuring a new way to play, with scavenging, surviving and adapting, Dayz brought a whole new aspect to the Arma environment. Whereas before, you would ignore enemy weapons, explosives and clothing, you now needed to loot and make sure you had enough bullets, food and supplies for any situation...
Whereas before, you'd be dissapointed you'd died, and have to respawn at base or restart the mission, Dayz stressed, and panicked you. If you died, you would probably lose your gear forever, lost in the Coyote Backpack of that ghilie bandit at Sniper Hill.
Additionally, the game branched out and expanded tremendously out of Vanilla Dayz.
Modders added bases (my favorite), new guns/sounds, new maps, new vehicles, a new economy system, and SO MUCH MORE!
If a game truly has the best modding community, it's Arma.
I hope, that Bohemia continues to create and enhance the Arma experience, in future installments and updates, fixing glitches and annoyances, like physics, destruction, medical treatments, and more.
But if you can get a group of 2-3 friends, get in a group chat, and load up this game, it will amaze you with a brilliantly crafted, Tactial masterpiece.
Arma 2/ Arma 2 OA: 9.5/10

This game is absolutely amazing! And let me tell you why.
First of all the visual style.
This game is a wonderful 2D metroidvania with beautiful surroundings and adorable characters that are animated really well. Personally I think the style is very appealing, with all the characters you encounter in your journey through the world, and of course how different every part of the world looks and is designed appropriately to what it is supposed to be.
Secondly the music.
Oh. My. Gosh. The music. It fits so incredibly well with whatever situation you're in. Music for fights get you pumped up, music for areas gets you wondering in awe, music for the calmer parts in the game gives you a break even for your ears. But no matter which piece of music you're listening to, it is wonderful.
Thirdly! The story.
As you find your way through the world, talk to some bugs here and there, and find notes written in stone, slowly the story unfolds. You start the game without really knowing what's going on, but as you play the game you will slowly find more and more hints of this amazing story for you to piece together. Just exploring the world and experiencing this makes you feel like you're really getting to know the world that has been built.
Fourthly? The controls.
Now I am one of those crazy people who decided it'd be a good idea to play this game on my keyboard instead of getting a controller, but guess what? It is very doable. Since there isn't a crazy amount of controls in this game it is easy to remember the keys to push. I can only imagine that with a controller it is even more intuitive. But not only the amount of controls is, in my opinion, just perfect. The smoothness of the animations after giving input is just great. There's an immediate reaction, without it looking weird. Everything that happens feels logical, control-wise, which isn't the case with every game, so this certainly made my experience an even better one.
Conclusion:
While I expected this game already to be super amazing, when I played it it was even more amazing than I could've hoped for. For me, this game has everything I want from a game. I very much recommend it and can only advice you to buy this game and go and put hours of wonderful experiences into it.

I love the Assassin's Creed games, and Black Flag is no exception. It is generally regarded as one of the better games in the series, and with good reason.  Great gameplay, characters, and story make an experience well worth playing.  While previous installments have had sea warfare, this takes it to the next level and makes it an integral part of the game.  You'll spend a good portion of the game on the high seas plundering ships for booty, while trying to survive massive storms with sea twisters and rogue waves.  That doesn't mean there isn't anything to do on land.  There is still plenty of the gameplay you've come to know and love, but the highlight is the sea. It's good to be a pirate, and before long you'll be singing sea shanties with the crew.

This is the game you want if you want to get into SoaSE at all.  This is the complete package, including all the DLC, a new graphics engine and 2 sub-factions for each of 3 original races in the vanilla game.  Rebellion is an odd mixture of a 4X game and an RTS and even an RPG to a degree (capital ships earn XP, level up, and most ships have 'spells' that they can cast).  The scale of the game is impressive, you can zoom in to view tiny fighters in high detail, and seamlessly zoom out to see multiple star systems.  This is far more action based than games like Civilization, but at the same time far slower than other RTS like CnC and Starcraft.  It is an odd mixture but it really works.  The new "Rebellion" version also introduced many new victory conditions, and while the game stays focused on military action, it is now not the only way to win anymore, which is a nice touch for mixing things up.  Any flaws I come up with are not really worthy of even mentioning, this is well polished.

Simply put, the game is flawed.
The AI is laughable at best, and this goes for both Civilizations and Aliens. For example:
1) The Aliens are always inclined to attack you even when you're peaceful with them or their foe is by far more superior. So, when my Brawler, an Affinity unit stands fortified near them, they will all attack and all die.
2) Some units like the Kraken, the strongest Alien in the game (I believe) can only move and attack in deep ocean. Therefore I killed a Kraken with the weakest ranged naval unit in the game.
3) The civilizations build armies but of the wrong kind of units. An ironic quote would be one from the game; "You fight with the army you have. Make sure it's the army you want". It seems both the army the Civlizations have and the one they want suck either way.
The new happiness system, Health, is dumb. You can really do nothing else to improve a low health level besides building a few specific buildings which are extremely sparse and lacking in the beginning (If you build "tall", if it's still called that in BE), and the system will just end up hindering your progress anyways to improve your level. Because, of course, a lack in health causes a lack in research, which stalls when you can next research the technology required to build something which will improve it. In Civ V, happiness was easy to fix thanks to the luxury resource system. However now it is all based 99% off of population, and that's significantly harder and more frustrating to fix.
The Research is fine, though the new Web feature and lack of advisor guidance when trying to pick what you want to research makes it significantly harder to stay decently caught up in worker techs and such whilst being able to grab an important technology for an Affinity.
The culture has not changed at all except for the social policies, now called Virtues, forming more around the new difficulties (and one around population).
These notes seem scattered, so let me summarize this. The game is flawed. It is a different beast than Civ V, and should be approached as such.
The AI choices and Research paths, along with the lack of personality (and animation? I recieved none) in the leaders causes for a large lack of depth in the gameplay. The game was monotonous and repetitive, and when I felt the game was going to get exciting as War broke loose, I left even more disheartened.
The spy system was pretty cool though, I'll give them that.
So, for the time being, I would NOT buy this game. I don't feel like I was even close to summing up how dissapointed I was when I tried it. In my honest opinion, Civ V with or without complete DLC is equal to or better than Civ Beyond Earth, respectively.
Do keep track of patches and note for changes in the AI and such. After a few patches and some DLC (which usually fixes a lot of things), then maybe this game will be worth the $50 Firaxis is asking for. Until then, I do not reccomend this game.
Quick edit: Replayability is huge though granted all the options. Also, if you are to buy the game, I highly reccomend you download the mods found here

As a massive fan of the Bioshock series and someone who was a little ticked that PC had to wait 2 extra days for this release, I'm appalled at how poorly the remaster was done.
If you play this game with mouse and keyboard, you're going to hit massive bugs within the first hour of gameplay. ALL of the issues that were present with the original release of the game have not been fixed or even attempted to be resolved.
In one hour of gameplay, heres every bug I ran into, sequentially;
* Changed a few visual settings, turned off auto-aim, hit enter to apply. Suddenly I'm set to gamepad mode.
* Changed my sensitivity from 3 (default) to 1; Small noticable impact, but atleast I'm not moving my mouse .2 degrees to the right and doing a 180. 800 DPI, btw. Considered the norm nowadays ffs.
* Going back into the menu with anything lower than 3 makes your menu sensitivity outlandishly slow. COMPLETELY different from my ingame sensitivity. Why it even changes in the menus where it barely matters is beyond me. This was always present in the original and makes no sense, why they kept it is beyond me. Oh, gamepad mode reactivated again.
* Changing your sensitivity twice in one area, then switching areas, causes your sensitivity to not only revert back, but literally lose 80% of the input movement you make. You move your mouse 9/10 of an inch and nothing happens; you move that extra tenth and the ♥♥♥♥♥ moves as if you're at default sens. Jumpy as all hell. I've also been informed this happens at random intervals.
* Any flashing effect (Lightning, TV screens, etc) with a visual that is displayed dynamically on the world doesn't seem to display correctly with 120hz or 144hz monitors. I haven't tested at 60hz, but it basically looks like you have a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of screen tearing where the effect is present.
* I have a Volume knob on my keyboard. For some reason rotating it opens my Map, even though it's not a "key" on my keyboard that can be bound to anything other than my windows sound. Rotating it fast enough crashes the game.
* The Director Commentary. Oh lord. This takes the cake for lazy. So the first one is after your first encounter with a Big Daddy where he murders the guy in front of you. I decided to click "watch now". What I got was a 720p (If even? I'm not entirely sure, but it sure as hell wasnt 1080p) video of an interview that lasted like 8 minutes, with artifacted, poorly compressed audio that forced me to remove my headphones from all the awful shrieking that came up. What really got me is that it's literally just a reuseable item in the world that can't be moved, it just pauses your game and plays the video with no UI or animation to help it connect better with the game. Then when it's over you're suddenly back in the game as if you never touched it, no fade out or anything just pop, back to rapture. They might aswell have just sent you a god damn youtube link. At least they mentioned that the commentary is full of spoilers.
* Oh look that flashing-screen-tearing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t is back with the Andrew Ryan Screen, lovely.
* Loaded into the new area where you get the Tommy Gun, mouse sens is broken again, change my sens back to 2, makes no difference. Restarted game and chose not to play anymore tonight.
Overall this is nothing more than a UI rework, higher res textures, and some seaweed+jellyfish etc models thrown in to make the eye-candy areas more visually stunning, I had hoped we'd atleast get the better models from bioshock 2 (Such as the changes to the little sisters, etc) Honestly, I wouldn't be nearly as upset with these bugs present if they hadn't taken those extra two days to wait on the PC release. I figured these issues were exactly what they were fixing and accepted it.
If you're new to Bioshock this game is still fantastic. Marvelous work-of-art of a game with fantastic storytelling. If you play with a controller, even better, no issues whatsoever. Just dont grab this game thinking you're getting an up-to-date, bug free title with the advanced settings and conversion success of other titles you see nowadays.
It's just weird to get Remastered versions of such a successful series that doesn't promote a new title or improve upon what was originally present.

There's the seat for an amazing game in Civilization: Beyond Earth. The familiar early-game curiosity of exploration, the interesting opportunity costs to compare, the (mostly) wonderous soundtrack, a non-linear tech web rather than the tech trees of prior Civ games, and other features make this Civ game start on the right track and feel like the start of something great.
But then things fall through. The AI prove to be lacking in a number of dimensions (poor military strategy and tactics, unengaging diplomatic offers), the game is quite unbalanced in places (internal trade routes are particularly overpowered, embarkation speed does not increase), and the quest system which has choices that are varying levels of balanced. There's plenty more I could go on about -alien (lack of) aggression,
More often than not, the game turns into a city-managing, trade-route simulator (usually after about turn 120). That's not entirely a bad thing though- there are some appealing, unique tile upgrades that only become available after researching mid/late-game techs, so you are then able to transform your city tiles as you see fit:
Need to really push for more technology? The Academy grants +3 science per turn (at the cost of 2 maintenance) and you can spam that sucker around a city to your heart's content! Need more culture? Pop up a holo-net satellite and add +2 culture to all the tiles beneath it. Surrounded by icy tundra? Terraform so that it yields a nice 2 food, 2 production, 2 culture.
There's a great feeling to look at your well-improved empire and knowing that it was once a lot of empty land and a swarm of wolfbeetles.
As the game is right now, I can only recommend it to Civ fans. The game shines with novelty in some aspects, but is rather dull and boring elsewhere. But regardless of whether you buy this game or not, watch the intro trailer and behold the sense of wonder that was meant to permeat every bit of this game, but hasn't quite reached Beyond Earth.

Great music with very soft lyrics that are hard to understand but pleasing to the ear. The characters all look absolutely amazing. There are a lot of cute scenes and personalities. The battle format is relatively simple, to the point of frustrating due to the lack of control you can exert over it.
The game itself plays out very similarly to Final Fantasy X on Playstation 2. Some key differences are the lack of swapping during battles, and there is absolutely no backwards exploring possible at any point during the game(unless you count the 'license to hunt marks' quest, which TBH is excessively long, clunky, boring, and thoroughly unrewarding aside from some ocassional monster battles). This in my opinion oversimplifies the game itself and makes it hard to appreciate it through remembering what you've done in the game, since you can't 'physically' take your characters back through the game and revisit various parts of the story. You literally have to either replay the game from start to finish or load up various save points that you made along the way, or else you can't go back to try to jog your memory at all. This is not the same as FFX because at least in that game, with admittedly a great many exceptions, you could backwards explore to jog your memory.
The side questing is very limited and totally unrewarding. It also feels forced, as if you have to do the 'side quests' in order to win the game. Well, not all of the quests feel this way. And part of it depends on your attachment to the characters. Still, I felt like most of the fun was in the game's story itself and the side quests just got in the way. It's a far cry from my favorite FF games in that regard. I guess half the problem can be traced back to how incredibly restrictive the game was and how time-consuming it is as a result to actually complete the quests. You literally have to spend like 20 minutes going across terrain just to get started on a quest if you making good time, another 20 minutes embarking on the quest, another 20 minutes completing the quest, and another 20 just getting back to where you started in some cases. That's easily over an hour if you hurry and don't mess up just to do one tiny part of the mark hunting quest.
By the time you're able to win the game, you probably powered up your characters just about as much as possible. And then you get to make them even stronger. For what? For more incredibly mind-numbing side-quests? No thanks.
One pretty neat thing that could be easily overlooked is the attention to detail with the weapons. You could appear to be holding a completely different weapon depending on what sort of elemental buff your weapon might be enchanted with, if it was indeed affected by a Synergist's spell. And the summons are somewhat entertaining, although you can only have the character you control do the summoning and only for whatever power they have access to. Also, the summons are basically your limit break. You can also use your limit break bar(it's called  Technical Points for whatever reason) for other stuff, but anyway you really have to use it wisely because it's not easy to regenerate at all once you start using it.
The game might be worth it for the story and the beautiful music as well as amazing graphics but when it comes to battles and quests it just doesn't deliver fun. Furthermore, if you play the game on your computer, you may experience extremely annoying glitches. One in particular that has plagued me from start to finish is this one where I can't exit the game when I wish to. There is a massive delay most of the time for that. Another one that is probably related is the trouble with alternating between programs while it is running. This can even mean that I have to hit the Start menu button before pressing the function key on my keyboard to either mute or lower/raise the volume. Coupled with the extremely time-consuming side quests, the glitches make this game suck up way too much time.

I got this remaster for free for owning the originals, and I recommend this edition of Bioshock, BUT BEOFRE YOU BUY IT PLEASE KNOW WHAT YOU'RE GETTING!
This Remaster makes the Original Bioshock much more friendly to High Definition Monitors and newer Hardware, and it makes the game look better with higher resolution textures and some tweaks to ragdolls and other physics objects, graphically...that's about all that was done.
However, There are some additional features as well:
-It has developer commentary ala Valve games, which are interesting.
-A Museum where you can view several original models that were scrapped during development of the original game, also interesting.
-Some additional gameplay content that I have yet to try as this review was being written.
-Bugs and glitches from the original game's release in  2007!
To curb expectations:
This game IS NOT a rebuilt from-the-ground-up Remaster the likes of the Halo Anniversaries, it does NOT make the game look like Bioshock Infinite's "Burial at Sea" DLC. (Which would have been amazing in my opinion, but I digress) Nor does it add anything new to spice up gameplay for players who've played it before like the Metro Redux editions, If this is what you wanted you will be sorely dissapointed.
If you have never played the original Bioshock I recommend the remastered edition over the original, It looks better and works better for modern hardware.
However if you played the original on Console and want the remastered edition on PC, I recommend this remaster...but wait until the price drops...there isn't a huge ammount of a difference.

[This game was free as of PC upgrade deal for both BioShock 1 and 2, and this review will focus solely on the changes and new features of the Remastered games. If you want a review on BioShock 1, I have one here:
]
Until this version of the game is signficantly patched and addresses its many problems carried over from the original version on PC, I cannot recommend this game. It's a damn shame because the Survivor mode is perhaps my favorite new feature for the series--and it's only in this game, not BS2 or Infinite.
For anyone defending this port or calling out disgrunted fans as being entitled, the original port was unnacceptable BUT could be understood with the disruption of GFWL. Infinite turned out to be a great port, so any defenses for BioShlock Retextured is inexcusable. They had their second chance, and they delayed this game for PC users.
The first major bug I came across is the drowning at the intro cinematic. It's either tied to the FOV, framerate or other graphic options features--which are anisotropic filitering from x1 to x16 and AA on or off--but it can be resolved if you set all the settings down to the lowest value AND you turn off the horizontal FOV expanded option. Once you reach the surface, you can turn them all on or you'll fall through the water.
Second, there is no FOV slider or option. Like the original, you will have to open up the Default.ini file and change the SetFOV to your preference, THEN you need to bring up %appdata% to find BioShock.ini to add to "w = MoveForward" with "w = MoveForward | SetFOV = X"--I have found to get a significant performance boost by making these two changes.
Third, there are audio desync issues, and reported by other users there are the same issues with the original's audio. I don't know of a fix for this, so I hope it gets patched.  Including these bug issues there are also gameplay bugs of all sorts like missing textures, and the mouse sensitivity issues are still here and it's practically mandatory that you turn on the aim adjustment option if you mess with the FOV.
Lastly, and probably the most aggregious, the "Save When You Exit" bug of BioShock 2 that corrupted your saves is still apparent, so always manually save and quit. NEVER use the save and quit option.
It's a shame that these issues, as well as general optimization problems--which I've had much better experiences with DOOM (2016) and Mankind Divided to give me the impression that this game isn't optimized well--are detracting me from some of the better qualities of this game.
The weakest of the list are the three new challenges, which are interesting little things but would be better to make those a part of the main game. Another weak bonus is the Director's commentary. While they are insighful from the videos I've seen, they are 5 - 8 min long (with gameplay footage edits) that are too much of a pace-breaker. They should be viewable from the main-menu so you don't have to hunt for them, and watch them, in-game.
None of the gameplay fixes of BioShock Infinite or BioShock 2's controls are included in this game, which is perhaps something I would be more angered by if it wasn't for the new difficulty mode, Survivor Mode. It begins with a stupidly high difficulty curve with Splicers taking more than seven wrench hits before the benefits of the new difficulty become more obvious. You'll realize this when you get your gun and can kill with a single headshot, and you get the Wrench Jockey to make the wrench more viable--and that's only the beginning of the changes.
Ammo, resources, enemy damage and AI behaviors, usage of eve, and the value for items, eve, etc. are all ramped up to provide the type of difficulty that works best for BioShock: Resource Management. This makes not only the planning, tactical side of the mediocre gameplay work better but makes the RPG (and "morality" system) stronger by making "every bullet [(and resource)] count!"
(As an added aside note, developers, stop making the BEST mode of the game tied to the hardest difficulty. There is a reason people love Ranger Mode from the Metro series and Hardcore Mode from Fallout New Vegas, and not the Survival Mode of F4; we like to have difficulty modifiers to our preferred difficulty so we can gradually adjust and get better to the changes.)
This difficulty inclusion is the only reason, aside from the new textures, I would ever recommend this version over the original because the original can be fixed while this one remains to be seen if 2K or modders will come to the rescue.

True sea-based exploration at its finest. Between making a new boat, foraging for food, fending off pirates, and sailing off into the sunset, I have had hours fly by with ease before I even notice its happened. There isnt any building or magic or anything like that, the game is actually rather simple. It focuses solely on the exploration factor, with a small part on combat and "survival". Theres money and some merchants, ruins and ancient relics, pirates and giant spiders galore, but the primary focus on the game is sailing into the distance and finding new lands to explore. Honestly my only two issues so far are that the music does not play nearly often enough and that there isnt enough to do while sailing. These are seriously minor complaints and do not detract from the value of the experience as a whole, but they have to be said. The music is atmospheric and beautiful, but it rarely pops up. And sure, you can fish or manage your inventory while sailing, but if you want to go off into the wild blue yonder in a small sailing boat against the wind....youll be sitting there for a while. It would be nice to have some crafting or smelting or something to do during that time. Maybe charting a map or a captains log to fill out, something that fits the theme. Either way, it is still a truly wonderful experience and sometimes just sailing in itself passes the time. It isnt finished, but what it is has enough potential to make it easily one of the best exploration games of its genre. Honestly, the only reason I dont have 50+ hours dumped into the game by now is because I get so absorbed into each time I play it that I have to limit myself from playing on days I have to work, else I risk losing hours of time without realizing it! Definitely recommended, 10/10, gold star, thumbs up, etc etc.

TL;DR Salt is a great exploration game, but the mechanics like combat and crafting fall short.
Salt is a bit of a disapointment for me.  The whole point of the game is to explore, and let me just say that Salt IS a great exploration game.  However, most of the mechanics were poorly concieved and/or do not function well.  Combat is less than appealing, as there is very little to do besides click and swing your weapon repeatedly.  Archery is frustrating in the least.  Crafting is, if not well thought out, reasonable.  The killer is that you need to simply spend large amounts of time gathering resources with virtually no gaurentee that you will find them.  Logs spawn randomly, as far as I can tell.  I would love to see features where you can harvest wood from trees, and rocks from cliffs, but until then, your only way of gathering resources is hopping from island to island searching the ground for stuff that (hopefully) has spawned there.
Combat stinks, can't figure out how gravity affects arrows, and grinding for resources all take away from the truly fun exploration aspect.  I could tolerate this, but unfortunately the detract from the game dramatically.

I'll begin with Orcane, and he's the one I play most.  This guy is a killer whale (orca) with legs.  Why does he need legs?  For kicking♥♥♥♥♥  His special mechanic is a drop of sludge he can fire and place anywhere on the stage, and also acts as a projectile to disrupt your enemy's recovery, or to provide recovery options via is up-special, or a trap (down-special, and forward-air) that can screw your enemy's approach (This is how you ruin the advance of Zetterburn and Wrastor players since they open with projectiles and dash after it hits).
Next is Zetterburn, if you couldn't guess it, he's all about the fire.  I haven't played him, but there's a lot of them out there.  He's pretty deadly if you let him fight completely on his terms.  He also relies on a DoT mechanic by lighting parts of the stage on fire, and if you are hit by the attacks that do that, or walk into the fire you'll begin to take damage.
Here's Wrastor.  Remember Captain Falcon and Falco from Super Smash Bros?  Well, they got gay and decided to have a love child.  He's a bird with aviator goggles.  His special mechanic is that you launch a tornado, and it leaves a line where your movement is faster in that line after the tornado.  He also accels in air combat, and his strong attacks (think Smash Attack) all require you to be in the air to use.  He also doesn't double jump, he flaps his wings and pentuple jumps.
How about Maypul?  This is Rocket Raccoon's♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off brother who runs around cutting people with leaves and seeds and♥♥♥♥♥♥  His brother got to go to space and become friends with a living tree named Groot, while this guy got stuck using his tree pals as weapons.  His mechanic is obviously the trees, you throw seeds onto your enemy, and bait them into your down-special and it wraps them up.  His smash attacks have long distance but not a wide hitbox.  He recovers by holding his up-special to use a vine to jump back up on stage near his enemy.  His down-air (or dair) also spawns a root from the floor of the stage, allowing it to hit anyone on the stage regardless of how far away he is from the ground.

Pros:
The game gives you a nice alternative to the run and gun style of most survival games.
You always feel like you need something else, even when you're group is in good shape, adding a need to keep playing.
It's possible to go the entire game without entering any active combat.
Cons:
The game takes a very stern stance on murder. At one point, I was exploring an abandoned house, and the description for it strongly suggested bandits. I was sneaking around without taking anything, looking for any signs of armed thugs. A woman spotted me and ran off. Note that I still hadn't taken anything. A few moments later, a man came up behind me with a shotgun and yelled "Die, B*tch!" I qiuckly charged at him and stabbed him with my knife before he could fire, killing him with 3 thrusts of the blade. I assumed that the building was taken by bandits, due to this attack. I took what I could from the building, ignoring the "private property" signs in the item boxes, since bandits don't deserve these supplies. I ran out of the building, passing the body of my attacker, along with 2 women grieving over it. After this, it said that my character was broken, and I had to send another member of the group tp talk to her for a few minutes, greatly slowing down my progress. The rest of the group were "sad" as the game told me, and I was greatly confused by this. Why is murder always bad? I hadn't stolen or attacked anyone, and I hadn't even pulled out my blade before this man attacked me. Funny thing is, giving children medicine for their sick mother, or helping board up a neighbor's house so that her and her daughter wouldn't be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and killed didn't seem to effect my group at all, other than a brief entry in their diaries. My point here is, what's the point of doing anything good in the game when there are no benefits for it, and a single act that the game finds "evil" will completely dismantle your chain of progress?
Overall:
The game is fun, even if it takes a few restarts to get the hang of it. BE WARNED: The game is a mouse clicking game where you control multiple people, not as I first thought, which was that you control one person with WASD and simply command your group to build your base while you're away.
8.5/10
