This game is simply beautiful. A true work of art. Sound was great and the art style was appropriate and stunning.
The main objective in this game is to survive as the mother badger and to help the baby badgers get food and to protect them from predators. As the badger troop trudges on, they encounter many obstacles, such as hawks, coursing rivers, and raging fires. Along the way, the mother can kill smaller game and pick fruits growing on trees or in the ground to give to the children. As the children eat more, they grow more, and become less of a liability.
I've never become as attached to a main character as I was to this mother. Maybe that's just because these cute little animals are adorable (when the mother isn't leaping 20 feet and killing mice). Regardless, I enjoyed my journey with this family, and even gave the young ones names (Sam and Daisy were my favorite, don't tell the others.)
It's a short game, but I think the overall experience and possible ability to start new journeys once the ending has been reached make up for that. I'd buy it again in a heartbeat.

For a game built upon the concept of slipping by unnoticed, Hitman: Absolution is certainly doing the opposite. It’s standing conspicuously amongst today’s fad-driven modern shooters and me-too multiplayer hopefuls, middle fingers extended. A slow-paced, single-player focused sneak ’em up, Absolution looms in stark opposition to many of the most pervading trends in gaming today. It cares not for the overly delicate, their minds rendered dull and flabby after years of being prodded through corridors blasting anything that breathes. Absolution delights in letting players skulk through it expending few bullets at all. It’s a game that wants to let you think for yourself.

Many consider this the Classic shooter that set the benchmark in modern FPS graphics. I agree, you still require a beefy system to be able to enjoy Crysis for what it is, a graphical monster with story attached.
Its a solid shooter, giving the average player around 7 hours of shooting, dodging, cursing and of course, death by physics. One of the major plus points this game deservers, is the fact that Nomad (the main character you play) speaks! Many games today just don't have a character you can identify with so this puts the game in the same legue as Dead Space 2.
Graphics are top notch, extreme but not over the top, you'll get lost exploring if you've got the power to turn it to at least HIGH. You'll enjoy it, trust me. Controls are nothing to cry home about, simple layout which all shooters have and the story like will have you interested and hooked till right to the end, where movie cliches start to bog down the actual kicking♥♥♥♥♥and taking numbers. Enjoy.
Final Rating: 4 / 5

If you can get past the absolutely horrible and amateur story (that feels like it was written by a 15 year old in the 90s), there are 4 or 5 good, somewhat open-ended levels. The rest are very linear.
Shooting mechanics are good, and the "gamey" aspects of the game are quite well done. The stealth system is crazily unrealistic. Like enemies have to be able to see you for 5 seconds before they can "see" you, and they either don't notice you or point their guns at you, no "i thought I saw something" where you maybe have a couple seconds to get away.
The story really is very very very bad, and I didn't really like that the majority of the real assassination targets you get are over-the-top sexy women. The others are: a mentally challenged character, a few hillbillies, and 2 "big boss" type guys. Very lazy writing with only a couple really dislikeable bad guys to kill.
Graphics are very good, although it depends on how you feel about overuse of lighting effects - this game uses a LOT of extreme lighting effects that might start to irritate you after a while.
Anyways, the gameplay IS very solid if you can get by the "gamey-ness" of it, and the somewhat poorly implemented stealth system. There are a lot of unlocks that boost your score to encourage multiple playthroughs, and a couple of the levels give a couple drastically different paths to completion depending on the disguise you choose, so you might replay a few levels in an "arcade" kind of setup.
The multiplayer is fairly fun, where you can design your own jobs and send them to other players, but there aren't too many people playing them anymore so unless you have friends playing, don't expect the contracts you design to get played much.
I look forward to the developers combining the graphics and shooting with the larger, more open levels of contracts, and hopefully hiring somebody out-of-house who can right an actual story and maybe reboot the franchise since the current Agent 47 and his world has unintentionally become a weird sort of Austin Powers sendup.

Ok it has been some time since I have posted a review of Riders of Icarus.  After logging over 4000 hrs of game play I can tell you all without a doubt that this game is absolute garbage.  I will try to list some of the major issues with this game and the people that run it.   Game crashes constantly.  Familiar taming success rate is ridiculously low.  Weapon and armor crafting takes days to get the materials due to daily time gates and then you have a high chance of failing to craft the item.  If you do get lucky and craft it, the stats are just garbage and most of the time completely unusable by the class you are crafting it for.  Tempering armor and weapons is a joke.  It is easy to temper from +1 to +10 is pretty easy, but from +10 and above it requires elluns to buy "insurance" so if you fail to temper you don't lose a level of tempering, ie 10 back to 9.  Elluns can only be obtained from the cash store or from quests that only give about 30 a day.  The higher in lvl you go up to lvl 25 per piece of armor or weapon the more elluns it costs for the insurance. TL;DR
This game mechanically blows while graphically appealing.  If you want to live the fantasy life of a pirate then I highly suggest this.  The pirate section of the game is fun yet lacks progression.  There's a large map with lots of stuff you explore/pillage and I certainly will be spending more of my hours doing so.
Before you read the rest of this guide, an important distinction that I think I should make is this; This game is not a GOOD game, but it is an ENJOYABLE game.  The game itself is glitchy, with terrible controls, that has little difficulty (except with some naval), and has alot of immersion breaks.  But yet even with that, I enjoy this game.  Explanation below.
World:
Now As the world of this game goes, it (as a whole) is kinda boring, there's nothing in the world to get you invested with it, it feels like a map and you don't ever feel that it is more then a map.  However, the map, is good.  There's so much to explore and little details that make it rewarding both through ingame rewards, beautiful scenery, or just interesting level design.
Graphics:
Man these graphics are stellar, I could mindlessly sail around in the water for hours straight and just soak in the views.  Although there are some spots with really bad textures, the majority is really well detailed and gorgeous.
Story:
Disclaimer, I haven't completed the story yet and am going off of the 13 hours I've played so far.
When I first got this game, I thought I would completly abandon the story asap and just go pirating, that was what I was here for, a pirate game, not an assassin game.  Strangely enough though, I find myself enjoying the story.  Although there are some leaps in the story that make me scratch my head, I feel that the writers of this game didn't want to go with a Assassin Creed Story line, focusing mostly around the Assassins and Templars.  Instead, the writers decided to take the mandatory "Assassins and Templars" and wrap it around the theme of the game, being a pirate.  A story as far as I've gotten is a massive treasure hunt, one that the protagonist hungers and uses the Assassins/Templars as a side attraction.  Although I feel that may change in the future.  (If the level of assassin/templar interference remains at this rate, I feel I will find myself greatly enjoying the story)
Music:
When setting an atmosphere, the music is probably one of the most important parts in a game.  This game does... okay with their music.  The music sets the atmosphere well enough, but is bland and unoriginal.  Not the type of music I would ever listen to standalone.
Gameplay:
Here's a core of what makes the game both good and bad.  The melee combat in this game is a complete joke and unchallenging at all.  As long as you counter enemy attacks and smash you LMB, you will end out on top of every fight.  The controls of melee are also disgusting as I constantly find myself jumping and climbing ontop of stuff I wish to walk around.  When sprinting in this game, they have the feature that makes it so you automatically climb stuff you walk infront of.  Now I think on paper this is a nice idea, however in practice I loathe this feature as I feel like whenever I get close to anything while sprinting, I climb it, with little control over where.  (For those of you who play Overwatch, think Widowmaker's grapple going to some place you had no intention of going to.)  However, there is still a redemable part to the gameplay, the ships.  The ship combat is fun and can be challenging (especially going after legendary ships).  Naval fights feel flawless and easy to grasp, with a interesting learning curve as you try and max/min each of your weapons.  When it comes to harder fights, you often find yourself having to use some strategy to out maneuver your foes, something I wasn't expecting in and Assassin's Creed game.  The majority of the time I've spent with this game is sailing around finding ships with good hauls to take, and I enjoy it immensly.  Going back to the bad though, the stealth in this game is a joke.  As long as enemies dont see you, and you don't shoot a gun next to them, you're virtually invisible.  I often found myself just sprinting around stabbing enemies in the back with zero thought.  When I play stealth games, I want to think about my actions and plan them out to make sure I don't get caught.  Having the stealth be so simply really disappoints.  As a final topic in gameplay, who the ♥♥♥♥ thought that adding stealth ship sections was a good idea.  It makes no sense how the pov of the ships work and ships are slow and can't move quickly, leading to parts where a section you thought was clear suddenly has 5 ships looking at it as they all decided to turn their bow towards that area.  To further rant, the detection range of the ships doesn't make logical sense AT ALL.  The ship fov works like that of humans, but with a tiny circle around them.  In reality, you can't just sail a few yards behind a military ship and not get noticed, since someone on deck will see you and point it out.
Progression:
The progression that was allowed for the ship was very disappointing.  The upgrades were very standard and you only gain 1 new weapon.  Interesting upgrades work so tha they completly change how the player plays, allowing the player to manage their upgrades to play how they want while also adding variety.  I also went into this expecting to be able to get bigger and better ships, however, it seems I have been mistaken.  I sadly see the possibility that I get bored at staring at the same ship hit waves for another 30+ hours.  Adding the ability to get a new ship would vary the gameplay and also add more progression.
Mobile Game?!:
A feature of this game that I'm currently neutral on (but slowly leaning towards disapproval) is the mobile game feature where you manage your own ship of fleets.  Again, good in concept, not so good in game.  I would love to be able to control a fleet of ships, however they work identical to the World of Warcraft Garrisons/Class Halls.  You go to the table, select the mission, choose the best ship, and then wait for a few hours as they complete the mission.  I'm not even completly sure what gameplay effect this feature has, if any.  It seems like it has potental but just like Blizzard, they ruined it. f fleets.  Again, good in concept, not so good in game. This is the game you want if you want to get into SoaSE at all.  This is the complete package, including all the DLC, a new graphics engine and 2 sub-factions for each of 3 original races in the vanilla game.  Rebellion is an odd mixture of a 4X game and an RTS and even an RPG to a degree (capital ships earn XP, level up, and most ships have 'spells' that they can cast).  The scale of the game is impressive, you can zoom in to view tiny fighters in high detail, and seamlessly zoom out to see multiple star systems.  This is far more action based than games like Civilization, but at the same time far slower than other RTS like CnC and Starcraft.  It is an odd mixture but it really works.  The new "Rebellion" version also introduced many new victory conditions, and while the game stays focused on military action, it is now not the only way to win anymore, which is a nice touch for mixing things up.  Any flaws I come up with are not really worthy of even mentioning, this is well polished.

Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion includes all the previous expansions and the core game, whisked and combined into a standalone which is astounding value for money.
RTS4X stands for "Real Time Strategy; eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, eXterminate", simply put: It is a strategy game that has a huge overlay of space-empire micromanagement and birds-eye-view strategy, whilst keeping the real time battles simultaneously active.
This game truly is a space opera, as huge battles take place whilst perhaps your strike-fleet is sneaking around the back to hit the enemy where they least expect it. Maybe you are sending your spaceships to different solar-systems or plunging into the depths of a worm-hole, to seek the treasures (or dangers) on the recieving end.
The game has similar aspects of the game Galactic Civilisations and Star Trek Armada, mixed and refined into a stunning, heart-pounding, yet relaxing game.
If you love space games, empire games and RTS games, this is going to tickle you.

This is a great little game that is very fun as is and has a lot of potential.
It is a platform fighter (AKA "Smash-clone")  It uses many of the same concepts as Smash and is fairly technical.  The key difference so far is that there are not blocks or grabs/throws.  Instead of a block you have dodge/parry button.
The dodging works similarly to Smash.  However, if you hold still and hit dodge you will parry. The parry works somewhat like parrys in Street Fighter III.  If you parry an attack, you recover more quickly than the attacker, which gives you a chance to counter or escape.  Since there is no block, grabs/throws are not really needed.
Also, there are no items.
The balance of the characters seems good so far and each character is pretty unique.  The netcode for online play seems to be more than adequate as far as I can tell.
Seems to me they just need to add more characters and make the 4 player free-for-all available online and we will have a great little Smash alternative for PC.

Salt is a true gem of a game that has captured my attention and inspired my imagination in a way no other game since Terraria has done for me. This game places no expectation or urgency whatsoever on the player in terms of goals, missions, objectives, etc., instead providing those gameplay features and allowing the player to pursue them or ignore them entirely. Playing this game is supremely relaxing, personally reminding me of summers spent sailing the seas of Wind Waker. Only the bare minimum of direction or guidance is provided, which is a true rarity among today's games dominated by quest arrows and nagging tutorials (and yes, I realize most of those options can be disabled in many modern games, but still...). The sense of wonder of exploration and adventure has stayed very fresh in this game and I'm looking forward to many more hours put in. And finally, if you've ever wanted a game in which you can do nothing besides scavenge fallen wood, mine for rock and gems, shoot apples out of trees with a bow and arrow, and hunt dastardly fast yet ungainly deer, well maybe you will discover as I have that this is your game!

Graphics:  2D setup that combines the detail of Shadow Complex and the art style of Limbo.  Everything is dark and brooding, which really sets the overall tone.  Their lighting system is a thing of beauty as well:  rays of light shine through broken walls and windows, fire barrels give a nice ominous glow in the night.
Audio:  Somber acoustic guitar soundscapes reminiscent of The Last Of Us play during the day, and the night scavenging missions feature very tense, suspenseful string and synth arrangements.  Environmental sound effects like artillery shells landing and the crack of sniper fire constantly remind you that you're never really safe.
Controls:  Point and click adventure style.  You navigate around the environment by clicking where you want to go, objects you can interact with in the environment have their own separate icon.  While in the safehouse, you control each character independently by selecting their character photo then giving them their own commands. Navigating the menu system is simple and straightforward.
Gameplay:  Everything is randomly generated at the start, so no play through is the same.  The safehouse sequences are fairly routine.  Build this, repair that, eat, rest.  The game really comes alive when night falls and you have to decide what to do with your survivors.  Sickness, hunger, and injury are very serious threats to your group, and losing anyone significantly increases your risk of having the whole thing come crashing down on you.  Managing your survivors is key to getting through the siege.  There's also significant danger when it comes to the overall scavenging:  rolling over those weaker than you and taking everything they have makes you a target for vigilantes and decreases morale, and some of the more well-stocked areas tend to be heavily guarded by hostile military forces and other survivor groups who have no compunctions about killing anyone who sets foot on their turf.
My one major complaint is the lack of a tutorial or tool hints on the environmental icons.  It doesn't take too long to figure stuff out, but the initial learning curve can lead to some restarts.  There are very few bugs, which is always a plus.
Overall Score:  9/10

I love how you can capture animals and have them be your mounts, or your pets (they make the pets have Kawaii faces (which I love)), and all you PETA people, you can release them back into the wild. I love the music, I love the fighting, I played this for hours not realizing how fast time went by. There are a few bad things I might add. I don't like how you have to pay money to release a mount. Despite all of the bugs and paying mounts it's still a really good game, and I finally found one that I can be hooked on ever since Runescape. The music and graphics are very pretty. There are a large number of tameable mounts, so there's likely something that will suit your tastes. For the most part, it's a pretty solid game. although I've had a couple of system freezes, normally when I've tabbed away during a long loading screen, which have required a hard reset to fix, just because the game seems to stay in front of even the Task Manager.
My biggest problems with this game are that mounted combat feels clunky, I couldn't get invested in the story (WHY are level 1 characters guarding the princess of the country as she travels across her kingdom? I can only assume they're all sleeping with their superior officers, because otherwise, you'd want at least a few of your best guarding her), the starting area (Berakka forest, or whatever its name is, I don't remember) is just plain boring, some of the quests feel like they're for characters several levels higher than they're defined, and the reasoning behind why there'd even be the option to seal your mounts into your weapons seems pretty thin on the ground. Many of these mounts are named characters, but you can repeatedly capture them, and then permanently compress them into enchantments. Also, why would your mount change size?
A lot of my complaints come from the "capturing" of the mounts. You technically create a "familiar echo" of the mount in question, which then changes size to fit your character. In addition to this, you can't actually use any weapons while mounted, unless you have the right generic weapon (a crossbow or lance). All of these things just feel like arbitrary decisions to enforce.. balance, I guess?
If you enjoy grinding to get your rewards, then this is a good game, but it was far too grindy for me. You can't even reach max level without taking on the secondary quests, which just got boring quickly.

This game is amazing. It deserves best indie game of the year for sure.
As a product, because of the cheap price and the amount of content and the QUALITY of the content, it's a 10/10 MUST play.
As a piece of art, strictly without taking how much it costs as a factor, it has some problems. Some parts are kinda tedious, and some parts feel not as fledged out.
But thinking it through about 7 out of 10 times I complained about something in this game was me complaining there wasn't more. I mean, there is A LOT but Team Cherry managed to create a world so inmersive with a lore so interesting, that I was always wishing for more. And that's not a bad thing.
The animation work is astounding, and the musical score is top-notch. Even though it has this somber overtones throughout, it doesn't take itself too seriously and has some legit funny moments. And it's also cute as ♥♥♥♥.
The amount and quality of content was a really nice surprise, clocking my first run through the game at 36 hours. My second run took me 40 hours, but because I went for 106% completion. And you should go for it since its endings are amazing and the DLCs are amazing. Specially The Grimm Troupe added the hardest (and coolest) boss in the game. Can't wait to get another DLC (for free!!) and to pay for the one after that. I just can't get tired of this game.
As a work of art, I give it an 8/10.

If you've already read other reviews, I'm mostly going to echo some of the same sentiments.
Civilization Beyond Earth really seems to take away a lot of choice that I grew to love (And be extremely frustrated by) in Civ 5.  This game really let's you do whatever you want; and although I enjoy a good sandbox, there just isn't too much decision making here.  You can level up in any given tech direction, affinity, or culture at will.  The only exclusionary forces to how you progress are the minor bonuses you chose to give to your military units.  Every other bonus you can get can just be min/maxed by playing the game longer.  In the end every empire I create comes out to be the same min/maxed plot-of-land expansion as the one I played before, despite all the options given to you in the beginning.    And the end game is just completely unfulfilling.  There's no lead up, or breakdown of the game; not even an option to play just one more turn! It's grayed out for me every time!  It just ends, and unless you're really quick at reading text before the box pops up to tell you it's over, then you may never know.  Yeah, that's right, the text box at the end is the same stock message for every game, with no details concerning who won, or how.
I do really enjoy the level with which you can customize your society, and that the NPC's and cities change in design depending on your affinity, and I will still continue to play this game,  but I don't think I can recommend it as it exists right now.  I guess we'll just have to wait for some DLC.

When this game released on PC, I was extremely excited because I never got the chance to fully complete the game on PlayStation 3. Since I no longer own any consoles, I never thought I'd get the chance. However, when I saw Final Fantasy XIII pop up on Steam my jaw dropped, and I pre-ordered with excitement. Once the game released however, my excitement faded. What I had expected to be glorious 1080p 60FPS on max settings, was actually 720p bouncing from 24 to 30 and to 60FPS constantly making the game look stuttery beyond belief. I was instantly turned off, and told myself I'd wait for a patch.
As of a few weeks ago, they announced a graphical options patch, and I was then excited again to play the game. I was steadily waiting for it to be released, but then all of a sudden I had the urge to get to the game. I started playing December 1st, and while cringing at the frame rates and graphical infidelity, I pushed on through doing the several same chapters I had done before on console. However, around Chapter 5 I really got sucked into the game again, and began to ignore the performance issues.
This may be the most critically hated Final Fantasy game to EVER have been released, but honestly, it's not, and you shouldn't believe the hate. I personally don't mind the linearity, so that may be the main reason. The characters all have great character development, although the game does feel as if Vanille was the main character, and not Lightning. It seems there was a shift in the characters somewhere in there. At first you find Hope and Snow both rather annoying, but around Chapter 8-9 you really start to enjoy them, and once all the character's struggles have been presented, you really feel one with the cast, and can't wait to hear more.
The gameplay system used in FInal Fantasy XIII is quite phenomenal if you ask me. Party Members earn different abilities with Crystogen Points, or CP, using them in the Crystarium, and can be earned by going through battles. In the Crystarium, there are different sets of roles. These roles and their effects are:
Commando: Low chain bonus, but maintains chain rather than it falling rapidly.
Ravager: Massive chain bonus, but will lose quickly if not having first used a Commando role before-hand.
Medic: Cures ailments of party, giving health and eliminating negative status effects.
Sentinel: A tank role, has all enemies focus on them while absorbing damage immensely.
Sabotuer: Inflicts negative status effects on enemies such as Slow, Poison, etc.
Synergist: Opposite of Saboteur, will give positive status effects on party members such as Haste, Shell, etc.
Each role plays a very important part in this battle system, and when coupling them with Paradigms, it becomes extremely strategic. You create your own Paradigms by customizing, or generating them, allowing you to pick what role your party members have, and you can switch these Paradigms mid-battle. Low on health? Switch your party members to Medic roles to quickly regenerate health. Need to deal massive chain bonuses? Switch to Tri-Disaster which contains 3 Ravagers blasting away at an oppoinents Chain until staggered. Once an opponent is staggered, you can greatly increase the Chain Bonus percentage, and deal immense amounts of damage to your opponent. The only downside to the Crystarium is you don't fully unlock it's capabilities until Chapter 10, where you can then use any role on any party member.
I haven't fully completed the game yet, but am hoping to sometime this week, and then am looking forward to the end-game side missions, and collecting of items to earn 100% of the Steam Achievements.
I would recommend this to anyone who is looking for a fast-paced RPG game, with decent character development, and plenty of content. I do however suggest waiting until the graphical option patch has been released, and I will be editing this once it has. Game on!

For those who are worried:  This is a picture perfect, if not improved, port of the PlayStation 3 and XBox 360 release.  It is worth the 50-60 GB you are going to eat up on your HDD.
Minus the linearity of the storyline, Final Fantasy XIII delivers an interesting, yet confusing storyline that only playing the game through the entire story will bring everything together.  It truly rewards those who push forward.  Yes, the cast is not the strongest cast to be put together, but all who cry about the cast being immensely butthurt at all times in this game need to look at Final Fantasy VII.
The battle system in comparison to previous incarnations is refreshing, giving us the active battle style we are used to with all previous installments, but forces you to pay attention to everything and change your strategy throughout each battle.  The A.I. allies are not stupid, but sometimes you are better off taking healing/support roles on your own.  It forces you out of your comfort zone strategically.  Although it isn't a complete masterpiece, there are other games in the main numerical series (Final Fantasy to current) and direct numeric sequals (i.e. Final Fantasy X-2) that I could easily use for purpose of opinion on why this entry is superior to their predecessors.
Plus, the game offers a "post-complete bonus" by letting you continue to grow your party, take on new challenges, then smash the final boss again with your newly acquired powers to utterly destroy it.  True mastery and completion is something that takes many hours and understanding what the best party make-up is for each challenge.
Square-Enix needed to make a strong statement with the future of the Final Fantasy series, especially since it is now in the double-digits in entries.  This was a great way to make that statement, even with flaws.

No but seriously, Salt is an amazing game. There actually is quite a lot to do, even at this stage of development and you'll still spend hours playing it trying to kill all the named pirates, get all the ships, get the best armour, explore every island, etc. My favourite part though is that it isn't a punishing game in the slightest. It's "survival" in the loosest sense of the word. Running out of food only stops your stamina from coming back quickly, and as long as you have a basic club, you should be able to fend off most of the dangers of the world. That being said, you're never really truly invincible in the world and though there will come a time where you're pretty much self sufficient with your accumulated resources, it will take you a good while to get there. But the heart of the game is really about exploring the lovely landscapes, building cool ships, and watching the beautiful sunsets. So if you're looking for the Dark Souls of exploration games, this ain't it. But if you loved Eidolon or Proteus, you'll almost certainly like this. There's plenty to do already and plenty more coming with active updates and testing branches available for those who care about those things. There's plenty that still could be done (the UI could use an upgrade, the 2.5D grass could mesh better with the landscape, the AI movement could be better, etc.) but what is there is extremely promising and already a great pleasure to play with. I will definitely be following this game closely to see where it goes because I'm loving the direction it's taking right now. So try it now! There's a free demo, so you really have no excuse not to ;) Now if you'll excuse me, I must go back to being a pira- *ahem* an "explorer."

I bought this game because the premise was simple and from the video, the style was very neat - in a sense that it was interesting. It is, by far, 'neat'. While the game is fun, I had to change the controls to something more.. easily accessable. It took a little bit to figure out what to do, since it just throws you into the game.
First, I gotta say I love the models for the badgers and foxes. They're widdle and adorable. The noises and music are really nice, too. The second level gives you the 'creepy mood' without being over powering.
The textures are very... messy. Tiling textures can be a pain, but looking at textures sloppily added onto the objects is also a pain - on the eyes. The textures are nice, but since nothing seems to tile, it just looks like a big, unfinished mess to me. The grass patches are obvious squares that go in alternating directions. It wouldn't take too long to easily make the textures they have tile, becuase they are already quite simple; full ambient, no shading. It is unique in it's own little style, though. You quicky get over it and enjoy the game. I think at first I just found it rather jarring.  I think my biggest pet peeve is the sky at night. Would it really be so hard to add glowing dots rather than what they have?? It looked like the cieling to a children's bedroom.
The camera seems to get weird during some places, and it doesn't matter if it's close up or far away. Sometimes it just... does a weird 'thing'. Turns itself around? Suddenly too sensitive? It's hard to explain, but it's super prominent in the second level, which was hard to explore. The levels aren't linear - which is usually a good thing - but I find it easy to get lost, only being able to know where I've been from the holes of wild growing.. turnips? I thought they were potted plants, at first. Hehe.
Anyway. The game is simple; maybe too simple. It's still fun, and I feel really bad for losing 2 cubs on the second level! If the textures tiled nicely, and didn't look like they were done in 10 minutes, this would be an awesome little game. It's easy to get attatched to your cubs once you figure out what you have to do, which can take a while to notice. From a distance, the environments are kinda pretty~
10$ is actually quite a lot considering, so I'm glad I got it for $2.50.

Graphics:  2D setup that combines the detail of Shadow Complex and the art style of Limbo.  Everything is dark and brooding, which really sets the overall tone.  Their lighting system is a thing of beauty as well:  rays of light shine through broken walls and windows, fire barrels give a nice ominous glow in the night.
Audio:  Somber acoustic guitar soundscapes reminiscent of The Last Of Us play during the day, and the night scavenging missions feature very tense, suspenseful string and synth arrangements.  Environmental sound effects like artillery shells landing and the crack of sniper fire constantly remind you that you're never really safe.
Controls:  Point and click adventure style.  You navigate around the environment by clicking where you want to go, objects you can interact with in the environment have their own separate icon.  While in the safehouse, you control each character independently by selecting their character photo then giving them their own commands. Navigating the menu system is simple and straightforward.
Gameplay:  Everything is randomly generated at the start, so no play through is the same.  The safehouse sequences are fairly routine.  Build this, repair that, eat, rest.  The game really comes alive when night falls and you have to decide what to do with your survivors.  Sickness, hunger, and injury are very serious threats to your group, and losing anyone significantly increases your risk of having the whole thing come crashing down on you.  Managing your survivors is key to getting through the siege.  There's also significant danger when it comes to the overall scavenging:  rolling over those weaker than you and taking everything they have makes you a target for vigilantes and decreases morale, and some of the more well-stocked areas tend to be heavily guarded by hostile military forces and other survivor groups who have no compunctions about killing anyone who sets foot on their turf.
My one major complaint is the lack of a tutorial or tool hints on the environmental icons.  It doesn't take too long to figure stuff out, but the initial learning curve can lead to some restarts.  There are very few bugs, which is always a plus.
Overall Score:  9/10

Below you will find the Riders of Icarus Ranger’s Fury DLC review for PC. Riders of Icarus is developed by Nexon America.
Ranger:
In the new DLC released for Riders of Icarus—Ranger’s Fury, the addition of the ranger hero class as well as a new zone and dungeon is a welcome addition to the Riders of Icarus franchise. The cornerstone of this DLC is of course the new ranger class which specializes in ranged attacks with crossbows and is the first ranged physical damage hero in the game. Although ranged attacks are the main niche for the ranger class, when it comes to close quarters combat the ranger is not limited to ranged attacks and has a variety of melee abilities as well. Kicks, leaps and specific abilities requiring a lance to be equipped allow for rangers to engage in melee combat while mounted and inflict devastating damage. In my experience the ranger class played very smoothly and the combat felt very satisfying. I was worried at first that the ranger would be very squishy and vulnerable to damage accompanied with less mobility compared to an assassin. However the developers have given the ranger a plethora of defensive abilities and damage reduction cooldowns/passives which make mitigating damage much more manageable. In addition, the design of both the class in general and melee abilities offers a nice contrast in gameplay for a primarily ranged class.

At the time of writing this review I have beaten Hollow Knight 3 times, first "normal" playthrough, second speed completion one and third steel soul completion. I have also revisited the game couple times to check and play with new, free content that was added. Since the time Hollow Knight was released this february it has firmly remained in "game of the year" slot for me.
The game is up there in the difficulty scale, but I greatly enjoyed my experience. Hollow Knight is challenging, harsh and often unforgiving, but also made me learn. With every hit/death I knew what went wrong and how to try to improve. Basic combat in this game is a simple thing, you swing your sword, up, down, left and right. There are special charged attacks you can learn, but they are also easy to execute. There are some very harsh platforming sections but I noticed that the game saves the most difficult ones for optional stuff.
The visuals are absolutely amazing, environments are lovingly crafted with great attention to details, giving each level a distinct character. This effect is enhanced by absolutely amazing soundtrack (one of my favourite game soundtracks ever). Enemies and bosses are very well designed, they vary greatly depending on where you are and range from almost cute to deeply disturbing.  NPCs (and our own character) also leave nothing to be desired in design compartment, I greatly enjoyed meeting them and uncovering their stories.
I should mention that there is no hand holding in this game, this beautiful world is vast and you can go where you want as soon as you have all skills. In fact you can go to a lot of places without having them, and that's the part of the game that causes some people problems. There is an NPC who will point you in the direction of your next skill, but the game won't point them out to you, YOU have to be the one to make a detour to talk to them. (Honestly, they aren't hidden or that much out of the way, but they also aren't "marked" as someone who can point you in a direction in any way) While I personally enjoy that aspect of the game I know many people won't, and may feel confused about what to do next.
One thing I found somewhat tedious (that has been partially fixed in free Hidden Dreams content update) is backtracking. You'll backtrack A LOT, no way around it. Especially if you, like me, are a completionist that has to sniffle out every single collectible, every single secret (and there is plenty of those).
From technical side Hollow Knight is also doing great. In all time I spent playing it I only encountered two or three small cosmetic bugs and one who forced me to restart the game (I lost maybe 10 minutes of progress). All of the bugs I have encountered had since been fixed.
All in all I can't recommend Hollow Knight enough and  don't regret a single hour spend with this game. Every time I go back to it I feel the same rush of excitement and wonder as the first time I played it.
My one advice would be to play it "blind" and savour the experience.

Easily top 3 of the entire AC franchise. Fully worth the purchase, especially if you happen to find it on sale.
The story follows Edward Kenway, grandfather of Connor from AC3. The gameplay is unique to the series in that you pretty much have to be a pirate in order to upgrade your ship and progress through the game. No complaints about that. But one criticism about the naval combat is that, for whatever reason, the game doesn't let you fire chainshot from your ship's broadside cannons. This isn't a huge deal, but when it comes to the battles with the "legendary" ships of the line, it would have made the combat easier and more historically accurate to be able to disable these behemoths from a distance before moving in and boarding for the kill. But, enough about that.
The world of Black Flag is vast, rich and deep. Even with 130+ hours logged in the game, I haven't seen all there is to see, collected all there is to collect, or completed all the side missions. After you've completed the main story, there's still much to do.
Highly recommended for fans of the AC series and first timers alike. The story doesn't really depend on you completing AC 1-3 in order to appreciate it. In fact, it takes place before AC 3 and Rogue so even if you played them in sequence, you'd technically be playing them out of chronological order, anyway. If you happen to be a fan of the TV series "Black Sails," you'll find it interesting to see how characters like Jack Rackam, Anne Bonny and Edward Teach (Blackbeard) are portrayed. Jack Sparrow's character seems shamelessly ripped off Rackam, by the way, but I digress.
Unlike AC 1-3, the "overworld" is no longer from the perspective of Desmond Miles, but of a regular employee of Abstergo Entertainment who uses the animus like just another PC application to access Desmond's ancestral memories. These ancestral memories, once known only to Desmond, have now been all complied in Abstergo's servers which malfunction from time to time during the game (there's a story to the overstory. kind of a seemingly unnecessary element altogether, but I suppose it adds some variety). In the end, we see that the Assassins vs. Templars conflict is still alive, leaving the door open for an untold amount of potential sequels.
My personal favorite AC title overall, and one of my all time vidya games. Buy it now.

I bought this game when it first came out, for the XBox 360.
After a few hours of playing it I put it down and never bothered to finish it, considering it one of the most disappointing releases from SquareEnix I had ever seen.
Years later I see this show up on Steam for $15, and decide to give it a second chance, to see if all of the shortcomings that drove me to quit this game in the first place would ever be overlookable.
Well, after about 80 hours of gameplay, I've decided that FFXIII was indeed better than my first impression dictated, and after completing the entire main story I would say the game deserves about 7/10.
The major downside to this game is just how long it takes for it to open up to you.  So many game mechanics are introduced only after several long hours of gameplay, but once they are there and fully unlocked the battles are actually quite engaging beyond the "repeatedly press A to auto-battle" mechanic that you start off with.
I think the biggest disappointment comes in expecting this to be the same kind of game as prior FF games, which was to be expected considering the name.  There are no towns, little in the way of sidequests, and a majority of the game is spent traversing long linear dungeons taking one battle after the next until you reach the next one.
But that's not to say that the game didn't eventually become fun.  It just took its sweet time getting there.
Glad I decided to give it another chance, and I'm definitely looking forward to the sequels to hit the Steam library.

FF XIII it's a classical JRPG, turn-based combat, a compelling storyline for a fantasy world, the two main characters (Light & Snow) are gorgeous and they're full of emotions. Graphics and design are pure eye candy, the music is great and follows the game perfectly, scenery is fantastic and the playability is suitable for casual players.
Hardcore JRPG gamers can find this game linear, read ahead please.
Graphics are gorgeous, period. The design of the entire game seems to be crafted in fine detail, from the start you feel that it's a AAA game... amazing cinematics and instantly you get the feel that the game is giant, and it is. You will travel through cities, wildlands, undergrounds, towers and futurist digital scenaries.
In two words, compelling + emotional. Almost the entire music is instrumental/classical and piano, however there are modern instruments too. It helps to tell/play this story very well, tracks like Blinded y Light or Fang's Theme are amazing, but there are many more... Sunleth Waterscape, Born anew, and Chocobos from Pulse are my favs... I ride a Chocobo just to hear that tune... great!.
The composers has achieved a perfect distinction from previous games, but has got an amazing new soundtrack full of emotion.
* You can play this game with just the keyboard, that's good for laptops, travelling, etc. Controls are easy to remember, the viewpoint is right, the automatic mode to fight helps a lot, i think. The paradigm switch animations are useless, but not annoying.
* You can switch from any role at any time, but you must choose wisely the abilities that you develop on each character.
* The FF powers are included; magics, healing, close combat, eidolons (special help), equipment, character progression, etc.
* There are no inventory issues, or worries about inns, or stores.
*  60% of the game is about traveling (linearly) to accomplish the main story... the rest of the time you can wander around two big maps in the world called Pulse. Moreover, there are teleport gates to easily go back and forth.
* Replayability can be done to get into higher levels, accomplish all the side missions, etc.
Overall, playability was carefully designed for casual players, but for hardcore gamers that want to choose what magic-power to use too. Lightning's "Army of One" is one of my favs.
You play a big storyline  about fate in a distant world called Pulse, and then there are four side stories (Light & Serah, Snow, Fang & Vanille, Hope & Zack). It seems there's no room (and time) for wandering around...the game as is, is about 60GB (100 hours gametime).
The characters are clearly defined, the heroes, the supporting ones, healers, and so on. The character design and backstory is compelling, the blend between cinematics and in-game aminations is excellent. A FF game, period.
You will fight against robots, betrayers, wild creatures, and more.  Fights are well balanced, specially if you take care of developing the right abilities for each character. The Ochu is one of my favs., wtf moments...
I've played without a glitch, I like the game as it is. However, some people want the classic JRPG experience at full, this game do not contains the section to role-play; exploring towns, Inns, markets, and crafting the equipment.
I think the story and the whole game was too big (3 DVDs on Xbox) to include the JRPG experience at full. IMHO.
Personally, I've enjoyed this game a lot... thanks Square.

THIS GAME. IS. AWESOME! Best $15 I've spent in a LONG time! Unlike what people have been saying, it's really not just a Smash clone. It's so similar, yet so different. Similar in a good way, so it feels natural to Smash players. Different in a few MAJOR factors: No blocking, no grabbing, no ledges, and every character is unique in some way.
Want an ACTUALLY stealthy character? Forsburn is perfect. A character that can teleport between "portals" they lay down? You won't find anyone like Orcane in Smash. Or how about someone who can make ENTIRE WALLS right below him, instantly? That would be Kragg.
So basically, this game is different enough from Smash to be fun for Smash players, yet similar enough so it's easy to learn. I HIGHLY recommend this game to anyone who likes Smash, or anyone looking for a good, easy to run fighting game that's good for partys.
Complaints: Spam is a little hard to deal with in this game, especially Zetterburn fireball spam. That's really it. I do wish they added support for the Gamecube to USB adapters, as Gamecube controllers just feel much more precise than Xbox 360 controllers, but that's just a minor complaint.

Definite Pro: Music, Setting (environment is beautiful and exotic...only fault is it's without 1080p support at launch), combat system with lots of abilities and weapons and customization (although you won't get to do it until about 1/3 through the game), beautiful cinematics.
Controversial, but still Pro for me: Characters and Plot. Lightning, Snow, Sazh, Vanille, Fang, Serah, all interesting characters in their own right. The story is cryptic at first...lots of undefined terms will be thrown at you. Definitely need to focus on the game to notice the subtle social cues and dynamics between the characters (esp Hope and Light or Vanille and Sazh). People give Lightning a lot of hate, thinking she has no personality, but that simply isn't true. There is a difference between having no personality and a repressed, reserved one. I will agree, however, the characters lack charm, suave, panache, etc., but they are relatable and lovable nonetheless.
Con: Super long "tutorial", i.e. the game does not give you full front-seat driver access until about 1/3 of the way through the game. You won't be able to choose your team, team leader, or diversify roles for a while. Also the game is not open-world, which severely limits replayability. I personally think this isn't a big problem, because the game is super long (dare you to finish it in one, or even 2 sittings, definitely take a week AT LEAST if you're a casual gamer). However, end game does give you freedom to keep going and max things out if you wish.

Blockstorm is a FPS developed by GhostShark and released May 21, 2015. It's basically a Minecraft inspired FPS.
So there's no singleplayer or story mode, there's only two selling points for Blockstorm: Multiplayer with 6 different game modes, and the in game editor.
You can select quick match if you don't care about the server or how many people are on it (it will only join official servers, and try to stick you into games with more people), or you can select your server with "choose match".
As I've already stated, there are six game modes: Death Match, Team Death Match, Capture the Flag, Assault, Castle Battle, and Hunt.
Most people are familiar with a majority of the staple game modes on this list... Death match is you vs everyone free for all styled. Team Death Match is Red team vs Blue team. Capture the Flag shouldn't need to be explained unless you had no childhood: you get the other teams flag and return it to your teams flag
. Assault is basically "control point" gameplay, one team defends, the other tries to get on the point to capture it. Castle Battle is defending your teams chests, and attacking your enemy teams chests, it's the only game which starts with a build phase. Lastly "Hunt" is basically killing stuff or destroying objects to get an item you run back to your control point to get your team points.
Each game mode has a time limit and sometimes a score limit, some have special map related rules or weapons, and as advertised you can destroy almost everything.
The weapons used in the game are mostly staples, before you join a game you can customize your loadout, you have your rifle, SMG, Sniper, and Shotgun. There are side arm weapons, and utilities like Grenades C4 and Rocket launcher, and lastly your knife/melee. What is different is the shovel and block. The shovel lets you dig through blocks, and the block lets you set blocks... You are limited on how many blocks you carry though.
I have saved the best for last, the "editors" have a lot of Potential... You can customize your own character, you can create custom maps, you can also upload your work to the steam workshop for others to see and insult!
Actually I didn't like the editor at first, but I think I'll make a level or two just because I messed around with it and started to get a feel for it. You're welcome to look it up and tell me how terrible it is!
Honestly this game isn't for me, I played for a few hours and find myself longing for something else... The achievements are only able to be earned on official Blockstorm servers, most of them are grindy... There is a player base for this game, so that's good for the game. But I'll be taking my marbles and leaving.
If you're looking for a minecraft-FPS, there are plenty out there, but this one delivers what's advertised so go ahead and pick it up if this is what you're looking for.
For early access, this game is a blast. It's a seriously good time waster and if you want a game that stimulates speed and precise combos, you definitely want Rivals of Aether.

It took a good 5 minutes in the game (including loading screens and bootup) to realize this was a literal copy and paste from the original game. It's noticeable that they did quite a bit of retexturing, but that's pretty much the full extent of their work.
Same low-quality sound.
Same old somewhat awkward animations.
Same old weird non-reflective, plasma-looking water aesthetic.
Same old excessive use of bloom to compensate for the lack of other visual effects.
Same old bugs, and a few new ones.
Hell, some parts of the game aren't even retextured. And even if you could possibly be satisfied with an incomplete retexture, you'll later realize that an enthused fan could have made a better retexture mod for Skyrim than a 2K-funded studio.
In conclusion: The only new things about this remaster are the bugs.
Edit: After looking at screenshot comparisons, there is a possibility that there are some instances in which the originals look better than their respective remasters.
Some might think I have no reason to complain, since I technically got this for free. But to be honest, you'd probably have a better experience playing the original than the remaster. So for those who did not get this for free: Don't buy the game; You'd be better off with the original even if it cost you $5 more. To those who got this for free: Just play the goddamn original.

Do you want a Super Smash Bros. Melee that isn't Super Smash Bros.? This is the game you want.
It's a very fun and potentially very competitive fighting game heavily inspired by Super Smash Bros. Melee. Unlike the majority of fighting games out there, your goal is not to make the enemy HP bar deplete. Instead, you hit them to make them weaker and weaker, so that you can launch them off the map, making them lose a life (Other than the one they lost because they're too addicted to this game, if you know what I mean). This game relies heavily on chains of combos to rack up damage on your enemy and finish it with a strong blow to launch them back.
If you like fighting games that are different than most others and very enjoyable, then pick this one up, it's worth the price. Actually, it's worth more than the price.
Also, if you've played competitive Super Smash Bros. Melee, many of the techniques you've picked up such as wave dashing and edge guarding can be applied here.

It's the Civ we all know and enjoy but bland and lacking innovation or vision.
On the positive side of the equation the game is stable, the Aliens spice it up a bit, the tech web allows a lot of options in research order, quests are included as part of the victory paths and the affinity system is cool.
But there is so much that could be better.  Trade routes require excessive micromanagement, the quests are one dimensional, there is no surprise or story around the Aliens (e.g. more powerful units), the Aliens do not become aggressive quickly enough, the factions and leaders are bland and alike strategically, the victory screens are appallingly lame, the differences in the various worlds are very minor (opportunity lost to add massive replay value by having unique features on each map), the Diplomatic AI is inept, there is no story beyond the intro movie, and there are no Colony Governors (so it can become quite micro intensive on large maps).
I'll play it plenty regardless because I enjoy 4X so much. But for those that have limited gaming budgets, the game represents appalling value for money.
This game really is just a reskin of Civ V and feature wise we've gone backwards from a Brave New World. We'll need at least one expansion just to get to Brave New World level. There really is no excuse for this given it's the same engine.
Secondly on Steam the game cost is US$90 in my region (Australia) with the price set by the publisher. Yes you can go elsewhere (e.g. OzGameShop) and pay about US$50, which is what any avid gamer would do, but more than a few casual gamers will spend US$90.
You put those factors together and it's clear that management at Firaxis are focusing on milking the cow.  I would rather they had a vision for the future of 4X games and led the pack. Ironically, a focus on leading the pack is likely the better long-term business strategy anyway.
As Devildog said in the eXplorminate review:
"despite many cries of frustration from fans and well documented examples, leads me to believe that they’re both incapable and unaware of how much we hate these things."
Unless you are a huge fan of 4X games and Civ, I do not recommend this game.  Either wait for Expansions to improve the game and buy it during a sale or purchase Endless Legend instead which is a vastly superior game.

Battlerite is a PvP battle arena game.
The gameplay is completely skill based, and there are no elements of randomness. It’s all about reaction time, juking, landing skill shots, and teamwork. Games are played in rounds, which eliminates the snowballing effect that occurs in MOBAs. There is a very high skill cap.
There are many champions, all having very unique abilities and roles. The champions are well balanced against each other.
Between each round you can pick battlerites, which are bonuses for your hero’s abilities. This allows for a variety of playstyles and opportunities to counter the enemy team.
If you enjoy the fast paced fighting aspects of MOBAs, I recommend this game.

Several points to be made about this game
1. Interesting concept. Seeing the other side of war is intriguing.
2. It has a simplistic, yet interesting crafting system.
3. The sense of needing to survive is pretty intense.
4. It's combat sucks a**. You click to attack, and hope that you hit before your enemy. You will die, unless they are unarmed. I mean, I can understand a brutal, and punishing combat system if either a) you could use skill to avoid damage, or b) you could go stealth, which brings me to my next point
5. The stealth system sucks a**. You literally have no indication as to whether you've been spotted or not until they shoot you...even when you're in the cover, you can be shot at. Sometimes they run, sometimes they warn you as they attack, and sometimes, they just sit there for a minute, and then attack you.
5b. You can see the sound they make, and that's suppose to allow you to sneak by them, but they move so fast compared to you while sneaking that it's quite pointless. There is also almost nothing that seems to block line of sight, meaning, if they are anywhere near you, you will get spotted, and die.
6. No tutorial, nor did it explain anything. So, for the first 10-15 minutes, you'll be walking around your house, rather than running. No key binding list, so you can't check that either. This is a unique game. This is a game for people who enjoy dry, British humour. It has the kind of illogical wackiness you'd expect from Monty Python, Terry Pratchett, or Douglas Adams. You wander around an office building as a cheeky narrator provides sometimes helpful advice, and sometimes incendiary criticisms. No, you don't fight or collect anything. It doesn't take that long to beat, but there are quite a few endings, many of which I never would have found without looking up online. There's even a way to enter cheat codes to walk through walls or shoot rockets. One of the achievements requires you to play all day long on a Tuesday. I didn't get that one. I know I can just change my system clock to trick the game and just leave it running and minimized for 24 hours straight, but that would drive up my electric bill. I can't have that. So again, it's not particularly long or challenging, but it is funny. Made me laugh. Every choice you make, every path you take, he'll be watching you. And taunting you. That goofy, British narrator. Why the Police homage? I don't know. They're British. Not a huge fan of Sting. Stewart Copeland is the real star of the show. Where was I going with that...? Oh yes! You'll find that the path branches off frequently. Many forks in the road. I tried to take the road less traveled and all that. I found myself constantly saving so I could quickly go back and check the other way. If you do what the narrator tells you, that's one ending. If you do the exact opposite of what he tells you, then he gets upset, but you get another ending. If you memorize the main path and get through it faster than he can talk, he gets upset and I don't think it changes the ending at all. There's an achievement for going through the main path as fast as humanly possible. I couldn't get that one. I pressed the W key as hard as I could. Anyways, I'm not about to give you financial advice, but I think 15 bucks is a bargain. Anything less would be...well, more of a bargain, I suppose. If you've read this far, you probably already have the game. If you don't have the game yet, you probably decided if you were going to buy it or not long before reading this review. If you are still on the fence, try reading Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy or one of the Discworld novels. If you've never seen a Monty Python film, you can't go wrong with The Holy Grail.
This review is receiving an unnecessary update on 11/24/2017 to coincide with the current Steam Awards and a particular badge related quest. I haven't played the game recently, it hasn't received any new content. So why continue talking about? Because it's just a fun, quirky game. It doesn't need any new content. What new content could they even add? Even more endings? A random Terry Gilliam cameo? Maybe an extended ending to show what Stanley did afterwards. Does he find a new job? A sequel might be nice to answer that question. But wouldn't a sequel just ruin the magic, the mystery, the mood? Judging by Stanley's bizarre day at the office, do we even want to know what sort of shenanigans the cruel universe will rain down upon him next? Perhaps it's more fun to speculate. I would hate to see him at another boring office job that also suddenly becomes interesting in the worst way possible. That would be redundant. What if he explored the house from Gone Home, and the British narrator went into lengthy explanations about Street Fighter, the X-Files, VCR's, and other relics from the 90's? I'd play that. And then there could be crazy alternate endings, like the house could get sucked into a vortex and the narrator could start talking about how it's so derivative of Poltergeist, and how the reference doesn't even make sense because the film came out in 1982 and the 2015 remake was "bloody awful".
If there ever is a sequel, spinoff, remaster, etc., then Stewart Copeland should write the soundtrack. Do you even know how many movies and shows he composed music for? Dozens. No joke. What I really want, more than another Stanley game, is another Oysterhead album. So anyways, I still recommend the game. My original review and recommendation remain very much intact. And now I should get a badge or something. Sweet.

Shelter, or as I like to call it "The Badger Game" is a potentially PTSD-invoking first person badger game. You play the part of a single mother badger, desperately trying to lead your helpless badgerlings to safety. Not only do you have to feed the little guys, but you must navagate perils such as swooping raptors and road-kill hungry carnivores with a penchant for badger flesh. At least - I think there are cars eventually, but I don't *actually* have first hand experience with them so they may not actually exists. If they *do* actually exist the drivers may or may not actually intend to hit and/or kill the critters.
I can't with a good conscious recommend this game because of the psychological trauma that I endured after one of my baby badgers, Two Stripes, was swooped up and carried off by an eagle within twenty minutes of starting the game. I found myself falling into a swirling pit of despair, shouting "MY BABY! MY BABY!" It was all for naught, Two Stripes was lost forever. I have yet to resume the game.
Or, if you want to support an indie game about badgers, go for it. In fact, go for it.

Riders of Icarus is a highly addictive RPG game with a lovely community and great features in the game. The thing that makes RoI different to other RPG games is that there is the "taming" feature, where you collect or craft marks for different familiars (mounts) and tame them for yourself to ride freely. The familiars in the game look absolutely amazing, from dragons to pegasi to cute little desert kittens. The developers take their time to put effort into the game; for example they make sure they are up to date with public events such as the christmas festive event and valentines day event. The community is very kind and there are rarely any scammers (although let's face it, there will always be scammers in rpg games). The graphics are very lovely; probably the best graphics I have seen in a game for a little while. The only things about this game that aren't very good is the constant hours of grinding and glitched/random disconecctions, however if you're very patient then this game should be recommended to you.

And there really isn't any story or plot in this game, but it makes you think about the deeper things that you normally won't think about. Nowadays, I've been playing and looking for games that's 'different' from others.  And I truly hope there are more games like this one.  I highly recommend this if you want a unique and wonderful gaming experience.

This game is, at the moment, nothing more than a "production line" type of game. A very intricate and complicated one.
Granted, a very interesting one too, given that it's still EARLY ACCESS.
But I can't see the final game to be any more than this.
I can't "feel" the background of the story. It's supposed to be about the "survivors" of the mother of all climate changes, but then right from the get-go, you find out that there are...corporations to trade with. Uhhhh....
There goes the backstory.
So apparently, human economy and industry outside your domed colony has survived all these years that the colonists spent in cryo-stasis.
Would be nice if we could have a backstory to these "corporations" that fit in with the rest of the backstory. How the heck did they survive all these years? Who the heck were their clients that they did business with? It can't be just the survivors in Project Aura. They were all asleep until now.
So, like I said, it's nothing more than a very intricate and complicated "production line" type of game. Your first moves would probably be to "buy" a cargo plane and materials to build it's hangar and awaken the right kinds of colonists to operate this facility, so you could go out of your dome to look for raw materials. Once you have food and water self-sufficiency, you'd probably aim to built some kind of industry, or expand your food production capabilities. Whichever, at this time, your concern would be to sell stuff that you acquire/manufacture. Recycling within your colony is given a premium. You even get to recycle your colonists' #1 and #2. You send out your planes to gather all sorts of garbage, and turn them into something useful.
If you're into this type of games, then you'll love this game. I can't say that I am into this kind of game though. I do find it quite interesting, but sooner or later, it may just end up like how Banished ended up in my Steam Library.

If you enjoy managing large civilizations and snowballing your way to victory this is not the civilization for you.  Everything about this game is balanced to produce smaller civs and increased interactions between civs.  This may be great if you play multiplayer, but for a single player fan like me, it takes away from the experience of leading mankinds first intersteller colonization.  Rather then wanting to climb over that next ridge, see whats there, and then optimize for the best city placement,; I'm forced to race against AI cities that are dropped right next to me.
This game is definetly not an updated version of Alpha Centauri.  Some of the innovations are great, the use of satellites, autoupgrading units, explorer expiditions, and affinities.  But other things are just off, the ability to cross oceans so soon after landing feels wrong.
The tech web is a very mixed bag.  Compared to past Civilization games that had a linear tech tree based on history, it makes perfect sense that in the future you could choose which path to pursue.  The problem with it was that I always felt that there was maybe one or two optimal choices.  Pick wrong and you would fail.  You need health, you need energy, you need better weapons from affinity choices, and you will always feel pulled by the choices.  In past civs there was always some slack with the tech choices.  Rather than techs giving me choices and rewards, I feel tense everytime I open the research window.
The virtue menu is also innovative, it gives you the option to customize your civ.  But everytime i play, it feels like there is only one good tree.  You have to take prosperity, anything else and you will fall behind the AI.  Maybe in multiplayer it would be a different story, but in single player it seems anything else is a waste till you max it out.
The civilopedia is awesome.  This may be the most narrative of all the Civilization games and the fiction inside the civilopedia had me opening the game just to read it.  And that shows a big problem with the game.  I was more interested in reading the civilopedia than playing the game.

Like I said at the start...great potential... :)

Within the first 5 minutes of the game, I notice that two major issues, FoV and mouse acceleration, which plagued the original game, are still infact present in the remastered version of Bioshock.
This port is sloppy as hell, but it isn't Arkham Knight-tier bad. The game looks marginally better than the original 9 year old game, but you'd honestly expect better graphics considering how old this game is. It looks better, but not that much better.
While many legacy bugs carry over from the original, the port is at least tuned to run well on modern PCs, something the original Bioshock struggled to do. Sound clipping that was an issue in the original is no longer present. It also doesn't crash when ALT-TABbing like the original.
All in all, this is a medicore port for a near decade old classic. I definitely suggest picking it up at some point, but you may not want to do it right now if you don't want to encounter annoying bugs.

-

-orbital layer

Here's what's missing:
-city states (stations are a downgrade in complexity)

-a UI that helps.

Basically this game is a reskinned and simplified version of Civ V.

There's a promising core here but as of June 2015 the game is not worth playing.
The tutorials do a terrible job of explaining how the game actually plays. You'll learn what most of the buttons do but not the overall picture. They show you how to set up the *second* production step for basic food (raw seaweed+fertilizer->food rations), then dump you into the game. Good luck figuring out where you're supposed to get those ingredients to start with.
The graphics are surprisingly good for this type of game, but it's only skin deep. The camera controls are finicky and won't let you zoom out enough to get a decent panorama view. Buildings look interesting and many have cool work animations, but there's almost zero information conveyed. The salvage planes flying in and out are pretty cool; now if only I could distinguish between the three types, or what materials they're carrying. Even the platforms that you expand onto lack clarity. You have to build the floor and the power system separately (again, something the tutorial and help screens fail to explain). The difference between an unpowered platform (that you can't build on) and a powered platform (that you can) is a thin line around the edge that glows red.
The UI is your worst enemy. You'll find yourself clicking through the same menus over and over again because the important controls are hidden behind three layers. Meanwhile, there are eight top-level buttons that have hotkeys. These include three rarely-needed status/upgrade menus, one temperamental and out-of-theme building menu, and two menus for features that *aren't implemented yet*.
There's no good overview menu. It's hard to even manage your inventory to see what items you have and what you need; forget about seeing the flow of production in your colony. You can't even see whether your buildings are working or not without carefully mouse-overing each one. And if you do see something is stopped, you'll still need to click through to figure out why. Did it run out of input materials? Did you forget to click the "run forever" button? Did you click that button, but not the "restart when new materials are ready" button?
And if you forget what this building is even producing, don't worry, that's an extra click. On each production line.
As previously mentioned, key game components are still missing, notably the research system. This actually wouldn't be a big deal except that the system is half-implemented. So you can building research labs and produce research tokens (color-coded science items), but then the only thing to do with those tokens is sell them on the market.

So far I love this game and I can honestly recommend it to fans of the metroidvania genre. You will 100% get what you searched for!
There might be a lot of things copied from compareable titles like Guacamelee (most of the skillset is a 1on1 copy -> level design is easy to foreshadow because of that, Controller Mapping is almost the same, Dream World switching), Salt and Sanctuary (combination of Soulslike with Metroidvania; campfires = benches, Darkness as a main leitmotif in the game design), Ori and the Blind Forest (superfine animations/cuteness, ambience, simple story with huge emotional impact),
BUT: the game still feels so well-polished and fresh that the mixture still amazes me to full extent. I'm 20 hrs in so far and I still feel like the vastness of the world overwhelms me from time to time. There is so much to explore and discover and the Charm System is so much fun to fiddle around to find the perfect perk combinations that adapt to the difficult bossfights and tough-spot situations.
I will keep this updated when I'm more advanced in the game, but so far it's been a blast if you can live with the fact that it doesn't invent the wheel anew and you are a fan of the genre.
Get it while it's still on sale, you won't regret it!

Rivals of Aether is, as you've probably gathered at this point, a Smash Bros style game. It sets itself apart by being more aggressive than Smash has become and having extremely unique characters. Ever character has their own little set of gimmicks and tricks, such as Kragg's ability to create a pillar and block that effectively act as part of the stage until destroyed, or Orcane's ability to lay down a puddle he can teleport to or "burn" for a blast of bubbles. As a result most of the characters play quite a bit differently and become fairly technical (though some are still fairly simple to pick up and play; notably Zetterburn and Kragg). It gives the game a sense of depth I feel Smash is somewhat lacking and really reinforces the differences between a so called "platform fighter" and a standard fighter. Stage awareness becomes much more important as well as an understanding of your opponents capabilities.
The game also has some key differences from smash in terms of standard gameplay, namely that ledge grabbing is not a thing, all characters can wall jump (gaining a second use of their recovery as a result) and there's no shielding, only "parrying" (which stuns opponents for a period based off how powerful the move was). As noted previously, the game is more aggressive, and this is partially why. Recovering becomes a lot trickier with no ledge to grab and having to effectively time your "shield" makes it harder to turn back an offensive. Oh, and unlike later Smashes, comboing is very much a thing in this game.
With that, you may be wondering if this is a game you should try casually. The game, while more aggressive, is still quite accessible to new people. The more aggressive mechanics aren't burdensome for the most part and just require some adjustment. About the only thing to keep in mind is that wave-dashing is in game, and while infinitely easier than Melee, is still something casual players will likely to find too much of a pain to bother with. This shouldn't effect most players anyway.
NOTE: Currently the game is early access, and online is 1 vs 1 only on random stages with no hazards. If this is a dealbreaker for you, you may want to wait.
So honestly, I strongly suggest giving this game a shot. For fifteen dollars getting an awesome Smash-esque experience on the PC is super worth it.

Just like many other reviewers are saying, this is pretty much hearthstone with MTG.   The tutorial and campaign system is great for new players, and the multiplayer matches can satisfy the "cardboard crack" itch for us experienced paper players.  It is also exciting to see cards from the new "Origins" TCG set in here as well, and to learn the lore behind the more iconic planeswalkers.  Overall, this is the best MTG video game and is full of potential, as long as Wizards is able to update the content when new card sets come out (about 4 times per year), which they have stated they will do.
My only complaint is that as of now, the cards from Origins are rather limited, and we are missing some key planeswalkers.  Wizards has been vague on whether or not the rest of the set will be added, but we shall see.
