This is the story of a man named Stanley.
Stanley worked for a company in a big building where he was Employee #427. Employee #427's job was simple: he sat at his desk in room 427 and he pushed buttons on a keyboard. Orders came to him through a monitor on his desk, telling him what buttons to push, how long to push them, and in what order. This is what Employee #427 did every day of every month of every year, and although others might have considered it soul rending, Stanley relished every moment the orders came in, as though he had been made exactly for this job. And Stanley was happy.
And then one day, something very peculiar happened. Something that would forever change Stanley; something he would never quite forget. He had been at his desk for nearly an hour when he realized that not one single order had arrived on the monitor for him to follow. No one had shown up to give him instructions, call a meeting, or even say 'hi.' Never in all his years at the company had this happened, this complete isolation. Something was very clearly wrong.
Shocked, frozen solid, Stanley found himself unable to move for the longest time. But as he came to his wits and regained his senses, he got up from his desk and stepped out of his office.

Hitman: Absolution is an excellent and my personal favorite addition to the Hitman series.
First, I'll talk about the story. In Hitman: Absolution, you are sent to complete a hit on a woman named Diana, who betrayed the agency. After you assassinate Diana, her dying wish is for you to protect a girl named Veronica. I won't go to deep into the story, but I'll say that you're no longer completing hits that someone gave you, but you're completing them based off of personal interest. Overall, the story wasn't the best, but I found it overall satisfying. I mean, there is only so much you can do with a story revolving around a player who is a hitman. But, none-the-less, I felt satisfied after finishing the game. I do have one complaint, though, I wish in the end, I could've had the choice whether to spare or kill Travis at the end, rather than it cutting straight to a cutscene right as you enter the sanctuary. Instead, the "final boss/bosses" are 3 well-trained body guards protecting Travis from Agent 47. Which was a bit challenging with the trip mines, but I was able to stealthly garrote all 3 of them on my 1st try.
Now, onto gameplay mechanics. Hitman: Absolution has a point system that either rewards you or takes off points based on your actions. This does two things, in my opinion: It adds a feel of competition for you and your friends to see who can get the highest score at the end of a mission. It also rewards you for stealthing it, and deducts points if you don't. I view this as sort of unfair. I'll explain why: The game upfront doesn't really explain to you that stealth is encouraged. I've seen many movies/TV Show/etc. where Hitmen are in it, and they didn't approach a hit stealthily. This gets on my nerves a bit because it seems like the only thing that you could do to get points was to stealth a mission. This didn't really affect me because I love to stealth things. But for players who love to go in gun-blazing into a situation, they might've been dissappointed. I mean, the least they could've done was give you less points, rather than giving you negative points.
Besides the point system, Hitman has a few features in stealth-related games that are pretty common. Things such as detection meter, hiding behind cover, etc.. What really sets this game apart from other games like it is the amount of different ways to kill a target, and the fact that you can blend in by disguising as the people you're around. I'll start off by talking about the different ways of killing people: As Agent 47, you can approach by killing a person with many different tactics. You could either approach a situation using the equipment you have such as your garrote or silverballers, or you could interact with some of the things that are in the target's environment to set a trap for the target. I'll give an example: In the mission where you are in Little China (I don't remember the name. Sorry), you can find poison to put in the target's food. If you successfully complete this, the target dies and you leave the crime scene undetected of doing anything to kill him. I loved this feature because the kills were awesome and extremely creative. I also really liked it because it was something that I had never really been exposed to in a game before in a genre like Hitman. Now, onto disguises: This was another thing I loved about the game's mechanics. I loved having the ability to sneak past people by wearing a disguise I picked up by either killing/knocking out an enemy, or by finding one lying around. It made me feel like I didn't have to deal with every enemy in an area, and that I had the choice to sneak past people to remain undetected. They also did a really good job making it to where it isn't extremely overpowered either. The reason it's not overpowered is because enemies can get uspicious of you still if you are wearing the same clothes they are. A solutution to this, though, pressing CTRL to do an action to get rid of suspiscion. The downfall to this: It eats up your instinct pretty fast.
One final thing I like about the mechanics was the fact that the missions got progressivley got harder as you got through the game. I love this feature because I hate games where it makes you wonder: "What the ♥♥♥♥? Why is this the final boss or mission when it was super easy?" or "What the hell? This isn't Dark Souls. Why is it this hard in the beginning?". Hitman: Absolution is able to hold this factor throughout the campaign with harder levels or missions after each one you complete. This feature may be pretty common with a lot of games, but I have played certain games where this feature isn't in it, and it makes you feel like the game was super easy or super hard.
Now, I'll begin talking about something that is new in this addition of Hitman: Hitman Contracts. Hitman Contracts is essentially someone creating a contract for you to complete in a certain way. It tells you what you must use to kill the person, what to wear, etc. in order to fully complete the mission. I really, really liked this add-on because it gave me something to do after I beat the campaign, rather than just playing through it again on a higher difficulty. What made this the most fun for me was the amount of creativity and imagination the community had. One of my favorite Contracts was when you were told to kill three hippies in the stoner apartment floor of the apartment. You had to use a bong to kill all three with a bong, and you had to be dressed as a scarecrow. It also isn't very hard to create your very own contract for players to complete either, which is nice for people like myself who aren't that skilled in level design or having that bright of an imagination. Overall, I thought this was something that was very creative and a nice way for the community to have an impact on the game. It was also a really nice addition to an already great game.
Conclusion: I really recommend this game to you if you are a fan of Stealth games, like myself. It offers hours of fun and replay ability. This was definately one of my favorite games of 2012.
*Cliffnote: I've read rumors online of Square Enix and the company that makes Hitman have gotten into a bit of a fight, so it's doubtful that there will be a new Hitman for a while. (Please correct me if I'm wrong on this.) :(

Sins of a Solar Empire Rebellion, is one of the greatest RTS 4X games of all time!
Please Note: however that the other Sins of a Solar Empire games have the some of the exact same content as Rebellion, so do not purchase those other games. With that said, Sins Rebellion is more of an expansion that a brand new game, because it has all the content of the previous three Sins games and new content of its own.
Now on to the review, I will use a pro and cons list, first pros.
Pros
1) Has one of the best tech trees of all time, with lots of things to research to make your units better, and also your planets to. There is a tree for defense, offense, diplomacy and finally fleet. Defense has most of the research for your planets. Research includes increasing tax revenue and production, as well as unlocking things such as mine’s, and increasing the hit points of structures. Offense deals solely in your unit’s abilities, health, and damage; you research items from this tech tree to unlock units. Diplomacy gives players the ability to win the game without destroying too much stuff, also allows friends to become enemies and enemies to become Allies. Fleet research has to do with increasing population cap for both total units and for capitol ships allowed to be fielded at once. Once Fleet is fully upgraded hundreds of ship can fight on each side.
2) The population cap itself is very large. Scale of battles is often large too, comprising of more than 200 units on each side by middle, end game.
3) Playing against Easy AI is an effective way to learn the game before jumping in to verse other people. The Easy AI will challenge first time players, they are hard enough to challenge but not eliminated the human player, which gives players time to learn the game.
4) There is a very large variety of units to deploy in the game that serve a magnitude of purposes, although you do not need to use all of them, the game does encourage diversity. Mainly there’s 3 kinds of units: Damage, Support and Defense. Damage units attack the enemy directly with lasers, bullets and missiles. Support units hang back and provide specially abilities, such as planet destroyers and aircraft carriers that deploy strike craft. These units on their own cannot defend themselves effectively; they depend on damage units to protect them at all times. Defense units can increase the hull integrity and shields of your own forces, and can provide devastating abilities that protect your fleets.
Sins is a game that is easy to learn but hard master. With so many different units you can field in battle, supported by so much research and strategic options, tremendously increases the replay ability. Now onto the Cons.
Cons
1) Unfortunately Sins does not allow the player to engage in battle on actual planets, but considering the scale of the rest of the game, this is not a big issue.
2) You cannot intercept or engage enemy units while on their way to one of your planets. In other words you cannot battle anywhere but the planet’s gravity well. This I would have loved if they added. You can only battle in the space surrounding a planet which is called the gravity well, and that is it.
3) In order to travel to other planets you must use phase lanes. Phase lanes are how planets are connected to one another, and in order to get to your last planet you must go through the other ones in the middle. In other words, you cannot simply go directly from your first planet all the way to your last one, unless you play as a particular race that has that ability earned middle/late game to do so.
4) Default game speed is quite slow, resulting in battles dragging on longer than what they should. This is an easy fix if you go to settings to increase game speed. Recommended level is fastest for everything.
5) All Sins games have support only for one processor. If you have a 2 core, 4, 6, or 8 will not give you a performance boost because they are not supported. But on a happy note this game does allow you to change many settings for graphics, making this game one of the most compatible with an extreme range of hardware. Most old and new laptops can run this game just fine.
6) This game is more like DLC then a new game. As stated at the top, do not buy the other Sins games, buy this one only.
Final Verdict
9/10 Excellent
This game is an example of above average work, there is no bugs, glitches or problems with this game whatsoever, although there’s a few features I’d like to see added perhaps in the future. Hopefully the next Sins game will make some or all my dreams come true.

The game seems interesting at first but it's very disappointing once you get the whole idea. It's extremely slow and boring. It feels like nothing happens. Increasing speed doesn't help game still feels dead.

Creating a colony is a very slow process. Production is micromanagement nightmare.
You start with very basic, the food, you need to buy, build, employ lots of stuff and citizens to produce the most basic food.
Every building needs a director which comes from colonist pool the "Vital Reserve" they are random so if he is not there you wait or exchange one of the colonists for the one you want at a price.
After director you need to buy blueprints for production, e.g. Seaweed fattening and Seaweed drying blueprints. And of course you need farmers and operators in each blueprint.

As a huge fan of Civ V it really pains me to write this review, given how excited I was for this game.  If you're completely new to the franchise, I would only recommend buying this game if you really just need a turn-based sci-fi fix, and even then I would recommend you consider other options first.  If it's a turn based strategy you're looking for, I would strongly recommend  you instead buy Civ V complete, as it is a much more diverse and enjoyable game.
To the veterans like me, I would point out my main problem with this game: no matter what type of victory you are striving for, your colony will look roughly the same every.  single.  game.  from the inside out.  Doesn't matter what faction you choose.  Doesn't matter what bonuses you choose beforehand.  Doesn't even really matter what victory you are going for.  In this game there is virtually no need to change  your strategy for different conditions.  This could not be less true in Civ V.  Take the three peaceful victories in Civ V (BNW), Culture, Science, and Diplomacy.  Think of how drastically different your strategy has to be to achieve each of those.  Consider how different your empire looks, where your gold is going, the focuses of your cities and the wonders you shoot for.  The contrast is incredible.  Now consider Beyond Earth.  Not three but four victories can be condensed to one similar description: research select essential technologies, build a thing, build more things for that thing, don't let that thing get destroyed, win.  Seriously.  Even vanilla Civ V was a little bit more varied, and that's saying something.  I expected exciting new challenges out of this game, not one new concept that could be done in four slightly different ways.
TL;DR - This game doesn't feel complete.  It basically only has two different types of victories, both bland.  Wait for the expansions.  Enjoy Civ V in the meantime.

Bioshock is arguably one of the best games ever. The remaster does it no justice.
When I first loaded it, the first thing I noticed was that the graphics were only marginally better. No big deal. At least I was getting 150 Fps! Then the screen started flickering because of electrical flashes. Again, no problem. I thought I would turn the vertical synch on and clear it up. The game crashed. Okay. Started it up again, smacked vertical synch up and gave it another shot. 60 FPS, no flickering and all seemed well. I wanted to look at the map. I hit the button and had to wait a couple of seconds for the map to come up. Nope. It wasn't a one time deal. It happens every time.

UPDATE March 23, 2017.  The game runs great, looks great and plays great. It is still as fun as ever. Unfortunately, it still locks up my system from time to time if I attempt to view the map. I am going to have to assume that this is as good as this product is going to get. Six months with no change is too long. Stick to the good old reliable version and have fun!

Rivals of Aether is, as you've probably gathered at this point, a Smash Bros style game. It sets itself apart by being more aggressive than Smash has become and having extremely unique characters. Ever character has their own little set of gimmicks and tricks, such as Kragg's ability to create a pillar and block that effectively act as part of the stage until destroyed, or Orcane's ability to lay down a puddle he can teleport to or "burn" for a blast of bubbles. As a result most of the characters play quite a bit differently and become fairly technical (though some are still fairly simple to pick up and play; notably Zetterburn and Kragg). It gives the game a sense of depth I feel Smash is somewhat lacking and really reinforces the differences between a so called "platform fighter" and a standard fighter. Stage awareness becomes much more important as well as an understanding of your opponents capabilities.
The game also has some key differences from smash in terms of standard gameplay, namely that ledge grabbing is not a thing, all characters can wall jump (gaining a second use of their recovery as a result) and there's no shielding, only "parrying" (which stuns opponents for a period based off how powerful the move was). As noted previously, the game is more aggressive, and this is partially why. Recovering becomes a lot trickier with no ledge to grab and having to effectively time your "shield" makes it harder to turn back an offensive. Oh, and unlike later Smashes, comboing is very much a thing in this game.
With that, you may be wondering if this is a game you should try casually. The game, while more aggressive, is still quite accessible to new people. The more aggressive mechanics aren't burdensome for the most part and just require some adjustment. About the only thing to keep in mind is that wave-dashing is in game, and while infinitely easier than Melee, is still something casual players will likely to find too much of a pain to bother with. This shouldn't effect most players anyway.
NOTE: Currently the game is early access, and online is 1 vs 1 only on random stages with no hazards. If this is a dealbreaker for you, you may want to wait.
So honestly, I strongly suggest giving this game a shot. For fifteen dollars getting an awesome Smash-esque experience on the PC is super worth it.

Game reviews can be quite tricky to write. Attempting to provide an interesting, yet insightful, treatise into a videogame using only the power of words that good old Dr Johnson has provided is a talent mastered only by the few. Get it right, and you can go onto a successful career writing for Marvel, get it wrong and you become such a laughing stock that you have to move to Japan. One thing that I have learnt, however, is that a review should base itself upon what the game actually does, not that which you wish it would.
So I shall attempt not to denigrate this Civilisation 5 scenario pack too much for copy pasting the rather lacklustre diplomacy model from its parent. I won’t mention the occlusion of core aspects of its spiritual predecessor like the planetary council, or clearly defined visual differences in faction cities. I won’t fuel the “games are being dumbed down” crowd by highlighting the oversimplification of the terraforming model, no longer can you raise a mountain on the west side of a nation, to reduce its lands to a dustbowl. And I certainly won’t highlight the complete absence of any “movies” that would traditionally accompany the completion of a wonder, or even the victory of the game. Indeed, just because I think that having spent five to ten hours conquering a procedurally generated landscape that a pleasing animation showcasing the type of victory that you have secured doesn’t mean that many other people won’t find a text message stating “congratulations, you won” as equally satisfying.
Instead, I shall concentrate on what the game actually does.
Unfortunately I doubt this will improve the general perception of the title either.
Yes, its basically Civilisation 5 with a purple repaint, so if you hated that there is no need to read any further. This is not the game you are looking for. Indeed, I might ask why you think it would be?
So what you have here is Civ 5. Set on another world. With half the aspects of the parent game cut out. There are a few differences, policies are replaced with virtues, but they operate in the exact same way, and the tech tree has been replaced with a tech web.
The tech web, however, could actually lead to some interesting multiplayer games (if anyone ever actually plays Civ in multiplayer). With Civ, if you are at the same tech level as another player, you are basically utilising the same units with the same bonuses. However with the web, you may well have a completely different set of buildings and units whilst still being at the same tech level. Hell, if you are behind technologically, but have concentrated on a more militaristic build, you stand a fighting chance against a more technically advanced, though more pacifistic, nation.
That said, and this is really the greatest flaw in the game itself, the lack of any discernable characteristic between the playable nations.  Many have criticised the lack of leaders present at launch (snigger) citing that Civ 5 released with 18 playable nations compared with Alpha Centauri: Weight watchers editions 8. However with the original game releasing with 7, this is a bit whiney. The problem is that the leaders present lack any discernable or notable personality. There could be a thousand leaders for all the difference it makes. Admittedly, its much harder to graft a personality onto a fictional person from a fictional future organisation than it is to imagine Gengis Khan of the Mongols as a bit of a bad♥♥♥♥♥conqueror on a horse, but twenty years (more or less) after release, Sister Miriam Godwinson and Chairman Yang can still be name dropped into a review and any gamer worth their salt will recognise the characters. This bunch of generic, committee members will be forgotten by Christmas.
Incidentally, also when you will almost certainly be able to pick this game up at the expansion pack price point that it should have been released at.
The AI is up to the usually civ standard. And by that I mean its♥♥♥♥♥♥ I’ve played on a few difficulty levels now, and am still waiting for someone, ANYONE to declare war on me. No matter what I do, no matter what I say or how I act, the AI tends to stay resolutely defensive, and when war does inevitable break out, its forces can be taken apart faster than a UKIP policy manifesto.
That said, the inclusion of a “satellite” layer where you can build and launch satellites to buff either your cities or your military adds another layer for the AI to fail at, and for you to exploit.  Personally (Of course, I’m not writing the opinion of anyone else here!) I find the inclusion of satellites to be the most interesting addition to the game. Finding the best way to use your satellites to most effectively buff your nation and provide killing fields is an exercise in planning all by itself.
Certainly its more interesting than the “affinity” system, which has been implemented in a nonsensical fashion. The theory of aligning yourself with purity to humanity, embracing technology or becoming one with your new home was certainly compelling. Whilst it is more expensive in research,  the ability to chase each path simultaneously is possible, which renders the “choice” rather ineffective.
If you liked Civilisation 5, then you will certainly like this. It is, minus some small variations, the same game after all.
However if you are looking for anything new, or groundbreaking, then I’m afraid you will need to go beyond: Beyond Earth.

TL;DR: The game feels empty, the AI bland and broken, the wonders underwhelming, and overall the game is too limiting. The game is rough, unfinished, and horribly overpriced for the end product. This would be labled as
, as in, wait while we put in more features and fix up the game to match the appropriate expectations and price, not a finished game. I highly doubt I am going to pick up any expansions for the game as the big flaws are in the fundamental game mechanics. It would need quite the overhaul.
One thing I have absolutely loved in Civilization Games is the ability to explore through technology. In your standard Civ game you can go through and research every single technology, listen to every bit of dialog, see what the game has to offer at every step. Unfortunately, this is not possible in BE. The Tech Web forces a player to get a few basic techs to build up the base of the empire and then rush towards an ending of some sort. There is no exploration of a tech tree and there are several, dozens, of techs that I have never see and probably never will, no matter what direction I choose to take the game. They just don't fit into any victory style at all and if I were to get them then I would be throwing away the game as the AI would have reached the game winning techs first. The leaf technologies I greatly enjoy, as a concept, but taking time to reesarch most leaf technologies takes away from researching more powerful branch technologies. There is no real tech advantage to researching most of the leaf techs unless you are trying to get more affinity.
The affinity system is cool but there really should be more upgrades for your individual units. Making specialized units, personalization, instead of the bland generic soldier unit, that's definitely a missing point to me. The upgrades they get are cool, but ultimately the soldiers are cookie cutter and that's just uninteresting. I was honestly surprised at the lack of options to get more affinity points. I assumed there would be more small things you could do in the game, option things, that would give you points in the areas based on your choices. Instead, all the affinity points are found in technologies, which really dictates how you play the game from turn one.
Early game warfare just isn't possible. Arguably, warfare at all just isn't possible. Take one city and the rest of the world hates you for all eternity. The Civs are pacifist, even in cramped settings (like eight players on a small map) and the aliens become obsolete mid-game, making Harmony nearly worthless. It's easier to stomp on the aliens and take their land than to co-exist and watch them get slaughered by someone else. Played right, as it happened in one of my games, the aliens can be a deterrant from other people landing on your shores, but that is certainly a rare occurance. On the larger maps, aliens break entirely, often spending the entire game just sitting in one tile, blocking off an entire region from anyone's access. Aliens are not fesable as a game mechanic past an eight player map, and even then it's a risky proposition. That's not to say I do not like the aliens, I do, but they need to be polished, as does every single aspect in this entire game.
The game is rough, empty, unfinished, and horribly overpriced for the end product. This would be labled as Alpha Early Access, as in, wait while we put in more features and fix up the game to match the appropriate expectations and price, not a finished game. I highly doubt I am going to pick up any expansions for the game as the big flaws are in the fundamental game mechanics. It would need quite the overhaul. I love Civ games, since Civ I, but this is just a disappointment.

As you may or may not know, this game is heavily inspired by Super Smash Bros. but more specifically Melee. Veterans of Smash will already be accustomed to most concepts this game has and will quickly adapt to the slight changes made from Melee. But for players who have never played Melee or Smash in general will be quickly alienated in the online, advanced techniques from Melee like Wavedashing and Teching are in the game and can change the flow of matches quite quickly. At some point I personally think that the Dev should include some sort of tutorial, when the game has been fleshed out enough, to introduce these concepts to players.
For actual gameplay the game is solid in nearly every aspect possible. Most characters are well balanced (Aside from Maypul and Zetterburn in most cases) and have amazing designs choices for gameplay. With two more characters on the way I hope to see the roster grow even more, possibly to the point that the game will be balanced enough to never have 20XX associated with it.
The sound track and stage design are both spot on and are extremely memorable, I hope that later stages can keep with this trend. Stages have two different types, Aether and Basic, with one being marketed more towards casual party play and the other for the competetive crowd (The greatest choice ever made). With story mode coming out soon™ I openly welcome changes to nearly everything.
Tl;dr: Fix online, balance characters a bit, and more everything!

To me, Salt was an insta-buy. Usually, I am hesitant about buying into an early access game, having gotten burned myself when devs would all but take the money and run. However, Salt is an early access gem, and I personally feel that this game will achieve huge things in the future.
The magic of Salt is it's atmosphere. Looking at the sun through a bamboo thicket and seeing the shadows stream through to the ground, wistfully shifting back and forth as the trees sway in the breeze. The way the ambient environmental sounds change as you travel from a beach into the inner part of an island. A quiet sunset that turns the sky a bright red hue. This game is dripping with cool scenery, and the Wind Waker-esque visuals really help it's case.
Oh, and speaking of Wind-Waker, Salt's gameplay reminds me of that game's wonderful open world sailing, mixed with (for those of you who are old enough to remember) exploring the island of Myst. But don't worry, there aren't any annoying puzzles. Salt is purely about achieving open world zen through gentle, thoughtful exploration.
I've sailed to many islands in my short time with Salt, and I have to say that the procedural generation is amazing. Every island I've visited has been unique. Never have I seen a cookie cutter layout, or one of those Diablo 3 style map-is-the-same-but-ever-so-slightly-changed scenarios.
I feel that one of the reviewers here on Steam said it best when he likened playing Salt to the first time you fired up Morrowind. Like, "WHOA. I've got this entire alternate world open to me?!" It's that excited feeling you would get as a kid, entering into a fantasy world where you could just simply be. That feeling is one that Salt has in spades.
Highly recommended.

After many years of competitive DotA, competitive WoW arenas and casual HoN/DotA 2, I'm now at a point where I don't have hours upon hours at hand to play a lengthy game where I have to gear up a character for weeks or farm lanes and woods for 1 hour. I'm at a point where I want a game that has instant action, but is hard to master. This is exactly what BR is.
Don't be fooled by other reviews though, this is NOT DotA 2 with no creeps, it's a totally different ball game. It's a high paced, adrenaline-packed game where you need complete mastery over the mechanics and cooldowns of your character every single second of every round, with no breathers (like stupid trips to recharge at the fountain).
Watch some gameplay, wrap your heard around the fact that it's not click-to-move, but top-down fixed camera WASD (like Helldivers or Forced), and be mindful of your choice!
Once you've decided that this is the right game for you, don't worry about its Early Access status. As oposed to countless other games, this one is perfectly playable in its current state and will only get better with time.
Each with their own learning methods, but I'd recommend reading the great guides on
, checking the BR Reddit which has great collections of educational links, and watching youtubers like Teldo.
Moreover, like so many other things in life, BR is great when played solo, but even greater when played with friends.
To wrap things off, I'd like to wish Stunlock Studios the best of luck with the coming months. I really hope they manage to turn this game into a huge eSports success because it has all the right groundwork to become one.

Clocking in at just over an hour for a single playthrough, Shelter is a wonderfully unique experience that doesn't overstay it's welcome. It doesn't have too much mechanical depth, but it doesn't need it with such a concise experience.
The story is touching and explained entirely through gameplay. I won't spoil anything, but if you have any heart at all, you will care for your little pups by the end. The game forces you do deal with frightening or difficult situations, and you really feel for the babies that you don't have any real control over. Also, whether it was intended or not, Smokey The Bear ain't got nothin' on this game.
It was an interesting and unique experience and I enjoyed my time with it, but that time is basically an hour, with nothing else to unlock or experience, with no divergent paths for subsequent playthroughs. The only thing that can change is how well you play the game, as that directly effects whether or not your pups die along the journey. It is basically the game equivalent of a short film that you'd see after the trailers in a Pixar Film.

I'm not going to spend too much time describing this game because you should experience it yourself if you are going to play it. If I had to put it in two sentences though I'd say: "Shelter is a game where you play as a badger in a forest where everyone and everything hates your species. Especially birds".
The game itself is actually very pretty! The artstyle they used was really interesting and it has a few great "background shot" moments. Soundtrack is pretty mesmerizing. Stuff you don't usually hear in video games.
There are some problems with framerate and some pretty harsh pop-in. Pop-in is something I would never want to see in an "experience game" like this. It does a good job of pulling you out of the experience.
Shelter is not a long game (1 hour if you don't rush through it) but I didn't feel like it should have been longer. It teaches you a thing or two about nature. For full price I can't recommend it but for heavily discounted price get it. You should look up some similiar "experience" type of games like Journey, Dear Esther and Stanley Parable and if you are not afraid of lack of gameplay then get on this. It's not the best of its kind but it's definitely not the worst either. If you have it backlogged get on it instead of reading this. It's definitely worth your time.

This is the story of a man named Stanley.
Stanley worked for a company in a big building where he was Employee #427. Employee #427's job was simple: he sat at his desk in room 427 and he pushed buttons on a keyboard. Orders came to him through a monitor on his desk, telling him what buttons to push, how long to push them, and in what order. This is what Employee #427 did every day of every month of every year, and although others might have considered it soul rending, Stanley relished every moment the orders came in, as though he had been made exactly for this job. And Stanley was happy.
And then one day, something very peculiar happened. Something that would forever change Stanley; something he would never quite forget. He had been at his desk for nearly an hour when he realized that not one single order had arrived on the monitor for him to follow. No one had shown up to give him instructions, call a meeting, or even say 'hi.' Never in all his years at the company had this happened, this complete isolation. Something was very clearly wrong.
Shocked, frozen solid, Stanley found himself unable to move for the longest time. But as he came to his wits and regained his senses, he got up from his desk and stepped out of his office.

This is the first AC game I played. Great introduction to the series. Now I've played III, Unity, and Syndicate as well.
Definitely buy this. If it's on sale, you should just scroll up right now and press Add to Cart, because it's an absolute steal for anything less than it's non-sale price. A bargain even if it's not on sale.
The protagonist is Edward Kenway. He's not an Assassin, but he becomes one throughout the main story. The main story is only ok. It doesn't totally make sense why you're going to such great length to find what you're looking for, but whatever. I especially liked the very first mission. A great mini tutorial and showcase of the environment.
The world of Black Flag is absolutely spectacular. The West Indies are beautiful and jam packed with things to do. The three cities of Havana, Nassau, and Kingston are somewhat small, but they all look pretty different. I LOVED Havana.
The rest of the world is huge. Luckily, you have a ship with which to traverse it. The Jackdaw is awesome. It's impressive that ship combat is more diverse than regular combat. Yes, there is a lot of sailing and naval combat in this game, but it's a joy, it really is. You can upgrade your ship, and unlock more weapons and abilities as you go. Some people call this more of a pirate game than an Assassin's Creed game, and I can understand why they would say that. But there is still plenty of sneaking around and diving into haystacks.
There is just sooooooo much to do in the huge world. Mayan temples to discover, islands to explore, sunken ships, smugglers' lairs, enemy forts, and much more. You can even go hunting for whales and jaguars.
Basically, everything you would want to do, anything you can think of, is possible. PLAY. THIS. GAME.
Note: The Sea Shanties are (and here is where I run out of different adjectives and synonyms for great) spectacular! Really adds to the ambience. Thanks for reading.

I have been playing CIV, all it's branches and spin-offs since the first days on the AMIGA. And not once did it let me down. I have spent thousands, if not ten thousand hours of my life playing CIV, in one version or another. CIV is one of the very few games I purchase in advance, because I want to play it as soon as possible. I even took a vacation for the launch of Beyond Earth. And I looked forward to write an excellent review for it, because usually CIV earns it.
I played for three days. Then I decided to play something else. Didn't touch it again.
This game has potential, there are a lot of clever ideas and the whole setting is a really nice one. But as of now, it is full of bugs that should not exist as those where working mechanisms in CIV V (like diplomacy or firing achievments) or should have been fixed a while ago (like the endless animations when air units attack) or are just shoddy coding (like the unit upgrade screen) and although I cannot really say why, it does not feel like a full game.
And while at its core CIV V/BE still is (IMHO) the best 4X game on the market, Beyond Earth falls behind comparable games in aspects like depth and storytelling. And I think this is critical. Sci-Fi is a genre where the "far, far away time/place" allows to tell thought-inspiring parables about humanity and it's questions, needs, ambitions and fallacies. And while CIV BE tries to achieve that, it falls short. Which is especially disappointing because of the excellent job Alpha Centauri did in this regard a long time ago.

I myself really loved Final Fantasy games in the old days, but when Square joined with Enix, FF games were not what they used to be. The only things that were satisfying in FF13 are the graphics and the sound, but everything else just couldn't get worse. Here's a quick view.
Gameplay:
There are a couple of things I don't like. The first thing is how linear the game is. The whole game is a corridor run, except for Chapter 11, which can be refreshing for a couple of hours. But to get there, you need to play at least 20-25 hours, and in my opinion it doesn't worth it. There are no towns to buy stuff and talk with people, shops are included with the Save Points instead. Also you can't change your party until Chapter 9, which is another disappointment for me. If you don't like the battle system, I wouldn't even suggest to dive in, because it won't get any better.
The other thing I disliked is the upgrade system. Could be great potential, but turned into a trial and error thing, and you won't get anything good unless you sacrifice most of your loots. You don't get money after fight, instead a loot sometimes, and this is where you can utilize them. For that, upgrading is a painfully slow process too, and when you find a new weapon, they look worse than the one you already have.
And then there's the Crystarium, the one thing you need to max with grinding to even stand a chance against bosses. The problem there is that the game limits your levelling until you defeat the next big boss, so if you reach that point and fail, your only choice is to come up with a better strategy. Now I did like the sphere grid in FFX, but this one was boring levelling, you actually had to push the button for a few seconds just to unlock the next bonus. Only thing you really need from this tree is the Health upgrades, and of course the rare abilities, ATB upgrade and Accessory slot. Also the costs for upgrades gets ridiculously high as you unlock more stages, trying to limit your progress even more.
I also don't know why the menu needs to always shows an exclamation mark when you get an item. Not just when you get an item you never had before, you also get it when you obtained after battle or BOUGHT it in a shop. Talking of shops, why do I need to select the amount of accessories I want to sell when in each item slot I only have 1? These are minor details, but they seems to be pointless in the game.
Last thing about gameplay is the difficulty. Now many people say it's easy, others say it's hard. In the PC version we got easy and normal mode, but as an experienced rpg player, I went with normal not knowing what him me. It was challenging, lots of battles testing your endurance with random encounters having as much health as all the FF7 bosses altogether. If you know what you're doing and keep buffing/debuffing, you can get to Chapter 13 easier, but if you think you can live without them, you are in big troubles now. This buffing/debuffing must just reminded me of Treasure of Rudra, a Square game that I actually enjoyed. It was also difficult, but at least it was fair. You do get the Eidolos to help you in difficult battles, but they are not helping that much, plus the time you are spending with them you are expecting much more. I didn't liked the summons in FF12, and I didn't liked them now. They should do them the old but simple ways.
Story & Characters:
For me these things are important. But for the story, after a few hours I just gave up. I did watched the cutscenes, but didn't really added too much for the game. If I could see what would be the point of all this, it'd be much better, but sometimes you are just there wandering aimlessly. In a game as linear you expect a story so strong to keep you going, but this is not the case. What I heard from others is that you need to read the datalog to understand everything. The game should show you what you do need to understand.
And for the characters. No matter who you are, you will find a character you dislike from the party or simply hate. It could be the big talk Snow, the cheerful Vanille or even Lightning, but for me the worst was the wimp Hope. I hated that character so much that I refused to put him in my party again after the game gave me the option. I don't know why they did this, but Square proved before that they can create likable charactes, even if you can't relate to them. Maybe if we could care more about the characters, we could care more about playing with them.
Conclusion:
I did try to like the game, but it failed me. You still feel encouraged to try the game, then get ready for 40 hours corridor run with long cutscenes and exponentially increasing difficulty. If I'm going to purchase FF on steam, I'd wait for FFVI, FFX or an FF VII remake, which would be the best thing from Square Enix anytime in the future.

Hmm, who would have thought something like this could work out so well? A game about a mother badger feeding and protecting her cubs from the dangerous wildnerness that constantly keeps you on your toes.
The game consists of 5 levels, each one with a unique theme, the first being a sort of calmer, introductory level to teach players the mechanics of the game (feeding, hunting and hiding), quickly moving on to the scary Night time, an hostile environment that easily scares the cubs, having them running into the predator's den. Then, you'll deal with a rainny day, traversing through overflowing rivers that might just drown you if you're not careful, after that leading to a Fiery forest, trying to keep the flames at bay.
All this while trying not to be caught by an eagle, the "antagonist" of this game (or is it?), concluding everything in the last level, a constant hide and seek between the two species.
This was an unexpected game, with a unique graphic style, and very beautifully done! The game brings a feeling of persistent consequence everytime a cub is lost, since there is no going back after one has been killed. As a result, you're constantly on your toes, and, despite its limited length, it's totally worth the time and money. There's the possibility of multiple playthroughs, trying to save as many cubs as possible.
Overall a very positive experience, which I'll go through at least once again to see how different it is after a good grasp of the  ways of surviving. I'd advise anyone looking for something different to play it.

Designed as an experiment to see how far you can ramp up the gamma in the Unity engine, the scientifically accurate
primarily serves to teach kids that badger cubs are omnivores that eat a grown cat's RDA every hour. In an epic play full of deep & morally relevant messages about adolescence, parenthood and the circle of life (sans Elton John), you are assigned the part of Badger Mommy, genetically engineered not to need any food whatsoever herself, and you bid your time (your hour, to be precise) babysitting your most adorable [citation needed] kids along a reasonably linear path of invisible boundaries, not passing go or collecting $200 until the game eventually runs out of scripted encounters. In the meantime, this corridor shooter without any shooting will hurl tons (I measured!) of emotionally charged music out of your speakers. Functionally it's a bit like a third person Lemmings game with the Lemmings following you 95% of the time, furthermore devoid of the various joyful abilities proper Lemmings have. Worth the purchase (or the effort of playing) only for the peculiarly jolly Predator-esque airborne takedowns Badger Mommy can perform on the various hostile mobs inhabiting Gammaland.
Length: 1 hour
Evils: Unity; scripted as much as any CoD campaign; omniscient bird AI; bugs
Replayability: You can hypothetically strive for a perfect playthrough. Depends on how often you'd like to endure "dat gamma".

Short version: This may be the single greatest thing of any kind ever made. I will never love another human being with the same fiery passion I love this movie, and I would marry it if I could. I may start a religion dedicated to it. It is so packed with awesome that I there were moments when I seriously expected my head to explode and my computer to fly out the window and go on a rampage. In short, it's a pretty good movie.
In slightly more words, Kung Fury is a weird masterpiece - short and low budget, but what an experience! Not a second wasted, nothing boring or unnecessary, just sweet, sweet weirdness from beginning to end. It's full of brilliantly executed anti-humour and absurdity, as well as cheesy clichés taken to the extreme.
The 80's references, the low budget feel (with added effects to simulate a tired, old VCR tape), and the balls-out insane jokes could so very easily have turned this thing into just another lame, trying-to-hard train wreck, but the legends at Laser Unicorn pulls it off with marvelous panache. They also managed a rare feat by living up to the hype this thing has been generating ever since its Kickstarter campaign, which is quite an accomplishment in itself.
If you appreciate absurd comedy, crazily overblown clichés and the eighties, odds are you'll fall in love with this gem. I just watched it for free, now I'm off to find Laser Unicorn's website and throw money at them. Not because I have to, but because I urgently want to. It really is that good.

Battlerite is a PvP battle arena game.
The gameplay is completely skill based, and there are no elements of randomness. It’s all about reaction time, juking, landing skill shots, and teamwork. Games are played in rounds, which eliminates the snowballing effect that occurs in MOBAs. There is a very high skill cap.
There are many champions, all having very unique abilities and roles. The champions are well balanced against each other.
Between each round you can pick battlerites, which are bonuses for your hero’s abilities. This allows for a variety of playstyles and opportunities to counter the enemy team.
If you enjoy the fast paced fighting aspects of MOBAs, I recommend this game.

I picked up his gun. Rushed to the second floor and crashed all the firepower I've got onto these nasty mercs. Some more loot. Nobody will be robbed by you anymore I thought.

Survive. Survive at all costs...I thought.
...
We have made it through...not without losses and tough choices though...
As many have asked, I will add short review as well.
In this game your target is to survive throughtout the war. With stylish graphics and soundtrack combination you will actually feel yourself in the war times. A lot of choices you will have to make during a single run will add up the atmosphere just as much as other things do. You will hate yourself for the choices you have made. You will search for an explanation for your violent crimes trying not to associate yourself with bandits. You will see how moral can be twisted and how people can change while fighting for survival. Game is extremely punishing for wrong choices. You can loose everything in just couple of days. Even if you have food, goods for trade, weapons, workshops etc. With several sets of starting characters, decent-sized world and several random events the game has a certain replayability. With all the drawbacks and flaws the game has it is still a truly unique experience in the Steam store and it is far deeper than many zombie/post-apocalypse or whatever survival games currently on the market. The overall great and deep atmosphere covers up all the flaws so you can easily name it an outstanding game. I do.

This is the story of a man named Stanley.
Stanley worked for a company in a big building where he was Employee #427. Employee #427's job was simple: he sat at his desk in room 427 and he pushed buttons on a keyboard. Orders came to him through a monitor on his desk, telling him what buttons to push, how long to push them, and in what order. This is what Employee #427 did every day of every month of every year, and although others might have considered it soul rending, Stanley relished every moment the orders came in, as though he had been made exactly for this job. And Stanley was happy.
And then one day, something very peculiar happened. Something that would forever change Stanley; something he would never quite forget. He had been at his desk for nearly an hour when he realized that not one single order had arrived on the monitor for him to follow. No one had shown up to give him instructions, call a meeting, or even say 'hi.' Never in all his years at the company had this happened, this complete isolation. Something was very clearly wrong.
Shocked, frozen solid, Stanley found himself unable to move for the longest time. But as he came to his wits and regained his senses, he got up from his desk and stepped out of his office.

***Early Access Review***
This is probably one of those games that I least expected to get addicted to.
Its a city builder that (at least for me) had a rather steep learning curve. Typicly that makes me walk away and not return, but thankfully I was persistant this time and kept doing new city after new city unitl I finally got the tech tree right. Hopefuly, the tutorials will get an overhaul and be made more compleate as the current setup is very lacking.
The visuals are sub-par compared to other games within this genra and era, but the layout and mechanics does make up for it enough so as not to become a problem. I do like how that the tech tree is rather well spread out, and its made up so you are not fixed into one path, but there are certainly those that are easier to follow than others (for example, I like to make money by spamming water/seaweed. Its low value compared to others, but easy to complete and avalible at game onset). The diversity of the crew that you can recruit is also a nice touch as you need to pair up the best citizen with the job in question. A good idea is also to give the ability to shoehorn in other citizens when your optimal choice is not readily avalible so you still do get room to play if your impatient (I'm a perfectionist so I typicly wait for the right citizen to spawn)
One of my favorite compontents is the blueprints for building contruction. It gives you a lot of versitility early and late game. To start you can keep things small but later on when you want to start building mega-complexes to limit staff needs (have one director instead of four, and only two workshops instead of four). Plus altering existing bluprints does not affect existing constructs which can be very handy. I would like to see the blueprint areas to expland slightly by a few more squares, but that is more of a nice touch than a requirement.
Another component of the game that I very much enjoy is the recycling theme. While its a great nod to enviromentalisim, it does play in a huge part of the mechanics of the game. To start with you rely heavily on money, but once you get your infastructure up, you rely on cash less and less as your ability to produce your needs rise. Additionally, very much of what you build for your city is recyclable, allowing you to nuke-n-pave your city as you learn the game and expand without signifigant punishment as (at least in easy mode) you get 100% of your materials back.
My biggest complaint, which may be fixed as the game develops, is the pacing of the game early on. It can take a large amount of patience to get your colony self-sufficent in the early stages until your able to produce food and plastic(or)metal on a sustainable scale. One reason is that your still reliant on having a cash income to which you can only gain by selling what you produce, but another hangup is being able to awaken the right staff at any given time. Right now, your randomly presented a list of staff that can be awakened to join your colony from a list of one to a dozen, and quite often I found myself waiting for a technitian or director to pop up just so I can get a building to even be funtional. Yes I could have pluged in other staff, but as I said above I am a perfectionist. What I would like to see is the ability to force-select a particular junior citizen but at a high cost so one does not have to wait for the RNG to give up your need.
Overall I do belive that once polished it will be a fantasic game and for those looking for something a little different than the typical city-builder and is looking for a challenge, its a good game to pick up. I hope the makers will continue to give us updates to enjoy. Be warned, it can be quite a timesink once you get hooked into it.

Hey, its not as good as previous games, but for me its definately a recommend. If you're new to the series, you'll have zero problems with this game, but if you're a player of previous games in the franchise like myself, there may be a few things that bug you.
First, let's say there or two huge (and vastly different) ways of approaching this new installment to the Civilization franchise as a person that has played previous Civ games:
1. The Hyper-Critic: You've been playing Civ 5 all your waking hours for the past two weeks before this game came out, and if the game doesn't meet your standards you might murder someone.
2. The Casual: You've been waiting for a long while for this game, and really just want to see an above-par addition to the Civilization series.
I, if you haven't already realized, fit into the second category. I do have my issues with this game, but it has spectacular visuals, great music, and a lovely, but cracked, overall design. You must also remember that this game is not Civ 6, but rather a side-game to the Civilization series and that should be kept in mind while playing this game.
One of these things that have bugged me slightly are the strength of the aliens, which seems (this may not be correct) to be way higher than that of the player. Another is that this installment seems to move away from the idea of having each civilization be a major role in gameplay. By this I mean the individual civilizations don't really seem to matter, with the bonuses given to each being largely unimportant, and the general atmostphere between using different characters quite lacking. Once again, these problems will not impact new players, but it will bug fans from previous games.
Both of these problems can be easily fixed in future updates and any DLC's that may come in the future.
One this I love about this game is, being a huge fan of Civ 5, it feels like the old Civilization I love, but with a lot of the old problems fixed, and a new life breathed into it with all the sci-fi aspects and great spy, new technology web, and aliens. This, and the excitement of a new and updated Civ game greatly make up for all of the little annoying bits I mentioned earlier.
So, before you go off and rip someone's jugular out from anger that this game isn't overwhelmingly incredible, please consider what I have spent my time writing out for you here.

I would imagine most people looking into this game have at least played other versions of Civilization. If you come into this game expecting it to be similar to previous versions, you will probably have a hard adjustment. While similarities can be found, they are quickly masked by a convoluted tech tree and a new "affinity tree". I do like the refreshingly new content and a new spin on a turn based strategy, but it seems lacking in some of the fundamentals to make a game like this exciting for repetitive play. The main one being that there are only 2-4 upgrades per unit, which are massive buffs. To the point it takes 5+ of the undertech'd units to kill a unit only one tech level above them. It is a very rigid technology step approach compared to a gradual technology slope in previous civilizations. One research completion makes night and day difference in military strength, abilities, population, etc. Hours of playtime are easily ruined with one simple misstep, and each decision becomes more critical than the last. This is a colorful, electronic, strategized version of Jenga... just don't be the one to let the tower fall over!

It's still the exact same garbage PC port the original Bioshock was.
Many of the same bugs the original version of Bioshock had. Mouse sensitivity changes upon dying/other schenarios, the game will chug along and stutter at random parts for seemingly no reason at all, alt-tabbing causes the game to go into windowed mode until you either exit and open the game again or you toggle on windowed mode and toggle it back on in the settings, theres no way to remove mouse acceleration. They successfully made a 2007 game look like a 2012 game.
This is literally just the same half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥PC port with a new coat of paint. And the new coat of paint is not even that good looking. Bioshock looked fine, the game was made 9 years ago, and it still holds up graphically for a game that old. So far I have not noticed anything that really jumps out at me as being improved graphically other than the models and some lighting changes. You can give me comparison screenshots all you want, and honestly, you won't notice any of the graphical upgrades while you're actually playing the games as most are just slightly better lighting, and some slightly better textures and modeling.
Now you may be thinking "Well alright, I will buy the original version, and save some money." Well too bad! You can no longer buy the original games on their own, you HAVE to buy the remasters in order to get the original games bundled with them. At first I was happy they gave the games away to anyone that already owned the games on Steam, until I found out about this slimey move on their part. They are making you pay more by taking away the option to buy the cheaper games.
That being said Bioshock itself is an average at best game that was overhyped at the time, and is still overhyped (especially Infinite) by people whos experience with RPGs consist of puddle deep games like Skyrim. The combat was clunky, the game was never scary in the slightest (and I say this as someone who gets scared by the toaster in the morning), the game had some horrible level design especially near the end of the game in places like Point Prometheus and The Proving Grounds, some parts like Arcadia and once again Point Prometheus were almost painful to crawl through with how boring they were. And The game was too easy and didn't take any thought to get through. I have beaten the game on survivor without vita chambers and the only moments that were any sort of a challenge to me were the early Big Daddy fights, only because you don't have many weapon options to kill them with. Later fights are easy because you get more weapons and Plasmids. If you want any tips on how to beat the game on survivor with no vita chambers, all you have to do is use Gene Tonics to upgrade the wrench so you can kill every normal enemy in a few hits, get the weapon upgrades that are with the exception of a few are in plain sight and easy to find so you can kill the Big Daddies and bosses easier. And there you go, you can get through the whole game running at enemies and hitting them over the head with the wrench without any thought or strategy.
If you want to play Bioshock and you're nearly 10 years late for the party find a means of getting the original version at a cheaper (or free) price. If you own a last gen console, you're in luck! Every EB Games (Gamestop's Canadian Branch) I have been to has had both Bioshock 1 and 2 in the $5 bargain bin because they have more copies than they know what to do with.

I'm not sure what all to say about this "remaster" except that it is a huge disappointment. I understand that new releases need some time to iron out issues, but this game still has bugs from the original 2007 release present. How can something so trivial such as mouse acceleration and button mapping be so difficult to fix?
The game visuals seem somewhat improved, if not mostly sharper textures and improved lighting, but the overall graphical issues detract from what makes this game special. There are at least a dozen instances in the first few levels were lighting strobes and textures still pop-in. Switching graphic settings would be nice, minus the fact that you are only given a single slider to adjust quality, whereas the original release had many different tweaks available.
The sound in this appears to also have been either downgraded or heavily compressed. Using a pair of hi-fi headphones, I can hear quite a bit of static hiss in voice dialogue and sound effects. When the AI talks, it is hard to judge distance as it sounds like they are always nearby, directly in front of you. The original soundtrack is still there, so at least this version has that going for it.
Menus and hacking are a complete mess. If you attempt to play with a keyboard and mouse, hacking becomes very difficult if you plan on using the mouse.. as there are quite a few issues with the mouse 'locking on' to items as well as horrible mouse acceleration issues.
I really wanted to revisit Rapture, but this "remaster" has me going back to the original version of the game. This needs a LOT of work to fix all of the above issues as well as some game-breaking bugs being reported. For the time being, I would strongly advise waiting until this is fixed, if that ever happens.

Due to the Steam Sale, I wound up picking a few games to add to my collection. One of which being a short indie titled called "Shelter". You play as a mother badger guiding her 5 pups through the woods to find a new home. Why? Because your small den won't be big enough for 5 quickly growing badger babies.
Along the way, you need to feed them, protect them from fox (which they will eat if you manage to kill one), keep them from the preying eyes of eagles, and from the dangers of wildfire and rushing rivers.
I managed to make it through the first time without a loss of offspring, so all five happy little fat badger babies made it to their new home.
The ending was special.
A very artisticly styled game that you can spend about an hour on to finish the story.  It was like watching an old story book moving around and easy to find yourself narrating it as you pitter patter around on your little badger toes.
The replayability isn't overall very high, although if you didn't manage to make it through the first time with all 5 babies, challenge yourself to.

After many years of competitive DotA, competitive WoW arenas and casual HoN/DotA 2, I'm now at a point where I don't have hours upon hours at hand to play a lengthy game where I have to gear up a character for weeks or farm lanes and woods for 1 hour. I'm at a point where I want a game that has instant action, but is hard to master. This is exactly what BR is.
Don't be fooled by other reviews though, this is NOT DotA 2 with no creeps, it's a totally different ball game. It's a high paced, adrenaline-packed game where you need complete mastery over the mechanics and cooldowns of your character every single second of every round, with no breathers (like stupid trips to recharge at the fountain).
Watch some gameplay, wrap your heard around the fact that it's not click-to-move, but top-down fixed camera WASD (like Helldivers or Forced), and be mindful of your choice!
Once you've decided that this is the right game for you, don't worry about its Early Access status. As oposed to countless other games, this one is perfectly playable in its current state and will only get better with time.
Each with their own learning methods, but I'd recommend reading the great guides on
, checking the BR Reddit which has great collections of educational links, and watching youtubers like Teldo.
Moreover, like so many other things in life, BR is great when played solo, but even greater when played with friends.
To wrap things off, I'd like to wish Stunlock Studios the best of luck with the coming months. I really hope they manage to turn this game into a huge eSports success because it has all the right groundwork to become one.

I feel that the main reason why some people get turned off by the combat is that they expect this to be a full action game with dodging like TERA, but that's not what it's about. This is a traditional MMORPG combat style but with more fluidity, the dodge mechanics aren't exactly "dodge", but escape/positioning mechanisms that differ from class to class (mages with teleport, rogues with sidestep, ranger with backstep, etc).
The only major complaint I have so far is a few combat bugs (the only bothering one so far is charge skills not working on certain terrains), but I have hope that this will be fixed, especially if people give this game a chance and the company can have a bigger budget.
TL;DR: Don't listen to the haters demonizing this game, it's really awesome (especially once you reach lvl15, which doesn't take too long). Judge it yourself, try the game. It's free anyways, so worst case scenario is you'll get a couple hours of fun for free. You're reading this review so chances are you're bored anyways, so why not?

This is an extremely fun game with lots of options for building your farm.  It simulates the activities of a farm well enough without forcing you to become over micro-managey.  Certain licenses are taken with reality to make it palyable... for example, cropse mature from seed to harvest in about 24 in-game hours. You can advance the clock to pass the time, which you will need to do early on when you only have one field. Once you have a lot of fields going, this is less necessary.
The only real criticism I have is that when you advance time, activities do not speed up. For example, if it takes a seeder 25 real seconds to seed one row of a given field, if you go to 5x time, it still takes the seeder 25 real seconds, only in-game, it takes the seeder 2 minutes 5 seconds. Thus if you run on fast time on a big field, the first seeds you laid down for harvest will be ready for the combine before your seeder is even done seeding. That doesn't make much sense.  Ideally, if you speed up time, the vehicles should move faster too... A tractor moving 25 mph should be able to travel 125 miles on 5x time speed. But it doesn't. It still only goes 25 miles in a real hour, but since time has passed 5x as fast, your tracter was actually moving only 5 mph in-game.
The time issue is really not a huge problem, however. The solution is to leave the clock on 1x while seeding, and then 5-15x for most other activities, and then 120x if you are just waiting for time to go by. Just don't forget to switch it back! I've doen that a couple of times and made a mess of things.
Pros:
- Nice graphics and sound FX
- Super fun to drive tractors and combines around
- Lots of development potential -- 20+ fields to buy, many kinds of crops and farm animals to raise
- Engaging and interesting
Cons:
- Clock speed settings don't work quite the way they should
- Tutorials do NOT explain things in enough detail
- I find starting out already with a loan to be very frustrating. I am in massive debt from day 1, even when I manage my finances wisely.

Disclaimer: I've only played this through once!
A lot of folks are saying that Civ:BE is essentially Civ5 with a new skin. I'd have to disagree. The technology web instead of the tech tree lends itself to an entirely new way to play the game, and for those who prefer straight lines, it can be a bit confusing to navigate when you get far enough into it. What's nice though is that if there's more than one option below a particular "branch," you don't have to learn both of them; you can just select what you want. The Virtues section is fun, too, with its vertical and horizontal synergies. Loved that!
One thing I wish was included was a full-on description of the different "sponsors" in the game. Perhaps it's just me, but I wish I was able to read about the leaders of each faction before being able to select them. At the very least, I wish they'd tell you which bonuses they started you out with. (This point may be entirely moot, however, because I was so eager to start the game when it launched that I just sort of picked one and ran with it!) As well, I wish that you were able to keep better tabs on the different "stations" that you meet in the Diplomacy screen like you could with the City-States in previous Civs.
Overall, I think this is a fun new addition to the Civ collection and I'm excited to start my next map. :) Cheers!

I had great fun until I got into the late game, where I discovered the game is horribly broken and unfinished.  The AI is subtarded, feeble-minded, mentally defective, has cerebral palsy and in most cases is very passive.
I allied with one of the AI Kavithan colonies in a game and Polystralia declared war on them and immediately attacked in one turn. Because I was an ally the game automatically declared war on Polystralia for me before my turn even started, and every single faction in the game including my ally declared me a war monger, which is essentially a PERMANENT debuff that makes diplomacy incredibly difficult, and some times outright impossible. Even after immediately making a peace treaty with the offending nation my alliance with Kavitha was broken and I was on my own for the rest of the game.
Up to that point I had been sending my ally enormous amounts of resources for free and even gifting them cities, and none of this was taken into account.  I thought this was just because of the affinities or some random seed of the AI but I tested this in several games and found that this is a feature of the AI regardless of settings and affinities.
I literally spent several days working on one game in particular and after over 500 turns it wasn't even worth continuing.  After a week of playing I've seen everything the game has to offer, every game feels exactly the same. The non-domination "victories" are cheap, if you aren't the victor you won't even know which nation won. It's a token victory with absolutely no depth, no feeling of resolution or that you've actually established a significant colony.  All you get is a popup window with smugly written text and a button to return to the game title.
The affinities are meaningless aside from some specific bonus upgrades for military units.  At the beginning of the game the AI announces its approval or disapproval of you regarding how you treat the native species of the planet.  If you attack the "aliens" (nonsense term that needs to be changed, since we are the aliens), colonies with the harmony affinity will condemn you with a diplomacy debuff. It gives you a sense of responsibility and the impression of significant depth. But later in the game even AI colonies with maxed out harmony relentlessly attack aliens.  You can't ally with alien nests even though you can adapt their species into your colony. Aliens are all the same on all planets (Really!) and there is no evolution that can happen to make them more intelligent and build colonies of their own, actually competing with the humans.
The leaders of colonies will gradually change their aesthetics depending on which affinity they choose, but aside from that they are extremely bland and monotonous.  There's also no way to declare them war mongers when they assault each other over frivolous things.  There's no reciprocation for being an extremely helpful ally. If your ally asks you to go to war with an aggressor and you accept, your ally will think you are a war monger. Also, during said war if your ally has a border touching the enemy and one of your satelites touches even one of your ally's tiles, even if it is a defensive satellite they will get angry and condemn you for it.
You can't really call this a brand new game, as it is really just a reskin of Civ 5 with a few mods applied (and a significant amount of content removed). There is so much wrong with this game I'm not sure an expansion will help it, but if you want to play it, instead save some money and get Civilization 5, which is a far superior game in every respect. Wait for an expansion for this game and then see if it is worth purchasing. Do not buy this before you try it for yourself.

UPDATE 2016-09-17: I actively avoid thinking about this game. Unlike Civ 5, which had a shaky start and got progressively better with its expansions, BE stagnated and finally collapsed under its own misbegotten bulk. The Rising Tide expansion somehow managed to make the faction balance even worse than it already was, at which point the developers threw up their hands and walked away. As such, this sad husk of a game that never lived up to its lofty heritage and goals lies now on the rubbish pile of gaming history. Crack out your Alpha Centauri if you want the better Sid Meier space 4X experience, which really speaks volumes to how poorly this game fared.
GOOD:
+ New setting for Civ franchise (well, new for the core Civ games - see SMAC)
+ New paradigm for "civilizations" i.e. sponsors and a re-configurable starting bonus system
+ Stations system doesn't block out expansion as much as city-states did in Civ5
BAD:
- Abandoned by the developers
- Faction balance never achieved, further ruined in expansion
PROGRESS:
+ I don't know if I will ever love the affinity system, but after the patch, the progression feels more natural; most of the time the decision is somewhat arbitrary, but that might be intentional (you can change it after all)
+ Affinities less thoroughly anchored to the tech web after a revamp of the game's quest system
+ Wonders are now clearly marked in the tech tree
+ Trade routes are now separated if they are previous routes, which makes managing them less tedious; trade system received a major overhaul in the Fall Patch
+ Victories are still underwhelming, but defeat at least tells you what happened now
UNFULFILLED WISHES (formerly WISHLIST)
= Demographics in core game - a mod exists that delivers these statistics, but they are not included with core game for some reason.
= Espionage still needs work -  I think further expansions will flesh this out like they did in Civ4: Beyond the Sword and so forth. There are some mods that expand espionage options, but I cannot as of yet comment on their effect as I have not played with them yet.
= Diplomacy not fully fleshed out yet, though the AI doesn't make extortionate demands for favors like the initial release; maybe some personalities for the stations like the city-states?
= No global systems aside from alien aggression i.e. no weather patterns like Alpha Centauri (expansions maybe?)

The big question concerning Beyond Earth is: if you played hundreds of hours of Civilization V already, is BE worth it?
I'd say it is. Beyond Earth certainly stumbles a bit, the different factions aren't varied enough, there are only 8 of them, some of the maps really don't feel all that different from the regular Earth maps from Civ V, Wonders feel lifeless compared to their Civ V versions (since they're all technobabble and the only picture you get of them is a blueprint, I couldn't even understand what some of them were supposed to do, lore-wise) and most importantly, the game really isn't all that distinct from Civ V.
But it's the small differences that make Beyond Earth worth it. There's the stuff from Civ V it throws aside, like luxury resources and Great People, which were just a hassle and added little to the overall experience. The addition of Quests (small decisions you make concerning your existing buildings) and Virtues (basically the philosophical leanings of your civilization) make all the difference, and actually change how you play the game a lot more than the Ideologies did in Civ V. The Aliens are great too, the keep the whole game a lot more active, with less turns where all you have to do is click the "Next Turn" button. And they look a lot less ridiculous than a bunch of axe-wielding barbarians running around next to atomic power plants and rocket ships like in Civ V.
With a couple of expasions, I think Beyond Earth will greatly surpass Civ V. As of now, it doesn't have quite as much content and charm, but the turn-to-turn experience is a bit more interesting and new enough to entertain Civ veterans.

The game itself is pretty solid. It's not the bet FF game by far, but not the worst like many people say. There are some pretty meh ones out there besides FFXIII.
FFXIII is criticized for being too linear. Well, it is (more linear than other FF titles).
