While the version of the game might be better on PS3, it was very unpleasant on PC.
I've a read a few other reviews and I don't seem to share some of the same problems they have like the black bars and crashing. I can comment on one issue I had and that was the controls stopped responding to my commands after a few hours of playing. I wouldn't be able to ALT+TAB out of the game and sometimes I would have to rely on it to get my controls back, at which point they would continually scroll through menu options making selection a timing-based thing. This was particularly horrible during battles and swapping paradigms. Since the game has been out for a long time I will be brief in my review.
Pros:
+ Good English Voice Acting - I didn't know you could play it in Japanese, but I don't particularly want to hear a Japanese guy voice a black guy.
+ Good Music - I owned the soundtrack before owning the game, so I played a vast majority of the game in silent minus the cutscenes.
+ The Paradigm System - Once you can unlock swapping team members, the possibilities for battle styles becomes interesting and a lot of fun.
+ The Crystarium - The game, as a JRPG, is obviously going to be grindy in a way and the Cyrstarium makes you feel like you're getting results from mindless battles.
+ Rendered Cutscenes, and Character Portraits - Great art and attention to detail. Characters are expressive and it's nice to watch the cutscenes.
+ Lots of Lore - Kind of necessary to explain some backstory when the names for the entities in the game are so stupid.
+ Upgrades and Disassembly of weapons and accessories - Pretty cool system but it feels like I'm throwing a lot of items at something and it only gets a little bit better.
Neutral:
+ Linear Paths and Gameplay - If you don't want to think, this game's map is good for that. Go down every path the NPCs don't is my general rule.
Negatives (oh man, and are there ever negatives):
+ The ♥♥♥♥♥iest camera ever - Like it really just sucks major♥♥♥♥♥♥ There's no visual feedback to let you know that the camera can't be turned in certain areas and it defaults to an awful location. Its turning speed is incredibly slow and you can't change its settings except for inverting its axis.
+ Defaulting to Auto-battle can just make battles "Press Enter To Win"
+ Grinding gets significantly less effective in a short amount of time - Enemies offer less CP and abilities cost a LOT more.
+ You can't freely move in battle - Which may seem obvious, but characters just wander around as they please and can get hit by AOE spells at low health.
+ No option to turn off animations for changing Paradigms - At first it starts of by focusing on each character and this ACTUALLY TAKES TIME IN BATTLE. While you're transforming, someone can die and you're basically ♥♥♥♥ed.
+ Can't control other members in battle
+ When your Leader dies, it's game over - Even though other characters can learn to raise other team members from death!
+ Bland characters
+ Sometimes difficult to understand map - Trying to find Marks to hunt and I can't figure out where they're meant to be.
+ Characters can't actually walk straight - They default to North on the minimap, but the map actually starts turning slowly while walking so you start walking diagonally in hallways.
+ Limited settings interaction
The list could go on, but I can't really think of anything else at the moment. This game reminds me of Ni no Kuni but it sucks as a port. I'd play it as a PS3 game, but not as a PC game. I'm going to stick with it and its sequels just because I've come this far.

Magic Duels isn't for everyone. But it's definetly for Magic fans like me who doesn't want to make overtime to have a competitive deck. Gold is pretty easily made compared to other games. Though not given away because they still want to make some money at some point and content is easily unlockable.
Once you get the maximum number of cards you can get (4 common, 3 uncommuns, 2 rares, 1 mythic) You're never getting it again. So there's a maximum number of packs you can buy and you don't have to deal with useless copies.
Gold is earned as followed. You can play VS. AI to get 5,10,15g for Easy,Medium,Hard AI respectively and you get 20g for a VS Player win. There's some Daily quest which can give anywhere from 20 - 60g.
there's a 400g gold cap (Quest doesn't count toward gold cap) (at the time of the review there's a random bug and the gold cap won't reset someday but it's usually back the day after.
For the moment, there's only 3 modes you can play. Vs player, Vs AI, And 2 headed giant (2 vs 2) The AI is "Decent" sometime it's dumb but the fact that it gets all the cards makes it win from time to time.
There's only 1 set of cards for the moment but it's been confirmed every paper set they releases will be added in part (70-80%) in the game for players to buy with in game currency and real money. So the pool of card, even if limited for the moment, will probably get way bigger eventually.
And the question everyone is asking of course... IS IT PAY TO WIN??? The answer isn't simple. Magic by definition as always been a Pay to Win game. The more cards you get the more option you have the better deck you can make. In this game... It's controlled by the fact you can't make a "all mythic and rare deck" Since you can easily unlock all the content (Of course it's gonna take longer for free players) You can always compete at the highest level. I personally get my gold from AI and i'll jump to PVP when i'm happy with my main deck.
So Overall. Card arts are amazing. Gameplay is pretty good. AI is a decent adversary (though you will win way more than you lose if you're a veteran) 2HG Is pretty fun in CO-OP there's no in game chat though so get a friend from your steam list or skype or just deal with the persons decision.

I'm a big fan of city building games and recently there haven't been a lot of them that have been done very well. Project Aura seems to be in the process of becoming one of the greats in the genre.
It's still fairly raw and has issues, both minor and major, but overall it's been very enjoyable. The current tutorials do a good job of showing how to do things, but not what to do or when so the learning curve is a bit steep. I trashed my first 2 attempts to play the game when I realized some assumptions I'd made were wrong. So be prepared to learn as you go and make some mistakes along the way.
Thankfully you don't get punished much for making mistakes, buildings can be demolished and 100% of the materials used to build them reclaimed. So if you position something incorrectly or realize the building you built isn't what you needed you can just knock it down and you lose nothing but time.
Your citizens require food and water, but it's no real loss if they go without for a while. The worst that can happen is they leave your city and you just have to wake up some replacements. In fact the only current way to really lose the game as far as I can tell is to never feed your people until they all leave and you don't have enough credits to wake up replacements. There are UI elements for hazard warnings and weather disasters, but currently they don't seem to be implemented so the game world appears to be danger free for the moment.
I can't be sure, but it looks like all the buildings are available from the start and I haven't found any use for a couple of the items you can have your citizens construct. I'm guessing they'll be used in the Technology Research part of the game once that's implemented. The quest system also isn't active so there are no objectives to complete other than seeing how big you can build your city and I haven't found any sort of 'endgame' either.
Most of the materials you need to build things can be purchased using the ingame currency, which is how you'll start out building your city. But once you get some basic infrastructure built you can start collecting resources and making those materials yourself. It can take a while, but that's what x8 speed is for (shift/+ for increasing speed, shift/- for reducing speed).
At the moment I have 2 key gripes about the game:
1. There are some UI sound effects that aren't controlled by the ingame  volume sliders and will always play at maximum volume...it's extremely annoying
2. There's no way to tell your food producing buildings to deliver their goods directly to the Larder so you're constantly having to manually refill it. It's not a big deal for basic food/water because you can produce them far faster than you'll consume them. But it's a major hassle with the special foods because unless you're devoting a large portion of your population to farming there's no real way to keep up with the demand so you're constantly draging and dropping food items like tomatoes and baked goods from your inventory to the larder.
These 2 issues combine to make the experience just as annoying for your housemates and neighbors as it is for you unless you turn off your sound, which isn't a real loss considering there aren't any warning sirens or voice acting outside the tutorials atm. But the music is nice and the sound effects are good and I hate playing games without sound :(
At the end of it all though I still recommend this game wholeheartedly to anyone that's a fan of city building and micromanagement games like SimCity, Banished, and Prison Architect. 4/5 stars from me on this and it clearly has potential to become a 5/5 game if they finish it well.

To be clear, this isn't an awful game. However, as a remaster, you expect it to improve on the game's graphics, and maybe touch up some of the gameplay issues from before. This game kinda does one of those, and completely ignores the other.
Graphically, the game does look better...sort of. Yes, the textures are better, and it supports 4K resolution, but those are really the only graphical improvements. In fact, my main issue with the game is th COMPLETE LACK OF OPTIMIZATION OPTIONS. They boil down to antialiasing, antisotrophic filters, and FIVE resolution options. That's right, only five resolution options. If your screen has a slightly less common res, like my 1360x768 monitor, you either have to deal with the screen cropping out part of the UI or trying to squint at your screen as it tries to display a lower resolution. Also, if your computer can't handle the settings as they are, you can't change a single thing to help yourself. I suppose that you could play the original version, seeing as how they are bundled together by default, but why should somebody have to install a 20GB game, just to find he can't run it, and then uninstall it and reinstall the original? Couldn't they have just included lower graphics options? But graphic shouldn't be a big issue, considering my mediocre PC could run it at 60fps.
As far as the gameplay and story go, it's exactly the same as Bioshock from 2007. Killing lots of enemies with your weapons and plasmids, doing whatever Atlas says, and, of course, hacking every piece of machinery in sight. Lots of people complain that issues from the first game weren't fixed, but frankly, those are far and few between, at least in my opinion. But don't expect the game to make any mechanical changes to the original. In short, if you liked Bioshock before, you'll like it now.
Overall, seeing as how this is the only way to buy the game on PC now, and it really is an excellent game, I have to recommend it. I really wish the remaster had more going for it, but for anybody who loved the game before, or hasn't ever played the game before, I'd say it's worth picking up just to go back to Rapture again.

While this doesn't change my opinion on the game's lack of in-game optimization, hopefully customers will find it helpful.

If I'm going to pay money for a supposed 'game' then it should be able to have descriptions applied along the lines of 'engrossing', 'entertaining', and 'fun'.
When I gave this game a try, as of 17/3/2015, I napped half the time.
Therefore 'engrossing', 'entertaining', and 'fun', cannot possibly be applied.
I'm exceedingly sorry I spent money on this.
I really -REALLY- hope it improves as admittedly I find the background story/concept attractive. However in it's current state I CANNOT recommend paying for it.
Some feedback I would give to the dev from the time I've wasted on it so far:
- "Are you ready?" confirmation is redundant.
- If you're going to have a time scale (cycles/days), and give the ability to adjust the game speed, then the passing of time should be linked to the adjustment of game speed. It would probably have meant I wouldn'tve ended up falling asleep at the keyboard. Also, letting the player know that 'cycle' basically equals a game hour would have been a good thing. Also (again), when you do get the link between adjustment of game speed and the games actual speed fixed, I'm thinking there'll be a few players (I'm one of them) who'll want faster speeds than x4. x10 would be good. Perhaps even faster, I'll have to see what it's like at x10.
- Why can't I have maintenance modules separate to other work modules and then link them so that one maintenance module can be applied to multiple work modules?
- Why am I applying multiple transport modules to the same pad? Why can't one transportation module apply to all buildings on the same pad?
- The degree of experience of employees affects the rate at which the module/part works, and also degrades. In which case, why can't I expand the building, after it's already been laid down, with additional module/parts for the ones that are falling behind?
- If I'm told there is 6 new people available to wake, then there should be 6, not 4 or 3. And yes, I did check the different tabs for the differing experience levels.

Shelter is an experiment in what the medium of gaming can provide as an experience. It goes outside the mould of standard gaming conventions and instead chooses to tell a tale about a Badger mother who must look after her cubs while traversing vast distance in search of a new home. While the game is only about an hour long, it is one of those games that any game connoisseur should not miss out on.
If you are only into games for the pointless grinding and getting as many hours out of a single game and exposure as you can until the value of that experience essentially approaches zero, this game is not for you. If you enjoy seeing the breadth and scope of the medium, and enjoy playing a large variety of games, this one is worth a look.
Overall this game is a welcome venture into a way of play that should be expanded upon in the future to fully reach it's potential.

Salt is effectively proof that Minecraft would be more compelling if you could build and live on a moving ship. (I make the Minecraft comparison lightly, as Salt is very much a different beast entirely.)
I would like to describe my feelings coming out of the Demo, though.
First I started playing, and decided "Well, this isn't much, but let's try and build a boat." After some time running around, laughing at the terrible pirate models (Yes, they're cute, but I still don't like 'em.), failing to kill a deer, and not understanding how to craft at all, I finally make a raft. Then I sail around the islands that I started on for a bit. And then I get bored with that, and sail off into the endless void. Then the music kicks in. And I feel shivers down my spine. And I feel hope. Excitement. Joy. Elation. "My word," I think to myself, "This is exactly how I felt when I first started playing Morrowind and realized that I had this entire world at my disposal! So much to see! So much to explore!"
I heartily recommend this game to anybody who loves the thrill of exploration. It made me feel things no game has made me feel in a very long time. Good work, Lavaboots.

Since the world is randomly generated from a seed it can be rather expansive but right now content and gameplay components may be found to be somewhat thin. If you're curious at all about a survival and exploration game set in a beautiful environment, check out the demo. Check out the discussion forums. I suspect you'll purchase once you experience a taste of Salt.

This atmosphere is executed brilliantly, the art style, music and pacing all lending more to it, allowing you to really put yourself into the space presented to you with your poor, semi-displaced trio of housemates.
I've played a lot of survival games and all of them have one conceit or another to explain the situation (zombies, spiders, zombies, aliens, zombies etc.) but the more realistic story in This War of Mine (a story being played out in the world in a number of places right now), in my opinion, lends it a more visceral, wholly real, experience.
If you're a fan of the survival genre, or a fan of artistic, atmospheric games, I'd suggest that you will not regret handing over your money for this one.

The game has you managing your supplies by determining who gets to eat, and who gets medical treatment if sick. Gathering supplies from outside (Only at night since it’s safer) has you putting your home at risk from looters if not properly protected. Also building improvements like barricades, beds, booking facilities, moonshine stills, all help to keep your civilians alive. Even keeping the house warm with a stove becomes imperative, when deciding to use fuel for either cooking or heating.
The game has no tutorial or instructions on what the best approach is, rather it’s left up to you. Do you want to survive? Help others? Become bandits and rob others? Even take part in the war by attacking military posts. All rather difficult tasks, and none really goes through as planned.
My game started off with three young men, Marko, Bruno, and Pavle. Bruno was the cook who feared venturing out, caring only for survival. With the mentality, better them than us. Marko and Pavle the strongest of the two as far as scavenging and defending. As the game progressed I ran into an elderly man named Anton who excelled in creating items and gave him shelter.
The game has you investing in your characters and fabricating their personalities in your mind as you make choices that put them at risk. Towards the end of my game winter sets in and supplies become scarce, while sickness becomes more common. Pavle ends up dying trying to back home through Snipers alley, an obvious reason why it’s called that. Marko dies trying to steal supplies from bandits that own a brothel. Left with a sick Anton and the cowardly Bruno. I set Bruno to avenge Marko as a last ditch effort. I imagined Bruno having lost his fear in desperation and anger. Making him kill three armed men with a shovel as he ambushed them from different locations of their hideout. The risk brought in a big reward.

A heart-wrenching, gripping story about the other side of war that we never give thought to in the endless stream of FPS war games that get released month after month. "This War of Mine" puts you in the pilot's seat of the struggle people the world over have faced when war shows it's ugly face, and it does a brilliant job of driving the point home. It doesn't matter who you are, what you do, or how much money you have. When War comes to your home, it is indiscriminate in the suffering it inflicts. You start each game with three characters, each with a small bio, and more of their story and personality is revealed as you survive longer and longer, and as you are forced to make more difficult morale choices. And just when things are at their hardest, when supplies are hard to come by and your closest friends have fallen at the hands of people who were only defending their own livelyhood, the ceasefire comes. But even that respite from the pain and suffering is momentary; The game then recaps all the choices you'd made, good or bad, and it lists when your survivors stopped being survivors. Each character you'd taken in is also given a brief epilogue, and I can tell you that it is enough to bring tears to a grown man's eyes when you them.
Just as important, the gameplay is smooth, simple, and fun. I didn't find any noticable bugs or glaring flaws, the game didn't ever feel overly tedious (Sometimes the base-management, specifically having to make all of my survivors go to the fridge to eat something every single day, watching them all crowd around a ladder to get to the upper floors, etc) and overall the entire game was as enjoyable to play as it was to experience.

I really wanted to like this game, and for the first few hours I really did. As you can see by the number of hours I spent playing, I stuck it out because I really wanted to recommend this game. In the end, however, it just didn't pan out.
It starts out with a lot of promise, but it gets tedious after a few hours. There are seven types of collectibles strewn about the world (treasure chests, hidden treasure chests, treasure maps, message-in-a-bottle, animus fragments, wild animals to hunt, and sea shanties) and they take forever to collect. Some are more enjoyable to get than others. The sea shanties aren't that bad, but you have to go chasing after them which can be a hassle depending on what sorts of challenges you like. The buried treasure chests are challenging to look for, but if it's not your cup of tea then the search can be irritating. The collectibles on the tiny islands in the middle of the ocean are the worst because you have to dive off the ship and go swimming to the little islands to grab a chest, then go swimming back. It takes forever!
Granted, you aren't required to find most of these collectibles, but if you want to afford upgrades so that you can stand a chance in combat later on then it's a strong recommendation (or if you're a completionist, of course). Boarding ships gets especially tedious after the hundredth time, and there are many unskippable animations and mini-cutscenes that play the same every time you do a certain action. Eventually your patience will wear thin and even sending your fleet on trading missions will become dull and obnoxious. I don't know how bad the tedium would be for a casual player, but I really don't want to spend several hours trying a "lite" playthrough to see if it's possible.
The story is so-so. Fortunately, most of the time is spent in the animus. And most of the time you just play a piratical action-adventure; until it takes a strange turn into pirates-meets-sci-fi. It's honestly not that bad, and the setting returns to normal at the end, but it could have done without. For what it's worth, the story is a mostly fun adventure and the characters (in the past) are pretty interesting, even if they're not all loveable.
Pros:
-Some fun weapons. My favorite is the berserker dart.
-Sailing the high seas can be pretty fun and/or relaxing.
-SEA SHANTIES! YOUR CREW SINGS FOR YOU!
-The soundtrack in general is great.
-All the strengths of the previous AC games are here.
-More customization. Outfits, custom parts for your ship, and renovations for your manor.
-Famous pirates such as Blackbeard and Charles Vane make an appearance. Characterization in general is pretty well-done. Kenway is charming and most of the characters are full-fledged and engaging.
-Wide variety of settings. Sail around the caribbean and dive underwater at certain spots.
-At times, feels like a big-budget "Sid Meier's Pirates."
-Fast travel is a godsend.
-You can pet dogs. Obviously Ubisoft had their priorities straight.
Cons:
-The tedium is hefty, especially if you are a completionist. On the bright side, you can collect most of the collectibles early in the game and get them out of the way. At mission 4 out of 13 I was able to get almost 75% game completion.
-Some stupid scripted set pieces that look good in a trailer for E3 but make for bad gameplay. On more than one occasion I was delayed from completing an objective because it was "too soon" for the game's liking. Also, the canned animations that play the same way every time something happens! If one more stupid frickin' eel jumps out at me from the seaweed, so help me....
-If you don't get all the sea shanties in close succession, then the first ones you find will become tiresome from hearing them so many times. Fortunately, you can turn off shanties and then turn them back on once you've collected them all.
-No one cares about the animus or the "meta-story arc." Just have an opening and ending cutscene in the modern day and then let us swashbuckle in peace in the middle. To be fair, there is far less modern-day stuff in "Black Flag" than in past installments.
-Swordfighting can be frustrating because many of the soldiers are very adept at blocking your attacks.
-The main game is pretty short. I usually consider this a good thing because I like games to be short and sweet when possible, but not in this case. I feel that the developers placed too much importance on collectibles to drag out the game's length instead of focusing on real substance. There is even DLC that allows the player to spend less time playing the game. This is good in a way, but also bad because it proves that the game shouldn't be this long. The amount of collectibles is insane. They could have added more missions or sidequests instead.

If you like competitive Smash Bros, get this game. It may look like a simple copy-and-paste of SSBM for the Gamecube, but this game is NOT just a Melee clone. For starters, it removes the mechanics of shielding, grabbing, and ledge-grabbing. Shielding is replaced by "parrying", which is an alternative to counters from Smash. So basically, no one's Down-B slot is taken up by some stupid counter. The absence of ledge-grabbing makes off-stage play intense and gratifying. Combo potential, on-stage and off-stage, is fantastic. And of course, it's no competitive Smash-style fighting game without wavedashing and L-cancelling, both made way easier. And the characters are unique, some invent new ways to control the stage (like Orcane's puddles or Forsburn's smoke), while others take inspiration from well-known Smash Bros playstyles and revamp them. Forsburn takes aerial and tilt inspiration from Marth, but his Side B creates a clone of himself that reminds me of Ice Climbers. Wrastor has the unstoppable airgame of Jigglypuff, but his attacks on the ground parallel Captain Falcon, Falco, and Meta Knight. Zetterburn, the game's main mascot, takes Bowser's strong attacks and mixes it with Fox's specials. But even with these comparisons, experience in playing Jigglypuff will not translate over to Wrastor. Experience with Bowser will not make you instantly understand Zetterburn.
So, a recap: Takes best parts of competitive Smash Bros and revamps them, combos and techniques are easier to learn for casuals, characters will remind you of popular Smash characters but make them new. Oh, and the music and art are great as well.
I'll rate this game A Bag of Chips/10. It has all you love about Smash Bros, from the competitive to the casual. And it adds awesome advancements to the game, making it accessible for all players but still appealing to the competitive audience. It's all that Melee is, and a bag of chips!

knowing that this was still a poor worked-over port, i used the GeDoSaTo tool from Durante to unsure i had full-hd graphics with more or less 40-60 fps (people have to get to know their PC better before shouting that they have such a high-end setup that doesnt work), the tool works wonderful with the game and makes it a better experience as on the console. without, the game has overall performance difficulties, reason for that is most likely the fixed resolution of 720p at 24Hz (or something like that). therefore the game and the system has unnecessary extra work, that heavily slows down the game.
i'm eager for the december 2014 patch for this game to see if SE can bring the game to a performance that is rather standard for most games released today.
i will keep my opinion about the story to myself, except that you have to play all 3 FF XIII titles to get the full FF experience, i'll wait for that till i'll played all 3 here on steam (have played all three on the console)
as for gameplay - i am fond of it, because it gives the hardcore FF-fan the chance for nice strategic battles and weapon customizations later in the game, while giving new players the platform to play a FF title without getting too deep into the FF mechanics which turns out unforgiving every once and a while.
i highly recommend this title to all, who wants to play a FF, but dont want to spend an additional 100+ hours on sidequesting, farming, revealing story-related secrets, etc. BUT i would wait till SquareEnix has patched it properly, otherwise the easy to use GeDoSaTo tool is free for download (and if possible support Durante's great work!)

Everybody who likes Smash should get into this game!

A poor game to begin with. Missing probably half of all the things it takes to make a good RPG worthy of baring the Final Fantasy name. First of all, the story line is confusing and shallow as hell, the characters were outrageously cheesy at best, especially Vanille and the world felt so small and closed that it drains your desire to even bother to see what might be out there other than what the waypoint sends you to. The game was also painfully linear and lacked any real depth. I played through the whole game in less than 40 hours which really sucks since the average FF title takes about 70 hours to complete. Another disappointment was the battle engine which was confusing, unecessarily flashy and overly automated making it very difficult for you to coordinate battle tactics according to your particular gaming style. Secondly, battles get longer and longer as you progress through the game which, I think hurts the whole game experience. I play Final Fantasy for its story telling, diversity and overall gaming experience. When I spend 80% of the game time fighting monsters, 15% watching ridiculously long cutscenes telling a really confusing and shallow story with annoyingly cheesy character personalities and 5% developing my characters with an okay development system similar to that of FFX, I will generally have a very forgettable experience and would probably never want to play the game again if I even bother finishing it.
In conclusion, this is a clear example of how the folks at Square-Enix think they can just crank out whatever garbage they want, slap a respectable title on it like Final Fantasy and ship it off for its loyal fans to waste their money on. Its like they dont even try to make good games anymore. I've played better indie games made by tiny bands of dudes working with budgets a fraction of that of SE. Final Fantasy XII was the first indicator that SE was getting lazy for me. The game was generally good but it was the first game I played that really lacked a good story-line. The story started out really good but really started falling short toward the end; almost as though the project ran out of budget money and was forced to cut its story-telling short. Either that or they really did just get lazy with it.
Dont waste your money on this title or on ANY of the following FFXIII titles, unless you can get it on a Steam holiday deal for a couple bucks and you happen to have 40 hours of your life you want to throw away.

While Project AURA is still in it's early stages, it is a fantastic simulation of creating/running a colony after a climate disaster.  There is a ton of potential available, and by the looks of it the devs are tapping into it from the amount of commuity interaction, and updates.
There is a good portion of mircomanagement, you decide which colonists you wish to awake and where to employ them.  You control the food, production, and resource gathering.  As well you contol which buildings you want operating, what the function of some of them are, maintenance management, while keeping an eye on your power requirements.
Depending on start-up options, the game can be more challanging by having less startup credits.  Even on normal there is a limited amount, so funds should be managed carefully until a good balance of production is established.
For people who enjoy playing a simulation that is not extremely fast paced but requires a little bit of mircomanagement, this is definitely worth playing, and supporting it's future developement!  Highly recommended!

I started playing Magic just before 4th Edition of the core set was released. Since then, I've dropped in an out, assembled and sold collections, played both physical and digital. As someone who no longer plays the physical game (cost/time), this digital version of Magic really stratches that itch. Overall I recommend giving this a try, regardless of your experience (of lack thereof) with Magic.
Pros:
* Free to Play: No need to drop several hundred dollars on a collection. If you have the time, you can play matches against the AI or random opponents to earn in-game "gold" with which to purchase more cards. Several "story mode" ladders exist with prebuilt decks that progress as you win matches. These are great for someone who wants a quick fix without the time/investment of collecting cards and building a deck.
* Hints/Tutorials: There is a pretty detailed tutorial system in place. While the "story mode" ladders exist to slowly introduce complexity as a form of tutorial, each new mechanic is given an optional, standalone mini-game that is made available the first time that mechanic appears in any story mode or AI battle match.
* Deck Building: There are two modes for deck building. In the first, the game guides you through creating a deck for any/each of two-color combinations, suggesting which types of cards to use and automatically adding land. In the second, you are given full control over building a deck, with decent filters for searching for just the right card.
Cons
1) If you let the game go idle for several minutes, it loses its server connection and will not reconnect until you return to the main menu, effectively losing any progress (story mode progression, gold earned from a victory) you've made since the last check-in. There are server connectivity issues with the game that many are blaming for this issue, but I have the SAME issue happen frequently in the iOS version of the game. Let the game idle too long, connection is lost until you restart.
2) While this game is multi-platform, there is NO ability to sync your account between platforms. I've been playing on my iPhone for two weeks, but that progress (and, correspondingly, my card collection) is not available while playing on Steam. Seems like a lost opportunity.
3) If you build a deck using the guided mode, you are not given the ability to manually edit that deck afterwards (instead you are forced to start from scratch). It can be frustrating to have a pretty good guided-build deck which you know can be improved with one key card, but not be able to just add that card.
4) No draft or sealed deck tournament modes. Single-duels (1:1, or 2-headed) only.
Notes:
I've not have any of the technical issues that other players seem to have experienced. I am always able to connect at start up, have not seen gold disappear, have not received "unlimited" gold, and have had no graphical/visual issues. Your mileage may vary, of course.

When I saw the blocky/voxel art style I was expecting something like Team Fortress 2 where you complete comical objectives and stuff, take like 20 bullets before dying, and blocky comic mischief.
What I got was an Ace of Spades clone with advanced customization features. Nothing makes sense when you get killed by silent entities from across the map because the sound doesn't travel well enough. You don't even hear bullets hitting you half the time. Much less does anything explain the collision when digging trenches I got stuck at least 5 times in the same trench because my feet kept getting stuck or something. Stuff you shouldn't be able to dig through, you can dig through. Stuff you shouldn't be able to break, breaks.
This game is 1-2 hit kills. Guns are bulky and don't shoot straight, even at close range, much less seldom aided by its ironsights feature. There are very few sound cues so you can only rely on your health bar to tell if you're taking damage. Zombies poke you to death.
This game feels VERY unfinished. Its as if they had literally taken Ace of Spades, increased the model resolution of players. The guns don't shoot where you aim, there's little to tell if you're doing damage other than a thin bar above your target, and nothing makes sense.
This feels like a beta. Not a all worth 5 dollars. I'd pay 99 cents for it because thats about all the enjoyment I got out of it, most of that $5 probably goes towards coding those editors. The editors and character/weapon/world customization are the only things they did right; its a shame its all to waste because the gameplay is nothing like you'd expect.

About This War Of Mine:
This War Of Mine places you in the lives of several civilian survivors in a war torn, besieged city. In order to survive you will have to forage for food and supplies while avoiding conflict as much as possible. Basic elements such being cold or hungry are major factors in determining how long your people will survive. Will you make it to the end of the conflict? Will there be stories you tell your children about 'the war'? Time will tell as you experience the war firsthand.

I love post-apocalypse fiction.  The atmosphere of helplessness, being lost without a guide, without a chance, without hope.
This War of Mine does so many things so well right out of the gate.
You are not a regenerating messiah from the depths of a vault.  You are not a techno-industrial cyber-soldier.  There are no faceless zombies to absolve you of ethics.
You will feel frustrated because you cannot keep your survivors fed and healthy.  You will feel helpless and scared when you notice footsteps coming from upstairs while you are scavanging a house.  You will feel something for the people you have to rob or even kill to survive.  It's a hard game.  Not immensely difficult, just hard.  Cruel.  Unfair.  Such is life. In. The. Apocalyse.

I bought this game last night, pretty much sight-unseen. It was then suddenly four in the morning.
I'm not sure how much credibility a review written after five hours of gameplay can hold, but I thought the first sentence probably covers whether or not I'd recommend it.
In terms of actual reviewy type things, I can tell you this:
The gameplay is excellent, filled with the tension you'd expect to experience living in a besieged city. This atmosphere is executed brilliantly, the art style, music and pacing all lending more to it, allowing you to really put yourself into the space presented to you with your poor, semi-displaced trio of housemates.
I've played a lot of survival games and all of them have one conceit or another to explain the situation (zombies, spiders, zombies, aliens, zombies etc.) but the more realistic story in This War of Mine (a story being played out in the world in a number of places right now), in my opinion, lends it a more visceral, wholly real, experience.
If you're a fan of the survival genre, or a fan of artistic, atmospheric games, I'd suggest that you will not regret handing over your money for this one.

The game has you managing your supplies by determining who gets to eat, and who gets medical treatment if sick. Gathering supplies from outside (Only at night since it’s safer) has you putting your home at risk from looters if not properly protected. Also building improvements like barricades, beds, booking facilities, moonshine stills, all help to keep your civilians alive. Even keeping the house warm with a stove becomes imperative, when deciding to use fuel for either cooking or heating.
The game has no tutorial or instructions on what the best approach is, rather it’s left up to you. Do you want to survive? Help others? Become bandits and rob others? Even take part in the war by attacking military posts. All rather difficult tasks, and none really goes through as planned.
My game started off with three young men, Marko, Bruno, and Pavle. Bruno was the cook who feared venturing out, caring only for survival. With the mentality, better them than us. Marko and Pavle the strongest of the two as far as scavenging and defending. As the game progressed I ran into an elderly man named Anton who excelled in creating items and gave him shelter.
The game has you investing in your characters and fabricating their personalities in your mind as you make choices that put them at risk. Towards the end of my game winter sets in and supplies become scarce, while sickness becomes more common. Pavle ends up dying trying to back home through Snipers alley, an obvious reason why it’s called that. Marko dies trying to steal supplies from bandits that own a brothel. Left with a sick Anton and the cowardly Bruno. I set Bruno to avenge Marko as a last ditch effort. I imagined Bruno having lost his fear in desperation and anger. Making him kill three armed men with a shovel as he ambushed them from different locations of their hideout. The risk brought in a big reward.
However returning home he only found that Anton froze to death in his bed. Bruno was now alone, suffering depression, but getting what he wanted from the start, just to survive.

Civilization Beyond Earth is at its core your basic Civ game that has seen several iterations over the last 20+ years and yet always seems to have something up it's sleeve to give it that individual uniqueness.  Although many see this as an offshoot of Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri, it is far and away a different experience.  Civ B.E. takes all of its cues from the past, such as different levels of experience, map size, etc., but the environments are based on exoplanetary research and data as we know it and replaces the nations with corporations and their various motivations at the forefront of this race to win at all costs.  The addition of virtues and affinities combined with the updated Tech Tree makes for interesting choices for how you move forward in the game.  Playing it as a Civ Vet or first timer, the learning curve isn't as steep as with other games and the community has already provided many interesting mods and add-ons that have enhanced the core product tremendously.
The game has plenty of room to grow and with a robust community supporting it, Civilization Beyond Earth is guaranteed a long life on the PC for some time to come.

How people can downvote this game is ... unfathomable! And here is why:
The game runs on a version of the Civ5 engine, correct, but the game it self isn't Civ5. Comparing it to Civ5 is - for a lack of a better word - idiotic. The game is - to use a popular term - "vanilla", and Civ5 is at it's 3rd major expansion. Doesn't anyone remember Civ5 "vanilla"? It was a horrible mess with broken AI, random crashes for almost everyone, random resource hogging, graphical glitches... and i can go on! This list for this game however - is almost nonexistent!
Some say it lacks personality. How? Yes you don't recognize earth and earths history along with the game ............ and thus the title ... Beyond Earth. If you are upset by this fact, then............ i really don't know what to tell you! However for everyone else, what gives this game more personality than Civ5 in some ways is:
The barbarians are gone, instead you get a race of aliens which you can actually interact with. I personally always found the barbs in Civ a bit lackluster, since you never got to do anything but fight them. I know my country at least was actually formed by tribes comparable to the barbs joined up and formed a country. The aliens are much more interesting than the barbs
The tech and wonders still have their quotes, and so does the different leaders. I for one find most of them to be on par with Civ5 - however it is all made up, so yes - you won't recognize it, and yet there actually are a ton of it that seems VERY plausible and makes sense.
The culture tree is also a welcomed addition in my book. It is less powerful than in Civ5 - which i like! It makes the transition from new nation to high tech an power nation much more fluent.
I could go on and on. This game is NOT a bad game. Downvoting it is mental! is it a 100/100 game? No - it isn't but a 80-90/100? In my book it is!

As of v2.11:
Project AURA is an interesting take on survival city builder formula - think Banished or Anno 2070 (but more focused).
It has quite fancy graphics that again remind me of Anno 2070 a lot. And I'd say that's a good thing.
The number of buildings in the game is quite limited (even with more coming soon), but that's not a big problem, because all the flexibility comes from building configurations, not the building themselves.
Yep, same building can do different things by swapping out Blueprints that are used for production (at the moment there's not too many alternatives for blueprints, but this is something that can and probably will be easily extended).
Add here the fact that all your citizens / employees are actual NPCs with separate skills, desires and stats.
Plus the fact that you need to manage power consumption / production to make sure your dom protects your from disasters.
Plus the fact that you need to manage food and menus to make sure everyone has enough nutritions, etc.
And you get a pretty sophisticated city builder with focus on surviving in hostile environment.
I haven't encountered any serious bugs during my playtime.
Most of the issues the game has are pretty minor and mostly related to UI and UX, which means they can be easily fixed.
I must note that as of v2.11 only sandbox mode is available, and the time flows pretty slowly, so be prepared to spend hours upon hours in the game to achieve a nice town.
If that's not your kind of gameplay - I'd wait until campaign and quests are introduced.

Shadow Warrior 2013 is without a doubt the most positive experience I have ever had playing a modern-retro first person shooter.
Let's start off by talking about the gamplay.
The combat in this game is simply fantastic, and there's no other way to put it. Weapons feel impactful and you never feel critically low on ammo, although even if you did somehow run through your entire supply, it wouldn't matter, because the sword in this game is easily one of the best I have ever used in a game, let alone a first person shooter, and once fully upgraded, can easily tear through low tier enemies. Speaking of tearing, I
to talk about the gore. While usually I would consider it a part of the Graphics section, the gore system in Shadow Warrior 2013 plays a very important role in the gun (or sword) play, with precise shots and strike tearing limbs off of enemies and stopping them from using certain attacks. Not only does this look freaking awesome, but it also does a number on the weapon feel, and goes pretty far in making the guns seem like they're shooting more than just pebbles at your enemies. If it were based on gameplay alone I would recommend Shadow Warrior to any FPS fan, but it offers up so much more in addition to the already great combat.
Running on FWH's proprietary "Road Hog" engine, the game musters up an impressive and often stunning level of visual quality, while also maintaining a rock solid framerate throughout the entire game. Models and textures are of a significantly high caliber, backed up by great lighting effects. This is all backed up by the extraordinary levels of detail crammed into the environments, with plenty of secrets to find, this is classically detailed level design at it's finest, there's just frankly more detail here than you could fit into an a less linear game.
If there's one aspect of this game that surprised me more than any other, it was definitely the story. Playing as Lo Wang (voiced by the excellent Jason Liebrecht), you make your way through 17 unique levels to find several peices of an ancient sword, and eventually
Along the way you meet Hoji, a demon who can seem like a bit of an a**hole at the begining of the game, but by the end feels like a true lifelong friend. The writing is far better than most would expect, especially from a game based off of what was essentially
. Naturally, there are d*ck jokes, but the comedic timing and delivery is just right, and they never overstay their welcome. The dialogue will often make you chuckle, but also knows when to let the jokes take a back seat for other emotions. Has an ultra-violent first person shooter ever made you cry? If not than this one just might. So if you'd like a tear jerker to go with your "tear jerker" jokes, this game is for you.
Based off of my comments you may be able to tell by now that I'm a pretty big fan of this game, and because of that, my review might not be completely un-biased, to say the least. However, if any of what I have said interests you in the slightest, I implore you to give this game a go, if you're anything like me at all, you'll have a blast.

This game is a totally unique experience. There's pirates in my AC game - there's an assassins in my Pirate game - two great premises that taste great together. Finally, the age old question of pirate vs. ninja can be answered... they'll join forces. Blow the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everyone. Cruise the seven seas looking for chicks and then suck down a cask of Grog.
Enter the main character - a drunken pirate with probably one of the most interesting back stories in the entire series. He's not the son of an assassin - he's not the daughter of a templar - he's just a guy who wants money. You can't argue with that. But he's got strange abilities - and they only get better as he encounters the series tropes and heroes who turn him into a weapon. As the series goes on this main character grows from a selfish pirate whelp to a selfish pirate captain to a selfish pirate king - only to realize, in the final act, that the whole selfish thing not only cost him his family; it cost him everyone he ever cared about. When he finally buckles down and goes to work you really feel like he's made a journey. Like you were a part of his development. This is not a main hero who is very heroic. He's a bit of a♥♥♥♥♥♥.. he's REALLY a♥♥♥♥♥♥ Granted, the world he grew up in the - the environment - how could he be anything BUT a♥♥♥♥♥♥ But it's his development from♥♥♥♥♥♥to a good man (not a hero - he NEVER becomes a hero - he ends the game as a good man and very admirable for the fact that he knows he's still broken) that really sells this story and sets it apart from most of the rest of the AC tropes.
Ground Combat in this game is the same as combat has ever been - if you're new to the series you'll pick it up very quickly. If you're a series vet... what's to pick up? Apart from a few new bells and whistles it's AC standard. A lot of people look on this negatively - but for me it's a positive. The Arkham games and Shadow of Mordor ripped the combat from these games for a reason - it works. It's not complicated - it's good fun - it works. Why get rid of it?
Ship Combat is refined from AC3 - in fact, everything from AC3 is refined. No longer does it leave the bitter taste of buggy development in your mouth. This is a fine quality product worth savoring. You turn your ship - you blow the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of stuff - and then you♥♥♥♥♥♥ pillage and plunder. Much like the ground combat it's very straight forward. The only real difference is that you can be attacked by more than one enemy at the same time.
The crafting system is the same as it was in AC3 - outside of costumes you won't really bugger with it. It's just less of a headache to buy all the stuff you need. Further, about midway through the game, you've got so much gold coming in that there really isn't a THING you can't buy. The costumes - sadly - are almost all reskins. You've got a blue outfit - a red outfit - and a black outfit (seriously, what other color would a Ninja Pirate wear?) and three or four 'unique' outfits that mostly just remove the hood.
The World Map is IMMENSE. There is a HUGE amount of space to explore - moreover, there's space within the space that you can explore. AC heard you like exploring - so they put some exploring inside your exploring so you can explore while you explore. For me the game was about 40 hours long - that's almost a full week of gameplay for me :P the collectables and bonus content hidden across the worldspace will keep you playing for two or three times that as my gametime shows.
All in all this game is what it says on the tin - Assassin's Creed Black Flag. It's pirates and ninjas. It's every gamers dream. Don't let the dated screenshots and the fact that it came out three years ago fool you. This game is a gem. Buy it.

I have been a civ fan for as long as I can remember.  I remember my first all-night gaming sessions were on original civ games staring with the original Civ, Civ II, Civ III, and Civ IV, as well as Alpha Centari.  I played all of them, but skipped over Civ 5 as I had moved on to other types of games at that point.  I have now come back to Civ for the new Beyond Earth.
Since I didn't experience Civ 5 much (played during trials sometimes), I do not have much criticism about whether this is a big upgrade or not from Civ 5.
I wrote a really positive review first, but after playing a couple of times, now, it is very forumlaic and too easy.  One of the AI attacked me, I successfully defended, then it asked for peace and gave me a city! WTF!?  I didn't even attack him at all or make any forward momentum toward their territory.  I simply defended my own space and kicked the crap out of them.  I was actually trying to play passively in the game.  So, it is a bit strange.
I did enjoy this game immensely at first.  There are so many variations in styles to play and there is no longer the idea that you just stack as many military units as you can and zerg your way to conquest.  Nearly every game I played on the old civ games ended with my military domination of the opponents.  Not so, in Civ BE.
However, as I played a couple of subsequent games, I realized it is basically the same thing repeated.  Even though the customizations are nice, the AI is bad, and the game becomes pretty forumulaic.
The victory conditions are quite interesting stories, but are generally too easy with the contact victory as well.  It is almost like they dumbed this version down.  It is no longer necessary to simply wipe out all the other players and dominate with military affairs.  In addition, you don't need to have so many different kinds of military troops.  Something that would quickly annoy me in previous games - upgrading my troops - happens basically automatically now.  In addition, the number of types of troops are not overwhelming as they have been in the past.
The tech web is really great allowing you to diversify your scientific discoveries greatly, moving from one to another quite quickly.  The affinity system and the virtue system should also allow for a great amount of variety of play.  However, it seems now that the desired affinities and virtues are becoming formulaic as well.  I keep choosing the same ones to win and it just appears to easy.
I give it a so-so thumbs up after playing it a few times.  For me, primarily because I didn't go through Civ V, I have a sort of bias toward the game.  But I wish they had made it a bit more meaningful in the different variety of choices and improved the AI.  Seems like they always just cheat to give the AI more advantages rather than actually improving its performance.
Its probably not worth the price at this point unless you have a lot of disposable income.

Project Aura Review
So I started playing this game thinking it may be a civilization kind of game or at the very least a trimmed down version of it. Sadly what I found was a game touted as Beta when the game barely qualifies as an Alpha.
The first black eye comes in the tutorial system, not only is it short(which to some may be a blessing)but also entirely inadequate for teaching you the game. Some people like going in blind, but you game should at least the absolute basics, which it kinda does and doesn't.
Next sucker punch is no rebindable keys or even a listing of what the keys do. I understand it's beta, but that kind of thing takes all of five minutes to do.

Overall, Project Aura is a great game concept centred around a strong environmental message. Pixel Quality Games have hit the balance of micromanagement and survival difficulty perfectly, and created and extremely addictive game. My only criticisms are that some of the mechanics are unclear, and many of the menus are difficult to navigate. However, Pixel are welcoming all player feedback and I am sure these minor issue will be finessed in later updates. I can't wait to see the final shape of this game and will continue to play along throughout its development.
Project Aura is the first venture for Pixel Quality Games, and has received widespread community support through Steam Greenlight. Aura is a survival/strategy game currently in Early Access. I am a big fan of the concept behind this game. The developers are aiming to make an engaging gaming experience, while conveying a message of sustainability, and climate change awareness. In support of the message behind the game, the devs are also contributing 2% of all game earnings to environmental causes that will be selected through voting, on social networks.
At sometime in the 21st century, global warming multiplied by human activities was responsible for the extinction of most of the life on Earth. Those who survived built floating cities on the ocean surface. Within each city the survivors slept in cryo-preservation, awaiting a time when they could awaken and rebuild.
The player is in charge of one such floating city, and must build the structures required to house and support the newly awakened survivors. All of the building materials required can be purchased from the market or gathered and recycled through various colony structures. Players are also responsible for assigning each survivor a job in the colony, and must take into consideration the natural aptitude of each person.
Food rationing must also be managed throughout the game, and players who do not construct a food production line early on, will inevitably watch as their colonists slowly starve. I had a great time building structures and gather resources, and it is very satisfying reaching the point of colony self sufficiency.
Aura is in the first stages of Early Access, so making a colony self sufficient and then maintaining its population growth is all that's on offer at the moment. Even with these limited mechanics I got hooked easily on this title and I can't wait to see the inclusion of, research goals, quests, city energy shield management and many other mechanics in the final release. There is an in game tutorial included with the Beta, but it is a bit bare bones, so I recommend reading the forums before starting, as some of the key bindings are not obvious but are needed to facilitate the experience.

Firstly, for a bit of a back story (Feel free to skip to the actual review):
I originally noticed the game on steam greenlight back in February of last year. It seemed interesting enough, so I supported it. The next day, I logged on and noticed it had been fully supported. Ok, so now the wait. Pretty soon after, I noticed that about 3 minutes after I logged in one morning, an announcement was posted that their website just went up and preorders were now available. Keep in mind during the wait between, videos and such were posted as teasers. Within 3 seconds of the announcement going up, I was already on the purchase page clicking order (I was actually the first to preorder the game). After ordering, and checking the timeline, the wait was on. Then after almost a year later, the day finally came when keys were being sent out. I had a problem receiving my key at first, however it was quickly sorted out. Shortly after it came out I imediately started playing to learn as much as I could about it, and have used that knowledge to help develope the Wikia for it along with Nomeg.
Now for the actual review:
1:) Tutorial
After initially playing on Beta 1 (Before steam early access), I noticed the tutorials were a bit too quick. They didn't cover everything in Beta 2 (They still don't, this should be improved later on). You were able to fly though them all in about 10 minutes. The graphics are excellent, even on the lowest settings (Which I play at simply for recording purposes). It covered most of the controls in game very well, as well as a few other details which are very handy. One thing that they didn't seem to cover for the actual sandbox mode, is how to get certain objects such as fertilizer. After playing around for a bit, I was taken back to the employment tutorial, and I realized that all buildings have employment setups (This includes the residential buildings). With that in mind I was able to start production on fertilizer, however it's a slow process and the the tutorial also didn't go over how to speed the game up, and still doesn't (Again, should be updated later on). Other then the few things it doesn't show you how to do, it was an enjoyable experience.
2:) Main Game (Sandbox mode)
Upon the launch of the sandbox mode, You are taken into a blank "Atlantis" looking platform center. At this point, it's easy to become confused and make it seem like you were robbed out of about $15. However, after playing around enough, I was able to find the market place and find the objects I needed to purchase in order to start on residential housing. From there, I focused on getting a steady steam of items in work for my colony to self sustain itself. Doing this was a bit tricky, as the tutorial also doesn't go over how the production cycles work, how to maximize production cycles, or even tell you what buildings can do what. The building menu lists the name of the building, however not what it does or needs (excluding materials, it does show this, I meant as in worker types, etc.). The layout could use a bit of a change to include a description of what the building does and such in my opinion. Another thing I noticed is that sometimes the errors were a bit buggy (before the hotfix) and would show in spanish, even if the game was set to english. At points, there were also times were I was confused why there are still things in the current version that shouldn't be there (Since they aren't fully working, turns out this was to save time for the next release) and why certain things weren't working such as the shields or extra cargo storage for ships. In the current release, the risk factor tends to skyrocket at points, and will sit at 100% even though the system that's being developed for it (Can't tell you guys what it is, but you're going to like it) isn't implemented just yet. There were also a few other bugs that are there, but overall, nothing that greatly effects the gameplay itself. Now while the game does just toss you in with minimal help from the tutorial (at the time of this review), and some may give it negative reviews because of that, keep in mind there were other games that did the same thing and turned out to be highly supported. Games such as Life is Feudal and Banished do the same thing. Now, please keep in mind as an early access beta game, I am basing my review off of the gameplay itself, not anything else since this is how games at this stage should be rated.
Graphics: As a laptop user, it's hard for me to play games at max settings sometimes. This game can be hard on my computer from time to time, especially while recording. That being said though, even on the lowest settings, the graphics are still very well done, clean, crisp, and smooth. I've tried changing the settings, and between High and Low settings, there is very minimal difference from what I could tell aside from the animations and extra particles. 10/10 for graphics.
Sound: The sound at times can be annoying, particularly when in the main menu, or when dragging objects around from one place to another (loud annoying base sound, rip headphone users). There is also a lack of ambient sounds, however this will be added later on. For now though, there is a very nice background album, very reminiscent of kerbal space program. Given the futuristic theme to the game, the music fits in well for it. 7/10 on sound.
Gameplay: The overall gameplay isn't bad. It isn't necessarily good, however it isn't bad. While it could use some improvements and will be receiving some, the current core gameplay tends to leave you feeling like it needs something more. As for what, I'm not sure, we will have to see on a future update. The gameplay is smooth, however due to the lack of what the tutorial teaches you, it's also a bit challenging. It adds a nice mix for a while, until you get the hang of the game, which then leaves you feeling empty and at times, bored. It has a nice blend of micromanagement to it, and an overall decent feel. Most of the GUI is well designed, although as I mentioned earlier, some of it could use a redesign especially when it comes to the construction menu. I will give the gameplay a 7/10 as well. As I stated, it could use some improvements and I know some are coming, however as I stated based on the current gameplay it's decent. Not bad, not good or great, but it's playable, and enjoyable for the most part.
Why I recommend this game:
Let me put it to you like I did for NoBull and a few others when they asked me what this game is like. If you like Banished, Anno 2070, SimCity, or X-COM, then you will like this, because the basis is like Banished, meets X-Com, meets Simcity in a sense with an Anno 2070 plot. Or as NoBull reworded it, it's like Banished and Anno 2070 had a baby and this is that baby. It currently has the potential to become a great game, given enough support and feedback. The devs are constantly talking to players, getting their opinions, and working with people when they have problems with bugs or other problems. It runs like a dream on low end machines unlike other city builders or survival simulators, yet that maintains clear, crisp HD look and feel. If you manage to brush aside the little bugs and issues with the current version, the gameplay is very enjoyable, and is easy to play for hours on end (So much so that you will probably lose track of time). Also some of you may wish to wait to purchase it until it becomes more stable, however I would like to remind you that playing with bugs may be worth it in the long run, since we all know after games come off early access you will be spending more money on it (Which for some may not be a problem, however I am addressing the ones that can't always afford to do so).
Overall, I give the game a 8/10 rating.

Now that the horrible launch has been fixed and the no background bug is gone, I can finally write a proper review of the game.
First the positive aspects: The game looks and feels polished, and the cards look excellent as usual.
For a FTP game, the business model is quite fair, if you're good at Magic, and put some dedication into the game, you should be able to get all the cards in a reasonable time by spending about 20$ in booster packs to give you a little push ahead.
The fact that the game will grow together with paper Magic means that this version shouldn't get stale as time passes, that's also why I won't criticize the card pool too much, the only issue is the lack of chaper removal, else, it's quite good considering we only have one basic set's worth of cards to unlock, and the free starting pack, which includes a very good amount of mana fixing, this has been generous of WOTC.
The bad aspects: Considering the previous versions had a chat lobby, I can't see why they removed it for this game, also, even though I don't play 2HG, I definitely think 2HG games vs random opponents should award gold. Finally, the difficulty level of some of the story missions is high for a product that is aimed at teaching the game to newcomers, some of the campaigns are unbalanced in the sense that the second or third duels are hard because of your less powerful deck, and then the last duel is actually easier than the previous ones because your deck has been improved, so you should have some patience and be ready to restart those duels a few times.
The veredict: if you play Magic or are curious about it, you should definitely download this game, it's free so you won't lose anythning.

Before reading on, I thoroughly suggest you download the demo for this game (available above) before investing money into it. It's early access and by no means near completeion, thus making it's price of £11 quite a gamble.
My experience with the demo was fulfilling as someone who's looking for something calm, peaceful, and relaxing to play. Although mush of the game's content is missing from the demo (not surprising), it allowed me to get an insight into what the game has to offer me as of now, and what it may offer in the future.
It was satisfying to control my raft as I sailed across the waves between islands, and - aside from the simple, yet altogether beautiful, graphics - felt very immersive.
My first encounter with an enemy, a pirate carrying a sword, was interesting - the combat in this game is simple and predictable, and provides users with the typical "attack", "powerful attack", and "block" features present in most games of this nature. Impressively, the combat in this game, although sometimes predictable (the enemy I fought only had one single attack) was an enjoyable quick break from the usual serenity of the rest of the game. Hunting, similarly, gives a small sense of achievement, and the rewards follow suit.
The scenery is very eyecatching and I have taken lots of screenshots of this game already, from the vast valleys in the islands to my boat drifting on the surf. There are substantial amounts of graphical settings which allows this game to be played on a wide variety of machines (and on high settings, I can safely say that I am impressed with what the graphics of this game has to offer).
Crafting in the game is easy and simple, as well as logical, and there's a decent variety of crafting recipies already. Like most games, there is a slight learning curve (not just in crafting, but in respect to the whole game), which serves as a little challenge for new players.
There is lots of content in the game already, which is surprising considering how new it is. The developers have promised future updates, however having had the game for such little time I can't vouch for them. Any improvements I'd like to see in the game are very likely to be added in the future.
Altogether, I find no bad points to make against this game. It does what is promised, and providing the developers stay faithful to their noteworthy creation, my rating of 10/10 shall stay as it is.
Please, before you purchase this game, do your own research. As with all early access games (and this game is VERY early access) you're paying for what a developer has promised you. I must say that the current game content is not worth £11 - what the developers say they will be adding, however, works out as quite a good deal for £11. Early access games are a gamble for the consumer, and this provides no deviation from that. Purchase with care.
I, myself, am glad to be a part of this game's development, and will be eagerly participating on the forums.
10/10. Let's hope it stays that way.

Salt's Early Access has been one of the more interesting survival games I've played lately. I personally have grown tired of the Zombie Survival games out there and Salt brings back a more realistic and exploring feeling without all the zombies. Although you may encounter a random giant spider sometimes, it's definitely not hard to kill and they don't lag around in any way. You will have to fight off pirates as well on certain islands, but there aren't hordes of them and escaping from them is usually pretty easy by just running back to your boat.  There are a couple different kinds of boats you can craft to get you to the several islands all different from eachother. Some having abundances of food and materials while others house pirates and other threats, you might even stumble upon some ancient ruins and find a nice simitar or sword. You may also stumble upon a pirate ship floating out in the ocean. These require some maintenece to repair and get working again and also hold a locked chest with valuble loot inside. Killing a pirate Captain granted me a key and I was able to access the chest in the ship but from what I have read you can get these keys sometimes from regular pirates or if you happen to come across a merchant, you can trade or buy one from him. It's the only thing thats really useful that they sell at the moment, The other stuff can be found quite easily. The worlds are created via seeds and anyone using the same seed will experience the same generated world. You must hunt and scavenge for food in order to keep yourself alive while sailing from island to island. Getting lost is probably one of the easiest things to do in this game especially if you have a urge to explore a lot like I do as exploration plays a huge role in Salt. Take note of the different types of Pirates you encounter. One I found to be really useful was the Cartographer Pirate.  Upon killing and looting his body I was able to get my hands on a compass which really made things a lot easier when it came to navigating the almost identical looking islands. The game is single player only which is one thing that bummed me out a bit as I would love to be able to explore this world with a friend, but it is still very interesting. As far as graphics go, The art syle is great, the textures and models aren't that impressive until you see a sunrise or sunset which can really make things look beautiful. Overall the game looks very promising for its future and I will definitely continue playing this. The developers are very active with the community in the forums and I see them replying to almost every post which is what we all love to see with these Early Access games. I definitely reccomend picking this game up if you like Survival and Exploration games. You won't be dissapointed.
Please take note. This early access and there will be bugs. Don't purchase unless you understand this.
I give thee a rating of 8/10 and can't wait to see the stuff added in the future.

Aside from good-looking UI and generally alright graphics, the actual content of the game feels uber Early Access.
Still, I somehow got over 10 hours of something out of this game, so I'd be a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to give it a negative review. However, it should be noted that, in its current state, this game is nowhere near worth 15 EUR. I sincerely hope that the developers will deliver in terms of what they're actually promising: "Pirate Action RPG". Considering that they are still updating their game, it's not entirely unlikely that this will eventually become a robust game.

Deathspank Thongs of Virtue. More of the same. Exactly the same. Same gameplay, Same UI, Same items. Same enemies. More thongs. Many more thongs.
As much as a sequel can often be completely worthless because in an attempt to innovate and streamline it loses what made the original so great the opposite is also true. A sequel that does nothing new whatsoever will often feel hollow and foolish.
Deathspank Thongs of virtue is one such sequel. It's a very simple action RPG that relies heavily on a quirky sense of humor that attempts to poke fun at the RPG genre in general. Unfortunately while the humor and silly art-style could carry the first game both have been worn quite thin by now and you are left with just the shallow action RPG that form the base of Deathspank's gameplay.
Nothing has changed other than the story and if you have already played the original Deathspank this won't be much different.
You should note, this game has a game breaking bug that corrupts your savegame if you exit the game at certain locations. The developers fixed the bug but never shared the update on STEAM. You have go find it yourself on the Steam forums and manually fix your savegame. Guess EA is rubbing off on them.
Not really a game I'd recommend buying if you already played Deathspank. If you're new to the series you can safely pick either although playing both will be a stretch.

Before anything else, I have never played past Hitman games and my opinions in this review is based only in my experience with Hitman Absolution.
I can understand why the majority of Hitman fans were disappointed with Absolution — It is infected by modern day game mechanics. Agent 47 has a Detective Mode-like Instinct that enables him to see behind walls, highlight items, important locations, see the enemy's walking pattern, and enables him to execute a slow-mo auto kill move (mark targets and Agent 47 auto fires). I do understand the reasoning behind the Instinct ability, but it's just too convenient. Fortunately Instinct is limited in higher difficulties. If you're tired of sneaking around, you can always shoot your way through. But that ruins the point of the game and I only use it when my cover was blown and too lazy to restart.
Enemy AI is, most of the time, stupid. When I switched to a different corner, the guard in front of me didn't react. I have to be visible for a few seconds before he notices me. Unlike, say, Metal Gear Solid or Deus Ex Human Revolution, the guards react and take caution when they notice something passed by. In Absolution, they just ignore any oddities they see.
My biggest complaint is the scoring system. They deduct points by taking out enemies, killing civilians, getting spotted, etc. You earn points by disposing bodies, getting specific items, etc. You'll get an overall score after you cleared the level. You get the highest score possible if you go purely stealth, I think. Sure it encourages you be more stealthy, but there are times that I want to get noticed. For example: There's a guard in front and I'm in a guard disguise. A way to eliminate this guard is to lure him to a dark corner. I approached the guard, notices me I'm not one of them, does not attack, 1,350 points deduction, I move away and he follows. I raise my hands, disarmed the guard, knocked him out, and hid his body and gained 135 points. I really like this bait tactic, but the score deduction is discouraging and I ended up tossing stuff around to attract the guards. It's not fun.
On the plus side, game controls are very good. Sticking and navigating Agent 47 to walls is wonky at best, but it's still functional. Stealth take downs and gun combat is good and satisfying. Agent 47 moves like a tank, so don't expect to roll around during firefights. The visuals are very impressive. Everything is so vibrant, detailed and areas with large crowds are a thing to behold. The game has a lot re-playability because of its checklist system. You get bonus points if you get all the weapons in the area, killing enemies with environmental hazards, collecting disguises. Avid item collectors will find this enticing. If collecting is not your thing, you can go to Contracts and beat community-made objectives.
Overall it's an okay stealth game. I like it and most likely I will replay the game again and 100% every level. For die-hard Hitman fans, Absolution is the cancer of the franchise, but to some it's an entertaining game that lets you garrote nuns.
