I really wish I could recommend Beyond Earth as it is now. After pouring hundreds of hours into Civ 5, Beyond Earth just feels like more of the same. It certainly has some interesting elements, I can grant it that. The backstory/lore is fascinating, aliens aren't always hostile (unlike Civ barbs), and the Affinites can add some intersting gameplay mechanics. There is; however, a rather bizarre design choice of making affinites dependant on certain resources. If you don't have access to certain resources, you, basically, are just forced to miss out on unique buildings/units. I understand the intent behind this idea, but having your starting location/initial resources essentially dictate the playstyle isn't a good thing in my opinion.
The tech tree also suffers from a very poor UI design that can make it confusing for new players to navigate and plan out tech paths. Wonders are very lackluster and very few of them are actually worth the resources to build. Upgrading troops via affinity level could have been interesting if there was a wider variety of choices and/or more visual differences outside of changing colors. The in-game decisions made based off of what you build are possibly the biggest missed opportunity. Each choice made should, in my opinion, have had a positive and negative effect tied to it. Then the choices would actually have weight to them instead of just deciding on which positive outcome you want. The lack of any religious or in-depth diplomacy mechanics also threw me off since the Civ 5 expansions basically made those features such a huge focus. Guess we have to wait for DLC?
If all you want is vanilla Civ 5 in space, then Beyond Earth is exactly that so pick it up. Otherwise, it'd be best to wait a few months for more mods to be created or just wait until the first expansion.

I was hoping for Alpha Centauri 2.0.  I got Civ 5 with a new skin.... Definitely not worth the full price.
Do you remember Alpha Centari?
Do you remember the Datalinks with all it's cutting edge information on technology?  Do you remember the secret project videos, with insightful commentary from the leaders, or quotes from Aristotle's Nichomachean Ethics or Sun Tzu's Art of War?  Do you remember the brief videos when you finally cornered and defeated the leader of a rival faction?
How about how you could terraform and change the landscape to your liking?  Do you remember how you could customize your troops from top to bottom with weapons, armor and special abilities?  Do you remember how you could create floating cities, if you wished?
Well, Beyond Earth has nothing like that.  The biggest innovation, which I am not even sure is a plus is the technology web.  Instead of it branching off, you work your way from the middle to the edges of the web, and and each main technology has a few sub technologies.  I found myself just researching as many technologies with the particular affinity I had chosen, because that is the way you upgrade your troops in this game.  You focus on one affinity, then as you acquire more technologies that are in line with that affinity, you get to upgrade your troops, and pick one out of two  attributes.
The terrain is quite interesting, and I still do not know what all the resources I can get are, or what they do.  But some are required to produce certain buildings and others for certain troops, kind of like marble or stone is to buildings and horses and iron for troops in Civilization games.
Most aliens you encounter are quite weak.  They are merely the Beyond earth counterparts of barbarians and do little to hinder your exploration, unless you run into an aggressive Siege worm on land, or an aggressive Kraken at sea.  The Aliens get relatively weaker and eventually disappear once you and your fellow humans have settled most of the planet.
You get quests througout the game, but they seem a bit forced and do not add much to the game.  Most of them consist of picking an extra attribute to a building you just finished.   There are others that compel you to research a certain technology and explore a bit.  But even that is very superficial.
Diplomacy is the standard stuff, but actually leaves a lot off the table if you do not have a cooperation agreement.  You can give away stuff in exchange for favors, so that the other faction "owes you one", but these favors are usually not worth much. Full disclosure, I've participated in a couple of the playtester builds earlier this year. I make a point to never support a game on early access, but my experience with the playtester build was what convinced me that it was a worthwhile investment. There are currently six playable characters and five stages, and training and local/online multiplayer are the only playable modes in the game. Dan Fornance has stated that the full game will have eight characters and stages, a story mode, and a wave-based survival mode when it's released next year.
If you're a Melee veteran looking for a platform fighter to fill the competitive void that recent Smash games have left behind, or if you're looking for a Smash Bros. style game for the PC, this is the one to get. The controls are very responsive and fully rebindable for both controllers and keyboards. For people who want to play with Gamecube controllers, there is no native support for the Mayflash adapter, but there is a guide available that shows you how to add it manually.
The characters in the game are incredibly well designed, both mechanically and visually. While Zetterburn is more or less a shoto of Wolf from Project M, there are some mechanics and moves that make him unique. Same goes for Wrastor, who borrows heavily from Meta Knight and Marth. The rest of the characters are all unique in their playstyles, with my personal favorite being Forsburn. Since there are no items in this game, each character has special skills to make up for it. For example, Kragg can summon a pillar of earth underneath him as his special recovery move, which I don't think I've seen in a platform-fighter before, let alone any other fighting game. This does lead to concerns about character balancing (Kragg, for instance, is kind of ridiculous), but I'm sure those will be addressed in later updates.
Is it worth paying $15 for at its current state? I would honestly be hesitant to say yes. There is a lot missing from this current build, but what is there is really well polished. The fact that I purchased this game says a lot to how polished it is thus far. If you're still on the fence about this game, I'd suggest you wait until at least the full character roster and stage selection is included.

First off, let me just say that Bioshock is one of my favorite games of all time. It's definitely a game I would recommend to anyone interested in an atmospheric, story based shooter. The original version is still available and you get it in this package if you didn't own it already. I honestly didn't see any problems with the original version. When it was announced they were remastering it I wondered why. It still looks fine even after 9 years and the PC port was manageable even with the mouse acceleration/sensitivity problems.
This "remastered" version seems more like a glorified retexturization which isn't what this game deserves at all. It still has the original annoyances of the old version with limited graphics options and poor mouse navigation in the menus. Any bugs that were in the original are still here in this version.
Honestly the graphics improvement isn't that noticable. Like I said, the original looks fine in my opinion. And unless you've played the original extensively you probably won't be able to tell the difference unless shown a side by side comparison of the two. It feels like they just added HD textures and called it good.
What annoys me the most is that you can't buy the original versions separately, you have to get it in the bundle with the remastered edition. Which means the cost of buying the entire Bioshock series went up by $20. Kind of makes it hard to convince people to try a 9 year old game when its as expensive as it is.
So to whether or not I recommend this version. I don't know. To me it just feels like a lazy way for the developer to cash in on the franchise again after 9 years. I still love Bioshock, but I'm just disappointed with this supposed Remaster. But if you haven't played the series before, this is probably the way to go. So I'll give it a thumbs up.

This is going to be fairly short and informal review based on this edition of the game. Bioshock is one of my favorite games and this review has nothing to do with how I feel of the original, I am just reviewing the content of the Remaster.
I come to you today, launch day of the Bioshock Remaster for us PC users, with nothing but disappointment. This "remaster" is extremely lazy for us PC users, especially considering there are
graphics options in this new release compared to the original release. I'll add that not only are there a total of 5 or 6 options, but the new textures look even less detailed than the original's in most cases. The "new" lighting is still behind in terms of modern industry standards and even with the slightly improved Anti-Aliasing you don't see *much* of an improvement.
I will add that despite being a remaster, I am experiencing issues with this version of the game that I never had on the original, such as a crash around 10 minutes into Rapture. Yep, I can't even play the game past a certain point as it crashed every time, without fail. On top of that, there seems to be some terrible lighting issues. When looking at a flickering light source, it appears to have improper texturing so the lighting isn't displayed properly, it's choppy and inconsistent.
Overall, this is extremely disappointing. I was hoping this rerelease would breathe some life into such a beloved game series, but instead we're stuck with more problems than the initial launch of the game. I cannot recommend purchasing this remaster even for the price of $20USD, it's just a lazy and broken port.

CONS-

Now if I haven't said repetitive enough, just wait 'til you hear what comes after you beat the game. In terraria, one of my favourite games, hard mode is introduced after a while and new enemies appear, new ore, new enviroments and a lot of stuff for you to gear up against the horde of increasingly difficult enemies. That game is hard. Now, in this game, 'hard mode' just means the whole game is repeated, except your most useful tool, the anti-grav well, is no longer available. Also, all enemies now follow your grav wells. This game is tedious.
I feel sorry if you are a completionist, because what this means is that you have to go through the whole game twice, in which the game normally is hard enough, this time you have no way of avoiding enemies as grav wells are your only means of movement, but all enemies follow this.
Enemies, by the way, just means the sprites half your size of ninja stars and bouncing balls that come in straight lines and 1 hit you, with no way of you being able to destroy them or attack them (unless they are yellow, in that case they follow your grav wells, which is pretty pointless if you need to USE THEM YOURSELF?!).
tl;dr: not even worth £1 this game. I actually got a profit of 2p from this game because of a sale and trading cards but if i bought it now, not worth a penny.

An insanely huge 50GB download, and a severe disappointment.   This is *NOT* a Final Fantasy game.   It's a collection of long, non-interactive cut scenes interspersed with wave after wave of repetitive FF style phased combat.
They've cut out everything that made the classic Square games classic.  All character development is handled through the cutscenes.  There's absolutely no exploration anymore.   You just view the superlong, boring cutscene (or you skip it) and then proceed to wave after wave of fights, at the end of which is yet another cutscene.
You don't actually get to meet any characters or interact with them.  You don't get to explore your base.   You don't get to talk to any of your team NPCs.    I'd say this is Final Fantasy Lite, but there's nothing lightweight about this when it requires a 50GB download, and a promised "update" coming this december.   If Steam and square stick to form, that "update" will probably require yet another 20GB or so download for a few lousy graphical enhancements.
I thought it might be worth buying at 17.99, but if I'd known, I'd have saved my money.    It's not worth the money.   It's definitely not worth tying up your connection to download.

All in all, C:BE is a disappointing and soulless entry in the Civilization franchise.
To start with, let's talk about what they did right; the game is visually stunning (for a strategy game, that is).  The gameplay is basically the same as Civ V as well (which is not a bad thing all things considered), and the mechanics they have added - with one very important exception - are positive.
Now, for the bad.  That one exception I mentioned? That would be the affinity system...arguably, the single most important change in this game over all the other Civ games.  As it stands now, shortly after release, the affinities are not well-balanced at all, and tends to lead to players choosing the one affinity to win outright to the exclusion of the others.  Also, the AI factions have preferences for which affinities they will concentrate on, meaning that certain factions are basically doomed from the start.  The affinity system brings another problem with it; the lack of unit differentiation.  Everyone has the same basic units at the start, but as your faction evolves, so do your units.  This isn't a bad thing, but by the end of the game you've been fighting like versus like continuously, wishing for some faction-based flavour.  It would stand to reason that a Supremacy PAC might have a slightly different armor unit to a Supremacy Franco-Iberia, but sadly that isn't the case.
This brings me to my next point; there is no flavour from one faction to the other.  Obviously in previous Civ games, where we look back on history and can find any number of things to differentiate one faction from another, looking to the future isn't so easy.  That said, the developers had a blank canvas to work with, and chose to put nothing on it, stating that it was up to the players to make their faction in the manner they choose.  An admirable goal, to say the least, but it just doesn't work in practice, as there just isn't enough differentiation between factions of similar affinities.  On that note, in the lead-up to release, the developer released all kinds of backstory to the game, outlining who the leaders are, what their beliefs are, what the history of Earth was like in the lead-up to the game - it was a very rich story (or at least it had the makings of one), and absolutely none of it appeared in the game.  Because this is a Civ game in space, it will inevitably draw comparisions to Alpha Centauri, whether the developer wants it or not.  What AC did so well, and what continues to make it such an exceptional title to this day, is that all of this backstory was in the game, and it told a rich (if depressing and dystopian) story as you played through to the conclusion.  Each faction had a very different emphasis, and each was both good and bad in its own right.  The lack of lore and backstory just makes this game feel like a soulless mod for Civ V, sadly.
Speaking of conclusions, the victory conditions of C:BE could use a lot of work.  First of all, several of the victories feel more like busy work than anything else; my first game, I played through to an Emancipation victory, where you send soldiers back to Earth through a gateway to "emancipate" them (presumably, emancipating them from their boring, weak, all-natural bodies).  This sounds good in practice until you realise you'll be sending a minimum of 20 units through the gate, which can only send one unit per turn.  So, 20 turns of basically waiting as you send one unit at a time through this thing...great.  I understand that there have been other "make-work" type victories in other Civ games *cough*spaceship*cough* before, but this is a whole new level of tedious.

A boring reskin of Civ5.
I quit when I suddenly realized I was making myself to make that one more turn. Nothing new was going to happen anyway.
In 30 minutes I lost that feeling, I was doing something meaningful; I was simply gathering resource to gather more resource to build that victory condition. Hard to say exactly why, but in CivV I constantly feel like I am choosing a way for my people to develop. Here, I dig res.
Things I did not like:
- Resources are a copy paste from CivV with different names. Not bad in itself, but not good either.
- Civilizations are all the same. Bonuses differ, but leaders do not feel unique. Just random talking heads saying all the same. No feeling "that civ has a background" like in CivV.
- Civilizations do not do anything interesting. The only things I got from them was "stop killing these aliens" and "give me something, and I will be grateful to you for that". Was fun the first time I received these, but then they just kept spamming same messages repeatedly. They never tried to push me in any manner.
- Units are all the same. They start to differ when you develop an affinity, but still, they feel all the same. Just units, able to deal damage. I did not feel the need to think like 'ok, i will place an archer behind that militia so that if the barb moves that way, he would be blocked and if that way, he will be stuck in mountains'. Just push with whatever...
- Units have no tactical promotions. They just increase in strength (the only promotion is +10% str). In CivV I had to think whether I want strength bonus to deal with barbs, or ranged def to attack a civ soon.
- Units get upgraded to next tech tier at once. No need to plan your finance to be able to upgrade the army for upcoming war. Just research the tech.
- Tech web is confusing. It is probably not bad, but confusing. The development variants are quite numerous (which is good!), but unless you studied and memorized the whole tech web, a good decision cannot be made. Each time I opened the web I pondered for several minutes, thinking what I would get from a tech, and which techs I will access after that. I do not want to spend time studying game mech, I want to feel I can make a valid, if not optimal, game decision on spot.
- Wonders are stuff you build to get resource bonuses. No wonder picture, just some blueprint. No short and clear description what that thing actually is. No feeling you build something unique. Just another resource factory.
- Caravans now originate from each city and have to be assigned manually. You also have to remember if you have max number of them in every city. Tedious.
- It is probably just me, but I did not like the landscape colors. Overall, the land is bleak and inexpressive. Again, I liked it first, but it became a boring view soon.
- (Fun part) In intro, a priest is crossing the Russian vessel before launch. I know they really do it (sadly) nowadays, but flying on holy spirit is a slap in the face of science. Disliked it.
Things I liked:
- Affinity system idea. Not how it was done.
- Aliens. Piu-piu.
- Space theme. Unit models look good.
Definitely not worth the money, probably not worth to play at all. Might get better with DLCs, but unless they get REALLY positive reviews, it is hard to believe BE will ever surpass CivV.

Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag is an action-adventure stealth game with open world environment from Ubisoft. It is the next installment in Assassin's Creed series and a prequel to Assassin's Creed III in terms of storyline.
Desmond Miles is dead, but his legacy continues. An unknown Abstergo Entertainment employee is doing research on Desmond ancestors in the familiar machine called Animus based on Desmond samples where he dives into the history of the one of many fearless and notorious pirates, Edward Kenway.
Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag like Assassin's Creed III, get some gameplay change and improvements again. Most improvements are very good and makes the game more fun and entertaining. The story takes place before the event of Assassin's Creed III, you play as Edward Kenway, grandfather of Connor Kenway, and a father to Haytham Kenway. In some location in this game, like in the city of Havana, we can go back to the building climbing style of gameplay, while in most location where it's not a city, the tree climbing still present a lot. But the best thing this Assassin's Creed has to offer is sea battles, piracy. While not on mission or on the way to mission location, you can engage and loot Spanish or Her Majesty ships, fleets or convoy and loot them for money and resources. Ship-to-ship battles has been improved a lot in this game that most of the time you will forget the mission and do some piracy instead. Sometimes I wonder how a small Brig can take down 2 big Spanish Galleon without a scratch and live to tell the tale. But those moment are awesome. But that just only one of many new features in this game that you can try. There are other things you can do like hunting sharks, wales or any of those extinct fish, explore undersea shipwreck and gets eaten by sharks, attack and conquer Spanish and/or British coastal forts, or maybe you just want to play checkers here. Sadly the Assassin's Brotherhood feature has been taken out in this game and replaced with Kenway's Fleet new mini-game. But many of these features are great, and there is still more to see.
Graphics of Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, for me, I don't know, I don't see much difference with Assassin's Creed III, except the effect on the sea. Sea can be very unpredictable here, sometimes the waves are calm, sometimes you have to face a small tsunami or hurricane which will damage you beloved ship. Performance of Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag is good, I haven't encounter any bugs or glitch and the game runs smoothly.
In multiplayer, mictotransactions are back, I don't know why Ubisoft do that, but it's not like you have to buy them, so no harm done here.
Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, in my opinion, is the second best Assassin's Creed after Assassin's Creed II, ever. I recommend this.

Sim Players are passionate when it comes to driving, flying or even riding the vehicles that have either thrilled and amazed us during our childhood even still do today which is why we take time out to write great reviews .. so I’d just like to add something to that ……
It’s always a shame to read about the disappointments that a fellow Sim Player has experienced instead of reading about their delights as they have taken the controls of their favourite consist and proudly taken passengers or goods from their chosen station, port or yard and delivered them on time having faced realistic challenges of schedules, other transport or sometimes signal failures and adverse weather conditions - that inner sense of achievement (and self-pride) is all we really seek - Yes they may be after all only simulations of real modes of transport –BUT…. be it an incredible landing of a fully laden 300 ton Boeing 747-400 on a real time flight from Singapore to Heathrow - Microsoft Flight Simulator perhaps -  where you take care of the Jumbo's flight deck and using the array of true to life switches, levers and dials as you descend gently down to terra firma – EGLL runway 21 to be exact to the [imagined] sounds of cheers and applause of your satisfied passengers and crew. Or that inner voice that says 'yees!' when we finally arrive at the depot and park up our Flexi-Bus for the day OMSI 2– its late, the sun has set, both outside our windows (if we care to look!) and within the Sim… but we don’t care.. We’ve driven with diligence and skill, we’ve hit n hurt no one and managed to pick up and drop off everyone without a hitch… that’s what matters.. That’s why we play these Simulators –
That’s what Sims do for us! - They fulfil our innermost desire to be a part of something that we admire, to take control of the very vehicles that we venerate and are in awe of – Hours of our lives are spent recreating the paths taken by Road, Rail, Air and Sea in order that we may share the experience in some intangible way of that of the Driver, Pilot, Captain, Fireman, Soldier and Doctor? within us all – all this achieved speedily at the flick of a mouse button and without the arduous years of universities, specialist training and professional advice and preparation, we will not suffer any loss of limb if we make mistakes as we learn the art of take-off and landing, nor will we face litigation and inevitable imprisonment from the families of the loved ones that we lost at sea due to our lack of experience of sailing cruise ships, or even suffer from docked wages from South West Trains for continued late arrivals at London Victoria… Friends our desire and task is a simple one … to Simulate through our chosen modes … without the Wind, Rain, Ice, Snow or Insurance Costs ever affecting or view of our chosen destination -
To Dream the Impossible is what drives the human spirit – But to deny someone of that dream is to deny them of the very lust for life ….. So keep dreaming keep ‘Simming’ and whether it’s by Air, Sea or Land may your journeys be filled with fun, passion and excitement –
Sim on!  n Smile as you go!

As a first time Hitman player, I think this game is decent: not something fantastic but not god awful horrible either. The aspects I like the most about this game are the stunning graphics and the idea of the community-based Contracts mode, though they should've allowed modding. Some things in this game that really rubbed me the wrong way are the check point system, the disguise system, and the overwhelming linearity of 99% of the levels. My biggest annoyance was that the game didn't include a Half Life-like player-initiated save system because this would allow you to experiment with the game (for example, assassinating a target) without having to go back and redo all the progress you made. While there are branching paths to take, they're pretty short and they usually all lead to the same place. The linearity severly restricts player improvisation, and when restarting checkpoints, it's very frustrating to pretty much have to do the same things all over again (which of course also discourages player experimentation because you don't want to redo what you did for the last 20 minutes if♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan). A few of the levels like the King of Chinatown one and the Layla assassination mission had a nice balance between linearity and open worldness.
I give this game a 7/10.

ภาพจัดว่าโอเคลื่นสบายตา เล่นแสงและเงาได้ดี เท่าที่เล่นมายังไม่เจอบัคเกี่ยวกับภาพเลย กด ESC เพื่อวางแผนไม่ได้ (มันจะเบลอแบ็คกราว ทำให้เราวางแผนล่วงหน้าไม่ได้ว่าควรจะทำอะไรก่อน - หลัง)
Gameplay จัดว่าโอเคเป็นแนว Survival ที่ฉีกออกมาจาก Survival ที่ล้นตลาดอยู่ทุกวันนี้ (ถ้าจะนึกภาพให้ออกคือ Survival แบบ DayZ แต่อยู่ในเหตุการณ์แบบ Metro) ตัวละครเราจะต้องเผชิญหน้ากับมนุษย์ด้วยกัน ซึ่งมีทั้งคนดีและคนไม่ดี การกระทำของเราจะส่งผลโดยตรงต่อตัวละครอีกด้วย อย่างเช่น ถ้าเราวิ่งไปหยิบของจากตู้เย็น บ้านของคนชราโดยที่เขาไม่อนุญาติก็จะทำให้ตัวละครเรารู้สึกผิด

This War of Mine is an excellent example of a game whose plot had never crossed my mind before, but I never knew how much I wanted it.
The game throws you into a war ruined world, with 1-3 randomized survivors. Your job is to get them to survive. In some ways, this is easier said than done. All survivors have certain skills, like being a good cook or being able to run quickly. Some survivors have addictions, like tobacco and caffeine. You have to use these along with general scavenging and smartness in order to survive.
The graphical style is very unique and very pretty. It's presented in 2D with a charcoal/pencil sketch style. You're able to zoom in and out on the landscape and your characters, which allows you to see the additional detail put into them. The character portraits, or "faces" are all of real people. The 3D models resemble the portraits, and they also added tiny details like blinking when selected.
Sound is very immersive, and can make certain situations very tense. You'll hear gunshots in the distance, or someone pounding on a door, among other things. The music is very fitting for the environments, and I found myself really enjoying the tunes.
Controls are simple, mostly done with the mouse. Click to select characters, and click where you'd like them to go, similar to a point and click adventure or something like The Sims. Option menu has a good amount editable, covering basics like sound volume and AA to changing if you'd like the pencil graphics to be more sharp or soft. Interface is also nicely designed and easy to navigate.
Overall, it's refreshing to see a survival game that doesn't have to do with zombies, and a war game that doesn't have to do with soldiers. This War of Mine is an excellent experience, and stacks up well to many more extensively priced and AAA games. It is definitely worth your $20.

My HQ and my team were falling apart.  We were sick, hungry and weak.  Night came and it was time to head out and scavenge.  I picked "Quiet Home" due to its lack of danger and apparent surplus of supplies.  Up until now, no notification of danger meant only rats and hungry (but kind) strangers were present.
After arriving, I picked up a few things in the front yard and then after entering I see an elderly couple talking.  The woman is distracted and annoyed, the husband is supportive and strong.  Her mind has been corrupted by Alzheimer's and he has made it his final aim to provide safety and shelter for her.
I walked around the house while he nervously asked if i was a bandit.  I didn't answer him.  He got more worried after each item I would pick up or opening his refrigerator.  While I didn't threaten him directly, he soon became paranoid for the safety of his wife and yelled out "HIDE! HIDE!".  She ran upstairs while he went downstairs to the basement. I found him huddled and sobbing.  I brought my shovel down on him, he cried out for help and ran to a locked door.  I finished him there.
The mentally disadvantaged wife eventually shuffled through the same room and upon finding his body she kneeled next his corpse and began crying softly.  Her mind was gone but not to the point where she couldn't make perfect sense of the situation.
I stood behind her, aware that I had forced her to live the rest of her confused life alone.  I did the unthinkable and brought the head of my shovel down on her neck and she died violently, curled up next to the corpse of her husband.
LOOTED HER BODY AND FOUND TWO DIAMONDS.  TEAM CAN SURVIVE FOR AT LEAST A COUPLE MORE DAYS.  WORTH IT. 9.8/10.

I only played this game for only two hours and I love it already! This game puts a totally differant spin on the survival genre. (Forgive my spelling if i make a mistake.) Let me just start off by saying why I like this game. For starters is the art style. Its unique and breath taking at first glance. The shadowing, the colors of the clothes they wear, every detail that went into this went to good use. Another reason i like this is because it is the first game (at least that ive played) that has you actually survive in a war zone without the use of zombies, creatures, etc. This game has just humans and raiders which to me is interesting. The survival of the game is just that, surviving. You go out to differant locations that some are abandoned, some are not, and scavange, trade or fight for supplies such as bandages, food and other things to help your group. Characters are given a background so you can read on what they are and even what they think of other characters and current events. The game also doesnt just give you a weapon and say "Heres a shotgun, go shoot people." You have to work for your weapons, go craft them with supplies you gathered, find them in buildings you scavange or loot them off people you killed. The building you live in isnt always safe and you have that risk of being raided yourself and you need to keep your group armed and supplied to fight off unwanted guests. There is also tradeing in the game where a man comes to your house and can give you things in exchange for supplies you have. When you do something bad it impacts your characters. Example: I went out to go scavange for supplies like food, water and meds when i went to a house. In the house there was a couple, an old man and woman. When i walked in the man (obviously) didnt take to kindly to me entering their house so they kept an eye on me. I did something wrong and they bassically hid from me. When i returned home after stealing from them my character just said "Heres the bandages. Dont ask how i got them." And was sad. Another person in the group was also sad due to the action the man did. Choices matter in this game, good and bad. Crafting is a good use in either crafting tools to help move rubble, bust open doors or make weapons such as a knife. The combat system is very simplistic but not ground breaking. Press on a character and hope it hits? Ive only done combat a couple times so i cant complain on it. The only couple of bad things is interaction with NPCs  and the combat. You can interact with only certain NPCs, the only ive been able to is whoever knocks on my door at the house. Everyone else just says "I have my eye on you" or "Dont cause any trouble." I just wish there was a little more interaction like with the couple i robbed. The combat is very simplistic to me. I at one point had to fight a man who had a knife and i had a crowbar, there was just a reticule on the man so i just kept clicking that. Sometimes i would hit, then he would hit so I guess what im saying is to me its just very simplistic and basic. All in all though this game is DEFINATLY worth picking up if you like survival genre. I would give this game a 8.5/10 and i would recommend this game most definatly.

I'm going to write a review about how Final Fantasy XIII, but keep in mind I will ignore the well known performance issues because they will be fixed by December and it's not worth rating down a game entirely just because of its performance problems.
Let me say first of all that I've been excited about its release on PC for a very long time and I couldn't be happier when I released it's on Steam finally.The performance problems didn't make the game less enjoyable for me because I've seen worse type of problems but I'm sure it made many other people used to constant 60 fps.
Anyway to start,the graphics are amazing for its requirements,the game itself as everyone knows is locked in 1280x720 resolution but  a modder created a tool called Gedosado which scales the game to up to 1080p or even 4k, even though the tool needs some work it's enough to make the game playable in high resolution until Square Enix patches the game.
You'll get carried away in the game's story:the entire time that I've played the game it felt like I was in a movie (firstly because the cutscenes added up are around 8 hours),so that idea made it exciting,what will happen next? The story has a little bit of everything in it:action,drama,romance,comedy,mystery and as you progress through the game the story deepens and you'll find yourself caught up in it,you'll want to know more about each character and how they can change their fate.
The soundtrack isn't less amazing than the rest,perfectly orchestrated you will fight each battle with more eagerness and you will sometimes want to enter a fight (even though not necessary) just to listen to the music again.
The characters themselves have a very unique personality and as the story progress they become better people,learning from their past mistakes,it's hard to pick a favorite because in the end you'll like something about each of them but it's them as a team that you'll love the most.Although you might find Vanille a bit stressful sometimes when she has too much optimism but who wouldn't want to be like her in daily life too?
The most important aspect is the gameplay and it's what gives the game its name,it's identity.You could say the game is a real time turn based rpg.It will feel too easy at the beginning of the game and you'll feel like the game is for the novice gamers.Not at all,the beginning of the game just prepares you for the harder parts later in the game which I might say are almost impossible even on the easy difficulty.
The bad thing about the gameplay is that it's linear,even though the environment is big,it's not an open world game but it almost feels like it.Things are pretty straight forward from the beginning to the end of the game but it doesn't make the game less fun if you consider all the other good things about it.From my point of view it's worth buying and it's not even too expensive.Do not let the entirely negative reviews about it stop you from playing it .The problems will be solved as I said above and even with the current issues the game is still playable.Hope this review helped,enjoy the game if you intend to buy it!

This game is a bit weird. It's cheap, no doubt about it: the voice acting is relatively trashy and the dialogue is cheesy, it all feels like it belongs in an 80s action movie. The atmosphere feels like it was lifted from 1999's Medal of Honour: Allied Assault and put onto a new engine with actual physics. The story pacing is a bit weird, with plot points either ganging up on you so that you don't know what actually happened until the post-level slides that explain it, or they leave you hanging for eon-long levels where nothing meaningful seems to happen.
But, it used this premise before it was cool, it used this setting before it was mainstream. You could almost say its a hipster version of ww1 shooters. My only gripe is the accuracy of the rifle you use for a large part of the game. Its better to compare its accuracy to that of a pistol than that of a rifle, but barring that the combat is engaging enough. You might be tricked into thinking this is a game where ranged combat is king - its not. Melee is where its at, the entire fury/health/adrenalin mechanism feeds into this in the same way that the new DOOM's glory kills do, seriously, the bayonet is more useful than the gun attached to it, and later when you're running around in subterrainian cathedrals this point is emphasised even more.
Ultimately I would summarise this game as a cheap Dark Messiah of Might and Magic set in WW1 with MOHAA graphics. I'd reccomend anyone looking to kill some boredom.

This is, by far, the best Final Fantasy in the franchise; if not, it is certainly the most modern of them.
Every time I sit down and play Final Fantasy XIII again, I find it to be even more thrilling than I remembered.  It's hard to get all the negative reviews and fanboy hatred for this title out of your head when you look at the game; until you play it.  Then the stunningly detailed visuals, the most coherent story in any FF game to date, and the deep many-layered characters pull you into an immersive world; two worlds, to be exact.
Alright, that's the short and sweet bit up top; that's the synopsis.  Below will be a page-long point-by-point rebuttal of the common view of this game; so that you folks who are trying to gauge if you want to spend your hard-earned money on this can get both sides of the story.
So, to begin; all the criticism and hatred a lot of people have for this game is, in my mind, just them being nostsalgic and whining (fanboy syndrome).   What people hate about this game, I love.  What they say breaks the game, I say is the innovation that Square promised would revolutionize the JRPG genre.
Let's start this list!
1) Linearity:  This is the number one complaint you hear about Final Fantasy XIII, "It is too linear."  Compared to what?  Fallout and Elder Scrolls?  It is, in my humble opinion, exactly as linear as any traditional JRPG usually is.  It's just waaaay more in-your-face about it.  The story AND the paths are one-directional.  Spoiler: You're on the run from folks.   The story is driven as though it were a tightly bound book.  Each page you turn is filled with exactly what you want and need to continue through that leg of the story; not with a bunch of ancillary baggage and side-quests that make the real story feel like some fading memory.
2) Story:  This is the second complaint I tend to hear; people say that either the game is too story-driven, or that it didn't even attempt to have a coherent story.   This section will contain mild spoilers.  I will use broad generalizations, no names, just themes spoken of in broadstrokes:
You start off in the middle of a holocaust (big props, Square); you're being sent to die for fear of contamination from an alien, hostile world.  You escape your bonds, you help stop the holocaust, odds are stacked against you, you run through hugely cinematic warzones, better than anything Square has ever done before.  Compelling from minute one.   The story then unfolds that there are two worlds, and they are at war with one another.  Your world (Cocoon), is made to seem like the haven of all humanity and the perfect paradise, but you learn it is darker than you thought.  There are these magical inter-dimensional type demi-gods (Cocoon Fal'Cie), they built your world, and they fight against the world below (Pulse) and its demi-gods (Pulse Fal'Cie).
Compare this to my favorite Final Fantasy, FFVIII, and tell me that the story is less coherent.  FFVIII's story sports some child soldiers brainwashed in a floating terrorist/mercenary training facility in the sky!  They all grew up as kids in an orphanage, but not one of them remembers this because of mental heatlh damage resulting from military hardware they're required to use as...child soldiers.   You race through many nations and warzones to find that powerful Sorceresses control the face of world politics.  Then you find, in fact, it has always been one Sorceress, who can bend time and possess people.  Then she, in fact, kompresses all time-space into a kind of purpl'ish goo that you have to navigate through to reach the end-game.  Honestly, and I love FFVIII, but that story is ridiculous.  It would be hard-pressed to survive in novel form.  FFXIII, however, could easily make a novel.
3) Voice Acting/Character Design:  People appear to hate Vanille, Snow, Hope, Lightning, and maybe Sazh and Fang too. Vanille is an upbeat young woman that sounds a bit 'slow' at first, yes, but I think they invented a fictitious accent (Pulsian) for her to use; which startles us Earthicans at first.  Snow is the archetypical hero; this isn't new.  Every Square game has a Snow.  Remember Zell?  Snow is way less annoying than Zell.  Imagine if Zell were voice-acted.  Now imagine Zell said the things Zell said in FFVIII, in a wheezy, energetic, high-pitched voice. I'd have let Zell die repeatedly.  Snow has a good voice-actor, it's just his lines are sometimes cheesy.  He's a self-proclaimed hero that's crushed by the guilt of his own failures.  Of course he's blustering.   Lightning, they claim, is one-dimensional.  People who say this didn't play the game, or don't understand the idea of character development.  She starts cold, she learns to trust.  The characters are well thought-out, look beautiful, and have remarkably well done, grade-A professional voice-acting.  For those that disagree, go back and play FFX and listen to Titus' grainy whining voice (that sounds like he's narrating from in a bathroom), then tell me FFXIII did a worse job.   People complain that Lightning is a trophy female protagonist with no personality.  She's essentially a better, female Squall, in my opinion.  They both can't trust, they both have deep pains from personal loss and people they failed to protect.  They're both strong and silent.  They both use gunblades; but Lightning's is ten times as awesome; exactly like Squall, but ten times as awesome.  That about sums her up.
4) Music:  The best, period.  8 and 16-bit scores do not compare to this symphonic magnificence.  The music fits the setting, the mood, and it flows.  The battle theme is light years beyond anything Square has EVER done.  Thank god I don't need to listen to jarring synthesizer techno while I save the world anymore.  Square has always excelled at making original, moving soundtracks; this is by far their best.
5) Visuals: Like a slice of an LSD-induced dream that was rendered into a game by Pixar.
6) Terminology:  So, I've read reviews of people ragging on this game for all it's jargon, "What's a Gran Pulse? A Fal'what? Gestalt? Is that a german seasoning?"  There's like, seriously, ten words or something you will need to learn.   Gran Pulse and Cocoon are worlds, the only two worlds in the game, so it's not like they're a galactic compendium of planets you have to remember.  Fal'Cie are the demi-gods, a human bound by a Fal'Cie's magic to serve them is called a l'Cie, a human that fails to complete his focus given to him by the Fal'Cie becomes a C'ieth (like a zombie).  That's about it, really.  The rest is just come-and-go.  Gestalt is just a meter you fill when you beat up the summons you're trying to acquire.  It's really a trite complaint.  Every RPG has it's own jargon, let alone FF games.  GF's, materia, mako energies, Ivalice, Shinra, etc.  FF is renowned for it's own jargon.  Jargon, in this context, just means unique story concepts.  Unique story concepts generally mean more attention to detail, more depth of story, and more immersion in the end.
7) The Battle System:  People either hate it or they love it.  I think it's, by far, the best battle system in any FF game other than XII.  The people that complain it's too simple are playing on easy mode.  I die routinely, and I am a twenty year veteran of RPG's.  Once you reach Pulse, there are regular mobs that are like mini-bosses, and there are daunting challenges all around you.  It's a new system, but not at all shallow. The infamous 'auto-battle' is a feature you can choose to never use with one menu option.
All in all, the fanboys' critique seems to be irrational, raging nostalgia lashing out with venomous spite at a masterpiece that failed to reach their dreams' fondest hopes.  In other words, they got let down and took it out on Square.   This game is easily 9/10.  The port has no graphics options, beware.  It runs fine on my PC, though.  Square will patch the game in December to fix this.

Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag is an action-adventure stealth game with open world environment from Ubisoft. It is the next installment in Assassin's Creed series and a prequel to Assassin's Creed III in terms of storyline.
Desmond Miles is dead, but his legacy continues. An unknown Abstergo Entertainment employee is doing research on Desmond ancestors in the familiar machine called Animus based on Desmond samples where he dives into the history of the one of many fearless and notorious pirates, Edward Kenway.
Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag like Assassin's Creed III, get some gameplay change and improvements again. Most improvements are very good and makes the game more fun and entertaining. The story takes place before the event of Assassin's Creed III, you play as Edward Kenway, grandfather of Connor Kenway, and a father to Haytham Kenway. In some location in this game, like in the city of Havana, we can go back to the building climbing style of gameplay, while in most location where it's not a city, the tree climbing still present a lot. But the best thing this Assassin's Creed has to offer is sea battles, piracy. While not on mission or on the way to mission location, you can engage and loot Spanish or Her Majesty ships, fleets or convoy and loot them for money and resources. Ship-to-ship battles has been improved a lot in this game that most of the time you will forget the mission and do some piracy instead. Sometimes I wonder how a small Brig can take down 2 big Spanish Galleon without a scratch and live to tell the tale. But those moment are awesome. But that just only one of many new features in this game that you can try. There are other things you can do like hunting sharks, wales or any of those extinct fish, explore undersea shipwreck and gets eaten by sharks, attack and conquer Spanish and/or British coastal forts, or maybe you just want to play checkers here. Sadly the Assassin's Brotherhood feature has been taken out in this game and replaced with Kenway's Fleet new mini-game. But many of these features are great, and there is still more to see.
Graphics of Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, for me, I don't know, I don't see much difference with Assassin's Creed III, except the effect on the sea. Sea can be very unpredictable here, sometimes the waves are calm, sometimes you have to face a small tsunami or hurricane which will damage you beloved ship. Performance of Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag is good, I haven't encounter any bugs or glitch and the game runs smoothly.
In multiplayer, mictotransactions are back, I don't know why Ubisoft do that, but it's not like you have to buy them, so no harm done here.
Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, in my opinion, is the second best Assassin's Creed after Assassin's Creed II, ever. I recommend this.

There were parts of the game I loved, and found memorable -- but there were almost as many moments when I found myself cursing the game for its flaws, and wishing I'd never bought the thing.
My overall impression of Hitman: Absolution is that I was always wrestling with the dang thing -- not all the game aspects work well, and at times I felt like I was really struggling to find the fun.
Should you buy it? I'd say don't bother, unless you're willing to put up with the bad alongside the good.
And whatever you do, don't pay full price for the game!
My opinions, anyway,

Getting playable FPS
The user ScottiePrimo from the GoG forums found a fix regarding the low FPS.
1) Download the following...

1.1) Unrar the downloaded file (DSWin8.zip) and you should have two files in the extracted folder (ddraw.dll and aqrit.cfg).
1.2) Place these two files into your "Steam\SteamApps\Common\Robin Hood" directory (in with the game.exe).
2) Download V2_02_90_build.rar of DxWnd from...

(I've been advised by other users that the newer versions don't work for the purpose of running this game.)
3) Unrar and inside the extracted foler and run "dxwnd.exe" as administrator. Go to "Edit->Add", in parameter "Name" set the name as Robin Hood.
4) In parameter "Path" choose the .exe file of the game (in my case it looks like Steam\SteamApps\common\Robin Hood\game.exe).
5) In the "Main" tab, under "Generic" untick "Run in Window".
5.1) Also in "Main" tab, under "Position" set "Window initial position & size" to X=0 and Y=0. Set "W" and "H" to your native resolution (in my case that's W=1920 and H=1080).
6) In the "Video" tab, under "Windows handling" tick "Modal Style" and under "Color management" tick "Set 16BPP RGB565 encoding".
7) Next in "Input" tab tick "Hide Cursor". If the cursor flickers on the main screen of the game don't worry, it works fine in-game.
8) Lastly click "OK" in dxwnd, if all is good it will show a green circle before the name of the game in DxWnd. Launch the game in Steam (Not in DxWnd itself, DxWnd runs in the backround!). You may get an error/alert that says something like "SetHook: proc=GetAvailableVidMem(D) oldhook=26b3e0". If this happens just press the Return key on your keyboard. If you can't select the error/alert window use Alt+Tab keys to cycle through the open windows. This part is just a bit of a trial and error, I don't know why it happens but you can get past it.
9) You will need to start DxWnd every time before you launch the game. When you close dxwnd, answer "Yes" to save the options that you changed. That's it...
I hope these fixes work for you aswell and if they do then have fun playing! :)

With the proliferation of technologies such as computers, smartphones and the internet, it is easier to see and more apparent than ever that the world around us is constantly changing. And not always for the better. With militants ravaging the Middle East, rebels vying for control of Eastern Ukraine, and the conflict between Israel and Palestine still raging on, its difficult not to feel like things are sliding towards a tipping point, a new global conflict even. Games depict wars, real and fantasy, all the time, and, if the likes of Call of Duty and Battlefield are anything to go by, those kinds of experiences are very popular. But we don’t often find ourselves connecting or giving a second thought for the civilians caught in the crossfire, trying desperately to survive. This War of Mine turns things on its head, you aren’t a soldier, kitted out in the latest combat gear, you are average citizens trapped amongst the fighting, doing whatever is necessary to survive. It’s brutal, thought-provoking, and yet another sign that games have matured as an art medium.
This War of Mine doesn’t simply tell the tale of a lone survivor, caught in a war zone, instead you’ll have dominion over three randomly selected characters (initially) and guide them through each day, trying your best to keep them fed, healthy and as happy as they possibly can be. Luckily, they’ll have the relative safety of a small dilapidated house to take shelter in.  It’s not much but it’s a good starting point. By scavenging inside, or at other locations, you can collect materials to fix up the house to make life more comfortable for the inhabitants, and you can build beds, stoves, radios and workshops. These little extras help to keep morale up and depression at bay. Materials don’t come cheap in the middle of a war zone, though, and somebody is going to have to pay a price for them – be it in coin, or in blood.
Running low on food and medicine is not an option if everyone is going to make it to the other side of the war intact. The brutal lengths that you may have to go to are uncensored and unglorified, and while murdering an elderly couple for their food and jewellery may initially shock, it becomes second nature after a while. And that’s the grizzly reality of war: sometimes, you must be absolutely ruthless to survive.
These realisations can deeply affect your survivors, and they may become deeply troubled by the events going on around them. Each has their own mood indicators highlighting whether they are hungry, tired or depressed, and their effects are almost immediately apparent. Characters who have fallen into depression will drag their almost lifeless bodies around the squat ruminating over the events that have happened, asking themselves ‘why?’. Other characters may take note of this and try to help by talking with them. Each character also keeps a diary with details of the events from days gone by; depending on the situation you may see your characters attitudes change before your eyes. Characters whom have murdered others may initially regret their decision, only to accept it later as an inevitability, required in order to stay alive. This War of Mine may sound emotionally draining to play, and it is; 11 Bit Studios have struck a delicate balance and created a title that is as entertaining to play as it is emotionally compelling
Each day is split into two sections which see your survivors fixing up the house to make it more comfortable during the day, and going out scavenging at night. Some aspects of the game have a “The Sims” feel to them, with you having to tend to everyone’s needs such as feeding them, keeping them comfortable and dispensing medication if they are sick. Scavenging at night can be very dangerous, especially if you intend to come home with anything useful, so it is wise to stay armed. A nifty crafting interface allows you to create all manner of different items such as lockpicks, axes, shovels and hack saws, which can be used to reach particularly valuable loot. Each scavenging location requires careful consideration before you set off though, and you’ll pay the price if you go out without the proper equipment. It is very easy to lose characters to militants or, other, better-armed survivors.
Sometimes, while out scavenging, you’ll encounter other violent and non-violent NPCs, and whether you engage them or no is up to you. Combat isn’t particularly in-depth but it doesn’t need to be. You can switch from scavenging mode to armed at the click of the mouse, but your adversary may become aware and attack you. Simply clicking on an enemy is enough to send you stabbing/punching/shooting in their direction. The impact doesn’t come from the combat itself, rather the effect it can have on your character – and you. As aforementioned, whilst out scavenging at an old cottage we found a friendly old couple, relaxing in their armchairs. Sadly, their number was up before we even caught sight of them; our fridge was empty, we had no valuables or medicine. Luring the old man down to the basement, we began beating him mercilessly with a shovel. “Don’t leave me!” cried his wife, as we set about her. We couldn’t help but pause for thought – would we do the same in a similar situation?
This War of Mine isn’t a delight to look at, but its aesthetic is expertly crafted. The city is awash in dark blacks and greys which inspire a feeling of desolation and despair. unfortunately we were subject to a number of graphical glitches and stuttering issues, which should be patched out post-launch.
As a game, This War of Mine is sensational, as a story it is gripping, but it is as a statement that it makes its biggest impact. Whilst most of us (hopefully) will never know what it is like to live in a war zone, it’s important to know that there are people, like us, out there surviving in horrific situations. It is an unforgettable survival horror game, but not as you know it. 11 Bit’s presentation of war is candid, undiluted and bound to leave a lasting impression.

Commentary?! Sold!
Or rather, it was free. I imagine paying for a remastered version of an older game--repackaged with the same bugs wholecloth--might put off some buyers. I played Bioshock originally on consoles, and never picked up the Steam version I purchased. So a free upgrade is a great excuse to get back into it. Make no mistake, this is still one of the better-crafted gaming experiences you can find.
For that reason I recommend it: If you've played it before, if you know what you're in for, if you know Bioshock, you want this (and will get it for free, I believe?) And the developer commentary is worth it, although it, too, assumes you've played the game. If you haven't ever touched Bioshock before, you're getting what you'd get anyway, just prettier and with some achievements (and bugs.) But now, developer commentary, a lovely museum, lots of fun new things that really makes it worth it, I think.
Caveats: controller support make the wonky controls easier to handle. Also ran fine on my 1920x1080 display, so can't speak to anything beyond that.

Picked this up thinking it would be a fun time-waster. I wasn't expecting a first person game to have effective sword combat, as most of them seem to get repetitive. However, Shadow Warrior impressed me beyond what I expected.
Story: 8/10
Kind of hard to follow at some points, but quite a unique and interesting storyline. The characters are all voiced excellently. Some of the jokes made me laugh out loud, though most seem kind of forced.
Gameplay: 9/10
The combat is where this game shines most. Carving up demons is oh so satisfying and the over the top blood effects only make it better. Oh, there are guns also, they have a couple of uses. I only give this a 9 because there is an annoying bug where if you dash down even a small flight of stairs, you can die and be sent back to the last checkpoint. Also, the boss fights are kind of the same strategy every time: dodge, shoot the glowy piece of armor until the glowy thing appears then shoot that.
Music: 5/10
Meh. Kind of repetitive.
Level Design: 7/10
The levels seem to drag on at points, and most of the game is a "Go here, kill a horde of enemies, look for the glowing door/switch, repeat" formula. However, the game does vary up the level themes quite nicely.
Overall: 8/10
A great game that is definitely worth picking up on sale. The gameplay was enough for me to want to keep playing it. The game is also a decent length (took me around 7-8 hours to play through).

Unless you got this for free if you own this and Bioshock 2 (With or Without The DLC) I reccommend waiting for a fix and an eventual price drop. It's not a terrible remaster but it is defintely a lazy one at that.

I gave this game a fair shot, but I absolutely have to say I hate it. Between technical issues, horrible sound design, and seriously dull gameplay have to make this one of the worst shooters I've played in years, possibly ever.
Starting with technical issues, you'll find plenty of bugs while playing and weird performance issues. One of the most annoying things at first was the game offers no vsync option, which I just forced in nvidia control panel anyways. However, whenever firing any full auto weapon or using the melee attack on the glove weapon you get later in the game, I experienced major stuttering and frame freezing. It would sometimes even just show one frame until I let up off the button I was using for the attack. This game uses the same engine the Painkiller games used, which while it is a good engine, it has some issues. One of these issues is EXTREMELY long loading times. Expect 2 minutes to load a chapter. A little less than one minute if you load a save in the same chapter.
Next is sound design. The voice acting is on par with Crash Time 2, just absolutely cringeworthy. The main character seems to have been voiced by two actors, which isn't the case, but it goes to show how inconsistent it is. Just wait until you come across Zimmerman midway into the game. On top of the horrific one liners your character blurts ou, expect some of the most obnoxious, dull soundtracks you've ever heard. You hear the same battle track for nearly the entire game up until you reach chapter 6.
And the worst thing of all, is simply the gameplay. The weapons feel weak and useless, the enemies are dull and uninteresting, and in many cases tanky as hell or even unkillable. Sometimes you need to just rush to the next segment by simply sprinting by the braindead enemies. This can also be easier if there are lots of enemies, since corpses actually have collision with you. So if you've got a big stack of bodies in the way of a small doorway, have fun. Weapon selection is clunky and plain confusing, with a poorly implemented dual wield system. On top of that there's two different melee buttons and a special attack button that is barely used. The controls are awfully overcomplicated.
The plot is also simply laughable. Upon completing a chapter, the chapter is basically recapped in a cutscene with a nearly entirely different story. Its jarring and leaves you wondering what is even going on. After defeating a boss later in the game, you walk out of the room to end the chapter. And then the cutscene shows something completely different.
The only positive thing I can say about this game is that the graphics are pretty good and the atmosphere is decent. Otherwise, I really can't say anything positive about it. I really wanted to like it, but I also kind of walked into it expecting it to be Painkiller. This is a terrible shooter, and I highly recommend you spend your time playing anything other than this. I gave this game a good shot, because some people say it gets better later on, but the farther I got, the more I got disappointed and ran into even more bugs.

First of all, I don't think that this game is complete trash. As a big Civ fan I enjoy it...for about the first 150 turns.
My biggest issue is the health system. Health is essentially the replacement of happiness just with one huge thing missing. There is no happiness from resources anymore. If your not a Civ 5 veteran you might not have such a big problem. As for me i'm use to ending games with 30+ population cities. In Beyond Earth, I have trouble getting 3 cites to double digits without going negative health.
The ways you are able to gain health are from a couple virtues(social policy), a couple quest decisions on increasing health on health buildings, and Biowells later on. The issues with this is that the virtues take so long to get that by the time you have the "luxury" of obtaining it. All the good city locations are taken by A.I.'s that are able to get 5 10+ cities to my astonishment on even low difficulties.
Now in Civ 5 we first got religion that gave us ways to boost happiness
Then we got Brave New World that gave us ideologies that had high boosts for happiness
Will we get things like this in expansions, 99% yes.
But Happiness by itself was useable to expand...Heath isn't.
So it's not because there is only 8 nations or basically 3 map types. I can't recommend this game because it just makes you miss Civ 5 than embrace Beyond Earth.

I've played a lot of a lot of different Civs and I don't expect Beyond Earth to be any different. It's fun, adds enough of a spin on things to keep it fresh, and is worth the price (or whatever it will be on sale). It is also not comparable to SMAC any more than Endless Legend or Pandora are. While all of these games try to have a bit of a narrative structure over the game, the lack of multiple voice actors, interludes, wonder videos/art, and customizable units make it much less of a space opera than SMAC.
Rather than going into deep details, I'm going to list the basics, my favorite part of the game, and my least favoirte part of the game. Outside of that, if you have played Civ 5, you'll know basically what to expect.
Best Part - the interaction between the Culture, Affinity, and Tech trees. The fact that much of your military might is dependant on your highest affinity number is interesting and has opened up a lot of strategy space on the tech web, rather than having to just rush each military unit upgrade to outpace others.
Worst Part - the book-keeping. Civilization has been an excellent game at having fewer city improvements that mean more. Improvements in Civ:BE are a game of inches rather than miles, and only late-game do the big scaling bonuses come into play. This result is, sadly, that you end up clicking a lot of buttons to get the same effect. It takes the same # of turns, just more clicks. This feels like false agency. Trade routes are the other issue: now that they're capped per-city it is impossible to get around assigning 2-3 per turn at minimum. Additionally, Trade bonuses are so crucial that even one missed route is a major issue, so these clicks can't be skipped without giving up a lot. Considering that it is obvious what the best choice is (depending on whether you want money or production), there is not a lot of gameplay there outside of denying people you are suspicious of of trade routes.
That said, the game is excellent, and will be even better after a bit more balance. The AI in particular could use some help.

I am sad to say, but I would pass on Beyond Earth as a title unless it happens to be on some super cheap steam sale.
There is a lot of new stuff to be seen in BE, including a few features that I would love to see in Civilization proper, such as Quests, Orbital, and a non linear progression. However, many of the bugs that were in the Civ 5 engine come along through space here too.
Early game is perhaps the best part of the game. You start off alone and weak, hoping to not anger the planet as you explore and get your feet wet. However the longer you play, the more you come to realize the blandness of the game. Quests are there, but they tend to only play a minor part of the game as a whole. You end up feeling you have a lot to do, but none of it really matters. The AI is some of the dumbest ive ever seen in a Civ game. They almost never directly confront you, and even if they decide to war against you, they wont do anything with it.
TL:DR Nice concept, but feels hollow and empty. It has the makings of greatness, but for now, it is just mediocre.

You start off with three people hiding out in a ruined building with a war raging around them, and you have them craft during the day and go scavenging at night.  To me it feels like you're the cast of The Walking Dead except instead of zombies it's a war that's got you scrambling to survive.  Very fun and compelling, it's definitely got that "one more turn" feel that great games have and couples it with some choices you won't make in other games like "these cigarettes I just rolled... do I let my group smoke them all or do I take them over to the bombed out hotel to trade them for rat meat?"    I can see how parts of it might get repetitive after a while, but most games do.  I'm finding it highly entertaining if a little bit depressing.  I definitely recommend it.
Edit/Addition 16 hours in:  I've been asked if it's fun. It's "fun" like Schindler's List was fun. Ok... not exactly like that but it's dark, it's depressing, and sometimes your game ends by having your last surviving character reach a point where she just can't take it any more and slits her wrists. Is that "fun?" I don't know. But it's making me think like few games ever have, and for me that's an amazing experience.

BiT Evolution tries so hard to have nuance and offer something unique that it is unfortunate that it falls flat on itself. Platformers have a plethora of genres they inhabit. BiT tries to emulate Atari-style platformers, then switches to gameboy, before attemping to jump to 16bit efforts that resumble Rocket Knight. The issue is that these gameplay styles offer little new to the player. The goal of each level is to finish it using a sort of neat death mechanic that allows you to keep playing from a dark-souls-like afterlife/dimension before you can return back to where you were. This other area in each level is harder to navigate, but why would I choose to go there if I can finish the level quicker in the initial area? There are also collectable orbs in every level, but they don't seem to do anything. Why should I collect them? The final sin that bothers me is that the game struggles to show me how to do new mechanics. It spends a lot of time telling me through dialogue and story sections. These try to add substance to the gameplay, but they are annoying and lack any real depth beyond references to games from that period of gaming. Platformers are about gameplay.
You can see that the developers really tried hard on this game and I think there is a great gem buried here, but they need to go back and look at what makes each game they try to emulate unique and learn why game series like Mario and Kirby are so wonderful.

With the proliferation of technologies such as computers, smartphones and the internet, it is easier to see and more apparent than ever that the world around us is constantly changing. And not always for the better. With militants ravaging the Middle East, rebels vying for control of Eastern Ukraine, and the conflict between Israel and Palestine still raging on, its difficult not to feel like things are sliding towards a tipping point, a new global conflict even. Games depict wars, real and fantasy, all the time, and, if the likes of Call of Duty and Battlefield are anything to go by, those kinds of experiences are very popular. But we don’t often find ourselves connecting or giving a second thought for the civilians caught in the crossfire, trying desperately to survive. This War of Mine turns things on its head, you aren’t a soldier, kitted out in the latest combat gear, you are average citizens trapped amongst the fighting, doing whatever is necessary to survive. It’s brutal, thought-provoking, and yet another sign that games have matured as an art medium.
This War of Mine doesn’t simply tell the tale of a lone survivor, caught in a war zone, instead you’ll have dominion over three randomly selected characters (initially) and guide them through each day, trying your best to keep them fed, healthy and as happy as they possibly can be. Luckily, they’ll have the relative safety of a small dilapidated house to take shelter in.  It’s not much but it’s a good starting point. By scavenging inside, or at other locations, you can collect materials to fix up the house to make life more comfortable for the inhabitants, and you can build beds, stoves, radios and workshops. These little extras help to keep morale up and depression at bay. Materials don’t come cheap in the middle of a war zone, though, and somebody is going to have to pay a price for them – be it in coin, or in blood.
Running low on food and medicine is not an option if everyone is going to make it to the other side of the war intact. The brutal lengths that you may have to go to are uncensored and unglorified, and while murdering an elderly couple for their food and jewellery may initially shock, it becomes second nature after a while. And that’s the grizzly reality of war: sometimes, you must be absolutely ruthless to survive.
These realisations can deeply affect your survivors, and they may become deeply troubled by the events going on around them. Each has their own mood indicators highlighting whether they are hungry, tired or depressed, and their effects are almost immediately apparent. Characters who have fallen into depression will drag their almost lifeless bodies around the squat ruminating over the events that have happened, asking themselves ‘why?’. Other characters may take note of this and try to help by talking with them. Each character also keeps a diary with details of the events from days gone by; depending on the situation you may see your characters attitudes change before your eyes. Characters whom have murdered others may initially regret their decision, only to accept it later as an inevitability, required in order to stay alive. This War of Mine may sound emotionally draining to play, and it is; 11 Bit Studios have struck a delicate balance and created a title that is as entertaining to play as it is emotionally compelling
Each day is split into two sections which see your survivors fixing up the house to make it more comfortable during the day, and going out scavenging at night. Some aspects of the game have a “The Sims” feel to them, with you having to tend to everyone’s needs such as feeding them, keeping them comfortable and dispensing medication if they are sick. Scavenging at night can be very dangerous, especially if you intend to come home with anything useful, so it is wise to stay armed. A nifty crafting interface allows you to create all manner of different items such as lockpicks, axes, shovels and hack saws, which can be used to reach particularly valuable loot. Each scavenging location requires careful consideration before you set off though, and you’ll pay the price if you go out without the proper equipment. It is very easy to lose characters to militants or, other, better-armed survivors.
Sometimes, while out scavenging, you’ll encounter other violent and non-violent NPCs, and whether you engage them or no is up to you. Combat isn’t particularly in-depth but it doesn’t need to be. You can switch from scavenging mode to armed at the click of the mouse, but your adversary may become aware and attack you. Simply clicking on an enemy is enough to send you stabbing/punching/shooting in their direction. The impact doesn’t come from the combat itself, rather the effect it can have on your character – and you. As aforementioned, whilst out scavenging at an old cottage we found a friendly old couple, relaxing in their armchairs. Sadly, their number was up before we even caught sight of them; our fridge was empty, we had no valuables or medicine. Luring the old man down to the basement, we began beating him mercilessly with a shovel. “Don’t leave me!” cried his wife, as we set about her. We couldn’t help but pause for thought – would we do the same in a similar situation?
This War of Mine isn’t a delight to look at, but its aesthetic is expertly crafted. The city is awash in dark blacks and greys which inspire a feeling of desolation and despair. unfortunately we were subject to a number of graphical glitches and stuttering issues, which should be patched out post-launch.
As a game, This War of Mine is sensational, as a story it is gripping, but it is as a statement that it makes its biggest impact. Whilst most of us (hopefully) will never know what it is like to live in a war zone, it’s important to know that there are people, like us, out there surviving in horrific situations. It is an unforgettable survival horror game, but not as you know it. 11 Bit’s presentation of war is candid, undiluted and bound to leave a lasting impression.

It's very possible the Game Boy/NES/SNES era levels are more exciting, but you have to play a

The game works, it functions just fine, so if you do not mind the monotonous
