I played this game on the PS3. I think I spent a little over 10 hours on it. I hated every minute.
Why? It was exactly what everyone said it was.
Flash forward to just a little awhile ago, and I just completed a play-through of the PC version. I, well, I liked the majority of it.
Why? It is exactly what everyone says it is.
Confused? Yeah so am I. Hmm..It sounded clever in my head. *shrug*
Apologies in advance. This review is going to echo nearly every other FF13 review out there. Everything you've heard is true, but not all of it is actually bad. In the end, everything is subjective. What doesn't work for you might work for others, vice versa, and all that good stuff.
The plot to FF13 is pretty dang convoluted. This is mostly due to the fact that you're dropped into the game with hardly an idea of what's going on. All these made-up words are being thrown at you, and everyone sounds like an obnoxious jerk. This is completely understandable, since Lightning and Snow are two of the first characters you meet. Basically the story goes like this: become a l'cie, get sweet powers, run down several corridors, punch the space pope in his stupid face, and try to figure out how not to become a cie'th (crystal zombie). Once you understand the basics you can switch your brain off and watch the pretty cut-scenes.
This game does take about 15 hours to reach its full potential. A good portion of the game is spent under some sort of limitation. Lightning and company split up more often than a Scooby Doo cartoon. This means two-person parties, and an overlong tutorial. This is the second-most draining part of the game, ESPECIALLY compared to prior Final Fantasy titles. I could be getting so much done if I was playing any other FF. I could play through FF1 twice, reach space in FF4, get involved in some major sidequest in FF7, and so on. The only FF title that compares in this regard is FF10. Even that game gave players a full-party before they left the first town (Zanarkand doesn't count because it's a city).
Despite this, FF13 is still very much a game. This is due to the huge emphasis on combat. It's a fantastic battle-system, probably one of the best of its kind. If anything, the limited freedom forces the player to learn how to actually fight, since grinding for level-ups is a non-factor for those 15 hours. This makes for tons of opportunities to learn the ins and outs. Everything from when to switch paradigms, which enemies to focus on, and cutting out all of the in-efficiency (spending too much time healing, not staggering enemies fast enough, etc). There's a lot that goes into each battle, even in the 2-15 hour time-frame. The boss battles are superb.
When you finally arrive at Gran Pulse, that's when the real game begins...eh. At first I was really excited to reach this portion of the game. I couldn't wait to explore a world and move in a direction besides forward. Honestly, while I appreciate what Square-enix was going for here, it could have been done better. The biggest annoyance is that there's just so much running around. The major side-quest involves cie'th stones. Find a cie'th stone, kill the monster it directs you to, and collect a reward of some sort. All this running around gets old, especially if you're not quite adept at dodging battles. Warp-points and Chocobos are available after enough progress is made, but I really could go for an arena or a list or something. However, if I could just choose what monsters I wanted to fight, wouldn't that make Gran Pulse just a bunch of filler to wander around in? Hmm....well it's pretty. At least there are a nice amount of character-specific scenes while exploring.
Grind Pulse is also where the game starts to bury you in busy-work. Like any good J-RPG, the world is going to end in less than 10 hours, everyone is about to die, but what's stopping you from spending the next 30 hours making your party super strong? Aside from getting those all important stat bonuses through the Crystarium, you're also going to want to upgrade your gear. It's that moment where you realize that "Hey! I can make my weapons really powerful!" but you're flat broke. Trying to get cash is the #1 biggest problem I have with this game.
Yes, I could use cheat-engine to give myself all the money I could ever need. But forcing the player to take shortcuts isn't good game design. Hell, nowadays game-developers are trying to sell us shortcuts. Buy my way to level 99? Why do that when I can just youtube the ending for free? The only legitimate (?) & logical(???) way to make good money is by killing giant turtles with Vanille's death spell. The amount of money necessary to max out a weapon's capabilities is FREAKIN ABSURD. Square-enix probably figured that if they didn't have all this nonsensical grinding, the game would be 5-10 hours shorter, making it less valuable in the eyes of consumers. Either that or they just really hate completionists. Is an extended vacation in Grind Pulse necessary? Not really. Sure battles will be more difficult, but that can make them more appealing. Despite my issues with this portion of the game, I appreciate its inclusion.
In all fairness, this method of getting the strongest weapons is somewhat an improvement over FF10's. I mean hell, would you rather dodge 200 lightning bolts? Collect those godforsaken butterflies? Ride a chocobo and get those crazy balloons? Turtle-grinding gets zero points for imagination, but at least it's less hateful than soul-sucking, marriage-destroying, world-ending minigames from satan's party-hole.

I actually grew to like the main cast of FF13. The ever-popular Sazh is naturally my favorite of the group, but everyone else comes into their own....eventually. The villains are throwaway trash however. I don't even blink when they're introduced and then unceremoniously discarded. Space Pope is pretty decent, but he's not even a factor for most of the game. I guess it's a side-effect when the first several hours are spent just trying to figure out what the hell is going on. There are a handful of other characters, like the tough mom, woman who wears a bikini to battle, some freedom fighters, a guy, and....yeesh. I can't remember any of these geeks.
I shouldn't have to mention this, because you already know, but Square-enix did a crap job on the port. Durante and his Gedosato program bailed SE out, as FF13 looks really nice at 4K, downsampled, or whatever other high resolution you can force. The frame-rate is still horrendous. At least an update is scheduled for next month. It's too little too late in my case, but I can't complain too much. I just played through the game didn't I? Oh well.
Speaking of...why didn't I quit this game? This has been bugging me ever since I finished my play-through. I went from hating FF13 to liking it. Both times I knew exactly what I was getting into. Maybe it was a change of attitude. Maybe I realized that the glass can be half-full (of corridors). FF13 definitely requires an investment. For a long-time FF fan like myself it was severely off-putting, but I stuck with it, and I'm kinda glad I did. The battle-system is fantastic, the music is excellent, the characters and story...have their moments. Overall this is a very solid entry.
Getting $5 worth of card drops was nice too I suppose.

Now the things I don't like: boring leaders (they sound dull and uninspiring), boring units (there's only to be 3 types of units, vs unique units for each civ in Civ V), boring music (I played my own music when I play, and I  - Civ V's music was awesome with the peace and war themes), boring wonders (I had to look through all the wonders the first time, although it's quite easy to see that the ones that need more production are the wonders), some virtues are OP (propserity - bottom right with -25% health - and the other health benefits in that tree, make that area the new Tradition tree. When I won through victory, the ending was so anticlimatic, and I went "That's it?". It's quite obvious that similar mechanics like religion will be in the game eventually: I want to worship Space Gandhi. But until I can, I can't really recommend this game at the regular price.

Beyond Earth is a decent CIV5 spinoff, but suffers from a lot of balance issues and design problems. It also fails spectacularly at the idea of being the spiritual sucessor of Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri (SMAC). The game has a lot of interesting ideas, but fails to implement them in a balanced and meaningful way.
The Tech Web is interesting in theory, but does not work well in conjunction with the Affinity system. After a few games you will find yourself using the same early game tech path over and over again - and during the late game you will ignore most other techs and just focus on those that grant you points for your preferred affinity, regardless of the actual tech benefits. The tech web ultimately fails to promote player choise and, once more, locks him into first-order tech strategies.
The Orbital Layer is another mechanic that has potential, but there is little incentive to use it. Even the highest difficulty levels can be won without ever launching a satellite. Interaction is limited to button pressing to shoot down other satellites with cities or artillery units.
The victory conditions for the Affinites sound interesting in theory, but in practice they just boil down to clicking "NEXT TURN" once you have setup up the prerequisites. Purity also requires the player to manually summon a unit each turn and guide it to a settle location, while Supremacy needs to send military units back to earth - again one unit at a turn. This turns the last stage into tedious micromanagement, boring the player instead of hyping him up for the victory.
The aliens in Beyond Earth are another interesting idea, but feel quite passive. Unlike barbarians in CIV5 they will never pillage improvements (except for random siege worm movement) and never attack workers or cities unless the player provokes them. While aliens present a challenge during the early game, they fail to scale past that phase and become utterly pointless during the mid and late game. Even the first unit upgrade is enough to tilt the balance in favor of the player - and once you have the first Affinity related unit you can one-shot every alien unit but the (rare) siege worm. To add insult to injury, the game offers an early game building that prevents aliens from getting close to your cities - and this building also has a secondary ability to grant alien immunity to all your trade routes.
Stations are the successors of city states from CIV5, but are less interactive and more often than not less useful than other trade route options. They also have the annoying tendency to drop down in your primary expansion areas, blocking large chunks of the map for your settlers unless the disappear from having no trade or you forcefully remove them - which requires early military investment, a quite bad strategy.
Lore-wise the game has actually a lot of interesting details, but it utterly fails to present them to the player. The only way you will have access to the lore is reading the (not very eye friendly designed) CIVpedia. AI leaders only have two main lines in the diplomacy screen that they will repeat over and over again. The techs feature quotes from different leaders, but fail to grasp the depth of the quotes from SMAC. In addition to that, all voicework for techs and wonders is done by a single voiceactor, so they feel even more bland. All of these issues combined give the game a lifeless and uninspired tone.
Many useful features from CIV5 are gone. You can no longer continue playing after being defeated by the AI, there is no strategic view and the game provides no direct post-game info. The UI design is pretty bad and in some cases hides important information from the player (like quest rewards).
The aesthetic design is not very pleasing. Pale colors make it hard to read the map, more often then not you will have trouble to see if a tile has Miasma on it unless you zoom in quite a bit. Borders can be barely visible and different terrain types look confusingly similiar.
Apart from these huge design issues the game suffers from severe balance problems. To name the biggest ones:
- The health system is mostly pointless. You can drop deep into negative without suffering any significant consequences. You can only stay positive by selecting the Prosperity virtues.
- Trade routes are so powerful that they dwarf all other options in the game. They also require manual adjustment every 25 turns - which is more than annoying, because you will have 3 trade routes per city.
- These two problems combined make ICS (Infinite City Sprawl) the best strategy in the game: Just place as many cities as you can and you will have an advantage over your enemy. Disregard the terrain to search for a good spot - just place them at minimum distance.
- Unit balance is terrible. Tier I affinity units dominate everything and as your unit upgrades progress some units fail to fulfill their specified roles - for example, gunners are better at sieges than artillery units during certain affinity levels.
- The AI is utterly incompetent, even worse than in CIV5. I have been able to win on the highest difficulty level in my 3rd game - and I rarely played past medium to high difficulty in CIV5.
- Only a handful of wonders are actually useful. Most of them are simply not worth an invest of science and production ressources.
- Diplomacy is pointless. There is no need to ever trade with the AI unless you desperately need a certain strategic ressource. Deals offered by the AI are extremely one sided, so you have no reason to ever  accept one.
Now this is an impressive list of shortcomings, but I would like to remind you that CIV:BE has to go up against the well polished CIV5 and the stellar SMAC. The game itself is not a complete failure, but compared to these two other titles it is lacking in many areas.
Until the problems with balancing and basic design issues have been resolved, I sadly cannot recommend this title for full price. If CIV:BE  goes on sale for 25 bucks you may consider getting it if you liked CIV5. Overall I'd advise you to buy and play the original SMAC - if you can bear its 15 year old graphics and the horrible UI. You will get a great game with interesting game mechanics, better immersion and a more interesting story - at a much lower price.

Don`t get me wrong, over the last couple of months the Team back over at Lion's Shade has clearly improved the Game a lot but at the same time parts of Tempest still seem to be as bugged as they were on the day the Game launched last year also those Bugs have been reported dozen of times by now.
Missions doesn`t moving forward even if you had done everything you were told to do, bugged Battleships that jump from one position to another and/or don`t attack at all, lack of Animations, Missions description that show you into the wrong direction, Missions where you have to Kill X Enemies but the Mission will only proceed forward if you have first a good standing with the fraction which doesn`t make any sense at all,...
Sure since Tempest is the first bigger project from Lion's Shade I could accept those Bugs/Glitches and more on but I can`t since over the last couple of weeks one new DLC had launched while the Game is still till today bugged and a Developer should never ever launch a DLC for a Game that is clearly not yet polished enough.
Considering that Lion's Shade is charging for the Treasure Lands DLC around one third of the Main Game you would expect that it should be therefor out of any Major Glitches but as you might have already guess again the DLC wasn`t free out of Bugs and as the Main Game too has it's own issues.
All this is very sad since on the other hand as already mentioned in the introduction Tempest could have been the Sid Meier Pirates! Game everyone of us have been waiting for since years to dig their hands into. It`s all there and yet it still feels like the Game should have been another year in Development before it was released and then over the last couple of months fixed while parts of Lion's Shade have already moved on to Aventarium.
I could probably rant about what went wrong with Tempest so far while listening to the Tempest Soundtrack from Vadim Krakhmal that is available on Steam and on
too which is one of the Highlights of the Game or how many great Battles I had encountered while I was playing the Game for around twenty hours so far or how many times had made me giggle like a small Girl because some of the Missions were just funny but in the end I probably would have at some point in the future again encountered a Game Breaking Bug and had to search for some time till I would find a way how to bypass it or like in the end just closed the Game down and give up on it.

This is one of the Games that you either like from ther first moment and enjoy therefor playing or hate with so much patience that it does hurt.
Special since it does have so much potencial it did hurt me each single time when i had encountered one of those Bugs/Glitches that are still in the Game because some of those are only still in the Game since the Team back at Lion's Shade were too lazy to fix them after more then two years because some exist even while the Game was in Early Access which goes way back to 2015.

Just because the FileSize does fit on a Mobile Device nowadays doesn't mean that the Game was developed on Mobile and then ported on the PC. It was the other way around and if you claim in your Review something else you are full of hate and don't remember that the Game was on Steam years before a Mobile Build was even talked the first time about or even planned by Lion's Shade.

One of the focal points of the series, AI and it's suspicious behaviour towards 47 is done in the cheapest way possible. The AI is at the same time too easy to fool, but too difficult to bypass with disguises, another key element of the previous games.
They will rubber-band you so hard, you cannot approach levels in any previously logical manner. You'll have to adapt to the dumbed-down gameplay. Sometimes you have to distract guards by throwing things at them instead of around them because there are scenes in the game where the AI isn't ready to be distracted by nearby sounds yet.
Theatrics and graphics are used for eye-candy, retrying annoying scenes involving bears and slow-mo may occur. Melee combat is done with QTE's, assassinations completed mostly in cut-scenes. Disguises won't show up in these cutscenes either, by the way.
There's completely arbitrary features like the forced-in scoring system, and the online whatever's. Getting Silent Assassin on each mission is sometimes terrible because it is way too easy, or terrible because the level is built in many sections, and you'll have to try them over and over again to get it exactly right... Or the way the game wants you to complete it. Meaning the tutorial level made it seem that you might not be able to get SA on all levels at all.
The story is good, yet the writing's awful.
Having a vat-grown clone like 47 be more human than humans to safeguard a potentially deadly-in-the-wrong-hands-assassin-girl is a great concept. However there's some lore bringing new unnecessary elements into the plot about 47's past, which are yet another slap in a fan's face. Although It would be more ok if the rest of the game wasn't so bad.
Speaking of faces, Diana's is just blurted out from the start, and seeing as it had been kept a mystery all this time, I feel it would've been more acceptable if there would've been some anticipation to seeing 47's dear handler for the first time through the players' eyes.
Writing tries too hard to make 47 appear more human. 47 is also less intelligent as before, trying to fibre-wire a man thrice his size. Plot device > actions befitting of the character.
Your part in all this will not be to play as 47, but guide him through extremely linear levels, possibly doing some small distractions because hiding in plain sight will never work. Sometimes you'll actually be given the chance to do the assassination yourself instead of a cutscene.
I got this from a midweek madness for 6€'s. And i'll recommend it at that price! It is worth 6€'s to see how a good format of game can be ruined.
My advice for Absolution? If you're like me and've played the previous games, don't be like me, and set your game on easy, say "Eff the scoring system" And just blaze through the levels so you can experience the semi-bad story as quickly as possible.

If you are looking for a game with a great campaign, then this is not a good game for you. If you are interested in military firearms and vehicles, as well as spending some time getting used to controls then I recommend this game fully. Arma 2 is the best game that I have played. It can run decently on almost all computers and has so many features that make gameplay interesting.
Arma 2 is a combat simulator based around a fictional conflict between the US and Russia in Arma 2 and the US and a fictional middle eastern governement in Operation Arrowhead. In order to play on almost if not all multiplayer servers you need to buy combined operations, not just Operation Arrowhead. This will give you all content from Arma 2 and from Operation Arrowhead. All content is worth the price.
If you are debating between buying this game or Arma 3 I really can not give a definite answer to which is better. Arma 2 is in some ways easier, but in some ways not. In Arma 2 the stamina system is much more simplistic, unlike the more realistic system in Arma 3. Arma 3 also has a 3d editor, making mission creation easier (in my opinion). My largest issue with Arma 3 is that it requires a much better computer than necessary for Arma 2.
ARMA 2 Multiplayer:
Some people think that Arma 2's multiplayer is dead. It is not. There are multiple Domination servers that have 20+ players on them at once. Many domination servers have decent team work, and are really fun to play on.
MODS:
Arma 2 and 3 both have mods that increase realisim, these are ACE 2 and the ACE 3 mod. These mod adds many features and in my opinion makes both Arma 2 and 3 feel even more realisic, with better physics and more interactions with objects. In my opinion I think that Arma 3 is a more accessible game for gamers that like fast paced FPS games, but Arma 2 is more tactical if you are not part of a large tactical clan like Shack Tac in Arma 3
Specifc Arma 2 Mods:
Mods worth looking at. You can find them all on
- ACE 2
- Advance Little Bird
- Unsung Vietnam
- Invasion 1944
- Celle 2
- Hell in the Pacific
- Lingor
- Fallujah
DAYZ:
I have never been a big fan of this mod, but if you like that sort of thing then there are still a good amount of servers that have plenty of people playing them.
Conclusion:
Arma 2 is a game for a sepcific group, and I think you will know who you are. Although I did not play Arma 2 when it was the most popular, it is still a great game to play, sepically with good friends.

Really unique theme and feel to this game.   You start off with three people hiding out in a ruined building with a war raging around them, and you have them craft during the day and go scavenging at night.  To me it feels like you're the cast of The Walking Dead except instead of zombies it's a war that's got you scrambling to survive.  Very fun and compelling, it's definitely got that "one more turn" feel that great games have and couples it with some choices you won't make in other games like "these cigarettes I just rolled... do I let my group smoke them all or do I take them over to the bombed out hotel to trade them for rat meat?"    I can see how parts of it might get repetitive after a while, but most games do.  I'm finding it highly entertaining if a little bit depressing.  I definitely recommend it.
Edit/Addition 16 hours in:  I've been asked if it's fun. It's "fun" like Schindler's List was fun. Ok... not exactly like that but it's dark, it's depressing, and sometimes your game ends by having your last surviving character reach a point where she just can't take it any more and slits her wrists. Is that "fun?" I don't know. But it's making me think like few games ever have, and for me that's an amazing experience.

---In short:
It's like Return to Castle Wolfenstein and Painkiller if they were made by a monkey.
Don't play this game.
---In detail:
Necrovision is one of the most miserable FPS experiences in recent memory: there is absolutely no redeeming quality, not an ounce of fun to be found in this unpolished chore of a game. None of the weapons are fun to shoot, none of the enemies are fun to kill, you are constantly being shot and swarmed from every direction, to the point the developer decided it was easier to give you a giant regenerating health bar and make you almost immortal than it was to clean up their mess.
The game starts in the trenches of World War 1, where you fight German soldiers before quickly moving on to zombies and demons. This is the better part of the game, though the broken game mechanics (aiming down the sights actually decreases your accuracy) ruin the experience (hilarious sections wearing a gas mask which completely obscures the screen, making you almost blind). About halfway through, the game turns into a first-person hack n' slash, which means it throws hordes of infinitely respawning enemies your way, making you opt to sprint past them instead of fighting them half the time.
The story is dreadful, told through interminable cutscenes plagued with the worst writing and voice acting you have heard in an FPS, or via 400-words letters/audiologs that nobody in their right mind will listen to (what with the terribly equalized audio making their hilariously bad fake german accents completely drowned out by the music) let alone read. The very act of moving around is a pain: you are constantly tripping over dead enemies or the rubble scattered around the levels, often finding yourself propelled through the air by the broken physics. The enemies are all bullet sponges that take way too long to kill and half of them possess undodgeable hitscanning attacks, which means you will almost constantly be taking damage.
In order to proceed, the game sometimes expects you to do something that looks like you're breaking the game, like jumping on top of the heads of a group of zombies coming out of a gate that only stays open for a few seconds.
The music feels like it's missing half the time: you'll be fighting a huge (and terrible) boss in complete silence; same goes for many sound effects that are flat out missing. What's not missing are the enemy phrases and your awful d-o-u-c-h-e of a character's one-liners stolen from Serious Sam, which are so few in number and repeated so often that they will drive you insane.
Avoid this game like the plague.

You learn about farming techniques and processes for many different sectors from crops to animal husbandry to forestry. All aspects of the game are fun in their own way. There is no goal, deadlines, levels, or in-game achievements to motivate you to complete things. Yet I find myself engorged for hours on end doing the same thing over and over.
Mod community is big, there are many sites out there and incredibly detailed modders creating additions to this game. When I feel like I am getting tired and don't want to play, a new mod hooks me back in. The challenge in managing your finances and planning your next big purchase makes this a real life simulator.
Multiplayer is okay, I've played a few times and it's very laggy. Other players kind of skip around when connecting to slow hosts on the international server. But you yourself run just fine and it's a good way to play with new equipment before deciding to get it for yourself.
If you like simulators, as close to real life as you can get simulators, this is worth every penny. The modding community is large to keep this game fresh with every new mod you add.

With the proliferation of technologies such as computers, smartphones and the internet, it is easier to see and more apparent than ever that the world around us is constantly changing. And not always for the better. With militants ravaging the Middle East, rebels vying for control of Eastern Ukraine, and the conflict between Israel and Palestine still raging on, its difficult not to feel like things are sliding towards a tipping point, a new global conflict even. Games depict wars, real and fantasy, all the time, and, if the likes of Call of Duty and Battlefield are anything to go by, those kinds of experiences are very popular. But we don’t often find ourselves connecting or giving a second thought for the civilians caught in the crossfire, trying desperately to survive. This War of Mine turns things on its head, you aren’t a soldier, kitted out in the latest combat gear, you are average citizens trapped amongst the fighting, doing whatever is necessary to survive. It’s brutal, thought-provoking, and yet another sign that games have matured as an art medium.
This War of Mine doesn’t simply tell the tale of a lone survivor, caught in a war zone, instead you’ll have dominion over three randomly selected characters (initially) and guide them through each day, trying your best to keep them fed, healthy and as happy as they possibly can be. Luckily, they’ll have the relative safety of a small dilapidated house to take shelter in.  It’s not much but it’s a good starting point. By scavenging inside, or at other locations, you can collect materials to fix up the house to make life more comfortable for the inhabitants, and you can build beds, stoves, radios and workshops. These little extras help to keep morale up and depression at bay. Materials don’t come cheap in the middle of a war zone, though, and somebody is going to have to pay a price for them – be it in coin, or in blood.
Running low on food and medicine is not an option if everyone is going to make it to the other side of the war intact. The brutal lengths that you may have to go to are uncensored and unglorified, and while murdering an elderly couple for their food and jewellery may initially shock, it becomes second nature after a while. And that’s the grizzly reality of war: sometimes, you must be absolutely ruthless to survive.
These realisations can deeply affect your survivors, and they may become deeply troubled by the events going on around them. Each has their own mood indicators highlighting whether they are hungry, tired or depressed, and their effects are almost immediately apparent. Characters who have fallen into depression will drag their almost lifeless bodies around the squat ruminating over the events that have happened, asking themselves ‘why?’. Other characters may take note of this and try to help by talking with them. Each character also keeps a diary with details of the events from days gone by; depending on the situation you may see your characters attitudes change before your eyes. Characters whom have murdered others may initially regret their decision, only to accept it later as an inevitability, required in order to stay alive. This War of Mine may sound emotionally draining to play, and it is; 11 Bit Studios have struck a delicate balance and created a title that is as entertaining to play as it is emotionally compelling
Each day is split into two sections which see your survivors fixing up the house to make it more comfortable during the day, and going out scavenging at night. Some aspects of the game have a “The Sims” feel to them, with you having to tend to everyone’s needs such as feeding them, keeping them comfortable and dispensing medication if they are sick. Scavenging at night can be very dangerous, especially if you intend to come home with anything useful, so it is wise to stay armed. A nifty crafting interface allows you to create all manner of different items such as lockpicks, axes, shovels and hack saws, which can be used to reach particularly valuable loot. Each scavenging location requires careful consideration before you set off though, and you’ll pay the price if you go out without the proper equipment. It is very easy to lose characters to militants or, other, better-armed survivors.
Sometimes, while out scavenging, you’ll encounter other violent and non-violent NPCs, and whether you engage them or no is up to you. Combat isn’t particularly in-depth but it doesn’t need to be. You can switch from scavenging mode to armed at the click of the mouse, but your adversary may become aware and attack you. Simply clicking on an enemy is enough to send you stabbing/punching/shooting in their direction. The impact doesn’t come from the combat itself, rather the effect it can have on your character – and you. As aforementioned, whilst out scavenging at an old cottage we found a friendly old couple, relaxing in their armchairs. Sadly, their number was up before we even caught sight of them; our fridge was empty, we had no valuables or medicine. Luring the old man down to the basement, we began beating him mercilessly with a shovel. “Don’t leave me!” cried his wife, as we set about her. We couldn’t help but pause for thought – would we do the same in a similar situation?
This War of Mine isn’t a delight to look at, but its aesthetic is expertly crafted. The city is awash in dark blacks and greys which inspire a feeling of desolation and despair. unfortunately we were subject to a number of graphical glitches and stuttering issues, which should be patched out post-launch.
As a game, This War of Mine is sensational, as a story it is gripping, but it is as a statement that it makes its biggest impact. Whilst most of us (hopefully) will never know what it is like to live in a war zone, it’s important to know that there are people, like us, out there surviving in horrific situations. It is an unforgettable survival horror game, but not as you know it. 11 Bit’s presentation of war is candid, undiluted and bound to leave a lasting impression.

I didn't want to write a review before 100%ing it to fully understand the shortcomings of this game. Now that I finally have, I can talk about it somewhat fairly. The truth is that there's so much wrong with this game that it's hard to recommend it to just anyone.
I enjoyed the combat system. The faster paced paradigm shift system (similar FFX-2's ATB/dressphere system) was a refreshing take on the turn based combat that FF12's didn't really provide. Shift canceling/ATB canceling also provided a lot more depth into what may look like simple combat mechanics. The story was acceptable but had major pacing issues with the first 10 chapters feeling overextended, while the last 3 chapters were much more enjoyable and interesting, yet shorter. What really stands out in the game however, are the visuals. Everything from the prologue to the end is a gorgeous vista of sci-fi fantasy, with a decadent high-tech society clashing against a beautiful yet raw planetscape. Eden in particular stood out for me, with it's beautiful architecture and sci fi-esque atmosphere.
However, the infamous graphical issues, the random crashes that occur and the ESC key essentially being a one button Alt+F4 are major issues in this game. It's depressing to see a fan-made fix that was made in one day is still the only option to fix this heavily broken game. Squenix recently patched, and I was hoping for some official fixes, but all we got was a simple pop-up change to ask if you really wanted to quit the game when you hit ESC. Not even an ingame message but for me it distorts the current game screen and freezes it. Only by Alt-Tabbing do I see an off screen dialog window box asking me whether I really want to exit the game. I knew Japanese pc ports had a terrible history, but this one is almost as bad as the Dark Souls port (at least we didn't need GFWL). Technical issues aside, the pacing is terrible, you don't actually get to use the full combat system for the first half of the game. Sidequests are replaced by what is essentially hunts from FF12, the Crystarium system of leveling is extremely shallow with the bare minimum of choice. Animations are often clunky and slow for the kind of fast paced combat the game uses. These are some of the most obvious probelms you'll encounter.
Overall, it isn't a terrible game. However, it's got so much wrong with it'll be hard to finish or enjoy, even for the seasoned RPG fanatic. It's a definite oddity in the consistency we've seen in the FF series. While it did have some very good areas, it's crippled of it's potential. I wouldn't recommend this to anyone unless they had the tenacity to see it through, and even then they might regret it.

Simply put, this is a hollow shell of what a Final Fantasy game is. Compared to the Playstation 1-2 classics (FFVII, FFVIII, FFX, etc.), this will be the least intersting, challenging and interactive sequel of its time. For starters, this is a completely linear story, no exploration, no interaction with people, no shops, no towns, no side quests.
While I typically don't mind being on a rail of an expansive story, the narration is by far the worst ever told where so many terms are comfortably used without properly introducing the player what the hell it all means; thankfully they included a datalog to explain all the necessary, but apparently too trivial to incorporate in real-time, information. Final Fantasy XIII intentionally skimps out on a lot of details to reveal a bunch of cheap "twists" that you have an inkling is going to happen or something of that sort as you play through.
The biggest gaffe to the game is the strategy, or lack of. It's so bad that I am actually writing a proper review for this game. Final Fantasy XIII does away with all sort of customization both in leveling as it is a shadow version of Final Fantasy X's sphere grid and equipment consists of an Accessory Slot and Weapon Slot with no real way to improve them besides chucking found items and boosting their stats. It's not very complex, elaborate or even that cool. For the majority of the game, the weapons hardly vary and pretty much offer better stat of your two stats: Magic/Strength (Magic/Physical). Since there are no shops in-game, you do all your purchasing through randomly placed books that let you buy items, save and upgrade your weapons, no real interface, customization or aesthetics, just menus and menus.
Let's not forget
. You don't control all three in battle, you control one and switch "roles" of all three when you want to be more aggressive, support/healing or more defensive/disruption (slow, haste, protect, etc.). It's a very unique system, but limiting in strategy and even more limiting in how to approach foes. To add, you don't get to control any three characters for the majority of the game, so you're individually leveling different characters and their stories throughout most of the plot. Their leveling is slow and some roles (such as the Sentinel Role or Saboteur) gets only one ability or two abilities. It's cumbersome, slow and hinders the entire pace of the battle for what they thought was an innovative system.
Everything that made Final Fantasy itself is gone: No Blitzball or Triple Triad minigame, no collectible Guardian Forces, nothing. Eidolons are the equivalent, but they're awkward, lifeless and there are very few of them. You summon them, they can do a limited amount of attacks and then they vanished. There is no real grandiose spectacle of their attacks that I would consider on par with the other games and certainly not as memorable.
The characters are also the most disliked people in the entire series. Without a clear antagonist highlighted or underlined for the majority of the game, you turn your hate towards the main characters who are very shallow in backstory and mostly hypocritical ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, I'll summarize it for you without any real spoilers (most of these are the premise of the game):

Agatha Christie couldn't even use this character. She is the summation of every dramatic asian show you've watched and went "oh brother". Your eyes will roll like a locomotive as soon as you hear her speak and then listen to what she says, does and is so blatantly bothered with (but keeps up a happy appearance).

I will preface this by stating I know I am not going to get review of the year for my comments on this. I have been playing strategy games for years (well before steam) and the Civilization series since Civ 3; and this is by far a huge disappointment to me. Many people are comparing it to Civ 5 before the expansions, having purchased it on launch I definitely found rough edges which over the past few years and two expansions later have been fleshed out to be one of the best Civilization games, if not the best imho - but Beyond Earth is, well it's not even rough around the edges. Many other players have spelled out the issues I've also found with Civ: BE such as:
-The factions are absolutely lifeless, boring, and might as well just be the same cardboard figures with different coats of paint to distinguish
-The AI is insufferabe
-The Technology Tree is an absolute nightmare/mess to navigate although one is able to see what everything does at least so it's not like it is a complete mystery.
-Very little depth to this game what-so-ever.
-There is very little immersion for the player - I found myself looking at strategic resources and having no idea what correlated with what resource (in Civ 5 you know iron is going to be important for early warfare for example).
The strategy genre, specifically the 4x turn-based style has been getting a lot of releases as of late, I'd pass on this until the game is more fleshed out and not only play something that doesn't feel like an "Early Access Game" but probably doesn't cost $50.

DISCLAIMER: This review is based on game version 1.0.0.574, and includes no DLCs apart from the pre-order (Exoplanets) bonus. I will update if I feel the need and/or if they [Firaxis/2K] have brought enough changes to the table to warrant it.
I'm going to start off by making something clear - I will be comparing this game to Civilization V quite a bit. Why? Several reasons - first of all, it's based on the Civilization V game engine. Second, they've decided to brand it "Civilization", rather than something that'll avoid association with earlier games in the series. And lastly - it is pretty much a re-skin of Civilization V. (Yes, this is a term that will rub some people the wrong way, but in this case - it's pretty close to the truth.)
I will be focusing, point-by-point (starting with what I consider to be the negatives), on the development direction they've taken this game in, since and in comparison to Civilization V. (The last iteration, i.e. with all expansions included.)
So without further ado;
-CONS-
1) Content.
This is a very broad criticism point, but examples include that there are far fewer civilizations ("sponsors"), and they have NO unique units (not even different skins, not even different colors), NO unique buildings, and very few unique "effects" (several nations had quite unique twists on gameplay mechanics, in Civilization V) at all. In addition to that, most traits you get from the different sponsor and cargo choices are extremely simple - basic stat increases, just like the world/national wonders. (See below.)
There are also less luxury resources, and NO natural wonders. (Strategical resources seem to be about the same, i.e. quite few.) The alien life forms are IDENTICAL, they look and behave exactly the same no matter what different planet you're on.
There is no religion (before you start to whine about the concept of religion in the future - watch the intro. No religion, hm?) present whatsoever.
The amount of world and national wonders is reduced, and they are ONLY gained through specific research options - there aren't any bound to social policies and/or other gamplay mechanics. The effects they give are also a lot more simple, usually very basic and incremental stat increases. (Energy, Health, Science, Culture, etc.)
Unit variety has been reduced, with very linear upgrades for every unit available (some get an extra effect that can change their behavior, but it's very conservative) and, probably the most laughable concept transfer from Civilization V, veterancy. Each veterancy level in Civilization V gave you several options on how to promote your unit(s), that could change how they'd perform in a number of different ways. Now you have one option. ONE. FREAKING. OPTION. (If you exclude the option to heal it, if it has been damaged.) EVERY. LEVEL. Oh, and your units are capped at level 3-5, depending on what you're fighting and what you have researched. Same promotion every level, just incrementally improving combat strength - nothing more.
City states ("Outposts") are now pretty useless - they do one thing, and one thing only: act as trading partners. You gain incrementally increasing benefits for every trade route completed with the outpost. Sadly, the trade route system has become a lot worse in this iteration of Civilization (more on that later), so the benefits aren't all that much to write home about.
Great persons and great works have been completely removed.
2) Mechanics - this will be broken down further:
A) AI, worker AI in particular - tightly integrated with the fact that tile improvements have become an absolute smorgasbord, and the fact that workers are A LOT slower to perform their tasks in this iteration. In short: virtually, no matter how many workers you have, they'll just go around roughly the same tiles and keep replacing the improvements they just built (that took 10+ turns to build), just because you've managed to research something they believe is better for that tile. Screw the fact that there are unimproved tiles in the next city, the workers will just muppet about and replace improvements en masse. While this can be alleviated with the use of "Workers do not replace tile improvements" - you'll instead be stuck (or stuck micro-managing) with early-game tile improvements. Explorer AI is not great either, inconsistent at best (the reasoning behind setting up an expedition vs. not doing so in auto-explore mode is hard to figure out as a player, for example).
B) Civilizations - mentioned in the content section. In short, they are bland - both in character and gamplay. They lack diversity, or any real personality to them.
C) Starting - you are extremely locked in terms of where you settle your first city - which may have benefits, but certainly has its drawbacks as well.
D) Trade - trade routes are now more exclusive, trade routes to city st... outposts are now limited to 1. In addition, you have a per-city maximum, which means you'll have loads of trade units late-game. And with the higher rarity of outposts (compared to city states) and the 1 limit on trade routes to them, you will not be able to gain a lot of resources from them, unless you're close to another major civilization. Basically, internal trade routes will be far more likely than foreign ones. Also, the duration is a measly 25 turns, which means you'll have idle trade units more often than not, when getting into the mid-late-game.
E) Social policies - far more linear (only 4 trees, compared to 9 in Civilization V, and that's excluding the Ideology system - which has no equivalent in BE), and not particularly improved. The options in Civilization V weren't great (quite a few basic stat increases), but they sure aren't better in BE.
F) Miasma - present, for some inexplicable reason, on every planet in the universe, apparently. Dangerous, spreading, contaminating (or nourishing, with the right affinity). Might be interesting in theory, but it gets slow REAL fast. Especially early-game, when you have no means to protect yourself from it, or limit the spread.
G) Orbital units - stationary units that can not overlap at all, for some inexplicable reason. (Collision risk is not a viable theory, as the individual cover they provide is significantly different from each other - compare a miasma repulsor and a solar satellite, for example.)
H) Voice acting - broken English can only take you so far. We've (humanity, collectively), in relatively short time, gone from having little knowledge of other languages than our own, to learning quite a bit about it at an early age. What's the plausibility of everyone speaking as bad English as virtually all the voice actors, in the future? It's just an annoyance. It'd be better to have them speaking their native languages, if you implement advisors of different nationalities.
3) UI and misc.
The UI feels like a dumbed-down (yes, another word many will shrug at) version of Civilization V's. Several elements are scaled up in size (for some inexplicable reason), information is more scarce (well, maybe because several gameplay elements have been removed, as well), especially in the city screen.
-PROS-
These don't need to be grouped up, these are the only specific elements I feel are a distinct step in a good direction.
1) Affinity.
If this had worked better (i.e. hadn't been granted by specific research, but rather actions and more diverse quests and tasks), it'd be a great thing - as it stands it's just a decent concept.
2) Quests.
This could be greatly expanded, but it's a nice idea to be able to choose different options for buildings, units and so on.
Bottom line:

Fair warning: This is an iphone/tablet game, which funnily enough is available for less than half the price it's sold on Steam on Google Play, and iTunes.
The Good:
-Considering the entirity of the game is just over 400Mb (it's designed for phones) there's a lot in there.
-Ship to ship combat is interesting and kinda fun.
-The overland map is a great idea and takes a lot of the tedium out of sailing from A to B.
-There is a lot of attention to detail in some areas, e.g. in first person your captain is holding a map of the world.
The Bad:
-The graphics take you back in time 10 years
-Boarding is so bad it would be hilarious if it wasn't so infuriating
-The UI is very counter intuitive
-You can't save/load games
-The quest system feels like an afterthought, most descriptions are very weak, and kill x of y quests don't update leaving you having to guess/remember how far through you are.
-The controls feel unresponsive
-You can't arrange your men in combat, you have to leave combat to do that (I can't yell for people to climb down from the sails and defend the ship?)
-You can't arrange your canon loadout outside of combat (I can't prepare for combat? What?)
-Despite being allied with a certain faction, they'll attack you if you're using "the wrong" flag, and sometimes they'll attack you if you're using "the right" flag.
-Trade feels like an afterthought, there are no indicators of whether a location is a better or worse price.
-Crewmen don't gain experience in combat despite the store page inference, you have to spend your own experience on them.
-It takes 50 skill points to acquire an ability, you get 1 skill point for each ship killed......
-NPCs steal your kills: If you do 95% of the damage to an enemy, then an NPC scores the final shot, no XP/faction gain for you!
-No LoS mechanic, you and the enemy can shoot through rocks/buildings/other ships.
-Battles with allies/Rescue missions are poorly thought out, it's in your interest to let all your allied ships be destroyed as then you'll get their loot without penalty.
The whole thing feels very much like an early access title, despite the obvious limitations of porting a tablet game to PC with another year or so of development this game could be great.
The unfortunate thing is this genre is very limited in choice, there are only a handful of titles available to players. So while I'm giving this a negative review, if you like this sort of game you can either get it, or carry on playing Sid Meyer's Pirates!

This is a game about a Pong ball that saves two worlds: the "rendered" world and the "code" world.
The primary gameplay mechanic is traveling between these two worlds. To enter the "code" world, you must die in the "rendered" world. To return, simply find a portal. Some obstacles in the game can only be overcome by switching between worlds; for instance, you may ecounter an impassible wall in the "rendered" world, kill yourself on some spikes, and then see that the wall isn't there in the "code" world.
In addition, there are 20 "pixels" scattered throughout each level. I cannot see any purpose behind these other than to get an achievement for collecting all 1,200 of them (and one achievement for collecting all of them in one level). If you are a completionist, expect to spend way too much time collecting these things.
Overall, the level design and controls are adequate, and in some cases quite nice, for a 2D side-scrolling platformer.
The game is spread across four major graphical periods roughly corresponding to the Colecovision, the Nintendo Game Boy, the Nintendo Entertainment System, and the Super Nintendo Entertainment System. Between them all, there are 60 levels (plus boss levels). My biggest complaint about this game is actually that it's too long. By the time you have reached the fourth major graphical period, the formula has gotten old. The developer does spice it up a bit with slight mechanic alterations between graphical periods, but it isn't enough to freshen "find the pixels and go to the end of the level".
Overall, I would recommend this game with the recommendation that you don't try to get all of the pixels. That should put the length right into the sweet spot.

This is literally one of the best survival games that I've played in a while, and if you look at the games I play - I'm REALLY into this genre. You begin with several characters picked out of a pool, each with their own unique background and skillset. For instance; Bruno is a great cook, Marco is a good scavenger, Katia is good at bargaining, and so on.
The immediate task becomes scavenging the shelled building that you'll be living in, and clearing away rubble. Once it hits 8:00 pm every night, it will be dark enough to attempt to scavenge in the dilapidated buildings in the area. More open up each night, and they each present their own unique challenges. Some are inhabitied by people, or perhaps being scavenged by others who are just trying to survive. Oftentimes they'll be friendly enough, unless you try to step on their toes while they scavenge; other times - you may be in for a fight.
There are other obstacles to worry about, as well. I've encountered situations where there were snipers covering a street, and if I tried to cross at the wrong time - I'd be just another victim. And the victims are many, as in any war. You'll encounter children, and adults who may need your help - but that help can be just as dangerous as a knife in your back. The medicine that saves their loved one, may soon be needed by yours, as your people come down sick or injured quite regularly.
As the temperature drops, you'll need to start heating the rooms, and trying to keep your peoples' spirits up. You'll often have chances to barter with other survivors, and sometimes a knock at the door can be the very thing that saves you, when you're running low on one thing or another.
This game does an excellent job of enforcing the concept that war is hell, and the casualties sometimes end up being civilians like you and I. You genuinely feel bad if you're forced to steal from other people who are just trying to survive, but sometimes the choice is between them and theirs, and you and yours. The moment I built a radio and turned it on, I immediately thought of the civilians caught in the middle of the current hostilities in the Ukraine; people who were living normal lives, and now find themselves caught between two groups laying waste to everything around them, as they struggle for dominance.
In conclusion, This War of Mine is a unique experience in the survival genre; I've survived zombies, plagues, and every armageddon imaginable...except the one that happens every day in the world around us. The micro apocalypse experienced by men, women, and children in countries you don't even know the name of, right now. Saddest game of the year? Maybe. But it's a game that makes you give a crap about something outside yourself, and that is truly a rare experience - well worth the price of admission, and then some.

I got this game with the Yogscast Jingle-Jam collection on Humble Bundle this last Christmas season, and after the holidays had passed I decided to give it a go. Overall I found the game enjoyable, though it did have its frustrating elements as well. While I give it a positive review, I'd say it's more accurate to say my opinion of the game falls in the mid-range.
Pros:
-The game's aesthetic evokes the broad nostalgic eras of gaming, with each world representing a specific game type and art style: Atari 2600, Game Boy, NES and SNES, with plenty of references throughout. References are primarily to the video games they represent, though there are a few other references thrown in here and there as well.
-The World of Code and Rendered World Elements add some variety to level design and let you see the game world from two different sides.
- Plenty of levels to explore (60 in all, plus a challenge mode)
- Responsive controls that are quick to learn
Cons:
- The story is rather haphazard and flat. There is an implication of a larger mystery/plot, but it's only at the end it feels like it ties together. Each world/gaming era feels very self-contained and could be its own (albeit short) game in its own right.
- Your abilities don't really change much between worlds, making most of the themes differences aesthetic.
- You collect "pixels" throughout the levels, but at no point is it ever made clear why other than because they are something to collect.
- Some levels are very frustrating to full complete - getting through the levels is not hard, but collecting all 20 pixels in each level can sometimes result in a lot of back-tracking.
-Occasional glitchiness, chiefly with Boss 3 (exiting the game and coming back again made it work) and sometimes transitions betwen the Rendered World and the World of Code double-kill you when you spawn in a spot you shouldn't in the latter.
Overall, I don't regret playing this game. It was a classic platformer with nice aesthetic variety, plenty of game references that make you go "hey, I know what that's from!" and plenty of levels to burn through. However, unlike great classics like Super Mario Brothers, Megaman X or Donkey Kong Country, this is not a game that is easy to just sit down and play for hours; it was good to play in bursts, but not for binging.
Pick it up on sale, or if you already have it, give it a go! It doesn't break the mold, it feels like there was something more that it was trying to be, and sometimes it's highly frustrating, but it's a fun distraction when you want a solid platformer.

Extremely depressing, brilliantly executed game.
In terms of atmosphere, the game world is a foreboding, gritty construction piece - and it lends itself to building a true atmosphere of the hardships faced by civilians during war time. Uniquely however, the game itself does not build its atmosphere with pre-constructed set pieces or otherwise; it instead, simply creates a sandbox environment for you, in which you carve your own story. In speaking, "This War of Mine" guides the player towards making their own choices; and suffer the consequences of them.
The game world is unforgiving; if you steal medical supplies from the elderly, you may return to their household later in time, to find them dead. Your character will experience traits of depression, and blame themselves. Other characters in your own household will form their own opinions on your crimes; and typically, it all boils down to a case of "it was them, or us". While you may feel remorse for your actions, this feeling can quickly be removed by having your own stronghold raided - and seeing your own medicine stolen while you have a sickly team mate is an equally bitter pill to swallow, in knowing that the most reliable method of ensuring your team mate lives through his illness, is to return back to the wilderness to scavenge (read: steal) medicine from wherever holds the least risk.
The art style and graphical fidelity contained within This War of Mine, is of an unusually high standard for an indie release. It does not attempt to go for a "timeless" look with cartoon-like, or niche graphical styles (bar a small pencil-shaded effect); instead, it strongly holds itself up against the expectations set by modern games on the marketplace, delivering a well-crafted, aesthetically pleasing (albeit quite depressing) design.
In terms of gameplay, everything is where it should be. Better support for keyboard movement would be appreciated for camera panning; but outside of that, it's your typical mouse-controlled side scroller type controls. Nothing to break, nothing to fix. You'll spend a great deal of your time planning out your next actions, rather than diving straight in and hoping for the best; at least, if you want to survive more than a few minutes. This War of Mine is slow paced, and rightly so; it's a large step away from the high octane, modern war games as of late.
One unique feature which I've come to love is the fact that the storyline is procedurally generated; as in, your unique characters will craft their own unique storylines, based on the actions carried out by the you as the player. They'll write in their diaries, and try to justify their actions to themselves; leading to a broad, unique experience and storyline on each playthrough.
A great deal of respect can be offered to the developers themselves, for avoiding the "early access" route, as many survival/crafting type games have taken to date. Instead, This War of Mine delivers the full experience from the get-go; and it's not an experience to be missed.

Let me first say that this is a terrible port.  If you meet the minimum or even recommended specs chances are you will not be able to play this game in an enjoyable state.  You will need something almost double the recommended to actually play this game at a stable framerate even on normal settings.  I've owned this game for a couple years & am only now getting around to playing it because it's just such a bad port.
That being said, this game is actually really good & I wish I could have played it sooner.  It isn't without it's faults, however.
-Large Open World to Explore
-Lots of Collectables & Unlockables
-Fun Gameplay
-Good Story
-Ship Battles
-Gameplay can be frustrating at times
-Collectables are mostly used as a "Gameplay Time Extender"
-Some Story Missions are just kind of dumb or trial & error
-Earning Money relies on "Kenway's Fleet"
You play as an employee at Abstergo Industries, a private company built on Animus Technology that records & edits genetic memory data to make movies.  You are part of a team going through the Genetic DNA Memories of Subject 17 who's biological history makes him one of the most valuable subjects for Animus Technology.  As you "play" through his genetic memories you soon find that things are not what they seem.  An ancient conspiracy emerges about an age old war against Assassin's & Templars bordering on the deranged shows itself & you are soon tasked by your superiors with finding out about something called the "Observatory" as soon as possible.  Playing through the memories, you are in the role of Edward Kenway, a Privateer/Pirate of the early 1700s who's friends with Blackbeard himself.  You must use all yours & Edwards resources in order to find out about the Observatory & what power it holds.
The game starts off witha thud that turns into a bang.  Eventually, after 4 or so hours, you are in the actual meat of the game with your own ship, crew, & island hideout.  Everything is upgradeable, but not everything is useful.  Your house, for example, has about 3 upgrades, all of which do absolutely nothing.  You get multiplayer rewards for upgrading it completely.  Yea, that's what we want from our Single Player games, Multiplayer rewards.  Anyways, not everything is all bad.  You can upgrade your ship, your weapons & armor via crafting & add other new additions to your island hideaway like hookers, a bonfire & a tavern.  Most of which are still pretty disappointing.  I bought the bonfire thinking it would be this big epic burning man celebration on the beach, but it turns out it was just a camp fire with people around it.  Whoopie.
Upgrading your ship is the most important thing you can possibly do in this game.  You get materials for it by taking down other ships or raiding plantations stockpiles.  Each ship you take down you can either add to your fleet, lower your wanted, repair your ship, or just sink the bloody thing.  Sinking is easier but cuts your booty by about half.
The Fleet is a sort of mini game where, each ship you capture can go on trade routes to earn money & random loot for your mansion to display or to equip on yourself or your ship.  I don't really like the idea of RNG loot systems, but this one's alright.  It's set up kind of like a Mobile game, where you take out enemy ships on routes, then send ships that are capable on the voyages which can range from 5 minutes to actual days to complete.  It's a waiting game, but it's also the best way to earn Money in the game.  I don't like that, if you don't use this minigame you are basically gimped for coin.  Money in the actual game itself isn't easy to come by & chests are filled with paultry sums that don't add up quick enough for what you need to buy.  In my travels in the game after about 40+ hours of gameplay I've maybe run across 40k total, while just sending ships out to do missions netted me over 100k by just turning the game off & waiting for missions to complete.
Combat & platforming is also a mixed bag.  Sometimes it works perfectly, other times it's janky as all hell.  At times, Edward will run wild clinging to walls & jumping off of every little thing you don't want him to, while others he does exactly what you were trying to do.  During combat, sometimes counters just don't work & you'll be stuck in a quick succession chain attack by one enemy.  Others, they will always work & you'll never get hit.  The biggest issue I have though is how poorly designed the combat system is in general.  Simply attacking an enemy takes about 4x longer to kill than a counter kill, so there's really no point in attacking first as it just leaves you open.  You're better off just countering or throwing a smoke bomb & instantly killing everyone around you.  There are those cool bad♥♥♥♥♥moments when you are on a freeflow combo killing spree that make attacking worthwhile but it's just a less effective way of dealing with enemies.
Then there are ship battles, which I must say are this games bread & butter.  Far more time was spent perfecting ship combat than the melee combat.  Starting out, you can't take on squat but as you upgrade your ship you will be able to take on the dreaded Man O'war vessels & even add them to your fleet.  Then there are the big Legendary Ships which are meant to be taken on only when you've fully upgraded your ship & those fights are doozies.  You get mortars, cannons, heavy shots, fire barrels, chain shots, & quick shots that target vulnerabilities you've made from other attacks.  Oh, and you can ram the crap out of other ships.  Once you get a big ram, you can pretty much monster truck your way over smaller ships with ease.  As you keep attacking ships, your wanted level goes up which summons Hunters, which get stronger & more frequent the higher level your wanted gets.  You can use your wanted level as bait to lure out better ships to add to your fleet or get more materials to sell or upgrade with.
The crafting in this game is basically copy/pasted from AC3.  You'll need to hunt animals & use their hides to add/upgrade your arsenal & defenses.  The difference is now, you can hunt whales & sharks.  The best way for me to describe these fights are comparing them to the big aligator boss fight in RE4.  You harpoon them, latch on & they pull you around & dive down to hide.  Then, they attack your ship if you don't hit them in time.  It's almost the exact same formula from that RE4 boss fight, just replace the big crocodile with sharks & whales.
There are also random events in the game like the White Whales or Trade Routes that give good coin or loot.  These appear as blue R-Boat symbols on your minimap & are available for limited times only.  Once found, they automatically share with anyone on your U-Play friends list so your friends can do them, too.  Not your Steam list, though.  So, if you have a lot of Steam Friends but not U-play the share feature is basically worthless here.
Finally, the collectables.  These range from simple chests, to missions, to Animus fragments & there are a ton of them.  Doing them all will take a considerable amount of time & probably extend gameplay by at least 3x.  I say this as I remember the one mission that put 3 animus fragments in jump off points that forced you to treck back through the entire Island again after getting each one.  Literally, extending gameplay of that one mission by at least 3x.  Some collectables do this, others are simply put on the path so you can get them as you progress.  I don't know if there's a reward for collecting everything, since I haven't done it yet.
If you are looking for a great open world adventure game with a Pirate theme & have capable hardware, then this is worth the buy.  It's frustrating at times but the pros do outweigh the cons in the long run. Just be aware that this game isn't perfect.  I'd go on, but I'm out of characters to type.

One street, enemies, slash slash, then some wood, enemies, slash, slash, then some dialog uncovering some very average unexciting story, again some street slash, slash, etc.. For seasoned FPS players, I can give this game 5 maybe 6/10. All points just for technical side of game, which was without any bugs or flaws.
In summary: younger gamers, or gamers which appreciate gory FPS game where you can cut your enemies with katana - recommended. Also if you appreciate watching on ******* bunnies. :)

Rivals of Aether is a game clearly inspired by the Super Smash Bros. series, but with it's own innovation on the formula. The core idea is the same: Deal as much damage as possible to your opponent as possible, while taking the least you can. Higher damage means you get sent farther when hit, ultimately resulting in players being sent flying off stage, either colliding with the end of the screen and dying, or being forced to try and make their way back to the stage with their opponent actively trying to prevent it.
If you're looking for a fun fighting game featuring some stellar game design, you've come to the right place.
If you are a fan of Smash, you absolutely need to play this game. The unique mechanics it brings to the table make it familiar but also a breath of fresh air.

When I first bought this game I had big hopes for it to be great and that it would have stunning graphics. And I sure hope I would have read any reviews before purchasing it... Because what I was stuck with was a extremely poorly optimized game which ran in 720p with no graphics options whatsoever. However, there was still hope for me, within just A DAY the work of ONE man was enough to give me what I craved for. Full HD resolution... Something that should be the absolutely minimum to be supported. Then when I today saw that Square Enix had released an update I got quite excited, so I rushed to the news feed to see what they had updated and this is what I saw...
"Hello,
The FINAL FANTASY XIII team have been working hard to improve your experience on Steam and we're happy to announce the following changes will be rolled out.
■ All versions
A request-to-confirm notification, will now appear when you try to quit from the full-screen mode. "
Is it not enough that they have yet to be able to do what a single man was able to do within a fraction of the time they had to develop this game, but then they go out and post that they have been working HARD! This makes me rather upset, I would never in my life recommend this game to anyone and it's a shame, it's most likely a pretty decent game which have rather stunning graphics when you are able to play it in 60fps 1080p... However, I can't recommend a game where it takes the developers over a month to put out a fix for something as mundane as the fact that the ESC-button simply shuts down the whole game. A fix like that shouldn't just take less than a day to fix, it shouldn't even have been there from the start.
Square Enix have made great games and I really mean great games. With stunning visuals and great storytelling, however, if this is how they wish for their PC-versions to be, then I'm sad to say that I no more will buy a game from them. At least not until they prove that they have learnt their leason.

I thought it would be a chore to play this game from the reviews. I only got it because it was 5 bloody dollars. The weirdest part is that it took about 9000 steam "Show me random games I dont want" quenes to find this thing, and at 9000 all you see are dating sims and anime games.
So to put it plainly, lets ask why we play games. For me, more often than not, having fun is a big part of it. This game is FUN as HELL! The way its set up make it so you never really stop feeling like a total badass. A dedicated kick button like bulletstorm or return to castle wolfenstien, added to a ridiculous assortment of guns, added to doom style combat (dont take cover, bullets are nerf darts to you but theres hundreds of baddies) and finishing moves for melee, dual welding a pistol and about a thousand other weapons, such as another pistol, throwing knives, shovels, dynamite, etc.
This is not a night at the opera. This is not where you get dressed in uncomfortable clothes so you can go and look like you are a person with advanced tastes. This is movie night with your friends, where you make sure no one is looking and pop die hard or some other goofy action movie in. This is endless make-you-feel-like-a-badass fun and I am actually ANGRY at other reviewers for having a problem with that! I can't even convince myself to get off this game because its bringing me back to the nostalgic old days of wolfenstien and doom where games were meant to be fun gore pits of sadistic laughter.
So yes, again. Voice acting and story are pretty awful and oftentimes your character will go "Oh whoa! you again" to literally nothing as if the devs thought youd take some time to look out a window to catch a glimpse of a fleeing monster. Your character, in the nicest terms possible, is a ♥♥♥♥ing massive redneck (Who is also demon posessed and occasionally shouts at the baddies in a sadistic demon voice) and he is meant to be that way, and its HILARIOUS. You get to dual weild Watercooled machine guns, if that gives you any idea how far on the awesome meter this game went for.
So once more, yes, stop being a stuck up snob, cough up 5 bloody dollars and have a fricken ball! 5 bucks for hours and hours of stupid fun? 5 bucks cant even buy you lunch anymore.
A toast to stupid good fun, and a big single finger salute to all the snobs out there who have a problem with it! TALLY HO
One last point, this game makes a MILLION references to other games like it, Ive heard references to the painkiller series, to redneck rampage, to doom and wolfenstien. Tons of silly one liners referencing other great games make this game a little bit of a parody of the very "Shoot all the things" genre itself.

Been through the game 4 times now and most of the reviews of this game are spot on.     It is a good but flawed game.   The flaws can come out in future patches, and i have no doubt that one day this game will be as fun as Civ 5 if Firaxis puts the same work into those.
The problem most people have with this, and i agree is that this is a $50 AAA title, it should be more complete than it is.
The Good:  There are some incredible moments in this game.  Taking a giant maisma spreading Rocktopus and invading the world with a green gas that heals your troops and damages enemies is just fun.
The Bad:  its easy to say balance, balance can be fixed in future patches, but for the life of me i cannot understand how the current trade route system made it into this game.  Any game designer who played this game once should have put up the red flag and said.... guys i dont think its really fun managing 30-50 trade routes, maybe we should re think this.
The Ugly: The endings.   This is also something that is inexcusable to me.  Games are about critical thinking and pay off.    To "reward" your players with the equivalent of a loading screen win or lose, no information, no cinimatic, it just feels lazy.    You have 5 different victory conditions, thats 5 different stories you could have told, give the players some pay off for spending 6 hours playing your game.

Performance on a Nvidia Intel based system is a fluent 60fps with everything maxed ( Google how to use Nvidias built in upscaller) I know a person who has a full AMD system that is struggling but I think thats more to do with his APU than anything else. Id say anyone on something modern GPU wise will be pretty fine.
Once they are done releasing the series that ff13 has including x2 and lights return then playing this will also be kinda needed to have any follow on the story.
FF13 x2 is a totally free roam game for those that want such things has no linear path for you to follow at all.
