Unfortunately I cannot recommend this game, because of how buggy it is.
It has a really cool idea and some really great sprites for sure! I really like the whole feel of the game. I bought this in a Humble Bundle, and I did not buy the bundle for this game, so it was a bonus for me. I also played this game in offline mode, so it may say that I have no hours on record, but I have played for almost 4 hours total.
A friend of mine got an error after the second boss. There was a Code Error dialog box that popped up. We're not programmers, so we don't know what it actually meant. But that doesn't look good in a final game (even if it did let him progress).
After playing through multiple tries of the third boss (I spent 1.5 of the 5 hours that I played this game just on this fight), I finally beat the boss. It gave me the achievement for beating the boss, and then glitched and made me redo the entire fight over again. Frustrating, right? So I went ahead and tried a few more times, and I finally beat it a second time. It did the same thing. I was about ready to give up entirely on this game at this point. I read a forum post where this issue was reported to the developer of the game in June 2015. The developer mentioned that they would fix the issue in the next update. Meanwhile, this issue still exists in January 2017. I ended up getting lucky on my third win of this fight that it did not make me redo it, but after all of that frustration, it was very difficult for me to finish this game. I did it, but everything was a breeze after this fight, since there were far less glitches towards the end, at least.
Multiple times throughout the game when I would teleport to the pixel world, it would spawn me inside of a wall, which was an insta death apparently. A few times I got stuck in floors, too.
Also, the default sound effects volume is painfully high in comparison to the music. The sounds can get very repetitive and hard to listen to after playing almost an entire game.
Overall, the game would be recommended if the huge bugs were fixed. But right now, it makes it very had to play. It's about on-par with Crisis City from Sonic 06, and that is saying something.

First of all, I would like to state, that I don't like very much this Steam reviews policy, yes or no, 0 or 1. I believe that it will not give you very precise results about game quality/not quality in the end, even if many reviews are all summed up together.
And I have a problem with such reviewing with exactly this game. 0 or 1, yes or no, as I am not clearly inclined to neither 0 or 1 in this case. In the end, I gave the game 'not recommended' as my subjective opinion.
I am seasoned gamer. I remember 8bit era, from FPS I remember everything from first Wolfenstein (1992) on PC. Regarding this game, technically: nice gfx, game has good controls, you can enhance your skills while progressing through game, this also work quite well (at least for this 2hours I played a game). Game has its funny moments, fortune cookies were my favourites.
But.. it's booring.
If you are younger player, I can recommend this game with score about 7/10. Nothing super special, but it works well, from technical perspective, nothing is failing. And if you are younger player which do not have tons of games (especially FPS) played already, I am sure, that this will not be such boring for you, as it was for me, just because of fact you played less games. Nice humour, lot of action, not many games out there, where you can hack'n'slash with your katana, almost without using any other weapons. If you can get this game for a good discount price, it's really ok.
But, if you played lots of games already, unfortunately there will be almost nothing, with what this game can attract you. Everything was here already and already in better quality. Few funny moments were not enough to keep me focused on game. I caught myself, how I was swinging with katana through enemies and I was thinking about something else, absolutely not paying attention to a game. One street, enemies, slash slash, then some wood, enemies, slash, slash, then some dialog uncovering some very average unexciting story, again some street slash, slash, etc.. For seasoned FPS players, I can give this game 5 maybe 6/10. All points just for technical side of game, which was without any bugs or flaws.
In summary: younger gamers, or gamers which appreciate gory FPS game where you can cut your enemies with katana - recommended. Also if you appreciate watching on ******* bunnies. :)
Other gamers - especially seasoned gamers. Not recommended from me. Nothing new, just repetitive slashing with scripted events. One scripted event following another scripted event, tied together with some uninteresting story. At least in my case after 2 hours of gameplay (4 levels), I was not giving a **** to story behind this game, and there was nothing which was driving me to go to another level.

this game is fun, and i would recommend it, but with some stipulations.
I wanna start by saying i found this game at pax west, and had a really fun time playing it and talking to a couple of the devs. they seemed like cool dudes really passionate about making a good roguelike. and when you play the game you can tell that they have put and are continuing to put lots of time into making the game fun to play.
I will say this - i wanted to *love* this game. I *LOVE* roguelike games. its my favorite genre and i have hundreds of hours into binding of isaac and games like it. I also love action rpg games like diablo and etc, so the fusion of the two seemed like an awesome idea that i wanted to be amazing.
Where i take issue with the game is here:
Take a game like diablo (1/2/3) hardcore mode. Health in that game is easy come easy go. You will take unavoidable damage regularly while playing, but its not only trivial but a major part of the game to stock up on health items. In d2, you'll have a belt full of literally 16 full health potions. So you have a game formula of If you die once you lose your character, and you can take unavoidable damage regularly, BUT you also have excess access to health items.
Now take a roguelike like binding of isaac or enter the gungeon.
It's not so easy to come across health in those games, and if you die once you lose your character. *BUT* you practically never take unavoidable damage or damage unexpectedly. That is to say - everytime you get hit in binding of isaac you're like: oh yeah i let that bullet hit me or i walked into that poison or whatever.
The thing about this game thats been bothering me is that it doesn't have this balance of either of the previous 2 games.
1.If you die your game is over.
2. health is EXTREMELY difficult to come across
3. you incur unavoidable damage regularly.
If you're playing a melee hero, you *CANNOT* avoid taking damage. whereas if you're amazing at binding of isaac you can not take a point of damage for almost the entire game.  This would be okay if health wasn't SO DIFFICULT to come across. you can buy full heals at the end of every level but 1. it makes for a less fun experience and 2. it doesnt address the issue of life in a big level.
Example: the sand worms in the desert. When they spit poison on the ground, you are guaranteed to take a few points of damage because the ground is active immediately. The damage should not begin for a second or two after the visual cue, making it avoidable for the player.
Other problem: for the bow character, the optimal strategy is to basically spam your defensive move nonstop, because the I-frames keep you almost permanently invincible. So how you play her is: spam defensive to one side of the map, shoot your bow 3 times, spam defensive to the other side, bow, defensive, bow, defensive.
Thats the optimal strategy. its right there, there is no other way to play her if you want to do the best.
and its not fun.
The rock golem on the other hand has a much more fun and dynamic playstyle, But then you run into the unavoidable melee damage issues.
Final issue is this: in games like binding of isaac and enter the gungeon, the visual cues for damage sources are SO OVERT. you absolutely cannot miss an object whose frames will cause you damage. It causes you to rarely feel like you took damage where you shouldnt have - which is incredibly frustrating.
In this game, because of the nature of the models and enemies, as well as the visual noise of the map around you, its not easy to tell when an enemy or object is emitting damage frames. I'll find myself being like what the ♥♥♥♥ how did that ♥♥♥♥ing fly just hit me thats ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Stronger visual cues for when you're invincible vs not, when an enemy can damage you vs not, would go a LOOOOONG LONG LONG LONG LONG way imo. because i find myself just being frustrated when i die. whereas in a game like binding of isaac, you almost always see your death coming. In this game i'll abruptly die and be like oh welp run over that was lame.
No words are enough to describe this piece of art!!

The germans start using necromancy and other forbidden things, resulting in the death of a lot of your comrades. Despite that, you start fighting your way through the enemy lines and deeper into the killing fields.
With a variety of weapons supporting you, you are fighting zombies in different shapes, resulting in a generic, repetetive and some times boring combat. The only thing changing is the overall enviroment, meaning you will sometimes be in trenches, sometimes in tunnels, sometimes in buildings [..]
What makes me not recommend the game? Well, for one its the just now mentioned, not very good executed combat, and on the other side it's the bad story writing. It just doesn't feel like the Developers thought everything through, despite the idea beeing such a great one.
Another killer (heh) for me was the really over the top buffed bosses. Bullet Sponges are not real until you tried fighting those.
Hint: The game does not seem to allow screenshots. But maybe that was a problem on my side. Do not buy this from germany, as you will get a low violence version, resulting in even more unsatisfying combat.

Pylon: Rogue is a fun game for those who enjoy difficult action RPG's. This game does mix elements of roguelikes well with it's core mechanics. Pylon: Rogue is no shining star currently, as there are issues of balance and controls. This review covers all content up to the Fire and Ice update.
The game does a good job on making combat enjoyable, with a nice variety of enemies as you progress the game. Enemies only damage the character when they attack, so when each battle has a nice ebb and flow of offence and defence. The navigation map and dungeons have a decent pallete of color, with some subtle variety in dungeon layouts. Dungeons also have a nice risk/reward system where fully clearing a dungeon (instead of just booking it when the exit is revealed) gives a mighty boon. The three characters (Moneydin, Ranger, and Golem) offer unique playstyles from their movesets, which helps with game logevity.
Where the game falls short of being amazing is due to two core elements: dependency of good drops, and having blocky animations/controls. Going through the game is challenging, as players are dependant on luck to get health drops for any damage taken as well as getting upgrades to help in future stages. The only current element of choice is in the shop, which is still random assortment of upgrades. One notable issue is getting upgrades (in shop or as drops) that are pointless because the character already capped that upgrade. The blocky animation/controls is mainly centered around the defensive skills for each character. There is either noticable startup or after-delay from the defensive skills where the character cannot perform any action; some characters also make it difficult to determine visually when they are invulnerable to damage. Aiming light ranged attacks is frustrating, as there is no aim controls. Characters must face/walk in the direction they attack. These elements create a high learning curve need to succeed in the game.
The only progress gained between playthroughs of the game is unlocking new upgrades available for the next run. While the unlocked upgrades do help, it doesn't feel very rewarding for the effort. While this may be alright for more purist rougelike players, I would love to be able to build up a legacy/mastery of each character available. Either through improving starting funds or improve starting stats.
Overall I've had fun with game and hope that it continues to improve. There's plenty of hours of entertainment to be had with this game, but in it's current state not all would enjoy the learning curve needed to progress.

Necrovision - one of *those* games that would really worth to be remade from the very basics, because besides of it's ideas it's filled to the brim with terrible choices and implementations. Hitbox, view, weapons, protagonist style, enemy attacks, sounds - so many thing could be improved. Do you really want to play it? Play it. Are you curious if it's generally worth playing? The answer is a really, really solid no.
TLDR about mechanics: weapon selection is unreliable, headbob is super nauseating and actively prevents gameplay, level and enemy design is boring + last levels is artifically hard with deadly pitfalls and HORDES or knockback enemies. These make the game an unfair chore instead of a fun, or challenging shooter.
The story... let's say it's unique. WW1 happens, then zombies, wraiths, trolls (?)...  a dragon appears, later you defeat mandatory evil german scientist's giant scorpion tank with your walking tank (yes.), only to later realize the vampires, living underground are corrupted by the demons whom Zimmermann allowed into the world, so you have to fight machinegun-wielding vampires, later ratmen equipped iwth flamethrowers while throwing fireballs and stakes out of your magical weapon, only to fight Satan in hell after taking a flying trip with a dragon. YES. THIS IS THE STORY.  I don't know what they were tripping on, but let's just ignore this....
Let's say the ideas are okay. But then I'm still left with a game where I can have 6 items cycling on my key 1, later I have magics on 1 (really bad idea, only forward cycling) AND my one-armed guns, and I have to cycle all 4 with my mouse wheel. Meanwhile keys 6-9 are not even used. What the hell....  and if weapon changing troubles wouldn't be enough, there are a lot of melee enemies who attack by dashing "through" you, as they constantly clip though you. They shriek, they sometimes not even visible because they are IN you, and you are also experiencing the worst headbob I've ever seen. Using submachine gun in iron sights is a trip for seizure-land, and even just ogres being around means a MASSIVE shaking effect that means useless aiming. And as you fight mostly undeads, headshots are a nice way to kill, otherwise it takes 3-5 times more shots. Now if you add this info together that they can stunlock you because you can't aim...  Then on the final levels when you can even fall down into lava they introduce enemies that jump at you, knocking you back super-hard (while using a stock sound asset), because there are no way to make those levels be more hated than that.
If not for the bet/promise that I will finish the game, I would have stopped around chapter 2-3 out of 12...it would have been a definitely better decision.

I came into this expecting a fun and ridiculous romp through the 80's and its various weird foibles and preoccupation with cops, martial arts, and explosions, and it certainly does deliver on those, but it...still wasn't more than okay.
The good news is, it's ridiculous, and the visual style is absolutely perfect.  It feels very 80's, and the action sequences are over-the-top and fun to behold.  It feels very much like what an immature CEO would cook up while binge-watching American Ninja and Bloodsport.  There are even some legitimately cool moments, and some of the jokes, whether poking fun at the 80's or just how inept the main character is at the traditional 80's pre-asskicking puns, are genuinely hilarious.
Unfortunately, there isn't much more to it than that.  The biggest problem I had with the movie is that...well...the eight deadly words.  I didn't care what happened to those people.  No one has any personality, so there's no one to really root for or even hate.  I just...couldn't bring myself to care.  Even the jokes didn't feel organic to the characters making them.  They might as well have been said by backflipping table lamps.  Thing is, this would have been fine if there weren't so many lulls in the action.  If it was flat characters and a neverending action sequence, it would probably have been one of the best movies of its type, but the way it was paced just seemed to want there to be more to the characters than there were.  The absurdity of the premise, meantime, just...wasn't.  The movie just...put the premise out there, counting on it to be funny just from that, so it didn't try to do much that was novel or interesting with it.  Thing is, it wasn't funny to me, so it fell flat.
It's really a shame.  This could have been amazing, but like much of the 80's, it just ends up being forgettable past the style.  Really, the Hoff's music video is most of the best parts of the movie already, so watch that if you want the Kung Fury experience.

Probably one of the most controversial games in the whole saga, up there with XII and XIV 1.0. And boy, does it deserve it!
It does some things well, some things are okay and a bunch of'em very bad, which leaves a taste sweet and sour at the time.
The story starts slow, not knowing what's happening besides there are baddies out there and they wanna kill you. As you progress the history, everything starts unravelling in two timelines, the days before the first one (when you start playing) and in the present (by moving the story forward). It gets quite chaotic sometimes but nothing a quick read on the Datalog cannot repair. As boring and bad was the beginning, I think it changed up to good. From "we bad you good" it changed more into a grey-ish tone at the end, were you cannot feel but think "Damn. He had a point.".
The visuals are stunning, but I've a hard-one for this kind of art, so take that with a pinch of salt. The game suffers for some low level textures that don't mesh well with some of the high res one. For example, in some upclose scenes of Ligthning, everything is detailed but the grip from her gunblade isn't. Maybe it was a problem with my own system but damn.
The music delivers, as expected from a FF title even though it wasn't composed by our dear Nobuo Uematsu. If you're curious to hear some of the best tracks of the title. you can google "Born Anew" (Watch out for the spoilers!) "Blinded by Light" or the heavier "Snow's Theme".
Aaaand the gameplay department. The most controversial of things. In this game, you can only control your main character (that you can change and it's useful to do it due to special skills of each character) and the other ones will act accord a role you have set up (Damage dealer, debuffer, healer, tank...). It starts slow due to not having too much options/party members, but boy it does well later on! You have to constantly switch paradigms to react and adapt or fail on your quest.
Finally, as a port? It sucks so hard ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s could do a series with it. I mean, pressing ESC in fullscreen closes the game without a warning! WTF SE?
Get Durante's GeDoSaTo and fix it by downsampling (game's locked at 720p in vanilla) and having 60FPS.
In the end? Worth the 10 euros. I beat it on 35 hours (story) and farmed a bunch outside of Steam and started doing sidequests. Game clocks at 90 right now and have to still beat the hardest optional bosses.
Already had beaten it on X360 so had an advantage on some encounters and what-to-do. Even if it was a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ port, the PC community always stands up.
Pros:
·Stunning visuals and music
·Interesting gameplay and difficulty
Cons:
·Longass tutorial (Pretty much 10 hour long)
·Doesn't feel like the old FF games without a big space to travel around besides an area you unlock later in the game. No overworld map, city visit...
·Such a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ port. God bless Durante for fixing it!

Feed in tiny portions. While many people have heard that fish require a "pinch" of flake food each feeding, giving them too large a pinch can give the fish digestive problems or make the tank dirty and unhealthy. Whatever type of dry food you are using, only put in as much food as your fish can eat in 3 to 5 minutes. If you put too much food in the tank, scoop it out with a fine net.
Warning: Betta fish should be fed much less than they can eat in 5 minutes. Two or three small pellets per betta is sufficient.
- Soak pellet foods before feeding. Because many aquarium fish have small stomachs, pellets that absorb water and expand in size may cause digestive problems or bloating in your fish. Soak the pellets in water for 10 minutes before feeding so they expand before the fish eat it, rather than in the fish's stomach.
- Feed the fish once or twice a day. Because it is much easier to overfeed most fish than to give them too little food, one feeding a day may be safer. However, if you are careful to give them small amounts of food as described above, you may feed the fish twice a day. Some aquarium owners prefer this because the fish become more active and interesting to watch during feeding.
- Look for signs of overfeeding. If a trail of poop is hanging from your fish, their intestine may be partially blocked due to overfeeding or the wrong type of food.[12] If the water gets dirty enough that you need to do a water change more than once a week, you may be overfeeding the fish, or the tank may be overcrowded. Reduce the amount of food per serving or the number of servings per day to see if the problem goes away within a few days. Ask an aquarium store employee or fish raising hobbyist for advice if it does not.
- Spread out the food so everyone gets some. Even within the same species, the larger or more aggressive fish may not leave enough food for the other fish. Reduce the chance of this happening by dividing the food and adding it to more than one area of the tank, or by sprinkling it evenly across the entire water surface.

I really enjoyed the music of this game, the art style, and much of the gameplay. It's a platformer in which the graphics and gameplay advances a bit as you go along, much like in Evoland, albeit at a far slower pace. There are four worlds, the first two of which each contain 12 levels followed by a boss fight, and the latter two which each contain 18 levels followed by a boss fight. The game presents the first world as an Atari game, the second as a Gameboy game, the third as an NES game, and the fourth as an SNES game. You'll see a few enemies that are obvious references to enemies from other games, and plenty of jokes and references to games of yore as well. You would expect those, and they're pretty fun.
I already said I liked the music, but seriously, the music is quite awesome in this game, so I'm mentioning it again. One thing that's a very nice feature in this game that sets it apart from other platformers is a realm you enter when you die, which is like a sort of mirror version of the world with various differences, enemies and collectibles of its own, and this gives you a second chance to find a portal back to the normal realm, or even use the other realm to move ahead a bit in the level before finding a later portal to cross back over. It's nice! You don't run out of lives or anything.
In fact, the trailer for the game itself specifcally says "you will die. But you always get a second chance," and it shows you dying, then running around in the other realm and going back through a portal. Cool, huh? Except when it flat out lies about you
getting a second chance that way. The third boss of the game is positively infuriating. You are running away from the boss, and if she catches you or you hit anything in the environment you shouldn't, you pass over into the other realm. Guess what? The other realm is packed to the brim with spikes on the ceilings and walls with no portals, so it's impossible to get back to the normal realm, and you die after a few seconds of invulnerability when the floor/wall/ceiling spikes touch you because you can't proceed without touching them.
I've probably died 40+ times trying to get past that part so far, and it took what was a charming and mostly relaxing game for me, and turned it into a profanity-spewing evening for me. It's an aggravating "tonal shift" in that the rest of the game follows the "second chance" principle promised by the trailer, but this part does not. I wouldn't mind the second chance lie if they at least had a well-placed checkpoint during the dash away from the boss, but there's not, so I had to keep redoing really easy stuff which takes a minute every time before hitting the parts that are generally fatal. The farthest I got was to a wing powerup located up a couple of vertical jumps, just before a long stretch of spikes in the distance. Every single time I make it that far, the boss touches me and I die, and have to start the whole thing over again.
If you'd like to know how difficult this was, if you've played Ori and the Blind Forest, I beat that game, and it had boss-dash stuff in it that was pretty aggravating. Anywho, this boss spoiled the good mood this game had been putting me in and left me angry and cut off from playing through the SNES portion of the game, which is a part of the payoff to getting through each world. I'm not claiming to be very good at games, so you might enjoy this game if you're skilled enough to pull off the escape from this boss which is handled differently than the advertising claims and differently than the way you play the rest of the game (never forced to rush until now).
I, however, do not recommend this game to anyone who isn't highly skilled at games, or you may find yourself stuck by a segment of the game which it does nothing to prepare you for in regard to the sudden pacing. Getting stuck is annoying, but getting stuck by part of the game that comes out of nowhere and is nothing like the rest of the game is just cheap.

An evocative, atmospheric action platformer with essentialist design that fuses classic and modern mechanics alike.
Nothing in terms of gameplay is original in this title, but then again, you probably have got more Call of Duties than platformer games. The magic of this title comes from how it approaches player progression and its world designs.
Nothing feels tedious in Hollow Knight. Exploration, character progression, earning currency, advancing story, backtracking are all fused together and have a seamless feeling of being paced just so. Although you could grind, you will quickly learn that it is pointless as you gradually aquire currency while trotting through the fairly linear progression of the game. The world may seem big and open at first, but you get restrictions as to where you can go based on a large number of your abilities, hence the linearity. Speaking of a platformer game, the abilities we're talking about are fireball, slide through the air, off-wall jump, ect.ect. Your character start as a vanila Mario-with-sword and gets one significant ability every now and again as you're exploring the game. Each time you get one of these, new areas become availabe to you, and you will clearly know where to go. You do not get lost in this game even though you're also exploring the game.
Itemization and customization are minimalistic, but in the same time, significant, as the passive abilites provided alter the game mechanics in a very noticable way. For instance, most of your enemies are on a hit counter from your sword. Some take two hits, some take three, ect. If you use an item that somehow damages your foes more, that is a big change.
You do get a few places that have got a quirky platformer design, places that your ordinary, run-of-the-mill Mario would not be able to go. Provided he is not flying, that is...Thankfully, you do get out of your ordinary Mario state pretty quickly :D. Those may pose a challange, but are mostly side content that does not impede progress, plus, the difference from person to person will be based on practice alone. Keyboard is absolutely fine for the game, despite what it says from the beginning.
The game, as a whole, is not difficult. It is a Metroidvania platformer action-reaction, so the learning curve will vary. I do not think it will become annoying to anyone though, especially since you also have players choice in combat.
With all the boring necessities out of the way, this brings me to my favourite part about this game: Art and Character design. People, perhaps somehow liberally, compare it to Dark Souls the First. One could argue about differences and similarities, but I think Hollow Knight deserves it's own rather than comparison because its world is unique. From the characters, to the music, to the story, the atmosphere, the places you explore, Hollow Knight holds independently as to how it presents itself. Take that you loot-box-infused tripple A's. And this, surprisingly, will be end of this section. I will not spoil anything for you guys. Just enjoy this little game.
If you like playing video games, I think, you will, at least, appreciate Hollow Knight. You may very well end up liking it a lot.

Ok so where to begin. First off you're going to read a dozen great reviews of this game that are pretty generic. They claim the game is the best, should have been game of the year yada yada yada. I'm here to tell you all that is bull crap!
let's start with graphics and overall look of the game. The graphics are pretty indy, polished but nothing the PS2 couldn't have put out. The color scheme is mostly bland and black and white at times. The art direction of the game is awesome, however. It appears to be inspired from Miyazaki, and Don Bluth, that steam punk secret of Nimh look. Now on to story... um where to begin. It's not intuitive at all and nearly non existent. I won't spoil things it kinda comes together as you play and at the end but leaves you wondering: why am i doing what i'm doing (other than just completing the game). This game is suppose to be "Metroidvania" , that means it has a an extensive map that allows for backtracking and powerups along the way that help you explore more of the map.
I'll break this down into what it has in common with those 2 games (super metroid and castlevania symphony of the night). Like symphony of the night you have a sword, you can double jump, and smash walls to reveal secrets. Like super metroid there are a couple of items that make navigation easier: like a mantis claw and a moth wing that allows climing on walls (or rather wall jumping), and the ability to dash forward in the air or ground. Unlike both of those games you can still be significantly damaged by early level enemies. Castlevania and metroid also offer a progressive difficulty level that eventually plateaus allowing for navigation and exploration. Hollow Knight fails in this category and yields to what most indy games do: tedious monotony and unforgiving deaths. ( I will add that I kinda enjoy a Nintendo level difficulty that allows me to push the limits of my platforming skills)
Controls: This is where the game falls on it's face at times. It recomends playing with a controller. I played this with a wired Xbox one controller licensed by Microsoft. That said, the controls are very very unresponsive at times. you have some excellent navigation abilities with jumping that allows you to maneuver in the air. However, if you take damange your jump is limited and the B button (the charge to heal/ spell button) becomes unresponsive. for instance if you take damage and begin to hold B you will not charge a heal. you must take damage wait until your knight lands and stands up before you can heal. This can really throw off your game, and is something you will have to get use to very early on to be able to take on some of the challenging bosses. If you fall into a pit or a bed of nails your knight will respawn. once respawned your ability to jump is non existant, yet you can move forward and back. If not careful you will simply walk right back into the pit. There are also several challenges that you must do a jumping downward strike in order to bounce  your way across an obstacle. if you make the slightest error there is very little recovery time, not to mention you must hold the analog joystick at an angle to bounce forward. If you are off by a little you will simply slash foward and fall into the trap.
Bosses: Bosses for the most part are challenges on the level of R-Type where you must master their paterns of attack with little to no opportunity to heal. This is especially difficult with bosses that have "random" projectile or lazer attacks that do massive damage, depend on where you are standing, and if you are lucky (and i emphasize luck) enough to be in a location where they are not hitting. Often you are forced to rely on a pattern of charms in order to afford you the opportunity to best said bosses. This coupled with the damage system is reminiscent of the legend of zelda. The worst of it can  be that you are trapped fighting the same boss do to the death system. If you die fighting certain bosses/ trying to solve certain challenges you must try to recover your spirit. You'll end up fighting your way back to that location with less mana (souls) which becomes very redundant due to save locations. I wouldn't gripe about this at all if you didn't lose all the money you had in dying (it can be recovered by taking back your soul).
tutorials and game instructions: doesn't exist and I solute the designers for not putting them in the game. A game should be uncovered and explored, it's part of the journey as a player as well as the hero.
The game has frustrated me but pushed me to continue. I don't recommend this for casual gamers at all. Be ready to dedicate a minimum of 40 hours to this game if you want to beat it. There are multiple secrets and challenges as well which require more game play. I give this a 7 out of 10 . It's by no means game of the year, but it is pretty fun. symphony of the night blows it out of the water, it's a fun dirivitive though

Pylon Rogue is an excellent top-down rogue-like, it brings a refreshing combat system and a unique environment to the genre.  I highly recommend this game to those that enjoy rogue-like's.
The gameplay is solid, you manually move your character and attack, there is not auto attack or click-to-move.  There are two classes (currently) to choose from a palandin or ranger, melee or range respectively.  Each class has their own unique skills, 1 main attack, 1 defensive ability, and 1 active skill.  You can find items throughout your current game session that grant passive buffs.
how the game works, there is an overworld map.  You choose a stage and complete them.  Within each stage are multiple locked rooms.  The goal is to find the exit, to do so you have to clear each room to find the portal.  You do not have to clear all the rooms, but if you do so, a bonus chest appears with items.
I don't really have any negatives for this game, overall it is a positive experience, it has a great foundation to build upon.
The dev's are super active and helpful in the forums, definitely stop by and ask any questions or suggestions you may have.
From a hours to price ratio, you will definitely get your money's worth and more once content starts getting released.  This game is a must have either now or later down the road.

NecroVision is another one of those last generation games on Steam that you wish you could give neither a thumbs up or thumbs down, but rather a so/so recommendation. That being said, there's more reasons to not recommend this title than there are to inspire you to purchase it. Developed by Farm 51, the same company that brought us Painkiller: Hell & Damnation, NecroVision takes place during the first World War; more specifically the year is 1916, and you play as Private Simon Bukner, an American soldier who was recently recruited into the British army.
Things start out interestingly enough, and you will find that the game captures your attention for the first five or six levels out of the twelve that it houses. After the halfway mark though, the title ends up taking a series of weird twists and turns that detach it from its original selling point. The idea of having a zombie FPS shooter that takes place during World War I is interesting, and the first handful of chapters do a great job in capturing the era of the early 1900's. In fact, they have a very Return to Castle Wolfenstein quality to them, but soon afterward you will find yourself battling through hellish and industrial maps that are more Painkiller inspired than anything else.
The plot ends up changing from World War I soldiers battling zombie hordes, to throwing vampires into the mix. A weird change up, yes, but not totally a write-off. However, soon after the prospect of vampires is introduced, the game then decides that it wants to be about humans and vampires versus demons, and then demons versus vampires, and then demons versus demons; needless to say, NecroVision cannot really decide what supernatural horror entity it wishes to focus on at all, but after the first set of levels the zombies are absolutely nowhere to be found, and neither is the World War I era focus.
Flip-flopping plots, enemies, and levels aside, the voice acting for Simon seems to fluctuate just as often. Since he is from the southern part of the United States, sometimes he'll have a southern accent, sometimes no accent at all, at times his voice will be deeper than others, and other times he will sound completely demonic. There is absolutely no consistency here with anything, including the sound level mixes that see to it that some dialogue gets completely lost within the gothic aria soundtrack during cutscenes. It should also be noted here that if you're a fan of subtitles, you will notice a lot of grammar mistakes and the inclusion of lines that aren't actually spoken. To its credit, the environmental graphics of NecroVision still hold up today and can be compared to Call of Duty: World at War.
There's also the matter of the excruciatingly disorienting motion blur and headbob effects; the former of which you can turn off in the graphic options, but it doesn't seem to do anything at all. More often than not, I found myself having to look away from the screen every once in a while as I was fighting armies of enemies, since every hit causes the screen to blur and jostle around. Not to mention, the massive troll and orc looking foes that contribue to the almost motion sickness inducing special effects by stomping around. So if you're prone to motion sickness, or if you have any medical conditions that could be triggered by this, most definitely steer clear.
The gameplay is primarily your standard FPS game, with the added bonus of a large arsenal of fun weapons and guns. Nearly every level has a giant boss that you'll need to battle. About halfway through the title you will also pick up a "Shadow Glove" that will allow you to use spells such as fireballs, ice, and stakes. Other mechanics that contribute to the uniqueness of NecroVision are being able to perform combos, such as chaining a melee hit with a gunshot, and the fury meter which will cause you to be able shoot and reload faster the more quickly you dispatch foes. You're also allowed to slow time down with the focus ability, so that you can concentrate on getting much needed headshots; as anything even remotely humanoid will take forever to kill unless you blow their brains out.
When it comes down to it, NecroVision is just plain weird. While I'm all for that, it's not a game that's weird in a good way. If it had just stuck with its original plan of being a World War I zombie FPS, instead of trying to have all kinds of unwarranted plot twists and dimension shifts, it would've faired much better. To be honest, I had to force myself to continue playing after the sixth level, as the game just became inane and dull at that point; even with its large arsenal of guns and plethora of enemies. Be wary, as this title does like to completely freeze up on occasion, and may cause you to hard crash your PC on Windows 10. If you've really run out of World War I or horror FPS games, then give this one a shot when you're bored. Otherwise, leave this one until you need to scrape the bottom of the barrel.

This is the first time I ever write a review/opinion of a game before actually finishing it, But since I own and finished the original Bioshock, and I just spent over an hour playing this remastered version, I simply don't understand why so many people are complaining.
Let's start with what I noticed so far.
1-The visuals have been completely revamped, the textures look a lot better and more defined, water effects are improved, and the lighting effects, and shadows look a lot better than the original. Anyone saying the visuals look the same, or are hardly improved, need their eyes checked, or maybe play the game with something better than a potato. I played both games, and as soon as I started playing this Remastered version, I noticed a HUGE difference. An overall much better experience when it comes to the visuals.
2-A lot of people are complaining about the mouse acceleration issue. I have used gaming mice with adjustable DPI's for years, and when I played the original Bioshock I was already using one, so I personally never had this issue. On this Remastered version, I adjusted the sensitivity setting to 2, and the DPI on my mouse, and the experience is perfect for me. No issues of any kind. People who claim/ or people who are experiencing mouse issues, should at least try to search the forums for help, or try fixing the problem themselves for more than 5 minutes, before posting useless reviews complaining about a new version of an absolutely amazing game.

This is Blockstorm, a new FPS about blocks and customization. It may look generic, or a shameless rip-off of games like Minecraft or Ace of Spades, but seriously, don't be fooled, it is a lot more than you think.
Overview
Blockstorm is a multiplayer only shooter set in a world of blocks, where you build, destroy and customize. As a shooter, it follows the classic rules of an FPS: precision aiming, crouching, jumping, running and noiseless walking, everything you'd find in other shooters out there. However, it relies on player interaction with the map to make matches the more dynamic they can be. This interaction happens in the form of building and destroying.
By using the provided equipment, players are able to tear entire buildings down, create alternative paths, blow up walls, build stairs, reinforce, connect structures, anything you might imagine. It helps making gameplay distinctive and unique, according to what players come up with in-game.
Weapons are pretty much common to any FPS, being them: assault rifle, light machine gun, sniper rifle, handgun, two shotgun types, sub-machine gun and machine pistol, each of them dealing a given amount of damage to players and blocks. Explosives are also available: C4, grenades, claymores and RPG, which are the most fun weapons you have at your disposal. Finally, you have the shovel and the placeable block, which will be the main tools you'll be using to modify and customize the battlefield during game time.
To help map makers create a larger array of maps, NPCs are also available. For now, there are two types: zombies and automated turrets. Zombies have simple spot-and-seek behavior, and can be used in any map kind. Turrets work as defensive structures, and can be used in any game mode. Both of them can be configured with a nice array of settings, like health, movement speed, etc.
Some maps will let the player man a mech, which is equipped with rocket launcher and gatling gun, and is capable of hovering and performing high jumps, making it a good tool to navigate through the map and clear enemies out.
It also provides amazing tools for those who like to customize or create their own content. Maps, equipment, NPCs, characters...anything can be created or customized in the blink of an eye and made available in the workshop.
Game Modes
For now, there are six available game modes:
Deathmatch
Universal game mode: kill anyone to score.
Team Deathmatch
Universal game mode: kill enemy team to score for your team.
CTF
Universal game mode: get enemy flag and deliver it to your base to score for your team.
Hunt
Original one: obtain blocktanium atoms from zombies or blocktanium pods and bring them to your base to score.
Castle Battle
Original one: destroy enemy chests and throne to score while defending yours from enemy attacks.
Assault
Original one: a simplified and asymmetric version of territory domination, where one team must dominate a target, while the other must defend it.
All of them work quite well, and each one has a good selection of built-in maps.
Balancing
Weapons are very well balanced, and they will only get overpowered in the hands of an overpowered/skilled player. Before each spawn, you are able to choose your loadout, each gun adds weight to your loadout, and the general rule is that the most damage and destruction power means the slowest run speed, so it is almost impossible to rampage around without being exposed to enemy attacks.
Built-in maps are also pretty well balanced, rarely encouraging camping, as it means, most of the time, acting as target practicing, not to mention being quickly dispatched with a C4 from behind a wall.
You can find the best suitable play style for you as long as you get used to the loadout you decide to use, for real, without relying on overpowered damage or movement speed.
So, by the way it is for now, game is well balanced.
Customization
Blockstorm's main and strongest feature. Almost everything can be customized. All editors are based in the same idea, and every content produced with them can be shared (via workshop, or in-game), and locked, if you wish to keep it only to yourself.
Maps
A powerful editor lets you build maps ranging from all degrees of complexity, being you a master architect or just a newbie in the world of map building. Tools are available to speed up building process, such as brushes, default forms, paint tools, selection tools, etc. Map editor allows you to toy with many different settings, such as environment, weapon slots, weapons available while spawing, boundaries, and other variables that can be applied to your map. Another important feature is the ability to create prefabs, which are useful tools to reuse something you might want in more than one map.
There's also a terrain generator that helps you create the initial settings of your map, with a decent array of options, such as size, height, type, etc.
A tinting tool also lets you add a hue layer over block textures, expanding even more the possibilities.
Every built-in map is also fully customizable.
Characters
Characters are the skins you wear and determine how will your player model look in-game. Character editor lets you build your own character, by using the same tools available in map editor. For now, you are able to edit each body part separately: head, torso, arms, legs, hands and feet. Arms, legs, hands and feet are mirrored. The way it is right now, it is impossible to implement different body parts for each side, but in fact, it won't never ruin the overall quality of it, neither prevent you from creating a good looking character. Character default skeleton can't be removed, but the limits around it are reasonably good, good enough to make any adaptation, and anything but creativity limitators.
Game comes with a good selection of built-in characters, which are fully customizable, and can be used as models for easy implementation of any other character you might think about.
It uses a different idea from the map editor, using colored blocks instead of textured ones.
Guns
Every gun and piece of equipment present in the game, except for C4, claymores and grenades (and the placeable block, of course), is customizable.
Each customizable gun or equipment works as the starting template for a custom version, and like characters, they have a default skeleton, which can't be removed, and, unlike character editor, some guns are pretty limited in terms of new possibilities and sculpts that wander too far from the default skeletons.
Like the character editor, this editor uses colors instead of textures.
NPCs
Turrets have a similar editor to guns and character editors, being based on colored blocks, with also a default, fixed skeleton. It will let you build each part of it, with decent space.
Zombies can be customized in the same way you would a player character.
Mechs
Mechs are also fully customizable (within the limitations of a default skeleton, like guns and player characters). Leg and arm parts are mirrored. Body, waist, right hand and gatling gun can be edited separately, and both hand and gatling gun have no default skeleton.
Community
Now this is where Blockstorm gets the high ground. Here we have a friendly community, with players that like to discuss and give feedback, and developers which actually listen to what we say, and that's a really big thing.
Server Availability
For now, there are a lot of server types, including TDM only, DM only, ranked servers with workshop content, etc. Most servers become full during night time, but it highly depends on the time zone of your country. You will, of course, find toxic players while playing, but there is a report tool ready to use, should you find it useful to warn the community.

As someone who has put in 800+ hours in Civ V and god knows how much in IV and III, it sucks to admit that I'm pretty dissapointed with CIV:BE. Overall, it's a fun new experience, but doesn't compare to Alpha Centuri and its UI is begging for a patch out of the box.
Summary:
+Affinities are a great expansion to how your units and cities look like.
+Enhanced narrative through sidequests / city state colonies
+Social policies have been put into 4 trees and it works well!
+Harmony affinity / alien units are pretty rad!
+Terrain generation is really cool and has good variety.
+Spying has been improved so you can stage a Coup and snag an entire city if you're successful.
- [~personal] I'm not a fan of how units are perma upgraded now.
- [~personal] CIV:BE feels like it chose visuals over gameplay
- No natural wonder equivalents [ Gimme a badass Volcanoe that gives +8 science!]
- No religion of any kind [ Gimme cyber future religion!]
- UI could use a LOT of color differentiation [ In the Tech Tree I can't tell what's a building and what's a wonder].
- Affinities should function like ideology [Once you pick one you stick with it rather than juggle 3 of them].
- [~personal] Another thing that bogs this title down is the limited expressions and butchered fake voice acting for some leaders (Slavic Federation and Brasilia; Kozlov's voice is just some Berkeley hipster reading off Google Translate with a Russian accent / which is odd because Catharine's voice in V was 100% authentic. )
+/- Trade works the same way as in Civ V, and thats ok I guess.
+/- Diplomacy is exactly the same and thats ok too, I guess
+/- No Nukes / Mass Destruction
+/- No Space Mongolians / Space bandits
At the end of the day, while it does offer a brand new experience, an impressive terrain script and an expanded narrative in the form of quests, I cannot recommend this game in its current state at its current price until it's at least patched and some gameplay elements are significantly improved.

Want to experience the worst netcode in the history of online gaming? Do you enjoy balance philosophy that revolves around the phrase "wouldn't it be cool if"? Then look no father!
Let me just start off by saying that I've been looking forward to this game for a long time. I was a frequent tournament-goer for Super Smash Bros. Melee years back, and after watching Nintendo ♥♥♥♥ up the following two entries in the series, I'm sure there were plenty of people like me who were excitedly anticipating a game in the same vein that was actually designed to be competitive. But alas, the excitement did not last long. But hey, let's start with what's good.
- The art style and sound design are pretty freaking great. There's obviously been a lot of love poured into the character sprites and animations and you can really feel it. The stages in kind are wonderfully detailed, especially that giant plant who will ruin your day repeatedly on the treetop level. The music and sound effects all fit in with the aesthetic are are really a treat most of the time. My only complaint here is that some things are just a little too similar to Smash Bros. to the point where it feels less like "inspiration" and more like "copy paste".
- The game (at least when it's offline) runs just as smooth as you would hope it does. It's easy to link attacks together to create dynamic combos just like you would in Smash Bros. Landing lag is virtually non-existent so the game maintains a very fast pace that is certainly tailored to the preferences of Melee players like me. It's great.
Okay, now let's move on.
- The netcode. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥is it bad. It's like Super Smash Bros. Brawl all over again. If you want to get good at this game, you better learn how to play through a soft delay at minimum to 3+ second input lag at worst. Matches that actually feel smooth are so rare that when you finally get into one you'll start playing badly because you'll be so used to the lag. And with no way of seeing your opponent's ping before a match, you have no way of filtering your matches. "Early Access" isn't an excuse at this point when so many other Early Access games, especially ones like this that are born for online play, have near perfect netcode right out of the gate. But hey, maybe I'm just spoiled by the buttery smoothness of Rising Thunder's dream netcode.
- Parrying. There are actually some huge key differences between this game and Smash Bros. that chance the way you play the game pretty radically. Number one is that there is no blocking or grabbing. That system is replaced entirely by parrying. Now on paper it seems like a good way to make the game a lot more aggressive and keep characters that would otherwise be way too safe on their toes. On paper. In application parrying makes the more defensive zone-control characters even more powerful than they would be if they just had a shield or even just a spot dodge. Why? Because unlike parries or perfect blocks in other games that just give you a frame advantage, a successful parry in Rivals of Aether puts your opponent in a stun state that allows you to counter attack. This effectively means that unless you opponent is being juggled, using ground attacks is suicide because you will simply be parried and destroyed. It doesn't bother Wrastor too much due to his heavy aerial emphasis, but it screws over every other aggressive character and turns fights between defensive characters into an even slower affair where both sides are afraid to go in for the kill because one parry and they could be dead. It's a huge example of "cool idea, terrible execution".
- There are no ledges and instead everybody gets one wall jump that also resets their up special. This, just like parrying, was clearly an attempt to make the game more exciting and aggressive but actually ends up removing a substantial amount of depth from the game. Now if you haven't played Smash Bros., ledges are, as you might expect, the corners of the stage where characters could traditionally "latch" onto. This meant that everybody's recovery was in practice a little bit better than it seemed because you didn't have to get back onto the stage, just to the ledge. But the ledge was more than that. Because it also gave you a brief window of invulnerability, it served as an analogue to the "wake up" scenario in many traditional fighting games. Just like in wake up situations, the disadvantaged player has decision priority and must make the correct decision to get back into a more nuetral position, whereas the advantaged player is trying to guess that decision and punish it. Rival of Aether's wall jump reset replacement accomplishes almost none of the same depth that ledges provided, and instead creates a situation in many matchups where the recovering player has such a ridiculously limited range of options that recovering is not a matter of outplaying your opponent but instead simply hoping that they make a huge mistake, and that's never good design.
Now, as with all Early Access games, there's always room for improvement, and maybe, in time, these issues will be improved upon, but at the time of this review, I simply cannot recommend this game at all, even if you are a Smash Bros. fan. By all means, hit that "Follow" button to keep an eye on this game's progress, but don't fork out your dough yet.

Due to my comment on the game being a "Total Conversion with half of the content any TC normally has" I feel that due to me changing that view just a tad, I give this game another go, removing my own disappointment as what I try to do for reviews.
The game is actually fairly decent, though there are a few things that made me disappointed in it, though from the eyes of you, a consumer who has not bought this yet who likely doesn't have civ 5 yet and hasn't previously known about this game.
So the game borrows from civ 5 a decent amount. Mainly just obvious mechanics bits like yield types, tile movement/tile shape (which the shape is actually more graphical ofcourse) and research, while other mechanics have been changed/expanded to be a bit more realistic.
The game is really fun starting out, better than ever, the early game is filled with options and is alot more fun than I previously realized. The mid-game does have a decent number of other options aswell with the affinities included, they make the civilizations slightly more different between one another which helps make player civs less samey and installs some variety.
Unfortunately, the late-game sadly is hurting for the moment. Not much to do in the late game with the victory types mostly being... well samey, all of them requiring more than 20 turns, a couple needing large stockpiles of money.
Due to my body trying to troll me and actually suceeding (Which is entirely unrelated, had possibly spoiled eggs in dinner), I will instead now link Angry Joe's video review of the game as it pretty much shows nearly all of my favorite and least favorite bits about the game...
Save for how settlers create outposts which slowly grow into cities in 5-7 turns and must be defended until then. Which is a pretty fun and neat feature since it can allow you to deny expansion if you have vision over the land enough near an AI.
Overall, I'll rate this game at a 5/10. It could use some expansions, patches and just some TLC and I could easily see it getting more enjoyable than Civ 5 is now with all expansion DLCs. Only time will tell.
I personally can only hope that Beyond Earth can stand the test of time... until the next civ game inevitably makes it old news, potentially expanding upon BE or simply dropping it like how Firaxis did after AC's Alien Crossfire expansion which I hear was a disappointment of similar proportions, but I have never once palyed it in my life and that kinda bums me out.
Feel free to get it if you're more convinced, I do recommend it. Due to personal preference, it's not a strong recommendation, more or less a shaky one suspended upon the condition that the game be updated and just given more love which it honestly could use.

: Very weak. This is (To my knowledge) the first Hitman game where they really attempted to give more depth to the protagonist, 47's, character. And it..... left much to be desired. The overall plot within the game wasn't absolutely terrible, but very predictable after awhile and the ending was extremely anti climatic and quite frankly, stupid. This is mainly where the game falls flat on it's face for me, had the plot actually had some interesting points to it I might have really really enjoyed this game more, but it didn't. The characters were very colorful, but I never felt connected with them. That being said, I did very much enjoy the game overall, mainly because of the gameplay itself, where Hitman games really shine.
-------------------------
: The gameplay in both Hitman games I've played (Blood Money and obviously Absolution) have been exceptional (At least in my opinion) delivering exceptionally open ended levels with set targets or objectives, and plenty of optional objectives and challanges. To condense it,  a typical mission has at least a solid dozen ways to kill your target, ranging from a wide variety of methods. From poisoning, sniping, dropping objects on, pushing off cliffs, blowing up, planting explosives, shooting with a giant whale harpoon, disguising as a decorative samurai and stabbing as they walk by, spiking cocaine, dropping a car on them, embedding an axe in their skull, to electrocuting them, or setting up a gas explosion; the options are virtually limiteless. There are multiple ways to approach a target as well, from taking a maintenance uniform as disguise, to running in guns blazing, sneaking along back alleys, blending with a crowd, or disguising as a scarecrow and creeping through a cornfield. And of course, general killing and mayhem is super fun as well, tossing guys out windows, strangling, throwing a knife into their head, and then silently disposing of their body in a leaf mulcher - this Hitman game makes it just plain fun to kill people. And since that was, of course, the objective of the game, to kill targets, it nailed it. Combat and gameplay in Absolution is superb.
There is a very nice point system built into Absolution as well - the game automatically tracks your poitns (Based on how silent you are, headshots, signature kills, if you were spotted, etc.) and uploads those scores at the end of each level to their leaderboards. Then, if any of your Steam friends play that level themselves, they'll see your highscore displayed at the top when they begin, giving them a little incentive to try and beat your score, and vice versa. Some people do not like the points system but I thought it was a good way to encourage stealth and I found myself specifically reloading levels to try and beat my friends score.
It is also worth noting that Absolution can be a VERY, VERY hard game, if you want it to be. There are 6 difficulty settings in the game - the highest difficulty offers you no assistance from outside intel, much more enemies per level, much harder objectives, and overall increases the difficulty to near impossible, presenting even the most hardcore Hitman fans with crazy challanges.
: If you have played Absolution and liked it, or are at all interested in Hitman games, I would recommend also checking out Hitman: Blood Money
-------------------------
: The graphics in Absolution are very very nice, and in many ways unique. The developers use of glare, bloom, and FOV make the game a bit harder to run for some, but pay off in very deep graphics. I did notice that the FOV and everything else combined, didn't present the most crisp graphics, but it did provide a very atmospheric feel to it, and certainly felt as if it fit the game. The colors were especially rich and vibrant. The settings in the game varied greatly, some missions were in noisey crowds in Chinatown, others in nightclubs, some in hospitals or secret facilities, and others in the dusty streets of small towns. These varieties in settings provided a constant changing backdrop to your murders and always presents new ways to kill.
-------------------------
- Yes, the game has so many options of how to kill, as well as extremely hard challanges such as finishing everything silently, or 'Suit Only' (Meaning you complete everything without taking a single disguise) and offers enticing options for replaying missions.
-------------------------
: Hitman Absolution delivers very fun gameplay and a great challange on most missions, and while the plot felt weak, I would recommend the game.

Yes, despite being 2014, if you click Esc, you quit the game. No questions asked, anything. Can you imagine after a hard fight pressing Esc to, you know, breathe a little, that was hard!.. Nope, you'll have to repeat that one again. Horrible, horrible idea..

Then comes the storyline itself. Despite loving the Final Fantasy storylines, I actually would love to, you know, PLAY! While I was playing this I got the impression I was playing 15 minutes, seeing a 20minute cutscene, playing for another 15minutes.. The cutscenes are breathtaking, mind you! I just rather prefer playing instead of seeing a movie of it..
The whole amount of space needed to play this game is ridiculous...60 GB?! Like, really?? I'm on a laptop here; needless to say, I felt the need to part ways with some of my most loved games for this.. well..90% of them... That's a no-no here as well.
The graphics are nice, the gameplay is nice as well and the storyline is compelling, all in all. Just expect HOURS of cutscenes and plenty of GBs taken from you.
I still think it's a good game and overall playable and enjoyable, so go get yours today if you're okay with the cons.

This is a difficult game to review... one of the most difficult I must say. On one point the game is awesome and briliant that you want to shout out: 'PEOPLE PLAY THIS GAME IT IS AWESOME!' and at the same time there are things about this game that are utterly garbage and stupid that make you wanna scream warnings: 'STAY AWAY FROM THIS'
This game is hard to get into and easy to bounce off and never try it again. Let me go into some details... the begining is horrible, this aint no Call of Duty shooter that is for sure so people who are rather utter amateurs of this genre will most likely say: this game is f*cked up and unistal, but I am used to difficult FPS games so I just went through it. It gets a bit better later but not perfect and the know how to do stuff in this game aka tutorial is almost non existent which is very bad cause this game has some interesting mechanics that arent typicaly find in most FPS out there.
Another bad thing is chaos... there is so much chaos and it gets extremely difficult to grasp with your mind what is happening as you get constantly and heavily receiving damage (luckily this game is more like serious sam/quake/doom style so you can take quite a few hits). Also the storyline is really bad, and actors are quite bad. And there are many glitches and 'something went wrong with the script' moments but I didnt find any game breaking bugs that would ruin the game for me. Yes it is very rough around the edges and you can feel the low buget this game mustve had but at the same time I cannot ignore the many great things this game has that are hard to find in games these days...
Despite poor storyline the lore of the game is very good and has a great atmosphere. The whole WWI trenches mixed with horror gore that seems heavily inspired by Clive Barker's style is great, it feels even greater then Return to Castle Wolfenstein horror elements and I would even say that it is slightly better then Bloodrayne. The whole world is dark, dirty and devastated. I really loved the vibe this game has despite the poor storyline.
The other thing that is most awesome is fighting and physic model. You shoot off head, arms and legs of human (or human like) enemies. It creates a really juicy gore feel of firefights and gives you the 'sick satisfaction' with every kill.
I love zombies, and here there are lot of moments where you fight a horde o zombie german soldiers and with the gory elements mentioned before it creates a mix that for me it has this special charm to it. The overal shooting is really difficuly to adjut but once you start to 'feel' the game more you start to get much more fun from it and that is where I am right now and that is  why despite all the flaws and problems this game has, I must put my thumb up as I found what I came here for, it wasnt pretty and painless but in the end satisfining.
I wish they could create a remake of this game where they polish and improve the bad things. Overall the idea behind this game and some feauters are truly uniqe and briliant

Long ago, I played the demo of this game when I was a child. It was one of my favourite games ever!
Now, I get the full game and I can tell that this is a very good and enjoyable game to this day!
How can this game tagged as a mixed one on Steam??? I check the majority of the negative reviews and most of them are just complaining about how this game is lagging/doesn't work on their operation system at all. I feel that this is not fair at all, people are going to miss an awesome game. D: It's just a very old game so it needs an optimization! Still, it's up to you to buy it or not! Get it cheaper: I bought mine for 2 tf2 keys! I hope they will do something against this lagging stuff too.
For me it's running good, no lags or anything bad!
Anyway, back to the game:
I really like the atmosphere of this game, the map/model makers did a good job on it. The castles, the forest and the towns are idyllic and beautiful!
Sounds and music are also golden in this game! The song of the Sherwood is one of my favourite songs.
The characters are well made, everyone has useful abilities, my favourites are Will Scarlet (although, he has a very agressive playstyle, he got a slingshot which can take out people without killing them) and Little John (he is definitely not little but I like how he wakes up his fainted teammates and generally he is good against big crowd)
For now, let me tell you what is the bad thing in this game (because nothing is perfect!):
Just one: The zooming... just why did they add that? :V It's very pixelated when I zoom in and when I zoom out it's too small for me. Maybe the zoom out is useful.
To end this, let me share some tips to this game if you are a starter in this game:
-Pick up every scrolls and give money to the beggars! A scrolls can tell you many useful information like: characters' abilities, warnings and they can reveal soldiers who are  in "shadows". What's more you can spawn more scrolls by giving money to the beggars! You can add more money to him for more informations but it's  a waste of money if you give money to the beggars then he says: "Oh sugar!" or something. If he says that, don't give him more money because he will not give any information to you!
-Try to not kill so many soldiers if you can! A lot of Merry Men are going to join to you after every missions,if you don't kill many people! Those guys are very useful in the Sherwood Forest: they can make arrows, herbs which are actually "health packs" in this game. I don't prefer them in combats untill they are more skilled in fighting but you can still bring them to the missions as extra teammates!
-Know the characters' abilities, how they can fight and train them in the Sherwood Forest in you leave them there if you go to the mission (or just leave them to make arrows or something, it's up to you)!
-Collect the clovers! If your characters die, you can use these to bring them back! If you complete some tasks to the poor citizens they will give you these clovers!
That's all! Have fun with this game! :D

Black Flag (new) - October 2014
Well, looky here; it's another Assassin's Creed game. I am of mixed opinion on this series; they are good enough titles that they keep me playing through to the end but increasingly I am finding it difficult to justify the purchase of the next iteration because the games are so similar to one another. Why spend $60 on a new game when I can get the same experience from the half-dozen other titles already in my collection?
Black Flag has the usual excellent production values I've come to expect from the series. I personally think that AC3 was slightly better looking, but maybe that's just because I prefer the craggy cliffs and forests of the American Northeast. Nonetheless, as expected the visuals are gorgeous and the game features some great sound and voice-acting. The motion of the boat and the waves is especially delightful.
But increasingly the franchise is leaving me cold as far as the gameplay is concerned; the story missions aren't particularly fun to play, and the wide-open world is mostly there to hide the endless collectibles. To be fair, the collecting mechanics are difficult for me to resist (it feeds into my OCD), but it feels a lot like make-work to artificially extend the game's length. Not to mention the game would probably be over twice as fast if not for all the interstitial - and unskippable - animations that play whenever I performed an action, from opening a menu to search a body. Sure, they only take one or three seconds each, but that really adds up over time.
Oddly enough for all of its apparent size the game-world still feels too small; I could only access small parts of each island, and the oceanic gulfs between them could often be crossed in less than a minute; by the time I got my ship up to full speed, it was time to slow down to prevent my slamming into the next island. The ship-to-ship combat is satisfying, although the boats feel both too maneuverable to be realistic too sluggish keep me from cursing their truck-like maneuvering in combat. Meanwhile, melee combat is the same as I have seen in the last six iterations of the franchise, albeit somewhat more streamlined; it's stylish but not exciting.
As is expected from the franchise, the story is as dreadful as ever, although the characters are a touch more likable than in earlier games (although given how impersonal the protagonists of the franchise are, that is not saying much). The "real-world" segments of the game  are an annoying bunch of mini-games that are better off skipped. Black Flag is also buggier than earlier games.with odd graphical effects like ship's sails getting stuck in the air or the AI scripts not running. None of these bugs are show-stoppers but it indicates the effects of Ubisoft's pushing the franchise to a yearly release.
It's hard to bash the game as it is not /bad/; it is just not a particularly engaging or exciting series anymore. Assassin's Creed the gaming equivalent of factory-baked white-bread; tasty but not nourishing. I recommend it, but with the understanding it is pretty much the same as any of the other Assassin's Creed games; if you've never played any of those games, this is a good one to start with, but if you have, Black Flag isn't going to offer you anything significantly new over the other titles, so you might as well invest your time and money in some other game.

What is BiT Evolution?
BiT Evolution is a platformer that starts out in the style of an Atari game, then changes to Game Boy, NES and finally SNES style. Throughout the game you have 12+12+18+18 levels, boss fights excluded. Each level holds 20 pixels. The clou about this is that the protagonist changed between two planes, and in each plane there are some pixels.
The graphics are fitting for the systems they try to represent, although as the developer admits in the forums, liberties were taken when those enhanced the gameplay. As an example there is no sprite flickering in this game, rather the graphics feel smooth and with each system different.
The sound is the usual for platformers, but the background music is excellent. Most of the music can be heard on Soundcloud, the link is
- but not everything. An especially catchy tune from the levels 4-10 to 4-12 is missing from there, yet it should provide a great opportunity to hear the music style.
The game can be played entirely with a controller, which I did. The protagonist has different jumping patterns for each simulated system. There are two special abilities for the hero as well, learnt or found over the course of the game. The first one is rolling, which like in Metroid makes the character one "square" high. Rolling can be used as a weapon against some enemies, others can be defeated by jumping on their head, others not at all. The other one is to glide, enabling easier jumping as well as being necessary to advance at certain points.
The main point of the gameplay is the ability to change between two planes of existence: In the rendered world, the hero BiT must be hit by an enemy to get into the world of code. There he must find a portal to return to the rendered world. While the beginning and end of each level are in the rendered world, more than only a few times is it necessary to switch between the worlds to advance through levels. There are numerous collectibles, called Pixels - 20 in each level, to be exact - which are spread between the two planes. If one does not hunt those, the game loses most of its fun, Many pixels pose a mini-challenge to get to them, such as letting oneself get hit in the right spot or rarely navigate through a tight jump or two, but most are just spread around and wait to be found.
After the game is beat, which takes around 3 hours without and probably around 9 hours with pixel hunting, a challenge mode opens. I only played 20 levels in it, enough to get the final achievements, but from what I saw so far it also has different concepts of challenge in each world. The Atari world is flooded with enemies while the Game Boy world rather demands dexterity when jumping.
While throughout the main game there is a checkpoint in each level and getting hit in the world of code means being set back to the checkpoint once passed, the checkpoint is not present in the challenge mode. Some of the challenge levels require frustration tolerance, but by the short length of them the difficulty is comparable to some easier Super Meat Boy levels - always possible, but sometimes only after knowing what to do, after learning the timing.
A great thing is that you can enter beaten levels at any time again from the world map. In the challenge mode, all levels are unlocked so they can be played in any order.
All in all, what remains is a Jump'n'Run that has obvious flaws, thereby can't be recommended to everyone. Only those who go for 100 percent completion, who want to hunt all the pixels, get all the gold stars and Steam achievements will get the most out of the game. Those who just look to rush through will have 60 levels of rather short length. For those looking to play through everything the levels might seem too many at times, but playing in short bursts at the own leisure redeems this. Speedrunners also might find the game attractive since levels are short and can be replayed easily at any time, although pixels once collected will remain collected even upon death or beating a level.
Recommended: Mainly for completionists who want to get every hidden/difficult pixel and those enjoying a pseudo-nostalgia trip with quirky humor, otherwise for people who play in short bursts over several sessions.
