Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag is a HUGE open-world, pirate-themed adventure game where you sale the ocean with a crew and your very own ship to find treasure, maybe complete the story or ignore it and just pirate.
Have you ever gotten yourself into something that was way over your head? You realized "woah, this is going to be way more work then I was expecting"... That is how I feel about writing this review.
After playing AC Black Flag for just a couple hours I knew writing a review was going to be a nightmare because there's just SO MUCH STUFF!
So I must come clean and admit: I'm not really sure this review will be adequate. I plan to make a youtube review where I can hopefully outline my thoughts in more detail and with better control... But until then, you've got this mess!
Your story begins in 1715, you are Edward Kenway, thrill seeker, sailor, scoundrel... Pirate. Edward left his would-be-Fiancée and everything that he knew to set sail for the Caribbean.
Along his journey he ends up making contact with the assassins, you know... the assassins with a creed? Yeah, those guys. For reason I will not spoil, he eventually is won over to their cause and helps them... But not before he has a jolly good time pirating!
Oh wait, you just got pulled out of a simulation... What's going on here, you thought this game was about Pirates in the 1715's! Here's the thing, you're actually "playing" the memories of Edward Kenway for a company called "Abstergo Entertainment".
They claim to be gathering footage for an up and coming Pirate movie they're doing on the characters in the 1715's and they need your help because you're naturally gifted with this "memory-brain-meld" technology.
I could write a few more paragraphs on the story, but lets just say things are definitely not as black and white as they seem, between Abstergo and their goals, or the people *YOU* work with, for that mater.
I could break the gameplay into a ton of sub categories, but for simplicity I'm going to focus on the two main combat features: Kenway's fighting/stealth/etc, and naval combat.
Kenway himself has quite the assortment of secondary weapons, even several different primary weapons, and don't get me started on the pickup weapons! Weapons for days!
Kenway at first just goes to his dual swords for combat, but eventually he gets the sneaky-sleeve-daggers. There's probably a formal official name for them, but I'm calling them sneaky-sleeve-daggers.
Depending on the weapons being used the animations are different, so a counter with swords looks and FEELS different then a counter with daggers, or even a counter when unarmed or holding a pickup-weapon.
The Hand-to-hand combat is tailored for ambush striking, and then running away and finding a place to hide. Or you can be a man like me and duel your way through the English lines. Optional: you can also die a lot like me, because you're playing the game incorrectly.
When Kenway obtains himself a ship, he names it the Jackdaw, a Jackdaw is a small bird part of the Crow Family
. The Jackdaw starts out quite fragile, but as you loot and pirate around you get enough money and resources to upgrade her.
And Upgrade her you do... with guns, armor, cargo, aesthetics, sails, ammo, crew quarters. Trust me when I say that you're definitely investing in this ship.
Now comes the part I was skeptical about going into the game... Sailing a ship.
Hands down, this was one of the most awesome and freeing sensations in the game! When you're sailing well, and can direct your ship where you want to go, the game is golden, couldn't be better. But when you're pinned between an enemy ship, and getting mortared by the local fortress... That magic dries up faster then rain in the Sahara.
So the Naval combat is touch and go, as a whole it adds to the experience, and definitely doesn't bog down the gameplay in my opinion. However, I will note that some of the most difficult challenges in the game involve the Jackdaw, so when the game says "Hey, you should upgrade your ship before you do this Mission", You darn well toot'n should upgrade that crap. If you don't you have no one to blame but yourself for how much death you'll have!
Here's where we come to my final note about the gameplay... specifically when dealing with the Jackdaw. You will hit literal walls that you cannot pass unless you go pirate-farm for a bit so you can upgrade your ship. Some people might be able to get by without it, but I had to go explore around, you can't really shoot straight through the story.
Even though the story is quite linear and you can go from story chapter to story chapter, there is a type of "gear check" that is in place to slow you down. AC Black flag was designed to take loads of time to play, to some people believe it or not, that's a turn off for a game! To others it's like "YES, inject that into my arm with an IV please, ahhhh yeah".
I knew this review would become huge... I haven't even been able to get into the finer details of the different weapons you unlock for Kenway or the Jackdaw, the mini-games, the multiplayer
, special events, getting world completion, uplay, uplay achievements... OH CRAP UPLAY!
Hey, Hi! did you make it to the bottom of this review?
, Uplay MUST run in the background even if you boot the game through the steam client. That's one of the biggest gripes people will probably have about the game, other then getting stuck on ambient objects while trying to parkour... ACK! I couldn't even talk about the parkour!

Ok, after I finished Ori, I must say my expectations were quite high... But this game... man. This game exceeded them all.
First of all - the most important aspect of any game of this kind - the gameplay - controls are tight, nearly perfectly spot on. The combat is fast and with the charms, you can customize your character quite freely. The abilities are mostly quite standard for the genre but aforementioned charms modify you enough to keep things interesting at all times.
The graphics - while not as... technically advanced as Ori for that matter, Hollow Knight has absolutely stunning visual design - the locations are beautiful and unique, and create this grim, gothic atmosphere, mixing beauty with dark mood. There is really nothing I can complain about at all - the whole thing is strange at first, but not as strange to feel random - the whole strangeness of the world is actually very coherent.
Audio - well, it is a masterpiece - beautiful soundtrack, fitting the mood at all times, and other sounds do not lag behind as well, even the voices of the characters, imitating speech - they are still filled with personality, like for example when you fight Hornet or Dung Defender - you can't forget this.
Story - well, you can clearly see the inspiration from Dark Souls, but at the same time it is not a mindless rip-off, which is nice. The story itself is dark, sad and propells you through the game very well. A lot of lore in this one, told in cryptic ways, through scraps of dialogue and visuals both. Show, not tell, as they say, and this game nails it.
As a testimony to how good this is - there are some games that I purposefully delay, because I do not want them to end. And this was one of them.
So... How about the difficulty - I would say it is well balanced. The fighting is done well - it is difficult enough and almost never feels too easy or too difficult. A lot depends on your strategy and charm selection. Even the hardest bosses are ultimately very fair, though some may require very, very precise timing.
As for platforming - the basic platforming is easy enough, with some tougher sections the first time you enter each area - but once you unlock numerous shortcuts, movement is quick and smooth so you never really feel punished for exploration, which is a very nice touch and an example of expert design.
There are couple of locations that reach near BS difficulty though - but they are either optional (Path of Pain...) or required for the best possible ending, which is supposed to be a challenge.
One more thing - I love that devs show that they care about the game - with free DLCs already released, both with solid, awesome content, seamlessly implemented into the game - it just shows their dedication for the already great thing they created.
Do I recommend it? OH YES, I do. Hollow Knight clearly goes into my top 10 list.

It's a very generic platformer, maybe too generic.  The game had potential, but ultimately it fell flat for me. An evocative, atmospheric action platformer with essentialist design that fuses classic and modern mechanics alike.
Nothing in terms of gameplay is original in this title, but then again, you probably have got more Call of Duties than platformer games. The magic of this title comes from how it approaches player progression and its world designs.
Nothing feels tedious in Hollow Knight. Exploration, character progression, earning currency, advancing story, backtracking are all fused together and have a seamless feeling of being paced just so. Although you could grind, you will quickly learn that it is pointless as you gradually aquire currency while trotting through the fairly linear progression of the game. The world may seem big and open at first, but you get restrictions as to where you can go based on a large number of your abilities, hence the linearity. Speaking of a platformer game, the abilities we're talking about are fireball, slide through the air, off-wall jump, ect.ect. Your character start as a vanila Mario-with-sword and gets one significant ability every now and again as you're exploring the game. Each time you get one of these, new areas become availabe to you, and you will clearly know where to go. You do not get lost in this game even though you're also exploring the game.
Itemization and customization are minimalistic, but in the same time, significant, as the passive abilites provided alter the game mechanics in a very noticable way. For instance, most of your enemies are on a hit counter from your sword. Some take two hits, some take three, ect. If you use an item that somehow damages your foes more, that is a big change.
You do get a few places that have got a quirky platformer design, places that your ordinary, run-of-the-mill Mario would not be able to go. Provided he is not flying, that is...Thankfully, you do get out of your ordinary Mario state pretty quickly :D. Those may pose a challange, but are mostly side content that does not impede progress, plus, the difference from person to person will be based on practice alone. Keyboard is absolutely fine for the game, despite what it says from the beginning.
The game, as a whole, is not difficult. It is a Metroidvania platformer action-reaction, so the learning curve will vary. I do not think it will become annoying to anyone though, especially since you also have players choice in combat.
With all the boring necessities out of the way, this brings me to my favourite part about this game: Art and Character design. People, perhaps somehow liberally, compare it to Dark Souls the First. One could argue about differences and similarities, but I think Hollow Knight deserves it's own rather than comparison because its world is unique. From the characters, to the music, to the story, the atmosphere, the places you explore, Hollow Knight holds independently as to how it presents itself. Take that you loot-box-infused tripple A's. And this, surprisingly, will be end of this section. I will not spoil anything for you guys. Just enjoy this little game.
If you like playing video games, I think, you will, at least, appreciate Hollow Knight. You may very well end up liking it a lot.

Before we begin; let me make a few things clear/put a disclaimer or two if you will:
- This was my very first time experiencing Final Fantasy XIII (FFXIII) on any platform.
- I played it with no extra addons or tweaks such as GeDoSaTo's Downsampling Tool or SweetFX settings (all in the name of preserving artistic integrity and all that).
- I have indeed beaten the game as the "hours played" will tell you with some optional content missed out on. Which means that I may have potentially spent even
time with the game.
- Played with English VoiceOvers (VO) for this playthrough and should be able to add a line or two concerning Japanese VO in this review as an update.
That said, of course...
Let us not beat around the bush. FFXIII does have some issues right off the bat. First and foremost, the game's resolution is locked to 1280x720 (720p) and no more. For some of us using say, laptop screens (like myself) that was not an issue, but if you have a 1920x1080 (1080p) screen on hand then there is some tweaking you will need to implement to have your game making full use of your screen's real estate. This may include making literally upscaling the resolution through your GPU's Control Panel using a customized profile OR using the aforementioned GeDoSaTo Downsampling tool for the required tweaking.
Secondly, there have been numerous reports of serious framerate stutters even on high performance GPUs. Most baffling in my opinion are some instances (at least according to forum postings) of users coupling older PC builds e.g. a Q6600 Quad Core Processor with a GTX 2** series card having a much smoother gameplay experience right out of the box compared to newer rig and GPU configurations. Personally, I did have a relatively stutter-free experience save for one late game "town". During battles, absolutely no problem regardless of the effects going on onscreen.
Lastly, the usage of a supported controller alleviates any framerate issues for some (used an X360 controller throughout my playtime). Reports of problems ingame with the use of KB + M are recorded on the Steam Forums for this game.
FFXIII does possess a passable story, if not one that is rather convoluted. Further, the explosive nature of its prologue doesn't help matters much in setting up an overrarching context for the plot. That responsibility falls on the extensive ingame Datalog (codex/encyclopeadia/database) and various flash-back cutscenes peppered throughout the narrative. I actualy liked slowly piecing together the disparate threads prevalent in the story. However, I am mindful of the fact that all the reading you'll have to do to make sense of the lore can be a drag to some. This is a tale that for all its flashiness is quite frankly a slow-burner. It's execution cannot be considered the best, but as the start of a totally new mythos for the Final Fantasy series (since being fleshed out by Type-0 and later FFXV), it's a good start. To be honest, if I had played this at release during 2010 with no knowledge of the two sequels in XIII-2 and Lightning Returns, I may have felt rather short-changed because playing through this and even reaching the finale, you get the feeling that the story is far from done.
Assuming you do not have any preconceived notions on how the game should look, then you may agree with me that FFXIII is indeed a looker. The art direction on show is in keeping with the vision the developers had for their game 4 years ago (if concept art is anything to go by). The production values for the cutscenes have sky high production values as is typical of a Square Enix RPG flagship production. The downside here is for all the grandeur and wide-open spaces you keep viewing, you are essentially running through very pretty ingame corridors. We probably will never know whether this was due to hardware limitations at the time or just a bewildering design choice... Needless to say, it did not bother me as much as I thought it would. This may have been because I viewed this as serving the needs of the story as it was being presented to me. It was grating, sure, especially since these are LONG corridors for the first half of the game, but not enough for me to consider them a deal-breaker.

Now let us spare a moment to appreciate the work of a certain Masashi Hamauzu-san. Music Director for this title. His compositions are a bit outlandish with some infusions of rock, jazz and orchestral pieces peppered throughout the experience. His work is definitely not in tune with your typical epic scaled FF game, but it eventually grows on you.... in a very good way. Special mention should be given to the main battle themes, the chocobo riffs (FF isn't FF without chocobos) and certain cutscene moments. Square did not skimp on the ambient sounds either, either during battle or just plain exploration segments (yes, exploration does exist in this game, but detailing where and when here would be spoilerrific on my part).
In a word FANTASTIC... while in combat. This is truly where Square really experimented. You have your menu based system that is literally on a "Realtime" timer (Active Time Battle segments) or a much slower variant. All commands are mapped to Abilities and cost ATB bar segments. This is rounded off by Techniques and Items usage. The beauty of this system is that this can be tweaked farther using character roles referred to as "Paradigms" with access to different abilities within each paradigm. For instance, offensive magic with the Ravager (RAV) or physical combat with the Commando (COM). So for your party your set up paradigm decks which you can then switch on the fly during battles to unleash some fascinating battle synergy between characters. Factor in the fact that you have certain roles tailored for each character and the possibility of unlocking special moves and an AutoBattle feature to save time, then you have yourself a very nuanced and deep combat system. Needless to say, your uncontrollable AI companions are quite smart for the most part. Sadly however, FFXIII lacks any sort of extra minigames that have been the staple of prior series outings. The closest to these being some late game content that bravely tries to play the part, but fails... also, ends up being incredibly challenging. Left these sections halfway done (at some 68% I believe) and proceeded to complete the last few sections of the main story. Of special mention is the Crystarium, your level up hub. Think a streamlined version of FFX's Sphere Grid and you'll get the idea. A more user friendly variant that is easy to max out if you pay attention.

The game is a beauty in terms of looks, yet lacking the expertly crafted illusions of "freedom" of prior entries.... It's certainly a divisive title to be sure, but a necessary experiment by the developers that may not have paid off big time. For its current price here on Steam this title is still a steal and knowing that there are upcoming sequels that should flesh out the story further, then I have no qualms about recommending this game.

Defy Gravity is a game about using the Gravity Gun (Hmmm...where have I heard that before?) which creates Gravity Wells (Oh, that's new) in order to complete feats beyond the rules of generic platforming. Wells, retract and attract, can be fired by using LeftClick and RightClick, or LT and RT if you do so desire to use the controller support, and allow you to fly around like a space eagle, or a bluetit on LSD. Only two of each well can be fired at any one time, though, to prevent flying over the entire level like some kind of intergalactic eagle.
The mechanic is certaintly a hit for the game, and will most certainly attract fans of games such as Portal, and other physics-based puzzlers, and the platforming is smooth, with firm controls. Any msitakes feel genuine, and you know it's your fault and not the game's. It's not blunderingly difficult, but it's not easy either, which also brings back the feel of Portal, which I like very much. It may take a few attempts before you can get past a puzzle, but that's to be expected, and as an added bonus, you feel great when the soloution suddenly comes knocking at your brain's door.
The XBOX controller intergration is nice too, and for PlayStation fans, the D-Pad acts like another joystick, bringing the 2-joystick feel, but actual DualShock 3/4 intergration would have been preferable.
I have very little negative points for this game, except for the fact that the mouse cursor cannot go past a certain point in front of you, but can go anywhere behind you. I don't know if it's a bug, but it's still hindering. The presentation of the menus and such isn't too spectacular, either, but you won't be seeing many in this game.
Overall, the game's intriguing mechanics and solid, feel-good platforming make this game a winner. Pick it up while it's this cheap, because it's well worht the 18p, or the £1.85 otherwise.

As someone who has played Civilization 5 for 250 hours I can say that while this game is very similar to Civilization 5 it has enough differences to be worth the price tag in my eyes. However as the game is likely to recieve expansions and dlcs that will take it from a great game to a fantastic game it may be worth waiting for a sale before buying. My review will mostly be comparisons to Civilization 5. With this in mind here are my thoughts:
Interface;
The interface design on the game is tightened up a bit on the main screen. Its a bit more sleek. However as a result some information is a bit small and hard to find at first as a result. Very functional and works just like Civ 5 for the most part. The biggest interface complaint is the Tech Web. The mostly blue and white coloring along with the almost unnoticeable difference between wonders and buildings on it makes it a chore to look at and sort through. Fortunately mods are already coming along to fix this so its not as big an issue as it might otherwise be.
AI:
A little better but the same as always. The game explains why the AI hates or loves you though so their reasoning is a bit more transparent. Unfortunately the AI is as dumb as always and having played on Gemini difficulty mostly they seem to barely present a challenge to an experienced player. As usual it seems like the main thing that keeps AI players afloat is the massive amount of cheating they do but in this game it seems like they don't do quite as much of it. The staggered spawning doesn't really matter because the AI returns to parity quite quickly. All in all its the same as its always been with the AI in Civilization. I  personally find the AI to be the weakest part of this game just like in Civilization 5.
Civilizations:
What has been lost in variety from Civilization 5 has been made up for by balance and customizability. Providing a series of mostly balanced options the game offers you a chance to customize how your Civilization starts and prevents the first 5 turns from playing out mostly the same every time. While I do miss some of the more fun and unique units and buildings from Civilization 5 I think the system used here is overall better. The loss of Civilizations with terrible bonuses is good. These Civs do seem to lack personality but to be honest they never had personality in Civilization 5. Any personality attributed to the AI by players was created by the implied history of America for example.
Gameplay:
On the surface it appears to be incredibly similar to Civilization 5 and in a lot of ways, it is. Units can't stack, the map is hex based, resources are reskinned but the same, ect. Despite this the game plays quite differently with aliens proving more dynamic and challenging than barbariens ever were. Spies have been revamped and are both more useful and interesting. Trade routes work on a by city basis as opposed to a global limit encouraging massive trade empires. The culture trees promote far more diversification and interesting strategies with their synergy bonuses. The tech web, a huge change to the previous tree system of Civ 5 diversifies each Civilization far more than unique bonuses ever did and allows for many interesting strategies. Except for the Domination all the victories have been revamped creating interesting ways for players to win and allowing for a lot of time for other players to interfere. Expeditions and resource pods create more variety and must often be fought over by the aliens squatting nearby. Miasma while often irritating makes positioning all the more important. Sattelites, one of the bigger new additions have many varied and useful effects on the land beneath them. I could keep going on but in the end while most of the changes feel small in my opinion they all add up together to create a game that feels and plays very differently from Civilization 5. It is certainly an iterative sequel but it is a different game from Civilization 5 in a myriad of ways.
I am greatly enjoying my time with this game warts and all and I look forward to the dlc and expansions that will make it even better.

I really feel let down with this release.  I was looking forward to it, having enjoyed Alpha Centauri immensely.
Some goods:  It's a reskinned basic version of Civ 5.  Familiar style of resources and city management.  Some variety in allowing you to alter structures to work to your play style.  An interesting way to develop and 'specialize' units.
Some bads:  It's a reskinned basic version of Civ 5.  For $50 Firaxis released a rushed game.  There are at least 4 mods that should've just been in the game.  Like color coded units based on faction, color coding on the tech tree, and some real faction differences that make chosing a leader have consequences.
That said, some opportunities were created and then totally botched.  First off the aliens.  If you leave them alone, they leave you alone.  Eventually you reach a stalemate with them.  I went all harmony then had to blow them up anyway as they occluded my city squares.  I get less interference from hostile factions during 'peace time' than I do with these aliens I'm 'melding' with.  If the planet and aliens are coordinated, then the AI could be better than 'barbarians minus the fighting.'  Firaxis created a great opportunity with a neutral 3rd party, then totally threw it in the trash.  Harmony should let you coexist at least, tame them maybe, grow them at best.  Slaughter/enslavement should see domestication, bio weapons, and other such.
Many of the wonders make me just wonder why I'm building them.  Unlike previous editions, wonders and achievements in Beyond Earth are rewarded with underwhelming monochrome.
Leaders need real variety.  Are they all just megacorp/region conglomerates?  Some religious fundamentalists, weathly aristocracy, mad scientists (like a crazy Bill Gates), and others are all much more compelling than 'future guerilla fighter from brazil.'
Having affinities is an amazing idea.  They are also very underwhelming, and non mutually exclusive.  They allow unit 'evolution' and specialization, some good and some meh in game bonuses, and help you break into a victory condition.  My half alien, half cyborg, humans first movement wins games....
The interface.  Oddly sized city management windows, poor/no city management options, nigh impossible to find clickables (look for a '+' and an 'eye'), and little differentiation in tech benefit icons, be prepared to hunt and wade through the interface.  Once you've learned it, it's easy enough to manage, and manage you will...  very few automation options are available.
My recommendation?  Wait.  Do not buy this game yet.  It is a stable alpha playtest masquerading as a 'complete' game.  The graphics are nice, but it doesn't feel like anyone worked on the mechanics, it's just a Civ 5 port.

This game is quite literally the best game I have ever played. It has the top-down view of a MOBA but the similarity ends there--it cuts out the cs farm, click to move controls, snowballing and leaves you with pure skill based, short CD-based arena deathmatches. This is definitely a competitive game, so if you can't handle getting owned by better players on your way to improvement don't say I didn't warn you. Yes, each patch some champion emerges as seeming "OP" but this is nothing new in class-based pvp games. The development team already have a very polished game with core mechanics that feel better than many full-release games, and have been adding more heros and balance changes every patch/hotfix. Everything the development team has put forward makes me confident in my purchase, and the gameplay itself has had me hooked for 100+ hours in the couple weeks I've had it.
tl;dr: If you like competitive, skill-based pvp games, can handle learning from losses and adapting to progressive balance fixes pick this game up I guarantee you won't regret it.

Initially, I wanted to play the game peacefully; scavenging but never stealing, growing foods when I could, trading for whatever else I needed by growing tobacco and crafting cigarettes. After repeatedly failing to keep my characters alive, as they met fates such as freezing to death, starvation, sucumbing to sickness, or being murdered by armed thugs, my morals began to fade.
I started a new game, and I was done being the victim. I crafted a knife for Pavle, my chosen assassin, each night going out in search of trouble. Like a trained hunter, I’d stalk bad guys as they made their rounds in a building. I'd jump out of the shadows, the armed thug caught totally off guard as he smoked a cigarette, quickly stabbing them to death. I was ruthless, meticulous, and my characters were living great. That is, until I slipped up and one of them shot Pavle in the back as he tried to escape. Things went downhill after that. Pavle survived, but nursing him back to health slowly depleted my limited resources.
Another night, as Pavle climbed through the window of a fortified home, he came face to face with an armed female guard. Pavle quickly dispatched of the girl, but what came next chilled me to the bone. As the girl’s lifeless body lay on the floor of the home, I heard footsteps coming from the floor above. Pavle hid in the shadows, waiting for the next victim to show their face. This time though, instead of a heavily armed thug, all Pavle saw was a grieving mother. She ran to her daughter’s body, falling to the floor in tears as she held her murdered child. As Pavle emerged from his hiding place, she screamed at him, just wanting to know why he was doing this. The unfortunate reality of the situation was that Pavle still needed the shotgun that poor girl was carrying, and nobody was going to stop him from getting it.
The profound weight of his actions had begun to take a toll on Pavle. Severe depression and sickness had started to creep in. Still, when Pavle was physically able, I sent him back out into the night. More dangerous encounters led to Pavle suffering another gunshot, this time worse than the first. As he returned home, empty handed and bleeding profusely, I knew what would come next for my once glorious killer.
With Pavle returning with an empty backpack, I only had enough food to feed 2 people. Someone would need to go without. As I looked over my 3 survivors, all hungry, Pavle stuck out as being a particular problem. He was very hungry, bleeding at an unprecedented level, and severely depressed. With the extremely limited resources on hand, I knew there was little that I could do to get poor Pavle back to 100%. So I stopped feeding him, and I stopped bandaging his wounds. I told myself it would be much easier with him gone, scavenging for 2 should be much easier than for 3. He died 2 days later from his injuries, a hero to some, monster to countless others.
These horrible actions weren't Pavels though, they were mine. I was the monster responsible for murdering a mother and child. I was the executioner of countless men and women that were likely doing the same as I was, whatever was needed to survive another day. In my quest to keep my companions alive during the war, I lost something just as important. My humanity.

Full Video review -
As the game starts you find yourself in control of three civilians in a shelled house. Each of your civilians has different backgrounds, inventory space and a main skill for example good cook or skilled scavenger. Your first objective is to scavenge through the house and find materials so you can build basic equipment like a cooker for food, beds, heater and other essentials.
The aim of the game is to get your group of civilians to survive through the war or if they all die the game will end. Each time you play the game you are assigned a random group of characters. Not only is this random but the length of the play-through is random, sometimes the war can last 30 days other times it can last months like in real life the length of a war is never certain. Both the location on the map and the things you find there are randomly generated too, which ensures replay-ability so each play-through you have will differ in some way.
Graphically the game is fantastic, the way the art direction has been done is very well thought out. The game is a grim one and its reflecting in its dark color palate. The game looks like it has been done with a charcoal scheme and then they've added a pencil shaded overlay which blurs the lines between computer generated graphics and hand drawn art. Sound effects are top notch everything from bombs going off in the background to the opening of doors. The soundtrack to the game is wondrous providing great atmosphere and emotion in the background as you play.
The controls are fairly simplistic and nearly everything simply requires a mouse click. Once a character is selected you can use the left mouse button move them or interact with an object. Clicking with the right mouse button has the same effect but makes the character run instead of walk so keep your fingers nimble as you never know when you might need to get away quickly.
The game works from off a day and night cycle. Its too dangerous to venture out in the war torn city during the day. The day is used for keeping your civilians needs met like feeding them, making sure those who were up all night guarding or scavenging get some sleep and of course treating the sick and wounded. The day is the only time you can make equipment and build items.
In terms of crafting you automatically start off with a basic workshop in your base from which you can build basic things you need to survive such as a heater, beds, water collectors etc. You can also build other more specialized workshops such as the metal workshop which you can use and upgrade to craft weapons, ammo and armor. All these workshops can be upgraded so you can gain access to more items to craft such as upgrading the herbal station will eventually allow you to craft your own medicine and bandages.
Everything costs something in the game after all its all about survival. Crafting items will cost you parts and materials which you will have to gather or trade for. But before you even consider crafting more complex items or even basic ones you first need to see to the needs of your group. Each member will need food and this can be done in various ways. First should you come across raw uncooked food and vegetables you can cook these at a cooker to create meals you'll also need water and fuel. You can also eat vegetables and such without cooking them but it does not satisfy hunger like a proper meal. You also have canned food which is usually pretty rare to find and very valuable, just one canned food counts as a complete meal and can be a life saver if your low on other food supplies.
Once night comes along its time to decide what you want to do with your people. The night, like the day is dangerous but its safe enough to try and scavenge for food and resources. When the night comes you'll enter the city map screen. This is where you can assign who does what for the night be it guarding the shelter from looters, sleeping and of course assigning someone to go out scavenging.
Truthfully scavenging is where the game comes alive. The locations you can scavenge vary and more are added as your progress. You can visit everything from houses, schools and hospitals to supermarkets, military outposts and more. Moving your cursor over a location will tell you what you can expect in that location, not only does it give you an idea of what supplies can be found there but it will also tell you if there have been reports of people inside and if there's possible danger.
Once your selected character is at a scavenging location they will automatically be in scavenging mode which includes the sneak stance. It's often best to try and get what you need quickly and quietly as drawing unwanted attention can have lethal consequences. So you scour the location you will come across various obstacles like mounds of rubble, locked doors or even grates and bars. With the right tools which you can craft at your home base you can overcome these problems however tools are either one use like lock-picks or have limited durability like the shovel.
You will be able to scavenge the same location more than once after all you won't be able to fit an entire locations resources into your little backpack. This is helpful as it means you know the lay of the land when returning to a previous location but don't get complacent, just because the location was void of life the first time doesn't mean other scavengers or worse won't be there upon your return.
While out in the city you will come across all manners of people who are just like you and trying to get through. Inevitably you may come across individuals who will want to do you harm, this may be some looters, raiders or soldiers. Dealing with hostiles very much depends on the situation, factors include how well armed you are, how armed they are and how many enemies your facing. Often sneaking past or making a run for it will ensure survival but you may find yourself having to fight. Sounds from rooms you have no line of sight in can be heard and seen with a red circle appearing. If you hear footsteps, it could be an armed soldier or just a scurrying rat, you never know until you look.
I certainly feel that the games vision has been achieved. As a video game it hits all the right marks, solid mechanics, great art and sound but what tops it for me is the events and it's sandbox nature. Not only are you creating your own story as you go through but it's a deeply meaningful one. The game has both feel good experiences and experiences that make you sick to your stomach. Through the characters, events and game play a powerful message is sent to you as the player. I grew attached to every character I had in my party and the people I met. The whole game was a gripping experience that left me as a gamer wanting more but as a human being truly distraught at the realities of civilian life in a war torn city. For all these reasons and more This War Of Mine has easily become one of my favorite games of the year and is probably my indie game of the year by leaps and bounds. There is a lot of mature content in the game so it's certainly not for younger audiences but for everyone else I certainly would say to pick it up and experience it for yourself.

BiT Evolution is a pixel art 2D platformer that harkens back to the the sidescrolling days of 'Bubsy' and 'Super Mario Bros.'. I know there are plenty of games I could list by comparison that are probably better games, however, I think the developer did a great job in recreating that feel of the genre with a twist of their own.
Pretty straight forward in it's approach 'BiT Evolution' drops you into the first world where you must jump from platform to platform. Jumping on top of enemies kills them and just about everything can kill you.
For instance, the first jump you attempt to make is impossible. There is a good reason though and why I like this game. Whenever you die you are teleported to an alternate dimension that is parallel to the world you are playing. If you die in this world, however, you will reset to the beginning of the world or the last checkpoint.
As you play, each level picked from an overworld map has 20 pixels that you must collect. You will fight your way through the generations of platformers from Atari to Nintendo, from the 70's to the 90's. So you will see levels that remind you of Mario and Mega-Man, and many others.
BiT Evolution is a well done game that is the 2D platformer version of the rpg hit 'Evoland' and well worth the playthrough. Go check it out now on Steam while it's 15% off.

Ah, Final Fantasy 13, how I avoided you in the the past during my time of running away from JRPGs (especially those with the FF title). For that, I apologize. While you are not Final Fantasy 6, 7, 8, or 9, you are still something to behold and I am very glad that I am playing through you now.
FF13 marks another entry into the Final Fantasy series's departure from the midly open world maps and puzzely dungeons to more of a linear, novel-like story. The combat is fast-paced and very active feeling amost real-time, and it takes some getting used to. This is the series's natural progression from what FFX started quite some time ago on the PS2. Some will love the beautiful story, rich characters, amazingly done character models, and decently engaging fights, while others will hate the 'hallway' style presentation of the linear direction of the story.
Honestly, though, aren't most FF games (and JRPGs for that matter) linear. I don't know many times in FF7 where you go off the beaten path in the course of the story except to do a few extra things.
My advice is to sit back and enjoy the story and beauty of the game and save up your thirst for open world for games like Skyrim and what-not.

Shadow Warrior is a bold reimagining of the classic 3D Realms’ shooter from independent developer Flying Wild Hog (Hard Reset) starring the legendary and quick-witted warrior Lo Wang. Combine the brute force of overwhelming firepower with the elegant precision of a katana to annihilate the merciless armies of the shadow realm in an exhilarating and visually stunning transformation of the classic first-person shooter.
Story
Shadow Warrior tells the offbeat tale of Zilla Enterprise’s corporate shogun Lo Wang as he is ordered to acquire a legendary blade of limitless power by his deceitful employer. Betrayed and left for dead, Lo Wang learns of the blade’s connection to ancient gods from another realm preparing to push our world to the brink of destruction. Now the reluctant hero must become legend through a masterful combination of gun, blade, magic and wit to uncover the truth behind the demonic invasion and banish evil back into the darkness.
Features
Shadow Warrior Reborn – A bold new vision of Shadow Warrior elegantly blends classic first-person shooter gameplay with thrilling action, inventive combat, and a contemporary retelling of the hilarious legend of Lo Wang.
Elegant Swordplay – Unsheathe your legendary katana to slice enemies apart with precisely targeted swings or unleash fluid combos and special attacks to cut down hordes of enemies with one swift pass through the enraged hordes.
Upgradeable Arsenal – Utilize every gun in your formidable armory – from stylish revolvers and quad barrel shotguns to explosive-tipped crossbow bolts and laser-guided rocket launchers. Each weapon offers several unique upgrades to increase power, speed, and add devastating alternative firing options.
Mystical Powers – Call upon mystical powers to protect yourself and paralyze your enemies or use their own severed heads and still-beating hearts to bring them to their knees.

+/+ Graphics are breathtaking.  Both technically and artistically.
+/+ Fun battle system.  The Paradigm system is unique and the battles are fast paced.
+/+ Many excellent and challenging boss battles.
+/+ Option of both English and Japanese voices.
+/+ Interesting and well developed story & characters.
+/+ Great sound track and sound effects.
+/+ Includes steam features (trading cards, achievements, and cloud saving).
+/- Lots of cut scenes (50% of the game is a movie).  Note: you have the option of skipping cut scenes.
+/- Extremely linear.  Not very many choices or side quests for a large portion of the game.
-/- First ~12 hours are not very challenging, followed by an increasing difficulty spike.
-/- corridor level design.
-/- No towns or other friendly locations.
-/- Terrible English voices. Note: if you wish to enjoy FFXIII use the Japanese voices.
-/- Lacks steam workshop.
-/- Bad port (locked at 720p, not consistent 60 fps for certain users, lacks other graphic and control options).  Note: Most of these issues can be fixed via GeDoSaTo.
-/- Steam in-home streaming does not work.
-/- Limited choice in leveling system.
-/- Large download size (50 gigs).
Verdict: 7.0/10.  A mediocre port of a solid game.  There are not very many modern JRPG’s on steam and it’s great to see the flagship series, Final Fantasy, arrive - even if it’s four years late.  For better or worse, the game feels like an interactive movie; lots of cut scenes and linear gameplay.  Both the story and gameplay are fast paced and action packed, however, and provide an entertaining journey.  The game does open up quite a bit but it takes about 20 hours to get there.  If you are a fan of Japanese culture and/or JRPG’s, then I’d recommend checking out FF13.  If not, then stick to one of the many excellent western RPG’s.

If you're reading this and you own either Bioshock or Bioshock 2 then great news! Bioshock Remastered should now be in your steam account.
It's probably a good idea that you know my PC set up before we continue so you can get an idea of how your PC will handle the game and for the purpose of this, I'll be taking a look at the first Bioshock as that's the oldest and because it's my favourite.
PC Specs:
CPU: i7 5930K 6-Core
Motherboard: MSI X99S Gaming 7
RAM: Crucial Ballistix DDR4 32GB
GPU: GTX 980 Ti
Now lets begin!
First of all, those silly devs forgot to put mouse control in the menus and instead, opted for arrow key control. Great! Good start. Is it 2016?
Anyway, let's go into the menu and see how many great options there are.
Basic menu options. This this is disappointing, especially to not even see the same options that we get in Bioshock Infinite. Also no borderless windowed mode, that's a killer. This is the level of control I expect to see from an XBLA indie game. Not to worry, onto playing the game!
As to be expected, the game runs great on my machine. No flickering, no hitching and no FPS drops to be seen anywhere. The game looks good and seems to have had that smudge effect removed from the original, while still retaining the Bioshock atmosphere we know and love.
You can see in the image above that everything looks much sharper and clearer than it did before. It makes an already great game just a bit more playable for the gamers out there who can't stand outdated graphics. Let me make this clear though, this is not a complete overhaul and is a touch up at best. I can't complain too much because 2K gave the collection to everyone for free on PC, and I've had no performance issues since booting up the game.
If you want to relive a classic or haven't played a Bioshock game before, then Bioshock Remastered is an excellent way to get started. Just don't expect too much. If you want to take a look at what a complete overhaul looks like, have a look at Systemshock and the great the work the team are doing on that game.

Arma 2 is the best way to experience a realistic military war. Why? Because it's a military simulation, not a military FPS. The best way I can describe it to newcomers is that it's a much more realistic version of Battlefield.
The best thing about Arma is its realism. Everything is realistic, which is really cool. There's realistic weapon ballistics, like bullets ricocheting off of hard surfaces or going through surfaces but losing speed depending on the surface. Different calibers go faster and lose different amounts of speed through different surfaces, and even penetrate surfaces smaller bullets cannot. And, of course, bullets are affected by gravity over long distances. There's a good amount of different multiplayer modes, from the popular DayZ and Life, to my personal favorite: Domination, which is a PVE war across one of the many great maps Arma 2 has. Domination is tense, and every game is different, along with its great enemy AI. The maps are detailed and varied, containing cities, villages, and big hills and mountains. There's a great amount of weapons and vehicles. There's even an average single player campaign. There's a mission editor where you can build your own missions and large scale wars. There's so much content here for the money!
The game is demanding on your PC. Unless you have a high end i7 with a powerful GPU, you won't max this game out. Luckily, since it's an older game, I can pull off a mix of Med, High, and Very High settings at 60 FPS with dips into 40s and 50s. I found that disabling antialiasing gave me 10-30 FPS without making the game look super ugly, which is very important when I want to hit a consistant 60. Crouching and standing force you into a stop, which can be annoying when you're trying to escape from enemy fire. Reloading also does the same if you do it while standing still. Luckily, you can reload while running, which I remember you couldn't do in Arma 1. The multiplayer servers for the original Arma 2 were shut down due to Gamespy going under, so there's no Arma 2 servers. The only way to play multiplayer is through Operation Arrowhead. So, if you're buying Arma 2 to play online, get the Combined Operations bundle, which comes with Arma 2 and Operation Arrowhead. For maximum compatibility with servers, you'll want the complete collection, which I would personally recommend. I also noticed the game can be a bit buggy at times.
Arma 2 is a fantastic mililary simulation, and one of the best PC games. My sights are set on Arma 3 in terms of future purcheses. I recommend getting the Complete Collection, which is Arma 2 with the OA expansion and all it's DLC, for the maximum amount of content and compatiblilty with MP servers. I read on Steam discussions that on a great sale, the price of it drops to as low as $7-10. I got it for $15 in a Bohemia Humble Bundle, which came with Arma 1 Gold Edition, Arma Tactics, and Arma 2 Complete Collection.
Should you buy it?

Having played a good amount of Civ 5, I think this game is an excellent addition to the series. It's not Civ 6, if that's what you weer expecting, but it is innovative enough that it feels very different from 5.
Beyond Earth trades 5's diversity for much more customization. 5 launched with 18 Civs, while BE has 8 sponsors. In BE, assuming you specialize in just one affinity, you will only really have 10 or so units (not counting orbitals). However, as you get your level in any affinity higher, you will unlock upgrades for your units. Each unit (with the exception of carriers and unique units) has 1 neutral upgrade followed by 2 upgrades for each affinity. Each upgrade increases the unit type's strength as well as allowing you to choose one of two perks that will be permanently applied to all units of that type AND all it's upgrades.
The perks are different for each affinity, which, in conjunction to the other bonuses aquired from each affinity, means that each of the 8 sponsors plays differently with each affinity. This makes 24 sponsor-affinity combinations, and that's if you pick just one affinity to specialize in. Unlike the idealogies, which affinities seem to replace, you can balance 2 or 3 affinities, or you can have one primary affinity and one or two secondary affinities that you only have a few levels in. You could potentially use affinities differently with every playthrough.
In adition to the vast affinity mechanic, trade is much more emphasized, with two trade routes per city. The victory conditions are innovative and very different from each other. Espionage uses G&K's base but expands on it to the point that it is a much more prominant mechanic. The quests system gives you both minor objectives to work towards while you pursue victory, while also implementing a decision system that allows you to chose a permanent bonus for each building type in your colony or choose different solutions to problems, with various rewards including affinity bonuses.
The game is far from perfect, and I am hoping that an expansion will fix some of the minor problems. However, I can definitely reccomend this to any fans of the Civ series.

One of the best exploration platformers I've ever played.  Easily ranks up there with classics like Super Metroid or Symphony of the Night.  Brilliant music and sound effects with crisp visuals and smooth gameplay.  The audio work in particular on this game is amazing- character voices, sound effects and environmental ambience achieve the delicate balance between distinct but not distracting.  The music pulls you into the environment and complements the visual atmosphere perfectly.
My two major criticisms:  First- the amount of work the game expects of the player in order to discern anything beyond the most rudimentary elements of the storyline.  I would argue that the story is immersive and interesting; it is deserving of more people that appreciate it!  I think it would have been more accessible if the player were given larger chunks of the story (and more deliberately.)
Second- At times it could be hard to figure out where I should go in order to progress.  This is inherent to the genre but I felt the handful of times I had to backtrack just to find the small thing I missed did not add much to the overall experience.  Perhaps something could be done with the mapping system to make loose ends more apparent.

Let me start out by saying I rarely take the time to review a game. Having recently beat this game I felt I needed to say a few things about it. First of all I did not like this game. I absolutely loved it. I didn't expect to enjoy it much going in but boy was I wrong. This little gem has ended up one of my favorite games of all time.
If you don't know what to expect, think Zelda style character progression + a Dark Souls push your luck monetary system + Megaman style bosses + the hardest jumping puzzles of all time. Now add in a unique world with insanely good art, great soundtracks and interesting characters. Boom, you have Hollow Knight.
This game is not easy. It will not hold you hand and guide you. It will make you yell in frustration. But once you finally beat that boss or finish that jump puzzle, oh man, the celebration is on. The combat is intense and fast paced with some really neat boss fights. There were a number of times I remember thinking, “Well, there's no way the next _____ can be harder.” I look back on my past self now and laugh at my ignorance.
Aside from the combat there were great little moments in the story that I did not expect. Things that really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off but also made me laugh (never trust a bug). Moments of awe after reaching some incredible landscapes, or pride after being bowed to. And just a general sense of curiosity at the world Team Cherry has built.
After over 45 hours of playtime I am still finding new things to do and am having a blast. For the price tag I am shocked at the value in this game. Team Cherry has also added multiple DLCs onto the game for free.
This game does have a few cons however.
Secondly, this game is NOT for everybody. If you're easily frustrated or don't like a challenge, avoid this game at all costs. If you are not scared to be tested however, prepare yourself for one hell of a ride.
I firmly believe this game will finish on my list of games up there with the only game I can really compare it to, Ocarina of Time. It's that good.
EDIT: Apparently I missed a patch adding mouse support. Thanks to Jonnymeboy for clearing that up!

Initially, I wanted to play the game peacefully; scavenging but never stealing, growing foods when I could, trading for whatever else I needed by growing tobacco and crafting cigarettes. After repeatedly failing to keep my characters alive, as they met fates such as freezing to death, starvation, sucumbing to sickness, or being murdered by armed thugs, my morals began to fade.
I started a new game, and I was done being the victim. I crafted a knife for Pavle, my chosen assassin, each night going out in search of trouble. Like a trained hunter, I’d stalk bad guys as they made their rounds in a building. I'd jump out of the shadows, the armed thug caught totally off guard as he smoked a cigarette, quickly stabbing them to death. I was ruthless, meticulous, and my characters were living great. That is, until I slipped up and one of them shot Pavle in the back as he tried to escape. Things went downhill after that. Pavle survived, but nursing him back to health slowly depleted my limited resources.
Another night, as Pavle climbed through the window of a fortified home, he came face to face with an armed female guard. Pavle quickly dispatched of the girl, but what came next chilled me to the bone. As the girl’s lifeless body lay on the floor of the home, I heard footsteps coming from the floor above. Pavle hid in the shadows, waiting for the next victim to show their face. This time though, instead of a heavily armed thug, all Pavle saw was a grieving mother. She ran to her daughter’s body, falling to the floor in tears as she held her murdered child. As Pavle emerged from his hiding place, she screamed at him, just wanting to know why he was doing this. The unfortunate reality of the situation was that Pavle still needed the shotgun that poor girl was carrying, and nobody was going to stop him from getting it.
The profound weight of his actions had begun to take a toll on Pavle. Severe depression and sickness had started to creep in. Still, when Pavle was physically able, I sent him back out into the night. More dangerous encounters led to Pavle suffering another gunshot, this time worse than the first. As he returned home, empty handed and bleeding profusely, I knew what would come next for my once glorious killer.
With Pavle returning with an empty backpack, I only had enough food to feed 2 people. Someone would need to go without. As I looked over my 3 survivors, all hungry, Pavle stuck out as being a particular problem. He was very hungry, bleeding at an unprecedented level, and severely depressed. With the extremely limited resources on hand, I knew there was little that I could do to get poor Pavle back to 100%. So I stopped feeding him, and I stopped bandaging his wounds. I told myself it would be much easier with him gone, scavenging for 2 should be much easier than for 3. He died 2 days later from his injuries, a hero to some, monster to countless others.
These horrible actions weren't Pavels though, they were mine. I was the monster responsible for murdering a mother and child. I was the executioner of countless men and women that were likely doing the same as I was, whatever was needed to survive another day. In my quest to keep my companions alive during the war, I lost something just as important. My humanity.

If you've never played a Bioshock game before, pick it up, but not if it costs more than $5 than the originals. This is definately the best way to play the
I had high hopes for this, but I should have saw it coming when it was going to be released for free to owners of the originals. I was expecting mechancics to be ripped out of Bioshock Infinite, then plugged in here so that it wouldn't feel as dated, however thats not the case. As far as I can tell, it is 100% the same exact original game, just with a few graphical upgrades added.
This means, a lot of the severly dated UI elements, controls, and sound effects, remain the same. Making it feel just a smudge more playable than the original. What they upgraded with the graphics even, isn't very extensive. I still find the Bioshock Infinite Burial at Sea DLC looks a lot better than this "remaster", and that came out years ago.
Because this game hasn't improved at all from the original other than graphical improvements, you still have a bunch of old engine problems that should be fixed today. Notibly, quicksaves. For some reason, whenever you quicksave it boots you back into a loading screen and takes a couple seconds to save, which defeats the purpose of the feature at all. This game also has the worst screen tearing I've ever seen in my life, requiring me to play with V-Sync on. Every now and again there are also crashes, and with the quicksave feature being as broken as it is, this can be pretty detrimental and set you back hours.
Another annoying thing is that all of my settings rarely save. Whenver I quit the game and have to restart, or it crashes and I have to restart, I always have to reset my display settings/keybinds. Which is incredibly annoying.
tl;dr they didn't really remaster it at all.
The game itself, however, is fantastic. Makes all of the pain worth it.
As a side thought: If they didn't mislead us by calling it a remaster, and rather labeled it as a texture-upgrade, I feel like it would've done a ton better.

I got this as a weekly deal for $0.29 USD and I must say, pick this game up if you are into puzzle platformers.
If you enjoy simple, yet challenging puzzle platformers, you will really like this game.
The aesthetics are very simple but good - the space background is nice to look at. The music is very good, quite a bit of variety and I have been playing to both listen to the music and enjoy the challening puzzles.
The controls are simple, however, you may need to practice getting used to manipulating the fields created by your gun - you can create gravity and repulsion fields. The learning curve is moderate, as the puzzles get pretty difficult once you reach the second half of the game - you will need to be good at timing to pass many of the stages.
You can create one active field of each type with your gun, and you can fire twice - you will refill ammo whenever you touch the ground/jump on an enemy. The fields are destroyed when you place a new one, or you can manually destroy them. There is a shield you can turn on to ignore the effects of any fields. You can also double jump.
Any golden objects can be affected by your fields, and many of the puzzles utilize this mechanic in a variety of ways. Your main hazard are purple lazers that will kill you on contact - your body explodes into several pieces (no blood), and this can be quite hilarious if you are dying within 3 seconds repeatedly and you consider the type of music playing (making it seem like less of a big deal).
I've been getting into a lot of puzzle platformers, and the ones where timing is critical to completing stages are my favorite. In DG, timing is essential in the later levels. There are also several ways to complete the stages, and, if you experiment and become proficient with manipulating your fields, you can even bypass a few levels without having to use the objects the game places to help you.
A very, very good platforming game, get it if you are even the least bit interested in this genre.
Definitely recommend!

Beyond Earth is a good game but very clearly flawed. It takes a number of steps back in personality, its suffers from a poor user interface and the AI does not deal with the new victory conditions in an interesting way (making the final moments of any game rather dull). Mechanically, Beyond Earth is still a very strong game though. It plays very similarly to Civilization 5, meaning that if you don't enjoy Civilization 5 then you won't enjoy Beyond Earth. If, however, you do like Civilization 5 then Beyond Earth is a nice, fresh take and certainly very enjoyable. If you've never played Civilization, then this is a competent title to get you into the series. The new mechanics such as the spies, the techweb, the changes to virtues, the affinities or the quests are all great aspects of Beyond Earth allowing for much more player freedom, and because of that it is still a very competent game. It’s not the best Civilization by any means, but it’s worthy of the series and in those 50+ hours I’ve spent, it remained highly enjoyable.

The battle mechanics are really interesting with the introduction of the paradigm system (role system, like attacker, healer, etc) and return of the ATB system. At first you can pretty much breeze through the first few bosses on a couple of paradigms, but later on you may have to craft some different paradigms to suit the needs of a particular situation (Barthandelus battle).
From all of the FF games I've played, 13 is one of the easiest, so it's great for the casual gamer who wants to enjoy a sci-fi esque story while not having to worry about grinding like crazy.
TL;DR: Great visuals, great music, easy game, very linear, little to no grind, somewhat confusing story.

I have over 1100 hours in Civ V, and over 40 hours in Civ: BE. As of today (30/10/14), I have finished all victory types except domination, and am working on beating the game on the highest difficulty.
Firstly I would like to say this game is *not* Civ V. It looks like like Civ V, has many features like Civ V, but it is *not* Civ V. This is also not Alpha Centauri. Much like XCOM, Civilization: Beyond Earth  is a spiritual successor to SMAC. It brings to the table many new features, many of the things we loved in Civ V, and a few things that need improvement.
The biggest difference is the new Tech Web. No longer are we confined to a linear path of building, but now we can branch out as we see fit, adapting to our enviroment, and investing our sciences as needed. This is a breath of freash air from Civ V, where going through the Tech Tree was almost formulaic. This allows for each game to be different in how and what you build, as well as allows you to quickly change plans should the need arise, and focus your efforts elsewhere.
Unfortunatly, the Tech web is not intuitive. Since Civ V is about history, even those who know little about the past still have an idea what Metal Working would be, or what a unit called "Knights" are. With Civ: BE, as this takes place in a sci-fi  setting, we now have techs like "Transcendental Math" and "Genetic Mapping". Figuring out all the new techs, buildings and units are a simple search in the Civopedia, and though I enjoy reading through the lore and learning about these, I do not believe many have that kind of patience. Most would want to just jump in the game and play.
Aliens replace barbarians, and do a good job. More dangerous than the barbarians, at lower difficulty levels they are hardly a threat, but at higher levels they spawn frequntly, and you cannot easily avoid killing many as you have to clear them out in order to expand. This causes the aliens to become more aggressive to you, and if you're not careful, you may find youself not only fighting the AI Civs, but the aliens at the same time.
Quests have been added to this itieration in the Civ franchise. Unlike Civ V, where we already know the stories and history of the civilizations, we do not have that with Civ: BE as it takes place in the future. Quests add a neat narritive to the game, and rewards for doing them are minor so as to not cause an imbalace, and can even be ignored should one choose.
The AI is no different than Civ V. To many players it poses some challenge, but to long standing Civ players, the AI is about as smart as a wet towel.
Worlds are colorful, and Firaxis did well in making the planets feel alien, and the music in the game is nothing short of brilliant!
The three aspects you can build your civilization around (Harmony, Purity, and Supremacy) are all unique, add great bonuses, and there's no penalty for putting points in more than one. I persnally encourage people to branch out, as even lower level bonuses are amazing. Much like the tech web, this allows for a different, less linear play style than Civ V did.
However, Civ: BE does have it's problems. Automated pathing for Explorers often leave them moving back and forth between two tiles, and automated workers will prioritize the best possible thing to build, which costs energy, so if left to their own devices they will quickly drain your economy! In the last game I just finished playing, I had a mine built on a hill, and when I discovered one of the mineral resources, it did not add the mineral to my total, allowing me to use it, nor could I overwrite the old mine with a new one.
Much like Civ V, after a few patches I have no doubt Civ: BE will be just as polished as Civ V. If you have played Civ V, and are looking for something different, this would be a good choice. If you're new to Civ in general, save your money for now, and invest in Civ V's Gold edition, where you will have a more polished game, DLC, and two expansions for cheaper price.
Civilization: Beyond Earth will not replace Civ V, but it is a good game to go to when you want something a little bit different.

Hitman Absolution… The first thing that I thought after playing this for a few hours was, “ugghh, I’m going to be getting a lot of colorful responses after I write this review”
So where to start; well I think I will state all the good things about the game before I start causing a riot to the countless number of people who complained to me to play this game. First of all, Hitman is a reboot of an older and somewhat classic series of game that many people are fond of. Now is this a good reboot? I honestly have no idea because I never played any of the older ones even though I have one sitting in the huge pile of games that now take up more than half the space on my desk. So I cannot answer as to if this is a worthy sequel to the previous games.
So on to the good points of the game, I must say that from the very start, the graphics are quite incredible; the developers obviously put a lot of time into creating these beautiful and interesting maps (well at least most of them were nice to look at, some were disgusting, but I will get to that later) Aside from the nice graphics, the developers also did a great job programming, there hasn’t been a single glitch and that is something I can’t say about most games today. Next is the movement and controls, so far these have been nearly flawless, agent 47 is very easy to control and there’s little to no hassle with irresponsive controls. I particularly like the cover system in the game. That was the only flaw in Dishonored, it was often hard to use cover and you ended up having to just lean back and fourth behind cover and it got a bit tedious when you had 50 guards after you. So this is a problem that Hitman Absolution beats Dishonored with, great cover system. Next is the story, the story is alright, it’s not good like Bioshock Infinite, but it’s not bad like Hard Reset. So there isn’t much to complain with as far as the story goes, sure it could have been better but we can’t have everything it seems, and this ties into my next point.
We obviously can’t have everything in a game it seems, and in this case, aside from the graphics, movement, controls and settings being nice, everything else pretty much fails in every way possible. Just for once I’d like to see a modern based game/movie that doesn’t rely on sex to be “interesting” I mean seriously, do we really need to include that to everything to make it “good”? I would say that it just downgrades everything overall. Now you may be thinking, “Hey! You're a female gamer, you won’t understand it, it’s a guys thing” Well I beg to differ, I may be a female gamer, but I really am not usually offended by sex in games or movies, I’m even a fan of Duke Nukem! I can usually bear sex in games, but Hitman is just disgusting in every way possible. For example, the very first target is a woman… nothing wrong with that, I’ve had many female targets in previous games, but did this target have to be in the shower?! Come on people, that’s just wrong! Why couldn’t we at least wait till she was out of the shower before we kill her? Then aside from this, they thought it would be a good idea to add drugs to the game. Christ, is this really necessary? Do we really need to add this to games? I understand this is an adult’s game, but that doesn’t meant it has to be filthy beyond all reason! Maybe if we were killing the people selling drugs, that would be ok, but nope, I just end up having to run around in a completely pointless field of pot. I was trying so hard not to throw up. That basically sums up how disgusting the game is, which is very. Now this isn’t the main reason I disliked the game; obviously I was able to get past that. However, the game is still terrible and a complete waste of time. After about two hours I found myself getting very bored and very disgusted….. not a good combination. Most of the game consists of taking out key targets, obviously, but it handles this in such a boring and uneventful way. Even though they put plenty of weapons in the game, they all function the same, guns shoot people (no $#!+), and everything else you can use to knock out your target. There are a few other environmental hazards, but they mostly consist of doing the same process over and over. In the end I just found myself incredibly bored with the entire game, I even looked online to see exactly how long the game was so I would know when this filth and boredom would end and I can start playing Tomb Raider again. When it comes to that point, I know the game sucks and I want nothing more but to finish it as fast as possible. Now you may argue that I was rushing through the game and didn’t play it properly, but that’s not true, I still took my time and I tried to do everything there is in the game… which isn’t much… at all. Then aside from this, they tried to put a concept where you can knock out people and take their clothes as a cover up, but of course this failed as well. Apparently every single plumber knows exactly who is and isn’t a real plumber. So even though I was playing the game “in disguise” people could still spot me from a mile away which just completely breaks the game and makes me wonder, “why the hell am I even trying?” I will admit that dressing up as a chipmunk was fun for the 10 seconds that it lasted.
In the end, this game is nothing but filth and boredom. Despite the fact that all the functions, controls and graphics are great, the game is still just flat out boring. I get the feeling that if another company made this game, it would have been great, less stupid and less disgusting. I’m getting the impression that this game was created by people with great technology and knew how to make a game function properly, but the overall concepts and ideas were made by a group of 12-year-old boys that didn’t know the difference between a pop-tart and a fish.
Overall, Hitman is a game that functions perfectly and has beautiful graphics, but has probably the stupidest and most immature ideas and concepts that I have ever seen in a game. I honestly believe that if a different company made this game with the same technology, and none of the stupid ideas, then it would have been amazing. But for now I will play Dishonored, Thief and Assassins Creed, the TRUE stealth assassination games.
My final rating for this game was hard. At first I wanted to give it a 2/10, but then I remembered how wonderful the graphics and the controls/movements were, so this is a tough one. I also want to mention that I’m not basing my rating so much on the filth in the game, but more on just how boring and mind numbing the actual gameplay is. In the end I found myself walking away from the game disappointed… not mad, but disappointed. I just wish the game wasn’t so stupid, but more fun instead.  So I’ll give it a 4/10.

A lot of people might call this  a mod for Civ 5, and I can see where they are coming from. It obviously has the same basic engine that Civ 5 had, and a lot of the same mechanics. The open nature of the tech tree allows you to develop what you want when you want it. A word of warning though, I learned in my first game that lack of forethought on the choices that you make can have a significant impact on your development, but I do like the ability to choose how you develop. The lack of a historical context definitely makes the game lose something, both in terms of confrontations and the personalities of the leaders, but I think that this is a relatively minor problem and the only real major setback it has. I played CivV since vanilla, and I can tell you honestly this game has a lot more polish then Civ V had when it launched. It doesnt mean it can't without more additions and maybe more personalization for the leaders but aside from that, it is the Civilization experiece. Civ vets will enjoy this game

After 30 hours of playing I feel like I can leave an initial review.
Pros:
Round based gameplay with no snowball. It's nice being able to make comebacks based on your skill and not just hope the other team makes a big enough mistake to let you back in.
Fast games. It's unusual for a best of 5 match to last longer than 15 minutes.
Movement and ability casts feel and look good.
Small team focus. There is a 2v2 mode and a 3v3 mode. Small teams make it much easier to find people/friends to party up with. Games are normally more fun for me when I'm playing with a friend and working together than just Solo Queue and this game makes it easier to get a full team of people you actually want to play with.
Cons:
Learning curve. The in-game tutorial is incomplete, it leaves out some key gameplay mechanics. There are plenty of youtube videos of people explaining them but it should really be explained in game to new players. Even so, you should expect to lose your first 5 to 10 matches without even winning a round.
Menu and party system lacking: While I haven't run into any in-game glitches yet there are plenty of out-of-game issues. Sometimes parts of the invite system are glitching and won't let you invite without finding your friend in the friendslist. Once you're partied up with a friend it'll sometimes just drop them out of your party after a game. I've also run into an issues twice after playing for a few hours where Battlerite with start hogging CPU (from the normal ~8% to all of a sudden ~80%) causing framerate issues. In my case a restart of the game has fixed it.
Summary:
In my opinion the pros outweigh the cons. All the drawbacks I see in the game so far are things that I imagine will be fixed before the final F2P release of the game. If you're on the fence about it and the price is a big deal I would wait until it goes F2P to pick it up. But if after watching gameplay footage you feel like it's the kind of game you've been looking for I would go ahead and grab it and have some fun. I know I've already gotten my moneys worth and I still feel like I'm just getting started.

A grim but realistic simulation of what it would be like to be stuck in your hometown if it ever came under siege during a war. This War of Mine has the player control a group of surviving civilians who must scrape together whatever they can to survive an armed conflict in a fictional region of the world, bearing a strong resemblence to more well known theaters of war such as Kosovo or former Yugoslavia.
Trade, craft or steal your supplies, and deal with the moral implications of your actions. Will you set up a thriving Moonshine business and trade your goods for medicine and other commodities, or will you go out at night to rob your neighbours and steal what they keep for themselves so greedily?
The choice is yours, but you must deal with the consequences...
PROS:
-The game always keeps you on edge, you can never quite sit back and relax...
-Getting useful supplies gives a feeling of accomplishment.
-Building and expanding your shelter pays off in the long run.
CONS:
-Bandit raids seem random, and almost always leave someone wounded.
-At the moment, guns are the Alpha and Omega, way too powerful.
