Quick Summary: Action / Horror First Person Shooter with mostly World War 1 weapons, though that changes about half way through the game. The graphics are decent for an indie game and gameplay is pretty basic shooting with partially regenerating health so you can run through large portions of the game.
You play Simon, an American soldier in Europe fighting the Germans in World War 1, but you quickly encounter far more dangerous enemies as the dead rise and demonic forces appear out of thin air. As you sacrifice your humanity and progress deeper and deeper underground, you find the ancient world of the vampires, who look like people in heavy bug armor (watch out for their vampire kung fu). For ages the vampires have held back the demons from invading, and now it’s up to Simon to do what they no longer can: Enter the portal to Hell and defeat the demon lords.
Right from the start of the game you’ll get some pretty pathetic World War 1 guns and throwable weapons. Most of the enemies in the game have enough life that it takes a few seconds of shooting to kill them. That means any more than 3 or 4 enemies at once can be a threat to you, especially when you run into the big dudes who actually run faster than you and take about 5 clips of ammo to kill. Like a lot of modern games, if you can avoid taking damage for a few seconds, your life will partially regenerate (up to about 60%). This means you can run past about half the enemies in the game (much harder in later levels with teleporting enemies).
An additional tool in your bag of tricks is the “adrenaline” meter which you charge up by killing enemies. The adrenaline can be used to temporarily slow down time, making it easier to avoid enemy attacks (or run away like me). If you take enough damage to kill you, and you have a full adrenaline meter, the time slow will activate automatically and you’ll actually become invincible during the effect. Unfortunately, during the time slow, your attacking and reloading is slowed down too, so don’t think you can just use the opportunity to blast everyone. Additionally, when you’ve started your descent underground you’ll acquire a special weapon with magical attacks (shadowhand). It’s not as cool as it sounds, but it adds to your arsenal.
Pros:
+I enjoy horror shooters (like Jericho) and despite having mixed ratings, the story is ok.
+This is a straightforward run and gun. There isn’t that much puzzle solving so if you just want to blast some enemies, you can do that. You have a little compass on your HUD that points you which direction you need to go.
Cons:
-The game crashes occasionally for no apparent reason. Also, I wasn’t able to Alt+Tab out of the game without the game freezing. There’s a bug causing blurry vision, but that can be fixed with a command line addition.
-The little cut scenes between levels are weird. Not only is the subtitling occasionally wrong, but they show and say things that don’t make much sense relative to what has happened in the gameplay. This is likely due to the game’s developers not being native English speakers.
Overall, the game is a mostly brainless shooter and if you’ve played the Serious Sam or Painkiller games, you should have an idea what to expect. The game isn’t awesome, but it’s not completely horrible either. 6/10

Rate: 3/5
First impression: Fun game but with some evident bugs. Recommended to the fan of the franchise. Others may want to wait a little for Firaxis to fix their ♥♥♥♥.
Review:
So, let's start with the essentials. I'm having fun, this is a fun game. If you're familiar with civ 5, you will start rolling pretty soon with BE. Basic mechanics and controls are the same. But the gameplay changed, changed a lot. You'll realize that immediately, as soon as you're prompted to choose a tech. The fact that there is no tech tree but a tech web is the major and often overlooked element of the game. One that will affect everything.
Ofc, because of the new shape of the technology dependencies graph, you may arrive at late game tech pretty fast: mid, early-mid you can already obtain the tech for the ultimate military units. But don't worry: you won't be able to produce them until late game truly arrives. Why? The answer is Affinity. Affinity is the mechanic that ensures technological progression is still paced at a reasonable speed despite the fact that you can rush end game tech so fast. You won't be able to produce units or buildings of a certain affinity unless you possess the required affinity level. Affinity levels are unlocked through research of affinity aligned techs. And here we arrive at the desired effect: despite the new flatter shape of the technology dependency graph, there is still a late game content.
Moreover, the auto upgrade mechanic of the military units is also a good balance mechanic. This ensures that even by not committing to military research (that unlocks powerful affinity specific unit classes) you can still get a good "passive defense" from the simple fact that you researched something. You're not "forced" to research a certain defensive tech: your "brute" will evolve with your civ, gain perks and combat strength and it will still be useful when the time comes of defending against giant robots.
I also like the quest system. It adds depth into the game, really introducing a little bit of "storytelling" in a genre that otherwise has always been so "impersonal" with its God like approach.
So my impression is that the gameplay is good enough. I can feel that it is not perfect, not yet, but yes I'm having fun. I'm sure the game will evolve with patches and exp packs in the future with more depth and variety. But this because the core of the game is solid. This is pivotal: if the game has had more stuff but was flawed at the core it would have been a failure with no possibility of comebacks. Instead cbe is core mechanics are pretty solid and fun now and the game will grow nicely in the next years with the DLCs yet to come (this is still a 2k published game, so there will be DLCs and a lot of em).
Let's move on the bad part. Bugs. Bugs bugs bugs. I'm not talking about aliens. I'm not talking of crashes too (never had one). Or cosmetic things like bad animations or silly leader sentences in diplomacy sessions (yea, it's plenty of bugs like that). I'm talking about gameplay compromising stuff. Like quests that doesn't work or with the text hidden by other objects on the GUI. And macroscopic bugs to diplomacy: like leaders who complain with you about something you did hundred turns ago and continue to do so and ask you to stop like forever despite the fact that you didn't do anything. I think Firaxis should be seriously ashamed for problems like those. I was expecting a micro patch to fix it right away. Instead they are still there. So disappointing. Let's be clear, the game is still fun. But those things are annoying and makes you seriously question about Firaxis QA branch.
So, my review is 3 stars over 5. They will be 4 as soon as all the gameplay bugs and the most macroscopic among the cosmetic ones are fixed.
P.S.: it looks like a tons of people complaint about the fact that this game is "simpler" than CIV5. Well, yes and no. If you compare CBE to CIV5 vanilla, CBE is by far more polished, deep and complex. But if you compare it to CIV5 with G&K and BNW DLSs... well yes, this game is lacking content. But this is kind of obvious, shouldn't be? Well it is for me, at least.  My opinion doesn't change.

We all know the gist of things; this is more like a DLC pack for Civ5 than a new game, except that it has all the bugs and glitches that a new game would have.  So, i will stick to reviewing the new stuff.
Having been an addict of Civ5, SMAC, and SMACX, I can tell you this is the spiritual successor to Alpha Centauri like Civ5 was the spiritual successor to DOOM.  They are both games and they both occur on the same planet, the similarities end there.  I won't compare BE to either of those games, because other than the graphics, BE would come up on the short end in almost every aspect.
I like the addition of the aliens.  They are unpredictable, strong, and as far as i can tell, there is no cap on exp gained by killing them.  In the early part of the game, running up against a worm is a real ♥♥♥♥♥, especially if it just moves around between two cities without getting close enough to for a city bombardment.  Racking up 1 - 2 points of damage per ranged unit per turn while the worm is destoying your roads can be a bit frantic.
The tech web is new and interesting.  So far, i'm not liking it due to the lack of logical progression.  But, maybe this is just something one has to get used to.
Having your units look differently and have different attributes based on your affinity is a very good concept.  Having them be upgraded only a few times and only via advancement in affinity level is not.  There are two upgrade "trees" and the affinity advancement grants you both a vast upgrade in strength, and an upgrade in "perks" at the same time.  This should be split so that tech advancement grants you the strength upgrade and affinity advancement grants you the "perk" upgrade, or vice versa.  This would allow 8 smaller upgrades per unit during the game instead of 4 huge upgrades.
The addition of quests to the game was also a great idea.  It was also well balanced and well thought out since some are very quick and easy, and some require 5 or 6 different steps to complete.  Kudos !
The leaders in the game are completely forgetable and uninspired.  I think the last time i played SMAC was 7 or 8 years ago, and i can still recall Zharkov, Miriam, Yang, Dierdre, Morgan, and Santiago, off the top of my head.  I finished playing BE 20 minutes ago and can't name a single character.
The affinities are a good idea, but they fall well short of their potential.  As an example, this is supposed to be a "living and possibly intelligent" planet with robust and somewhat intelligent natives.  Shouldn't they have a a reaction to each colony's affinity and actions ?  Shouldn't natives react with more hostility to those who are trying to dominate and transform the planet than they do to those who are more in harmony with it ?
The "wonders" in the game are pretty forgetable.  I do like that the wonders are far less likely to be game changers.  As an example (of both points), there is a science wonder that i can't remember the name of.  Once completed, if yields a +8 to science.  Significant and desirable yes, but not nearly something that will give one an unsurmountable advantage in tech.  I think the forgetable part could be addressed by using names that have more relevance to earth.  These are earthlings after all, they would likely name great works after historical figures and events, or even modern leaders.
My single biggest gripe is the trading system.  Once you have more than a few cities, you will spend the majority of your time renewing trade routes.  I suspect that this was a last minute addition or change since i never saw much in the line of negative reviews about it from the professional reviewers.  I also find it impossible that beta testers didn't complain this since it is by far the most annoying thing in the game.  If you haven't played, i'll give you an idea of what you are in for.  On one of my first games, i ran up 9 or 10 cities.  I was maxed out on trade routes (3 per city).  I didn't track how often a route needs refreshed, but i can tell you that i had to refresh 3 - 4 trade routes to 1 build order.  So, unless i was at war and moving large numbers of units, about 70% of my interaction with the game was refreshing trade routes.  It was so bad, that i quit the game and now i go with a max of 15 trade routes, or i can't stand to play the game.  So, to keep the game playable, i have to either limit my trade, or play on a small planet.  This needs to be fixed ASAP.  It is an easy fix.  Either have the routes last 2X-3X longer without a refresh, or better yet, add an automation menu with options such as: "select highest yield", "exclude player X", "trade only with player Y", "select lowest giveaway yield", etc.
How about some stats ?  I hate having to cycle through every city i control to find out which has the highest production, science, and energy output.  What about a build queue ?  If these things exist in the game, they certainly are not intuitive.
In the big picture, this is not a bad game.  But, the devil is in the details and in this case the minutae.  Where CIV5 and SMAC cost me lots of sleep on many a night, this game is inducing it by forcing me to micro-manage far too much.  As it is, if this game was in the $10 bargain bin, i'd say give it try.  But until the playability issues are taken care of, it is in no way worth full price.

First things first: let me list some important points which may very well influence you taking my recommendation seriously.
There is a tl;dr section at the end, if you want short conclusions.
With all of that out of the way, let's proceed with the recommendation, shall we?
Firstly I will address the port issue. And, my God, there is an issue here. What does this port have? 60 FPS. Theoretically. However these 60 FPS often turn into anything but 60. Sometimes you get 30. And sometimes it drops below even that. And if I may remind you, FFXIII is almost five years old at the time of writing. What does this port not have? Plenty of things, actually. There are no sound options. Half of the keys are not rebindable for some reason. On launch the game was locked at 720p with nasty black bars on all four sides of the screen (at least on my machine, maybe it's Radeon-specific). There is no way SE could not have made all the options and optimization. They just chose not to. To give Square Enix credit though, they listened to the fans and gave us dual-audio. Appreciate the option. The game is also quite stable - it only crashed twice for me in 87 hours of gameplay. The controls with keyboard and mouse are at least okay, but a proper mouse support in menus (instead of it just functioning as a mini-keyboard) would be nice.
UPD: As of December 11 the game now has resolution options (up to 1080p, so no 4k for you) as well as AA and shadow resolution. It's good that SE gave us an ear and implemented these, although the fact still remains that there were no graphic options of any description on launch. And the time it took them to respond with some action is, well, two months.
Now let us move on to the game itself. While I am strongly disappointed by the port quality, the contents of the game I am pleased with. Let me warn you: FFXIII is linear. As in linearly linear. In more ways than one. But is it really bad? No, I do not think so. This game is about watching cutscenes and fighting. If those things are good, then I myself do not care about linearity. And, well, they are. It also means that if you happen to dislike combat and/or cutscenes, you won't like the game either. The cutscenes are gorgeous and all, but the battle system is the highlight in my opinion, so let's talk about it a bit. The battles take place in real time with some turn-based limitations, where you have to make quick decisions while the action gauge fills. Your party consists of up to 3 characters (you can't choose them until chapter 10) and each of them has a role or a class. The combination of two or three classes (depending on how many characters are in the party now) is called Paradigm. Outside of the battle you can prepare 6 Paradigms and after that you can switch between them at any time in the battle. That is called Paradigm Shift and it allows you to quickly react to the situation at hand or to just choose your tactics on a whim. It turns already spectacular battles into something more interesting. Yes, you can just hit Auto Battle button and let AI do everything for you, but it's boring this way, and the AI doesn't make optimal choices considering AoE, buffs/debuffs and the type of your attack. Personally, I didn't get bored of fighting in this game even once. It's flashy, dynamic and requires some thinking to do right. It also has a lot of smaller nuances, like trying to initiate a battle with your enemy not noticing you (which makes the fight much easier) or character's action animation actually influencing his/her position (if during an attack your character is in the jumping animation, enemies may instead hit the ground or just cancel their attack).
The game opens up rather slowly with the first several hours being basically a lengthy tutorial in terms of mechanics, since they are introduced gradually, but there is a lot to learn. Exploration is practically nonexistent before chapter 11, where you get to roam an open-world style locations and do some side-quests, all of which (and I do mean all) are just "kill this monster" tasks. It's pretty dull, but since combat is fun, I found it more or less acceptable. Sometimes these quests even open roads to hidden locations with more challenges and items. Speaking about challenges, there are some rather nasty enemies, which are kinda hard to deal with. Not to mention, that there are enemies with 16 million HP capable of one-shoting an inexperienced party.
Some people say that FFXIII's story is confusing. I don't think it's true - the plot is quite straightforward, somewhat typical and predictable, but it gets the job done. Since the cutscenes are quite a spectacle and the dialogues are well voiced (at least in Japanese), I enjoyed the overall story as well. Especially I want to praise Lightning's and Fang's voice actresses. On the other hand, some characters do not match well with their voices until you get used to them. The characters themselves, by the way, are quite bland and rather uninteresting. They are typical for your run-of-the-mill Japanese anime/manga/VN. To give authors credit though, the way they explain the connection between seemingly unrelated bunch of people is rather neat.
I would also like to praise the game's setting. The worlds of Cocoon and Pulse, Mass Effect-style technologies and fear of magic wielded by pseudo-gods fal'Cie and their human servants l'Cie - there are a lot of interesting concepts, and the lore in general is compelling to say the least. I found myself striving to defeat some difficult optional bosses just to get a new piece of said lore.
The graphics. Even by default it's a nice-looking game, but with GeDoSaTo on it can be really stunning. Character models and lighting effects are especially good. Texture quality - not so much, but the game sure knows how to present itself and make it look good despite the lack of HD textures. And well, for a five year old game FFXIII is surely a looker. I've got a huge gallery of screenshots to prove that point.
A couple of words about the music as well: it's really pretty and provides a fitting atmosphere. Sometimes I found it odd, when the music contained real vocals, but it was beautiful nonetheless. I think, I will get the soundtrack for the game, which I don't do often.

I do recommend the game despite it having some rather major problems. The combat is great and the story is decent. It is quite a fun experience and the price point is laughably low. Best Metroidvania2DDarksoulsy on Steam by a country mile. Initially I was skeptical, it does a lot of things I wouldn't usually want - Dark Souls homage, it's loooooooooooooong and sprawling rather than being tight and "curated" (insert game critic hand gestures here), it attempts a depressive and bleak tone that comes across more maudlin than sentimental at first until you play it for a bit, it's got the same bloody "crawling around the platform" enemies that have been in Metroid games since the very first screen of the very first Metroid, etc. But it's all so well done and polished that I can't be cynical about it all. The areas are full of nice platforming challenges and it's never repetitive despite its size, and the ability/levelling stuff is perfect. Great fighting. Great jumping. A+ exploration. No pixel art. My previous fav was Axiom Verge, which had great design and sound but it was just the same old Metroid underneath. Hollow Knight felt new and original, but not in a gimmicky way, it's full of subtle novelties and slight changes to the formula rather than having one central aesthetic or design gimmick to differentiate it. There's bits of every good recent entry in the genre here: from the Paper Mario inspired upgrade system to the fiddly but extremely satisfying platforming. And those elements all felt different and fresh.
One big caveat:
The post-game bonus section contains one of the best, most satisfying hard platforming sections I've ever played in a game. But it has one point that's so arbitrary that it almost spoils the effect of the whole section. Ditto the final secret boss, incredibly unfun and felt like rolling dice. Why, after having some of the best extra content that I've ever seen in any title, indie or otherwise, this game feels the need to stink it up with a bunch of gitgud dyingisfun macho twallox I don't know, but I probably won't go back to it unless there's some good DLC on the horizon.

NAM has a slightly interesting history. It's was an example of a commercial modding team that was given the opportunity to make a full released game. However unlike Team Fortress Classic, it wasn't well regarded and generally faded from the public view.
NAM is a pseudo-sequel/pseudo-remake of an earlier total conversion for Duke Nukem 3D called Platoon TC. It is very similar however many of the graphics were completely replaced and the entire game was given new levels. It's so similar that players later ported Platoon TC to NAM.
NAM plays almost identically to Duke Nukem 3D. You have a mighty boot (reskinned as a knife), your pistol is a m16, your ripper is an m60, your shotgun is the same, your pipe bombs are grenades etc. The enemies are all vietcong footsoldiers who employ hitscan weapons. Imagine if you played Doom and all of the enemies were shotgun guys and chaingun guys. As a result, the game plays less like a run and gun, and instead more of a "quicksave constantly" sort of game.
I have to give the developer credit for the attempt but there is a reason why the game was forgotten. It's a very amateur attempt at a first person shooter and released alongside games like Half-Life and Thief the Dark Project.
But it goes on sale for 2$ usually, and for the price and the novelty of playing a Vietnam Duke 3D mod I think it's worth it. It also plays beautifully in eduke32 so you get widescreen, good mouse control and a good framerate. So it has aged technically better than some of the other Build engine games like Blood. So it's at least a playable experience, and one that piques your curiosity.

BioShock™ Remastered is a re-release of the 9 year old BioShock and comes with overworked graphics and additionaly with Director’s Commentary, Museum of Orphaned Concepts and Challenge Rooms.
In BioShock you are a survivor of a plane crash in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. You are able to make your way to an island where a submarine is waiting to take you to into the great depths below where the mysterious underwater city of Rapture awaits. The city is trashed and genetic freaks called splicers roam around, attacking anything that gets in front of them. In order to survive you will have fight through these Splicers and other oddities keeping your eyes and ears open for clues into what has gone wrong, how you may be able to help or how you can escape.
One aspect that makes the storyline work so well is the way it is told. BioShock uses a real time method of telling the story through random radio reports, overheard conversations and audio recordings.
You can choose from a variety of different weapons, anywhere from pistols and shotguns to chemical throwers and grenade launchers. Each gun has different ammo that you can use. There are also many plasmids that you can use. You can electrify the water to kill everyone in it, set people on fire, freeze them and then smash them with a wrench, among other things.
The graphics are not such a big improvement in comparison to the original version.
The sound of BioShock really puts you into the game. From the creepy things the splicers say to the background music, everything fits perfect.
BioShock builds a great atmosphere, it is a stunning game and definitely worth to buy.
Sounds 9/10
Graphics 8/10
Gameplay 8/10
Atmosphere 9/10

Not only that, there really isn't any way to alt+tab out of the loading screens without causing a meltdown... so you can't just 'come back when it loads.'
- Next, the actual game doesn't feel like an epic struggle to tame a new planet. Instead, it feels like a race to see who can develop the specific technologies to reach the scripted endgames the fastest. You have all these cool Affinity techs, but you barely hve time to take advantage of them ... instead you have to rush through you chosen victory path, only getting to really explore your affinity at the last minute. On the playthroughs I have tried to explore the Affinities as a primary goal, I end up losing to the factions that raced through specific tech web patterns early on. Basically, you have to metagame the hell out of it... not enjoyable.
- Finally, trade or die? REALLY? I mean, Earth just emerged out of 400 years of isolationism, and I am racing to this alien world that may or may not be habitable in order to establish a new planet in my own image (aparently as fast as I can) and I am suddenly expected to trade with EVERYONE? That is such a stretch of the imagination that I get mad enough that I almost shut off the game at least once a playthrough based on that fact alone.
So, No, Frixas, I am NOT  IMPRESSED with this latest offering.
It has some awesome features, and some novel uses of existing Civ mechanics... but you really bombed out here.

First of all:
I'm playing this series since the snes era, and I'm a big fan of it. However as you may guess, I got too old to hype a game just because it's called Final Fantasy and Square is behind it. That means, what you will read might be pretty accurate. Well it will be up to you to decide that of course.
Definetly not. How can I say that? Well.. Back then when Final Fantasy V and VI came out on SNES .. do you remember that? You could make decisiont which affected the gameplay and the story a bit. That was awesome. Deep character designs, well developed world and etc. After that Final Fantasy VII came out. You could still make choices but they made LESS impact on the story. However there were mostly improvements like the materia system, side stories and so on. That was obviosly a step ahead technicaly too. The story was better or worse than the previous ones, depending on your taste. Personally (as most of the players) I liked that pretty much. Than Final Fantasy VIII and IX came, and they weren't improved much likely rethinked compared to Final Fantasy VII. They were VERY good games and honestly..why should they change anything if it worked? They couldn't improve the side quests, secrets, mini games more, because of the hardware, so they just revamped the things and it worked.
Now time jump, and everything begins here... Final Fantasy X. Definetly a good Final Fantasy, however already lacking the depth in side quests. (Blitzball was awesome thou.) The story telling went into the "movie style", mostly because the character had voice acting. That was ok and we all knew that they have to keep up with trend and technic.
Final Fantasy XII... I think that was a "we don't know which way to go" game, since it was pretty much like the MMO version but in offline mode, with better story. Not bad, not good..and not because you couldn't enjoy it but it was a totally revamped thing. The atmosphere was ok.
Final Fantasy XIII Is what we got here. They went back to Final Fantasy X because I think they felt that this is better than the FFXII mmo style, and "improved" that. This is a success. More movie like, faster, more action based but...lacks the things what was still in Final Fantasy X. While there was still some "game" elements, like story development while you play, the feeling that you are respoinsible at least a bit for the things and so on, Final Fantasy XIII is more like a movie. You wont feel that you are making the choices, you won't feel that you are responsible for anything, you won't feel that your characters developed cause of you (more precisly, you wont get this illusion like in the older games), and you wont be sad when you finish the game cause your journey ends.
That's because we are in 2014 (or 2010 when the game was released) and the trend is the movie style gameplay. It's not as bad as you think, it's definetly a Final Fantasy, just not a game but a movie with many interractions.
Definetly, comapred to the J-RPGs on pc, this one is one of the best. Even if it's not good compared to the old Final Fantasy titles, It is pretty good compared to other J-RPGs nowadays.
However if Tales Of Vesperia and others will come to PC once, I think I will have to take this back... :P
If you like J-RPG and Final Fantasy, I think this is pretty much a good price. The port is cheap and lacks many things, but let's be honest: Who the hell plays games like this without controller?

Let's start this with a little story. I first started playing Alteil quite a few years ago. I was never good at it, but I enjoyed it anyway, because it was simple enough to understand, and had some pretty nice art. Throughout the years I would play this game off and on, and rotate between loving it and hating it. When this game had a kickstarter I debated on donating to it,which is incredibly rare for me to do,  but never got a chance. After it relaunched, and became Alteil Horizons, I was really hopeful that this game turned over a new leaf. I was horribly wrong. Fast forward to today, and I am just as disapointed as I was then. "But wait, the game has barely been out for a day at the time of this review, so why be so harsh?" I am being harsh, because I know this game, and I know it's developers, and how they've handeled it throughout the years. When this game was played through a browser, it had a multitude of issues, most of them preformance based, and it still has these issues now. My biggest gripe with this game, comes from the very fact that this has gone through a crowed funded relaunch, and now a steam release, and the developers have made no attempt to improve it, just push it out further.
Let's start out with some pros, to lighten the mood a little.
1. The game is fun, and simple enough to understand once you devote a little time to the tutorials.
2. The art is amazing, if that's your thing.
3. If you are a card game fan in general, meaning you dabble in things like Yugioh, Magic, Pokemon, ect, there are some great price compairisons, like how cheap packs are, as well as boxes, so long as you don't mind the fact that these cards aren't physical.
Now the cons.
1. This game does not run for♥♥♥♥♥♥currently. If you can even get through a game, it'll be a hell of a bumpy road. But the game has literally always been like this, so it leaves a lot of doubt in my mind about them ever fixing it. When I started a game it was laggy as hell, and it's not like this game is flooding you with amazing graphics that rival anything else I've already played successfully on my computer. Another lovely little feature is the poor excuse for a chat bar that its a flimsy see through box with a tiny X you can click on to open it up. But that's not my issue with it. When I opened it, it got stuck over my opponent's field, and I had to quit the game, because it wouldn't go away, preventing me from targeting my opponent's cards.
2. The interface is horrible to navigate.
3. The small, but devoted community is hostile, condicending, and has no pateince for new players. I have had multiple accounts, and all of which were met with hostility, and down right rude interactions with the veterain players.
4. I mentioned before that the game is simple to understand once you've done some reading, but by far the hardest thing to unerstand, and then in turn, come to terms with, is that strategy is near nonexistent in this game, since attacks, and some effects are completely RANDOM. That's right, you don't get to attack whatever you want, or whatever is within the range feature, it's completely random, and it completely screws with any possibly strategy. You do have the ability to use whatever is in your deck, rather than drawing into a hand. While this is a huge plus for me, you quickly realize that most decks, and card combinations are the same, and limit your creativity.
5. The pay to win side of this game is real, and it is brutal. I'm not one to really complane much about pay to win games, because obviously they have to make money somehow, but the scales are so far tipped in the favor of the guy with the bigger wallet, and it is enough to discourage any new players almost instantly.
(UPDATE 10/30/16)
So the game has been out for a couple of days now, and I've had a chance to try it out some more. It's still pretty buggy, and slow, but from what I have heard, they plan on working on it. I still wouldn't reccomend this game, unless you plan on putting quite a bit of money into it But, if you want to go through the slow and painful process of hoarding the in game currency through your limited wins you'll get with one of the four, quickly outclassed starter decks they give you, you can give it a try.
(UPDATE 11/5/16)
Good god, it's been nearly ten days, and this game is still horrible. The lag is slightly better, and I do say that lightly. This game is god awful, and though the developers repetedly claim to be patching it, I'm not seeing any improvement. Unlike most people, this game actually worked for me, but that let me realize it wasn't any fun or good. Apparently you will blow this game if you played commandos or desperados, neither of which I played, so I didn't really care. The graphics can't go higher than 800 x 600 (there was 1024 by 700 but it makes the screen so small not worth it). This leaves the screen a jumbled blocky pixelated mess. There is no tutorial to explain any of the controls or game mechanics. You hae these tiny scrolls that you pick up that explain bits and pieces.....why not just explain them in the game, why give me a tedious task of walking around the map getting them. There is no direction to the map. I had an X and a black dotted line but it was pointing back to the start of the level. So basically you just wander around hoping to find what you need. Apparently you can't fight most people, which I found from reading online, but the game doesn't tell you. Why would Robin Hood not be able to fight people?! But the stealth mechanics are so meh anyways. You can crouch and walk, but its too slow to do anything. You can only see 1 person's cone of vision at a time, which many people has pointed out is dumb.  I got seen from someone super far away and on a different level, made no sense. Also I went to knock out a guy from behind and suddently he was alerted, once again made no sense. Also sometimes just by walking I got heard and found out by a guy that was turned around, but then other times I wouldn't, more inconsistencies.
The combat is actually pretty fun for this type of game, with using your mouse to make different swipes. Some other things don't add up though. I walked in this room with this guy, but I couldn't interact with him or attack or knock him out, but seeing me he ran and alerted a bunch of people in the castle and they knew exactly where to find me......why have a guy I can't do anything about but that affects me? The level design is also poor. The first level you're in this big castle and there is no evident way to get around. There are multiple levels and doors you can't tell you can interact with, it makes it super confusing to get around. You basically just click somewhere far away and hope he finds his way there. But this leads to the other problem, you can't see inside rooms. I would be outside a room and once I opened the door or robin went inside I could see it, but by then it was too late because the people inside spotted me.......dumb. Also unfortunately the 2d doesn't work as a lot of time you feel the need to rotate the camera. I guess the game also has a resource management where you assign people benign tasks at your home base like chopping wood.......boring. All-in-all I would say get this game if you like 15 year old pixelated commando games with poor resolution. Other than that there isn't much here. 4.5/10.

This game is addicting. For the price, it's well worth your money whether you're looking to play Smash but don't have a Nintendo console or are already really into Smash. There's a lot this game offers. The character roster may look small, yes. Right now it has a mere 6 fighters with 2 more to be released by the game's launch, and only 5 stages with 3 more to be released, but the depth the gameplay brings to the table is so engaging that I find it hard for me to not look forward to coming back to it again and again.
The fighters take a lot from multiple Smash characters and mix them into one but a lot of their movesets and specials are so unorthodox from Smash that it's a breath of fresh air for avid fans like myself. The major differences you'll notice right away are that there is no ledge grabbing and there is no shielding. You can wall jump (usually) after doing your up special and you can parry attacks (hitting the block button exactly when the other person's move would hit you). It leaves them vulnerable for a second for you to counter-attack. It fits with the game's playstyle and it's really cool to see new takes on standard Smash mechanics.
Wavedashing is also here, and it's much easier to do than in any of the Smash games. No character has a short wavedash, so it's viable for everybody and useful to learn and apply to your fighting eventually. Overall I'd rate this game a 9.5/10, would be a perfect score but for real can we please nerf Zetterburn and Kragg a bit? Thanks.

There are a number of negative reviews complaining about the game client, but I didn't run into any of the major issues they complained about. No weird background tasks in my task manager. Hit the 'X' to close the game, and it quit fine. No super lag (just time to load things from the server). All in all it could use some more polish and some bug fixes here and there, but it's by no means unplayable.
Now that that's out of the way, let's talk about the game. The game itself, as many people have already written, is a highly strategic and creative way to battle other players. There's tons of interesting skills and combinations you can come up with, and so many different decks out there to try and beat. The four spheres offer a lot of variety in themselves, concentrating on defense, resource control, attack, and board control (roughly speaking). Within the spheres you also find a lot of variety, each features multiple "families" of units that can combo with one another. Each also has different strengths and weaknesses. And you can make a perfectly strong deck without combinations in particular, if you'd rather throw individually strong units together.
So is the gameplay itself compelling? Yes, undoubtedly. The fact that there's players who've stuck with the game for so many years attests to that as well.
Let's talk about the developers as well, for a moment. The developers listen to their playerbase. I used to play back when the owners of the IP were from overseas, and made bad decisions to try and milk players for every cent. The US team wound up buying the IP, and have since been making the game much more fun and more rewarding to play. No longer are you purchasing options limited to just throwing dice and hoping for good cards. Now you have real options to aim for cards you want, or spin the ol roulette if you're in the mood for a gamble. There's a single-card marketplace, where players can sell each other cards and get rid of duplicates! Not to mention some single player adventures, NPCs to battle, indepth, fun tutorials, and even a crafting system I haven't even gotten into yet. They've made the whole experience ten times better, and they're not going to stop now.
Balance is another important area the devs have improved, creating a subset of the huge card base that's qualified as "Horizons legal". Some cards, qhile fun to play, were just too overpowered or convenient, and I'm glad to see that they've tackled the issue head on. I'm confident future releases will be in the same spirit.
To sum up, if you're interested in a strategic CCG, give Alteil a shot. It's got beautiful art, lore and characters, and most importantly varied and fun way to take down your opponent. The client's not perfect, but the dev's are dedicated and it'll only get better.

About the context of the games original release:
This is from back in the late 90's.  Quake 2, Half-Life , and Unreal were out and the Build engine may have been "old" and outdated, but gamers weren't quite as snobby and picky back then.  Most of us pc gaming kids only had what PC our parents bought and were happy for anything that ran on them.   Honestly, we were still enjoying games made with the Build engine even after it was outdated.    It was a solid engine that ran fast on almost anything over a 50 or 66 mhz CPU.
About the game itself:
I personally passed on NAM back when it was in a large cardboard box on the pc gaming shelves of Wal-Mart and Electronics Boutique.  Being used to the more imaginative content of the ID software and 3D Realms games, a FPS set in an "authentic" setting based on historic events sounded boring to me.     Fast forward a decade and a few years, and I'm hunting down old 90's games I passed on just for nostalgia.
NAM is pretty impressive for a Build engine game.    The norm for any Build engine game (and almost any other FPS) from the 90's was to copy the Doom formula of gameplay.  "All by yourself, find the keys to open the doors to exit the level while shooting all the monsters."
NAM is on a scale beyond DN3D and it's Build engine brothers.   You've got actual air strikes with jets flying over. (triggered by the player a lot of the time), NPC's that help the player fight or replenish health (which can be told to follow or hold position).  A lot more speech and dialog than in the typical FPS of the era.  As well as the most convincing jungle that the Build engine could probably handle.  (most FPS of that era all took place in mostly indoor areas of metal and concrete.)
I think it's pretty fun in the same way that Shadow Warrior, Blood, DN3D, Redneck Rampage, Doom, Quake, Heretic, and Hexen are.    If you're used to nothing but modern FPS then you'll be lost and confused as there is no arrow pointing where to go and no NPC holding your hand and dragging you through the game.  You can die pretty quickly after you spawn on the first level.  You just have to learn the rules of survival for this particular game and figure out a strategy to avoid cheap death.   (although it really aids in the atmosphere of chaos and panic of Vietnam)  I quickly learned that you need to try to keep your back to the walls and stay low as much as possible, as the NK respawns and likes to ambush you around corners.  Also, random mortar shellings often strike out in the open.
Yeah.  NAM is a fun sprite based 90's FPS that doesn't totally follow the game design trends of the era.

Playing this game as is is a technical nightmare. The controls are awful and you can't change them, the graphics are an indistinguishable gray mess and you will not get a good framerate on DOSbox.  However this can be remedied quite simply by downloading the eduke32 engine and dragging the required gamefiles onto the .exe.  After swapping out the engine I realized that this game is actually quite good once the technical difficulties are resolved.  Especially in hindsight with all the other failed Vietnam themed games out there.  This game gets a lot of things right. Enemies hide behind trees, pop out of foxholes and sometimes seem to materalize out of thin air. the area is constantly being bombareded by aircraft and artillery, friendly fire is common and can go both ways, the M16 is a piece of crap that will "jam" on you at the wrong moment and get you killed (in this game you can't reloaded it manually, so you'll often pull the trigger only to reload, but like I said this does have a real life equivalent), stepping in the wrong place will activate a mine and insta-kill you. This game is hard, you will die a lot, you will learn to take cover, to fire blindly at bushes, to lob grenades like a madman and to never stay in one place for too long.  The sound in this game is actually quite good, even today. Airstrikes are looming and bombs are always going off, radio chatter is constant and enemy banter and gunfire is everywhere, it sounds like a warzone.  Again once I learned to play it right, in the Eduke32 engine with the music tunred off, and the doors in the background for atmosphere, I found myself really enjoying this game. It feels like a well thought out Duke3D mod and it feels like NAM.

This is the new game a lot of Super Smash Bros. fans have been waiting for. This game feels very fresh, but still familiar. I think I'm enjoying this more than any other Early Access game I've purchased. The graphics are nostalgic and crisp, the gameplay is very solid, and online play works very well if you have a reasonable ping/connection speed.
There's currently only 6 characters available, but 2 more are to be released when the game is officially out. There is a small handful of stages to pick from, each giving you a "basic" or "aether" variation. The "basic" versions remove walk-offs, stage destruction and stage hazards, presumably for competitive play.
Much like the smash bros games, each character has 4 sets of moves. Regular attacks (think tilts), areal attacks, heavy attacks (think smash attacks), and special moves. But unlike smash bros, there is no shield button. There is a sort of spot-dodge like button that can be used to parry, but requires very goos timing. Also removed is the ability to grab the ledge. Instead, each character has the ability to wall jump, and use their up-special a 2nd time after the wall jump.
Balance might need a little work, but it's all there. Also do yourself a favor and get a USB GCN adapter instead of using the X360 controller. It just works so much better, despite the extra setup work it requires.
After being very disapointed in Smash 4, it's great to see a game that's really had some time and love put into it. Fantastic game, and I would HIGHLY recommend it to anyone.

DOWNLOAD EDUKE32 BEFORE PLAYING
Seriously, EDUKE32 is a fantastic Build Engine Emulator and runs NAM like a charm. Comes with console commands, anti-aliasing, mouse movement and much more smooth jazz!
With that in mind, playing NAM through EDUKE32 isn't required but it is great for those who are on a nostalgia binge and can't get past the state of the current game.
NAM itself started out as a Duke Nukem total-conversion called "Platoon" and was pretty damn good for what it was, and while I'm not sure what led the dev team to jump into the indie-scene I'm quite glad they did, even if their product was panned at the time of release for it's engine and graphics.
Gameplay wise, NAM is quite hard and in some areas is unfair, with airstrikes routinely killing you moreso then the Vietcong scrambling out of the woodwork. However, the meaty gunplay and pretty damn articulate level design (for the build engine) kept dragging me back in. The Story included in the original manual is laughable but is not necessary to enjoy the game entirely. Just shoot VC and don't get blown up.
Graphics and sound is pretty good for the build engine but those who judge by graphics will not be pleased, as even at the time of release NAM wasn't the best looker.
Long story short, NAM is a brainless shooter and has a certain niche amongst older FPS fans and is a favorite in the Duke Nukem modding scene. So grab both NAM and Eduke and kick back for a couple of hours, but make sure to watch your head, those damn airstrikes will certainly get you more then once.

The audio work in particular on this game is amazing- character voices, sound effects and environmental ambience achieve the delicate balance between distinct but not distracting.  The music pulls you into the environment and complements the visual atmosphere perfectly.
My two major criticisms:  First- the amount of work the game expects of the player in order to discern anything beyond the most rudimentary elements of the storyline.  I would argue that the story is immersive and interesting; it is deserving of more people that appreciate it!  I think it would have been more accessible if the player were given larger chunks of the story (and more deliberately.)
Second- At times it could be hard to figure out where I should go in order to progress.  This is inherent to the genre but I felt the handful of times I had to backtrack just to find the small thing I missed did not add much to the overall experience.  Perhaps something could be done with the mapping system to make loose ends more apparent.

Let me start out by saying I rarely take the time to review a game. Having recently beat this game I felt I needed to say a few things about it. First of all I did not like this game. I absolutely loved it. I didn't expect to enjoy it much going in but boy was I wrong. This little gem has ended up one of my favorite games of all time.
If you don't know what to expect, think Zelda style character progression + a Dark Souls push your luck monetary system + Megaman style bosses + the hardest jumping puzzles of all time. Now add in a unique world with insanely good art, great soundtracks and interesting characters. Boom, you have Hollow Knight.
This game is not easy. It will not hold you hand and guide you. It will make you yell in frustration. But once you finally beat that boss or finish that jump puzzle, oh man, the celebration is on. The combat is intense and fast paced with some really neat boss fights. There were a number of times I remember thinking, “Well, there's no way the next _____ can be harder.” I look back on my past self now and laugh at my ignorance.
Aside from the combat there were great little moments in the story that I did not expect. Things that really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off but also made me laugh (never trust a bug). Moments of awe after reaching some incredible landscapes, or pride after being bowed to. And just a general sense of curiosity at the world Team Cherry has built.
After over 45 hours of playtime I am still finding new things to do and am having a blast. For the price tag I am shocked at the value in this game. Team Cherry has also added multiple DLCs onto the game for free.
This game does have a few cons however.
Secondly, this game is NOT for everybody. If you're easily frustrated or don't like a challenge, avoid this game at all costs. If you are not scared to be tested however, prepare yourself for one hell of a ride.
I firmly believe this game will finish on my list of games up there with the only game I can really compare it to, Ocarina of Time. It's that good.
EDIT: Apparently I missed a patch adding mouse support. Thanks to Jonnymeboy for clearing that up!

This game is quite literally the best thing ever. In spite of the overwhelming glitches, bad graphics (which also glitch) and extremely cheesy plot and dialogue, the game is extremely fun to play. Especially if you try to get good at it. In it´s surface, Necrovision is just a shooter, but actually, it is much more than that. It´s a shooter alright, but also a rhythm game, due to the way reloading can be sped up (which is crutial on higher difficulties) a bit of a mystery with the strange story-line, but most importantly: a complete mayhem.
Let me illustrate just how much of a mayhem this game is: assuming you collect a sufficient amount of Bonus Items, you gain some pretty crazy special abilities, that mix quite well with the magic you learn to use half way through the game (spoilers!)  one of those literally turns everybody around you into burning statues. You will watch the attacking enemies petrify and incinerate mid-swing while laughing skulls burst out of your infernal aura and pierce your enemies and your death-claw relentlesly unleashes one fireball after another...! No other game can do this.
Not only does Necrovision approach degrees of mayhem never before seen in another game, but its gunplay is rock solid. You get to dual wield everything, you can use melee weapons with ranged weapons at the same time, you can beat people up with a pistol (for bonus points!) there are many ways to approach the game. I ofter found myself returning to the earlier levels just to shoot people in the head with my trusty luger (which is absolutely brutal when comboed with rhythmical  reload acceleration) but those are unfortunately quite few.
The chief problems of this game is the lack of levels. It´s just too darn short for such a niche role. There is no other game that can satisfy one´s desire for destruction like this one, but to quench it 100%, it´s just too short (meaning, it´s got only a normal length campain, a bunch of challenges, and nothing more - no multiplayer of any sort) Due to this, I give this game a 8/10. Meaning it´s about 4 times better than Bioshock Infinite !GASP! which makes it a must buy. Make your mum proud of your Wampire World War achievements.

As someone who's played a fair share of platformers and puzzlers and has pretty defined opinions about design and what "difficulty" entails, this game started out as decently fun and interesting. I enjoyed the music, and the title screen background art got my expectations comfortably high. But quickly, it feels like the game runs out of ideas for level design using the gravity gimmick. It starts to feel like a mediocre free Flash browser game - long segments of jumping on a slow stream of orb enemies, repeated "use gravity to drag this platform around" bits, and a lot of areas where the solution to the puzzle is to simply use the same bruteforce technique a few times, because the inconsistent physics will net you a win. Some of the puzzles that brag difficulty turn out to be boring - you have to place a grav/anti well at a very precise point that you won't realize is wrong until a full 10 seconds pass, so you try just a little bit to the right, etc. A browser Flash puzzle platformer game is the best comparison really, because of the inconsistent physics and drawn out level design characteristic of them. And the "ultimate challenge," which is the game's sort of newgame+ hardmode, serves to limit your options to make levels feel even less creative to pass by removing anti-grav wells, and makes all enemies physics-based, allowing the often shoddy engine to make your play even less consistent than your first run. Ultimately, I gave up on that because I was bored, not challenged. Games like La-Mulana will leave you feeling challenged by the puzzles and platforming. Or, perhaps this game will as well. A lot of people seem to like the game, but I would have been bored of it if it were freeware. A lot of positivity about this game seems to repeatedly refer to the price point. A game at a comparably low price point which I will recommend in Defy Gravity's stead is Super Hexagon, a challenging game that tests skill rather than the sheer snoring patience required of Defy Gravity. Or maybe I'm wrong and don't know♥♥♥♥♥♥about video games.

BioShock™ Remastered is a re-release of the 9 year old BioShock and comes with overworked graphics and additionaly with Director’s Commentary, Museum of Orphaned Concepts and Challenge Rooms.
In BioShock you are a survivor of a plane crash in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. You are able to make your way to an island where a submarine is waiting to take you to into the great depths below where the mysterious underwater city of Rapture awaits. The city is trashed and genetic freaks called splicers roam around, attacking anything that gets in front of them. In order to survive you will have fight through these Splicers and other oddities keeping your eyes and ears open for clues into what has gone wrong, how you may be able to help or how you can escape.
One aspect that makes the storyline work so well is the way it is told. BioShock uses a real time method of telling the story through random radio reports, overheard conversations and audio recordings.
You can choose from a variety of different weapons, anywhere from pistols and shotguns to chemical throwers and grenade launchers. Each gun has different ammo that you can use. There are also many plasmids that you can use. You can electrify the water to kill everyone in it, set people on fire, freeze them and then smash them with a wrench, among other things.
The graphics are not such a big improvement in comparison to the original version.
The sound of BioShock really puts you into the game. From the creepy things the splicers say to the background music, everything fits perfect.
BioShock builds a great atmosphere, it is a stunning game and definitely worth to buy.

Defy Gravity's a pretty good game!
It's a platformer where you have the ability to place grav wells (a blue field that attracts you) and anti-grav wells (a yellow field that repels you). To keep you from just slowing launching yourself between points and never touching the ground, you're limited to one well of each type on screen at a time, and you can only fire each type twice before having to recharge on the ground or after bouncing off an enemy. The puzzles are basic, with you having to navigate hazards to reach the goal, and some levels where you aren't effected by your own gravity wells and can only manipulate the environment. Then, after you beat the game once, you're asked to do it again without anti-grav wells, changing the strategy of the game.
It controls well, it's fun to play, and it can be challenging without ever becoming unfairly difficult. It's a short game, but $3 is a fine price for it. If you ever see it on sale, though, you have no excuse not to get this. Definitely recommended.

Review: A squad based tactical VS Card game where you have to manage RNG AKA Alteil.
Story: 7/10
A card game needs little story, and while Alteil goes above to provide more the what you will normally see, there are plot holes and little lore to dig through. With so many characters, you can write an epic from them, but we have yet to see this in the game.
The story is, we are Iczers, teleported mages whom can summon others to do their bidding to fight for us. We fight because there is a war.
Gameplay: 7/10
There is a lot to learn, and a lot to think about in Alteil. Perhaps overly much so. The limited deck/file size of 25 means that every card decision is a troubled  one, but if you're one of those who likes a challenge, then this game is for you.
Or you can just grab a meta deck and think little of what cards you need. That works to. The powercreep is strong in Alteil, as good as the game is.
That aside, we have the concept of "rows", "range" and speed.
Speed determines which creature goes first. If two creatures have the same speed, it's RNG who goes first.
Range determines how far the rows your creature can hit if the row is blocked. If there's 3 enemy creatures in your creature range, which creature you hit is RNG.
When playing cards, we have open skills and grimores. the priority is grimore>open skill high speed >open skill low speed. If there are any ties, RNG.
UI: 8/10
With the inclusion of game speed (and the FF speed), I can now reward Alteil with a solid 8 in UI. It could be improved though, it's hard to drag cards from set to the field.
Art: 9/10
Art's great.
Sound: 7.5/10
It's not really to my preference.
Community 8/10
The people here are preety friendly and great.
CCG tools: 6/10
Auction house taking 15%, with the restriction of only paying users can sell. That's really to high isn't it? Card creation aka cauldron is a mess, unknowing, and unreliable useless tool right now. Even with recipes, the chance of you getting what you want is 40%, or less. Save your mats.
GM Events: 8/10
Tons of events, and events is where you will want to join in and play, because these are the best and most reliable way to get the cards you want. They come often. I don't have complains.
Meta: 5/10
Some files literally can't win against some files. Nuff said.
Final score. 7/10
Great time waister. Play if you like complexity and art.

---Fix 1: Windows 7---
If you are running windows 7 you may be able to fix the game via changing the font localisation files, instructions to do this are here:
This won't fix the bugs on Windows 8 but it might be good to do anyway.
---Fix 2: Windows 8 and Windows 7---
If you're running windows 8 or if the above doesn't work then download a program called DXWnd found here:
- After extracting the file run the 'dxwnd' .exe
- A little blank window will open, select the 'edit' menu and click 'add'
- A window with a bunch of options and tabs will open, fill them out as follows:
- "NAME:" = Robin Hood (can be anything you like)
- "PATH:" = C:\Program Files\Steam\SteamApps\common\Robin Hood\Game.exe
Note: you may have the game installed at a different location eg. "Program Files (x86)"
That's it, Hit OK and you should see 'Robin Hood' appear as an option from the window that was blank before.
- Select it and go >edit>run and the game will run smoothly
You will have to launch the game using this program or have DXWnd open when launching it from steam every time.
DXWnd is a hook program that you can use to get a lot of old games running smoothly on new systems, it won't hurt to replace the font files anyway if you still have some problems (in Fix 1). I didn't create DXWnd nor was I the one who worked out that it fixes the game.
is a trustworthy site for developers and you can get more support from the guy who made the program there if you need it.
This fix isn't perfect, I get grapical artifacts from the mouse on the menus and it's crashed once but otherwise it's run perfectly so far. Resolution looks a bit blurry, I'll add a way to fix that if I find a mod or work it out.
---review---
As for the game itself. This was one of my favourites as a kid! You have a small team of robin hood and his merry men that you move around like a traditional RTS, each unit you control has 3 or so abilities which are mostly unique. Robin can knock people out with a punch, frier tuck can tie people up with rope, little john can carry bodies etc. you'll have to combine these abilities to get through situations. You will want to avoid fighting, once a character is locked in combat it becomes dificult to escape and they'll slowly die, some characters can't fight at all; so the game is about stealth. Things happen slowly in this game, abilities are executed slowly, it's all a bit sluggish and clunky but that's not really a detriment. You'll be waiting for the ideal time to make your move and planning out your aproach. The sluggishness might feel lame for some people but it works fine for what you're trying to achieve. The levels are very well designed, they're open ended and have plenty of little areas that are a bonus. You'll clear one area and in doing so work out a solution for another area, these areas often wrap around and encircle each other. You can clear a level very quickly after you've figured things out but the first time around it may take hours. It's very satisfying.
If you aren't a fan of stealth or clicky isometric games this isn't for you. It's about tactics and stealth, not combat.
Their aren't many games in this genre and this game is up there with some of the best. Isometric stealth games are dead now but it's well worth the few dollars it goes for on steam to try them out with this one.

I was slightly worried when I bought this game because of all the reviews stating it has trouble running on modern PCs. I took a chance though, and I'm glad I did.
I do most of my gaming on my custom build (GTX 760, FX-8320, Windows 7), and although I was worried this game might have compatibility issues on that PC, I had a backup plan in that I also have an old Dell laptop with Windows Vista on it that I thought could definitely run the game if my main gaming PC couldn't.
After instaling the game first on my main machine and experiencing some extremely low FPS (especially during combat), I tried it on my laptop, where it ran perfectly. I'm so glad bacause this is really a fantastic game. Beautiful graphics of the isometric style (every environment/map looks incredibly detailed and good enough to frame as a painting on your wall), interesting gameplay (RTS style focussing soley on combat and stealth), and a story with a great narrative, voice acting and music that completely immerse you into the adventure. This game captures the essence of Robin Hood perfectly.
The bottom line is that this game is great and can probably run perfectly if you have an older computer/operating system. Even on a newer PC, it was still somewhat playable, but only if you reeeeeeeeally want to play the game and would tolerate such issues. Hopefully this game will eventually get an HD re-release like what Age of Empires II and other older games are getting, or at least some kind of update/patch to get it to work on modern machines.

I never cared for Diablo, so it's a bit puzzling that I put so much time into Torchlight, a derivative made in part by makers of Diablo & D2. Most tout D2 over Torchlight due to its multiplayer/larger class variety, but Torchlight's interface addresses my problems with the genre.
The main problem with ARPGs (esp. Blizzard's) is "tedium" & "excessive mouse clicking." Torchlight takes real measures to reduce both. You can hotkey commands to ALL keyboard numerals. You get an invincible pet that not only doubles your inventory, auto-attacks enemies, and can pick up items for you, but can be told "go back to town and sell your items to free up space." THIS IS HUGE. You're also CONSTANTLY getting new gear, which makes Normal mode a breeze. Alas, you still left-click to both move AND attack.
As far as aesthetics, I prefer that in this game, you can dual-wield GUNS and effectively set up machinegun sentry turrets. Hits have impact. Enemies can be pretty massive. One's even a chaingun mecha!

This is the new game a lot of Super Smash Bros. fans have been waiting for. This game feels very fresh, but still familiar. I think I'm enjoying this more than any other Early Access game I've purchased. The graphics are nostalgic and crisp, the gameplay is very solid, and online play works very well if you have a reasonable ping/connection speed.
There's currently only 6 characters available, but 2 more are to be released when the game is officially out. There is a small handful of stages to pick from, each giving you a "basic" or "aether" variation. The "basic" versions remove walk-offs, stage destruction and stage hazards, presumably for competitive play.
Much like the smash bros games, each character has 4 sets of moves. Regular attacks (think tilts), areal attacks, heavy attacks (think smash attacks), and special moves. But unlike smash bros, there is no shield button. There is a sort of spot-dodge like button that can be used to parry, but requires very goos timing. Also removed is the ability to grab the ledge. Instead, each character has the ability to wall jump, and use their up-special a 2nd time after the wall jump.
Balance might need a little work, but it's all there. Also do yourself a favor and get a USB GCN adapter instead of using the X360 controller. It just works so much better, despite the extra setup work it requires.
After being very disapointed in Smash 4, it's great to see a game that's really had some time and love put into it. Fantastic game, and I would HIGHLY recommend it to anyone.

I'm long time fan of Civilization series and I have very mixed feeling about this one - unfortunately on "No" side more then on "Yes".
On a good side:
First of all, I had a lot of fun playing it for first 3 or 4 times. Everything was fresh new, I had to learn a lot and this side of the game is as always very nice for me. Unfortunately  once I got those games behind me I find it hard to come back for more.
I love the quests implemented in this game - they really add a lot of depth - you can make different choices each time you play and your civilization will be affected by them - you can shape it to be a bit different.
There are a lot of problems with make this game either boring or annoying to play:
- military - auto-upgrading military units sounded like fun at start but then once you start war it's really really annoying. Your enemy's units can at any moment upgrade to a much better unit on the field. There are not that many units overall, which probably could be fine if they were not being upgraded automatically - but with automatic upgrades it feels like you have very limited toolbox to use for war. Also upgrades are way too big between levels, they should be more gradual. You need to get few points of affinity to upgrade a unit again and then it's like major change. So in order to win a war you basically focus just on technologies that raise your affinity for affinity's sake, not for anything that this technology brings to your civilization.
- economy - trade is especially annoying, in late game when you have 2 or 3 trade units per city, you constantly have to pick another trade target for them, every single turn. On the other hand trade is very powerful and without it your civilization will be in a disadvantage so you can't just ignore it.
- I also hate how this game no longer rewards me for playing. End game? Just one picture, no way to check my progress against other civilization, some pathetic text "you win" and that's all. When you get a new technology, it's described very poorly and quote that is read to you is usually poor, a bit stupid or non-sense entirely.
If you want to play this game you should probably wait a bit till it gets cheaper on gets some DLC/expansion to fix those issues. Right now I can't really recommend to buy this game at full cost. Myself I'll go back to Civ V.

NAM (also called NAPALM) is a first-person shooter set during the Vietnam War, developed by TNT Team and published by GT Interactive Software and released as a total conversion mod for Duke Nukem 3D in 1997 in MS-DOS under the name Platoon. Infogrames did a remake with better art with the product manager from the game Blood (One Unit Whole). U.S. Marine Sergeant Dan Snyder helped with the computer simulation training for American troops with a Doom army mod.
NAM was published on the Steam platform in 2014 where people can buy a virtual copy of the game.
A sequel to NAM is World War II GI which is also developed and published by the same studios and runs on the same engine.
In NAM you play as Alan Westmoreland ( also known as The Bear), a U.S. Marine Corps Sergeant during the Vietnam War in 1966.
In fact you are in service of the Central Intelligence Agency and you are genetic engineered to become a super human war machine.
You are given standard military orders and most of the time you wander alone or you are assisted by small teams.
In order to survive you have to fulfill several tours of duty in order to show that the side effect of the serum can be overcome.
During the game you have to deal with ambushes, booby traps such as anti-personnel mines, firefights, gas, air strikes, snipers, tanks, cannons and many more who will block your path towards the end of every level.
In some levels you receive help from AI U.S. Marines like a medic.
For me the game is everything except easy because of the high presence of hostile surprise elements in each level which I really liked because it makes the game quite challenging.
Saving multiple times while playing NAM is a good thing to do but don't do this when you are being shot or wandering through large open areas otherwise your saved progress can be a total disaster by limitless dying when the save game is being loaded.
I really enjoyed this game because of the looks and feels that blend in very well even though it is pixel art.
If you have played the Doom series, Duke Nukem 3D, Blood (One Unit Whole), Shadow Warrior, Redneck Rampage you will probably like this game because of the Build game engine.
I highly recommend this game to people who like challenging retro pixelated first-person shooters with great gameplay and level design, certainly when the game is on sale!

Necrovision is a strange game. Stuck between a myriad of styles and influences, it emerges as a blend between the atmosphere of classic world war shooters and the crazy mass murder party of games such as Painkiller, Serious Sam or Bulletstorm. The overall result is highly personal and depends heavily on your mindset: don't go into this game expecting an AAA shooter. You'll find cringeworthy cutscenes, amateurish voice acting, a pixelated GUI and weird bugs all around.
However, as soon as you get past its imperfections, you'll be playing a pretty crazy and fun game with a (surprisingly!) relatively readable storyline, zombie beheading, dragons, huge boss fights and lots of other nonsense♥♥♥♥♥♥happening in WWI. One of the biggest surprises was level design, which, although relatively linear, is huge, well planned enough, often aesthetically pleasing and with a very classic feel and pace.
On less positive points, the combo system is pretty bland and doesn't really feel well-implemented (although it can be fun). The weapons are also sub-par: the historical limitations are understandable, but for a game this crazy, they often slow the action to a crawl as you painstakingly bolt your rifle after every shot fighting giant demon things. Health is also a bit weird: medkits exist and are pretty abundant but are close to useless since your health automatically recharges up to about 75%; which breaks some of the classic appeal in my view.
Overally, Necrovision is a pretty fun experience if you're willing to forget its technical shortcomings and accept its particular brand of insanity. 7.5/10

Music/Sounds:
Nothing really special here but all the music and sound effects fit really well into the overall immersion of the game!
Community:
This game has a fantastic community, at least that i've come across! Plenty of people have helped me get to grips with features I didnt really understand. Also had lots of fun questing with random people i've come across while playing! If you do get this game send me a message, always looking for people to play with! :)
Not really anthing else I can say, but if your into MMORPG's you should really give it a go!

I pre-ordered this game for $60 after playing through Hitman: Blood Money because I was so enthralled with the concept of being, well, the hitman! There's just something about being given a contract case, studying the contents within, memorizing the face of your target, studying maps, and choosing the right weapon for the job. I need to maneuver my way through a riverboat to get to my target? Better stick with an mp5 - silenced. Need to assassinate the bridegroom during a wedding? Better handle it at a distance with the W2000 - silenced.
None of those things that I mentioned I loved from the previous game were in Absolution, which is part of why I was so disappointed with the title. Sure, the graphics of this game are more than a few notches above blood money, but the feeling of being the contract killer just isn't there. It feels like a Max Payne title with more (or less, depending on your play style) sneaking.
Although I'm disappointed with this installment in what was otherwise an absolutely wonderful series, I can understand why the game is the way it is. Agent 47 is an old dude. He's been taking contracts for over 10 amazing years, and it can't be easy with age. I just recommend thinking about this game as about Agent 47, and the relationship he built with Diana. The game requires a little less thought than the previous ones, but it still makes for a decent playthrough.
I highly recommend playing the previous games first.

This isn't the way I want this series to go. 47 shouldn't be on the run; he should be in control when he's on missions.
Main reasons: instead of relying on disguises to get you through missions, you have to duck into cover a lot, which makes it feel more like Thief or Splinter Cell. There are missions that are fairly uninteresting, but there are very fun kill missions. The checkpoints are awful sometimes, and I'd rather choose my own save points.. Taking out three targets with a lot of precision by 'accidents' whilst looking for checkpoints on the level in the meanwhile doesn't make it more fun. I am a long time player with hundreds of hours in Alteil and can never get tired of the deep tactical gameplay that Alteil. The best thing is that there is
. This means that you have access to all 25 cards from the start(+5 Soul Skill cards) and thus do not have to pray to lady luck for the luck of the draw. There are ways to get specific cards - you can use "point cards" and turn them in for a card of your choice(the amount of point cards indicates what rarity you can turn them in for). Alteil is hard and has a learning curve so it is not for everyone. I recommend this if you can put in a bit of time to learn. I have played tons of card games, including Infinity Wars, Scrolls, Eternal and Hearthstone. But there is no card game that excites me as much as Alteil.

I've been playing Alteil since 2011 and it's still the only card game that I've ever really enjoyed.
Alteil is highly tactical, and a great challenge whether you pay for cards or not. There are four 'spheres of influence'. Cards within these spheres tend to have similar traits, advantages and drawbacks. You're free to play with any sphere (once you've collected enough viable cards to make a deck) and even a combination of spheres if you plan your file well enough. You get access to your entire deck during a game, so you're not relying on luck of the draw. However, you do need to build up resources (called SP ingame - stands for spell points I think?) to play your higher level (and often more robust/powerful) units.
The learning curve can be rough, and chances are you'll rage now and then. Don't be put off if you're struggling - everyone started at the bottom.
Up until now, one of the biggest problems that faced Alteil has been their small player base. Hopefully this will change with the recent steam release. If you're someone who enjoys challenging yourself against other tactical players you'll absolutely enjoy Alteil. The card selection is huge, the art is fantastic, and there's still more crazy card combinations to be discovered.
P.S For those who wonder "how Free To Play is Alteil really?", there have been a number of very successful players who didn't pay a cent, and you wouldn't realise it if you faced them. You certainly get access to more cards at a faster rate if you're buying, but no amount of money makes you a smarter player.
