This is a worthy entry in the Civilization series and easily worth buying in its current form. Beyond Earth makes significant departures from the gameplay of Civilization 5, while retaining enough of the core to make its gameplay understandable.
The biggest change from Civilzation 5 is the change from a tech tree to a tech web. This allows more diversity in playstyle, but definitely takes more than one game to really understand. For instance, when do you unlock the ability to mine strategic resources? The technologies that actually USE that resource effectively will frequently be in a completely different part of the web. Its nearly impossible to truly ignore any part of the tech web, which can make it punishing for the first game that you use it. If you play through a game however, the tradeoffs become clearer when prioritizing certain techs, and soon it is intuitive which technology you get when.
Warfare feels distinctly smoother in this game than previous titles. While there is still usually a time period in every game where someone has significantly more powerful units than the other players, this happens in every civ game and does not usually last very long in this one. The basic units are upgraded throughout the game depending on what play style you choose. This means they remain the core of your army into the late game. Special units from advanced technologies are like an elite tip of your army at a handful of units, but you may have significantly more basic units. Combined with an orbital layer and military units that can use it, warfare feels deeper than in previous Civilizations. The AI unfortunately, kind of sucks at it. The AI has always been a flaw in the series, but it is unfortunate that it remains true in this iteration.
Aliens replace barbarians in BE, and in my opinion they are far improved. While they seem overly hard to make angry, I find they consistently give me some breathing room when dealing with AI expansion. Before an area can truly be controlled with a safe settlement, the aliens in the area usually need to be cleared. The time that this takes give you plenty of opportunities to expand youself, especially if you make use of explorers (who the aliens will never attack after 1 point of Purity). This makes the early expansions relatively stress free, even if competition over resources heats up later.
My experience with Beyond Earth can be summed up easily; this game has already started to suck hours out of my life, if you give it a chance it will do the same to yours. 10/10

It is basically a Civ5, but better and with a lot of promise for modders and additional DLC content. And it is in space! If you played Civ5, it won't take you long to get familiar with this one. So, how is it different (and better)?
First thing you gonna notice is advanced starting customization. Before landing your colonists on an unknown planet, you can choose from a wide array of bonuses that affect your early-game a lot. You can choose the profession of your colonists (for example, if you choose them to be Engineers, you will have +2 production in your starting colony), specifics of the spaceship your people are using to get to the planet (provides some map-related bonuses like being able to see all the shorelines on the minimap from the get-go) and what type of cargo the colonists took with them (if it is a weapon cache, you get a military unit right from the start). And even though some of the bonuses might seem not-so-useful and an optimal choice seems to be apparent, all of them are good for different strategies, which you can think of.
Second thing is the planet's wildlife, that replace the barbarians from the previous game. Basically, the concept is similar: there are alien nests which spawn aliens over time. But aliens can give you much more trouble at start, as their spawn rate is pretty high, and there is a few different kinds of them that can lazily stroll near your colony right from the start. And there are some really strong ones that you will not be able to handle for quite a while. Like that huge Siege Worm (48 mellee strength! One-hit your soldiers!). But the thing is, they are not always agressive and will never attack the colony itself, unless provoked. Sometimes, they might just chew on your explorer just for the heck of it when he gets near, and sometimes they might not give a heck while he trudges right in the middle of a big swarm of feral wildlife. But just try to attack them yourself - and you get an angry horde of bugs of different forms and sizes trying to kill your soldiers, digest your workers and raze your farms. One thing though, the aliens will never upgrade into having better units, so you will have much less troubles with them as you advance in technology.
Third thing worthy of note is that there is more to do with your starting explorers (scouts). The game still has an analogue of ancient ruins you can take with your units, but there are also various exploration sites you can conduct an expedition at with your explorers. The process itself is just like building tile improvements. Get the dude on the hex, tell him to conduct an expedition and wait for a few turns.
Fourth thing is a Tech Web. Instead of having to research all the techs over time, there are a few branching paths for your scientists to take and you are the only one who decide what to research first.
Fifth, and the best, thing is Affinity Levels. There are 3 different affinities, and by researching certain technologies and completing quests in a certain way will give you experience points towards one affinity. Different affinities have different buildings, different units and different means of victory. You can actually have levels in a few different affinities, but you will only get units from the highest-level one. And although all the units basically have the same concept we all are used to (close-range infantry, range infantry, vehicles instead of cavalry and siege weapons), units belonging to different affinities look different and have different bonuses. Like, a Purity-affinity Guardians (range infantry) have 50% damage bonus whan being garrisoned in a colony, while a Harmony-affinity shooter of the same tier is stronger when he doesn't have any units on the neighbouring tiles. Its really awesome.
The only complaint i have with this game is that the multiplayer games still have the very same problems with lags and players occasionally dropping, although not as often as it used to be.
So basically, if you liked Civ5, you will like this one a lot, just like i did. Just do not expect something totally new on a conceptual level. It is still Civ, after all!

The weapons look nice and are fun. Most of the enemy sprites, on the other hand, are pretty lackluster. The maps are very open, and there are multiple paths to explore. You often have to flank your enemies to survive. Playing a level for the first time you will often die from unpredictable airstrikes and other random explosions. Also there are very view details. Everything looks just green and brown. The maps are littered with invisible walls. Generally the level design is pretty weak in comparision to Duke3D or Shadow Warrior. The same goes for the uninspired soundtrack that was probably composed and performed by keyboard cat. Despite all of these downsides the game is still surprisingly fun! The voice acting is cool and there are even friendly NPCs you can interact with. If you love old "2.5D" ego shooters, you will have fun with this. I'll definitely keep playing. Only get it on sale though.

Civ. Space. Epic.
As with many modern titles from the Civilization franchise. The base game is just that - the base game. Some reviews fault Beyond Earth simply for the time we exist in where DLC is commonplace. That is simply unfair.
It is a tight little game. Although, not nearly as great an undertaking as Civilization 5, the game paces itself right. The tech web, affinities, and virtues systems all create a sense of freedom and flexibility. That you aren't looking to replay the triumphs or mistakes of the past, but forge new ones.
Beyond Earth is not without its minor flaws, however. The trade system could use some work as it is an integral part of the game, but suffers from a poor organizational interface. Aliens seem daunting at first, but come off being more or less in the background after a few playthroughs - no means to scale their aggressiveness either. AI for computer players seems less differentiated and outright strange at times. For example, AI players will call you out for killing their covert agents, which to me seems countertuitive to a spy game as a nation-state should be disavowing that they had any connection to a supposed spy. Second example, AI flip their lids that you removed poisonous gas (miasma) anywhere near their borders, which boggles the mind - how dare I help you clear that miasma! Finally, the icons for buildings, units and wonders lacks differentiation to the untrained eye, and even then is difficult to identify at a glance.
Unpolished? Yes.
Unfinished? Not for a base game.
Fun? Yes
Time will ultimately tell whether this game stands up to the greats and its forebears, but so far it is an enjoyable game.

Hollow Knight is a superb game, both in terms of quality and value for money. I went in expecting a standard metroid-vania experience but found a lot more. The exploration in this game is on par with the original Dark Souls, that sense of tension you get pushing into uncharted territory is so common in Hollow Knight along with the relief when you reach a familiar area or find a path out of a nightmare area. The map continued to expand and one up my expectations long after I thought i'd found the edges of the world. There is a platforming element to the game and it feels smooth, responsive and controls well with a controller or Keyboard (i personally recommend a keyboard but i'm wierd). For the most part the combat is the focus, and it works well with simple 4 way aiming melee attacks and some 'spells'. This adds enough complexity without it ever losing its focus and there are some intense boss fights that will put your skills to the test. It also must be said that the enemy variety, along with the environment, is extremely impressive for a game about bugs. To say much more would be spoiling an incredible and immersive experience. It took me roughly 45 hours to complete pretty much everything, looking forward to a second playthrough and future updates.
The game has also been recieving free updates introducing new content. Both of these so far have been of a high quality,  fit neatly into the gameworld and can be found on your first playthrough and not feel tacked on or out of place.

First take all the hype, skill and immensely replayable combat that a MOBA offers.
Then you take the out-dated control scheme that hasn't change since DotA was a Warcraft III mod, and throw it out the window in favor of something more snappy, akin to a top-down shooter.
You now have Battlerite.
I haven't played much but just dipping my toes into this game I can see myself having a lot of fun with it. The skill shots feel satisfying, the melee is fast paced, and the way the game simply plays is extremely exciting.  The whole presentation of the game works very well for itself, a lot of the cosmetic choices not only make the game look good but improve gameplay in manners so subtle you wouldn't quite notice them right off the bat.
The most interesting thing is how this game plays, controlls are similar to something like a classic-top down shooter but with cooldowns and abilities you'd find in any Moba, along with mechanics from games like Street-fighter in which you save up energy in order to fire off your ultimate, or instead use that same energry to fire off altered or super-charged versions of your standard abilities. It's got some crazy levels of depth for how far you can take the combat.  For the most part, a lot of characters do share very similar skill shots and AOE style attacks but thedifferences in stats and effects that come with them make them just another tool in that character's overall playstyle, so in a neat way playing every character feels more or less the same, but utilizing them different is where it count.

NecroVisioN is one of many old-school games out there. But it's not a generic arcade shooter. There is something that differs NecroVisioN from other shooters, modern included.
Story and setting:
The game is set in 1916, during the First World War. You play as Simon Bukner, a british trooper whose destiny is about to change...
The game starts in generic trench warfare scenario, but later we will find out that there are much worse enemies than germans.
Though, the storytelling is pretty confusing - that's the only flaw.
Overall story score: 4/5
Gameplay:
Gameplay and mechanics in this game are brilliant. There are two-hand weapon mechanics, enemy limb damage mechanics and even great close combat mechanics. For example, you can grab a knife and a Luger, a demonic hand and a Luger, and much more. Enemies greatly react to damage - you can shoot his leg off to make him crawl away in despair.
As in every old-school shooter, there are secrets scattered around the level. Talking about the levels, they are huge, taking an hour to pass, which is definetly an advantage.
Overall gameplay score: 5/5
Graphics:
The game is built on NecroEngine, which is a modified version of PainEngine used in PainKiller. The engine provides an amazing picture quality: the effects are juicy and loud and the designs are great.
Though, graphics in this game are pretty lame in comparison to nowadays standarts - "soap" textures and "rubber" people.
Overall graphics score: 3/5 (personal: 5/5)
Design:
Design is what gives this game an awesome feeling. Gasmask-wearing spiders; barbed wire-coiled, mutilated germans and vampires, gigantic underground strongholds and much more.
Overall design score: 5/5
To conclude, I definetly recommend this game to you if you need quality gameplay.
Overall score: 4/5, one of the best old-school games out there.

This game was a childhood favorite, though I lost the CD, and I had just enough in my steam wallet to purchase it on sale. I was really looking forward to savoring this classic and seeing if it lived up to my memories of it (and maybe to actually completing it, since I never did as a child).
However, all the menus, from the main menu to the in-game story scrolls have a mirage-like, oscillating blur effect obscuring the legibility of any of the text after a split second of legibility when it initially loads, except for the highlightable buttons once they're highlighted.
I'm on Windows 7-64 bit with a Radeon 7950 an intel iCore5-3470 CPU @ 3.20 Ghz (4 CPUS) ~ 3.6 Ghz, and 4 Gigs of RAM.
Has anyone found a solution to this bug or has anyone else at least encountered it? I can't recommend this game until this bug is fixed, though if it is fixed I will most likely give this game a thumbs up if my memory serves me right.
EDIT: I fixed the problem by turning off Morphological Filtering in the Catalyst Control Center. The game certainly lives up to my recollection of its enjoyability, especially for a little over $1. Beautiful, art direction, soothing music (except for the combat music, which is passable), fun characters, unique gameplay (closest comparison to gameplay-style I can remember right now is the Commandos series and this has a much more detailed and directed storyline with a rich cast of colorful characters on both sides of the unfolding conflict as the story progresses), a surprising amount of variation in the mission-types as the game progresses, and even a fair amount of unique, temporarily available side missions during the campaign and secondary objectives during quests that are part of the main story.
The game can be frustrating at times. Orders must be given carefully and in the heat and confusion of combat this can often be a tall order to complete. My main complaint is that characters insist on pulling the arrows they've just been shot with out as soon as they get shot and nothing will stop them from doing so. This animation often causes an unstoppable loop that will cause your character to be shot repeatedly by the same archer while taking just long enough to pull out each arrow for him to be shot again with another arrow that he will take the same amount of time pulling out, giving the archer just enough time to nock yet another arrow. I'm not sure that immediately ripping an arrow out of the wound as soon as one is shot would really be the smartest or most common reaction of anyone, but the rest of the game makes up for this glaring and common flaw in the game design. My tactics have become very focused on taking out archers quickly.

Super Epic. This is Final Fantasy regardless of whether the haters say so or not. Final Fantasy games always change up, some things you like, some things you might not. The characters are the best since Final Fantsy VI. Just like Resident Evil 6, you have to take the game for what it is, not what you want it to be and you'll enjoy it. It is linear for the first parts of the game, but it opens up on Cocoon and lets you quest and grind. Overall I'm enjoying it. You can see I've played 60 hours so far and I'm not even done with the game.
Yeah, it is a straight port. It's not cool that you have to mod it to get higher resolutions, but once you do, it looks much better albeit a bit less stable than I'd like. I save whenever I have the opportunity.
Well worth the money, but with all the HD remakes going around, it's a bit disappointing Squeenix didn't make this the definitive version, just by tweaking the code a bit and allowing higher resolutions.
Edit: After finishing the game, I still want to go back to Cocoon to finish the C'ieth stone missions. Too bad they didn't let you go back to Cocoon as it changed however. Still, best Final Fantasy yet and I'm aware it could get better AND could have more things like a more open world, etc. Can't wait for FF XV, hope I don't have to wait another 6 years.
I also have to add, just like any other PC game, people don't realize resolution goes hand in hand with dpi. I have a 1440p monitor, but it's only slightly higher dpi than my old 1080p 21.5" monitor. If you were to play this on a TV you'd be sitting alot further back and the aliasing would be unnoticalble. Being that this game was mastered for TVs, I find sitting further back from my monitor really makes the details seems alot smoother and more crisp. Either I'll get a lower resolution TV to game on to go easier on my GPU or when GPUs are powerful enough, I'll get a 4K monitor with at least twice the dpi.

To be trite, you could call this "musical pong." But if you're bad at it like I am then it isn't particularly musical, and it lacks the analog controls of classic pong. Instead you get to use your withered claw of a hand desperately clutching your mouse. Delightful.
Strawman cheapshots aside, I'll tell you the real tragedy of this game -- the visual design. You've seen this complaint in other reviews. In my mind, a game like this should challenge your reflexes and pattern recognition. Figure out where the dots are going and steer the paddle there with speed and precision.
doesn't want to do that though. Instead it obscures the visuals or otherwise tries to confuse you in unpleasant ways. Consider an infamous example: a couple minutes into the first stage you notice a fiery comet slowly descending from above. It continues creeping downward until it is covering a huge portion of the playing area, blocking you from seeing much of anything; the now nigh-invisible dots just whiz past the paddle while you squint furiously at the screen. There are many other instances of the game just trying to make it hard to see what's going on, and you feel like you're taking a frustrating eye exam.
But I mustn't forget the part of
that I hate the most: the menu. This is one of the worst menus I have ever encountered in a video game. You make a choice and a dot flies across the screen which you have to bounce back. This adds a ~4 second wait to making a choice, and if you miss the dot then your choice doesn't execute. That's more latency than a DVD menu and those are awful. This might sound like a petty complaint, but I have no patience for time being needlessly wasted. There's no challenge or fun there; it's just making you jump through a hoop. What a cruel design decision. This game is filled with such decisions which make it very hard to recommend.

Is a two person versus game. You go up against a friend and the two of you go at it grabbing up gold, emeralds, rubies and all sorts of other things. You can throw goats, horses, raccoons. And that's only a small sample of what goes on in this game.  The idea is to collect the most gold and toss it into your safe before your friend does.
At the time of writing this review, I chose the fast option as the Best option the game had was slowing down my mac's performance to show said graphics.  Yes folks you read that right.  This game can be played on windows and Mac. The visuals themselves look very detailed, the maps themselves are fairly large and the different landscapes are nice. Score 7 out of 10.
I will make a couple of notes of observation to the developer of this game though.  1. During my second run through of the middle map at one particular point on the mountain, i somehow managed to get a fairly quick red-disruption on my entire screen. it lasted for a second but it was worth noting, it happened sometime during my jump at the mountain.
The other thing I'd like to make note of is this, In the game there is a particular flow of water, that goes completely straight it just hangs there in mid-air, that's an indicator of where the map's proverbial wall is, I'd offer the opinion to fix that minor detail so it transitions smoother with the rest of the map.
At the time of writing the first review it turns out that my headset was to blame for the lack of sound.  The sounds were crisp and clear and fun, the music was perfect for this type of game and i loved listening to every minute of it. It's the sort of stuff you'd expect to hear in the great old west days. 10 out of 10
I have since found all the achievements in the game. That was real clever how you hid that unicorn!  The game would have been more fun with a pal, but me winning the whole game entirely by myself is also a lot of fun. I would say definitly don't buy this unless you have someone to play with.  For what it's worth, I like gold gathering/klondike style games and so i enjoyed myself.  I also decided to now increase my score of the overall fun because it took a lot of fun effort to get the unicorn so i'm adding an extra point to the original score i gave this game. 7 out of 10.
I would have enjoyed seeing a few more maps, but i was satisfied with what there was.  I again would suggest this game to a person who has friends. This is not a single player experience (and while i like winning, i also like a challenge). But yes  I do recommend this game to play, but play it with a friend.

Goldrushers is a delightful local multiplayer game that offers a child-like sense of wonder in its playful competition as well as its comical easter eggs.  What this game does is drop two players into a playground for a chaotic mess of hilarity with light hearted throwing dynamite at one another, exploring together to find an elusive unicorn, or just partaking in the ancient alchemy of converting coal into gold using slot machines.  This game really is about doing whatever you want with a loosely defined structure.
I did notice there to be a high sensitivity issue with the keyboard controls, so using a controller is a far superior experience.  Tutorialization isn't completely obvious so first time players, make sure to turn the settings on.  If the game appears to be lagging, try setting the graphics setting lower.  This will not sacrifice graphics quality all that much while still delivering a fun experience.
As it stands, you will get about an hours worth of content playing by yourself, but this game is meant for emergent play with a friend where you can play as much and as long as you want.  If you don't often have a friend around or prefer playing alone, the price point may be steep (get it during the sale!), but if you want to have a fun time with a friend, this game will definitely deliver an amusing experience.

Robin Hood: The Legend of Sherwood is an isometric strategy game in the vein of the Commandos and Desperadoes series. You control Robin Hood and his Merry Men as you undertake a variety of missions in various locales in an attempt to ransom King Richard and thwart the evil machinations of the Sherrif of Nottingham and Prince John. Your standard Robin Hood tale, if you will. The game features beautiful isometric graphics that still hold up to this day, the voice acting is pleasantly passable and the levels are well designed. You control your characters by clicking and dragging and fight your enemies by pressing down your mouse and dragging it around. It sounds a bit gimmicky but it's actually very satisfying to see your character twirl when you draw a circle. It also works surprisingly well. As other reviews have mentioned if you play the version steam gives you, it will lag terribly. This is because it uses the wrong font for the text in the game. If you download and replace the font, the game will run like butter. This game is highly enjoyable and is worth giving a shot if you're browsing steam or your library looking for something to play.

I like this game. I like it a great deal It is not without its difficulties nad challenges, but as several people have said before, if you look at where Civ V is today (the game from which this one got its skeleton), its clear that Firaxis still knows how to put together an excellent and lovingly balanced game.
I'm not entirely sure Civ: BE is there quite yet, but it is still quite fun. In addition, the things it does well are done beautifully.
Tech Tree:
The tech tree is rich, and it is wide. This means that you have to specialize to develop towards your victory strategy, and that you will be leaving things out as you do so. The way that they have the military units implemented do an excellent job of rewarding your choices rather than punishing your shortfalls. In addition, the "Steal tech" option is always valuable, as there is no way  that you have researched even all of the second ring of tech by the end of the game, so a little bit of free midrange tech is a nice little reward.
Culture Tree:
Again, they did an excellent job of rewarding your choices,  whether you choose to specialize or generalize. Every tree has rewards after so many virtues are unlocked, and every virtue tier has rewards for the same, regardless of which tree those virtues are in.
Military:
Units never obsolete, and the affinity paths that you choose (be they specialized or broad) allow you access to powerful benefits for the core units as well as affinity-specific units which further have some benefits for developing a secondary affinity. Fewer overall core units, but more choices than Civ.
Overall, I think this is a very good start. If Civ: BE gets the same degree of attention that the Civ V series has over the past couple years, I think that the things that really make it shine today will be the very things that will make it an overall richer game than Civ V is today.

Battlerite combines elements of MOBA combat, arena pvp and shooters. The game has a top-down camera, a handful of unique abilities for each of the diverse cast of heroes, and "battlerites" which are hero-specific talents that you choose  after each round of a best of 5. The result is an incredibly fun, fast-paced, fluid 2v2/3v3 competitive pvp game.
PROS:
-Well designed, skill based combat
-Unique heroes, good aesthetics
-Nothing pay to win in the chests
-Seemingly large and supportive community for the future of the game
-Practice mode to try out heroes already implemented, as well as bots
NEUTRAL:
-PvP Only
-High skillcap, fast paced
CONS:
- Competitive ranking system could still use some work (devs seem to be actively trying to figure it out)
- A lot of the skins just look like recolors
Despite being in early access, the gameplay is smooth and the visuals are nice. The heroes are all charming and well designed. For the most part, the skillset of each hero feels unique, although the different classes tend to blend together a bit. There is a chest-reward system incorporated into leveling up that gives various cosmetics such as skins, poses and weapon skins.
All in all, a very well done PvP-centric game that looks to have a promising future. Highly recommended.

This game is an interesting hybrid. On the one hand, I've seen it described as a survival game, and it's definitely a platformer (at least in building interiors) -- and I'm not a big fan of either style. On the other hand, it's an open-world game, and "pick up and play" (i.e., you can spend 15 or 30 minutes on it and most likely have something to show for it), and I love both of those styles.
I'm still early into it (and have restarted a few times as I learn more about how it works), but I've seen enough to confidently recommend it. The initial stages aren't too punishing -- at least once you know what's going on -- though you should expect to die and take it in stride while learning the ropes (you can continue from a checkpoint if you're non-hardcore like me).
Graphics are very low-res pixel art but they have a ton of character.
Ran into one bug that the developer patched within two days of my bug report. Also ran into a basement I couldn't get out of, but I can't say whether it was an oubliette or just my own failure to git gud. The jumping in general requires a little practice but is not bad once you get a feel for it. Damage inflicted on you in building interiors is fairly light so you have room to screw up.
Beginner tips:
* The game will say you shouldn't get too attached to your car, but try to keep it intact for the first couple missions; park a little way from the mission objective so it doesn't take collateral damage when you get into fights. You will have some distances to travel that will be impractical on foot unless you can take shelter in a building.
* To refuel the car, stand near it and Use your fuel can in your inventory. Don't refuel until the car runs out of gas, or you may get shortchanged.
* If you're initially timid, be aware that plain old fisticuffs can be quite effective. But don't go into the darkness and get mobbed. Wait for morning. The clock runs fast enough that it won't take long for the sun to rise.
* The developer was kind enough to respond to my begging for tips in the Steam Discussions; check out his response for a few additional ideas. If you're really interested in the game, check out the developer's website for some blog entries on how the sausage is made. It was fascinating to me but could be too much detail for some players.
* There are some YouTube videos that show how other people approach the game. Watching a couple of these was very useful to me. One commenter noted that Energy in this game (replenished by food and water) is similar to how a shield or body armor works in many other games. Haven't played enough to know whether this is an exact parallel but it seems right.
Looking forward to playing a lot more of this.

I enjoyed Final Fantasy XIII. Admittedly, being a PC-exclusive gamer for the last decade or so, I haven't played too many JRPGs lately, and I was frankly thrilled to finally be able to play a modern Final Fantasy game on PC. Final Fantasy VI (SNES) is one of my favorite games of all time, and I've briefly played but never beat (rented back in the day) FF 7, 8 and 9.
The game is as linear as they say, but I didn't really have a problem with it. I play Final Fantasy games primarily for the story and spectacle, and then the battles, and then very distantly the out-of-battle gameplay sections. FF13 performs strongly in the first two, so being pretty much completely linear for most of the game isn't really that big of a deal. I really enjoyed the story, and though some have complained that it's confusing or hard to follow, I found it easy enough to understand (though I did read all of the datalogs religiously, which definitely helps).
Some stuff I really enjoyed are some new "convenience features" that basically remove most of the things I find annoying about JRPGs. Namely:
-No random battles! You can see (and usually avoid) any enemy on the world map.
-Your party is automatically healed and cured at the end of every battle (so you don't have to micromanage all that stuff yourself all the time)
-If you die in battle, you can restart the battle immediately to try again, and it even starts you outside of battle so you can change your party/upgrades/paradigms or just run away. This even applies to boss battles!
-No grinding - the game is somewhat challenging (though there's also an easy mode you can switch to at any time), but I never felt the need to stay in one area and grind experience before moving on. Grinding is boring and it's exclusion will not be missed.
The battle system is really novel. You only control one character, and you have an "auto-attack" option (though you can still individually choose your attacks if you want). There are 6 different roles, and a combination of these roles is a paradigm. The main focus of battle is switching up your paradigms for the situation, sort of macro-managing the battle rather than micromanaging every single move. I found this quite an enjoyable change of pace from the same battle system that's been in FF for years.
As an aside: yes, the port is horrible, and it's absolutely shameful that they'd lock such a beautiful game to 720p. Fortunately this is easily fixed with the program "GeDoSaTo" (created by legendary modder Durante, who also fixed Dark Souls 1). The framerate is weirdly inconsistent during battles (bouncing between 30 and 60, despite sitting at like 30% GPU load, and 10% CPU load) but it wasn't enough to put me off from playing the game.
Overall I enjoyed my time spent with FF13. The game is absolutely gorgeous, especially at 1080p (I've taken several hundred screenshots during my playthrough), the story and characters are interesting (except Snow, ♥♥♥♥ that guy), and the battle system is fun and novel. My JRPG experience is admittedly a bit lacking, but I loved them back in the SNES days, and if FF13 is anything to go by, I still love them now.

People often say that this is a good game, but not a good Hitman game. They're right. It's not like Hitman—you barely do any proper assassinations throughout the game. For some reason Agent 47 is left to defend a little girl and the honor of his intel handler Diana, both which simply don't suit his character. And in regards to progress through the series this game went backwards in level design; the levels now are extremely narrow with little opportunity for variety.
That said, the stealth in this game is pretty good. People complain that it's a broken system on the hardest settings, but I disagree. I got through it without using any glitches on Expert (I honestly should have just picked Purist but I didn't like the sound of no HUD). The game is beatable, and it's fun sneaking through levels and picking people off silently. I recommend this game for this reason. You can skip it and wait for Hitman 6 though, which I expect to be this game + Blood Money's level design.

Hitman: Absolution can't decide what it wants to be and suffers for it. It's got a lot of different systems which are half baked at best and flat out broken at worst. The melee system involves you performing the same quick time event that half the time doesn't work. The disguise system ranges from useless to game breaking because only enemies in the same disguise can instantly see through it. The scoring and instinct systems actively encourage you to play poorly. As an added bonus every action is done with a context sensitive button press which will always screw you over once per level. While their are a few flash brilliance, the're all buried under the mountain of issues that plague this game.

Civ: Beyond Earth, for me is a rather enjoyable game. I recommend it to people who think as I do, and agree with me on my following statements. What I enjoy and like about this game will not be shared equally. If you are interested, try the demo before making a final decision, which is why it exists. A set of other people's opinions cannot garuntee you will like or dislike the game. I think a lot of the other reviews tend to miss that part.
BE, for me, has a certain charm. The amusing wonder/technology/affinity quips that play after researching or finishing one are good, subtle jokes that make the game stand out from Civs 2-5. They are the right level of incorrect to be believable. It fits the setting in a sense; the quotes and the mistakes are just possible enough that it feels like you are hearing from someone who is several hundred years into the future. But my enjoyment goes beyond that.
Civ 5, even with the expansions, felt like it had a lot of things that were simply not needed. I found little use or intrest from the espionage. Indeed, it became quite a pain to constantly have the other leaders beg forgiveness for failing to steal my technology, and I never needed to use my spies to do anything more than rig city-state elections. Here it can do a lot more for me. Is it particularly balanced? No. It is quite powerful. Still, a feature having a use beyond simply being an annoyance is a plus.
The units have been simplified. Perhaps over-simplified, as the types boil down to a paltry number. Still, in comparison to Civ 2-5, I find myself actually enjoying this. An increase of only perhaps 2-3 types of units;,a dedicated bomber, submarine, and maybe a cruise missile would be all I would want. Civ 5's unit types didn't change the fact that a set number were the best, and the rest existed simply to dig AI or players out of a hole when they had no strategic resources. In short, you never used them. So while I do agree that the units were over-simplified, I find it preferable to the alternative.
Great People are gone, finally. Number one way to over power other civs in Civ 5 was getting a few early foundaries/academies. They were highly unbalanced and the AI did not use them efficently enough. G&K made them even more game breaking by allowing you to purchase them with faith in the late game. Allowed you to snowball your lead in all areas way too efficently. New tile improvements can now replicate weaker versions of those tile improvements. Not the best way to handle it, but the AI actually builds these sometimes.
The aliens and their miasma are probably the most annoying part of the game. But even then, their existance is not necissarily a flaw. They start out as regular wildlife would; passive until you get close to their nest or you shoot them. Which makes sense. Chances are good that if you go hiking and see a group of wolves, they will leave you alone unless they are hungry or threatened. So to, does the alien AI act. Occasionally a siege worm might tromp through the outskirts of your city, but it tends to merely be passing through. Later on, your units will be a lot strogner than these more primitive creatures. Which, again, makes sense. When was the last time you saw a cougar with a rifle? Barbarians in the previous Civ titles were also generally behind and did not scale well either. I can't recall the last time I even bothered sending land units to do more than clear the camp they spawn from in mid to late game Civ 5. So why complain that the aliens don't scale well either?
The miasma, which is hard to see at times, is a bigger issue if you don't push hard for Harmony affinity. It can force your units to take awkward paths, or take a surprising amount of damage if they get caught in it. your explorer AI will also avoid it, leaving valuable crashes left untouched unless you manually give them orders. Still, it only matters early to mid game. Later on your workers are both immune and can clear it, and you can launch satellites that repulse it. By that time, you can normally use it as a buff if you want to be a Harmony player, and may just leave it; it provides no negative effects to tile yeilds.
I greatly enjoy the vibrant visuals of BE. It certainly LOOKS like an alien world. Some things tend to get a little lost, like the miasma or xenomass, but I enjoy it overall. A few things could look better, like the 'geothermal' resource. And the unit visuals are on the 'meh' side until they get their affinity skins. My main complaint is the same as it was with Civ 5. Wonders tend to explode outward from cities, sometimes appearing three tiles away if you have a lot in one city. Which is not particularly hard in either game. Obviously, this has no gameplay effect. It is just a personal annoyance wen I see a wonder several tiles off land, or something that should be central in my city (like one wonder called the Drone Sphere) way in the outskirts.
The tech web is a neat idea, though it seems a bit scattered. The progression of technologies makes, at best, a loose interpertation of sense. I feel it could be better organized, though since Civ is a turn based franchise the time it takes me to go and glance around the web is a trivial inconvenience. I find it odd that units/buildings/wonders are not color coded, and that I had to get a mod just for that. Yes, these things have a different icon outline, but especially with buildings and wonders it can be tough to see sometimes.
As with the tech web above, I find the UI quite navigatable and fairly intuitive. It's a little more colorful, and is slightly more simplified. The individual buttons are now slightly larger, which is also a plus. I can see why some people have an initial shock when coming over from Civ 5, but calling the interface 'hard to use' or 'more confusing' is a dramatization.
Choosing your starting options is a little more interesting, with a few of them being long term bonuses and others helping with only the initial landing. I can't say I've found Retrograde thrusters (+1 radius to landing zone) particularly helpful, nor the soldier unit. Starting with the extra tech or the worker seem to be the best ones. A little more balance would be nice between some of these options. If it were, say, two soldiers or a soldier and a gunner I might be inclined to choose that option. As always, production and science are king and queen.
Diplomacy is the weakest point of the game, for me. Still, it is at least slightly improved from Civ 5. I still normally find myself polarizing the AI quite a bit. Espionage actions, even ones that fail, do not seem to have an impact on diplomatic relations. I cannot compare this to Civ 5's espionage since I never bothered with such a weak facet of that game. Clearing or spawning miasma carries surprisingly harsh consequences and, despite the constant praise for not killing aliens early game, a mid game killing spree of several islands didn't bring any negative side effects. Except for a few siege worms.
The quests are about as useful as the ones from Midevial Total War 2 or Shogun 2 if you have played those  games. Trade routes are very profitable, unlike those introduced in G&K. The small 'bases' scale fairly well, but their bonuses are overpowered later on, especially if you delve far enough into the Productivity culture tree. No more religion or faith exist, though that had only a minor effect on gameplay in Civ 5.
Glitches and bugs are relatively few and far between. I have encountered a few, with my explorer not revealing FoW around himself and ruins/crashes not disappearing. I've had the map flicker once or twice a game, but that seems to be an effect of alt-tabbing rather than a game hiccup. More may exist, but I have not personally experienced them and cannot speak to their existance.

No more inventory management puzzles, no more clicking like an idiot all over the place to get the gold, no need to head back to town to dump your vendor trash time and time again! Just kill the monsters, take the loot and send your pet to town to dump what you don't want while you keep killing monsters and taking their loot. The only flaws I see are the limited choice in player classes and lack of multiplayer, but apart of that, this is a must have for fans of RPGs in the style of Diablo. And it has user-friendly mod support, to boot! A rare jewel in this sea of meh-inducing imitations.

Rivals of Aether is a platform fighter heavily inspired by Super Smash Bros. Melee. The thing that Rivals of Aether does different than Super Smash Bros. Melee is it automatically performs all the advanced techniques automatically. Wavedashing is more lenient as Rivals of Aether lets you airdodge while still in the jumpsquat state. Aerial cooldown frames are shortened when compared to Super Smash Bros. Melee. Aerials in Rivals of Aether are usually very easy to follow-up on due to how they position the character.
This is also where I would describe some of these choices as flaws. Due to the fact that many of the techniques from Super Smash Bros. Melee are simplified, there leaves little margain for error. What this does is gives every player powerful tools for no expense.
Overall, this game is a fun way to get into the competitive platform fighter genre. As competitive as this game may be described, it is definitely only a stepping stone. But if you want to get into Project M and later Super Smash Bros. Melee, this is the game to play.

Do you like Civ 5?  Do you like Alpha Centuri?  Good, then you can skip this game.
Beyond Earth is worse than both games in every concievable way.  The UI is exceedingly poor, for example a componant that should be entirely simple to implement like the world map is so tiny and horribly presented that it has been rendered entirely useless.  The information bar at the top of the screen is tiny yet cluttered.  The grid itself is ugly as is the fog of war.  The game itself is just so dark.  It's like being in a room with no windows and the only ligthing coming from an old 30 watt bulb that's been dyed blue (or yellow depending on the map).
What first seemed an interesting twist, the tech web is difficult to navigate and read.  Maybe after you dump 40 hours into the game you'll remember what upgrades are under what leaf and branch, but I grew sick of trying to find where that stupid tech was that let me harvest float stone (or whatever I was looking for at the time).
The game does a really terrible job introducing the new quest mechanics, and at no point did it ever explain victory conditions.
Religions and culture trees have congealed into a bland, overly condensed and boring set of 4 cultural trees you can advance down.
Leaders/states have no personality, aliens are little more than window dressing for each planet, and jeeze what an ugly planets they are.  Do you like blue on blue on blue?  How about puke yellow worlds with oceans of dirty water?  Then boy does Beyond Earth have some property for you!
Beyond Earth has unambiguously poor presentation, and offers nothing mechanically new or interesting over Civ 5, it strips away depth, yet some how it's become more obtuse.  If you're looking to get more out of this current gen of Civ I think you'll be much better served turning to the workshop than spending your money on this poorly designed and ill conceived addition to the franchise.

I will put the summary first as I know people have short attention spans, I would rather be playing games than reading about them. Here goes...
So everyone has been comparing this game to Alpha Centauri, for obvious reasons, it is one of the primary reasons I was interested in this game from the time it announced. It has very similar mechanics and the factions kind of resemble some of the characters it has 2 of the victories  (Transcendence and Domination) and 2 new ones (Emancipation and Promised Land) which are just mirror images of each other.
The game is 1.5 parts AC, 1 part Civ V and 0.5 parts something new, the game to me fails to live up to the title of spiritual successor to AC. Like with a lot of modern games alot of the intricacies of older games have been dumbed down in their more modern versions sacrificed on the altar of production value. The 8 factions are not that different from one another and end up just being skins, the affinities while being different ideologies can be played by any faction not much variation as to benefits as to who plays what.
There is no penalty for accumulating affinity points counter to your main affinity!!!! This should have been put in the game at least. There is no negative events to quests either general or buildng quests and that seems to be a lost element!!!
Conclusion: comes off a little flat however will still do well due to tried and true Civ mechanics, it does do a lot better in mid-late game in keeping your attention than Civ V and AC as in those games it can sometimes seem you are counting down turns to victory.
Score 7/10 for people who want to see AC reborn
Score 8/10 for people like me who really love Civ as it does do the mid-late game better in my opinion
overall purchase game when on sale unless you really wanted a Civ like game but played Civ V till you were tired. read on for more indepth stuff...
There are 8 playable personalities who are not as typecast as in AC. one expects them to play a particular affinity but I have 2 playthroughs so far and they have picked different affinities which is good on the strategic side (more on that later) but bad on the whole charisma, feeling out your opponent in AC and CIV V. They all get a small play style boost at the beginning  but it seems to fall short of AC as you can customise; on the plus side (similar to randomise option in both CIV V and AC) which adds a strategic element.
There are 3 affinities which are basically ideologies of AC only instead of 8 now there are 3 which are Purity, Harmony and Supremacy. Purity (Believers) is basically trying to remain human in an alien world although some of the technologies that are linked to affinity points do not quite add up. They are stylistically feudal: mech suits, paint and banners and tanks (early 20th century).
Harmony (Gaia's Stepdaughters), where you try to be one with the planet trying not to kill the alien life and eventually building alien life to obliterate the other factions. This affinity feels more true to its origins. They look organic and the special units are alien-human hybrids squads for the most part.
Supremacy (Cybernetic Conciousness from AC expansion that I didn't play) where you play as robots or at least in this case you become robotic over time and therefore the bases look very futuristic and units are some of the best looking in the game very robotic and angular.
This is where the strategy comes in it is very hard to pick your affinity before playing so if you wanted to play a particular character with a particular affinity then I have news for you. Each affinity has a strategic mineral attached and to a lesser degree a sub mineral which if you don't have any close to you it doesn't make any sense as almost all the special units and buildings use that resource. Purity has Floatstone and to a lesser degree Titanium, Harmony has Xenomass, some Petroleum and Floatstone(one unit) and Supremacy has Firaxite, titanium and petroleum.
The technology is non-linear in a sense similar to the option in AC where you could pick your own research or filter it for growth, expansion, science etc. This is where the strategy of the game is as with most Civ V games it is balancing the right research to your build: building important wonders to either further your cause or significantly hurt your competitors, helpful buildings that further science, production, health and culture and units to defend your cities.
The technology web is however poorly done even on my second time round, and having a good idea of what did what, getting lost in the web is too easy. I see there is a mod out now that colour codes the web I will probably download it as it is very difficult to tell exactly what you are getting when researching a branch or leaf outside of experience /staring at the screen for 10-15 mins each time you have to research something.
Health is similar to happiness in Civ V but definitely made more difficult in keeping with Prince and up difficulties in Civ. Even on Sputnik difficulty health is a serious issue. I like it it adds that hectic feel that Civ has on higher difficulties.
The aliens are well pictured in the game, however to me they are a bit tame, the ultrasonic fences and the first purity affinity being that explorers don't get attacked is I think overpowered. I think it should be that aliens don't attack you unless you are aggressive, but I would like to see siege worms taking out cities, waves of aliens taking out bases or improvements due to your aggression. Right now as it stands you can rush the purity affinity and use explorers as a fence against aliens which is what I did in the last game where I started 4 turns from a 8 xenomass nest with 2 siegeworms and about 8 assorted aliens running around close to my base.
The gameplay is a mix of AC and Civ V borrowing elements from the AC expansion as well.
Spying is better similar to Civ IV, air warfare could have been improved, satellite coverage and to a lesser extent warfare is a welcome addition would love to see on multiplayer.
Transcendence is basically the same with you connecting with the planet's consciousness in a process similar to AC, Emancipation and Promised Land is where you build a gate back to Earth so that you can bring more humans to the new planet (Purity) or you can 'cleanse' them of their inferior humanity (Supremacy). The only difference being some of the dialog leading up to the end and the look of your units.
What I would like: :)
The original context instituted where certain factions have certain playstyles and similar to Civ V where certain factions tend to be in jungle etc have the Supremacists closer to Firaxite etc. Keep what they have in the startup as an option where you can customise your experience again similar to AC.
This is asking for alot a scenario based on each faction almost like how Blizzard did Starcraft single player which could explain units the tech tree and alot of the lore around the planets example why this particular one, internal power struggles everything storybuffs like myself would love. They could sell as DLCs I would buy them.
Better aliens, more aggressive, more reactive, possibly evolve and get more difficult almost similar to xcom or become more organised as the game progresses.
Random events, to me outside of all the dumbing down has got to be the worst most glaring and include cheapest thing to fix.. The quests are interesting to read but the same each time (will recant only 2 playthroughs), it needs randomness!! Special occurences probably linked to achievements things that only happen when you play this char with this affinity in this way. I have almost 700hours in Civ V and I still occasionally see a civ or myself try to do something new and this to me has to be the biggest issue as this will prevent it from getting that strong community that Civ and AC has.

- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan

Reviews, videos, and pictures do not do this game any justice. This is a game you just have to play for yourself in order to understand why it's so good. This game went from a game I thought I'd refund to a game that is in my Top 3 games of all time. This game deserves a proper review.
First off, the visuals. I genuinely feel that they look better - or at least can compete - with Cuphead's visuals. I mean, just look at the screenshots above. There is a nice fluidity to everything, and the world feels complete. Backgrounds aren't just backgrounds, they're simply what's in the distance. The backgrounds in this game make you feel like you're in a level that's much larger than it already is. They're animated as well, and once again really make the world feel whole and complete. The combat is simple, and that's one of the best parts. But while the combat is simple, it does not mean it is easy in any way. You start out with 5 hearts, each being depleted by getting by an enemy. All the enemies are unique, which can vary on which area they are in. The enemies feel like they belong in the areas that they are placed in, and all their abilties/attacks make sense. You explore a vast world with secrets everywhere, meeting new friends along the way. The NPC's in the game are great with destinct personalities. After encountering an NPC once I already can remember their name and what they are like.
And the ♥♥♥♥ing music. There are only two games I would buy the soundtrack for - Hollow Knight and DOOM. The music fits the location that you are in, and there has yet to be a song I've heard that I didn't enjoy. It immerses you into the world and sets the atmosphere. There's also a real sense of progression, as some key features aren't even given to you until you progress through the Hallownest (the world) and discover new locations. This game can get very frustrating at times, no denying it, but it's all worth it. There is always something you can do to be on top.
The boss fights are also phenominal and unforgettable. They are all unique and a blast to fight. The length of this game all depends on you. If you want to explore the vast world Hollow Knight has to offer, going at your own leisure, backtracking and whatnot you will have tons of hours in this game. I only have about 14 hours in this game at the time I am writing this review, and while I feel I have gone through so much, I still feel like there's so much more left for me to do; and I love it.
I know this review wasn't the best, and was a bit all over the place. I didn't go too deep into the mechanics but that's not the point of this review. The point here is to simply just tell you what Hollow Knight as to offer and why you should give Team Cherry your money. There were times were I genuinely forgot that I only payed $15 for this game. Not to mention that the two DLC packs they released so far are
. While they do say that a controller is recommended a keyboard and mouse works just fine. One thing I will mention though is that if you at least change the attack to left click and dash to right click, neither will work unless you go into keyboard settings and then exit out into the game. A minor annoyance, but nothing that takes away from the experience.
Overall, Hollow Knight is one of the best games ever made and I've ever played, and if this game is even slightly interesting to you I highly recommend you go buy it. You won't regret it.

For this review I wanted to see how many games are dedicated to WWI. What I found  is they are not many and not too popular. Valiant Hearts and Verdun are most well known I think. There are few grand strategies, but i'm not in to them. The reason i started with this is NecroVision take place in WWI setting and this was the only thing I could think of to start the review.
You take the role of Simon Buckner, young american who join the British army to fight germans in 1916. After an ambush and the following fierce battle, everything for our hero turns upside down. Simon encounters supernatural phenomenon and realize that greater evil threatens to wipe humanity. To a certain degree it's the germans fault. They never learn not to play with fire. The story is not bad, it kept me interested through the whole game, but it's not memorable enough. You have to save Earth from germans, vampires, demons and whole other bunch of creatures. The good thig in the story is it takes to great locations.
Let me take a step back and look at the the settings. Rebindable keys, HUD and crosshair opacity are few of the good things in here. But in sound is missing speech slider. In some places people speak so quietly, I can bearly hear them. Subtitles help to understand what are they saying, but they in some places are not displayed. In video options you can change a lot of things – textures for weapons, people, envoirment. Also you have render quality, dynamic shadows and so on. But even if everything is on max settings the games is not a good looker.
The dev try and succeed in putting enough mechanics in the gameplay to differentiate from other FPSs. Not all are entirly original. When you kill enemy in non-traditional style, you are rewarded with Adrenaline and Fury. Adrenaline is basically bullet-time and later is used for one more thing. Later for it. Non-traditional ways for killing reminds of Bulletstorm, but here they are not that creative. Headshots with different weapons, kicking, melee and so on. When you manage to chain few combos, you gain Fury level, which in turns leads to, for the first few level, electricity coming from you and hitting enemies. For even higher level – incinerating them. For reaching maximum Fury, be on a lookout for hidden vampire artefacts. Each found increases one level. It's so satysfing to melee a group of bad guys and incinerate them.
NecroVision is FPS. And what you do in this type of game? Shooting and blasting enemies. How is the shooting? It's good. Weapons have arcade feel to them. They don't have recoil, but they also don't have Quake-like accuracy. If enemies are far away , you have to burst, because crosshair widens and the gun become less acurate. Weapons in 1/3 of the game more or less represent the time period the game takes place. Two pistols, rifle, sniper, rocket launcher, shotgun, heavy and light machine gun. These weapons are used in abovementioned 1/3 of the game. After that the game takes hard turn and starts to get more interesting. You get Shadowhand, SMG, shotgun, rocket launcher, and flamethrower. One of them raises curiosity. It's Shadowhand. It's metal glove with Wolverine-like claws. You can use it for melee or cast spells – fireballs, iron rods and freezing. All are useful. Shadowhand have one one more ability – raising the dead. When Adrenalin is on it's maximum stand to nearby fallen enemie and ressurect him to help you fight.
There is more. You can dual-wield pistols and machine guns. You are less accurate, but in close range is so satisfying to mow enemies down. In your right hand you can equip a pistol and in your left you can put another pistol, bayonet, shovel, granade, dynamite and gas lamp for setting enemies on fire. With shovel and bayonet you can melee or throw them. I killed a lot of enemies that way. Almost every murder gives you adrenaline.
There is a sprint button. Except for fast movement, you can use it with combination from melee and a gun to knock down a group of enemies. This and kicking are the best course of action if bad guys surround you.
I intentionally missed few interesting things, that will happen. I don't want to spoil everything, when the game turns 180.
Restoring health is done in two different ways. Generally, half of it is regenerating and for the other half you have to find med packs. This is through the first 1/3 of the game, which I will continue to mention. After that you will restore it by collecting red orbs from dead enemies or finding them in hidden places or breaking the surroundings.
When you are about to die, you get The Last Chance. Everything slows down to a crawl for a few seconds and you have manage to get away or die.
The level design through the 1/3 of the game are okay. Trenches, castles, dungeons, all standard stuff. But (there is a big but here) when you past that 1/3, the gets more interesting. Better and wider level design, better atmosphere. Gothic dungeons created from forgotten and vanished civilization, full with strange machines, electricity coming from tesla coils, dungeons filled with lava, strange railroad, leading to some uncharted and dark places, deep in the bowls of the earth. Here creativity of the developer shines. Great level desing!
In almost every level there are secrets to be found. Except the abovementioned vampire artefacts, there are also weapons, ammo, letters and golden chests to be found.
The sound here is not great. As I mentioned in the beginning some voice actors can barely heard and this is design flaw, because this is at certain places. The voice acting is good, but I don't like the main character voice and don't get me started with the one liners. They are not that good or original and you will hear them over and over again through the hole game. Music is almost absent. When is present it's good, but it's so rare to hear it. There is some ambient music and it's contribute for the atmoshpere, but it's not enough. The game needs more tracks and the music have to be played more often.
Enemies are fairly diverse. I know i'm repeating my self, but during the first 1/3 of the game most of them will be germans and zombies and few bosses. Eventually and gradually, new enemies will apear. Masked people that shoot you, other that make some kung fu kicks, when you are closer to them, imps, dragons and other flying creatures, two types of ogres and so on. I don't know what type of creatures are all of them, so I make up their species to get you an idea to some degree how they look. I almost had no problems with all enemies, unless they surround me. The ogres gave me headache, because they are fast and do a lot of damage.
Almost everything I said until now is what I liked about the game. However, there are few things I don't like and I think it's worth to mention them. Non of them are game breaking. One of them is the AI, when you ressurect someone. It's dumb as brick, always falling behind, you have to walk slowly and babysite them. This makes the ressurection useless. You can also see flickering textures on buildings. As a whole the game is not a good looker. Sometimes I didn't know where to go, I was confused by the level design. Some times I can jump over a fence, others I can't. Not always was clear where to go, but this maybe my fault. There tiny little bugs, but naybe the biggest problem is the first 1/3 of the game. It's fun, but it's just okay. But after that everything gets better – level design, guns, abilities, atmoshpere, enemies, everything! I get it from storytelling point, but some players maybe be turn off by this. Be patient and you will granted with awesome moments. As a whole it's rough around the edges, but entertaing. The game reminds me of Return to Castle Wolfenstein and Painkiller, this is a good thing. It's not as polished as them, but you can always do worse. I had fun, so I recommend it.

For me, the parts I always liked about MOBAs were the tense, memorable team fights. Unfortunately, in most MOBAs, that makes up only about 20% of the actual game. The rest is frustrating slog.
Battlerite basically distills down the best parts of MOBAs and cuts away all the fat. Just super fast-paced, skill-based teamfights that don't take forever.
As someone who plays a lot of games simultaneously, it's also refreshingly easy to come back to. It doesn't have weird, obscure skills that require constant upkeep (like last-hitting in many MOBAs) or require an up-to-date encyclopedic knowlege of items or character builds. Most of the characters in Battlerite seem to follow a relatively similar formula for the way their abilities are set up, as well. I don't feel like I've forgotten how to play when I pick it up after a lengthy absense.
I highly recommend it if you're someone who loves the memorable moments that come from awesome plays in MOBAs, but you find most MOBAs to be convoluted slogs that take too long and fill you with frustration.

Игра хорошая, но естественно не очень доделана. Например из явных минусов:
-Не привычный режим абордажа, нет игры от первого лица или третьего за персонажа, чтобы кромсать зомби, скелетов, офицеров, форты как в корсарах.
-Игра как я понял по сети, подразумевает не больше 3-ох участников. Хотя мне кажется, крутые баталии должны быть начиная от 5-ти игроков по сети.
-Нет возможности (или пока не нашёл), назначить к примеру первого помощника на захваченное судно, и продолжить битву или собрать эскадру. (только если играешь совместно с другими игроками).
-Если было действие например проплывающие корабли противника, а на карте в этом же месте сражается другой игрок, будьте готовы к неожиданному прибавлению противников от 3 до 6 штук точно (если pvp включен). Думаю пофиксят как-то это.
-Иногда выбрасывает в бой, вроде бы в нейтральных водах, а там стоит форт и он вражеский - итог, он начинает по тебе палить тоже. Иногда бывает противников к союзному форту выкидывает.
-Очень трудно с карты на карту переплывать. Через специальные точки-метки для перехода. Но естественно нельзя переходить, пока идёт бой. А ТАМ вероятность, вражеских кораблей очень большая. Постоянно там натыкаюсь. Разок было так, что я просто встрял против 6 противников, которые сражались 3 на 3. Но для меня было 1vs6, либо топить их ко дну за считанные секунды расходуя по залпу на корабль, или отплыть и ждать когда они друг друга сами перебьют.
-Пока ты плаваешь и собираешь вещи, тем более используя ускорение, могут приплыть ещё вражеские корабли, появится чудовижа, начаться ураган и тебе придётся продолжать бой. Будьте внимательны.
-Как мне пока кажется, малое кол-во кораблей. Я не встретил пока мановара, и ещё несколько типов кораблей. Которые хотелось бы увидеть. Может они будут впереди).
-Отвратительнейшая экономика. Ну прям очень. Можно купить товар со скидкой в одной городе, приплыть туда, где он дефицитен, и бывает так, что заплатив команде, довезя груз, продаёшь его дай бог в туже сумму. Я конечно не пробовал возить по 100 серебра, 100 столовых украшений и 100 шелков. Но уверен, что сильно с торговли в этой игре не заработать.
Но и плюсы:
+Видно что работа уже проведена приличная. Несколько усовершенствований и игра станет аналогом Корсарам к примеру.
+Достаточно умная система распределения команды. Паруса:скорость, манёвренность и прочность парусов. Палуба: Кол-во команды, стрелки и бойцы. Трюм или такилаж: Прочность корпуса, перезарядка орудий, меткость кажись зависит)
+Возможность играть нескольким игракам как мешать друг другу, так и помогать.
+Куча наций и пока что достаточно интересные квесты.
+Кракены и артефакты, которые позволяют делать те или иные вещи на пользу или во вред себе и противнику.
+Вполне логичная система водного боя.
+Очень логичная система захода на абордаж. Сначала нужно снять паруса противнику, чтобы его "обездвижить". И порубить желательно команду перед заходом, выставить своих людей в большей степени на абордаж. И только тогда взять корабль на абордаж.
+Как я и люблю, захватываешь корабли, продаёшь, остальные корыта топишь. Форт пока не взрывал. Ибо линкор только только получил.
Очень не плохо играем вдвоём. Поясню.
Я получил свой барк(смог взять и победить на абордаже, да так чтобы золото осталось, и при возвращении в порт у меня команда не разбежалась из-за неуплат. примерно на часе 7-8 игры. Фреган на 13. И Линкор на 17-ом часе.
Мой друг на 6.1 часу имеет уже Фрегат. Думаю к 10-ому часу игры, точно будет Линкор, если не будет тупить.
Ну и совет для игроков:
-Обплывыте корабль противника, если он остался один - сзади. И начинайте рубить ему паруса. Чем быстрее у Вас корабль, тем больше вероятность того, что противник не сможет дать по Вам даже 1 залп из пушек. А потом его можно брать на абордаж-топить и т.д. Но следите, чтобы у него не было артефакта на починку, иначе рискуете попасть под атаку всё равно. Я так захватил и Барк и Фрегат. Линкор вообще пришлось другой стратегией
брать. Думаю если бы npc не затупил, я бы его и не взял. А он бы потопил меня и союзников, коих было 5 кораблей включая мой и все фрегаты!)
