I will put the summary first as I know people have short attention spans, I would rather be playing games than reading about them. Here goes...
So everyone has been comparing this game to Alpha Centauri, for obvious reasons, it is one of the primary reasons I was interested in this game from the time it announced. It has very similar mechanics and the factions kind of resemble some of the characters it has 2 of the victories  (Transcendence and Domination) and 2 new ones (Emancipation and Promised Land) which are just mirror images of each other.
The game is 1.5 parts AC, 1 part Civ V and 0.5 parts something new, the game to me fails to live up to the title of spiritual successor to AC. Like with a lot of modern games alot of the intricacies of older games have been dumbed down in their more modern versions sacrificed on the altar of production value. The 8 factions are not that different from one another and end up just being skins, the affinities while being different ideologies can be played by any faction not much variation as to benefits as to who plays what.
There is no penalty for accumulating affinity points counter to your main affinity!!!! This should have been put in the game at least. There is no negative events to quests either general or buildng quests and that seems to be a lost element!!!
Conclusion: comes off a little flat however will still do well due to tried and true Civ mechanics, it does do a lot better in mid-late game in keeping your attention than Civ V and AC as in those games it can sometimes seem you are counting down turns to victory.
Score 7/10 for people who want to see AC reborn
Score 8/10 for people like me who really love Civ as it does do the mid-late game better in my opinion
overall purchase game when on sale unless you really wanted a Civ like game but played Civ V till you were tired. read on for more indepth stuff...
There are 8 playable personalities who are not as typecast as in AC. one expects them to play a particular affinity but I have 2 playthroughs so far and they have picked different affinities which is good on the strategic side (more on that later) but bad on the whole charisma, feeling out your opponent in AC and CIV V. They all get a small play style boost at the beginning  but it seems to fall short of AC as you can customise; on the plus side (similar to randomise option in both CIV V and AC) which adds a strategic element.
There are 3 affinities which are basically ideologies of AC only instead of 8 now there are 3 which are Purity, Harmony and Supremacy. Purity (Believers) is basically trying to remain human in an alien world although some of the technologies that are linked to affinity points do not quite add up. They are stylistically feudal: mech suits, paint and banners and tanks (early 20th century).
Harmony (Gaia's Stepdaughters), where you try to be one with the planet trying not to kill the alien life and eventually building alien life to obliterate the other factions. This affinity feels more true to its origins. They look organic and the special units are alien-human hybrids squads for the most part.
Supremacy (Cybernetic Conciousness from AC expansion that I didn't play) where you play as robots or at least in this case you become robotic over time and therefore the bases look very futuristic and units are some of the best looking in the game very robotic and angular.
This is where the strategy comes in it is very hard to pick your affinity before playing so if you wanted to play a particular character with a particular affinity then I have news for you. Each affinity has a strategic mineral attached and to a lesser degree a sub mineral which if you don't have any close to you it doesn't make any sense as almost all the special units and buildings use that resource. Purity has Floatstone and to a lesser degree Titanium, Harmony has Xenomass, some Petroleum and Floatstone(one unit) and Supremacy has Firaxite, titanium and petroleum.
The technology is non-linear in a sense similar to the option in AC where you could pick your own research or filter it for growth, expansion, science etc. This is where the strategy of the game is as with most Civ V games it is balancing the right research to your build: building important wonders to either further your cause or significantly hurt your competitors, helpful buildings that further science, production, health and culture and units to defend your cities.
The technology web is however poorly done even on my second time round, and having a good idea of what did what, getting lost in the web is too easy. I see there is a mod out now that colour codes the web I will probably download it as it is very difficult to tell exactly what you are getting when researching a branch or leaf outside of experience /staring at the screen for 10-15 mins each time you have to research something.
Health is similar to happiness in Civ V but definitely made more difficult in keeping with Prince and up difficulties in Civ. Even on Sputnik difficulty health is a serious issue. I like it it adds that hectic feel that Civ has on higher difficulties.
The aliens are well pictured in the game, however to me they are a bit tame, the ultrasonic fences and the first purity affinity being that explorers don't get attacked is I think overpowered. I think it should be that aliens don't attack you unless you are aggressive, but I would like to see siege worms taking out cities, waves of aliens taking out bases or improvements due to your aggression. Right now as it stands you can rush the purity affinity and use explorers as a fence against aliens which is what I did in the last game where I started 4 turns from a 8 xenomass nest with 2 siegeworms and about 8 assorted aliens running around close to my base.
The gameplay is a mix of AC and Civ V borrowing elements from the AC expansion as well.
Spying is better similar to Civ IV, air warfare could have been improved, satellite coverage and to a lesser extent warfare is a welcome addition would love to see on multiplayer.
Transcendence is basically the same with you connecting with the planet's consciousness in a process similar to AC, Emancipation and Promised Land is where you build a gate back to Earth so that you can bring more humans to the new planet (Purity) or you can 'cleanse' them of their inferior humanity (Supremacy). The only difference being some of the dialog leading up to the end and the look of your units.
What I would like: :)
The original context instituted where certain factions have certain playstyles and similar to Civ V where certain factions tend to be in jungle etc have the Supremacists closer to Firaxite etc. Keep what they have in the startup as an option where you can customise your experience again similar to AC.
This is asking for alot a scenario based on each faction almost like how Blizzard did Starcraft single player which could explain units the tech tree and alot of the lore around the planets example why this particular one, internal power struggles everything storybuffs like myself would love. They could sell as DLCs I would buy them.
Better aliens, more aggressive, more reactive, possibly evolve and get more difficult almost similar to xcom or become more organised as the game progresses.
Random events, to me outside of all the dumbing down has got to be the worst most glaring and include cheapest thing to fix.. The quests are interesting to read but the same each time (will recant only 2 playthroughs), it needs randomness!! Special occurences probably linked to achievements things that only happen when you play this char with this affinity in this way. I have almost 700hours in Civ V and I still occasionally see a civ or myself try to do something new and this to me has to be the biggest issue as this will prevent it from getting that strong community that Civ and AC has.

Vintage Year has its pros and cons, which we will be going over, as well as what its about, as well as what it is.
Vintage Year is a Indie Topdown Roguelike Shoot-em-up, that relies on strategy, speed, and stealth.
While playing you can collect corks, which can be used in the menus after you die to buy things like other unique characters, for example.
It can be compared to Teleglitch, Nuclear Throne, The Binding of isaac, and many other games like that.
You have been hired by a gentleman, who calls himself the Connoisseur.
He hires you do defend his familys wine from a group known as the skull faction.
As soon as you delve into the wine cellar, it becomes blatantly obvious that there are supernatural things going on.
Pros
-Weapon system similar to nuclear throne
-Cosmetic items, for me it was fun trying to find out how to get them all, and I even have a guide on steam about it.
-36+ interesting weapons to use.
-4 types of weapons, Light Weapons, Heavy weapons, Explosives, and Melee.
-Ambient and dark surroundings require you to move slow and carefully plan your route.
-Well-made effects, animations, and sound effects.
-Secret mechanics, which usually give bonuses.
-Doesnt require a well-built computer.
-12 unique characters, all with their passive effects, such as a 20% dodge chance, or a 10% life steal.
-Randomly generated levels, with traps, loot, and sometimes a secret area.
-Perks, although you can only have one in a game, the perks are all very interesting
-Cheap, its $2.99 on steam at the time that i made this video, and i doubt it will change.
-Fun little mini-games and challenges.
-Ambient Music, which fits the game.
-Supports English, French, Italian, German, Spanish, and Danish Languages.
-Unique and challenging bosses and minibosses
-Dark levels, and placeable light sources, which can be put out by spirits.
-Leveling, every few floors you will get to choose between upgrading your damage, speed, sight, or health.
-Visual leveling, your character will change based upon what you choose to level up, for example,
when you upgrade your speed, you get a bandana
-Create and share custom character designs.
-Lots of replayability.
-Steam trading cards
-Full controller support
Cons
-No difficulty setting.
-Downloading and using the custom skins requires you to use the files, which can be hard to find.
-The dashing is a bit weird, you cant just choose a direction and dash.
-You cant remap the controls.
-Sometimes the shooting is weird
-Minimal tutorials
-Slow moving bullets, although i think this is fine, its all based on the player.
I give it a 9/10
Would highly reccomend.
it is well worth the $3 in the first place,
but if it's on sale, just get it, you wont regret it.

I did not play much Civ V so I can't make much of a comparison like these other reviewers.
That said, if you like sci-fi and 4x this is a pretty solid game imo. For now there's 3 routes to go: Purity, Supremacy and xenophile (I can't recall the real name of the last one right now). Each gets unique units and paths to win.
The AI in the game can be absolutely brutal or incredibly bad. At one point the AI ganged up on me while I was about to win in supremacy, which I thought was pretty good. However on my domination victory game I was facing Franco-Iberia in war and they were doing a very good job of repelling and chipping away at my massive army which I had spent many turns assembling at their border. On the verge of believing I would need another 100 or so turns just to recuperate my losses the AI offers a truce with 6/9 of their cities and 10 turns of peace... that pretty much sealed their fate 15 or so turns later. Not sure what the AI was doing there (this was only vostok difficulty mind you)
The aliens in the game will unprovokedly attack your troops on occasion but in most instances they will leave them completely alone for better or worse. There is not much point in interacting with them aside from the quests given to you (great for affinity in your path) because even with the culture perks killing ayy lmaos (aliens) does not grant much science/culture/gold. This could possibly be improved.
As well I wish there were more cultures and there was more variance between them. in general they all play exactly the same. I know Civ V has exponentially more at any rate, perhaps updates/DLC in the future will fix that.
Overall 7.5/10

At first I was just wowed by all the pretty theatrics of the game especially with it being in the future but this title as you would hear from hundreds of other feels like an ambitious Civ V mod or just a pretty re-skin. I see where 2K comes from though. They found a formula that works really well! Why veer too far form a great thing? Especially when you're doing something as ambitious as moving the setting of your game that has been the same for the past 20 years to something totally new. SPAAAACE.
Sure the new tech web is cool and I get the new system they have for the units which I think is neat! The web allow everyone to advance at the same pace but in different directions.The unit system is a lot less managing 30 different units from 3 different eras and more focus on evolving your units based on your unity (or whatever the 3 paths are called). One land infantry unit, one land armor unit, one ranged unit, one flying unit ect.
A new Civ game should make me go "I will call in sick just to play one more turn." or "Ok. Seriously. One more turn. (900 turns ago)." But this game doesn't have the wonder and awe of a newly released Civ game. I think I'll hold off on playing this until expansions come out and really change up the game (at least im hoping it will). I'll drop by every now and then to put more hours in but until new expansions come out and really grasp me I think i'll hold off.

There are very few games that present themselves as well as Vintage Year. Along the way you’ll become imbued with paranormal abilities and find a plethora of weapons with which to dispatch your foes. What really sold me on this game, and what makes it stand apart from other top-down shooter roguelikes, is how much strategy is involved. Peeping from behind a wall, planting torches, and planning out an attack are not only par for the course in Vintage Year, but necessary for your continued survival.

Played this back in the day way more than I ever played DOOM, Blood or Duke Nukem.
The thing that always got me in this game is that there are no magical shenanigans, no demon invasion from other planes of existence and no alien forces to fight with, well, at least not that many. There is the whole "you're a genetically engineered experimental soldier", but gameplay-wise it's just a game about the War of Vietnam. The game really does a lot for immersion, putting you right in the middle of hell itself. There are several vietnamese and american bombers flying low all over almost every level, dropping bombs at random intervals everywhere, there are vietcong ambushes waiting for you, anti-tank guns, snipers, booby traps, mines, napalm and many other ways of killing or getting killed in this game. You'll play some missions during the night and you even get to use night vision goggles, which are actually helpful, by the way. In some missions, you'll get that Apocalypse Now feeling of being stranded deep in enemy territory and slowly going mad by all the♥♥♥♥♥♥you're seeing and doing. That's how good the atmosphere in this game is. Soundtrack really adds into it, some songs are downright batshit insane combinations of slow, eerie sounds and fast string instruments. It's amazing.
About the gameplay, expect the exact same as Duke Nukem 3D. It's as simple as that. NAM is just a remake, stand-alone game of a mod called Platoon made with Duke Nukem 3D. You move at the exact same speed, you jump the exact same way, you shoot and duck just the same. You have 6 weapons at your disposal, including a M-16, a M-60 machinegun, a shotgun, a KA-BAR combat knife, a granade launcher and a rocket launcher. While there is plenty of ammo for the M-16 and M-60, you'll have to think before shooting the other guns, since they are essential to getting out of hell alive and you won't trip into rocket ammo every 2 minutes. Talking about thinking, get ready not to run and gun. The game is hard as balls and, unless you already played it and know exactly where to go and what to look after, you'll be ambushed every thirty seconds and it takes only a couple of seconds of fire from a single guy to ♥♥♥♥ your game up. The game is really, really short: There are two tours of duty with six missions each, I've completed the game in only four hours, but I remember taking weeks of play when I was younger to find out how to play, where to go and how to stay alive.
If you like old 3D shooters and have a least a little bit of a fall for the Vietnam War, like most of us do, get this game, you'll love it.

This game is NOT Civ V with a fresh paint job.  In fact, I was slightly dissapointed the first few games when it didn't quite play like Civ V and I ended up simply grinding through technologies and developing my cities.  It seemed shallow and void of any meaningful strategy.  Then I got used to the progression of the game and started realizing there is a different strategy game underneath that is nothing like Civ V.
First, the addition of the quest system adds a variety that will change your civilization in small, incremental ways that end up really affecting your "civ" in a large way in the end-game.  There are 6 different victory quests that, if completed by any "civ", will end the game.  It's tricky to figure out which victory your opponents you are going for and prevent them from achieving it.  Deciding on which victory condition quest to persue must be decided early to optimize your approach to completing them.
Second, while it may seem that there aren't as many leaders for you to choose from, you basically create your civ from scratch at the start of the game by choosing the perks of your civ.  I liked this approach.  Some of the choices really change your approach to each match by allowing you to find ideal locations for expansion quickly or getting a jump start on research.
Third, the tech tree is now more of a "web" than a tree.  Mastering the progression of your technologies is probably the most important part of winning.  There are so many paths that one can take through the web.  Some paths are required to complete parts of victory quests.  Do you go straight for them?  Do you focus on acquiring more culture, production, expansion, or research first?  What is the ideal balance?  Here's where the strategy of Civ:BE really shines.
Finally, spycraft is so much better in this game compared to Civ V.  The covert operations mechanics can get very powerful, even to the point of capturing a city without even building a single soldier unit.  It can really change the tide of the game when you steal energy, research, tech, or city(!) from a competing civ.
If I had any complaint, it would be the UI.  It is so flat that it is hard to tell what techs are at a glance.  I find myself hovering the cursor over each tech to figure out what I'm really getting... every time I choose new research.  I can't really tell whether I'm unlocking a unit, a building, or a wonder without reading the discription.  It would be nicer to have some color or texture to denote the differences at a glance.  (EDIT 1/2/15 - Since this review, the UI has been tweaked a bit to fix this issue)
This is a worthy Sid Meier's Civ addition.  Just give it some time and forget (most of) the strategies you used in Civ V.

This game is bad.  Let's just get that out of the way right now.  If you're going into this game expecting a AAA style shooter (even for the day), you're going to be disappointed.  So why am I giving it a positive recommendation?  Because of what it accomplishes with what it had to work with.
This is a build engine game.  (Duke Nukem 3D, Shadow Warrior, Blood, etc.)  The engine is limited.  When it came out it was impressive, because its main competition was Doom.  What this engine excelled at was "work-arounds."
That's what the devs had to do to make something work using this engine.  And work it does.  There's a lot of little tricks used in this game, to varying degrees of success.  A lot of miscellaneous items were all actually the same item, with a different value - displayed in percentage - to determine what it did.  This also meant that there was one collectible item that was randomized.  It could be a health pack, it good be ammo, it could be nothing, it could even explode.  All the same item on the same map, just a different effect when you collect it.
Now, that does mean that a lot of things are not clear until you play with them.  But it does stretch what the engine was capable of, and give a bit more randomization to the game.
But, is that a good thing?  For most games, probably not.  But again, that is where this game differs.  This is not a traditional Doom or Duke Nukem 3D clone.  Not by any means.  The developers wanted to make this feel more like the war in Vietnam.  (Note: I, like many of you, am too young to have actually been there, but this is a stylized version anyway.)  The enemy is well hidden.  They hide in the trees.  They hide behind bushes.  They hide on ledges, and around corner.  The enemy is hidden, everywhere.  There are land mines, and claymore mines.  They are hard to see.  You have allied planes dropping bombs now and then.  Sometimes with little warning.
What all of this means is that you are going to die.  A lot.  And often in very unfair ways.  This game is cruel, this game is brutal.  This game is challenging.  And the ending is totally not worth reaching.
But it does make the game fairly unique.  It's a noble effort, and I think they pulled off the atmosphere well.
This is not a game for everyone.  There are also several signs that this was not a very high-budget endeavor.  Some of the graphics are off - and in the case of any indication from the player that you've hit an "end of level" switch - missing altogether.  (When you do so with Duke Nukem, you see his fist come up to press the button.  That is absent here.)  There are a few sound effects held over from Duke Nukem itself.  In essence, this is a bit of a Total Conversion.
But there is a lot to like.  Some of the level design is interesting and fun.  The enemies are not the standard fare.  The weapons are mostly reskinned and tweaked from Duke Nukem, however, there is a new flame thrower, and a sniper rifle which sadly does not zoom, but does have the scope effect.
Now, as a note, I played this game using EDuke32, in order to have it run more smoothly on my PC.  It does work fine in DOSBox.  You *CAN* change the controls, you just have to start with the configuration and go from there.  (Be sure you set "up" and "down" at the bottom of the keyboard config, otherwise you can't scroll through the menu.  And yea, that's pretty bad design.)  You will also probably want to adjust the mouse Y scaling as high as it will go, and note that what they call "inverted" is not.  This WILL make the default game play more like a modern FPS.
If you can get this game cheap, and you know what you're getting into, then by all means pick it up.  But just know that this game is going to be unfair, unforgiving, and jury-rigged together to give the experience.

Just got this game, and I've played through about half of it, and I keep thinking how much I would have loved this game as a kid.  It has the right feel for an old-school platformer, but it is a puzzle game rather than a shooting game.
It's designed like a classic 2-D sidescrolling platformer, but the trick is that you have a gun that creates two types of gravity fields.  One pulls you, and one repels you (along with some obstacles).  This makes it feel in some ways like a 2D version of Portal at times, although the feel is very different.
I am breezing through the game so far, but I have played a lot of puzzlers and platformers over the years and don't usually find them challenging anymore.  I think an average player would find this game very challenging, and it certainly is inventive.
So far, everything about the game is good from what I can tell, with one exception.  The aiming mechanic on a gamepad is a little hard to fine tune, and it's especially hard to aim when in motion on a gamepad.  This is bad as some of the puzzles are best solved with mid-air field placement.  Meanwhile, the usual gripes I have with this kind of game (bad hit detection, erratic controls, poor optimization, graphics glitches, etc) aren't an issue here.  The game feels pretty solid with the single exception of the aiming system.

You assume the role of Commander Video, a space alien created with nothing but dark matter and a series of beats. Once you're actually in a level, you play as a little yellow pong-board, and your goal is to block the "beats" that come toward you - they sort of look like little yellow squares. Different-colored beats have different behaviors, like bouncing off different materials ingame, the blue "beat", and coming back once you block it, making you have to hit it again, the orange "beat".
Now, that's just the main gameplay basis. This game would probably earn itself a positive view from me if it wasn't for a few key gameplay factors.
The first problem I have with this game, which a lot of other people have too, is the eye-burning graphics. The retro "feel" to the game could have been very good-looking, but blocking the "beats" were extremely hard due to so many things happening on-screen - like blinking beats, bouncing beats, and a whole lot of sparkles going around your pong-board every time you block a beat, although I feel that was the real challenge this game was presenting.
The second problem I had with BIT.TRIP BEAT is the hard-hitting learning curve. The first level (mind that there are only three) starts off easy, assuming the player knows what they need to do. Not too long later, the learning curve has such a sharp angle it's almost as if it's just a line. The game starts throwing different beats at you that you don't know about, and all too fast, too.
The final problem I have with this game is the lack of levels. Losing a level out of the three of them would be much less punishing if, let's say, there were 8 parts to a level. Selecting a level would let you select out of these 8, allowing you to go back to a place you messed up without having to play the parts before it.
Of course, there are positive things to this game - so much so that some of this is edited once I finished the game.
If these main gameplay factors weren't so sketchy, I wouldn't have a problem with this game at all. The graphics, at times, are really attractive and nice-looking. The retro feel of the pong-board and the 3D graphics and the background allow for an astonishing feel while you're blocking beats. The gameplay itself, the idea of blocking beats, is also a nice concept to add to the game. The music, of course, is the best part of the BIT.TRIP series - after all, the things are called BEATS! The music is hella awesome and usually fits the setting and current situation of the player.
Additionally, at the time of editing this, I have finished BIT.TRIP BEAT, and to be honest, the learning curve doesn't matter if you're up to the challenge. Though this may seem stupid, because of this one reason, I'm giving this a positive.
In conclusion, BIT.TRIP BEAT used to give me a negative review, but on the flip side, I gave this a positive for some odd reason.

A move forward in the Hitman franchise, but is it the one you would expect?
Hitman: Absolution is a huge improvement over the previous Hitman games, giving you more content, better graphics and a slightly more engaging storyline. However, if you're a fan of the Hitman franchise, you soon realise that quite a lot has also been taken away; the most important feature being freedom. Unlike the older games, Absolution keeps you under control. You can't just run around the mission area, kill a person here and there and then get back on track. With the addition of the mission points you have to limit yourself to focusing on the mission and the mission only if you want a good end score.
While some may not mind this, personally I find it irritating. On the other hand, the more you play, the less you think about it.
All in all, Absolution is definitely a step in the right direction and a chance for the developers to learn from their mistakes. While many fans of the franchise will not appreciate this to its full extent, it is a reasonably satisfying game for the casual gamer.

As a long time huge Final Fantasy fan, this is very hard for me, and I don't think there is really any correct way for somebody to write a review on this game. Whether you like it or dislike it, there will always be a large number of people waiting to hate you for it. But I'll share my thoughts at least:
I personally feel like 9 or 10 was the last true Final Fantasy game, then the world map disappeared, the battle system changed repeatedly, and of course, most areas became boring corridors in FF13.
I wasn't a big fan of 12, but it was still fine, and so far (about half way through the game, I think), I dislike 13 more than any other Final Fantasy that has come before it. However, my thoughts continue to change on it as I get further...
I started off very unimpressed by the boring areas, lack of exploration, annoying characters (or lack of personality, in Lightning's case), and I hated the battle system. I always enjoyed strategically giving commands to all my characters individually, but in this game, you only control the leader, and pretty much just give suggestions to the other party members. Granted, they're actually quite smart sometimes, but I just feel like I would be a lot more comfortable knowing exactly what everybody is going to do.
But as I got further, I started to accept things a bit more. The battle system is quite clever in some ways, the areas start to get slightly more interesting (I think), and despite what people say, there is actually some character development. I never thought I'd say it, but I've warmed up to the game, and even Lightning's character.
But at the same time, I think this is still my least favourite Final Fantasy (I've not played any other game in the FF13 trilogy yet). In fact, it's probably one of my least favourite JRPGs in general. And yet, I feel like the good parts are so good that it's still enjoyable and worth my time.
Anyway, I'm far from an experienced reviewer or anything, but to anybody on the fence about whether or not to try this game, I'd say:
Give it a go, but be patient with it. There were times when I just wanted to stop playing and give up on it, but I've continued onward and am enjoying it more than expected, for the most part. Give the characters a chance, even at their most obnoxious and whiny. They become more bearable, at least to me.
And that's about all I can think of to say about this game. I hope it helped in any way at all, but if not, oh well... I'm just sharing my opinion online, leave me alone!  D:

Gonna have to say no on this one really. It's not a terrible game by itself, but it's just a reskinned Civs5 that took 1 step forward and 2 steps backward. It added a few little nice things like the tech web, removed things they shouldn't have, and created a really basic system that doesn't have much depth like Civs5 did because apparently the game was too confusing to play(?).
-Military Unit promotions are dull, bland, and quite boring. The way affinity works with upgrading them looks cool at 1st because the units look different depending on the affinity path you choose. But it's just a simplified unit promotion from Civs5. You only get 2 options when the upgrade comes up. Where's all the dozen other promotions I could give my unit? Where'd that go? Why is it that a particular unit is always going to have the same promotions when built? I liked it when I could have multiple rifleman with different roles. One played the medic, one had huge defense, and maybe one had really good offense. You can't do that anymore. Every unit of that type now plays 1 single role. *KILLS* it for me.
-There's almost no unit diversity. For example, there's only 2 different naval units in the entire game. Really? ...Really?  ¯\_(ツ)_/¯
-Wonders are kinda meh. Not as many at all compared to V and most of them don't do much.
-The endgame is boring. No real units to look forward to, nothing changes. Plays like it does early game for the most part. Your turns also start to become unnecessarily tedious due to a few annoying things that I hope they do fix. One, being the trade routes. In this game you can get about 3 trades routes PER city you own. So once you start running a dozen cities or more, most of your turns you're going to be constantly reconfirming what that damn vessel/convoy should be doing. Again, and again, and again~
-The "Civilizations" or Sponsors I believe they call them are♥♥♥♥♥♥ They barely have any unique bonuses, no special units or buildings, and there's only 8 of them to play.
So OVERALL: Skip this and go buy & play CivsV if you haven't. It's cheaper and you get more content. Win win!

When you get down to it, this game is, mechanically speaking, more or less a clone of civilization 5 with a few modifications, none of which are earth shattering.
Of course, the same could be said of Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri, and while the developers of this game were quite insistent that it is not intended to be Alpha Centauri 2, it's quite clearly intended as a spiritual successor, and looking back, Alpha Centauri was, mechanically speaking, more or less a clone of civilization 2 with a few modifications.
Indeed, what made Alpha Centauri something special was the spectacular (and quite believable) worldbuilding, the interesting leaders, and the way the world and the characters were presented to the player. At first glance, Beyond Earth falls flat on its face in that regard: While most of the quotes accompanying the technologies are attributed to one of the game's leaders, they don't tell us much about the setting, the narrative, or the technologies you've discovered, nor do they do much to develop the leaders as characters. Just as bad is the fact that the quotes are all read by a single narrator, which divorces the quotes from the leader in queston; the fact that the quotes in Alpha Centauri were read by the character they was one of the big reasons those characters were memorable.
However, after going through the civilopedia entries on the various buildings, technologies, and wonders, I'm starting to warm up to the setting the developers have constructed. While the explanations given for many of the technologies, structures may sound like pure technobabble, most of the ones concerning my area of expertise (medicine) are plausible or at least theoretically possible, and the odd instance of improperly used medical/biological jargon seems more like honest mistakes rather than the result of a willful disregard for the use of the word "science" in the term "science fiction." These entires flesh out the game quite nicely, and, for once, actually gives a coherent explanation for what exactly the unobtanium we're finding on the planet IS; Firaxite is a high temperature superconductor which functions at relatively mundane temperatures, floatstone contains magnetic monopoles, xenomoss is a fungus analogue with a unique biology, and so on.
The fact that this is not presented particularly well is the biggest problem with this game when compared with Alpha Centauri, and while I enjoyed the game and recommend buying it if it happens to go on sale, I would suggest people who didn't enjoy civilization 5's gameplay avoid this game for the time being.

Stylish and uncompromising, but rough in ways that wouldn't be so forgivable at a higher price point.
Vintage Year is a low-key roguelike overhead shooter, and here roguelike doesn't simply mean "permadeath". Vintage Year embraces the old-school roguelike style of giving the player very little information and forcing them to figure it out. It mostly works, with the gameplay being simple enough that you can learn just by fooling around, and the fast-paced live-die-repeat gameplay helps this.
You never feel like you lose much progress by making a blind choice, but sometimes the very minimal UI can be frustrating if you already know how things work, you just can't remember which item is which. Some players will find the experimentation-driven learning very rewarding, but some may find it simply frustrating.
The gameplay is rather polished, but one major area shows weakness: enemy pathfinding. Levels are randomly generated and mazelike, and the enemies have an extremely hard time navigating if there is a hard wall between them and you. And this isn't something that comes up every once in a while; enemies literally do not know how to move around a wall to line up a shot. In some ways this works to the game's benefit; if the AI could navigate better then the already hard game would be even harder, but to see the AI fail so regularly is amateurish.
Vintage Year is rather difficult, since you have very limited health and it is only replenished by (very rarely) randomly found health pick-ups. Using all the tools the game provides you is vital, as is caution. Stumbling into a room without a very good idea of what's all in it can be deadly. While unforgiving, the difficulty feels fair, though one sometimes wishes for some kind of non-random healing.
The biggest failing is in the UI. It seems designed for a controller, but the gameplay requires precision I wouldn't trust to a controller. Frankly, if you're making a PC game, main menus that can't be navigated purely through the mouse are an unforgivable sin. And furthermore, the game is inconsistent: sometimes WASD can be used to navigate menus, sometimes the arrow keys need to be used. Sometimes things are selected with the mouse, sometimes with E, and sometimes, bafflingly, with the enter key.
Finally, the progression system is very minimal, only giving unlockable characters and cosmetic items for characters. This isn't a terrible flaw, but its implentation feels more like an ingame-currency DLC store than a true progression system, in that the things you unlock may not help you get further in the game at all, and are simply alternate options to enhance replayability.
Overall, the biggest factor in my recommendation is the price. At 10 dollars I would not recommend this game, when you could get Hotline Miami for the same. But at $5.49 it's worth a look if you like roguelikes or overhead shooters. I don't know how much more I'll really play this thing, but I've definitely gotten $5.49 worth of fun out of it.

Hollow Knight is a superb game, both in terms of quality and value for money. I went in expecting a standard metroid-vania experience but found a lot more. The exploration in this game is on par with the original Dark Souls, that sense of tension you get pushing into uncharted territory is so common in Hollow Knight along with the relief when you reach a familiar area or find a path out of a nightmare area. The map continued to expand and one up my expectations long after I thought i'd found the edges of the world. There is a platforming element to the game and it feels smooth, responsive and controls well with a controller or Keyboard (i personally recommend a keyboard but i'm wierd). For the most part the combat is the focus, and it works well with simple 4 way aiming melee attacks and some 'spells'. This adds enough complexity without it ever losing its focus and there are some intense boss fights that will put your skills to the test. It also must be said that the enemy variety, along with the environment, is extremely impressive for a game about bugs. To say much more would be spoiling an incredible and immersive experience. It took me roughly 45 hours to complete pretty much everything, looking forward to a second playthrough and future updates.
The game has also been recieving free updates introducing new content. Both of these so far have been of a high quality,  fit neatly into the gameworld and can be found on your first playthrough and not feel tacked on or out of place.

Edited AFTER beta patch 1.3b to a "Thumbs up".
The long list of changes included in patch 1.3b addressed literally all of my technical issues with the game.
Though since starting a new map I still haven't been able to fully test the forestry fix(es) due to lack of in game money, so far.
This of course didn't repair my corrupted save, but I have since found a beautiful free mod map "Old Ridge Farm" that both suits my personality and sense of aesthetics, so starting again has been as good as a holiday, (that new car smell).
Selectively adding suitable "quality of life" mods to the game from a smorgasbord of high quality free mod sites, has tailored the game to how I want to play Farming Simulator (2015).
I don't have much experience with game modders, but I am impressed by both the quality and quantity of mods available for this game.
I now practice a very strict backup process for my save folder every night, but the game is exceptionally stable ( except ONCE, which was devastating).
Buy this game, except if you are time poor, and even then, strongly consider getting this game.
Original:
I love this game, there are no win conditions, no artificial restrictions for you to unlock, no leveling up, no end game.
If you can afford the equipment (and the daily maintenance), you can buy it for your farm.
There are no "best" or "end game" equipment, just equipment that is better suited to what you doing, or your preferred way of doing it.
Most of my farm purchases were based on budgeting and economics rather than stats.
This is the game I play just to relax, and enjoy myself.
Everything is SO detailed, the lighting, the models, the animations, the weather, the day and night cycles.
It is the attention to detail that keeps me entertained while I am harvesting a paddock.
The game appears to be very well optimized as my aging GPU doesn't have any problems in providing a very smooth framerate.
The tutorial is probably the best one I have seen for being short, sweet, and to the point, so you can get on with the game.
The Modding community, and the quality of the mods for this game is huge.
My ONLY complaint, and it is a BIG one, is that trying to expand my farming into the much advertized FORESTRY, the game crashes with the unfortunate habit of deleting all the current save game files (XML's).
My current save has, or rather, had over 100 hrs invested in it.  I was able to retrieve an autosave backup, with only a hour or so lost, however continuing to plant more saplings caused the game to crash and delete the save files again losing a few more hours work.
Considering the amount of precious time invested, this to me is unacceptable.
Losing three hours is the same as losing an entire gaming night.
Despite my love of this game, I can't recommend this game until such an important feature, is fixed, and I personally hope it is fixed soon.

Unique idea that leaves a lot to be desired. It's a decent pong-based rhythm game with a cool soundtrack, but it gets repetitive pretty quick. Worse, the screen is usually way too busy to tell what's going on with a high degree of accuracy and the game includes *way* too many bright flashing effects for anyone with even with the slightest light sensitivity to enjoy pain-free.
I know that I had a lot of trouble playing it without getting migraines, and many friends I showed it to complained of similar light sensitivity issues. There's no way to turn them down or off (an increasingly common disability option), so this ends up creating a game that isn't really based on skill so much as it's based on your eye's ability to not freak out when exposed to all the lights. Decent fun if you get a copy for cheap, but not really worth it unless this kind of thing is *really* your jam.

People complain about the linearity of this game, but is it really different than any other Final Fantasy? An open world gives the illusion of choice, but the plot of every Final Fantasy game is linear. Rather than letting us "decide" whether to get lost on the world map or not, Final Fantasy XIII gives us interesting tactical choices. Every weapon you find can become an ultimate weapon. Every character is different and useful. The great feeling of trying out parties made up of different roles has been boiled down the core mechanic and we can make this decision many times per battle.
I don't think the linearity hurts FFXIII in any way. Rather, I think the useless decisions have been removed and we're left with just the interesting ones.

Glork is a great character with funny side-kicks and chatty robot friends which keeps the presentation moving along and adds a bit of levity with mini-skits between games.  There's small, totally-optional tasks to accomplish like run back and forth 10 times, which might get thrown at you randomly at the start of each game.  A few little tidbits that seem stupid on paper, but the devs used a light touch and only used these mechanisms to mix things up between games.
The shooting game is nothing earth-shattering but what can I say, I like playing this.  Far more than I ever liked Galaga, back then in 1981 or now on an emulator.

is a twin stick shooting dungeon crawler with roguelike elements. The basic premise of the game is that you've been hired by a gentleman who calls himself The Connoisseur who tasks you with defending his family's precious wine from a vicious gang called the "Skull Faction". As you venture into his wine cellar, however, it's clear that there's other supernatural forces at play.
The game is often compared to other top down shooters like
. Although both games share the same basic elements, they are quite different. Vlambeer's
has a faster, more arcade-like feel to its gameplay, while
relies on stealthy tactics and careful planning. At the beginning of every level, you're given an opportunity to scout out the layout of the room. This gives the player a chance to strategize the best way to tackle all of the enemies on the floor; you must eliminate all of the Skull Faction before continuing. Levels are also shrouded in darkness, making it difficult to peer ahead to keep track of enemy movements. To counter this, you're given a limited amount of torches to place, adding more of a strategical aspect to the gameplay.
For its $5 price,
offers a good amount of replay value. There's up to 16 different playable characters that you can unlock, each with their own unique perks. After every two completed levels, players have the chance to gain more perks, helping them continue through ever-increasingly difficult dungeons. Enemies, Mini-Bosses, and Bosses get progressively harder to overcome, making this game a suitable challenge for fans of roguelites and action games. There's a lot of the game that the dev has kept secret, leaving the player to discover the strange inner workings by themselves. Additionally, players can also unlock an alternate game mode, cosmetic hats (!!!), and mod their own characters into the game.
Still, the game isn't perfect. The controls aren't remappable, and at times, movement doesn't feel as smooth as it should. Some parts are a little buggy, such as sometimes getting stuck inside walls and strange spike trap hitboxes. Graphically, the pixel sprites lack the creativity and charm that
manages to capture, but the developer, Nooner Bear, makes up for it with a chilling atmosphere that keeps the player on their toes. He's still adding bugfixes and patches to the game, so it can only get better from here.
is a solid game that delivers a lot in a small package. It offers a good amount of replayability through procedurally generated levels, challenging gameplay, and many player unlocks. It definitely shines most as a quick game to take breaks with since you can go on quick runs to try and beat your high scores. This game is a great stepping stone into shooter roguelites and is definitely worth the asking price. You should definitely consider picking this up, considering the $2.99 vs. $12.99
asks for. However, both games have their own merits. Even if you own Vlambeer's popular product, this is a good investment for a different experience. If you like games that are easy to pick up and play but are difficult to beat, this indie gem is a good addition to your gaming collection.

If for some reason you've never played Blizzard's renowned Diablo franchise and have wondered about the fuss surrounding Diablo 3, look no further than Torchlight to answer your questions.
Runic Games consists of former Blizzard employees who worked on Diablo 2. As such, it should come as no surprise that the two games are extremely similar. Unfortunately, Torchlight has a few flaws that limit its potential:
Repetition. Maybe I've outgrown the dungeon crawler genre, but I couldn't shake the tediousness half way into Torchlight's 12 hour campaign. Gameplay is primarily mouse clicking and neither the enemies nor environments were varied enough to keep my interest.
The lack of multiplayer severely diminishes replay value. It's generous of the developers to add an infinite dungeon, but why should the average player care when he can't flaunt his spoils or successes?
I do applaud Runic's inclusion of an editor, allowing fans to prolong the life of Torchlight. Kudos to that!
Grade: B-

I remember playing Civ 3. It was my introduction to the series, and I wasn't very good at it. But I kept playing it, losing in new and different ways, slowing learning: an advanced unit could be destroyed by enough less advanced units; there are limits to what you can bulid, etc. Though I find this new game frustrating, I still find myself pulled back in like I was with Civ 3.
The short version: it feels like an uninspired add-on, and a lot of the new ideas don't work, but I keep coming back to it.
A lot of people voice the same complaints, so I'll just reiterate them quickly:
-boring leaders, boring wonders
-crippling health mechanic prevents expansion (not limits - prevents)
-aliens are the only thing that attack
In addition:
-The AI gets mad when you attack the aliens. It doesn't matter what they do to the aliens: if you attack the aliens (because they'll have no trouble attacking you), destroy miasma (toxic to 2 of the 3 affinities), or destroy their nests, the AI will all line up and condemn you, barring diplomatic exchanges. Not that they're useful, but they could be and they're not an option if you defend your territory. And, of course, the aliens get mad and swarm your early, pathetic military units.
-The tech web is nice, but you NEED to get health buildings right away, then affinity techs to improve your military (not a specific tech, but any affinity gains will improve your units), then quest-specific techs. So you could do anything you wanted, but a pragmatic player will find a path quickly to meet these needs.
-The favors system doesn't make sense to me yet, though I could come around to it. So far, all I know is that 3 favors and I can compel an AI to declare a war as I like. Though it's more expensive than just buying their participation.
I knew it would be similar to Civ 5, and welcomed that fact. I don't mind buying the same strategy game again because I love it so. But I hope the game improves prior to any DLC, because I'm not sure I can stomach playing this game much more as it is. I was drawn into the Civ series because of its historical ties: the French building Versailles, the Mongols conquering China, these things are real and can be done in the game. The future of BE isn't nearly as compelling as the history of Civ 5.
I do like having certain things at the very start, like roads and bridges. The sci-fi theme can be cool and the planets look interesting. Late game war is, in my opinion, much more interesting.
I'm still not sure about the aliens. I've found it helpful to think of the early game as belonging to 3 parties: me, my rivals, and the aliens. They're too powerful to be conquered early, but too weak to be meaningful in the late game. That mindset has improved my game, but I'm still learning.
All in all? If you liked Civ 5, you'll find something in this game too. It has plenty of room for improvement but I think Firaxis is up to the task.

Its a complete downhill ride.  It starts off decently.  It feels like a more linear version of blood money.  Then with each level advancement it just becomes more and more like some crappy splinter cell/sin's creed clone.
I managed to suffer through the entire game on normal and hard, and it was just complete torture on hard because it adds in a lot more guards.
Its not difficulty to stealth in this game, but nearly all of the stealth features are completely broken at random.
Throw a brick to distract the only guard near you?  LOL NOPE!!  A guard across the map goes "WHAT WAS THAT NOISE!?!" and comes to investigate while your target smokes a cigarette.
Purposefully run near a guard to get him to investigate the noise? LOL NOPE!!  Instead of going to where you ran to investigate, he goes to the run spot, continues past, continues to nearby stairs, goes to the 2nd floor, and goes "WHAT WAS THAT NOISE?!?!" 1 floor above where the noise was made, chasing you by accident the entire time.
Non-stealth isn't an option.  Why?  Because this is hitman, not some run n gun series.  No point in playing it non-stealthy.
This is how a typical hard mode run goes:
1.Observe targets path and interactions.
2.Figure a way to kill him with the environment, or kill him when he is alone.
3.Ambush him at a kill spot.
4.Kill him.
5.Get seen through 7 walls by 2 different guards.
6.Reset at last checkpoint and do it all over with your fingers crossed this time.
I don't want to review the bonus conditions...but they increase your score, which is the only way to get upgrades!
Collect everything in the level that can be used as a weapon?  omfg...how tedious.  I can't even see half of the crap on the ground that is able to be grabbed without using my LOLOLOLOLO HIGHLIGHT MODE.  The bonus kill conditions are just completely rediculous.  You can do the entire bonus condition 1000 times, but it'll never give you the bonus unless you are psychic and know that you HAVE to kill the certain person with a certain weapon at a certain time.  Its all trial and error, and therefor, technically, a bad game.
I really hope the hitman series is dead now.  I loved blood money and the previous games, but this is pure garbage.
Playable on normal though, if you ignore all bonuses and just LOLOLOLO shoot and xray vision everything.  Not fun, but playable.

Since I don't want to dissapoint you guys, I'll give you some tips about going well prepared to your first job interview!
Job interviewing never seems to get any easier - even when you have gone on more interviews than you can count. You are always meeting new people, having to sell yourself and your skills, and often getting the third degree about what you know or don't know. And, you have to stay upbeat and enthusiastic throughout each interview.Here are job interview tips to help prepare you to interview effectively. Proper preparation will help alleviate some of the stress involved in job interviews and the more you prepare, the more comfortable and successful you will be interviewing.
Practice answering interview questions and practice your responses to the typical job interview questions and answers most employers ask. Think of concrete examples you can use to highlight your skills. Providing evidence of your successes is a great way to promote your candidacy. Also have a list of your own questions to ask the employer ready.
Do your homework about the employer and the industry so you are ready for the question What do you know about this company? Know the interviewer's name and use it during the job interview. If you're not sure of the name, call and ask prior to the interview. Try to relate what you have learned about the company when answering questions.
Make sure your interview attire is neat, tidy and appropriate for the type of firm you are interviewing with. Bring a nice portfolio with copies of your resume. Include a pen and paper for note taking.
Be on time for the interview. On time means five to ten minutes early. If need be, take some time to drive to the interview location ahead of time so you know exactly where you are going and how long it will take to get there. Here's more on preparing for an interview.
During the job interview try to relax and stay as calm possible. Remember that your body language says as much about you as your answers to the questions. Proper preparation will allow you to exude confidence. Take a moment to regroup. Maintain eye contact with the interviewer. Listen to the entire question (active listening) before you answer and pay attention - you will be embarrassed if you forget the question. Check out these tips for avoiding job interview stress to help stay calm. Also review our interview tips for introverts.
Try to relate what you know about the company when answering questions.  When discussing your career accomplishments match them to what the company is looking for. Use examples from your research when answering questions, “I noticed that when you implemented a new software system last year, your customer satisfaction ratings improved dramatically. I am well versed in the latest technologies from my experience with developing software at ABC, and appreciate a company who strives to be a leader in its industry.” Here's how to make a match between your expertise and the company's requirements.
Always follow-up with a thank you note reiterating your interest in the position. You can also include any details you may have forgotten to mention during your interview. If you interview with multiple people send each one a personal thank you note. Send your thank you note (email is fine) within 24 hours of your interview.

Cory in the House is a television show, which aired on the Disney Channel from January 12, 2007 to September 12, 2008 and was a spin-off from the Disney show That's So Raven. The show focuses on Cory Baxter, who moves from San Francisco, California to Washington, D.C. with his father, after Victor Baxter gets a new job in the White House as the official head chef. The series marks a Disney Channel first, as it is the channel's first spin-off. This is also the only Disney Channel spin-off series to be broadcast in standard definition for the entire length of the show. Reruns of the series have not been produced on Disney Channel, or on Disney XD; however they continue to air on the Family channel in Canada. Raven-Symoné guest-starred, reprising her role as Raven Baxter in one episode. In 2014 Disney Channel started airing a weekly block called Disney Replay on Wednesdays nights, during which episodes of Cory in the House air alongside That's So Raven and Kim Possible, among others.

Ok, i've read some good reviews as much as i have read the bad reviews for this game. To start off NecroVision is a FPS set in the time period of world war 1. The game also uses the common mental toying all through the game. For example, you can walk into little dugouts where the soldiers slept and most of them are gassed so you go through stages where it becomes hard to see through the gas but when you complete whatever it is that you had to do you would find there was nothing in there. A great game of 2011 becomes frustrating in 2017.
I remember my feelings when I played this game long time ago. It was awesome. So much stuff to unlock, so much maps, so much gameplay time...
I saw Dungeon Defenders on discount and bought it for refreshing my memories.... and I got confused.
Dungeon Defenders is a mix of Tower Defense and Action games. It's also designed to play cooperative. You have a list of heroes for playing (4 for base game). Each heros is controlled like in third person action games. He can use melee attack, range attack and he can summon towers. Each hero has different types of towers. For example, Warrior uses traps which activates when enemies step in. Monk has aura towers. It covers a certain area with magic sphere.  When enemy is inside of thsi area he got aura effect (slow, damage or etc..).
You pick a mission. Each mission can be played solo or with up to 3 friends. Note, all missions designed as co-op missions, because they have a lot of entry points. So it's kinda difficult to play this game alone. Enemies come, you kill them, you get mana, you summon new towers, next way comes and etc. Usual TD gameplay but with a hero.
By killing enemies and completing levels you get experience for you hero and gold for equipment. After you reach new level up, you can spend Skill Points on improvements of your hero or making your towers stronger. There are a lot of hero levels and different items (but they are kinda all the same), difficult items. So you can spend a lot of time playing this game.
So, why do I give this game a negative review?
The game become outdated in 2017. It's not fun to play solo, but severs are empty. For 2 hours I have seen only 1 man of 85 level. The main gameplay is boring in 2017. It wasn't fun for me to run around the map and click left button of the mouse. The game which was Hero Defense for me in 2011 now become Clicker & Runner.
The difficulties are set. Enemies on Normal have 65 hp. Doesn't matter you play alone or in party of 4. But the same enemy of hard has 650 hp. So Normal is too easy, but hard is too hard. You need a teammate, but almost noone plays it anymore.
Also, base options are limited. You need to buy a lot of Stuff as DLC if you want fully play the game. It's kinda strange, especiall when the game is pretty old now.
Pros
- Innovative mix of genres
- A lot of stuff to unlock. More than 100 hours of gameplay
- Nice graphics even in 2017
Cons
- Very limited hero fight options
- Not fun to play solo. Low online find proper teammate. (When I played it was only 2 :D )
- Requires a lot of running around the map (collecting mana and opening chests)
- If you want to try different class, you need to play from the beginning and level up him (like in MMORPG games)
- All missions are kinda the same
- Base options are limited. New classes, maps, items are purchasable as DLC. Prices for 7 years old game are kinda expensive
There are a lot of reasons to not recommend this game. The only situation I can recommend it, if you have a 1-3 friends right now and you want to play co-op TD game. If you are alone, try Orc Must Die or 2th part of DD or other TD games. It's not pleasant to play DD solo in 2017, I assure you.

A friend and I bought this game to play multiplayer and had a properly horrible experience. This is a half-finished game and it should not be sold as a completed product. We did not try the single-player mode but my understanding is that there is no difference other than being alone on the map rather than with multiple players.
The game does have a tutorial to introduce you to the game, however it is woefully inadequate and leaves out some of the major mechanics of the game. This, in addition to the game not having ANY tooltips or visual indications on key objects makes for a rough experience. Or a steep learning curve if you wish. For example, it is not possible to determine the rewards of a quest, the difficulty of the same or the consequence of attacking an enemy or accepting “an encounter” until it is all over and done and you are presented with the result. Like your sunk ship or the loss/gain of reputation and/or resources.
Furthermore, views and panels such as reputation, open quests or owned assets are only available under certain conditions leaving you wondering and chasing back and forth looking for the information you would expect to be easily and continuously available at your leisure.
All this might have been overlooked if the game, once you become familiar with it worked reliably and was fun. It does not and is not. We suffered from already completed quest being offered repeatedly and if accepted promptly breaking, leaving you with no chance to complete or get rid of them. Quest events related to completed quests (quest reward collected and no longer in quest log) did not stop triggering causing all kinds of ridiculous situations where the game either became trivial, or impossibly hard at random.
And the only way to recover when you eventually succumb to the bugs and unfortunate mechanics is to go into “settings” (yes, where you change resolution and sound volume) and find a button labelled “reset game progress” which will allow you to start over. It took quite some time to find this misplaced function.
As if that was not enough, we were repeatedly disconnected without warning or indication other than that we eventually noticed we could no longer see each other on the world map.
So, the final verdict is: If you want a “Ships and Pirates” game, you should go for something else. E.g. “Port Royal 3” that even with its own short comings and faults works as intended, is enjoyable and reliable. This is a poor experience that will leave you unsatisfied and annoyed.
“No, No, No!” to quote a phrase.
Best regards,
DeAurion

There are many critiques about this game, ranging from comments like "THIS IS A DIABLO 2 RIPOFF!!" to "It's respectably unique in its own way."  In my own opinion, I definitely choose the middle.  Indubitably, this game is a derivative from Diablo 2 because many people do not realize that a few creators of this game were the original designers of Diablo 2, thus it should only make sense that this game is much similar to D2.  From my perspective, Torchlight is rich in color and original in some aspects such as merging the powers of a nercromancer and elementalist from D2 into one being: the alchemist.  While the story seems to build of it's own foundation, the gameplay is painfully like D2, making it unoriginal.  But if we really think about games these days, aren't they mostly built off of other games?  Overall, Torchlight is fun and creative in its own sense, but lacks originality in gameplay and graphic features.  Thus, I give this game a 7.3 (C-).
Signing out,

Glorkian Warrior wasn't remotely high on my wishlist, as somebody who tends to wishlist any decent shoot em up on Steam, and the only reasons I have it is because of a Very Positive Steam rating and because I was looking for very cheap games to get an extra Trading card during the 2016 Winter Steam sale. I decided to give it an install since it was a small file among the many cheap games I bought.
I honestly wasn't into the "Trying too hard to be funny" type of comedy I expected from the save devs as Potatoman and Dino Run, but upon play I becamed charmed by its handrawn appearance, silly cutscenes between game sessions, and cute sound effects including children announcing your weapon pickups - thankfully, it wasn't obnoxious at all. I saw no overzelous use of it's cartoonish them, except for the fact that you have to sit through the silly dialogue (which honestly didn't make me laugh, but it certainly wasn't bad at all), but you can skip to the next line quickly.
It plays much like Galaga - enemies fly in from the top and sides with various formation and occasionally will try to kamikaze attack the player. The player is always automatically shooting and can also jump (with air control) to dodge enemies and slight bullet hell patterns. Enemies occasionally drop different weapons which are effective, but whelming at best, and will slowly run out of energy. This energy can be partially refilled with crackers dropped regularly from enemies, which also count as credits that eventually unlocks minor mechanics such as bouncable basketballs or Tetris blocks during bonus waves. The enemy waves are randomly generated, and occasinally their are boss waves, bonus waves, or some weird wave including a strange giant head flying or bouncing around spewing semi-nonsensical, humorous quotes.
That's really it for the gameplay, but it is fairly easy to die, which the game expects unless you play very well. Like some recent roguelites, there is long term progression though the credit system I mentioned before, so you can play a few rounds and comeback later to make progress. My only complaint is that maybe the hitbox is too big for the bullet hell moments, but maybe I just need to GIT GUD. You can also get the OST seperately from Bandcamp if you wish.

To all those comparing this to Nuclear throne, Please stop.
This game is totally different and its really good but so different.
The only similarities are the details and bullets.
So now for the Actual Review.
Vintage Year , is a Rogue-like Topdown shooter, that relies on speed, Strategy, and stealth.
Your object is to clear the room to lock the door to the next level, Killing those enemies with your Guns.
( yes the gun system is similar to nuclear throne ) As in you can carry 2 guns and switch between them, there are Heavy and light weapons and explosives and melee weapons.
Killing Enemies and collecting ammo and weapons is fun : ), You gotta make every shot count to not run out of bullets and get stuck.
The game is always as dark as it looks in screenshots, you can place a limited amount of torches to light a small area ( they refresh after every level ).
After every few levels you gain 1 point , and can choose between 4 perks , and each of those perks can be upgraded once.
You have the ability to dash ( Although i'm not quite found of it ) But its useful to escape fights and dodge bullets.
Collect Corks, which is the game's currency , to use it to unlock new characters and customize your appearance which is a cool thing to have in a game like this , you can even change how your torch look like by buying new things in the store ( Dont confuse what i just said by thinking this game has micro transition , no it dont have it : \ just wanna make sure you get that )
Each character has its own passive effect, Such as +2hp or life steal, and 7 Extra passive effects that you can choose only one from, 3 starts unlocked and the other 4 you have to unlock yourself using Corks ( the game's currency )
The game is fairly difficult, cant say its too hard, cant call it easy, it categorizes between those 2.
Random generated levels, with traps, different enemies, chests, loots, secrets, and fun stuff to do all around, Each level is a bit small, Doesn't require much time to finish, but if you want to survive the game you'd need to do it carefully and not take much hits, the enemies are a bit trickery they move suddenly and shoot at you and they are not that easy to avoid.
I like how dark the game is, Forcing you to move slowly and not to rush into enemies, placing lights, observing your surroundings, The details and lighting are nice, the bullet effects and sounds are good, theres a spooky feeling to a game, i wouldn't call it horror not at all just ..spooky : ).
The boss fights proven to be fun, they are something that you don't see everyday, needs a good strategy and timing, and challenging to a certain level.
The soundtrack i'm not that into it, it gives the game this spooky factor yes, but it does not feel right for the game, i mean most of it is good but there are some parts that just doesn't feel good for it ( in my own opinion )
Edit : 1/16/2015 The dev was awesome enough to edit the controls , making E instead of The annoying Enter button, So the game is WASD , Mouse , and E to open doors and chests and in menu.
Story mode : Choose a character , and keep on playing from level to level to reach the ending ( not gonna spoil )
Battle mode : Basically a survival mode, you keep getting ammo and enemies spawning and well you kill them and see the highest score you can get ( Also can be used to gather corks ).
Kinda bums me out that the game has no Achievements, It would take time to unlock all characters and finish the game but achievements would give you a higher reason to go with it and to 100% the entire game.
Summing it all up as Pros and Cons
1 - Good style, using tactics and stealth, in this dark atmosphere instead of the usual ( Rush and kill sh*t ).
2 - Nice art in the game, pixelated with a good touch.
3 - A load of weapons to find , and characters to unlock, and enemies to kill, ( and 2 game modes <story> <battle> )
4 - Good effects and animations, Awesome level design, Easily Addictive type of Gameplay.
5 - Leveling up, venturing deeper, fighting bosses, surviving traps, a good challenge.
6 - Supports my monitor's resolution and runs on 60 fps.
7 - Cheap price, that brings a good amount of game time.
1 - Having no achievements or leaderboards for (Battle) mode.
2 - The Dash ability I don't like, because its used with the button Shift, and you need to be walking to dash and sometimes you'd need to do it quickly and you cant just choose a direction and just dash, and after you do there is indicator showing you when you can dash again , you just need to memorize the timing, and sometimes the character just wont dash unless i walk for a while.
TL:DR
"A very good rogue-like game for that price ? hell yes you should get it, has a dark atmosphere to it , use your stealth and strategy to conquer monsters and reach the final level in this randomly generated game" -

In a nutshell - Nuclear Throne's gameplay (at a slightly slower pace) + Cthulhu Mythosesque atmosphere + persistant unlocks = a light romp best enjoyed in short bursts.
Standard top-down shooter with an eery atmosphere, intensified by your need to put down candles in order to see your foes (which, by the way, you have a limited number of). You start off with four characters (my favorite giving a heavily increased rate of fire) and unlock the rest, either by completing hidden objectives or buying them at the shop. Additionally, you can unlock starting spells, which operate as a single and constant perk for the entire run.
Weapons wise, you're given a variety ranging from your standard pew-pew pistol to the more creative volcano cannon to get the job done. If you happen to pulp something particularly hard, character-specific flavor text will pop over their corpse (if you're playing as the Bear, it just goes "rawr" when someone is turned inside out).
I've got minimal playtime, yes, but I'm sure the game will keep me occupied for fifteen minute intervals for quite some time. It does a very good job of dangling the carrot of progression over your head to keep you moving along, while not forcing significant investments of time in one go. A very good example of a touch-and-go roguelite shooter.

There's no trick to this game. It is what it looks like. It's a roguelike top down shooter. The core gameplay is intense and quick, but not overwhelming like Nuclear Throne is. No random perks, the same perk tree every time. Random guns but every gun generally does the same damage as every other gun in its class. No shop. Ongoing currency just unlocks characters with slightly different perks. It plays lightning quick. The final act is a huge difficulty ramp though but it's still quite doable compared to other roguelike action games. Hell, the design is solid enough it could almost pass for a real arcade game rather than yet another roguelike. The pure shooting and dodging is satisfying. A nice relaxing game worth the cost.
It's got a more measured pace and tighter balancing than Nuclear Throne and I think that's for the best at the cost of NT's sheer love of random chaos.

The huge enemy variety and the random power-ups are what make this game great. You never know what's going to come next and how best to deal with it given the power-ups on offer at that point. The short cut-scenes in-between each level allow you to catch your breath before the next onslaught and the achievement system gives you a goal to aim towards.
Even after completing 100% of the achievements though, this game is still fun to go back to for a quick blast whenever you have a spare few minutes. I'd definitely recommend this to anyone who enjoys 2D shooters and is looking for something just a little bit different.

A very curious one. This is basically a Duke Nukem 3D MOD for people who take war far too seriously.
I am not one of those people.
I'd never have even heard of this MOD if it weren't for eDuke32 - I wonder if perhaps some of the same developers worked on it. Actually, I don't think I should call it a MOD as it's a standalone game which doesn't require Duke to play. BUT - it's not quite a Total Conversion as there are still some elements of Duke's art and SFX in Nam.
But yeah. It's a drab, deadly serious attempt at recreating the Vietnam war experience in the Build engine. It's playable, but it's VERY difficult - downright unfair at times. Perhaps that's the idea. I don't know. I like Duke because of it's hyper-realism. I don't buy games to simulate real life. That's what real life is for. And war is an element of real life I certainly don't want to experience.
If you do... then go for it. Knock yourself out. But I'm sure there are better war games out there.
