Final Fantasy XIII was originally released on both the Playstation 3 and Xbox 360 in 2009/2010 and brought Final Fantasy to that generation of consoles. The game and its subsequent sequels offer some of the greatest visuals, original music, and engaging battle systems that builds off previous games in the series' successes.
FFXIII serves as the introduction to the world and people of Cocoon, led by the "divine" Sanctum Fal'Cie, and whom are afraid of the world of Pulse that lies beneath their floating paradise. Lightning Farron is a sergeant in the Bodhum Regiment of the Guardian Corps whose life is changed when she is branded along with five others as a l'cie, a slave to a Fal'cie from Pulse tasked with the very destruction of her home. As she comes to terms with her fate of either fulfilling her 'Focus' or becoming an undying monster, she and her new companions are hunted by the military and hated by civilians. The story is a dramatic tale of six people that must put beside thier anger, fears, and despair, and make a choice...
Final Fantasy XIII is, like many other games in the series, one that demands some time to complete: Roughly 40 - 50 hours. Get ready to spend a week or so with this one. It is also a game that departs from many series staples, like exploring through towns and engaging in side quests. This means that the biggest draws for the game are its story and combat systems, which fortunately(in my opinion) get passing marks. The combat system in this game is called the 'Command Synergy Battle' system. Throughout the battle, you are in command of one character, the party leader, and the other characters in your group are operated by a surprisingly iintelligent A.I. that takes the best course of action in battle based on their selected roles and known enemy stats/weaknesses. There are six "classes" in the game: Commando, Ravager(magic attacker), Medic, Synergist(enhancing abilities), Sabeteur(enfeebling), and Sentinel(tank). Characters can develop their stats and abilities in the Crystarium by expending Crystal Points earned after the end of battles. Battles progress by switiching 'paradigms', or role combinations to best take advantage of the situation. Should you press the attack with a pair or ravagers and a commando to build up chain gauges? Should you put a sentinel on the field to soak damage while a synergist enhances your attacks? The choices are up to you as you try to weaken and 'stagger' enemies to submission. Trying to gain high battle ratings through skillful use of the paradigm system is surprisingly engaging.
A grand portion of the game is spent "on the run" from the military, and this informs a lot of the exploration segments. So much in fact that the game has been called(rightfully so) very linear up to a certain point where it opens up tremendously. Fortunately there's never a dull moment in the story, and many times I've found myself needing a break just because of how intense the story and battles can get. This game can be hard, make no mistake. If you aren't careful in certain conflicts, enemies can get some pretty quick hits that'll have you retrying quite a few times.
After originally having played Final Fantasy XIII on the Xbox 360 back in 2010, I've loved the the series even more with each new entry. The mythos behind Gran Pulse, Cocoon, and the beings that inhabit them create a dramatic story filled with great characters facing immense tragedy while trying to escape their fate as pawns in a Chess game being played by beings beyond their comprehension for reasons even more unclear. When it originally released, nobody was aware there would be a series of sequels released later, so a lot of the plot points seemed to be very hazy without the context provided by future games. I feel that this has become less of a problem with the release of Final Fantasy XIII-2(my personal favorite. Give this RPG a shot. It's different by a lot of standards, but I feel that it is an entry in the series with a lot of merits.

I do believe this game now sits in my #1 spot as best metroidvania game out there.
First off, the art direction is top notch. Reminds me of the games from The Behemoth, but a bit more refined visually. Character design is fantastic, sporting a very large variety of minions to slay, and bosses to fight. There's  many NPCs you'll run into, and all beings you come across stand out on their own, with very little cases of copy and paste here.
The game's environment is extremely expansive. I was not at all expecting to spend 49 hours playing a 2D metroidvania title, but here I am.
Hand's sweaty, feet sweaty, mom's spaghetti this game is hard! The difficulty generally scales well, starting off as almost a little too easy to controller chucking, vitriol-spewing hard  in the mid to late game.  This game does not hold your hand at all. It's extremely easy to get lost and not know what to do, which for some is a mark against it.
Gameplay is superb. Control is very tight. Hollow Knight is a paradigm for movement and combat and in a 2d platformer.
My criticisms are minor. I think I would have enjoyed the early game a bit more if it was a tad more clear where to go. I can see some players giving up in frustration given no direction inside one of the most expansive labyrinths of world in a 2D game. I know some hardcore players would be against a navigation mechanic but such a feature could easily be disabled in options.
The biomes bled together a little too easily. I wish they were a bit more defined from each other; fog canyon and city of tears are good examples of biome diversity. Furthermore, the game visually is a little too monochrome at times.
I tend to scrutinize the soundtrack in this genre given how high Super Metroid set the bar. I wasn't a fan of the score in this game. It wasn't bad but wasn't that memorable.
Criticisms aside, this is one of my favourite games of 2017, if not my favourite this year. If you favour metroidvania games, this game is well worth it even at full price.

Do you like Smash Bros.?
If you answered yes, you will love this game.
If you answered no, what the hell's wrong with you?

First and foremost, it's an extremely bare-bones port. No graphical options, no resolution changes, no nothing. You're getting a direct copy of the PS3 version that just happens to run on your PC, although it does come with the Japanese voice acting, the difficulty setting option from the JP re-release, and it runs at 60 FPS instead of 30 like the console versions. Also, the required specs (and the recommended ones, for that matter) are really low and you'd need a pretty terrible machine to not be able to run it.
Aside from that, it's FF13 and you probably already know whether or not you're going to like it. On one hand, it still looks gorgeous even for being 5 years old, the music is pretty good, and the combat's fun. On the other, the story is awful, the pacing is terrible, and it's excessively linear, so if that matters to you stay far away. I like it, and for $16 you could do a hell of a lot worse. To be fair, you could do a hell of a lot better too, but I think it's at least worth giving it a shot.

Like Smash? Then this game is for you, simply put.
By competitive players for competitive players. Though there certainly are options for the casual crowd, this game is largely designed for the level of depth, speed and fun brought forth by Super Smash Bros. 64 and Melee, tailored to boast the same accessibility of Sm4sh, with unique style and flair to give RoA its own identity.
In Rivals, gameplay guides character design. Since the cast is entirely original (with some animations borrowed from Smash) the devs have the freedom to keep the roster fit for specific playstyles. The goal for RoA was to create something more aggressive, and to accomplish that they threw out the concepts of shields, grabs, and ledge camping. Instead, we got parries, which are basically "power shields" that stun the enemy so you can punish them, and a very, very diverse combo game for all characters.
A lot of familiar mechanics show up in RoA: wavedash/land, dash dance, reverse aerial rush, and a slew of new advanced tech for the community to discover. Each character, based on one of four elements, has their own tech and traits that make them distinct. Zetterburn can light his enemies on fire for a DoT effect and burning enemies take increased knockback from strong (smash) attacks. Kragg, of the earth element, can change the stage using his up and neutral specials. He can create a giant rock pillar to wherever he is located, and pull a big, stone block to place and block enemy movement temporarily, or use as a projectile. Now apply that sort of diversity and clever design to the 6 others.
The game's small roster bolsters its ability to remain focused and balanced. Dan has stated that the game is to be balanced around 1v1s, ensuring that all characters have the tools they need to deal with any of the others and dittos of themselves. He's been very receptive to feedback, which is fantastic and an absolute blessing for a competitive fighting game.
All in all, this game has been incredible even before its release. Controls are smooth, art is beautiful, music is engaging and catchy, characters are unique, deep, and interesting, online play is (usually) smooth, and overall Rivals of Aether makes for a great platform fighter either as an alternative or supplement to your Smash collection.

It is amazing how addictive this game is.  I have been playing Farming Simulator for several iterations (since 2009) and I was not sure what to expect when 2015 came about.  The jump from 2009 to 2011 was dramatic, but from 2011 to 2013 left me scratching my head.  Was 2015 going to be (essentially) another patch release?
The videos showing up from the Beta work were very encouraging and as the release date grew closer, my mind was made up that I would take the plunge.  Even if it was really just another incremental release, my desire to support the developers was solid.
The day arrived and purchase I did...and am happy to have the 2015 version!  The graphic improvement is solid as is the game play improvements.  Forestry...finally we can cut out the pesky trees that are in the way without using the Giants DF editor.  Worth the price right there, but wait...there is more!  It is the level of detail that starts to become apparent that caught me.  Dirty implements, tire tracks and the like.  All help create an even more immersive environment.
Aside from the tree cutting ability, the developers really seem to have listened and now one can “hire” a worker to fertilize crops.  The cruise control has been improved and now can be used more effectively when loading trailers.  There are a few more crops that are available as well that require specialized equipment for processing.  All in all, I find it to be a great “next step” in the franchise.
So far, I have only farmed in Bjornholm.  I own about a quarter of the fields and have silos prepared to burst.  I have not ventured to play on HARD level yet, but my next career will be there.  I have also refrained from modding the game excessively.  I have a few extra vehicles, but mostly I am playing it stock still.
If you are currently playing 2011 or 2013, this is well worth the price of admission.  If you have not playing any of the prior versions, but are interested...again worth the price IMHO.

Shadow Warrior is one hell of a good Single Player game!
The plot: You (a high ranked... assassin-type of guy) have the mission to find a sword. You find it, bring it to your boss, and suddenly hell brakes loose. Demons, skeletons, mafia [...] there are countless enemies to fight.
The story develops very nicely and keeps you entertained - not only because of the sarcastic spirit that is following you around. You will want to know what happens next after each chapter!
The gameplay is more or less always the same. Different areas, different enemies, different ways to beat them. But, your arsenal of skills and weapons, plus the various enviromental extras do make each fight different. It kept me entertained for 10 hours straight! (excluded sleeping pause). By defeating enemies you will be able to learn new skills, upgrade existing ones, upgrade weapons and buy bonuses such as extra money, the ability to pick up specific demon heads as weapons etc.
There were only 2 level were i felt annoyed, but that was only because they were incredibly long and had repetetive fights. Overall the gameplay is very good!
Music & graphics are nice as well, i didn't have any complaints whatsoever.
After completing the game you will be offered to restart with all your existing upgrades - a good thing, but it also has a downside. You will have to play the game again. Which is, at least for me, a nono right now, because i do not think i would enjoy slaughtering all those demons again, just for the sake of completing all achievements.
Overall? Recommended! It is a very fun fps shooter / sword fighting game that can keep you very busy. The countless secrets and various easter eggs just add to the fun. Beware the bunny of doom.

what I like about the game:
it gives a new take on the life of 47, memorable movie-like moments that make you realize just how unstoppable and dangerous he is. yeah, the other games show how good an assassin he is, but he seemed halllow and robot-like to me, this one made me realize just how dangerous he is and how I one should not mess with him. and answer many questions I was left from previous games about the character itself.
plus the graphics of course.
what I didn't like about the game:
the instinct thing makes the game too easy, the removal of the syringes and agency support (customization, briefings, delivering weapons etc...), the broken disguise system (although I always liked to complete contracts with the original suit in previous games) and the fact that it wasn't a "hitman" game, more like "agent 47" game, let me explain, when I say "hitman" game, I mean hits, assassinations, targets that were only a person someone payed you to kill, and when I said it was more of a "agent 47" game, because it focuses on this chapter of the character's life and on making him a believable-existent-breathing-person rather than an avatar.
all the running away and hiding goddammit!! isn't he supposed to blend?
bottomline:
in order to enjoy this game you have to clear any expectation you were left from the previous games and board it as of it was completely new game, this one it's a chapter apart from the other hitman games, felt more like a movie about the character 47 going through a chapter in his life than a game about an assassin performing hits.
personally I'm satisfied with the game, after playing all the other games (blood money being my favorite) I was left with this crave to know more about 47, how he was and what he would do on certain situations because to me I felt 47 was very empty, like a robot that just sits in a cryogenic chamber doing absolutely nothing until Diana called with a contract. a "thing" was not able to talk to people, empathize, drive a car, or go to the store to get some tissue and bandages.
would I recommend?
to newbies, yes, enjoy this game, then play the previous ones immediately.
to fans, yes, but I advice dropping any expectation of this being like previous games and take more like a game about a chapter in 47's life, than a game about a Hitman doing hits.

This game has a neat premise though it is fatally -- unplayably -- flawed.
I really want to like it.  It has a nifty, but simple, premise.  I like the idea of marrying the concept of Pong with a rhythm style music game -- each successful hit adding in part of the song being played currently.  It feeds into the desire to flesh the music out, and really is one of the only ways to give feedback to the player that they're doing well.
However....  Retro design should not ignore more modern advance.  Fake difficulty, such as what might be found on the old NES, should never be acceptable in modern games.  Yet that's exactly what happens here.  Gaijin settles for screen-overpowering strobe flashes and moving backgrounds to, many times, completely obscure the player targets for half (or more) of the screen.  There may be other fake difficulty "features" in BEAT, but my eyes were thoroughly blinded halfway through the first song.  (I'm still blinking away the damned afterimages from the photography-quality strobing my eyes took in only about 20min of playing.)
Gaijin could have, and arguably should have, incorporated an adaptive difficulty to BEAT.  Something to randomize the patterns of the blocks or speed up the attack, should the player hit certain streak thresholds.  Or narrow the width or increase the height of the screen to reduce reaction time or increase the distance the paddle may have to travel.
At the very minimum, they could have taken a page from Beat Hazard's playbook and put in a control to reduce the intensity of the strobes.  That would deal with the whole "I like being able to see things when I'm done playing." issue.

Definitely containing stylistic inspirations of the classic Galaga arcade game, this was an enjoyable arcade game with many levels, aliens, and bonuses. Blowing up aliens quickly earns you more perks -- double lasers, fireballs, glorf gun, and such -- and also causes the aliens to drop "crackers" which you collect.  Crackers advance you to the next bonus's such as different graphics or enabling new perks that can drop that help you shoot more aliens.
While there is no 'end' to the game, I thoroughly enjoyed my 3.1 hours to unlock the last perk.  One unique thing that makes this different than a usual arcade game where you start over from the same beginning every time, this behaves more like where each game is a "Continue" of the previous game, but not exactly.

I selected a server and created a berserk class character. I met many people in my adventures until I reached level 16 and got bored. Berserk simply wasn't quite cutting it despite having a blade the size of a small skyscraper. Instead I made a priest. This time things were different. I felt like my life actually had a purpose now. From the very 1st level I was overwhelmed with my self-importance. I grabbed my scepter and rushed into the world.
I tamed my first mount - a unicorn-like horse. Probably imported from China. It was all fun and games until I was sent to a temple infested with spiders. What do I have to do? Clean it out. This is not the job I applied for. Spiders are nasty, I don't see why I have to touch them with my pure god magic. Why not let some dirty berserk take care of them instead? After that I travel on, slaying innocent fairies and stealing their water for some nefarious reasons.
I reach the capital city and king himself wants me to visit him. We chill, he tells me about his issues in bed with the queen, you see, she isn't happy. Not even best healing magic can help him. Being unable to help him, I head out for more outskirts action.
The pinnacle of my adventure was when I reached a village populated by werewolves. Werewolf! Werewolf? There. What? There, wolf. Afterwards I move further into the world, killing all. At one point I reach a Villa full of posh vampires. The very moment I entered the gate I saw green gardens full of nobility vampires enjoying their tea and discussing latest court gossip. Too bad for them, I had to slay them nonstop until they stopped moving.
Finally I go to a volcanic area. At this moment I knew I was gonna get my first dragon. There was only 1 issue. I could not until I was level 20. Allegedly if I was under 20, it did not prove my loyalty to the kingdom, making me unworthy of taming a dragon. I was stuck for 30 minutes doing same quest of killing turtles and harvesting their soul for the devil him self until I finally got enough turtle slaying experience to reach 20. The quester tells me "go into this fiery hole and catch that dragon". And so I do. I enter the tunnel and reach the dragon and mount it with ease.
I ended my adventure by using the megaphone to shout to the world, only to receive tons of harassing whispers in return. Did not expect to be bullied like that.
In later levels you start to feel weak as a priest, but that is not a bad thing as it adds additional challenge and requires you to think strategically to defeat your foes. It is not often you have to do that in the world segments of many MMOs.

Based on a graphic novel: The game is based upon James Kolchaka’s graphic novel ‘The Glorkian Warrior Delivers a Pizza.’ Kolchaka is the first resident of Vermont, a state in the New England region of the United States, to win the Laureate for best cartoonist. He is a prolific artist in the world of comics having written and illustrated for MARVEL with his ‘Hulk Vs. The Rain‘ short that was originally published in black and white in an unauthorized alternative magazine, he is the creator of ‘Monkey Vs. Robot’ and ‘Impy and Wormer’ which was featured in Nickelodeon Magazine. In 2012 he won the Eisner Award for Dragon Puncher 2: Dragon Puncher Island. Kolchaka is a very talented man with his talents spreading across multiple forms of the entertainment industry. He is also a rock musician fronting his own band, James Kolchaka Superstar, who have released nine albums. His artistry in the game is outstanding – everything looks precisely the way that you would want it to and is very easy on the eyes. It adds a tremendous amount of character to the game. It’s some of the best art work that I’ve seen in this genre of indie gaming.
Challenging play: Glorkian Warrior offers some of the most challenging game play that I’ve come across in some time. The mixture of Galaga-style shoot-em-up with platformer style gameplay works marvelously well. Deaths and hits generally always feel fair to me which is of vital importance. However,  I do take issue when the game expects you to jump and then has enemies flying down at you that are unavoidable. This is the only let down in what is a vitally important component.  Game play consists of constantly moving around the bottom of the screen while shooting – automatically – at enemies above and avoiding traps that are next to you constantly trying to kill you. The amount of power ups and their variety is one of the game’s key strengths.
Suitable for all ages: As the original title was intended for a younger audience the game is definitely accessible to younger players if you don’t mind them blasting space ships out of the sky. Although I do not have any children of my own I do feel that I am very education conscious. There is nothing here stopping children from playing the game. In fact, some of the video games that I played in my early education in school would have been much more of a concern than this. It’s animated violence and children would see much more violent things in their cartoons.
Good humor: What I loved perhaps most of all in Glorkian Warrior was the use of comedy. Again, it is something that all ages and audiences can appreciate but adults should not find too young. There’s a lot to like in the way that the story is told that will engage older gamers. It is good humor that will have you laughing when you’re not too busy concentrating on advancing further into the game.
Super Addictive: Glorkian Warrior is the very definition of a ‘one more turn’ game for me. This is accomplished through the superb unlock system in the game.  Every time you unlock something the next unlock feels as though its only a game or two away until you advance deep into the mid and latter parts of the game and only then does it begin to take considerable effort to get to the next unlock. Of course, by then, Pixeljam hope that you have improved sufficiently that the next unlock still doesn’t feel that far away. Unlocks include new power ups, birthday cakes, basketballs, ceramic cats – that the developer owns – and actual short comics that are a pleasure to read.
I thoroughly enjoyed Glorkian Warrior – Trial of the Glork. It’s a perfectly addictive retro-style shoot’em up cross platformer that will keep you playing. I would recommend it to everyone and in my opinion is Pixeljam’s best game to date.

Lots of people here are saying its bad and too similar to Civilization V.
I completely disagree.
This game offers a refreshing take on the Civilization series. I've loved previous Civilization titles, and although this game runs on the Civilization V engine, things are very different.
The tech web makes the game different each time. Rather than researching the next step to victory, you research what your civilization needs, whether that is food, science, culture or production. You choose the path and this makes your play far more individual than to any others.
Affinities are perhaps to some of you, a reboot of your ideology in Civ V, but if you just take the time to look a little closer. They are actually completely different ways of play, while ideologies gave you bonuses for production or perhaps a 10% science boost. Your affinity changes your military, your cities, what you can actually build and what resources its useful to have. It also completely changes your play style because you need to achieve a different victory.
Virtues, admittedly they do look a lot like social policies, but, again, delving deeper you'll see that they provide much better bonuses and are much, much more diverse and more open to individual play. You will get bonuses for specializing, or diversifying. And ultimately, this is the sole purpose for culture, so it had to be powerful, which it is.
Diplomacy is much the same as Civ V, however, they've balanced your relationship with the AI with the new favors feature. You will gain and spend favors so that you can perhaps get repaid when you gave the Pan-Asians some gold when they hit hard times, rather than the AI never repaying as they did in Civ V.
The aliens, unlike the barbarians actually mean something late game, they will either help or hinder you. Perhaps if you choose Harmony as your affinity then you can call worms, and create loyal versions of the native creatures, perhaps if you choose supremacy, they will constantly try and wipe you off the planet, the point is, they are relevant late game, because unlike barbarians, which could never do even a little damage to a city, they are dangerous, and can wipe out an explorer instantly, right at the start of the game.
Quests are completely new and give you bonuses right throughout the game, they are useful and plentiful. They will offer you an opportunity to complete a series of tasks, in return for a reward, often you get the choice, in order to advance your civilization in the way that you need to. This creates another way to customize your civilization and get a different play style to your opponents and allies.
The orbital layer is something that is not to be overlooked, you can launch satellites to improve the land around, shoot lasers down on your foes, improve science, culture, energy, growth, production and more. These can provide a strategic advantage in battle (I find that an orbital laser above an enemy city can prove useful...) and they can provide other advantages such as increasing stats or even defending against spies and creating strategic resources.
All in all. Civilization Beyond Earth is more replayable, more fun and more individual than Civilization V. Yes, there are some features that are pretty much unchanged. But there are also some new features such as the orbital layer, there are some well improved features, such as technology and there are some things that work better in this game than they did in any other before. I think its polished and excellent. It exceeds Civilization V in my view, and that's saying something because Civilization V was frightfully epic.

As of right now I played for 3.7 frustrating hours and though I want to continue playing this game I honestly can't give it a thumbs up. The game itself is promising and has a very good chance to become one of the most enjoyable pirate games. But in the current state (1.03) the downsites are too prevelant to recommend this game to others. If you are interested in this game look for gameplay material on youtube and some reviews of game magazines. Look at the many cool stuff this game has to offer but also be aware of the annoyances (and especially if they are fixed/patched by the time you buy). As so much already highlighted to positive side of this game I will only list the game breakers for me.
CONS:
- boring, uninspiring and grindy trade mechanic (no price changes, find a good route and grind for money)
- boarding lacks any kind of inspiration. You can't do anything besides clicking a few icons a few times and watch your crew fight.
- lack of ingame explanation. As this is somewhat of a general topic I will focus on the boarding mechanic again. Other than a few lines in the tutorial missions the boarding mechanic will never be explained in any depth. You can shoot a enemy ship down to nearly zero crew and board with your fully manned ship and nevertheless loose the battle. There might be a logical sense behind the outcome of this fight but the game will give you no indications at all why you failed.
As I already mentioned there are for sure many positive sides to this game and I really hope the devs will pick up on the baddies and fix them. In conclusion, I would rate this game to be decent (not good, not bad) in the current state. If you like pirate games and feel like experimenting give it a try, the base price of 15€ isn't that much of a deal.

This is not a new game. This is not even a DLC. This is a poorly executed reskinned mod of a de-contented original Civ5. Gone are the city-states, replaced with stations that are useless after turn 50. Gone is the logically organized technology tree, replaced with simulataneously complex and shallow tech web. Gone is the unit levelling system, replaced with two options: +10% or instant heal. So what was retained? AI bugs, when AI badgers players about a station destoryed 300 turns ago. Illogical computer actions such as declaring a sudden war after 200 turns of alliance while clearly behind in miltary, only to ask for peace and offer a city and all available energy ten turns later. Now, what was added? Great, at a glance, espionage system that upon playthrough turns out to be a simple linear set of assignments. Establish network - syphon energy - steal technology, etc. Miasma that could have been a great gameplay innovation would it no be so unbalanced in favor of harmony affinity. Buggy affinity system that causes AI to attack me for 'forgetting how to be human' at level 18 of purity. Ridiculously over-buffed trade system, allowing for virtually unlimited energy (read: gold). Unbalanced tile improvements (terrascape at 6 maintenance, anyone?). Moronic worker AI (yes! Terrascape everything!). An finally, difficulty levels worthy of a 3 year old. In the end, this game is not worth $50. It is not worth $10. It's an amateur mod hastily put together, along with an admittedly great reskin. I have played every Civilization game to datre, and I am severely disappointed that Firaxis decided to go down the Call of Duty road. Rest In Peace, one of the greatest francises in gaming history. Long live balding budget cutters.

Summary: Beyond Earth is extremely similar to Civilisation 5, to the point of worrying consistency. However; it introduces several systems that work very well within the science fiction setting and has great potential for growth later on with possible updates and expansion packs.
Pros:
-The engine is far more stable than Civilisation 5 and doesn't have as nearly as many issues.
-The Affinity and Intrigue systems are especially interesting are interesting to play around with.
-The Techweb is far more unique and requires more thought than the linear path of Civ 5 in which all techs will eventually be unlocked.
Cons:
-The game feels like a copy of Brave New World with a sci-fi skin, it has only a few features that seperate it from Civ 5, noted above.
-The AI is still a weak point.
-The factions and leaders are less interesting, along with the quotes. This was a staple of the previous Civ games and it is disappointing to see it falter here.
In conclusion; Beyond Earth is a decent title but has little innovation over the previous entries although it has a few new mechanics.  I would recommend this if you enjoy 4X games and Science Fiction, although it may be better in the long-run to wait for the inevitable expansions that flesh out the gameplay as Gods and Kings/Brave New World did for Civ 5.

I do believe this game now sits in my #1 spot as best metroidvania game out there.
First off, the art direction is top notch. Reminds me of the games from The Behemoth, but a bit more refined visually. Character design is fantastic, sporting a very large variety of minions to slay, and bosses to fight. There's  many NPCs you'll run into, and all beings you come across stand out on their own, with very little cases of copy and paste here.
The game's environment is extremely expansive. I was not at all expecting to spend 49 hours playing a 2D metroidvania title, but here I am.
Hand's sweaty, feet sweaty, mom's spaghetti this game is hard! The difficulty generally scales well, starting off as almost a little too easy to controller chucking, vitriol-spewing hard  in the mid to late game.  This game does not hold your hand at all. It's extremely easy to get lost and not know what to do, which for some is a mark against it.
Gameplay is superb. Control is very tight. Hollow Knight is a paradigm for movement and combat and in a 2d platformer.
My criticisms are minor. I think I would have enjoyed the early game a bit more if it was a tad more clear where to go. I can see some players giving up in frustration given no direction inside one of the most expansive labyrinths of world in a 2D game. I know some hardcore players would be against a navigation mechanic but such a feature could easily be disabled in options.
The biomes bled together a little too easily. I wish they were a bit more defined from each other; fog canyon and city of tears are good examples of biome diversity. Furthermore, the game visually is a little too monochrome at times.
I tend to scrutinize the soundtrack in this genre given how high Super Metroid set the bar. I wasn't a fan of the score in this game. It wasn't bad but wasn't that memorable.
Criticisms aside, this is one of my favourite games of 2017, if not my favourite this year. If you favour metroidvania games, this game is well worth it even at full price.
The earlier issues were patched, now the game runs smooth, no crashing, and supports higher resolutions, although some effects are pixelated.

Like Smash? Then this game is for you, simply put.
By competitive players for competitive players. Though there certainly are options for the casual crowd, this game is largely designed for the level of depth, speed and fun brought forth by Super Smash Bros. 64 and Melee, tailored to boast the same accessibility of Sm4sh, with unique style and flair to give RoA its own identity.
In Rivals, gameplay guides character design. Since the cast is entirely original (with some animations borrowed from Smash) the devs have the freedom to keep the roster fit for specific playstyles. The goal for RoA was to create something more aggressive, and to accomplish that they threw out the concepts of shields, grabs, and ledge camping. Instead, we got parries, which are basically "power shields" that stun the enemy so you can punish them, and a very, very diverse combo game for all characters.
A lot of familiar mechanics show up in RoA: wavedash/land, dash dance, reverse aerial rush, and a slew of new advanced tech for the community to discover. Each character, based on one of four elements, has their own tech and traits that make them distinct. Zetterburn can light his enemies on fire for a DoT effect and burning enemies take increased knockback from strong (smash) attacks. Kragg, of the earth element, can change the stage using his up and neutral specials. He can create a giant rock pillar to wherever he is located, and pull a big, stone block to place and block enemy movement temporarily, or use as a projectile. Now apply that sort of diversity and clever design to the 6 others.
The game's small roster bolsters its ability to remain focused and balanced. Dan has stated that the game is to be balanced around 1v1s, ensuring that all characters have the tools they need to deal with any of the others and dittos of themselves. He's been very receptive to feedback, which is fantastic and an absolute blessing for a competitive fighting game.
All in all, this game has been incredible even before its release. Controls are smooth, art is beautiful, music is engaging and catchy, characters are unique, deep, and interesting, online play is (usually) smooth, and overall Rivals of Aether makes for a great platform fighter either as an alternative or supplement to your Smash collection.

If you're looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

BIT.TRIP BEAT is the first of the BIT.TRIP games, a rhythm game in which you play as the left paddle attempting to prevent any pixels from passing you, loosely based off Pong. The pixels (hereafter referred to as "beats") travel from the right side of the screen to the left, in time with the music. Some behave uniquely depending on their color, and the player's score increases depending on how many beats in a row they are able to hit. Once you've hit a certain number without having missed a certain number, you'll move into a higher "mode" which has flashier graphics and higher scoring. Similarly, once you've missed a certain number without having hit a certain number, you'll go to a lower "mode" with more plain graphics, eventually losing altogether.
It's an excellent game, but can be rather difficult at times - there are no checkpoints mid-song, so much of the game relies upon memorization of patterns, and being able to anticipate what is coming up next via the music. That being said, there is a visceral pleasure at completing a particularly difficult part sufficiently to allow you to proceed further in the level - if you enjoy rhythm games, this is one of the best and should not be missed.

The Bit.Trip games have a decent reputation in the indie scene. So what about this one?
Well "Beat" is basically the Bit.Trip style on pong. Its by no means a bad game, maybe even fun. But do I recommend someone to buy it or even play it?
Not really.
The gameplay is simple. Its pong. Sure, there's a twist - lots of things come flying toward you to avoid and there's powerups.
There's only four levels or so so you can beat the whole game within an hour or two.
When I played through it, it was fairly difficult at the end. Supposedly an easy mode has been added so that's definitely a plus.
There's no story, but the art is alright. The visuals look decent, but the backgrounds are somewhat distracting. The music, as expected in a Bit.Trip game, is pretty good. Probably the best part about this game.
Like other Bit.Trip games, its pretty well suited for PCs with no problems at all.
Its a decent game, but I don't think its worth playing unless you get it from an indie bundle.
There's plenty of other pong styled games that are more interesting and do the style much better.
Overall, an ok game but its not really worth your time unless you're a die-hard pong enthusiast or like collecting indie games.

Defy Gravity is a tiny little physics-based puzzle platformer in which you manipulate your movement through the creation of gravity and anti-gravity wells, allowing you to conquer assorted obstacles.
Almost everything about the game is somewhat reminiscent of the big days of browser-based flash games. Fairly generic music loops, non-existent story, simplistic art style, and a pretty short length compared to most games on Steam (30-60 minutes for a basic playthrough, or 90-120 minutes if you're including all achievements/hard mode). The concept's not too bad, but the puzzle design is somewhat repetitive and the difficulty progression is very uneven (the final supposed-to-be-climactic puzzle is actually one of the easiest rooms in the game).
Overall, there are plenty of worse ways to spend an hour or so. Defy Gravity is definitely worth the summer sale price of $0.29 - especially considering it comes with Steam Trading Cards which you can easily sell back for more than that. At full price, however, the cost is a bit steep for the paltry amount of content here. Grab it if it's on sale and you have a huge fetish for physics puzzles, or not at all.

Explanation of this review: the installation options allow for different languages for the game, and each version gives replayability.
English version: Great game! Set in the great land of England, and what I consider to be the canonical version of the Robin Hood story. No such thing? There is NOW! Original legend's one thing, but as far as a story goes, this is the best, I think. The gameplay is deep enough, and so is the story. Amusing, too!
German version: Great game! Set in... someplace, I guess. I'm still trying to figure that out myself. Since German makes everything sound so epic, expect adrenaline rushes. Any Nazi jokes and I'll stick your fingers in a meat grinder.
Spanish version: Great game! Set in the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly humorous land of Spangland, the hero Robin Hood with his friend the Sneaky Stutely, this adventure is packed with humour! Spanish is always funny. I'm almost constantly laughing when I play.
Overall: Since translation does not affect the story, the story is top notch in each iteration. Surprisingly, the voice acting is fantastic in ALL three of these versions (and hilarious in Spanish), the difficulty settings are also great. Easy is too easy, perfectly imbalanced for the kiddies. Normal is normal for once, and good for the average player. Hard is too difficult for most people, but good for pros, and nicely realistic in that BLACK ARCHERS SHOOT YOU FOURTEEN TIMES WITHIN HALF A SECOND if you let them. Perfect realism, these are elite troops after all
However, immersion broken with the RED CAVALRY. THEY SLIDE VIOLENTLY AT OBTUSE SIDEWAYS ANGLES AND SOMETIMES MOONWALK AT YOU WITH A FLAIL, OBLITERATING YOU AT JET SPEEDS WITHIN A FRACTION OF A SECOND AND BAT YOU A HOME RUN

Lets take a minute to consider this, ignoring the port, ignoring how awfully Square Enix botched the Job on the PC version and lets take a look the game for a second and ask ourselves a single question:
Is Final Fantasy XIII bad?
NO IT'S NOT! I don't understand the hate towards this game, i understand that it has awful flaws. The cosntant tunnel runs being the main gripe, but gameplay wise is it bad? No! the combat system is actually interesting, the issue with it is that it isn't fully realized, they had an idea but they didn't fully execute a team wide combat system for some reason, but despite that its still a very fun and interesting combat system.
As for the story, it isn't as conveluted as most people might think, the main problem here is that the names of the "Deities" are largely similar to what the Human Drones and "Branded" humans are, but despite that the backstory is actually quite unqiue! I love the world buliding, the locations, the general universe and its all quite exciting if you think about it.
The main downfall storywise is the likability of the characters; Snow is overly passionate, Hope is all a bit too whiney at the beginning before gaining his Edulon, Vanille always seems like an awkward mix of Postitive and Depressed. but I feel like most of the issue here is fixed through the Japanese Voice Acting, because they deliver the lines much more genuinely than the English counterparts that go full ham and not enough ability to tone it down!
Besides what I see as the worst game in the Franchise - Final Fantasy VIII - comparitively its so much better, but I still see hoards of people give VIII a glowing score beause ♥♥♥♥ing nostalgia!
but its not much different to Final Fantasy X as a game now is it? I mean they're similar yet they both are hold in different acclaim and I think there is a reason.
Endless Corridors. Check. A plotline involving the destruction of a civilization through the transformation into said destructive force (Ragnarok and SIN). Check.  Character with a Shadey past and Moody demeanor (Lightning/Auron). Check. Token happy Ethnic guy with troubled past (Sazh/Wakka). Check. Scared healer needing the support of everyone who finds their feet (Yuna/Hope). Check.
Its scary how similar the two games and I think thats partially the reason.
but I feel like the main hate of this game is beacuse Square are realizing Final Fantasy is the same game year after year, and they've wanted to change that since XII/Kingdom Hearts.
So this was the first step in an entirely new direction. They want to keep the old souls happy, so they made Bravely Default, but they've come to realise that Final Fantasy can't be the same game anymore, they want it to be more of a cinematic experience.
Final Fantasy XV looks like the prime example of that.
edit: The PC version suffered from awful porting with no graphics options.
They somehow vamped up the graphics so much that when it turned it on after the update I literally♥♥♥♥♥♥myself after seeing the difference.
it looks so. much. ♥♥♥♥ing. better. than. the. console. counterparts.

Is it good?
Yes.
Is it GOTY good?
No. It's good, has moments, but it's not going to hold lengthy replay value of Civ V+add-ons until some massive DLC shows up.
Is it Alpha Centauri 2?
Hell no. The factions and leaders are much blander, and there's plenty of future stuff (terraforming! aquatic bases!) missing. Still, SMAC had its long boring stretches too. The game lacks a planetary government body, so the intrigue of that (plus a rare political victory) is missing.
Does it feel like Civ V DLC (the big packages, not the one-or-two civ packets)?
Unfortunately, yes. It's professionally slick and expansive, but it still feels like Civ V. A good expansion, though.
Does it feel like $50 worth of new game?
Response: How often does the word "wait till Steam sale" come up?
Is the AI better?
The diplomacy is a little less whack, but I'm still not impressed with the military from my Earth-hailing rivals. Or maybe because I play them off on each other and stab them in the back. The aliens, on the other hand, do prove to be a huge problem in the beginning.
Anything else?
Out of the box, it's much stronger than vanilla Civ V, which was a joke when it first came out. But just noticing the first offered mods on Steam -- color-coded tech tree to make identifying which techs give wonders and units, a real-world clock -- makes you realize the little bells and whistles that were missing. The creators were wise to distance themselves from SMAC comparisons.
The endings are big disappointments. No stats or replay, and the affinity victories are boring as hell to do against the computer. (Maybe the contact with alien race might be more fun; haven't done that yet.)
Getting the voice actors playing the leaders to read their quotes in the tech/wonder advancements would've been better in fleshing out the factions. Also, seeing blueprints of completed wonders and not the actual thing is incredibly stupid.
The affinities rely on a specific rare resource (harmony needs xenomass, so you'll need to break with peace with the animals logic and kill alien hives for it; the other two require mining techs); so your start position will likely guide your tech direction, not you wanting a cyber Slavic Federation or hybrid alien-human Polystralia.
Quests were a good addition to keep things interesting and keep yourself paced with the top dogs of the AI. I wish natural disasters of Civ 4: Beyond the Sword were back though.
Espionage is meh. More involved than Civ V but still limited. Needs more terrorism and success (spy does something minor = detected). Basically they're just 18 turn ATMs or science boosts.
I noticed on videos before the game was released players weren't buying new units or buildings. Sucks for them. It's actually far easier to buy what you need than in Civ V to crank out a sudden military build-up or have a new town catch up with the rest (or buy new stuff for the one taking 30+ turns to make a wonder).
You MUST take the option of having your trade ships and caravans sport ultrasonic barriers instead of your bases getting a +1 on range of keeping critters from your territory. Otherwise, you're spending energy and units guarding lengthy spots of the map from aliens snacking on your economy.
(Sometimes, slaughtering the legions of spawning barbarians near your trade routes was the most annoying bit of Civ V.)
I miss submarine and bomber units.

I emailed Wingware support about the text paste problem below (the email address is easy to find at their website).  I got a response in under 24 hours, which is a great sign of an engaged dev.  He suggested that the problem was likely due to security software blocking application access to the system clipboard, and mentioned webroot by name, which I have.  The solution turns out to be to allow the wingware app to access the clipboard in webroot (or other security software) configuration.
I made the change and now I can paste in the wingware editor.  Due to this excellent support response by Wingware, I am updating my review to "recommend", although it is still a little frustrating that this issue exists:  other apps are able to use the clipboard without needing an exception in security software policy.
But all software has little issues, and not all companies have this kind of customer focus and dedication to their product.  Now I am excited about Wingware again, and am looking forward to checking out all it's good qualities!  :-)

All the years, all the beforehand knowledge of this game's story and gameplay...none of it prepared me for how astoundingly bad this game truly is. I say this with zero amount of hyperbole - this game is by far, the absolute worst of the Final Fantasy series that I have played. And I've played 1-10, 12, Crisis Core, Dirge of ♥♥♥♥ing Cerberus, various Tactics games, and Echoes of Time.
But Final Fantasy XIII is on a whole different level to any of those which I consider to be terrible...which is a fair number. I'm going to describe, in detail, my experience with this game up to the point where I gave up. Prepare yourself.
The game opens up acting like it's Advent Children, because as we all know, Square Enix desperately wants to be a film studio instead. After Vanille decides to give a vague line about how after 13 days (ahaha, that's clever),♥♥♥♥♥♥started to hit the fan. Then we are greeted by our lovely heroine, Lightning. Wait, let me rephrase this - we are greeted by our unlikeable, idiotic, monotone, angry, selfish, loathsome, hardass, soldier turned rogue heroine, Lightning. She is joined by the game's token black guy, Sazh, who could be the only really likeable character in the entire game. They've boarded this train under the guise of wanting to be Purged by...someone, which means being exiled to Gran Pulse where they will probably be mauled by scary monsters...or something. But the real reason why they're here is to beat up some god robot - a Fal'cie called Anima which could be responsible for the Branding of Lightning's sister, Serah, and Sazh's son, Dajh. Their branding means that they are now a L'cie, which is a magic using agent of the Fal'cie to carry out vague, virtually impossible to guess instruction, otherwise they turn into spooky zombie robots. If they complete the instructions, they freeze in crystal for eternity...the...better result? I guess.
Lightning demonstrates the ability to smash a controller which frees all the train's captives for whatever reason and bounces around acting like the game has a good battle system. It really doesn't. Then, after a pointless boss battle with a mech that refuses to die, we are introduced to Snow and his rebellion which look like a ton of idiots...because they are. One has enormous blue hair, too and you will never take him seriously. These guys, called NORA, decide that they're going to rush in with no plan at all to defeat PSICOM or whatever because "heroes don't need plans". Get used to this hero talk Snow's got. That's the majority of his dialogue. But his sheer stupidity gets some kid called Hope's mom killed and him and some random Australian (because this takes place on Earth...no it doesn't), called Vanille watch. Vanille doesn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥and Hope wants to murder Snow because of it. So, in short, Lightning and Sazh want to go beat up Anima, Hope and Vanille and wandering around after Snow so Hope can beat him up, and Snow wants to beat up Anima because Serah is his fiancee. So, they all meet up, kill Anima, and the entire place explodes and turns into crystal.
Everyone drops into some lake thousands of feet below where they were without a scratch on them, and they discover they've all been branded as L'cie. So they discuss the shared vision they all had, briefly discuss what to do with it, and wander around doing pretty much nothing. I encountered some relatively easy monsters here and the combat system was no issue here. Sure, all the combat has been up to this point is mashing A in order to auto-attack everything because there's not many commands to work with yet, but it wasn't horrible...yet. Gotta love how I'm hours in (yes...really), and I'm still getting tutorials on random crap that can easily be figured out, or even ignored to continue letting the game play itself. The battle system works like this - everyone has set roles that they carry out, and you play the leader. And only. The leader. If the leader dies, it's game over, because even though the AI can do anything to keep the party going, they don't know how to rub a feather on someone. There are multiple roles a character can have such as Ravager, which is a mage, Commando, which is a melee fighter, and Sentinel, which is a damage sponge/tank/draw aggro guy. Sounds useful, yes? Snow's the only one with Sentinel at this point, and you don't use him after he stays behind while everyone else goes off. Then he's captured.
But back to the battle system, throughout the course of the fight, you will probably be spamming auto-battle most of the time, and when the time comes, you switch Paradigms. What that does is assign different roles to your whole party. You can use a full-on combat Paradigm to deal as much damage as possible, use a Support Paradigm to cast buffs on the party while someone attacks, you can use a Healing Paradigm to heal while you fight, or mix all those up in any way you want. That's it. It's not even all that strategic. If you're screwed, switch to a buffing/healing paradigm, then go back to a full-offense paradigm. If it doesn't work, go grind or something. Oh, you can choose to use abilties on your own accord, but that just gives the enemies more time to hit you since the battles are very, very fast and enemies are constantly attacking you. Not much room to do anything in combat, really.
So, after wandering this crystallized lake a while the mech from earlier comes back! He fell thousands of feet after being beat up twice, escaped being crystallized, and is now much more powerful even though he's clearly damaged. After finally killing him once and for all, the party decides not to make a single comment about it, and the game doesn't show it again as if nothing happend. They all have an argument about their Focus, which is the vague directions I mentioned earlier, and Snow stays behind to try and free Serah, which is obviously impossible, but he tries for a few hours and gets caught. Later on, Vanille finally grows a brain and comments on how the whole place is made of crystal. What a great observation.
Then the party comes across a random ruins. There's zero backstory, unless the game gives it in the datalogs where the story is made more clear (♥♥♥♥ing lazy), but it doesn't matter to the party since they're having so much fun wandering around doing nothing. They beat up a Garuda or some crap, and fly an airship out of there and into the sky.
Here, we are greeted by our villain, Barthandelus, who is under the disguise of Super Pope, Galenth Dysley making his appearence on a hologram TV in the ship. He makes a speech about killing people, and Sazh gets angry. Not much going on here.
I just remembered the flashbacks, but they don't matter.
Eventually, you arrive to a brown junkyard full of boring to fight Pulsework Soldiers which take about a thousand years to take down, annoying Targetting testicles that allow mechs to spam incredibly powerful missiles at the team, and some more "character development" for Lightning and Hope. See, they've decided to go off on their own, because Splitting the Party is always a good idea, and Hope makes a comment about how his daddy is mean and Lightning jumps over a wall and abandons the rest of the team. Have we not learned from Snow's one-on-many fight with PSICOM soldiers that this is a stupid idea? Oh, damn. I forgot that. Snow had an encounter with his spirit animal - I mean, Eidolon there, but screw that. There's another coming up.
Once Sazh and Vanille wander around, fighting the same monsters over and over again...and slow as hell considering they are both mages, they come across Hope and suddenly they are able to proceed. I probably got some events mixed up, but it honestly doesn't even matter.
And ♥♥♥♥, I'm almost out of room. Time to sum up the next encounter -
- Tedious, overpowered, too fast, Hope and Lightning are a bad combination. -50/1000

I enjoyed this game, however I can't exactly say it was good. It has every element that makes up a good story driven RPG. The characters, on paper, are compelling. The story, on paper, is interesting. The character development, on paper, is interesting and the combat is really fun. The game is gorgeous and the world, on paper, is interesting.
The problem is that nearly every element of the game is mishandled from minute one.
The characters are held back by atrocious dialog and awful voice direction (Although for the most part the voice acting is good).
The story is held back by awful pacing and a habit of extreme repetition as if the game doesn't trust you to understand it (and keep this idea in mind, the game not trusting its players - I'll get back to that in a bit).
The character development harkens back to the excellent systems of Final Fantasy 10, then manages to mishandle them in every possible way. It recreates the sphere grid, but with multiple classes per character; however each class is essentially one path with little branching and additional classes aren't unlocked later in the game; this turns the system into effectively grinding for miniscule stat increases between new ability unlocks. Item upgrades are very similar; grinding monster parts or gil to throw xp at them for miniscule stat gains. Again, the game fails to trust the player to make any in-depth decisions with their characters.
Combat, on the other hand, is very interesting and fun. Battles play in typical Final Fantasy fashion of pseudo-turn based with menus, however everything is much faster and the ability to switch classes on the fly (in the middle of a turn even!) makes for some fast paced and entertaining battles.
Again, though, there are problems. Final Fantasy 13 seems afraid to give you too many options early: not letting you even customize your party until nearly 15 hours in and limiting you to 2 characters at a time for much of the game, making early battles both less interesting visually and from a tactical standpoint. Not being able to switch character control in combat (your party lead is directly controlled, other members AI controlled) is also a problem, but less of one than it sounds - the AI does a good enough job of picking the right actions (based on your knowledge of the enemy to boot). Combat also becomes very repetative against some of the simpler enemies.
But now, for the gorilla in the room: This game is linear. It's linear as ♥♥♥♥. The phrase "corridor simulator" comes to mind. Square Enix creates a very interesting and potentially detailed setting, then renders you completely unable to actually explore or interact with it. Even when the game world opens up, you're still very limited in what you can actually do. Almost as if SE couldn't trust the player to figure out what to do if the game was more open.
And therein lies the game's largest fault; it doesn't trust the player to be able to do anything on their own. SE doesn't trust you to figure out the story, find your way in the world, figure out the battle system, or develop your characters without leading you on the nose for hours and hours.
In spite of all of this, I enjoyed the game. Combat is really, legitimately fun 90% of the time; despite all the flak the characters get from fans I enjoyed most of them (I stand by most of the criticism with the characters boiling down to awful dialog and direction); and the story is legitimately interesting until the later chapters (there's a bit of a deus ex machina at the end). I still recognize its faults though; there's bad game design right left and center here.
Some words on the PC port: it ran great, framerate wise. Controlled fine with M+KB and controller. The resolution locking is incredibly stupid but you can at least toss a hack on to set it to whatever you want. The escape key quitting the game is so hilariously stupid I can't even get mad about it; it's just funny. Had some minor FPS drops entering new areas and a crash here and there, but nothing major.
The pricetag is right on this one. At $16 you could do a lot worse provided you can look past this game's faults. Throwing a recommend here; with the caveat that if you can't see past the game's flaws you should just avoid it.

You're mission, colonize and prepare for the rest of the humans to join you, but you may have different plans. The technology you create and decisions you make may shape you into something much more. There is affinity (ideology) which you can take the path of Purity which holds on to humanity tightly and refuses to throw away it's past or turn into something else. The path of harmony, growing more and more into the planet itself and becoming more like it and it's alien creatures and using them to do your bidding. Then there's my favorite, the supremecy path, which evolves humans into cybernetic beings which in the end decide to return home using lightspeed technology and 'liberate' the humans on earth (in other words you make them join you or kill them). Which way you decide to go is up to you.
The mechanics of the gameplay are pretty much universal across on Civs series so it's easy to adapt and settle into this one. There are a lot of major differences between Civs 5 and this game though. A few key things I liked is they got rid of happiness and replaced it with a metric called 'health'. So luxury resources aren't really in play, but instead you build buildings and use 'vurtues' (policies) to keep that in check. Another thing I really liked about this game is you don't have to spend energy (gold) to upgrade military units. These units upgrade themselves as you progress through the technology web, and they change based on which affinity you follow.
What this game lacks is content. Yes I know it was just released and I'm sure they will come out with some great expansions/DLC but compared to Civs 5, this game is small. There isn't a very wide variety of units either, I feel like Civ 5 units could have taken Beyond Earth units easily in comparision.
Overall, if you like Civs you need to pick up this game, it is unique but holds on to the important stuff like the "If it's not broken don't fix it" concept, and they did that perfectly. I found myself missing a lot of things that I'd love to see put back in, like great people, more units to choose for combat, better diplomacy mode (I had to get info addict just to see what everyone has, a summary page upon victory (yeah, no replays or graphs or anything), and a simple calendar would be nice so I could see what year it is.
I give this one 8 out of 10 MF Falco's and I hope to see you Beyond Earth soon.

I do believe this game now sits in my #1 spot as best metroidvania game out there.
First off, the art direction is top notch. Reminds me of the games from The Behemoth, but a bit more refined visually. Character design is fantastic, sporting a very large variety of minions to slay, and bosses to fight. There's  many NPCs you'll run into, and all beings you come across stand out on their own, with very little cases of copy and paste here.
The game's environment is extremely expansive. I was not at all expecting to spend 49 hours playing a 2D metroidvania title, but here I am.
Hand's sweaty, feet sweaty, mom's spaghetti this game is hard! The difficulty generally scales well, starting off as almost a little too easy to controller chucking, vitriol-spewing hard  in the mid to late game.  This game does not hold your hand at all. It's extremely easy to get lost and not know what to do, which for some is a mark against it.
Gameplay is superb. Control is very tight. Hollow Knight is a paradigm for movement and combat and in a 2d platformer.
My criticisms are minor. I think I would have enjoyed the early game a bit more if it was a tad more clear where to go. I can see some players giving up in frustration given no direction inside one of the most expansive labyrinths of world in a 2D game. I know some hardcore players would be against a navigation mechanic but such a feature could easily be disabled in options.
The biomes bled together a little too easily. I wish they were a bit more defined from each other; fog canyon and city of tears are good examples of biome diversity. Furthermore, the game visually is a little too monochrome at times.
I tend to scrutinize the soundtrack in this genre given how high Super Metroid set the bar. I wasn't a fan of the score in this game. It wasn't bad but wasn't that memorable.
Criticisms aside, this is one of my favourite games of 2017, if not my favourite this year. If you favour metroidvania games, this game is well worth it even at full price.

The end has a decent boss fight, but nothing to write home about- for whatever reason, the story is what's supposed to grab your attention, and that's ultimately what will justify this purchase. If you're looking for a fun, more narrative-driven action shooter with fun easter eggs, fast, fluid combat, and tons of things to kill tons of ways, then this is your game.
However, if you don't care for narrative and are searching for a more hardcore gaming experience evocative of classics like Duke Nukem, Blood, or the older Shadow Warrior, you will ultimately find that this game falls short of delivering the same smart-as-a-whip map design and frenetic intensity.

Necrovision não é nenhuma maravilha mas tá longe de ser um fps ruim. A proposta do jogo é enfocar mais no combate do que na história, por isso as vzes tem umas coisas sem pé nem cabeça, assim como  zumbis e soldados que desmembramos a todo momento na engine de física divertida. O arsenal de armas vai desde tipos de pistolinhas, metralhadoras, snipers, baioneta, shotgun, até um canhão lá antigo e armas melle como espadas e pás também. Suggest, yes. Qualification, included.
The title "Farming Simulator" is correct as it is a very nice, beautiful recreation of using various pieces of farming equipment. What it is not, is a "Farm Simulator", designed to simulate actually running a farm. There is a complete abcense of any risk in this game. While you vehicles require an arbitrary daily upkeep amount, your tractor cannot break down at a vital moment just before harvest. Running at full speed off a cliff or into another vehicles has no effect or repercussions. There are no competing farms to undercut you or try to drive you out of business or market crashes that leave you with tons of surplus you cannot sell without taking a hit and everything can sit in your silos for years without decay. Where are the insect infestations that can ruin your crops or tornados or freak storms that can destroy parts of your farm? Why do you start the game with nice equipment and a 'complete farm' out of the gate? Why not one barn and build your structures as you go. And what point are the structures? They don't protect your equipment from rain or rust? No one steals your equipment as I have left it sitting in the middle of town for days.
I could go on and on but you get the point. It is a very pretty, mechanically solid rendition of what it is like to run around using various pieces of farm equipment but other than driving stuff to a dumper and watching a single screen for price fluctuations there is very little depth to the game. I know players will say, well that is what mods are for... no. Players should not be made responsible for fleshing out elements that really should have been in the title to begin with in order to qualify to really be called a simulator. Is it a bad game, not at all. But it really should be understood it is a game with no real risk, just keep playing and eventually everyone will own the entire map and 'win'.

Just a quick disclosure first: The game had some serious performance/lag issues on my PC. No idea what was up, but it felt like it was running at 15fps. Also had some bizarre flashing/blinking issue. Now onto the game! The game is a top down action/strategy game that plays like a stealth version Diablo or similar. You have objectives that usually involve reaching a certain area of the map that is patrolled by a number of guards or soldiers. In a 1-on-1, Robin Hood can hold his own vs. most enemies, but can quickly be outnumbered. The idea is to either knock out unsuspecting enemies, or use the environment to your advantage. The issues I had with the game are that I couldn't tell which objects I could interact with, and which would just move me right to a non-interactive decal. As well, I couldn't figure out how to heal myself; even between levels, damage would carry forward. I figure there is some way to do it, but if I have to look outside of the game to figure out the basics of the game, then I consider that a failing of the game. In closing, the game shows a lot of good ideas but has not aged well. Stealth and swordplay have been done much better in more recent games, and the game does not perform well on newer machines. Worth a try if you have it, but I wouldn't recommend to buy it otherwise.

Buying a "drama CD" as a video on Steam is a little weird conceptually, but as someone who liked the visual novel quite a bit, I found this to be cute and interesting enough.

I've put alot of hours into this game, and decided to do a review about it. Today, is the day I quit RoI. The fact why  I do not recommend this game is that after putting alot of hours into this game, you will not be happy once you have to quit it, because trust me, sooner or later you will, because you will get bored of it. Now, let's talk about the game itself. When I was searching for a new mmo, I came accross this game called "Riders of Icarus". I've never heard about it, it was fairly new, and reviews were more or less leaned towards positive line, so I was like sure, let's give it a try. When I came into character creation, I've picked DPS class, specifically assassin. Now, I LOVE tanking role, the fact I didn't go with tank in this game is because my friend wanted it, so I went with assassin. I was quite sure I'd reroll my class and change into guardian soon, but classes here are really well designed so I've stayed with assassin... all until today. I was literally bored when I created guardian, and trust me, I LOVE F*CKING TANKING IN MMOS!!! All taming mounts system is brilliant, it's very unique and very cool, maybe abit to grindy when it comes to having required materials to attempt a tame at the moment, but what would a mmo be without some grinding?? Dungeons were unique as well, they were satisfying when you completed them, and of course - when you drop a legendary item. There are also quite alot of world bosses, that drop already created so called "marks" used to tame heroic or elite familiars. And, with enough dps, you can even take on the world boss while not being in the group, and drop "box" (Term used by players when a certain player or group does enough dps to a boss (5% of his hp) so it gets normal looting box. If not 5% is dealt, only some gold is dropped, and that's it. No other items). But, now comes the catch. It gets very repitive and boring after a while, and sadly, developers play a huge role in this. Updates are piece by piece, fresh for a few days, and after that, same old stuff. You log in in the morning, solo a dungeon or two, join so world bosses fight -> repeat. Get heroic familiar mark, fail the tame -> repeat. Every.single.day. PVP is more or less non-existent. The current two raids are way too hard, so even mediocore players cannot participate in them, just because their gear is trash when compared to the one  required for the raid.. Drop rate is like really low, and game is leaning towards pay to win mechanic with every single game update. It pains to write this review, but that is just how it is. Also, there is another thing, that means ALOT of me. Player base. It's dying. Daily. It is very sad for a game with great potential to die out, just because developers won't listen to their players. Now, I don't want them to do whatever we say, but should at least think about it and include and think about our ideas. But anyway, 850 hours spent, I do not regret playing the game and putting so much hours into it, mostly because guildies made game much much much more fun, but as I said, it became too repetitive and boring. And... well.... dead.
P.S.: I could talk about this game for a day, I'd be glad if anyone has more questions about it, feel free to ask me, as I did not cover all aspects of the game.

This is the game where the wonderful Bit.Trip series started. Think of it as a pong game on steroids with an amazing soundtrack that interacts with events in the game. If this game looks difficult, it should, because it is. Many playthroughs will be needed to get through all three levels and great concentration will be needed to master all three. Normally games that have extremely high difficulty are plagued with being just that. A game that is extremely difficult but other than that there is no substance or goal to work toward. That is what separates this game from every home made game that is meant for nothing more than to test your patience. As difficult as the game is, there is so much charm that oozes out of this game to keep you coming back. The music like I said is absolutely amazing. It never gets old, and is always exciting when you progress to the next stage in the level, and the music gets more frantic. There's nothing more terrifying to let beats slip by you and hear that massive knock that lets you know you messed up. Miss too many and you get knocked down to a lower score multiplier. Miss even more and get knocked back into the 70's with a lifeless black and white screen with no other sounds than beeps. Fail to recover out of this will break you, then game over. Unlike most difficult games, this one gives you a chance to recover and stay in the game and it does it so well. Each level has an end boss and it is so satisfying to watch them blow up when you defeat them, because they are not easy either.
I own this game on the Wii where it was originally released, and while I love the Wii version, the PC version really has a huge advantage with the mouse controls vs. the Wiimote controls. The mouse control makes it much easier to keep your paddle steady and makes movements more precise. When playing on the Wii I can only make it through a quarter of the way through on level 3. On the PC version I almost made it to the boss. A bad thing about the PC version is that I have to run this game in windowed mode or else I get some mean lag in the controls when running full screen. Not sure why this is, but it's not a massive deal. Once you start playing the game, there won't be any time to look anywhere else on your computer.

Dungeon Defenders is a fun and strategic tower defence game. After putting in a decent amount of time and trying out different classes I have to say that this game is well worth the money. There is always something to do and while it can get a bit repetitive, it is well worth putting some time into.
Pros:
- Lots of classes to choose from,
- Able to add maps from steam workshop (you can add some cool and creative maps such as Helms Deep from Lord of the Rings),
- Customizing your character is easy to do, fun and can make unique looking characters,
- Easy to understand and follow what the game teaches you as you play along,
- Gameplay is smooth and the art style is pretty especially for a game of its time.
Cons:
- Online is dead. Best to play with friends,
- You have to grind a significant amount to get what you want,
- Can get repetitive especially if you're after a specific item.
All in all, I recommend this game if you're looking for a tower defence game. It has its flaws but there is a lot of fun to be had. Even more so if you are planning to play with a friend.
