I quite simply do not understand the praise for this game.
It's biggest problem is you quite simply never know where to go. The game has absolutely no conveyance of any sort to guide you toward a goal. I understand adventure games and you are supposed to discover the world and make your way through it, eventually getting to where you need to be.
But this game constantly loops in on itself, while heavily restricting what you can and cant do with many areas requiring abilities that you might not get for hours, and then its like ok where was that spot again? Guess I have no choice but to re-explore the entire labrynth once again.
The game charges the player for every single convenience. You pay to unlock fast travel spots. You pay for maps. You pay for literally almost everything. See a cool item for sale on a random shop in the dungeon? Hope you have enough geo or good luck remembering where they were.
This in addition to brain dead hit and run combat makes for a game that is simply a chore to get from A to B, and any sense of adventure is ruined by never knowing where you need to be to progress.
Compare it to something like Dark Souls. Obviously a top tier game everyone knows, everyone loves. Dark souls also winds in on itself and can be somewhat labrynthine, but you never feel straight up LOST, because it conveys exactly where you need to be without ever telling you a single thing. You can easily tell if you are going the right way. Enemies go up in difficulty, you find bonfires, and the divergent paths will meet up along the way and guide you to a boss. It is what is known as good game design.
Hollow Knight has none of that. It's just random. Everything loops around with non-sensically placed benches and almost non-existent means of fast travel, because the spots designate for fast travel are so rare and far from anything relevant. If you die the amount of work it takes to get back to your corpse will have you frustrated beyond words. Sometimes you wont even know how you got there in the first place thanks to the maze-like world and the fact that you may or may not have stumbled into the map seller. This is what is known as bad game design.
I don't consider the game hard at all. I consider it inelegant and frustrating. The agility expected of you to overcome some obstacles clash heavily with the imprecise skills the game gives you, and you will impale yourself on spikes or fall in acid pits the entire game.
It is a horribly clunky game in every sense of the word. Barring a beautiful game world with incredibly interesting character and world designs and ideas, it's unquestionably one of the worst designed games I've ever played.
The praise this game gets is utterly baffling.

Hollow Knight proves itself to me as the most enjoyable Metroidvania I've played to date. I won't pretend I am adept in the genre, but I feel I have had enough experience with the catalog of these types of games to have a feel for the common weaknesses they present. For me, the worst part about this genre is the heavy amount of backtracking required to move around the map. Hollow Knight tries it's very best to improve upon this problem, and surely does a great job at doing so. It hasn't abolished this weakness, but it is nowhere near as unbearable as some of it's ancestors are.
Depending on what order you acquire new abilities, the game can play out much differently in terms of convenciency. The way it unfolded in my first and only play through thus far, was acceptable. But if I were to do it again, I know exactly which ones I'd dart to first. It's another double edged sword of the genre; in attempting to allow the player to go whichever areas they happen upon first, the developer sacrifices the convenciency of certain upgrades that would have been far more helpful in the early parts of the game, and would have contributed a lot to the backtracking problem that is still present. Team Cherry makes the right choice. I heavily favor freedom over conveniency. But I would be lying if I said it didn't lessen my experience.
The art style is super impressive in nearly all the areas. The only place I got real tired of was Deepnest. It's lack of peripheral vision and it's refusal to extend beyond a black and gray color palette get tiring when traversing the area. Some may argue it's a necessary part of the atomosphere for the game, but I feel it is the opposite. Ignoring the existence of Deepnest, the rest of the game has this amazing ability to put you in a dreary place that certainly feels dangerous and grim, but they provide the player with these adorable glimpses of hope in various ways throughout that heighten the mood of the game and encourage me to go on. For example, there are dozens of these green worms hidden around every area inside these glass jars. When you get near one, you hear this little noise that I can't even describe, it's just cute as hell. These worms are present in Deepnest, but if anything that just made me realize that the adorable nature of the game doesn't only rely on the things you fight for, it's just as present in the things you fight against. Just look at the screenshots for this game and you'll see that very few enemies look like they were drawn just to be repulsive and antagonistic. As far as appearance goes, most seem as harmless as those worms.
Level design is never too confusing, every area is pretty different in the way they are mapped out. Some don't have as many shorcuts, but compensate with tightly woven pathways that are, I guess, more traditionally accesible. One of the coolest things I found myself really appreciating in the late stages of the game was how the areas connected to one another. (Specifically present in "Fungal Wastes").
Boss design is a great middle ground between challenging and enjoyable. My favorite part of the game by a landslide. Some were leaning on the easy side of things, but that's only because I would come across them wielding much more abilities and upgrades than I should have had when facing them. But this only happened two, maybe three times.

Grunt enemies are varied and always challenging when first meeting them. Some of the earlier areas become cakewalks when coming back for secrets and other goodies, but I think that isn't really a weakness, just a natural evolution of power in games like this. I don't mind it really. At times I felt super empowered when revisiting some of my worst enemies.
Soundtrack is consistently great. I hate to bring the area Deepnest up again, but It's worth noting that this area doesn't have any music. It fits the nightmarish look, but the absense of music falls in the same criticism I have with the artstyle of Deepnest. It's just so uninteresting to go through, a stark change of pace compared to every other area of the map.
The map size is enormous. I couldn't believe I was finding so many areas. Upon every new area discovery I would get this feeling like I never wanted the game to end.
Character and story wise, it works. Most of the side characters contribute to the atmosphere a lot. With characters like Zote and the Map Maker and a few more, I never felt like Team Cherry was taking themselves to seriously. When the times comes for drama, it supplies a healthy dose. But never overdoes itself.
I also have to note the economics of the game. With games like Breath Of The Wild coming out alongside this in 2017, I heavily favor a consistently challenging price range for items and upgrades. One of the biggest gripes I have with Breath Of The Wild is the ease at which you gain currency not even halfway through the game. Anybody putting in a little bit of discourse from the main story will find themselves with plenty of rupees to pimp link with loads of stuff, but the accomplishment of acquring these things becomes crippled by the ease of acquiring the currency to buy them. Hollow Knight never, ever, did this. Til' the very end, I was strapped for cash. This not only makes the items purchased feel accomplishing, but the sight of a floorfull of coins at the feet of your fallen foes becomes just as pleasing as the purchases. Note that it never got too tedious when trying to get money, it was just enough to delay certain items across the runtime of the game so that I wasn't ever at any point walking out of the storefronts with a full shopping cart.

Ok, I'm going to do a new review format, listing the positives and negatives of the game.
-Amazing graphics: Oh, they're so nice, especially in the cutscenes
-SOME nice environments: While many weren't so great (more on this in the negatives), the ones that were were just awesome.  Chinatown was my favorite mission, as you have to make your way through a very crowded area, trying to figure out creative ways to kill your target.  That's what Hitman is supposed to be about, right?
-Rewarding gameplay: I love how good it feels to get those more creative kills.  Why kill them yourself when you can drop a chandelier on them or electrocute them when they go for a drink of water?
-Contracts mode: This is a very fun game mode.  Basically, players can create custom contracts based in the single player levels of the game.  This means that you get to pick your own targets and murder them however you want.  This contract then gets posted for other players to try.  They can then rate the contract so that people can see the better ones.  This is way more entertaining than the single player game, and much harder too.
-Instinct letting you see through walls: Stealth games should not have a magical way for you to see through walls.  It adds an awesome feeling when you have to be super careful and you don't quite know where everyone is.  Even worse, it points out all of the places where you can do something special.  This makes "creative" actions much less special, as you didn't really have to work for it or experiment at all.
-The suspicion system: They made it so that the group of people that you are disguised as will just naturally suspect that you are an impostor, and the only way to avoid that is by burning instinct so that you can blend in.  Not only is this super annoying, it also doesn't make any sense.  How do all of the security guards know each other so well, and why can't they just say, "Well, must be a new guy."?
-The combat: You are SO overpowered.  It's ridiculous.  At first, I was not aware of this, as I would always restart from the last checkpoint if I broke stealth, but later in the game, I would sometimes snap and kill everyone before restarting.  It revealed that murdering everyone was not only viable, it was easier.  The only thing that can keep you from doing it is the point system, but that is so lame.  Stealth should be promoted through difficulty, not how high you will get on the leaderboards.
-The story/the bad levels: I am a hitman.  I am supposed to be a predator, hunting my target and feeling hardcore.  So why am I being framed for murder (with little to no convincing evidence, might I add) and constantly running/hiding from the police?  I understand that the developers were going for something different, where each mission was connected in a nice little story, but it becomes a bit uninteresting when you have sections where all you are doing is sneaking from point A to point B.
Overall, I would still recommend this game, as I found it to be fun to play, but it is flawed.  Hitman: Blood Money might be better, but I haven't played it in a while.  I should probably give that a shot.

If you enjoy being a sneaky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, this is a good choice. I enjoyed the difficulty of trying to get through a mission unseen and unheard.
Sneaking through an entire level without raising an alarm is tough. Doing it without anyone seeing you is tougher. Try to do it without a costume and without touching anyone but the target and the challenge is quite high. While it may take one or two or ten tries to nail that perfect hit, the feeling of satisfaction is completely worth it. This has been a mainstay with the Hitman series and is not lost here.
The in-game challenges in missions adds tons of replayability. An issue previous Hitman games had was not knowing of cool mechanics a level could contain. For example, I believe Blood Money had a giant chandelier you could drop on stage to take out one of your targets. That one was obvious. Others, not so much. With the challenges, you get a bit of a hint in terns of the name of the challege or the icon beside it. I found it pretty fun seeing all the different ways I could take out my targets.
There is some variety in missions. Not all are assassinations. Some may include escaping an area, while another collecting necessary items. Sure, the game is called "Hitman" but having a bit of variety never hurts.
If you are looking for a game that is all about run and gun, this isn't it. On the harder skill levels (I never played anything but hard or above) running into a gun fight is asking to die of lead poisoning. Also, the story tends to have completely over the top characters. With the gameplay itself quasi-realistic (one shot kills, no regenerating health apart from very rare first aid stations, etc) the ridiculous characters are a little much. The last qualm I have with the game is the fact that I don't believe a single character model creator has actually seen a real human female breast based upon the strip club level. Just sayin...
All in all, I do recommend this game.

This is one of the best games I ever played. This game has everything - humor, story, good game design, lots of details and my favorite - it runs in Linux flawlessly, which is an extremely rare case for games of such size that suppor Linux. Gameplay is smooth(no leading screens between different locations on a level). This game has secrets that are there to FIND them, and not accidentally get them. There are so many things that are done correctly in this game and are just wrong in many others(and still being done wrong in modern games). Like your character will not replace a mag in your gun if it is already full, he will do some other action instead. If you are at low health your screen will not turn red or simulate bleading from your eyes - it will decrease color perception instead. Your character will say that the fight was easy only if your health didn't drop below a certain threshold, and not when you barelly made it alive(just to sound cool and tough). There are many other small things that make you think: "Hey, that is not an ordinary game, that is a f*cking masterpiece". I recommend this to everyone who likes to play FPS. It also has some chalenging difficulty settings that most other games just do not have nowdays. If you play on heroic you will have to THINK first and THEN do. Like if you do not chose correct skills and abilities(during first levels) the first boss will just 1-hit kill you and since in heroic you cannot save-reload, you are done(though you still might be able to do it, you just need to be untouchable for around 20 mins)... Which is what a heroic difficulty is meant to be. Options in the game are also quite smart - you can toggle hints that show where you need to go. Level design is quite good, so for a new player it might not be clear where to go or what to do, and an experienced player might not want to have those kind of hints.

BIT . TRIP BEAT a pretty simple game to stumble upon, at least when you first look at it. This game is another addition to the well known BIT . TRIP series and it keeps the series golden with its creation not disgracing the series at all, this game unlike previous BIT . TRIP games is a mimic of the Classic Game Pong however it adds a rythem mechanic to it, hence the addition of BEAT in the title. The first minute of the game you will be wondering why you had bought this game asking why you would waste even a penny to it however as the levels progress in the game you start to realize the game isn't a peice of cake as you had originally thought, as the game progressively gets harder each second. When I had first picked this game up I had enjoyed it to my hearts content although I have to admit I enjoy most rythem games but I am in no way musically talented meaning that anyone can pick up this game and be good at it. Although this game is fun, it does have a few problems, some of which could be annoying, problems include, having trouble keeping track of the bits coming to you due to the background or having bad sight this is probably the worst problem I had to deal with as it really becomes noticable as the level progresses and this could be a major problem for people who wish to obtain a perfect in the game and they ended up missing a bit because it was apart of the background, another problem can be that you feel that your mouse is too slow to keep up with the bits however this problem can be reduced with increasing mouse movement, the final problem I had noticed was that sometimes you felt that your "player" was going to hit a bit due to your preception however you will end up missing by a inch, this may be a personal problem for me and may not affect others. Even with all the problems I would still personally recommend this game because it is enjoyable to attempt to get that Perfect for the level and trying to master the game by doing so, it is also fun trying to beat others on the leaderboard as Highscores have always been my favorite setting for games, the game also has an awesome soundtrack and as I suggested before you don't have to be musically talented to be good at this game. I would recommend buying this game when it is on sale as it can cause anger with the problems I have stated above, however this game should not be ignored when it is on sale because it truely is a great game.

Shadow Warrior is a first person shooter released back in 2013 where you run around with a plentiful array of weaponry with something as simple as a sword, to something as powerful as a “duke nukem” launcher, and to something as over the top as giant demon heads.
The gameplay is right as rain for this game. All the controls feel smooth and it is perfect for anyone who likes action. With the exception of some occasional puzzles and the drudgery of trying to navigate the hallways of Shadow Warrior with its lack of directional markers to tell you where to go other than making the doorway you need to progress through glow, this game is constant fighting. The first half of the game is very well paced with short 20 to about 30 minute missions where you get to fight through all different sorts of unique areas and meet all the different enemy types. From these weird flying harpy demons, to giant minotaur looking mini bosses, and to rolling exploding green poisonous de monic balls of death. If you're looking for solid first person shooting mechanics and controls, you've found it.
The graphics of this game look great for 2013 and still good today! The sounds compliment it all perfectly and there's a lot of things retro for anyone who is coming from the old shadow warrior game that this reboot is based off of. There's plenty of little hidden easter eggs throughout the game that you can find that I personally don't understand since I didn't play the original, but they still made me laugh every time I saw them. One con to note about the graphics though is that when you get up close and start cutting up human enemies, the animations seem to fall apart and appear retro in quality. I'm not sure if that's a feature or bad animation, but its very laughable in its lack of quality amidst the updated look of the game.
The story of the game is extremely comical and interesting if not entirely common to advance due to how much action spaces out story segments. It ended on a bit of a serious note which was a bit unsettling though since the game had tried so hard to be funny that a serious ending didn't really feel like it fit. It was however made comical because its the first time a cutscene ever shows your character in third person, where you get to see that they didn't bother rendering your character's head outside of reflections and you get to see yourself sitting there with nothing but a mouth and eyes, no face to to be seen. There's a lot that doesn't get solved in the game though, making it very obvious that there was going to be a sequel since the ending is very unsatisfying and in the end you really don't feel like you accomplished anything.
The games pacing is probably the biggest con the game has. While it starts out nicely spread and manageable with up to 30 minute missions…the later missions take 40 to about 50 minutes each which are extremely tiring when some of them don't even give you a cutscene to help advance the story, just some basic comedic dialogue with literally zero story progression. They start packing each level with larger and larger amounts of the same repetitive enemies jumping out at you after every couple of steps and it really just becomes cumbersome to carry on. What's worse is that they even start repeating the levels towards the end. You'll run through the same rooms and hallways more times than you can count with no sight of anything new.
There's a very strange delay whenever you hit the U key to upgrade your weapons and skills. It seems to get worse as the game goes on as well, but it either reverted to its original state towards the end or I just got so used to it I stopped noticing it. I'm not sure what the deal with that is but it was very frustrating to start which is why I feel the need to mention it.
Overall I definitely recommend Shadow Warrior. Even by today's standards this is still a good game. I give a 7/10. It was fun. It wasn't amazing, but this is probably the first arcadey shooter that pits you against the world with no friendlies and minimal story progression that I actually enjoyed, potentially the first one I've ever finished. Do not buy it for its full $40 price. You'll be paying $4 per hour of gameplay. Wait for it to go on sale, and then definitely pick it up.

Played my random roll a few times now, total about 2 hours. Shadow Warrior was a blast to play. It’s the reboot version from 2013. I’ve played a little bit of the old 90s version as well, prior. First off, the graphics are passable, but disappointing. It’s not that old but there were aspects to them that were almost downright bad. On the other hand, environments looked really really good and there are other aspects that look good. It runs very smoothly, though, so that also helps. I think I was in the 70-90fps range most of the time with my 5 year old hardware and there are a lot of monsters at times.
So I played two levels, each about an hour long. The game starts off, you are going to buy a sword from some old traditional Japanese guy, you get double crossed and you get imprisoned. Sometime in between conscious demons erupt from the earth killing basically everyone in the most gruesome fashion. They are your primary enemies. The low level ones are basically sword fodder and rush you with their claws. Later I came upon some other type that shoot glowing balls, and then some giant warlord one that shoots fire and has a gigantic sword. Basically just kite and shoot or go in swinging with my sword for the little ones. The AI isn’t anything spectacular, but I wouldn’t expect them to be. The humans are pretty much just as stupid though. I’m pretty sure I heard “I got something for you BLADE!*”
Combat is fast and somewhat frenetic. I used a sword 90% of the time. In the options you can change the appearance of the basic katana with a couple other things. Ice axe from Walking Dead (telltale? I don’t remember) some sort of bat, and the “penetrator” from Saints Row, which is a 3 ft purple d1ldo on a stick. Which is funny, especially when you unsheathe it like the sword and rub your hand along its length. I generally stuck with the sword though. With the sword you can also throw shurikens. Other weapons I got so far was a pistol that can be upgraded, a submachine gun, sort of like an uzi that is incredibly weak and almost worthless. A demon heart, that kills any low level demons in a very short radius. And then after I killed the warlord I could use his head (this is an unlockable ability) and it shot some sort of fire/energy from it’s mouth. You get a bonus in energy points (for ability unlocks) by doing a multitude of strike types against a group of enemies. Usually it just gets crazy fast though and I just hack away.
Story is actually pretty decent. After hell breaks loose, you are still after the sword, for some reason. It’s a pretty big deal. You get the help of some kind of magic being that gives you powers. You start with a self-heal. I unlocked a couple so far, one being a blast that knocks enemies in a line into the air “oh look, demon pinatas!” and another that knocks them down in a radius. As well as a Ki strike that is pretty powerful. And I think I unlocked so ki strikes give me health. I’ve died a few times when absolutely overwhelmed, especially in corridor type areas that have a lot of explosives like vending machines and cars (why does a coke machine blow up like a nuclear device?!).
The unlock section is pretty neat actually. For some you get tattoos, for others you color in classic Japanese prints, and then you can buy upgrades for your weapons with found money. I like it. Of course Lo Wang has his quips and remarks. They aren’t USUALLY repetitive, but I’ve heard the piñata joke enough times now.
Oh yea, and it’s really gory gross. Mutiliated bodies skewered on spikes everywhere. Pools of blood and smears and whatnot. Monsters get hacked to bits from your sword. A lot of things are destructible, but could be more. On the other side, there are some really nice classic Japanese artwork pieces on the walls.

Glorkian Warrior is reminds me slightly of alien invaders. You are in control of the alien Glork, and you are protecting your asteroid from invading aliens. The game play is simple. I really like the cute sound effects on show here,  the voices sound hilarious, and I love the characters Chloe, and Chloe. I loved the back and forth between the characters.
On a whole, while this isn't the sort of game that will have you sitting down for hours upon hours a session, it does offer something different, short bursts of fun which is sometimes all you need just to relax and take your mind off life.
Would certainly recommend Glorkian Warrior!

I have mixed feelings about this game.  It shows promise, but the development has been slow.
I understand Early Access games are a gamble --- some succeed, and many fail.  I appreciate that game developers  have dreams, ambitions, and hopes for their projects, as well as pride in their work.  And, I know that it's easy to be critical of the work of others, especially when you don't know or understand the details of what is happening behind the scenes.  (There is an old saying "Nothing is impossible if you don't have to do it yourself.")
But, Early Access games have to be developed and offered to potential users in the real world, and such potential users do not have infinite time or infinite patience.  Because competition for the attention and money of potential customers often can be  tough and merciless, developers need to temper their dreams and ambitions for their projects with a strong dose of realism.  There is another old saying --- "The best is the enemy of the good" --- that developers need to keep in mind to avoid letting their dreams and ambitions cloud their judgment about how much time and patience they can expect from potential users.
Even if the developers of Novus Inceptio succeed in fulfilling their dreams and ambitions for the game, the slow pace of their efforts is threatening to exhaust the patience of many potential users.  I hope they succeed, but am concerned that their slow pace could result in achieving success at a time when many potential users have exhausted their patience and moved on to other, more promising games.
Apart from the slow pace of the game's development, the crafting and building options seem to be overly detailed, not very obvious, and a bit too complicated.  There is a fine line between a crafting and building system that is too easy and not challenging at all, and a crafting and building system that is too hard and demanding to be worth the effort.  The complexity of the crafting and building system in Novus Inceptio leans toward being too detailed and too demanding that it threatens to be more of a boring grind than an interesting challenge.
As of December 26, 2017, I am leaning toward giving a thumbs down to this Early Access game because of the slow development and overly detailed and complicated crafting and building system.

Novus Inceptio is a survival RPG set to our planet, but far in the future. Despite of the fact that the game is labeled as a survival game, it is not a typical survival challenge type of a game.
DIFFERENT POINT OF VIEW ON A SURVIVAL GAME
Do not expect a typical survival challenge game, because survival elements are slightly at the background. On one hand, it is necessary to cover basic needs to survive, but these activities are not to bother you a lot, they rather intensify the world atmosphere. On the other hand, it is not difficult to get killed or to die as a result of some kind of injury.
THE WORLD IS NOT JUST A DEAD BACKGROUND
You can interact with nearly everything from the surface of the ground, bushes, trees, to your own buildings. In the game, no plant serves just as a decoration – would you like to pick up mushroom and eat it? Go ahead, nothing stops you. Even ordinary tree does not serve only as a source of wood, but offers other materials, too (bark, leaves, branches, resin etc.).
LIVELY RELAXING ENVIRONMENT
The game contains environment with natural time flow, following daily cycle and being affected by weather changes. If you stop for a moment and listen to the sounds of the nature you would recognize in which direction a wolf is hunting, you could feel the wind taking off, or you could just let yourself go while listening to atmospheric music and you could calmly relax listening to the whisper of leaves and the wind.
COMPLEX CRAFT SYSTEM
The game craft system is based on very difficult internal logic which requires individual production of every single part of the final product. As a reward for such game mechanics you get unique items, spiced with material bonuses, e.g. it is really important whether you craft from oak or pine wood. The game also offers an option of the craft system for those who don´t want to dive in tables and calculations.
MATERIAL BONUSES
The game contains a unique system of resources heredity which is used during crafting. Therefore it is possible to craft unique items with specific characteristics which happens because of the craft complexity.
UNLIMITED CHARACTER OPTIONS
The game allows natural character development. Only personal attributes, which you use, are enhanced. You have free hands to create a mix of specialization which you truly enjoy. You don´t have to think even before the beginning of the game about choosing a proper race or profession – character attributes are automatically adjusted according to frequent character activities.
CHARACTER AGEING
Yes, during playing your character gets older and can eventually die of age and therefore can move one generation further. The ageing system is our specific system of character level up. The age are experience points and a generation is a level. You dont´t have to be afraid of ageing, because it is natural way to level up, which brigs you bonuses and even better attributes.
BUILDING SYSTEM
Thanks to modular system, while building your new home, the only limiting factor is your creativity (and if not, you can always use ready-made houses). The difference in our system is in the builning process. First, you take your time and plan, only when you are ready, you start gathering material and finally build your dream house.
FARMING
You can build a farm around your house and grow plants needed for cooking a good quality meal or plant your own wood and bring some exotic plants from different biomes to your home.
ANOMALIES
In the world, there are many portals to different dimensions or times. In anomalies you can come across some unique rewards, but primarily you can learn new craft recipes which are essential for any crafting. But it is vital to pay attention to any danger hidden in those portals.

Overall, I think the game is off on the right track but there is a few things that can be a bit frustrating.  The progression is pretty slow, I spent roughly 4 hours and got a lumbermill going that only gives 20% success chance, and was able to get a 4x1 house and some basic clothing and equipment.
Gathering materials is very grindy because you always find yourself needing some part for another part.  I can see that once you get rolling, resource collection is faster...but ultimately it needs to be more accessible because if the intention is for this to be an exploration game, I didnt get out and explore much because I spent so much time trying to make the eqipment and starter home.  This is the same for pretty much everything, you need a bunch of something to combine it into a more robust thing, then turn those more robust things into a final something.  It's a little tedious and you always find yourself a little bit short on something.
Combat is enjoyable, its not just a hack n slash.  It is a bit clunky at times and you have to be prepared for certain encounters.  I got wrecked once by a lone wolf simply because I wasnt wearing a shirt.  In a real life situation, If I had a sword,  a wolf would get pretty messed up.  Sure I could get bit and bleed, but I could also cut the wolfs head off. Anyway, this wolf was jsut outside the start area and it either had too much defense, or my attack power wasnt enough...so I had to grind more just to go fight wolves.
Relating to level up and progression, I thought this was totally fine.  The whole age-thing is a bit odd at first, but you kind of just get used to it.  Skill perks and everything seemed fine.  One thing that I felt was unclear was how to obtain new skills...is the an experience bar that I missed?  Is the Age the experience bar?  What determines your age, and why does it climb so fast?
Overall, I recommend, but warn people that the game is a bit grindy and is def early access. I did enjoy the experience, despite the criticism mentioned above and I will surely check back later to see furhter updates.

I believe that this game is a step forward in the Civilization series. The game does has several aspects that are from Civ 5, since both games operate on the same engine. These similarities are not a lack of creativity, however, but a recognition that in Civ5 they got it right. If you were to browse my Library and the amount of hours I've put into games you would notice the huge gap between all of my other games and Civ 5. I have 485 hours into that game. When you develop a game series as successful as the Civ games have been you ought to know when certain aspects are great and that you should keep them and this is what Firaxis and 2k have done.
My only true complaint is that the diplomacy is copy and pasted from Civ 5, this is the only grievance I hold against the game. Other than that, this is a game worth getting and full of creative thought.

This review is aimed at newcomers to the Civilization series.
Sid Meier's Civilization®: Beyond Earth™ is the latest installment in Sid Meier's long running historical grand strategy series.Civilization®: Beyond Earth™ is being met with several bad reviews primarily due to the long list of complaints about the games similarity to Sid Meier's Civilization®: 5™.
Firstly, let me tell you a bit about the game's features.
In terms of story, Sid Meier's Civilization®: Beyond Earth™ offers a story, kind of, following a fictional Civilization®'s tale in future events. Sid Meier's Civilization®: Beyond Earth™'s main campaign, which is its primary attraction, is in effect a sandbox of the known world from 2700 AD. Sid Meier's Civilization®: Beyond Earth™'s map is exceptionally large, spanning from a rock to another rock, and from big rocks to small rocks. The player leads a faction of their choice through an futuristic strategical story. There is no variety between factions, for example, the Slavic sponsor's strength lies in their ability to provoke global wars, while their military is often inferior to the opponents'. Not all strengths and weaknesses lie in military attributes, some factions receive bonuses to diplomacy or trade. Some will also enjoy the few unremarkable landmarks scattered across the map, as well as the occasional alien making an appearance.
The gameplay in Sid Meier's Civilization®: Beyond Earth™ is two fold. Firstly, there is the world map, where the player will manage cities, build armies, research technology, and conduct diplomacy with other factions, among other actions. The sweeping map can be overwhelming at first for new players, as can the number of options and menus available. The game features a somewhat simplistic politics system, which varies greatly depending on what the RNG rolls. For example, while a player playing the American Reclamation Corporation (ARC) faction will vie for control of the senate against other patriarchy families attempting to avoid civil war while using intrigue to assasinate or slander opposing politicians, a Slavic sponsor will focus on proving that their warlord is worthy of leading the faction, to avoid an uprising from vassals. The characters participating in politics can also be appointed generals to lead your factions armies, gaining them fame, respect and experience. While the generals and troops of these armies will differ, the army can develop useless traditions, which do nothing.
The second part of Sid Meier's Civilization®: Beyond Earth™'s gameplay is experienced on the A.I. turn processing. When multiple A.I. need to conduct a turn, processing will commence. Usually this will take 2 to 5 minutes. This processing can be highly enjoyable as you may spend your time alt tabbed out of the application on activites you actually enjoy. Infantry, rangers, robots and artillery must all be moved in cinematic fashion.  Sid Meier's Civilization®: Beyond Earth™'s sound design, in terms of music, sound effects and voice acting all add to the intensity and excitement of the process.
The good:
Sid Meier's Civilization®: Beyond Earth™'s large scale battle's can be extremely fun. Seeing your planned tactics play out can often make one feel very strategically capable and outsmarting the AI with well thought out hidden units or a timed flank with robot can be satisfying. The sound design, along with some of the unit animations and a camera which aims to get you into the thick of things can make for an involving experience. The unit variety in Sid Meier's Civilization®: Beyond Earth™ is also a plus, with an astounding 3 different visuals based on your choice of the 3 affinities, and seeing how your army fares against foreign factions and adapting new tactics can be interesting. Unit abilities are also a plus. The multiplayer aspect of the game, while simple, is still enjoyable and provides a fun challange, though faction balance is still debatable.
The bad:
The world map in Sid Meier's Civilization®: Beyond Earth™ is not as engaging as in previous titles and feels dumbed down and simplified, while simultaneously seeming overwhelming for newbies, the food and populace happiness features, can still be frustrating and ballbreaking. The game's graphics can be best described as hit and miss. Sometimes, the game makes for eyecandy with a well timed shot, other times, the graphics seem lackluster and outdated. The AI, like in other installments, can seem incapable at times, providing no real challange and making outright stupid moves, including having bad formations in battle, denouncing you for so much as moving a unit within 10 tiles of their border or using no tactical finesse and simply rushing forward or standing still. Other issues with the game stem from the removal of features in previous titles, such as everything, making Sid Meier's Civilization®: Beyond Earth™'s characters less personal and seem more like generic numbers.
In conclusion, while still a solid game at core Sid Meier's Civilization®: Beyond Earth™ has many small gripes which deter from an amazing experience. The game can feel simple at times, and I predict in seeing the number of DLC rise. I would recommend purchasing this game when it doesn't suck.

I will recommend it, because I enjoy playing it – but it has a lot of flaws :(
I did actually enjoy the game, and I have also won both games I have played… maybe that is why :P – anyway, I can surely follow why people are complaining.
What I like about the game:
•	I love the theme (music, art, new-age-space-journey).
•	I love the new Tech-tree, especially that it is not linear but more dynamic
•	I like the idea behind Affinities, and that they is a mix of your nations behavior towards this new world, your military units and your option for winning the game (victory condition)
•	I like the critters/aliens in this game (they are more interesting than the barbarians in the old games) – however there is something about them that I dislike.
•	I love the small ingame quests that you will get, and I do also enjoy the virtues
•	I do also like the units in this game, however I want more…
What I dislike about the game:
•	I dislike the “favor”-system that you can have with an opponent. In a game an opponent owed my like 12 favors, however my opponent disliked me, and would never help me if I for instance wanted war against another opponent. The trade of was like, I will get 1 or 2 favors from you, and you will at this giving point get 2-8 strategic resources from me – when I tried to turn in all these favors they were worth nothing, like 1 energy (similar to 1 gold) pr. favor.
•	The logic behind the AI’s friendly/neutral/hostile behavior seems not to exist.
•	 As I can read, if you lose, - the game just stops without any information (which I can imagine can be a blast after several hours of gaming).
•	I am disappointed of the wonder-movies, I also miss seeing my city like in the good old civ days.
•	The aliens (critters/barbarians) of this new world seems to be a little too passive, and quite fast they become obsolete against your military units.
•	The game does lack some information through the game, and you have to keep track of everything by opening windows or using the F1-F12 keys. ;)
•	I never thought I would say this, but combat seems a little meaningless, due to the fact, that it is quite easy to defend yourself with city-missile-defense, a stationed rocket battery, and a few city improvements + maybe a hub.
•	It lacks content, in my opinion, I would prefer more units, more playable races/roles, more movies, more different terrain (one mentioned different planets), a larger techtree, more improvements… (That is just typically me, and can always be added).
There is prolly a lot of stuff I like/dislike about this game... but oh well..
Conclusion:
Well I guess it is a little disappointing compared to the other civ games, however I see a great potential in it, so hopefully they will fix it…
I enjoy playing it … I really do, but recommending this game is a little vague, since I am unsure that you will like it as much as I do…

Q*bert might be my favorite of the classic arcade games of my youth. I love the mind-bending perspective and the puzzle-game aspect to getting all the cubes lit correctly.
But this version is a tragedy. I got it on sale for barely more than a dollar, and it wasn't worth it.
I figured it was worth a few dollars just to have the original game on hand. But the classic arcade version is completely mangled, with oddly fuzzy graphics and muted sound effects. It controls ok, but there's something really off about the emulation here, and you can find better ports elsewhere.
The "rebooted" version is criminal. It's not actually clear that the developer has any understanding of what made the original game so brilliant to begin with. The transition to hexagonal platforms is perplexing for a number of reasons. Apart from destroying the three-way symmetry of the original pryamid (which is what allowed for enemies like Ugg and Wrong-Way to behave the way they did), it also means that Q*bert can choose from six different directions instead of the original four, and the controls are not remotely up to the task. They are mushy and imprecise, and going in the right direction feels like a matter of chance. You'll be fed up well before you bother to notice how boring and poorly animated the enemies are.
The game also comes with unforgiveable user interface problems. Despite being a simple reboot of an arcade game, the menus navigate poorly with a controller. And if you're playing on something like Steam Link without a mouse handy, you'll have to deal with a cursor arrow sitting in the middle of the screen unless you grab the mouse and move it out of the way first.
I love Q*bert, and I think he deserves a return to the spotlight (apart from being dejected and homeless in Wreck It Ralph). But it's not going to happen if he keeps getting plastered across broken software like this. A shoddy effort that wouldn't even be worth adding to your library if it were free.

Great game if you like operating equipment otherwise this game fails to deliver as a true farming simulator game.  This game should be called a farm equipment simulator as the farming aspect is remedial at best.  A true farming sim should involve all aspects of farming and not just planting and harvesting.
The financial aspect of the game is so simplistic that you might as well sell at the closest place available.  If you do decide to sell while the prices are up you will quickly find the prices change so fast that they will probably be lower by the time you reach a selling point.
The controls are clunky.  You can use your mouse to steer while walking but once you are inside a piece of equipment you are limited to WASD or a game pad with no option to use the mouse.
The world itself is empty and lifeless.  There is some traffic on the roads and some people walking around but they are in a line and walking or driving in circles.  There is really no interaction with anything.  The learning curve for the equipment is steep and unforgiving.  Not sure why there is a day and night cycle because you can't rest in your house.  There are no upgrades to your farm except to the equipment.
This game is not unlike SimCity (2013) in that the graphics are good, but there was not attention to detail or game complexity.  I would rather play SimFarm from the 1993 then this uninspiring game.  Save your money!

Playing Shadow Warrior is a weird experience, it starts nice, you quickly get inside the action you have two likeable characters a nice melee system a okey variety of enemies, so pretty much a good recipe for a fun time. Not really...
Again I have to underline that liked playing SW on the beginning, as I said, it got you right inside the action and you were slicing and shooting things to your heart content. But with time, the game showed her gameplay problems, which I will try to list in here:
1.Guns
The game has a good variety of guns, from a revolver to a rocket launcher, no complains here. The problem I have with them is that they don't have any "kick" to them, every gun feels like a peashooter, which makes them just plain boring to use.
2.Difficulty
Now, the game has 4 levels of difficulty. I started playing on normal but about half way thru I felt that I can go two levels higher. It's importent to understand that I don't have any problem with hard games but they need to be fair and making all enemies bulletsponges is just stupid. The devs clearly didn't understand that more enemies doesn't equal more challenge.
3.Level desing
First few levels were nice looking, they weer going for the japanese style architecture, but then it all fall down. Later on we were playing in plain looking cities, harbors, ships, warehouses it got boring quickly. In addition to that some levels were really long and very mileading. Sometimes I didn't were to go and there is no argumentation that this is a "Old-School Shooter", they are just badly made levels.
4.Boss fights
These are the cherry on top of a cake that made me quit while being 2/3 thru the game. The bosses are just horrible. They look okey but they are HUGE bullet sponges and just plain boring to fight with. Also they are badly desinged, and you can only kill them using bullets, which means you have to use guns and they have thier onw problems.
Overall I still liked this game weirdly enough, It had a nice cast that was making okey jokes (unfortuently they got stale after a while). The melee system is nice. The katana had some cool skills I have never seen before. But there just too many mistakes that were inside the game that I just cannot recommend the game. I still haven't touch upon the progression system that was very average.The story and optimization were fine, nothing to add here.
In conclusion, I do not recommend buying this game, maybe some SW fans will find enjoyment in this but I found this Shooter to be just plain average and boring in it's execution

I thought this game was pretty damn awesome. It reminded me a lot of the reboot of DOOM; that game was better for a lot of reasons, but that doesn't mean this one wasn't fun.
So, some of the good things: the sword is fun to use. There are plenty of ways to get health back, even in the middle of a fight, but there is no passive healing. It's a longer game than I was expecting, so you get your money's worth. Dismemberment is pretty good, makes you feel more powerful.
Now, the bad things. There are three mini-boss-type enemies, that are essentially big guys who walk around and let you shoot them for a couple minutes while little guys annoy you. In a game like DOOM, I felt like that worked, because you had big guns for the big guys, and they weren't all that big. Here, it feels like the opposite; big guys are bullet sponges, and a lot of the time you don't have any special guns for taking them out. Add to that the fact that all of their melees do damage randomly (that is, if I'm behind you, I'm sure there's a reason you lunging forward hurts me, but I certainly can't figure it out), and things tend to get annoying. Also, as other reviewers have said the map design isn't all that good, DOOM kept things interesting with verticality but this was more a case of flat rooms and corridors with walls to hide behind sometimes.
In summary, this is a genre I like. Sort of a throwback to the 'good old days' of first-person shooters, but with some new stuff thrown in. It's not a perfect game, but I enjoyed it, and I'll definitely look into playing the sequel.

With all of the garbage triple-A FPS games coming out each year, it's refreshing to see one take a few chances, and not take itself too seriously. However, Shadow Warrior does have its flaws that make it almost unplayable.
The melee combat is, in my opinion, the centerpiece of Shadow Warrior. Although it feels a bit "squishy" before you unlock any karma powers, once you have some actual tools at your disposal, it's actually a blast. For a bit.
Cutting through endless waves of relatively stupid demons is enough to entertain the player for a while, but there's a certain viscerality and tension-building that is very clearly missing. The maps are boring, and encounters are done on very level playing fields. Lo Wang has the ability to dash and sprint short distances, but that's about it as far as movement goes. In short, you will never find yourself jumping in this game. It's useless. After playing for a while, many fights against the greater demons become a repetitive cycle of kiting and slashing.
And by repetitive, I mean it. The only insane thing about the Insane difficulty was the amount of health some of the demons had. With every enemy attack being relatively easy to dodge (and on the off chance you DO get hit, you have an ability to heal with a channeling spell) the hardest part of the game is killing off the smaller mobs just so they don't block you to death. And after the hard part is over, you're tasked with slashing at the big dumb demon for 5 minutes with your butterknife. Boss fights take a literal (no joke) hour of constant shooting to down. It's almost comical how incorrect the pacing is. However, I can't speak for the easier difficulties.
Now, I would have actually been fine with the ridiculously tanky bosses, if the game actually let you use your sword on them. Because as it stands, it is impossible to kill any of the bosses using the sword (the most fun part of the game). There is a rather encompassing array of standard FPS weapons (including a crossbow, rocket launcher, whatever), but each of the weapons feels so ineffectual you are compelled to use the sword to have any fun. In fact, at the beginning of the game when you do pick up a pistol, it deals so little damage and feels so inaccurate that I thought it was an intentional design choice to convey the message: "USE THE SWORD INSTEAD, IDIOT," kind of like in Mirror's Edge. But alas, you're lost at sea with a broken paddle (or in this case, a BB gun) and your only way home, so you can play the REAL game, is to hold down LMB for 55 minutes.
The story is better than most.
The humor is cringey at times, and hilarious at others. Hoji, a clever and quipping spirit that you befriend, by and far carries the game's dialogue and makes it endurable.
All in all, Shadow Warrior seems to try to do what DOOM 2016 succeeded at: be a kickass, lightspeed, demonslaying simulator. It's just a shame that in this game, everybody that lives in Hell has adamantium flesh and blood.

Well... I'll give you few simple reasons and then let you to find out other reasons for yourself, ok?
Do not pre-order AAA games. Never. Please. You are supporting the wrong brain part of gamebusiness suits.
And be careful, whet it comes to all the "92 years in early alpha but pay-the-full-price please" games as well.
Luckily, Novus Inceptio is neither of these things. It's just a game with a huge potential.
All the usual fun stuff is already here: you can explore, fight, craft, build (=make your own house), farm, cook, level-up, be a botanist, forage  and so on. Unlike many other games, this time it's also made very well. For example crafting is so complex it even reminded me Wurm.

One of my favorite CIv titles to date (fav being Alpha Centauri, CIv 3 PTW, Civ 4 BTS). Most fun I've had playing Civ multiplayer in years. I've logged about 50 hours in multiplayer, completing 6 matches, and am absolutely in love with the title. Compared to the vanilla CIv 5 launch this is a vastly superior title.
There are SIGNIFICANT changes to gameplay mechanics that are enough to make the gameplay experience very refreshing for veterans of Civ 5. Here are some of them that I've found to be a great improvement over Civ 5:
+ The existence of aliens which serve as very strong barbarians help deter rapid expansion and promotes a healthier and tigher midgame rather than seeing one player or AI running away with the lead. Fall From Heaven 2 veterans (one of the best Civ mods of all time) will find aliens to still be too easy/lenient on the player but will enjoy the overall change.
+ City strength and hitpoints are much lower and require significant investment to improve. This makes warfare faster and keeps players in check from only rushing econ/tech.
+ Orbital layer units and vastly improved combat system. If the new combat system was a mod for Civ 5, it could be called Civ: Combat Evolved.
+ The new affinity system: I absolutely love this system. Each of the three affinities in the game have their own distinct strengths and weaknesses, but are still comprehensive enough to not be blatantly overpowered or deficient in some aspect. For example, even though you might think Supremacy is all about warfare, they actually have quite strong research options (via harnessing of special firaxite buildings) as well as economy options (terraforming satellites to spawn new resources onto your tiles). Whereas Harmony, which at first glance seems to be non-miltiaristic, has the strongest melee unique units in the game, but are deficient in regards to ranged combats.
+ Revamped tech tree that is closely linked to the affinity system. The way it's setup actually promotes hybridization of affinities - which is intentional by design AFAIK since affinity unique units can utilize other affinities to upgrade.
+ The new search functions and search filters are quite excellent, especially in the tech tree. You can even filter by victory condition, or search specific units and buildings to be highlighted in tech tree.
+ The new victory conditions that are linked to the affinitiy system are thematic, flavorful, and well balanced for multiplayer. They all require placing a wonder onto an actual tile on the map which can be destroyed by other players and sets the stage for some truly awesome multiplayer battles.
+ Quest system that allows you to adapt your buildings to your current needs in a given game.
+ Overall atmosphere of the game is hearkens back to Alpha Centauri and the planet customization is superb.
+ Threaded rendering support
There are a few gripes I do have with the game, but I believe these will be sorted out with patches or expansions in due time:
- Trading requires too much micromanagement currently. You have to renew convoys/trade vessels after a certain period of turns, which is extremely tasking in the mid-late game when you have lots of cities and lots of trade routes.
- Multiplayer netcode seems to be slightly improved over Civ 5, but still needs more work.
- Contact Victory is too easy to achieve compared to the other victory conditions.
- Only 8 "factions" on release = bare minimum to populate an 8 player map with unique civilizations. Fewest civs at release since the original Civilization.
- I miss civilization specific unique units.
- AI is quite poor at using anti-orbit strikes.
- Miasma sometimes blends in too well with terrain features.
- UI and filters could use some tweaking.
- Weird texture glitches immediately following multiplayer resyncs.

Ever thought how would it be if you were the last human on Earth? well, this is your chance to try and see how would it be.
Although the game is still on early access and has a long way until becoming a finished product, it offers a lot of fun and enjoyment. And lots of hoarding opportunities!
Pros:
- the most responsive, friendly and dedicated devs one can find
- beautiful graphics
- interesting concept and background story
- endless resources to be hoarded, stored, processed, transmuted, turned into useful, less useful, fun, useless, needed, not needed, random items
- crazed pumpkins and wicked witches (yes, yes, I know Halloween is over)
- the most responsive, friendly and dedicated devs one can find
- constant optimizations, updates and bugs fixing, sometimes in a matter of hours from being reported
- in-depth crafting system
- awesome crafting interface, one of the best (if not THE best) I have ever seen
- large variety of skills (some less or at all useful, but again, game is in early access stage, so countless future opportunities and functionalities to be added)
- seasonal events and rewards
- small quests to help players advance easier and understand game mechanics
- did I mention the most responsive, friendly and dedicated devs one can find?
Cons:
- you are all alone
- not a very big map to explore, and no dynamic changes to the actual map
- relatively hard to use building system, "bulky" and not so "friendly"
- no high end content (yet), once you maximize your main gathering/crafting skills, most you can do is build, moan, demolish, build again, moan harder or just moan more melodious
- no terraforming, no trees regrowing, no animal husbandry (taming, breeding), no vehicles or mounts
- limited cooked food recipes (good thing I like mushrooms!)
- slow processing raw materials
- still quite intensive clicking, right-clicking, carpal tunnel clicking, mouse-torturing clicking, more clicking
- no female characters and no character customization at all
One in all, the game is a little (unpolished) gem, with big possibilities, highly depending on players' support, suggestions and interest in the game.
Again, the dev team, as small as it is, does a terrific job and has an outstanding attitude, always ready to improve features, fix bugs, help new and confused players, add new content, listen to rants and generally being as involved as they can be.
If I recommend the game? with both hands!
For the price of a pizza or two, you're going not only to have a great time exploring, roaming, finding a place of your own, dying, eating mushrooms, building a house or three, sewing your own clothes, but you can also contribute to the future growth of the game and have the chance of seeing your suggestions turned into features and being added to the game.
Oh, and don't forget the opportunity of becoming a little (or a little more) addicted!

Right up front, I would say that Beyond Earth is a pretty good Civ 5 mod. That is obviously bad in some ways, good in others.
BE should have been a standalone expansion to Civ 5. One where you can continue with BE as the final era in Civ 5(either on Earth or transitioning to the new planet), or where you could simply spawn the new planet map as you currently do in BE.
The Good:
The quest system is good, and even better in how it lets you personalize your buildings. The building customization is something all Civ games could use, and could probably be expanded upon.
I like how there are many buildings that you can't build because of the route that you have taken in the tech web. I also like how you can still get all those buildings if you play a game long enough.
The orbital layer is well done(and should be added to Civ 5). I especially like when I can plant satellites that make resources appear. The AI also seems to make good use of satellites when invading you, at least initially.
I like the synergies found in the Virtue screen, and the general bonuses you get therein.
The Espionage system is generally interesting and useful.
The theme, style, and ideology of the Affinities works pretty well.
Having sub-techs in the tech web is good.
Could Be Improved:
Miasma is super annoying. Does every world have to have it? Need a map option to control it's appearance; everything between no miasma and complete global coverage.
Aliens... First, we need a map option to set the quantity of aliens or remove them altogether. Second, we need more than one type of alien. I am tired of fighting bugs after only one game. Maybe the next world could be filled with dinosaurs, or monkeys, or none at all, etc.
The terrain textures are very bland. I shouldn't have to stare at the map very hard or read tooltips to figure out what kind of terrain a tile is supposed to have.
The unit upgrade system is pretty boring. I like the affinity tie in with the style changes, but generally the system is too bland in terms of actual upgrades.
Unit names(Build Queue UI). My build queue is a wall of meaningless affinity specific names. Put the basic unit type somewhere in the name of the unit.
When I research vertical farms, I expect my farms to, you know, go vertical.
It seems like your satellites will only add resources to un-improved tiles. This makes me want to raze my entire empire so I can seed resources on those tiles.... Just let the resources seed under my farms.
The Bad:
New with BE
The Tech Web. It is futuristic looking, it has the sub-techs that I like, and it lets you go in any direction. The failing the tech web has is in organization and display of information. First of all, the web should be generally organized around the affinities. If I am going Supremacy, I shouldn't have to study half the tech web just to figure out my next move. I should be able to study a general area of the web, and then if I want to go outside of that, I can look elsewhere. I am not saying all supremacy goodies have to be in that one section, but most should be. Second, even if it isn't a tree, the whole thing should generally move in one direction so that you can look at each tier of techs with each other. If I am on the third or fourth tier of techs, I have to scroll all over this stupid web just to compare the competing options. Third, figuring out what each tech has to offer is a severe pain. The neat little icons you guys created just don't do the job of information relay. You need better icons, colored icons depending on type, and icons that visually show what affinity they belong to. Basically each icon requires a mouseover, and combined with the dozen other techs you need to study every 3 turns, this is very annoying.
Trade. This system is so micromanagement heavy. Why do I have to resend each trade route every few turns? With only 15 cities, 45 trade routes pinging off every half dozen turns with the horrible UI for choosing where each trade route will go next... This needs to be fixed. Trade is so simple in this game that it might as well be fire and forget. If players want to min/max this thing then give them the option to drop and remake routes.
Unit Management. Is there even a screen to manage units? Do I have to scour the map for idle workers? Can we get some worker automate options that is more intelligent than "Don't remove what is already there."?
The lack of any governmental system. You have 3 religions and no government. If the Civs are supposed to be your government, you need a full Virtues-like tree just for the government aspects. The current virtues are more economy based than government.
Siege weapons have to be set up? What kind of ridiculous reversion is this? I know you can get those late game upgrades that remove that requirement, but still. I can see why you wouldn't want players using them, with 1UPT making them godlike, but this isn't how you fix that.
Air Warfare is extremely weak and disappointing for such a futuristic era. Perhaps it was too strong in Civ 5, but it is pretty disappointing that more thought wasn't put into this.
No nukes or orbital super weapons? What kind of pansy future is this? The planet carver is useful but hardly awe inspiring.
Old from Civ 5
Diplomacy. When I see diplomacy text left over from Civ 5 it leaves me wondering why there wasn't a single person on the dev team with enough passion and an hour of free time to even make this a little bit better.
AI still doesn't know how to wage war on a 1 Unit per Tile battlefield.
The map generator. It has all the same failings as Civ 5 with some new map templates thrown in. Not enough map creation options for the player.
Why is it that such an advanced civilization still can not perform any useful task with a mountain?
Specialist management is still a pain in the butt.

Seria Hitman od początku swojego istnienia była produkcją wymagającą. Nie wystarczyło jej włączyć i po prostu przejść, kazała poznać się od każdej strony. Wszystkie misje, lokacje, przeciwników – gra wymuszała zaznajomienie się ze wszystkim i dokładnie przygotowanie się do zadania tak, jak na profesjonalistę przystało. Nie była jednak niesprawiedliwa – odpłacała się za swoje wysokie wymogi równie wysoką jakością. Wielka swoboda w osiąganiu celu, ciekawe zadania, wyraźny bohater. Taka mieszanka zaowocowała sporym gronem fanów i niezmiennie pozytywnymi ocenami. Czy kolejna część serii jest godna swoich poprzedniczek?
Największe obawy fanów wiązały się z trailerami i screenami, które prezentowały głównie akcję, krycie się za osłonami i jeszcze więcej akcji. Mnie też owa wizja Agenta 47, który pruje zza winkla seriami z karabinu niemało przeraziła, gdyż przed moimi oczami ukazała się groza w postaci Sama Fishera z granatami. Uspokajam jednak wszystkich, którzy moje lęki podzielali – nowy Hitman jak najbardziej jest przeciwny takiemu gameplayowi! Co więcej, zachęca do przechodzenia gry w sposób, który nie pozostawia po sobie choćby cienia obecności, jak to Cichy Zabójca działać powinien. Co więcej, w prawym górnym rogu mamy okienko, które wszystkie nasze działania punktuje, nagradzając za bezszelestne parcie do przodu. Wszelkie wykrycie czy napadnięcie kogoś, kto nie jest celem, skutkuje ujemnymi punktami, zmniejszającymi nasze szanse na zajęcie jakiegokolwiek sensownego miejsca w światowym rankingu – o mniejszej satysfakcji już nie wspominając.
Choć sposób ten pokazuje nam, jak bardzo dobrymi Hitmanami jesteśmy i jakie działania są pozytywne, a jakie złe, czułem się przez większość gry, jakbym występował w jakimś teleturnieju. Osobiście wolałbym, aby nasze działania były podsumowane na koniec misji, jednak to tylko taka drobna uwaga.
Otrzymywane punkty nie tylko zapewniają miejsce w rankingu, ale również odblokowują „ulepszenia” naszego zabójcy. Choć nie mamy wpływu na ich kolejność, to nie przeszkadza to aż tak bardzo, gdyż prawdę mówiąc nie mają tak wielkiego znaczenia dla rozgrywki. Należą do nich takie bonusy, jak lepsza celność podczas prowadzenia ostrzału, czy większy poziom instynktu (o którym za chwilę). Dużo przyjemniejsze są natomiast osiągnięcia, dołączone do każdego zadania. Choć większość z nich to „odnajdź wszystkie przedmioty, które można podnieść” znajdują się wśród nich również takie, co potrafią przekonać do kilkukrotnego przechodzenia misji, gdyż nie wszystkie można osiągnąć za jednym podejściem. Należą do nich osiągnięcia przyznawane za przejście całego zadania w swoim garniturze lub wręcz przeciwnie – przebierając się za wyznaczoną liczbę osób. Jest to dobry pomysł na uprzyjemnienie rozgrywki i zapewnienie jej dłuższej żywotności.
Agent 47 w tej odsłonie wyposażony został w coś, co twórcy nazwali instynktem. Ta nadludzka umiejętność pozwala na bardzo wiele, gdyż nie tylko jest w stanie pokazać nam ścieżki patroli i celu do zlikwidowania, ale również podświetla wszystkie osoby w okolicy, umożliwiając ujrzenie je przez ściany oraz zaznacza punkty, w których znajdują się przedmioty przydatne w wykonaniu misji. Ułatwia to grę na tyle, że osoby będące weteranami produkcji, chcące się zabawić w starym, dobrym stylu – samemu szukając sposobów na ubicie celu - odsyłam do opcji, gdzie umiejętności te można powyłączać, pozostawiając jedynie interesujące nas elementy instynktu. Zdolności Hitmana mamy szansę używać niemal bez ograniczeń.
Jest jeden wyjątek - gdy będąc przebranym za np. policjanta, przyglądają nam się inni stróże prawa i włączymy w tym momencie instynkt, to jego pasek będzie w dość szybkim tempie spadać. Naładować go możemy wykonując jakieś działania w trakcie misji, które przybliżają nas do osiągnięcia celu.
Jest to kolejna nowość w serii – wcześniej będąc przebranym, mogliśmy niemal bez problemu poruszać się wśród ludzi. Teraz działa to tylko na osoby nie należące do grupy, której ubranie mamy na sobie, co wymusza częstsze skradanie się – nawet będąc w przebraniu – i wykorzystywania osłon terenowych do ukrywania się przed ich wzrokiem.
Wiele osób grających w nowego Hitmana, narzeka strasznie na wysoki poziom trudności produkcji. Stwierdzenie to jest prawdą, gdyby odnieść je do innych gier pojawiających się teraz masowo na rynku. Jeśli jednak mamy za sobą poprzedniczki serii – zapewniam, że jest to najprostsza część, w jaką grałem dotychczas. Niemal każde zadanie podzielone jest na kilka fragmentów, pomiędzy którymi mamy zapis, na dodatek można znaleźć porozrzucane punkty kontrolne, pozwalające cofnąć się do nich w razie porażki. Jest to dużym ułatwieniem, jakiego w poprzednich częściach ze świecą szukać (a i cała latarnia morska nie pomogła). Do tego wszystkiego dochodzi instynkt, który nie będąc wyłączonym, niemalże prowadzi nas za rączkę, więc naprawdę nie mam pojęcia skąd biorą się wszystkie skargi na temat zbyt wysokiego poziomu.
Dla tych, którzy dalej utrzymują, że jest za trudno, dodam tylko, że instynkt pozwala zaznaczyć kilku wrogów naraz i patrzeć jak Hitman kolejno ich ściąga, jednego za drugim – co żywo przypomina „Mark & Execute” ze Splinter Cella. Użyłem tego tylko raz podczas samouczka i nigdy więcej nie sięgałem do tej plugawej możliwości… To przecież nie jest gra, gdzie się zabija (kogoś więcej niż główny cel).
Nowy silnik graficzny Glacier 2, to kawał dobrej roboty. Pozwala osiągnąć naprawdę ładną grafikę nawet na gorszych komputerach i nie tracąc tak wiele ze swojego uroku. Co więcej, zdolny on jest do wygenerowania całej armii ludzi i zaobserwować można to na screenach. Mało która gra pochwalić się może tak wielką ilością wyświetlanych ludzi bez spadku płynności. Masa zastosowanych efektów graficznych niemal wygląda odrobinę śmiesznie, gdy od łysiny Agenta 47 odbija się cała paleta barw, dosłownie oślepiając gracza, jednak blask ten wygląda naprawdę nieźle i ma swój urok. Szczególnie dobrze prezentuje się w silnym deszczu, gdy całe ulice są mokre i odbijają światło.
Udźwiękowienie również jest bardzo dobre i nie mam do niego najmniejszych zastrzeżeń. Jedynie brakowało mi Ave Maria w menu głównym, jednak nowy motyw również pasuje do gry i wyzwala w graczu emocje. Aktorstwo stoi na profesjonalnym poziomie, do niczego nie jestem w stanie się przyczepić w wersji angielskiej. W polskiej natomiast wyszło średnio, jednak jestem wielkim przeciwnikiem pełnego spolszczania gier – w końcu jak ktokolwiek mógłby naśladować głos Agenta 47, niezależnie w jakim języku?
Nowa część to jak najbardziej stary, dobry Hitman z kilkoma przeróbkami, które nie pozwolą zostać serii w tyle. W przeciwieństwie do Splinter Cella, zmiany te są dobre i gra nadal pozostaje skradanką, w której trzeba myśleć i planować, zanim podejmie się jakąkolwiek decyzję. Choć przyznaję, że w Blood Money czułem się najlepiej, to jednak Absolution jest na tyle dobry, że naprawdę bez wyrzutów sumienia postawić go można obok poprzedniczek.

For all I’ve wanted to, The Stanley Parable is... Well, a difficult game to review. It’s a very unique experience, one that tosses many things at you at a rapid rate; it’s mostly comedic, but also surprisingly dark at some points, and surprisingly deep and philosophical at others. The main problem with reviewing it, however, is that to talk about many aspects of it would be to simply ruin the experience for you – it’s something you really should be approaching nigh-on blind to get the most out of. Let it be known from the outset, then, that this is an experience that’s worth checking out.
Let me try and give you a little more detail if I’ve piqued your curiosity; you play as Stanley, a guy stuck in a mundane job, his only company being a mysterious narrator dictating every element of your life. As events unfold, the story twists and turns based on the choices you make, with the narrator reacting and responding accordingly to the many weird situations that can occur as you head towards one of the game’s multiple endings.  To say more about the story would ruin the point, but trust me when I say the situations you end up in are going to mess with your head big time.
For instance, it’s highly likely that on more than one occasion the narrator will suddenly pipe up and voice exactly what you’ve been thinking quietly to yourself for the past five minutes, in moments that startle you out of any autopilot mode you may have been settling into. At other moments, he might successfully manipulate you into doing something without you even realising it, or point out nonsensical or oddities in the world that end up throwing you for a loop. There’s one ending in particular which completely freaked me out, whereupon the narrator span off into a monologue which perfectly and eerily predicted what I was doing in the game at the time. There are loads of clever moments like this scattered throughout; things that can invoke an actual notable response out of you, and stick with you long after you’ve actually turned the game off. That’s something that even triple A titles can’t pull off consistently, and is therefore something to be commended.
The Stanley Parable’s not perfect, however, and there are a few criticisms that I personally feel can be warranted towards the game. The first is that I feel there are a few areas in the game whereupon whatever the game is trying to achieve just ends up not having the impact it might be aiming for, if indeed it makes any impact at all. This can be for a few reasons – sometimes things are just confusing, at others it feels like the game is trying to be too clever for its own good. For all The Stanley Parable does end up hitting certain notes perfectly, others do end up falling a little flat. It’s also another one of those titles where you’ll probably play it for a couple of hours at most and then never touch it again, so that’s worth bearing in mind if you’re sitting on the fence about things; waiting for a sale wouldn’t be the most ridiculous of things to do, if you were so inclined to do that.
Overall, though, The Stanley Parable is certainly a very unique and distinctive experience, and one that’s well worth checking out even if you have the slightest curiosity about it. It’s not perfect by any stretch of the imagination, but it’s something that’s nigh-on impossible to remain stoic to, and for that alone it’s worthy of your attention.
