I so highly recomend this game/sandbox. If you are looking for a game to tax your ability to survive, this is probably not for you (unless you don't like to pay attention to item stats, then you're likely going to bleed to death.) The mobs, while beautiful to look at, are fairly easy to dominate (at least up to generation 15, my current.) If on the other hand you are looking for a preaty, open world in which to build and craft this is awesome! Very grindy with a steep learning curve, but once you mount that curve (which happens fairly quick if you use the advanced crafting and pay attention to the stats) the view is incredable. Though you get all the basics; axe, sword, knife, armor, etc... for the housing/decoration items you have to go out and loot the 'box from creators' or fish them up. "Hey I found a purple curtain for my windows, oh I don't have the purple dye recipe, or the red dye recipe to even make the purple when I do find it." Found the recipe? Have you farmed the mats? Keep grinding.
Tips -
1  Use the basic crafting for you first set of weapons, tools, armor, etc... then go into the advanced and start thinking about what stats you want/need for various items. Some things you will want more than one of, Eg. a 'gathering' knife and a 'crafting' knife. Build a good crafting hammer early and keep upgrading it as you can, fewer lost material is time saved.
2  Transmute, transmute, transmute! When your out looking for that one-more-rhino-pelt for you new leggings have A-2A transmuting the next tier of iron for your next better sword. Also use the advanced crafting and look closely at how the stats will be effected, especially for pelts. Two wolf pelts don't give the same stats as one wolf and one deer. The same goes for branches, a T2 cherry from ((T0cherry+T0cherry)+(T0cherry+T0cherry)) will not be the same as ((T0cherry+T0oak)+(T0apple+T0elm)).
3  Burn low level mats leveling up your skills so you don't destroy (yep, that's a thing) as much higher tier material.
4  Build a good well and harvest/replant your crops (with a good rake of course.) A lot of time transmuting can be saved by getting higher tier materials to begin with. One exception seems to be metals and the 'plantable' mining nodes. I have not seen tiers for these, you just need a better pickaxe and mining skill to getter higher tiers of these. A second possible and rather limited exception is trees (which are a finite resource, they don't just regrow/respawn themselves, I highly recommend spending the age point(s) to get the chance to harvest seedlings unless you like barren landscapes.) While planting and harvesting higher tier trees gives higher tier logs, branches, leaves, bark, resin, and seedlings, transmuting branches up (as alluded to above) while time consming deffintely alows for higher stats.
5  'Harvest' every rock you come across and relish every piece of graphite you find. For me this has been the hardest resouce to come by and is needed to make steel, the alloy of choice for armor and weapons. You can buy it from the vendor stations for 400 PEK (or PEC,) but through transmutaion, that's almost 13K for one piece of just T5 Steel. The Tier system goes up to 10!
Long story short, I am loving this game. Like OMG it's 3AM I have to work in the morning, over 100hrs in the first 2 weeks loving this game. The developers apear to be hard at work with minor tweaks coming out every few days it seems. If you like watching/making numbers go up in a crafting/building game I suggest giving it a try.

Tacoma is a game developed and published by Fullbright, the same people behind Gone Home
If you loved Gone Home, then Tacoma is a definite steal. If you didn't like Gone Home... well tough
Tacoma starts with you entering a space station, in orbit between the Moon and the rest of space. Your task is to retrieve the station AI per your contract with the operating company, as well as any and all personal logs, desktop and holographic conversation records
You do this by passing around the station, playing through the recorded holograms, scrubbing back and forth to get the information you need to proceed. The world of Tacoma is dense and there's plenty of hints at a bigger picture for the universe of the game
Tacoma is a great-looking, touchingly written and brilliantly executed take on the "walking simulator" genre, where you explore an environment to reveal a story without much in the way of gameplay challenge
Of course, it's clear from early on that not everything is as it seems in this scenario. You may figure out some of what's going on before it's officially revealed, but there are definitely still some surprises in store for the shocking, thrilling ending
The game is over in less than 2-3 hours, but it's a really exciting and emotional ride through a brilliantly imagined future amd I highly recommend Tacoma, especially if you loved Gone Home before

I like a good story exploration/ambiance exploration game. Good is always subjective, of course, so my preferences not always were similar to what I heard from others. I like Dear Esther, for example, even prefer it to Everybody’s Gone to the Rapture but was mostly really bored in Gone Home. So I wasn't really that excited for Tacoma when I first heard of it. Damn, am I glad I decided to check it out, though.
Tacoma works similarly to how story exploration games usually, work, but adds a more interactive investigative element to everything, and also establishes a rather curious multi-layered mystery to the situation. You are a person sent on board a space station that suddenly got damaged and has only a few days left of oxygen, all right as the 6 people on board were getting ready to end the year of service and look into renewing their contract. Except, things look a bit off, and perhaps there was another reason for the accident, and that is something you will be investigating while watching the Augmented Reality recordings of the events on the station, following people around and watching them cope with this situation, and their normal life relationships.
It's a pretty simple setup, really, but the game is very smart about the storytelling and portioning the story bits you investigate, and also spending a lot of time on detailing every character personality. Voice acting is on point, as is the writing, and things just work together in a very nice simple way, that helps the game being very engrossing. You'll easily remember the characters, understand why they do what they do, get intrigued in their internal conflicts and then get through the whole story until its solid, if somewhat predictable (but not in a bad way), resolution in one go. Especially since the game will most likely take you under 3 hours to complete, even if you check, watch and read everything. Which some might find disappointing, but I'd say - the game lasts exactly as long as it needs to and tells as much as it needs to, so kudos to Fullbright on not doing the common mistake of adding pointless elements to the game.
If you're into story driven adventure games or story exploration titles, I would highly recommend checking Tacoma as soon as you get a chance. If you're not - hey, it's short and is a joy to play, so please do consider checking it out anyway.

Crafting - This is a unique system and once you discover the Advanced Production section, you will understand the impact of raw material bonuses. Every item in the game has unique values according to the material. Decides whether wood is from Pine or Oak, etc. You can make really interesting items.
Construction - There is small issues with the control over here - but it is not bad for early access. But what it is interesting - that you can plan the whole construction before you can solve the raw materials. The system is modular (and there are really many components in the game, but just do not have everything available from the beginning). I built a cottage (which is a ready-made house) and slowly try to build something bigger.
Survey - the map looks like it is not very small and contains a some different climate. Where are the different animals and raw materials. Just need to add more content - but otherwise it is fine.
I am satisfied and I recommend.

I love the way Tacoma tells its story. It uses the tried-and-tested environmental storytelling of Fullbright’s first game Gone Home, yes, but this time the bulk of the narrative heavy lifting is accomplished by augmented reality wireframes playing out recordings of Tacoma’s crew all around you in real time. It’s a brilliant mechanic, one that combines the classic audio log with something more akin to theater, allowing conversations to unfold naturally as characters drift from room to room, with the player able to follow one character around, then rewind and go elsewhere to see other events that transpired at the same time. The story told with those mechanics is pretty great too, a far-future tale of AI and space stations that nonetheless feels incredibly relevant to today, with workers struggling to work together to protect their rights and their jobs as automation threatens to make them obsolete.

Beyond Earth is very perplexing to me on if I like it or not. Mechanicly speaking, it still functions like Civ V but thats to be a given since it runs on that games engine. However the tech tree and unit tree are indeed quite different.
On the good side I love the new tech tree as you can branch out in any one or all directions at your choosing. This makes tech theft actually useful as each nation is certain to have something you do not. The orbital layer is also a good consept and does add a good dimension to the game since your artillary now has more than the mere role of city bombardment. My favorite consept was that I feel they FINALLY got an economy trade system set up RIGHT. The ability to have a physical convoy go to and from cities to which can be intercepted and looted is a grand idea that works very smoothly in the game.
The dissipointment is the lack of unit diversity. For a civ game it feels lacking in this department, especially given that its grandfather Alpha Centuari had vastly more customization to it. Diplomacy also felt fully lacking as it seems to have been watered down to its most basic levels, with the fewest options that I have seen to date. What stunned me the most was the sheer lack of in game cinimatics, especially for an endgame. After so much hard work to beat the game, especially after hitting the learning curve that I did, getting only a static picture and a one paragraph congradulations was a pretty heavy let-down. Given how much they put into the intro I was expecting a great deal more for an endgame reward.
Ultimatly I do still recomend this game, its worth a play and will certainly create a timesink for many fans of the series. For me, its probably mid-way in the Civ series in terms of favorites with Civ IV beign a the top, and 2 second (purely for nostalga value). I truly do hope that the game is added upon and given additional elements that was found in Alpha Centuari, or a satisfactory mod comes avalible via the workshop.
--------
Edit: After a day of thinking about my review, I have to accept that my recomendation for yes was out of nostalga. I cannot in good concience recomend this game now, at least at the price point given. This game is ultimatly a mediocre expansion pack that should have gone for only $20, tops. What truly kills the game for me is the sheer lack of reward for completing the game, too much of a letdown for me.

This is a phenomenal pirate game. For anyone who really enjoyed Sid Meier's Pirates but wished there was more, this is the game for you. A lot of other reviews say the ships feel good to sail, and they're right. They handle smoothly and wind does make a significant impact now (I imagine in the past it didnt, I've read complaints). Ship to Ship combat is fun, once you have a steady stream of income the exotic shots become much more important. Artifacts are a nice wild-card for these engagements too. They may become formulaic in how they start (Couple ships off port bow, couple ships off starboard) the fights never get routine unless you're sticking to pirating trade routes.
There is hardly any tutorial to speak of, and the quest system is a mess that has a bad habit of stealing ~5000 gold pieces to buy important quest items without my consent, but I would still highly recommend this to people that are comfortable playing open ended games, where your next prize is a significant upgrade to your ship.

This is a great game. I was a bit worried when I first booted it up becaue I liked the Knights of Pen and Paper but I have played some RPG style games in the past that were medieval and then did the space thing and really weren't very good. I think it was Puzzle Quest that I used to love and eventually they came out with a space version which I bought but found to be way less fun and enjoyable than the medieval one. This game however does it well, there is so much I love about this game and it really hits you hard with all the nostalgic references.
I've actually never seen a game so jam packed full of references to things I love, like Anime, Sci-fi, RPG's, Cartoons and other Video Games. The first screen has so many I just love seeing them all. He-man was there, Thundercats, Dinosaurs, Star Trek / Star Wars etc. So awesome. It's easy to tell the developers love a lot of the same things as myself and seeing it all there is so cool.
The art style and graphics are gorgeous and great to look at. The music is very nice for the most part and seems to fit in perfectly with the different themes of each world. The first planet for example is a sand planet and has an awesome space-western style song, Neo-Tokyo has an awesome sort of sci-fi Chill-Ambient style music, etc. Everything is so nicely polished and fits in perfectly.
As for the gameplay it's got turn-based combat which I absolutely love. It's a little bit on the slow side and on top of that you do need to grind a little bit, but that's what many old RPG's were like. You would have to level up your guys to take out certain bosses and get farther into the game instead of just running through.
The quest system is okay, I wish it was a bit more advanced but it does the job and more variety opens up as you make it further into the campaign. The game world seems small at first but does open up as well.
One thing I wish this had was controller support. While the mouse works fine, I would love to play this type of game while being lazy on the couch and using my controller with the steam link. That would be great. It is available on the app stores for smart phones and tablets and with the way it's designed it would be perfect for touchpads as well.
First Impressions / Gameplay Video
If you are a fan of Knights of Pen and Paper or old school RPG's you would most likely enjoy this as well. While it's very similar in many ways to Knights of Pen and Paper, it plays differently and has new things to do such as space ship battles.
I would definitely recommend this to RPG fans and there are a number of different devices you can play it on as well so give it a try if you like this sort of game. It's good :)

Galaxy Of Pen & Paper is a spiritual successor of Knights of Pen & Paper, by Behold Studios. It’s a turn-based rpg game that features questing and battles. The setting is what makes it different from hundreds of similar games: the game takes you into the role of a DND player, seamlessly shifting you between the “real” world and the “space” world. At one moment, you see the game master and players actively discussing game mechanics at the table, and at the next – their alter-egos, questing through space, picking fights.
The game is packed with not-so-subtle references to other space series and puns. Writing and wordplay are the strongest moments of the game. That also means you’d need to read a lot: between battles, there are a plenty of dialogues and character interactions.
Combat is pretty straightforward: you have two battle lines on each side (3 characters on every one of them MAX). Characters take turns hitting each other. If you want to succeed in combat, you’ll have to take advantage between skill synergies. For example, you could learn a poison skill on one character, and a skill that gives attacks healing effect on the other one. Or the skill that burns poisoned enemies. There are quite a lot of combinations and that make the combat fun.
The good thing is that since you are playing as a GM and a party at the same time, you can often pick the amount of opponents that you are facing. If you get a task to defeat 4 enemies, you can split them into batches of two and fight them two times separately. The difficulty decreases, but the amount of rewards also goes down.
One new thing that has been added is space battle element. It’s a minigame that essentially involves ships throwing dice, accumulating action points that can be spent on healing/attacking. One thing that I could not find out is the way to upgrade the ship health: right as you get your ship, you get sent into optional quests that involve destroying other spaceships. There’s a catch though. You can not see the strength of the ships that you are going to fight. So when I encountered a starship with 400 hp, it quickly annihilated my 140 hp ship. This happened quite a few times. There was also no way to escape from the combat like this.
One thing that could be improved is the character progression UI. All of the skills are mixed in one box, available to see from the start, sorted by price. In my opinion, this is not a right approach, as it can get quite confusing. It’s also not so easy to distinguish between learned and not learned skills, since they all seem to be bundled together. It would have been easier to group the skills in some ways (passive / active? Class/generic? Group by effect?)
The other thing is bugs: the game have quite a good number of them. I could occasionally open the character window in inconvenient game moments and then never close it. Once I’ve started a class questline (and failed it), the savage stayed with my party and when I got another party member – it has been placed in the same position and essentially I had two characters in one slot during the combat.
Overall, $14.99 might seem like a steep price – but I say the writing and the immersive atmosphere are worth it. However, there are quite a lot of bugs, so I’m a bit hesitant. I genuinely had fun while playing it, but be prepared to encounter quite some bugs as you play. The different reviews of the game mention bugs of different severity and one of the encounered ones was quite severe, but not absolutely gamebreaking. If you don’t mind the bugs – I can recommend the game to all of the RPG fans.

I saw this game awhile ago. It looked interesting, but I was not 100% convinced it would be a good game for me. Lack of a female avatarl usually doesnt do it for this gal =p Anyways.. it went on sale and I snapped it up.
Knowing this is early access please understand my comments are based on the games current state and playability as it stands, not just on future potential. The graphics are stunning and very detailed. The lighting needs some work still in some areas, like light shafts underground at the starting temple and shiney "wet look" rocks at night.
The harvesting system is incredibly detailed. It progresses from tier 0 through tier 10, and you can transmute lower level materials to make them into better versions of themselves.
Crafting in batch lots is a plus. This is especially useful when transmuting... which you will want to do alot to get better gear and tools. To put it into perspective it takes 512 T1 materials to yield just one t10 if you use transmutation to increase its tier. This is because it is a 2/1 ratio.
The existing building blocks for housing are well rendered and are fairly easy to create. There are also premade structures, work benches, furnishings, and decor. The building system allows you to prebuild and see how your building will look before actually committing resources to it. One thing to note is that when you actually finalize your build you will have to go into it in non build mode to apply materials to each part of the modular building you designed, as opposed to applying it to the whole build at once. This can be a bit tricky if you do not have some sort of way to get up high to apply roofs and materials on tall builds as you have a limited range.
There is a small PVE element in the form of natural beasts in the world. You can die if you aren't careful but death really doesn't seem to have a penalty in the game other than the inconvenience of getting your personal A2-A unit to a cloning station. Speaking of cloning, all your possessions and knowledge gets passed down to you as you progress. Once you age to 75 years (or die) you can make a new and improved version of yourself. When you do this you get generation points which you can spend to improve your character. Age alone earns you age points which can be used to improve your abilities.
I find the game enjoyable overall, but I do feel it is VERY grindy in crafting. Transmutation takes a long time. I have literally queued up 50 combines and walked away to do other things for an hour and come back to check and see my progression. Also, I do feel it uses way too many resources right now. Point in case, 512 T1 resources to get to 1 T10 is a bit extreme IMO. Also, there are some things which can be exploited, like relogging multiple times to get chests (there is one area with NINE of them).
Overall I would say yes, get the game. It has potential to be something great. The concept is definately a nicely developed one. The backstory is great. I think the dev is progressing the game the right way, slowly and with care, rather than just rushing it out. I look forward to seeing it come into its own!

Recommended, but just barely. Solid B game. Does some things like sounds/graphics very well, but other things are just very lacking. Ill list some of them and you can decide if any of this bothers you:
- Only one save file which you cannot reload on demand making all deaths/losses irreversible. Want to back up your save? Have fun finding it in the most obscure hidden location possible on your computer (AppData -> LocalLow -> Tempest)
- So many quests at once that they really lose their meaning and you essentially sail around vising every port with a green ! or ? to progress whichever quest is present there
- No voice overs, no NPCs, no portraits, feels very lifeless
- All open world spawns are always in the exact same place. You get 2 ships to the left of you, 2 ships to the right of you, and depending which flag youre sailing, some are hostile. They spawn always at the same distance, in the same place, fighting the same way, making the game feel very grindy. You get a bit more variety in the quests but even those are always predictable
- The game is too easy. Hard early on as you learn the mechanics and how it works, but later on its just a cake walk. You are never challenged. If there is an enemy battleship there will be only one other ship on the map, you. If there are three enemy battleships then there will be 2-3 other ships (friendly) to balance the scales. Only a few missions where youre outnumbered, and those are usualy wee little ships that die easily
- Your ship fires chain fire, not salvo. Its fine for the little ships, but the big ones end up shooting for like 5 seconds, while youre steering, still hitting the target even though you may no longer have it within your line of sight. It looks stupid and unnecessarily slow
- First person melee combat is stiff and rudementary. Doesnt add much to the game. Would have been better with some top down RTS play instead
- Lots of buggy quests with poor descriptions not indicating which zone theyre even taking place in. Sometimes if you simply play too long the quests can stop working all together until you close and sign back in

A lot of noise has been made about this port if you haven't done any searching around the steam community page or checked the user reviews much. Raging nonsensical rants asside a lot of what is said is true. The lack of resolution settings, graphical settings and sound settings are not available at this point in time. This does bother me and I don't want to say I am thrilled with them being ommitted from the game. All I can really say about it is for the future FFXIII titles they bring to Steam I will hope and expect them to add these options and perhaps maybe even patching this game to add them. On my end though I have had zero crashes, bugs and only on one occurance have I had major frame drops (a quick restart of the game and all was fixed).
As far as the game itself goes, I really don't have anything but positives to say about it. First of all, the music is fantastic. I am a fairly novice FF gamer (I've played 10 fully, 11, 14 and parts of 9 and Tactics) and the music is usually one of the best parts of the game. This one does not dissappoint and might even be my favorite of the games I've played.
Next I would like to talk about how beautiful some of the zones and scenery are in this game. There have been numerous times throughout the game where I stop just to look around and soak in the environment. For a game that came out in 2009 the graphics still hold up very well and have really impressed me. A few standouts to me were Lake Bresha, Nautilus, Sunleth Waterscape, Gapra Whitewood and Sulyya Springs. There is still more game for me to play so I wouldn't be surprised to see more beautiful areas.
The characters are also a positive for me in this game. It seems to be a polarizing topic but to me all of the characters show great development and it is very interesting to find out about how the characters are connected to each other (trying to avoid spoilers here, of course). Lightning is probably my favorite of the chracters to progress. She starts out very closed-minded and standoffish but opens up into a great character.
The story is also another positive for me. There have been a few twists and outside of the first 30 minutes or so I've never felt lost. I would definitely recommend reading the data log to fill in any holes the cut-scenes may leave out or just to reassure what you just saw or heard from the characters.
A part of the game that you will either hate, like or feel indifferent to (it's impossible not to have an opinion on it) is the linearity. It is definitely a restricted game (for the most part) as to where you can go and how you get there. If you are just interested in a heavily story focused game that doesn't involve tons of exploring you will likely enjoy the game. Personally, I don't mind the linearity of it at all because I am playing for the story and have never been a fan of grinding or getting lost in huge zones with random fights popping up every few steps.
When I originally looked into the game for the console I thought the lack of control of all the characters in the combat system would be a turn-off for me. How wrong I was. The combat in this game starts off slow but really picks up the further into the game you get and is an absolute blast. Boss fights always leave me thinking how much fun it was and the need to constantly switch paradigms quickly is chaotic at times. The dificulty level heavily picks up when you get to a completely new location (again, avoiding spoilers) and has challenged me a lot. I wouldn't say the game is overly difficult to the point where you want to throw your controller at the screen but it is far from an easy game. It has a nice balance of very tough and easy fights in-between.
Anyways, sorry for the ramble but I just LOVE this game and would definitely recommend it for the price of $15.99 or more power to you if you can get it cheaper. This seems to be a polarizing game but from my end I couldn't be happier with my purchase and hope you will be happy as well if you end up purchasing this title. Can't wait for to finish the game and the series.

Arcade games from the 1970's and 1980's were simple. You had a joystick and a button that controlled your character. The skills were dependent on the game. It made for mindless entertainment that eventually expanded into the medium we hold dear. How someone thought that bringing an idea like Q*Bert into the modern era would work is beyond me.
I have nothing against old classics being revived. Pac-Man: Championship Edition is a great example of modernizing a relic and making it feel brand new. Q*Bert Rebooted is not that example. Apart from mind numbing music and horrid level design, the only thing I enjoy from this reboot are the graphics.
How you can manage to mess up the control scheme to Q*Bert really boggles my mind. Gamepad support works, but barely. Often times, you'll press the diagonal direction required to make Q*Bert jump and he won't move. Other times, you'll swear you hit up or down only to have the orange puff ball jump to his demise.
For a game that is based on the idea of jumping platforms and not falling, it fails on a basic level to provide that. If I can't reliably control my character, how am I supposed to enjoy the game? For that matter, why do all the level designs recycle ad naseum until level 37?
You would be forgiven for thinking the 40 levels included in Rebooted would all be different. At first, the game mixes up the grids and keeps you guessing. It's not necessarily great, but something different that builds into new concepts is how classics like Mario can stick around.
Instead, after level 8, the game just recycles everything. No new concepts, no different grid structures; there aren't even different color schemes. It makes for a slog of an experience that feels like you're re-enacting Groundhog's Day. The enemy AI is also seemingly random, which becomes infuriating in later levels.
The game also has no true ending. Once you finish, you are greeted to a screen of "Look for Upcoming Levels" and that's it. You can't even get closure on this waste of a game. I'd say the unlockable skins give you incentive, but they can all be acquired long before you finish the "last" level.
To top off everything, even the emulation of classic Q*Bert suffers from control problems. It has all the content, but Q*Bert seems to have a mind of his own when it comes to jumping. If I'm not mistaken, some of the sound effects are missing, too.
Really, the only reason I bought this was because of a sale price. During the Winter Sale, I saw the game for $1. I could have done worse and paid the full price, but even my $1 feels wasted. I'd recommend steering clear at all costs. Q*Bert Rebooted is a prime example of exploited nostalgia.
P.S. Be weary of the reviews on the Steam page. One is listed as IGN, but is linked to a blog post on the site. I believe that is called false advertising.

.Game play.
You can use the WASD keys or the mouse in order to guide your ship. While doing so, you have the option of watching movement via a map overview or the 3D rendered ship, which can be seen in third or first person point of view.
In ports, you can hire more men, buy supplies, and pick up quests. Quests range from fetch quests to exploring certain areas of the map. Some have a bit of story attached to them and you'll also meet new characters. You'll be rewarded money, supplies, and crew for completing quests.
Along your travels you'll face random encounters and, based on your point of view, you can handle them in different ways. If you're looking at the map overview, you can click "auto" and the battle will be resolved based on your health, crew, cannonballs available, etc. Otherwise, you can use the button in the bottom left corner in order to zoom into the 3D view and battle in real time.
Your cannons fire from the sides of your ship, which means combat consists of trying to flank your opponent while using the space bar to fire your weapons once they've been loaded. You can use the mouse or the WASD keys to maneuver, but you'll still need to fire with the space bar. You can switch ammunition on the fly, but keep in mind that will reset your reload time. Reload speed can be altered, but doing so is a matter of risk and reward: faster reload speed means lower accuracy and conversely, slower reload speed means higher accuracy.
Your ship is heavy and cumbersome (this isn't just some dinky sailboat!), so much of your time will be spent trying to find just the right positioning. It's fun, but I soon found myself hitting the auto button rather than engaging as battles can take a while to complete.
You've also got a ship log with various information:
*Faction's attitude towards you: there are various factions you'll be attempting to sway and your relationship will decide who will attack you and who won't.
*Reputation: there are five possible reputations you can have for the various things you do. For instance, the spider is combat-related. It's called "paralyzing spider" and it allows you to deal twice as much damage to enemy sails. Reputation acts as perks that develop based on your play style, essentially.
*Game Progress: this covers how much of the map you've explored, the number of quests you've done, and how many hidden goodies you've uncovered in addition to how far you've traveled.
*Economy: how much in-game currency (Piastres) you've earned in one way or another and how much you've sold.
*Combat Actions: how many cannonballs fired, how frequently you've missed, how many enemies you've destroyed, how many times you've destroyed--and so on. Nothing too out of the ordinary here.
Your logs also keep track of your active quests, and the statistics of your ship and crew.
-My one complaint would be that there's not much of a tutorial for fighting or trading or... Anything, really. Leaving the tutorial box checked in the options menu means you'll get brief messages during battle or exploration regarding what can or should be done--without an adequate description of *how* you should go about doing those things.
.Soundtrack.
The ambient sounds are great. The crash of waves and the crack of thunder are tumultuous and they reflect the name of the game rather well. You'll also hear bells ring, seagulls cry, and the occasional shout of your men. The background music leaves a bit to be desired as it's a single track that replays over and over based on the occasion (exploration versus combat, etc). The songs are appropriate for the moments they're used, sure, but I would have preferred more variety.
.Graphics/ Art Style.
Tempest is beautiful. From the falling rain to the rough, choppy waves, to the ragged, flapping cloth of your sails the game drips with style.
.Longevity.
Despite the promises of an open world, it only took me a few minutes to sail around about half the map. Still, there are plenty of quests to do, so going between islands and completing them will keep you occupied for a good while.
There's also an online mode, though I can't say much about it because I didn't try it.
.Bottom Line.
Tempest is a swashbuckling good time that will give even the landiest of land lubbers their sea legs. If you're into naval combat and exploration, I can easily recommend this game to you.

- This short documentary consists in a series of interviews with several indie developers or people from the gaming industry that talk about their work. The information presented is rather superficial, and I would have expected the story to focus more on the inevitable obstacles or struggles that a team needs to overcome during the developing process or at least their victory moments. The lack of details makes this video meaningless, unentertaining and uninteresting.
However, it does convey the fact that most of the gamers nowadays play their video games without thinking about how they are created or about how much effort the developer team had put into developing them; sometimes they are way too quick to judge or criticize thousands of hours of work, without even having solid arguments.
This is why I think that maybe watching 'The Art of Playing' might help some gamers improve this attitude and become more appreciative towards the developing process, by realizing its complexity: hours of coding, testing, designing, recording the audio tracks, putting everything together – and all this done with mainly one purpose: our entertainment.
To all the developers out there, to all the testers, designers, artists, producers, directors: a big thank you for everything that you do for us!

Ultimatly, I'd reccomend this game.  50 bucks and I've got almost 40 hours on reccord, and I intend to get many more.  Compared to other games these days where 70 get's you a limited playthrough plot, Such as Watch Dogs, or a fun game that you can only enjoy with friends, like Destiny, it's a huge joy to play something I'm both familiar with, yet also learning something new. Even though BE had the advantage of building on existing CiV engine (which was also by no means perfect at the beginning, but have been improved over several patches / iterations), many aspects includnig trade route management feels lacking compared to existing systems in CiV. If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

was a pleasant surprise for me.  I went in with modest expectations, but its strong writing, deep world-building and good voice acting all lead to a satisfying experience.  It is short, but I recommend it for any fan of the environmental narrative/walking simulator genre.
One thing that I particularly liked was the justification for the flashbacks we get.  At the beginning of the game, your character agrees to have all their actions on the titular station be recorded.  In an age where we sign away our privacy to social media, often without even reading the terms of service, this is all too plausible.  But this then explains the origin of the recordings we see.  What's more, pay attention and it should be clear why we see the clips that we do.
This idea also lets us see the characters in several ways: as part of the group, one-to-one with their friends and alone.  The little differences in behaviour really help to build character and motivation.  Despite only seeing their faces in still images, the crew of the Tacoma felt very real and believable to me.  That in turn helped to make the setting as a whole verisimilitudinous.
If there is any criticism to make of
, other than its length, it is that it doesn't do anything revolutionary with the genre.  But, what it does do it does very well, and in this case I found that enough.  I definitely recommend it.

This would help keep it hidden while still guiding the player to where they need to be. Further, the platforming demands will definitely turn many people off because of how high the difficulty rises. I think that should be toned down some or more should be done to minimize frustration. I came to play a relaxing game, not try to play a 100% run of Super Meat Boy. The extra bosses are fine. Definitely a great game that I would recommend to anyone. Admirable, Team Cherry, and I only hope to be able to do something as well in the future. Keep it up!

The part that gets me, though, is that the learning curve is extremely steep.  When coupled with long stages, I just sit here going, yeah, I couldn't have learned how to do that in the time I was offered (because the game does a very bad job of teaching you of the upcoming mechanics), so I lose and then I have no interest to play again because the stages are so long.  It's just a massive snowball effect.
It would help if the graphics weren't so distracting to the gameplay.  Maybe I'm just getting old -- I mean, I am, so that's true -- but I have a really hard time following what the hell is going on. In Tempest you'll play the captain of a ship who roams the mighty seas is search of wondrous treasures, destroying any who dare to cross him. Although still an Early Access title, Tempest has a lot of content to keep you playing including a large open world for you to explore at your leisure, multiple quest lines, factions and combat opportunities, ship customization such as weapons, colours, your sails and figurehead, and various mobs such as pirates, sharks and kraken (so I've heard). You can choose to live the pirates life with just you and your crew or find an alliance with one of the various factions you'll encounter throughout the world. You're welcome to plunder your way to riches or try the simple life of a sea merchant trading loot for gold both are viable options, all the while enjoying the rich graphics the game has to offer.
You start with just you and your ship and a quest that guides you to a close port to get you started. Once there you'll find a few quests, maybe a crew member and you have a chance to explore the port interface a little and see the options such as hiring and distributing your team, ship customization, available quests and traders.  Every port belongs to a faction and you can see the faction flag beside before you dock your ship. You'll make alliances and enemies with these factions and that'll affect which ports will be peaceful and hostile towards you. There are various ports dotted all around the world that you'll have the chance to find either being guided by quests, or just as you roam.
You can move your ship in one of two ways, the first being the map screen. On this screen you can simply draw the route you want your ship to travel in. Any ships you might encounter along the way will appear as a small pop-up and you can choose whether or not to switch to the other interface and engage. The second way to travel is in the 3D mode where you actually control your ship the same way you do whilst in combat. The 3D mode is much more immersive and gives you the feeling of actually sailing on the oceans. If you zoom right in you can even drive in first person mode from the ships wheel which, if you can ignore the rigid crew member sprites, feels awesome. Whilst controlling your ship directly you can choose to play with your camera free or locked, switching between the two can make combat a lot easier.
Combat in Tempest is real time and consists of you choose which attack you want to do and which side of the ship you want to fire from. Different attacks have different ranges and different reload times but also increased or decreased accuracy depending on the attack you are doing. You can also choose which cannonballs you want to fire and this will determine the damage dealt to hostile ships. Though I enjoy the combat I don't understand why there is a chance to miss if I am 100% aiming at the ship in question. This doesn't work well with real time combat and I think the combat mechanics in game could do with a little bit of a rework. As you take hits your ship will lose some of it's health and over time your crew members will take damage and become wounded stopping them from being active at their posts lowing the overall efficiency of your ship. The more damage you take the more chance of your crew members dying completely and your ship sinking. Once combat is over you can loot all fallen ships (even those from factions you're allied with) which will be one of your main sources of income. If you sink after taking too much damage you won't die or get a game over, you'll respawn at a nearby friendly port but will have lost a significant amount of your wealth so sometimes a retreat is recommended or even just scavenging off of battles early on like I did.
Despite Tempest being fantastic in terms of gameplay the lack of a tutorial is something which hinders the game massively. There is very little that is explained to you and it did take me around three restarts before I felt I had a firm grip on what I was meant to be doing. Combat is almost impossible to learn without being sunk a few times and can become very frustrating. Also distributing your crew is never fully explained alongside what is affected by 'efficiency'. Things like this could be explained a lot easier by some text when you hover over options or icons but there is nothing currently. Right now Tempest desperately needs some tooltips. On the forums the developer has mentioned this is coming soon so I'll update this when that update is out.

What's funny about this game is that it is on par with games like the Elder Scrolls. Not for the fantastic story or whimsy - or basic naming (seriously, who the hell names their child "Dajh" (rhymes with dodge)) - but in the lore surrounding it. Makes for some worthwhile reading within the Datalog, not that many people actually read the dang thing.
What's funnier about the so-called In Depth Reviews on here are that 90% of the "Yes" reviews all have people who have actually played the game for any length of time, usually about 20+ hours. Conversely, 90% of the "No" reviews are under 10 hours of gameplay.
That speaks volumes, in of itself. If you're not really willing to give the game (port) a try, then why bother even playing it? Okay, opinion piece over.
OPINION OVER; ACTUAL GAME COMMENTS
++ Fantastic visuals (idc about the f***ing 720p stuff, it looks awesome, deal with it), and in HD too!
++ Gameplay is varied from insanely easy to incredibly frustrating (Neochus, anybody?), making for a good scaling.
++ Inability to (at first) choose your team may seem like a drawback, but it makes for a fun kind of learning curve, using everybody and their roles as needed (or required).
++ Lots of post-game things to keep you busy or at least entertained for a while.
++ Fights are fast; anything over 2 minutes is really weird, apart from boss fights.
++ Despite having low funds for the majority of the game, you really don't need money until you want to start upgrading weapons past tier 1.
Potions become obsolete quickly (or not with the right equipment) and you don't have to buy more unless you never use the Healer role, which is ridiculous; could make for a good challenge playthrough though. Phoenix Downs are scarce initially, but nothing should kill you save bosses early on (Chapter 3+) and you find a lot of shrouds, enough to last the entirety of the game if you don't use them all before every fight. It may take an extra 20-30 seconds, but when starting out, fight everything you see, and then do it over and over. Don't run away or around enemies, it only hurts you later on.
-- Story is meh, and holy batcave is it confusing for a first-time player. Fal'Cie, l'Cie, Cie'th... it's like somebody went out of their way to make this as confusing a narrative as possible.
-- Linearity is annoying as heck. Press up to go forward; and that's pretty much your movement options.
-- There is no way that an enemy with its back to you can see you sneak up behind them from 40+ feet away.
-- Some portions of the game almost require grinding, after long Chapters (parts) of having fewer enemies to fight.
-- Missions take forever because of distance, not the fighting; also, the chaining is very odd and disjointed.
-- No clear progression or idea of where to go for Missions, no minimap support, map problems, etc.
For example: To get the item that doubles CP (this game's experience point mechanic) you need to find the proper mission. It's at one end of the world; not so bad, a long walk maybe, but no big deal. Actual boss? Other side of the world,
Then to get to the boss, you need to be able to ride Chocobos - which requires another mission entirely - causing you to drop the current mission to get that one
, to warp / run back to the first, run / warp back
to the first area, use the chocobo to get to an out-of-the-way area, and then proceed to fight a boss that is A) Ridiculously hard, and B) Annoying. You are never once pointed in the direction of the next Mission for a chronological order, because that would make too much sense. Argh.
== Money drops would be nice, but whatever, it's easy enough to make money when you need it.
== Role definitions early on is good, until you like playing as one role specifically and only ever want to play as that role ever again. (Com, for me)
== Characters were... okay, I guess. Voices were nice, but they cut up every, single, chapter, four, hundred, times; just for dialogue that is primarily useless. Otherwise, nice.
== Just stop sometime and check out the view. It is stunning. Seriously; just take a few seconds and look around.

Pros, cons and tips. :)
Pros:
1. grafics, sounds, atmosphere. It's just a marvel to behold, especially if we look at how small the size of the game is.
Cons:
1. Little to no in-game tips. You have to figure out tons of stuff yourself or go to the discussion board (where is it btw, please, tell me if you know :))
Tips:
1. Pirates are currently the only faction you can get benefit from being in good relations with, so put on the pirate flag and work towards improving your reputation with them.
2. Quests are the source of income, random battles are more or less a maritime enjoyment, but they have little economic sense. Quest battles on the other hand are a different story, 50k gold for ruining some guys fort? It is there, though you have to be in good relations with pirates to get this one. :)
3. Forget earning by trading. You can, but quests are way better.
4. Run if you can't win. :)
5. Don't carry money and goods, unless you just got them. Sell goods, put up to 12k gold to bank (yeah, figure out how :)) and collect interest from time to time. If you have over 5k gold, buy upgrades or buy goods in cheap port (yeah, figure out which ones:)) and store goods there. If you get sunk with stuff on board, you loose some.
6. Don' try attacking forts until you have a better ship. They pack a punch and you need a good hp to withstand it. :)
7. You basically don't need pistols and boarding unless for the quests, so you may carry your pistols without equipping them (unless on a boarding quest) and use your crew on sails and cannons only.
8. Use spyglass to get info about your enemies in the beginning of a fight. Use Ctrl button to switch the glass on/off  (you probably should be sailing away from them and looking behind, right?). Spying info will include three bars for the targets: sails, crew, hull (same as your stats), so you can know for sure if you can win boarding before starting it and that kraken has only hull hp, so don't use shrapnel on it... :)
Also, multiplayer is accessible through the globe icon on the map. As far as I can tell, it is based on "rooms" system, so if you have friends, just put in the same room name probably? Or join random, me and some folks will be glad to help you out with some enemies. :)
P.S. One of the factions works as the bank, check out faction descriptions in ports.
Cheap ports have a green % sign on them. :)

Avast, me hearties! Are ye longing for the bygone days of wooden sailing ships ruling the ocean waves? Do ye crave the tang of salty sea air? Are ye jest unable to wait for weevils in yer bread to tickle the stubs of yer rotting teeth? Do ye long for the gentle touch of Scurvy as it sneakily weakens yer body and soul? Would ye give anything for a chance to see the mighty Kraken?  Well look ye no further landlubber. Tempest is set in the age of pirates. Ye command thee a small ship with an equally small crew as ye set off on yer high seas adventures. Ye don’t have to be a pirate though if ye don’t want to be. Pirates are but one of the factions that are willing to have ye fly their colours. The majority of the gameplay takes place on yer ship as ye quest around between the various islands getting into mostly optional scuffles as ye sail around.
In Tempest you are a captain of a fledgling pirate ship searching for your lost crew. Your main goal is to gain the wealth needed to upgrade your ship and keep it out of Davy Jones’ locker. You amass wealth however you like. You can be the scourge of the sea known as a pirate or live the respectable life of a trader. You might even become a pirate hunter. You are free to choose but if you cross a faction too many times, you will become their enemy.
Flags help to show who you are. Decorative flags make you look spiffier, factional ones show where your loyalties lay. You begin with a Pirate and a Merchant flag. Leaving the pirate flag equipped when you join a battle will automatically represent you as the Pirate faction. The same goes if you have another faction’s flag equipped. If you are flying the Merchant flag, you will join your allies to rally against the pirate menace. If you go against a faction too much, you will quickly find yourself unwelcome in any of that factions ports. On the flip side, your Pirate buddies will see you as a mighty pirate and new quests will unlock for that faction.
Controlling your ship is simple in both the 2D map mode and in the 3D high seas mode. While in map mode, simply click where you want to go and the ship will set sail but it follows the course without deviation. You could ram an island en-route. There is a better way to set your course. Left click and hold it down to then draw the route you want your ship to take. The map is accurate in that it has the authentic dullness of maps from the by-gone days. The high seas mode is where the game really shines. The highly detailed ships are seen at sea complete with crew. The oceans look amazing and the ambient weather and diurnal cycle just make this mode look breathtaking. The controls are as easy as in map mode. Press forward for faster and backward to slow. Left and right to turn and that’s it. Use your spyglass to see what you are up against. The spyglass has a really cool effect on your screen that gives the feeling you are actually looking though one.
Let me tell you a story. I had barely started the game when I decided to visit the various ports to see if I could find ships for sale and to see what I would need to purchase one. I battled a few ships on my travels while flying the Jolly Roger. I then encountered a fort that didn’t want me to dock in their town and attacked my ship. That was when I first encountered the monster. The malevolent Kraken attacked my ship! The Kraken’s tentacles began reaching up both sides of my ship in a furious attempt to pull me down into a watery grave in the briny deep. I’d love to say that I became more infamous than the Dread Pirate Roberts that day and won my freedom, but sadly I cannot make that claim. The combined fire of the fort and the Kraken was too much and my ship sank beneath the churning waves.
Sinking in this game is not the end. You lose most of your belongings and wealth though, so it is a wise idea to unload goods to your warehouse before heading out. Eventually I was able to afford a bigger ship with better guns and parts all around. I had a good crew and became a mighty pirate known only as G. Threepwood.
Combat in the game is straight forward. Your ship has arcs for your cannons and once your arc lines up with the enemy hull you can open fire. If you hold off your trigger finger for a moment, your shot will gain in accuracy. You can select the type of cannonballs you want to use and the reload speed and accuracy in which they will fire. The more accurate you want to be, the less firing arc you will have and the longer it will take between shots. Next, you have to figure out how you want to win this fight. You can go broadsides to broadsides if you are so inclined. I personally found starting out with a little bit of cowardice… I mean tactical retreating is a good way to get your wealth flowing in. Once I had longer ranged cannons I was actually able to sink enemy ships without them scratching my paint so I was quite happy about that. I admit that taking long-range potshots on the enemy is expensive in terms of cannon ball expenditures so I changed my cannons to short range and decided to kill the crew instead. I read a comment by the developer that ship capturing is something that is being implemented. Currently sailing close to the enemy and boarding only allows you to get supplies. One day I hope to capture an enemy ship and keep it as my own. For now, I will simply have to buy my ships and upgrade them myself.
The ability to upgrade is simple. You find parts you want and dock at a port. The port is straight forward and mostly the same everywhere you go. You see several icons to choose from and once you select the one you are looking for you will be taken to the respective screen. Here is where you buy and sell, hire crew, take on new quests, and retrofit your ship with parts you have acquired. Artifacts can also be added to your ship to give you special abilities. These artifact abilities help to separate Tempest from other similar nautical games and add a whole new level of fun to the game. Not all stores sell the same items so you will likely have to dock a few times before you find what you want. This is where the factions really start to come into play.
Joining a faction has perks besides just having a safe place to dock. Each faction has a joining bonus that you can’t seem to acquire elsewhere so you might want to visit each of the factions to see what they have to offer. Even if a faction hates you, it isn’t the end of the world. You can still equip their flag to suck up to them and eventually they will pardon you.
Considering Tempest is still in Early Access right now, it’s actually very good as it is. The developer is actively supporting the game and listening to the community. If you want your change to help shape the game, you might want to get it now. There is even a new area being worked on as we speak! Additionally, multiplayer is working already and is quite interesting. I have not played multiplayer as much as I have the single player so I can’t comment too much on it but from the looks of it, the game will really come to life if you play in multiplayer.

With a good blend of minimalism in focusing on simple pirate combat, combined with the details of a 4X strategy game; Tempest delivers that happy high-seas adventuring every land-lubber dreams about.
With trade routes to plunder, slave ships to chase down, coastal factions to ally, and some common mythological elements to battle, such as sea monsters and the kraken; you’ve got more narrative than just pirates.  Through the missions, story and mystery unfolds. Not to provide a spoiler, but the act of making alliances will cause certain events to take place later in the story. The Lion’s Shade dev team seems to be putting out updates weekly, if not more often. So, I suspect it won’t see a long wait for release. But, early access does not mean a game is less fun to read about and play. Although most games are built on a mechanic that needs to be finished before its fun, there are numerous games like Tempest that deliver a fully built mechanic that will provide hours of fun and excitement in early access.
The art is lovely. Those storm-wracked seas provide a magnificent backdrop for hours of gameplay on end. No cards yet, but you can look for some fantastic artwork from this game. An art book would be a welcome addition, as well as full screen backgrounds. The player chooses a banner to display, depending on faction alliances. With the dynamic weather, the beauty of the map motif, and the colorful graphic representations of faction flag and symbols; the game immerses you in an era in naval history that is legend.
Tempest has some errors & bugs, with occasional splicing of elements and waves, & wall glitches, but none of these seem to affect the enjoyment I get from losing everything I had acquired to this gigantic sea monster that appears out of the depths. As Shakespeare said in The Tempest, “He that dies pays all debts.” Losing everything in such a manner is incredibly nice, and 10 times out of 10, I would lose it all again when the game is fully released, with as much pleasure.

The game is played with the open ocean as the predominant view. Here in the 3D view you can spend as much of your time as you like in actual combat. Clicking the map button brings up a map overlay that is a fully functional navigation system. Your ship appears in miniature replica sailing across the map between various settlements. You set waypoints on this view for your ship to travel freely around the map. Interestingly, you can draw out the shape of the exact path you want the ship to take around obstacles. As you watch the ship sail, notifications pop up when you are encountering pirate raids, naval battles, merchant ships and the like. You can choose to click to the ocean view to engage those vessels in combat, or allow the AI to flee the encounter.
When you reach your destination icon on the map, you are switched to the ocean view at the port. There doesn’t seem to be much difference between the map view and the sea. It is like being on the ship looking up from the map on the captain’s table as a ship fires cannonballs at you. In some of the more dangerous harbors, I found myself knocked out of the crew screens by an attack from pirate ships near me. I had been fighting an intense mission, and had several injured crewmen, so I was trying to find meds in port, but kept being attacked while looking for them. I soon realized I needed to travel to a safer port to go shopping lol. And, ports carry a different selection of goods anyways.
Maneuverability is well-thought out. Setting the sails at half-mast (50%) will boost the ship’s maneuverability. Arrow keys control the camera, as well as a right click & drag with the mouse. The camera is fully functional 360 degree rotation on every axis. Zoom works with the mouse scroll-wheel. Compass cardinal directions are visible on the horizon as well, aiding in navigation. It’s quite realistic like being at sea with the captain’s tools in hand, and yet it draws to mind the look of 17th & 18th century maps & ships, like reliving the adventure of the Golden Age of Piracy.
The drag & drop interface is touchscreen friendly with standard WASD keyboard shortcuts, movement around the ocean is possible by using the left mouse button to click and set waypoints, just like on the map.
Your ship has a cone-shaped attack zone. The angle depends on the chosen accuracy mode. You can increase the angle with the Q & E keys. The attack zone lights up when you have an enemy in your line of sight. Fire when ready. It is entirely possible to turn on automatic firing in the settings. This causes your cannons to fire when anything comes in your attack zone.  The combat is what the game does best. The look of the battle scenes is reminiscent of the old BBC Admiral Hornblower series.
You are building a reputation at sea which varies after each battle. The game provides a variety of factions which figure into the missions. I noticed a few errors, like the Foggy Harbor mission sends you to Foggy Harbor, labeled Misty Harbour on the map.

You want a high level crew. You train them with experience points earned in battle by clicking on an arrow button next to each sailor. Rank appears to move from left to right on the boat decks, from Greenhand to Pirate in 5 different classes. A simple click & drag of the screen to the left will reveal the Tavern where you can hire additional crewmen. But, if you already have a full crew, you will have to put some Greenhands on shore leave to hire more experienced hands, just by dragging and dropping them into the Tavern. Of course, the Greenhands are always free if you’re broke. To add an officer to your crew, click on an icon on the left and choose any officer from the list below. You collect these officers from various missions, so you’ll have none at first.
First things last. :D Yes, every sailor worth his salt had to start out nowhere. You begin Tempest as a poor scoundrel with a bare bones ship and little options for upgrading. So, you’ll want to just have a look around at all the finery you don’t have, before heading out to sea to sink a few ships and claim your first prize money. Then you will be ready to buy some of those red-hot cannon balls and an accurate pistol to board future ships, and perhaps a trusty spyglass. Buy ship parts and upgrade them in port. Here you can focus on Sail, Boarding, or Gunnery efficiency. Dragging the screen to the right while in Goods mode will reveal the warehouse where you can store unused goods until you need them.
In the middle of a battle a mysterious ship on fire sailed up near me and began to lob cannon grenades into the air. His ship would glow with a strange blue artifact as well. He was bearing the skull & crossbones so we were allied instantly. I just tried to pick off the smaller ships around while coveting the firepower of this grand ally. But, the MP is the same map as single-player, with other players joining you at will & appearing on your map and in the sea near you, if they are logged in at the same time as you.
Combat to satisfy your inner pirate
Ship Navigation system that is fluid & fun
Dynamic Weather & day/night cycle

No cards or achievements yet
Early Access
Incomplete Tutorial
I recommend Tempest for all lovers of adventure on the high-seas, and pirates-at-heart. If you enjoy sea battles and navigation, then this game has all that plus sea monsters to die for. I rate Tempest a 10 out of 10 for combat games in the genre.

Syphilis has been called ‘the great imitator’ because it has so many possible symptoms, many of which look like symptoms from other diseases. When I saw the announcement for this game, my little 4X heart skipped a beat. Alpha Centauri is one of my favorite games of all time, and this seemed for all intents and purposes to be its spiritual successor. I counted down the days and hours until I could get my hands on what was sure to be a masterwork by Firaxis, eager to get home from work and wake my computer. With breathless anticipation, I fired up the game to find that Firaxis had indeed combined Civilization 5 with Alpha Centauri.
A couple hours in, I realized that after mashing the two together, they had also proceeded to remove the good parts of both.
The basic gameplay mechanics from Civ5 are in play here, and they've been polished up. The Tech Web is very nice in concept- each tech has two sub-techs you can research or skip at your discretion, and you aren't limited to a linear progression- but it ends up falling flat due to a horrible UI. All the little symbols denoting what advantages/advances the tech infers are laid out in plain white and often illegible. One spends most of their time on the tech web hovering the mouse pointer over these little gems to figure out which tech to take next.
Trade routes make a return, and they are a very powerful tool. Unfortunately, they're also very spammy. They have to constantly be manually set every few turns. In the later game when you have a bunch of cities, each with two or more individual trade routes, you can find yourself having to scroll through a list of available routes to find your previous route (rather than having an auto-renew option or putting the previous route up at the top for easy selection) FOR EACH TRADE CARAVAN. I often found myself having to perform this same task 5 or more times each turn, and it eventually became far more nuissance than feature. It really slows an already slow game down to a crawl.
Quests were a nice addition, though they could still use some work. These usually tell little self-contained stories which add a nice flavor and allow for a bit of roleplaying, while others tie into the overall plot. These sometimes involve performing a task like creating a particular building, founding a new colony near a specific resource, performing a particular covert action in a particular city, etc. Rewards for these can be things like energy, free units, free tech, and points towards an affinity. Most often though, quests involve just making an arbitrary decision between two (and ONLY two) choices. The rewards for these vary greatly and will tend to add permanent affects to your game (such as making farms have +1 production for your faction). After a while, I stopped even reading what the text had to say about the supposed situation and just picked whichever choice gave me the benefit I would find most useful.
Unfortunately, the quest system doesn't do context very well. It will sometimes give quests which cannot be completed. For instance, I was tasked with building a bio-fuel plant in my capital city. The problem? That building requires having an improved water with algae bloom tile and the specific city the quest required it to be built at was a full 8 hexes from the nearest water- completely landlocked, making the quest impossible. For the record, it was my starting city, so I didn't have much choice on where to place it.
One of the neater things plays out in the beginning. There are a lot of options to customize your starting condition. You choose a faction (or "sponsor", rather), choose what kind of colonists you want (laborers gives you a bonus to production, farmers to food, etc.) and a few extra little bits like cargo. The other factions do the same. Now, one would think that this should lead to vast dynamics and a different experience for each game. Sadly, this is the most glaring place where Beyond Earth falls flat on its face. None of these choices have any lasting impact. The seven factions have no individual identities- no strengths or weaknesses of any particular note or goals. There is literally nothing at the core of each which differentiates it from any others. The faction leaders themselves are little more than cardboard stand-ins, completely lacking any personality or ideologies whatsoever. Each one is as bland as the previous and all react to the events in the exact same way. In fact, there are only three ideologies to choose from: Purity, Supremacy, and Harmony. You gain levels in these ideologies through the techs you choose and quest decisions. You can have levels in several, not just one. Even then, these differing "affinities" only affect diplomacy so much. In more than one playthrough my closest ally had a different affinity.
Your affinity levels also determine your unit upgrades (and some units are specific solely to a faction advancing a particular affinity). When your affinity level goes up, you often get the ability to upgrade a unit to a new type, which makes the unit stronger and gives you a choice between two permanent enhancements. Unlike Civ 5, all of your units of that type magically upgrade to the new type with the new enhancement. No picking and choosing individual unit upgrades here or even having to go to a friendly territory and paying to upgrade. Nope, that ship floating in the middle of the ocean really did spontaneously grow an extra 30 tons of metal, armor, and bigger guns.
Diplomacy and espionage have taken a drastic step back from Civ 5. It's taken a step back from Civ 3, even. Both are terribly rudimentary, and the former has taken a particular hit from the faction leaders' lack of personality, ambition, and goals.
The five different victory conditions are interesting, though two of them make little practical sense. In the supremacy victory, the faction achieves victory by... leaving? In going for a military victory, you win by capturing every faction's starting capital. This option is locked out to you if you ever lose your capital- even if you take it back. In theory, you could conquer every city on the map and not achieve a military victory just because you lost your capital for a single turn. It was dumb in Civ 5, and it's dumb here.
Winning a game feels hollow and pointless as it gives you a small picture in a grey box, and a voice-acted quote before dumping you back to the main menu. When you lose, it doesn't even tell you who won or how. The whole endgame is unsatisfying on a level worse than Mass Effect 3. One could argue that it's the journey which counts, and sometimes it is, but in this case, I would state that one making such an argument probably ingested far too many paint chips at a young age.
The bottom line here is this: Beyond Earth lacks a personality, an identity, and a soul. As much as it pains me as a huge fan of the franchise to say so, I can't recommend this game in its current state.

To be fair I've never played the Hitman series before but have been a big fan of other stealth action games and shooters and consider myself pretty proficient and willing to retry missions 20 times to get them right.  However, Absolution is impossibly frustrating and I've just ended up deleting the game.  The primary frustrations are (i) the disguise system, which isn't well explained and doesn't seem to work well - once you don a uniform everyone else who has that uniform is instantly suspicious of you if you're in their line of sight, which I've seen extend very long distances or alternatively several inches - point being that it's inconsistent and therefore you have to reload/fail to see how it's working in particular scenarios and are often stuck wearing a uniform and cannot go back to being a civilian, (ii) there is no save system, just some screwy checkpoint system which works sometimes, and othertimes not, and if you reload NPCs that you've disabled or killed before reloaded will not be refreshed... (iii) the game is just boring in terms of story and creativity within each level.  After just walking around, which is usually too frustrating to do without being identified (I usually just kill everyone and then walk around the level at my leisure to explore before restarting) you can find the unique kills and the silent assassin awards... the challenege is then trying to execute that whilst tripping over very poor game mechanics, and this is complemented by (iv) which is that you cannot develop your character in terms of items or skills other than predetermined bonues which are not quantified or explained and which are received solely by virtue of finishing a level - I haven't seen any difference at all between getting say, 15,000 points at the end of a level or 115,000.
In the end, if you're looking for stealth action gameplay, Deus Ex is excellent.  If you're looking for the type of gameplay I expected from Hitman, which was an open world where you have the freedom to explore and choose creative assassination techniques, this doesn't provide that because the world is very linear, scripted, and you cannot interact with the environment except in pre-defined (and I will definitely emphasize "unintuitive" ways).  I'd say that not being able to interact with NPCs except potential combatants seems a major gap, but this might be a legacy from the series.  Likewise, the "instinct" element is superfluous and distracting - it should have been left out as it muddies the gameplay... feels like they implemented the instinct mechanic and then designed the game around it... you're required to use it so fairly straightforward tasks are never straightforward (plus, since when can Hitman see through walls?!).  I would also mention (v) the stealth system is not explained and compares poorly to competitors.

A fun scifi “walkulator”.
Plays with and also somewhat subverts classic tropes regarding AI and future megacorporations with a few pitfalls.
Vague spoilers follow:
My main complaint is the story that eventually unfolds and how it’s done. I’ve enjoyed a few walkulators before, lacking gameplay and means to affect the story but they’ve offered the player the gratification of uncovering a mystery.
But Tacoma robs you of that feeling. As just an archaeologist of past events, the player doesn’t get to actually discover the secret behind what has happened, but to merely watch a recording of one of the disappeared crewmembers doing so. You then learn the crew whose “disappearance” you’re investigating are safe and sound because they were in fact already rescued. So the secret didn’t die with anyone, and will eventually blow out regardless of the player character’s involvement.
Finally, the game signals that certain orders shouldn’t be followed because doing the opposite is the right moral action. But this is a walkulator, the player has no choice but to follow the story in its tracks. You then just continue with this queer feeling about what’s actually going to happen, only to learn the story doesn’t have a moral choice for the player character to make anyhow - the character’s in fact had an agenda all along, unbeknownst to the player. The game was trying to do a gratifying twist but just slapped me in the face.
So as the ending credits rolled, I was left thinking what the function of Tacoma is as a video game when they’ve removed the player from it entirely. A film is a far better medium for tricks like these because there’s no interactivity and the viewer doesn’t assume a character and their actions.
