Having finished Tacoma, I realized I would probably need to write a review in two parts, seeing how split I was on my opinion of the game. Not to say I wouldn't recommend it, overall it was a very well written and executed story, which I would easily take over a movie theater ticket any day. Here goes.
Tacoma's presentation exceeded my expectations on all fronts. Since
, Fullbright has stepped up the quality in both a visual and written sense. The art and sound direction is simple, but very stylized and suits the Science-fiction-mystery theme like a glove. Although the diversity card is a little forced, the characters are extremely well written and acted, and all of them have unique personalities and flaws without feeling too on-the-nose. You can listen to a single room's scenario five times over, because each character has a different encounter, a different dilemma going on at the same time, while still seeming interconnected. The story falls a little short in length, as Fullbright created a bigger world than the time they wanted to spend explaining it. However, there is plenty of optional exploration that can answer your questions and pad the playtime. All in all, Tacoma did a fantastic job of captivating me all the way through, with stunning visuals and environments, interesting characters and solid pacing.
With
sparking so much controversy among players, I was hardly surprised to see the political symbolism and undertones in Tacoma. The ominous talk of "gene screening", the [s]evil corporation[/s], the AI rights activism, it was hard to ignore that there was some intended meaning to it all. But what exactly was this meaning, this moral of the story? That slavery and genocide are bad? That couldn't be it. Maybe that companies can be evil? I have no problems with developers trying to push a message out through their medium, and I definitely have no problems with games that just want to tell a story, no morals involved. But when a game is so noticeably forcing a message, shouldn't it be clear what that message is? And if the message is one of the aforementioned notions, then it was a bit of a waste of time to use all that talk if the only payoff would be something everyone knows...?
A quick look at Tacoma as a whole reveals a visually stunning game, containing a short yet well written narrative, with all the right ingredients for a mystery/suspense. Deeper down, it has some issues in the core message, but if you are able to take it in as it is, as more of a cinematic experience than an interactive one, then Tacoma would be a fantastic game for you.

Oh. My. Gosh. The game had me in on it. The story in particular. I couldn't place the story at first, but then I replayed I figured it out. It plays off of the vague ending of Hitman: Blood Money.
I just gots to ask: WHY in the name of my mom's FUDGE is every contract so damn PERSONAL?
Gameplay: 10/10
The way this game was developed, oh my goodness! It has great gameplay mechanics and has a very good storyline. The storyline was pretty hard for me to comprehend at first, but after remembering what happened before the last level of Hitman: Blood money, I thought
. However it is STILL funny because of "AHH! B*TCH!". But I digress.
Graphics: 10/10
What would you expect from a Square Enix game? The graphics are intense. They help immerse  yourself into what is happening in the Hitman: Absolution world.
Controls: 9/10
The controls were confusing, but after some patience and persistance, (and practice), I managed to figure it out and get used to it. However, when I get spotted while in cover, and I press the  "Get out of cover" button, Agent 47 turns into a disobediant brat, and gets me killed because he won't get out of the cover!!!
Replay Value: 10/10
Replay as in the Absolution mode. Say, for instance, you completed all of Hitman: Absolution story. You can REPLAY the missions but maybe it is the same objective, but what matters is HOW you complete the objective. If you say, (And you won't), "Ahh, I completed all there is to Hitman: Absolution, even the replay stuff you said to do, now I am bored." Well, lucky for you, on the main screen, where it asks you to select Absolution mode or Contracts mode, Contracts take you WAY back to Hitman: Blood Money. BUT don't think contracts as boring as Hitman: Blood Money, it's way better. Every contract you take (other than the tutorials,) are PLAYER MADE contracts. Seriously NO coding experince needed, it's THAT EASY.
Side note: I made a contracts level if you guys want to try. Hope you enjoy!
Overall Rating: 9.8/10
"That's all I got, Homes," -Birdie

The story is not that long. But if that discouraged you from buying it, I urge you to (re-)read the Replay Value section of this review. I sincerely hope you enjoy the game. Dassit, bye.

Fullbright's taken their storytelling to the next level. Reminiscent of an immerse theatre experience, the player will rewind the same scene multiple times to follow different characters through the same 2 to 10 minute time frame, and they've deftly managed to weave those multiple paths to ensure that at no point in any of those scenes do you feel as if you're sitting around waiting for anyone to do something while others are engaged in conversation in another room. Once again, the experience is a short one, but we'll worth the cost of admission, particularly if you can pick it up at a discount.

I thoroughly enjoyed this game.   There is just so much to say and I don't even know where to start.   The good parts, is the various ways of completing a task/mission through the use of Challenges.   You can be ruthless and kill all in a very loud and visible way, or be more stealth about killing people.    Or you can be really sneaky and never hurt anyone but the intended target, or use disguises to sneak around people.   The weapons used are great and fun to experiment with and the number of unique weapons are just as fun too.   Story wise, I'm new to it but I understood most of what was said and it made sense.   The graphics are nice and crisp without affecting performance (for me at least).   Also, I haven't done it much, but the Contracts part of the game, looks very challenging since there are unlimited possible ways of creating them and completing them.   The only negative I have about it, is that some times it can be annoying to fail stealth, and failing stealth, can be disastrous.  And that when a checkpoint is activated, and you die/restart to checkpoint, you have to worry about the same enemies that you dealt with earlier since they get respawned.
All in all, I loved the game and am still currently playing it and don't see when i will quit for now.  I highly recommend this game for stealth-based enthusiast or anyone who enjoys things of that nature.

An unabashed, old-skool, hideously violent, borderline racist shooter; this is one hell of a tough game to review.
There's tremendous fun to be had using different weapons and abilities (you'll learn some ninja magic too), but there's also frustration built into the game -- namely the mortal-kombat-esque spell-casting on the D-Pad for joypad users, and the boundaries of every level -- you want to explore, but there's not as much to explore as you think.
That said, there are plenty easter eggs (about half of them are strictly adult humour), fast-moving action sequences, and a lot of 'almost too inapropriate' asian-based jokes in amongst the bloodshed.
Playing the game as it is -- a series of beautiful gauntlets -- it's excellent fun, and mostly fulfils the promises made in the trailer, but take that 20% pinch of salt as you see fit. In the end, finding original parts of levels rendered as the original game, wiitnessing hidden hentai showering, and brutally using and abusing the body parts of your vanquished enemies is a great romp.

I try my best to avoid one-line meme reviews, because they are Steam Review Cancer, but if I were to do one for Shadow Warrior 2013 it would read "It's Brutal DOOM, but with Wang jokes". If you don't know what Brutal DOOM is, there is a pretty fair chance you are not part of the target audience for a game like Shadow Warrior to begin with.
I thought this was a really enjoyable game that also has enough options for really enthusiastic fans that want to sink some time in (higher difficulties, a neat survival mode). The meat of any FPS game is combat and I found there to be no shortage of fun there. Simply put the game was very fun to play. The story is, frankly, a pretty muddled mess, but that's almost irrelivant here. The meat of the game is chopping and slicing your way through waves of demons, and the game does this well. I didn't find normal to be overwhelmingly difficult, but it is challenging in several key areas, and I'm sure the higher difficulties could get quite painful if that's your ticket.
For me there were only two minor negatives so let's get those out of the way. One, this didn't bother me a ton but it did some people I know, and I can understand it. There is some old school "hunt around looking for key to open door after you kill all the bad guys" in this, which I will file under Your Mileage May Vary. For me it was no real issue but some people will not enjoy this, that's fair enough. Two, for a game focussed heavily on swordplay (sword is your main killing tool, all the other weapons are more situationally useful), it is quite odd that the boss fights focus heavily on gunplay. I found this a strange creative choice.
I don't consider either of these particularly serious issues.
I had one crash during gameplay of the main campaign (roughly 16 hours, for me).
On the positive side, combat was satisfying. The sword is flat out fun to use. One of the reasons I was interested in this game at all was I loved playing as Krieg in Borderlands 2; a very against-the-grain FPS character who can shun guns and avoiding damage, to play a "hit me and I get stronger" and melee style of gameplay. So I was interested in trying another melee focussed FPS game. You get a variety of sword techniques as you go, each with timely uses. You also have plenty of chances to just hack and slash away if you like. The other weapons I found pretty much all of them situationally useful. The pistol is actually pretty decent when fully upgraded, very useful on flying enemies and in the boss fights, the SMG is great against these green exploding things that you want to keep at a distance, the shotgun was great against the big dudes that carry shields etc. etc. I found pretty much every weapon had a use that fit for me, and the upgrades allow you to pick and choose weapons that you find suit your personal style. That's cool.
If you like blood, boy is this a game for you.
Overall I liked the level designs. It's a throwback FPS with little side corridors, and secrets to find. The game world looks pretty cool on the whole, and there's a variety of settings.
Lots of fun dialogue. Stupid lowbrow jokes that work. One liners. Just don't try to make too much sense of what the heck is going on and you'll be fine. Overall Lo Wang was a fun character to play as, and there's enough here to break up the constant killing sprees and add a little levity that I found enjoyable.
Pretty good soundtrack. It's also included in both MP3 and FLAC format in the Special Edition, which is a nice bonus.
I got this on sale fairly cheap, and on the whole I feel like I definitley got my money's worth and more out of a full run through the campaign. A fun throwback to a style of FPS I tend to enjoy much more than the Modern Military Shooter end of the spectrum. At this stage of the game's life, it will probably go on sale fairly regularly and is definitely a worthy pick up for fans of old school FPS action.

"YOU GOT WANG!"
Shadow Warrior is a reimagining of the classic 1997 video game by the same title. This game is hilariously brutal and cheesy at the same time. You play as Lo Wang, a Chinese assassin working out of Japan. You are sent by your employer (Master Orochi Zilla) to collect the Nobitsura Kage, an ancient sword of unimaginable power, for him. Long story short, things don't go very smoothly, and literally all Hell (or Shadow Realm to be specific) breaks loose.
The game is played from a first-person perspective, through the eyes of Lo Wang. You can see your hands, you can look down at your legs. Combat is fluid, very quick and very brutal. This game has a lot of blood and gore, and flying limbs (which is quite entertaining to say the least). You fight against mostly different shadow creatures, demons if you will, and a few humans as well. More often than not there are hoards of creatures coming at you all at one time, meant to try to overwhelm you... but you can handle it, you're Lo Wang.
You start off with your sword (shurikens too), but as the game progresses, you acquire more weapons: revolver, submachine gun, crossbow, shotgun, flamethrower, and rocket launcher. You can also obtain the ability to pick up demon hearts and/or warlord heads. You can use all these amazingly fun toys against various baddies that show up in the game: crawlers, birdmen, trolls, warpers, mothers, warlords, shamans, berserkers... and the pitiful human enemies too. Also, if you come across a cute little furry bunny rabbit, and you feel so inclined to splatter its internals all over the ground over and over, you may come across a little surprise revenge of the bunnies moment, so by all means, use your toys on that as well.
Joined with you along the way is Hoji, a banished immortal of the Shadow Realm. Quite an amusing character, and to be honest, I probably enjoyed him more than the main character of Lo Wang. He may be kind of annoying, snarky and sarcastic, but quite amusing nonetheless. And he grows on you... like a fungus... but in a good way? But I digress. He helps you along the way both with his knowledge of shadow creatures, and his innate ability to find the whisperers, who are synthetic creatures that hold memories as well as parts of the scattered sword you're after. Despite part of his own memories being missing, he is quite helpful.
Aside from the normal enemies you come across, there are the boss battles. These battles take you into the Shadow Realm, and one-on-one with each of the other immortals, or ancients: Gozu, Mezu, and Xing. You only come across these bosses after finding a whisperer, retrieving part of the sword, and cracking open the lost memory of each. The boss battles require you to unleash all of your arsenal on their heavy armour before you can fully take 'em, take 'em out, take 'em down, do your... do your stuff.
I had a blast playing through this game. You will too. There are a lot of things to do. Sometimes the waves of enemies become repetitive, but hey that's okay. There are a bunch of secret pathways to find secret items. You can collect secret statues, pools of blood, and fortune cookies as well. There are achievements for doing such too. I played through this game 3 times. First, on easy for a very casual introduction to the game, where I could explore and find everything I could. Second, on Heroic mode, which only unlocks once you've beaten the game on any difficulty, and I did that for more of a challenge. Third, to find anything I missed, and I missed a lot, which is quite easy to do. But, I found all the statues, all the pools, all the cookies, and attained all achievements.
What a ride! If you haven't gotten this game, I highly recommend that you do. It is worth the full price, but quite often it goes on sale, and most times (or maybe every time, I don't know) that it does, it's at 90% off, I picked up the Special Edition for $5.49 CAD. Amazing deal!

First, it's free. That alone makes it worth trying out. The fact you get a flying mount really early into the game is also a huge plus. Is it amazingly fast? Absolutely not. But it beats walking.
At the moment, I have 30 hours on this game and I'm level 21. I easily could have done gotten to 20 in half that time, but I was enjoying the instances too much. The people behind this had the genius idea of adding not 1 or 2 difficulty levels, but 4 tiers of them with 5 levels per tier. Each difficulty tier has a slightly better armor set than the last tier. The difficulty isn't just mobs with more health and doing more damage, oh no. The bosses start upping their game too.
So far, I haven't seen any pvp, but I haven't exactly looked for it (which is pretty rare for me). Between the instances, taming, crafting and questing, I've had a good amount of entertainment. Crafting and taming aren't particularly different than your average MMO, which is entirely acceptable. The taming is relatively unique, though. In itself, it's a mini game of sorts. You hop on the mob, ride it around, trying to "break it in" by resisting it's movements and taking on screen queues. Once you have tamed it you can ride it around as a mount, or convert it into a pet that fights along side you (both of which gain experience and levels as you keep it out), or you can turn it into a gem that gives bonuses to your armor. By the way, you can, eventually, fight atop your mount, which has it's own skills to utilize.
I honestly don't have any negatives to state about this game that I wouldn't give the entire genre (grinding quests), other than I don't personally see that many people around. However, I'm still relatively low level and I may have simply not gotten to the populated zones.

The increasingly intense winds come in hard and violently thrust into the sails, the mostly wooden schooner known as The Bleeding lady rattles from the shock of the strong winds.  Captain Mean Jay Strong-bone sits at the helm, ordering his crew to sail directly into the storm even though he knows this may wind up being a suicide mission.  His target is none other than John Ripton, the vicious pirate wanted for slaughter a boat full of noblemen and woman.  Stong-bone knows sailing around the storm may ruin his chance of catching Ripton off guard.
A huge wave prepares to crash into the side of The Bleeding Lady, the fearless crew hold their positions and brace for the impact.  The wave smashes into the side with a loud "smash" and "crash", one of the crew members Harry Riggins gets pulled over board.  Harry was a good man, setting sail to help improve the lives of his wife and children.  Strong-bone makes a mental note to send Harry's widow word of his demise as well as a stipend of gold.  A captain always pays it forward, and makes sure the family of his fallen crew members get taken care of that is if he's a captain who wants his crews respect.  First more important matters are at hand, getting through this storm.
Strong-bone stands stoically at the wheel of his vessel, rain pelts him in the face, he squints and looks from side to side, he can feel it, a little further and the worst will be past, but not wanting to think too far ahead, he spins the wheel hard to the right....

Video Review:
Textual Review:
Tempest is an "open world" ship combat game which boasts including trading, piracy and racketeering, amongst other things. The combat in the game is quite interesting in nature and is "live action" with a nice set of graphics to finish it off. You're thrust into the world without a clue of what to do, as unfortunately the game does lack any form of tutorial or useful information (at time of recording the video). You will have to micro manage your ship, including its crew, ammo stores, damage and general cargo most of which is done at various ports you find on the map. Each crew member can provide various buffs / stats to your ship, so choose carefully! I found travelling around the map relatively boring and essentially its just used to jump from battle to battle, I would have personally preferred this to be more like a true open world whereby I could sail around, a bit like "Naval Action".
Positives:
+ Great combat system
+ Nice graphics during combat
+ The upcoming introduction of multiplayer
+ Ship customization
Negatives:
- I felt a lack of purpose or path in the game
- Lack of video settings - although it does make up for that with decent graphics anyway
- No tutorial or hits really leaves the player without a clue of what they're doing at the start
- Could get very boring very quickly
Verdict:
Definately worth keeping an eye on as introductions of new regions, multiplayer and other game aspects may turn this into a more interesting game.

This game is a sequel to a by-battle, choose your own adventure text-based adventure akin to your choice of an Napoleon-era romp, Choice of the Broadsides, Horatio Hornblower, etc, with nearly non-existent magic. Guns of Infinity improves over Sabres of Infinity in the following ways: it provides a more dynamic experience, with diverting or flavorful mini-storylines, new characters and romances, and considerably more nuance.
The first game, Sabres of Infinity, was largely a linear experience. You went from one battle to the next, with two chapter changes if you didn't make promotion. Guns of the Infinity follows your substantial decisions, writing four chapter changes (8 unique choices) for their divergences. If you retreated in the last game, you have a whole unique arc.
But this can also result in brevity. The game is long, but unless you replay or read the scenes, you won't see all the stops.
To help with replayability, the author has provided some flavor-enhancing storylines. This include a family, selective pasttimes and causes. But there are some caveats. Your family, in theory, provides more Austen sensibility, but with the amount of choices over your siblings, mother and father, effectively reduces to a money-bleeding vanity. Some decisions, like beatifying an old officer, do not show their full effect in the game.
The stronger additions are the romances. (When I replayed Sabres, I combed the choices for nearly an hour, before I realized the war-time romance was in Broadsides.) Your choices include an Adlerian spy filly and a fur-lined Duchess. (It looks like there was plans for knights-and-idealism Elson, but not moody-venerable-bryonic-hero Sir Cassius.) One note of caution though: only the spy has the full arc.
Guns still has a small cast like the first game. This is both detrimental and advantageous. In Sabres, you focused nearly entirely on your two friends/rivals/distant chums. This resulted in two strong characters. But I had no idea what my second-in-command did during the day. (Probably slept until I woke him up like Alfred.) The newcomers have more plans and preferences and ideas (and more importantly investments!)
The strongest is the spy. So if you do want to romance her, remember that there isn't much recourse in romance after the first (your character's plans for her) choice. It is easier to break up than choose intellectually and fall in love later, or go from friendship to love.
Flavor and love-at-first-sight decisions notwithstanding, Guns excells in its nuances. In Sabres, it was guns blazing into the quiet sun. Guns plays like Empire to a New Hope. Your commanders express their weariness at the loss of war more often. You get more inner dialogue.
To people familiar with war novels, the diatribe between the romance and cynicism of war may seem old hash. But the only way this story works is in its sense of time. This story is part 2, of a long campaign, and game. Whether your character goes for the war is hell mantra, or God save the King, is irrelevant. You make choices to a changing and growing world. Some choices are meaningless, a few vital, and others numbing in their repetition, (didn't I already make Theoden's charge?) but they are all cumulative.
Wars are made by the composite of many, many events, not any one shot.
Your decision to play this game is by the sum of all parts.

A cautious recommendation.. You've been warned.
At release this game is a very simple 4x title, built in the Civ 5 engine and lacks a lot of rather standard UI elements and gameplay components that fans of the Civilization series have come to expect…
Gone are the graphs and tables of data, as well as any sort of overview for things like diplomacy, economics or trade routes.  There is no way to check on the relationship between various factions, consult even rudimentary advisors or check world demographics.  Even things so simple as a clock on the HUD or different colors for each factions units have been skipped over here.. The only indicator that the spaceman with a gun is your marine and not mine, is the color of the symbol over his head.
From a gameplay perspective the game lacks any sort of great people, and fair enough.. Whose to say who the great people of this new world are exactly.. But from a gameplay perspective, the acquisition and use of a Great Engineer was a strategic choice that is simply not there now. Similarly, the different sponsors all have a unique ability, but they all feel rather lackluster and without any sort of unique units or buildings, they lack any character. Instead special units are tied to research and affinities in game.
The affinities system is like a combination of ideologies and religion in past Civ games.. and not the best parts of either. It has an effect on your interactions with other factions.. But it’s small.. They will still trade and deal with you, even though you are machine men and they are genetically-modified alien hybrids.. it doesn’t seem to matter all that much in the end. Worse is that it is tied directly to the research web (which by the way is much simpler than it originally appears) and so you gain the ability to use new unit types as your research progresses. Annoyingly though, those technologies are rarely the ones you need to actually progress and you will find yourself going back constantly to get access to artillery or aircraft… or boats..
Beyond Earth reminds me a lot of the initial release of Civ 5, back in 2010.. It was a competent 4X title, but everyone was disappointed after playing Civ 4: Beyond the Sword for so long..
Now too, we are disappointed. It’s not the Alpha Centauri sequel we all desperately wanted.. and it’s sort of a step back in some basic ways to the Civ 5 we have been playing since Brave New World. It’s curious why these things were left in this state, but I am hopeful that Firaxis will get it together and, like Civ 5 before it, Beyond Earth will grow into a more rich experience.
We’ll just have to be hopeful.. Cautiously hopeful..

EDIT 6/7/17:
Camtasia is now offically discontinued on Steam. This is a major disappointment, and I have since moved to another editing program. I hope that in the future TechSmith will offer a lower-cost Steam version of Camtasia that does not rely on the subscription model, but until that happens I can't recommend the program itself for its current price, especially when it lacks support for 60 fps which is essential for modern game capture.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
It's a solid program - I started with Camtasia 8, and so far 9 has been a big leap forward. Not as full-featured as more expensive software, and does have a number of bugs, but overall it's really easy to figure out, and the product support is significantly better than most of its' competitors. Try the demo out before buying.
For me, this basically hit that sweet spot between Windows Movie Maker and Sony Vegas. Keep in mind, if you have a lower-end PC, it's going to struggle, especially if you're trying to edit an hour of footage (or more), but if you're putting together a 10-15 minute video it'll do fine. The capture software is surprisingly good, but on rare instances it has crashed while trying to switch back to the editor and my footage was lost. Most of my capture happens on an external box, so this isn't a huge problem, but if you're planning to do all your capture in Camtasia you might want to test it yourself before buying.
As I said earlier, there are some serious bugs, and you need to save often. If that immediately puts you off, then you may want to look for a more expensive solution, but for a "consumer" program you get a lot with Camtasia.

Let it be said first: I do not judge how good a game is by its price. Absurdly cheap prices does NOT a good game make, though I am willing to forgive some of its faults as well as overall length, but a terrible game shall not be forgiven (*cough*AlphaPrime*cough*).
So why am I talking about that? Well, besides the absurdly cheap price (only 19 cents!), almost non-existent story and overall game length (1 hour, not counting Hard mode), this is a genuinely good game. In fact, I found it to be very enjoyable, especially with the game's marvelous soundtrack.
It's deceptively simple to play, but tough to master. You get your standard 2D platform movement & jumping (with a double-jumping jetpack that recharges mid-air), two types of shots (gravity & anti-gravity pockets) and a shield to protect you from your crazy physics manipulations. Sounds pretty easy, right?
And this is where the game's level design really shines. It starts off simple and shows you the ropes, but quite soon after it doesn't hold your hands and you're faced with proper puzzles to solve. You might need to repel yourself to get that extra boost to reach the ledge, or maybe it's not quite enough and you shoot a gravity pocket upwards to attract you and get high enough. Perhaps you'll need to stomp on enemies to get through corridors filled with deadly traps, and you might need to manipulate them too! Gold spinning blades flying towards you? Gold Platforms? Repelling them is usually the best solution. Sometimes you might have permanent shields on, others you might only be able to shoot twice of each shot in mid-air until you recharge on the ground. Needless to say, it keeps things fresh, more than enough for the hour-long experience.
If I were to have a major complaint, it would be the lack of variety, and generally every place visually looks about the same except for the backgrounds. Also, your character is severely lacking in animation, so expect very snappy animations when you look around and aim at things. Overall, anyone with a slight interest for physics-based puzzle platformers should definitely try it out.

A bit of mystery, a lot of good writing, and personal stories. Tacoma is a complete piece of art in the videogame medium. Around three hours long and well worth it.
The crew aboard the Tacoma lunar orbit station were met with a disaster, you're there to find out what happened. The game has a very clever in-game augmented reality user interface, a nice glimpse into the future of tech we will surely all use in just a few years. This is mainly what the gameplay consists of, this isn't a shooter game; it's a game about finding out about the crew (and the station artificial intelligence) as people , as employees on the station, and as victims to the disaster that struck.
The game looks good, has very nice animations and sounds great as well. A wonderfully immersive experience, with the moody ambients of the space station, the sounds of life from the crew's recorded logs, the lovingly crafted living spaces of the station. The attention to detail is staggering, this definitely doesn't feel like exploring a game level, but a real location with real people, who have real lives. Certainly was easy to become invested in their lives.
A hearty recommendation for fans of near future scifi, hard science, and good personal stories. Especially recommended for fans of Gone Home.

Bit.Trip. A series of rhythm games that originated on the Wii. As a result, the collection of games haven't really gotten the attention they so rightfully deserve. For what their simplistic controls and Atari style aesthetic hide is a treasure trove of unparalleled immersion and emotion.
Bit.Trip Beat is the beginning of the Bit.Trip Saga. The opening cutscene reveals that the mascot has been born and...well it's very abstract. Needless to say, It's the gameplay that is unique. At first glance, it appears to be pong. Just a paddle on the left and blocks coming from the right. But if you hit that block (called a "Beat"), the game makes a tone that actually goes in time with the music. And once that beat hits the right side of the screen, another tone is made, also in time with the music. Okay, this is pretty cool, I thought as I maneuvered the paddle up and down with the mouse to hit the beats back. And then I hit enough to rank up. The beats changed tone, they were more crisp and less chiptune and more electric. I "leveled up" into what is apparently Mega. The game has three modes of play: Hyper, Mega, and Nether. Hyper is where you start, and is where you start in every bit.trip game. Mega is one step higher with a less chiptune sounding aesthetic and more flashy animations. Miss enough beats and you will enter back into hyper. continue to miss beats and you will enter nether, a black and white realm that sound like the heart rate monitors in hospitals. if you miss enough in Nether, you lose and you have to restart the level. And for levels that last roughly 15 minutes and NO checkpoints, it is quite devastating to lose. But you just want to get back! That is the allure of Bit.trip. they are all difficult, but they are so much fun to play. When you enter Nether, you start to race. Feeling lost as if you are slipping. Few games can get this kind of urgency but this game, as well as its sequels, master this.
As you play, you start to think  you mastered the game. but then, the game just decides to throw in a new beat that you've never seen before. I personally like the final level. Some of the things that happen in that stage are pretty cool and I'll let you guys find out. All in all, this game is certainly worth the price tag. Get the soundtrack with it as well, you won't regret it.

Galaxy of Pen and Paper is an RPG with good combat mechanics and fantastic presentation.
The game has a rather odd but welcome setting taking place in the late 1990’s featuring a group of players going through a sci-fi roleplaying game. You don’t really control the game characters, instead you sort of control the players who in turn control their characters, if that makes sense.
The combat is the meat of the game and for the most part it works rather well. It’s a traditional turn-based system where each player and enemy gets an initiative roll which determines the order of the turns.
Your characters each have their own unique classes and abilities which you can change fairly regularly. This offers a nice bit of variation to the combat. You can even swap classes and characters out entirely to try new things.
The combat difficulty is variable depending on what you want to do. In most cases you can choose to have a battle at any point along with deciding what you are going to fight and how many of each enemy. You can make it very easy and take on enemies one at a time for a bit of an XP grind, or you can face off against many or more powerful enemies which will give you better rewards. It’s a nice little part of the game that makes it feel like you have control over the gameplay and story.
The combat can feel a bit repetitive after a while but thankfully each chapter and quest usually doesn’t outstay it’s welcome.
The space combat so far (after roughly 4 - 5 hours of play) is much more repetitive compared to the ground combat. While it happens less regularly, the space fights seem to always be against the same ship every time which feels very samey. The combat doesn’t progress quite as well with enemy ships mostly just getting more health as the game goes. This is by far the weakest portion of the game.
Where Galaxy of Pen and Paper shines most is in the storytelling and presentation. The developers have absolutely nailed the aesthetic both in the sci-fi element and the real world. The pixel art style is extremely well done, each environment and animation has a ton of personality and it greatly enhances the game as a whole.
Complementing the art and graphics is the fantastic writing and references throughout the game. Nearly every quest has some great comedic dialogue and callbacks to every sci-fi work imaginable. The developers really know their stuff.
There are a few glitches and some lack of polish on the product. The victory screen occasionally glitches out for no reason and I’ve run into two quests that didn’t have markers so I had to run around for a while to find the right place. Some have been reporting more serious issues but I have yet to experience them.
Overall, Galaxy of Pen and Paper will sell you best on it’s style and references. The gameplay backs it up nicely to an extent but gets a bit hindered during long boss battles or ship-to-ship fighting. That being said I’ve had a great experience so far and will absolutely recommend this game.

Finally, I'm getting lag/slowdown on a fairly high end system, which points to bad/sloppy porting or maybe a game programmed in Flash or something...
Overall, I generally never recommend games where "artificial difficulty" in the form of poor control, bad design and bad porting (lag in low-end games on a high end system), so I unfortunately can't recommend this one at all.

PRO:
+++ Leveling System (my favorite kind)
+ Pretty graphics
+ Beautiful UI
+ Good controls
+ Simple yet powerful building system
CON:
- Poor English translation (English is clearly not the devs first language, I still understand what they mean in most cases)
- Multiplayer not yet implemented but is coming
- No terraforming
This game is one among a sea of survival games, many of which I have played, this one stands out as having great promise, especially once multiplayer is implemented.  It is very reminiscent of games such as Life is Feudal, but especially Wurm.  The major difference here is that there is no terraforming and I do not beleive it is planned, which is too bad becuase that certainly adds a level of customization to the world.
While the game is currently only single-player, a full multi-player world is planned.  You can however currently join others in a chat while you play single-player, I assume this is done just to begin the infrastructure of the multi-player elements.
The thing I love most about this game is the leveling system.  Everything you do adds to your skills.  Repair an item, Repair skill goes up.  Make some twine, ropemaking goes up.  Chop a tree down, forestry goes up. ETC ETC.  This is how survival game leveling should be, it makes it the most fun for me.
I highly praise this game for its UI asthetics and controls.  The UI is simple but intuative and easy to understand.  The controls are pretty standard to other modern games.  You are given a WASD + Mouse Look for movement.  EF and mouse buttons and wheel for interaction.
The game is set in a sci-fi far in the future after all other civilizations have long been dead and forgotten in a somewhat "fresh world" sort of setting.  Despite the sci-fi setting you learn recipes from finding blueprints that allow you to create objects from every stage of development of the ancient forgotten civilizations.
I will also reccomend this game just simply for the amazing devs.  They are quick to respond to almost every issue and have fixed bugs the very same day as receiving the bug report.

DOC STALIN'S REVIEW
PROS
-Short 15 min maximum games (usual game lasts around 10 minutes)
-Very high skill ceiling
-Gameplay is clean as ♥♥♥♥
-Great servers (have DC'd once during my play time and it was from my side)
-Each character has so much depth to them and none of them suck
-Constant Updates
-Extreme Clarity with the Devs
-All in game purchases are purely cosmetic
CONS
- The UI could use some work but the devs have addressed that already
- Tutorial is not clear to all of the advanced mechanics in the game - but steam guides have you covered there
- You can get queued with people that just plain aren't anywhere near your skill level unless you turn on strict matchmaking - even then it can be spotty
- All the issues I am addressing here are almost non problems because the devs have addressed that they want to fix them.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay of this game could not get any better. The overall experience is clean as ♥♥♥♥ . NO ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t RNG. All skill and cooldown based combat. All the champions feel unique and alive. The core gameplay doesn't have any glaring issues.
The champion pool is under three categories. All the champions are rather unique but some of the ideas carry over to other champions such as counters. The first being ranged. Ranged champions as you would think are just champions that their main auto attack is a range ability. They have different mechanics such as a bow that shoots slower but hits harder and a shotgun that does spread damage and damage per bullet.  I would recommend playing Jade to understand the mechanics down for most ranged champions (again personal opinion). The second category is melee. This is as you would think their auto attacks are within melee range. This does not mean they have no ranged abilities. Also their ranged weapons have different ranges based on the champion.The last category is Support. This is mostly based on the fact they have a heal built into their main abilities.
I will not go huge into mechanics of this game because this is a review and I just wanted to give you a snapshot.
CONTENT
The game currently only has 14 champions last time I counted. They are adding new ones at the moment at least 1 or 2 every month which is pretty damn good for this type of arena game.
There are loot boxes similar to other games. They each drop 3 items. The first type is the silver chest which you can only acquire by playing the game(quests, playing a champion repeatedly, etc). This chest is pretty easy to come by and will give you a base start but can drop some sweet stuff. The second chest is the gold chest. These chests can also be purchased with real money in bulk amounts.  The last chest is the Legendary chest which is only able to get by leveling up a champions(you get levels by playing them) or acheivements. There are certain events that might throw one in there as a bundle like they did for the last champ that came out.
FINAL SCORE
9.5 / 10
Overall one of the best games I have played hands down. Great to pick up at any point and just play a couple of games then head out for the day. Devs are clear on their intentions which doesnt happen often. Buy this game and don't look back. I am by no means a pro at this game but hit me up if you want to play sometime!

An updated take on the forgettable 1997 original
Rating 5/10
The original Shadow Warrior came out in 1997, perhaps one of the greatest years for PC games which saw releases such as Fallout, Dungeon Keeper, Total Annihilation, Grand Theft Auto, Age of Empires, Star Wars Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II and Quake II to name but a few.  In amongst all those classic games it's quite easy to forget about Shadow Warrior, a cheesy Duke Nukem clone. So the question remains why did they bother update what was such a forgettable game?
The new Shadow Warrior plays very much like an old fashioned game, constantly moving whilst defeating hordes of enemies, if you stand still for a moment there's a good chance you'll be killed, especially on the higher difficulty levels. It's reminiscent to what they did with the Serious Sam series, trying to recreate old fashioned FPS gameplay in a modern game. In some ways it works but too often it feels floaty, light and with no real meat behind your actions. Battles are also far too repetitive and the game doesn't challenge you in any meaningful way. After the first couple of levels you've learnt how to master the fights, they do mix things up with some mini bosses but these are used to increase a fights length rather than provide a real challenge or change of strategy.
There are other issues which turn the game into a slog apart from just the repetitive battles and that's the bloated level design. Levels are too large, too bland, too similar to each other and it doesn't feel as though you are making any discernible progress. Countless grey corridors that lead to wide open spaces that then signal a new fight. Warehouses, harbours, offices, locked doors that require keys to be found and hidden secrets that require you to search every corner.  We've seen it all before and we've seen it done far better.
The story is really just an excuse to give the protagonist a wise cracking sidekick who really does crack wise. I can't think of a single time I laughed, it was as though there hasn't been 20 years since the original as they layer on the same lame joke. It begins to wear a bit thin about the halfway point. There is of course a story, something about overthrowing the head of a family of ancients in the shadow realm and stopping your one time boss from doing it first. This leads to perhaps the weakest part of the game, the boss fights. Again another throwback to the past, the boss is revealed and you find his weak spots, then spend the next ten minutes or so exploiting that weak spot. There's no challenge just a matter of patience
There are however some positives, it looks pretty in places and runs well. There's also a satisfaction to be had in beating some of the tougher battles and there's a sense of nostalgia as you do it.
I can just about recommend it but unfortunately much like the original it is a game I will forget about within a week until they make the next one.

Beyond Earth is not a huge departure from its predecessor, Civilization V.
Now that we've got that out of the way, I think your impression of this game might depend largely on your expectations. If you're expecting something revolutionary and different then you might want to wait for this one to go on sale so it's comparably priced to a DLC or an expansion and continue to patiently wait for Civilization VI, which Beyond Earth is not.
If you want a solid 4x game with great graphics, a gorgeous color palette, beautiful map terrain and cool resources, immersive music, an interesting premise, and chock full of sci-fi references, then you'll probably enjoy this. I can't stop playing it, I just want to test out all the new victory types and see what all the units look like after upgrades attached to each of game's the three affinities. Even though much of the game -- from the UI to the AI -- feels familiar, there's enough that's fresh that you have to pay attention to the details. And I keep finding myself pleasantly surprised by the new stuff I discover. And sometimes I find myself familiarly irritated by some of the things that have plagued most incarnations of Civilization games, like repetitive AI that offers insanely lopsided trade "deals" and then launches an attack a turn after telling you how awesome you are.
I really like the addition of quests to the game, even though sometimes it's difficult or even impossible to complete some of the tasks (also wow fragile explorers). Once you accept that though, the tasks you can do become a nice little addition to the game and a way to earn extra bonuses while you're playing.
On the down side, the end-game tends to drag a bit, and some of the victory conditions have "false summits" in which you think you are almost there but then find out that you have to have to jump through hoops for another 50 turns in order to actually win.
I wish there were some more statistical and information options for those of us who like to really delve deeply in our strategy games and think things through completely before committing to a path. I also wish there were more incentives to cooperate with the other colonies, like science and economic boosts for signing cooperation agreements. I'd have liked more emphasis on science, perhaps via the ability to enter into research agreements through diplomacy or the ability to trade techs like in earlier Civ games.
Overall, I'd say that the fact that I played the game for over 40 hours in less than a week speaks to its value, at least in my eyes. It's not perfect, but it's a lot of fun and it definitely has that "one more turn" factor that makes it a solid addition to the Civ family.

Q*Bert: Rebooted is a very fun game. I prefer the mouse controls personally, and it works great!
I never played Q*Bert in an arcade, but I've seen a few videos of it, and can say that the classic version plays pretty closely to the original. From what I can tell most of the sound effects are there, and it looks just like the original!
The new version is fun too though! It's the same basic game idea, but with a few added elements. There's gems, which you can use to buy new characters, there's stars, which are required to unlock new levels, and there's new enemies! The stars however did not recieve the best implementation they could have. You have you complete challenges to get stars, and there's 3 challenges per level. You have to play the level 3 seperate times to get them all, and get the stars for them, such as score 2000 points, or beat the level in under 1:10.
The enemies are interesting too, you have the classic ones all in a new style, and then you have the new ones. One is a boxing glove that punches you away, it feels a tad random when it punches you, but it's still a good enemy (frustrating though!). The next is a treasure that you chase around, I believe if you catch it you get 70 gems but I could be wrong.
The levels in the rebooted version get extremely hard (at least for me) later on. I'm still having fun though.
The final thing is the achievements, while I like collecting achievements for games, I feel like in this one it's random. I earned the achievement for winning the rebooted version even though I didn't beat it quite yet, the same happened for collecting all the characters.
This is a pretty good game for what it is though. It's a great way to bring back Q*Bert!

I've played Civ 3, Civ 5 (With Expansions), and now Beyond Earth. As far as the series goes, this is a fun game, although the complete Civ 5 still wins out.
Pros:
-I really liked the idea of the tech tree from the start. I dedicated more thought to it than the linear tree in Civ 5.
-The affinity system I feel provides a good substitute for the concept of advancing through new eras, and unlike in Civ 5   the eras you advance through are different based on your choices.
-The overall atmosphere of the game is very well done. The music is beautiful. The graphics are pretty and appropriately futuristic.
-The customization to your faction at the start is a nice addition. Most of it felt relevant mainly to the early game, though.
Cons:
-I want to see more factions! Space Germany, Space Arabia, Space ... Mongolia? I'm sure someone can come up with some better names, I just want more choices.
-Some of the written dialogue is identical to that in Civ 5.
Overall, I do recommend it. I'm having fun with the game and that's the main thing I look for.

The game is really fun. A few notes: I've only played KOP&P and it was on a tablet, I am a couple of hours into it and my highest leveled character is 29, so let's begin.
Gameplay:
The game brings it's usual turn based RPG system from the knights series, but brings a few editions:
A. Enemies can now be stacked in to groups of 6.
B. You can position enemies in certain positions with certain abillities.
C. You are able to chain together positioning in order to maximize damage of certain abillities. You can line up abillities to hit 4 enemies at once, you can line them up in the front or backline for an abillity that devistates enemies in a direct line, and you can even position it so that enemies under certain effects like confusion.
Classes:
You are able to unlock 4 classes on top of the 4 you start with. These classes are much more powerful than the actual classes in my opinion, escpecially the savage and medtech. The one critique I have is that some classes like the gadgeteer feel underpowered, and classes like the trooper and savage feel very much more powerful. Other critique I have is that you have no proper healer until you unlock the medtech class, which has completley overpowered healing abillities and end game (with SP items) your party won't be able to die as the healing abillities are overpowered with SP generation and you at most will use 1 SP item in major boss fights. I swapped off of the medtech class after realizing I was basically cheating with an overpowered class. But it is completley up to the player to use classes like these in order to play the game.
STORY:
The game brings it's comical 4th wall humor from the knights series. But due to it being online xainey activities happen. For instance, there is a point the game game (very early) where trolls enter your chat room, the GM takes this opportunity  and turns the trolls into a reoccuring enemy type throughout the game. It fits the setting perfectly. The game does have ALOT of troups throughout the experience.
SPOILER AHEAD, SKIP IF YOU DON'T WANT A SPOILER!!!:
-Time travel
-mother invading son's privacey.
-aincent guardians of the galaxy that protect it
-aincent guardians of the galaxy that protect the time stream
-evil doubles trope
-going from the end of exsistance to the far past.
-evil cults
-Changing the timestream for the worse
-Every single Star Wars Episode 1 and 4 trope that's been reused in so many movies, games, and shows it can't even be counted.
But these are all countered by the game's sense of humor. As it spins these tropes into a story that fits them well with smart writing. Yes you can still feel the jokes coming a mile away, but it is still keeps it fresh with good jokes unrelated to the trops that even tie into gameplay mechanics. The one major critique I have is the translation in chapters 4 and 5, as the writing makes no sense in some areas and leads to me having problems understanding the plot. But if you know your english you can avoid this issue easiliy with some thinking. I do think the game could be better however.
Overall the game is alot of fun and is worth your cash if you wish to drop it. If you like RPGs I think you will love it and if you play D&D (escpecially if you DM like me on occasions) you will love the humor and style. 8/10 from me as the gameplay is good but uses too many tropes from other sci-fi/JRPG medias.

MAZ! is another of my SG wins, and actually not a bad game. It's insanely easy though and the achievements are broken, so there is that. Ultimately, I just kind of zoned out, took in the music, and got into a groove until I died despite not hitting anything after getting to level 17. Interestingly, as long as you don't exit the game after dying, you can start over, only at the level you died at, but with a complete reset otherwise. That will guarantee that people can finish the game if they like.
It is however difficult to note any real transition other than the level number changing after what seems like a certain amount of pellets collected. Once you get used to the controls and the hit box for your mouse, it's cruise control from then on. You can easily coast through the game (until/unless you just randomly die as happened to me).
If you are OCD about achievements, I would stay clear of this game. Otherwise, it's a pleasant little experience with a nice music track and is just complete relaxing. In fact, for a few minutes, I really didn't even bother focusing on the screen. I could see everything I needed while just unfocusing my eyes like you would if looking at one of those optical illusion pictures.
I see no reason not to give this one a go. It's inexpensive and competent at what it does, totally relaxing once you figure out the game's patterns, and just kind of an easy time killer.
5.5 out of 10 (although if the cheevos and whatever bug randomly kills you are sorted out, I think I would rate it more like a 7 out of 10).

GOPP is a relatively fresh entry to the "of Pen and Paper" series-- it incorporates several elements of Chroma Squad's battle system while keeping to the overall style of the previous Pen and Paper games.
HITS:
-Interesting tactical combat that focuses more on group synergy than min/maxing damage skills. Rather than having four skills to distribute points into, characters now have many abilities that can be unlocked with skill points, four of which can be used in battle. It's very fun to find the best synergy between party members.
-Charming writing style that mostly avoids the common pitfall of reference overload
-Ship combat makes for an engaging diversion, though it isn't very deep
-Little secret objectives give incentive to explore
MISSES:
-Ground travel is sluggish, and going from ground to ship quickly got repetitive
-While it's fun to find good strategies for battle, most situations don't require varied tactics (the same "click until you win" issue that other games of the series had in some parts)
-At the time of review, the game had several bugs that, while not intrusive, were irritating
-There's no easy indicator to see what you've already found on a planet without landing on it (weaponsmiths, scanner upgrades, meta shop quests etc.)
CRITICAL MISS:
-The scanning system is slow, unnecessary, and very frustrating. Most of the issue is in the shop interface, which has no way to easily sell large numbers of items other than clicking one at a time (At one point I had 900 of a mineral, and had to click 700 times to sell it in bulk.)

I rather enjoy playing Novus Inceptio.
It has an overhead build view that requires some maneuvering, but certainly an improvement over the more traditional first person view.
Relatively well designed leveling zones, so you don't go from fighting a level 1 monster to fighting a level 7 one in the same area, which is breath of fresh air.
Performance is as expected from an early access survival game , made by a very small team, you could use an ssd, but it's not really necessary.
Large amounts of crafting recipes which have a chance to drop or appear in various places, so there is always lots of stuff to make , and plenty of chances to find the required materials.
It was very refreshing to play a survival game where you're not bashed to death by naked people in the first five minutes, I certainly hope the developer continues in this refreshing direction.
Combat was ok for me, ended up taking out quite a few mobs with the base gear and more and higher level ones, as I leveled up.
Overall it's an ok game , that should get better with time.

The first installment in the amazing Bit.Trip Saga, Beat is a game that at first seemed to just be a fun little pong-type game with an awesome soundtrack, but it then blossomed into a rich, creative series following the story (Yes, these games have story. It's actually pretty deep. Message me if you want to know it, or ask a dev or something. It's hard to find it online) of Commander Video as he takes down evil through various forms.  So, on to Beat itself
Beat has 3 levels, like every Bit.Trip game, and is as challenging as all of them. In this game, you take the form of a line that looks like a pong paddle, and you hit "beats", blocking them from going past and sending them back. The game starts off slow, but quickly picks up speed. It's pretty challenging, especially when you try to get a perfect score or go to the highest difficulty. If you're on the verge of buying this, I would say go buy it, odd are you will like it. Now, in the PC version, you control yourself using the mouse to move up and down, and it moves pretty smoothly, but make sure you dont have a crap mouse. In the Wii version, you make your paddle horizontal and tilt it forward and back, which is pretty good, but it's hard to go from PC to Wii, or vice versa. However, if you liked the Wii version and wanna grab it on here, I would recommend it. It also has a mini level that is portal themed, which is cool.
For the Bit.Trip series reviews, I will make a review for both the PC version and the Wii version, since sometimes they don't have the same scores (See my CORE review).
SO, final Scores:
Wii- Pretty fun game, can be hard to tilt your controller JUUUUUUSt right, but still a fun game! 7.8/10
PC- Pretty fun game, not as hard to get it just right, but then again, your mouse could suck. 8/10
Bit.Trip Complete- Check my CORE review for more about the game. 9/10

Torchlight is a delightful singleplayer game than will have you playing just-one-more-level till 3am.
Mixing the artwork from World of Warcraft and the gameplay from Diablo, this game brings the best out of both games.
Your choice of class is boiled down to a simple three choices - Brawler, Archer and Mage, and there is plenty of gameply to be had as each class.
If you're a hoarder of gear and equipment (like me), then this game is going to be both a blessing and a curse.
There is just so much to pick up, so many matching sets of armour to collect, so many jewels to craft, that your inventory gets a fair workout just in the first few levels.
Happily, you get a pet companion to act as a loot mule, but you'll still wish for more storage.
Overall, I'd recommend this game to anyone, and given the cheap, cheap price on Steam, it's almost a crime not to have it in your collection.
Noticeable omission of co-op play, but that is being addressed in Torchlight 2 - soon to be released in 2012.

Back when I had a Wii, this was one of the first games I bought from the marketplace.  It just seemed interesting.  On the Wii, it is in all honesty, probably my most played game (keep in mind I've played and 100%ed SSBB at least four times).
I don't really know how to describe a game like this.  I guess I'll start here: BIT.TRIP BEAT is one of the most intense rhythm games you will ever play.  It combines great 8-bit melodies with an uber-hard version of pong you play to the song.  The BIT.TRIP franchise in its own is very difficult.  Every game is a rhythem game that may actually drive you to rage.  Oh, did I forget to mention how hard these games are?  Let's just say it's somewhere between EVE Online difficulty, Dark Souls difficulty, and Super Hexagon difficulty.
The only real problem I have with it is the controls.  First, I would HIGHLY RECOMMEND not using the keyboard; use the mouse or controller.  Also, I wouldn't recommend a laptop's touch pad to substitute for a mouse.  I personally like playing it with the Wiimote, but that's probably just me.
Ratings-
Game Design-8/10
Graphics-8.5/10 (for 16-bit, you have to admit it's pretty damn good.)
Soundtrack-8/10
Replay Value-6/10
Final Verdict-7.6/10
Recommended buy price-$2.50 USD, or buy with the BIT.TRIP franchise pack.

This game has phenomenal potential, but has too far to go for me to reccommend buying this as is. A lot of the concepts are fantastic! I haven't seen much of a story or point to literally anything, but that may just not have been added or maybe that takes a while longer to get to.
You start the game as a clone. You live, die, and are reborn from the vats of clones left behind by someone long forgotten. The game is mysterious, and what story I did find was from the ruins of a long forgotten civilization much like our own. Exploring "anomalies" was really interesting and made things a lot of fun. I don't want to describe too much, as most of the fun is in the discoveries.
You definitely noticed that I don't reccommend this game. It's not that it can't be a great game, it absolutely can. It could possibly compete with the king of all Alpha titles, Subnautica. It really could be that good! It has the bones. I just don't feel comfortable telling people to fork over money for a title that needs as much work as this one does. Especially since any purchaser of Steam Alpha titles would be aware of, many alpha titles are often abandoned.
Sadly, the crafting was convoluted and ridiculously excessive to make even the simplest of items. Even if all they added was the ability to select what you want to craft, and it would auto-craft all of the base components necessary, that would improve things considerably. Even then inventory management is nearly impossible due to the massive amount of materials there are to gather. I love challenging, survival-crafting games, but backpack organizing simulator isn't really my idea of fun.
There is intermittent stuttering going on all the time. Throwing your camera all over the place. Good luck trying to survive against the cold, I have to look at the sky and run around and circles to get the campfire to actually appear above ground. Found some ruins? Get ready to play hopping simulator! Your character will get stuck on everything! A bottle, a random brick, a street curb, absolutely everything!
Again, stick this in your follow list, or wishlist, and wait for them to make some improvements. The massive bugs and lack of any streamlining may be due to them being more focused on adding content, rather than anything else. That is fine by me! I don't mind waiting, but that's exactly what I'm going to be doing, and what I advise any potential purchasers to do until improvements are made. I will periodically be checking in and updating my review. I'm eagerly waiting to see what these developers are capable of.
Edit: Still can not reccommend as of October 21, 2017. It has gotten much better. Far better in fact. However, there it still just has too far to go. There really isn't much to say that has changed. It hasn't changed much, they just made small tweaks that made things far less annoying, but the bugginess, the awkward and clunky animations. Crafting is less annoying but still not good. It would be far better if you could just select a recipe and it crafter all of the core components. As it is, you are just spending large sums of time crafting massive amounts of the same item, to make another item, as an ingredient for another item, that will be used for another item, that is needed for what you actually want. They release frequent updates but I don't notice much of a difference. This could be because of where they are focusing their efforts, but I just hope they aren't trying to keep up appearances, and don't actually have an end goal in mind for the game.
